And now once more —we
must warn all of our members
and sympathizers to keep away
from either the Republican or
the Democratic primary.
Most of them are probably
aware that at the primary elec
tion one can not “split” the
ticket. That is, you cannot
vote for a Socialist for a cer
tain office, and then also try to
help a friend on the Republican
or Democratic ticket for another
office—because the different
parties are on different sheets
and you can vote only on one
sheet.
In other words, at the primary
you must vote a straight ticket.
Otherwise you lose your vote
and weaken your own position.
And why should you vote a
"split ticket”?
The so-called “progressives”
are hanging on to the Repub
lican party for dear life. They
are hanging on to the party of
Calvin Coolidge and Andrew
Mellon and Albert Fall and
Harry M. Daugherty, and their
capitalist friends —who are in
absolute and complete control
of the Republican organization
and of the Republican policies.
They are the Republican party
—not La Follette, Ekern, Zim
mermann or Voight.

Now we can readily under
stand that a person honestly be
lieving in the policies of Calvin
Coolidge and Andrew Mellon,
must vote the Republican ticket.
However, why a person claim
ing to be opposed to these ultra
capitalist policies should vote
the Republican ticket —which is
the legitimate capitalist ticket
is beyond our comprehension.
The most honest progressives
admit that they do so only to
use the Republican label in or
der to be ejected. And that in
itself is dishonest.
As for the Democratic party
it has neither a fixed policy
nor a stated set of principles,
and least of all any competent
leadership. The Democratic
party is simply held together by
the “Negro” question down
South, and by office-seeking or
ganizations like Tammany in
New York and the “Grey
'Valves” in Chicago up North.
The “tariff for the revenue
only” which used to be the di
viding line between the Repub
licans and Democrats has ceased
to exist. There are almost as
many “high tariff” Democrats
now as there are Republican
and on the other hand, many
prominent Republicans do not
advocate the “high tariff” any
longer.

Any man voting the Demo
cratic ticket, therefore, is sim
ply throwing his vote away4-al
though it is a pity that we have
no opposition party in'our coun
try. The Democratic party does
not function as such, and a new
line-up has not taken place na
tionallv. We simply have two
capitalistic tickets.
Therefore, if you want to put
j your vote where it counts
whether you want it or not, you
must vote the straight Socialist
ticket.
The Socialist ticket is the
only one which means that you
are expressing your dissatisfac
tion with the present rule of
Wall Street and with the incred
ible corruption—and that you
are voting for cleanliness, effi
ciency and honesty in our pub
lic affairs.
There’s going to be a lot of
“anti-trust” trust agitation in
the next session of Congress.
Material is now being gath
ered by all sorts of politico-eco
nomic agencies for attacks on
bakeries, radio, electrical manu

end), motion pictures, and per
haps even banking.

ly having a large measure of

PODESTA PLAN
IS EXTENDED
BY MUSSOLINI
Change Has Approv-
al of Citizens Pre
mier Claims.
ROME—The Fascist government
yesterday abolished the election of
municipal officers by popular suf
frage, allowed since the kingdom of
Italy was founded in 1870.
The change was effected by the
adoption by the council of ministers
under the presidency of Premier
Mussolini of a decree extending the
podesta system to every city, town,
and village in Italy. This system
consists of the rule of an official
appointed by the central govern
ment. It already obtains in 7,341
towns of less than 5,000 population
and also in towns considered health
resorts and those in the earthquake
zone.
Says People Favor it.
About 1,700 places are effected by
the new decree. Rome and Naples
alone are excepted. Rome remains
under a special type of administra
tion with a governor, and Naples re
mains under the rule of a high
commissioner. Neither city has any
elected officials, however.
“The general favor with which
the podesta system was accepted,”
says the council of ministers in pro
mulgating the decree, “shows that
the people are convinced that the
choice of administrators of autono
mous entitles—towns, cities, and
provinces—by popular suffrage has
outlived its day and that the elective
s.vstem responds more readily to
modern conditions.”
Two Means of Control.
The first podesta decree, which
was adopted last February, was ?x
perimental, it is explained, and the
success it achieved in the small
towns has convinced the government
that the system is applicable to all
municipalities.
Another reason for the adoption
of the podesta system, it is said, is
the smoothness with which it will
function with the new syndieal or
ganization, giving the central gov
ernment two avenues of control, di
rect and indirect.

3 Per Cent Boost
In Cost of Food
WASHINGTON—During the year
ended June 15 the retail price of
42 principal food articles increased
3 per cent, according to the depart
ment of labor. Cmpared with June
15, 1913, it was 63.3 per cent higher
and is the highest price reached
during the 13-year period, with the
exception of 1920, 1919 and the last
half of 1918. In June, 1925, the re
tail food price was 58. G per cent
higher than in 1913.

HITS MONEY
CONTROLLED
GOVERNMENT
Declaring that the United States
senate must not be permitted to de
generate into a/board of directors of
public utilities or any other busi
ness, Theodore Roosevelt, in ad
dressing members of the Harvard
club at a luncheon in the Univer
sity club today, pointed out that the
trend of politics in the 1 United
States is toward a money-controlled
government, and that every day we
let go by without positive action
toward curbing it is a net loss, and
permits the rottenness to strike
deeper into the loins of the body
politic.
This Is Wrong.
“The Pennsylvania and Illinois
primaries this spring were a burn
ing disgrace,” declared Mr. Roose
velt.
“In Pennsylvania approximately
$3,000,000 were spent in the strug
gle for the Republican nomination.
“In Illinois apparently, the tale
is much the same. It is unnecessary
to say that this is wrong, for even
a child can see that this action not
only subverts the principle of the
primary but strikes at the very roots
of republican institutions.
“The paramount issue before us
today lies in curbing political activ
ities that will result in our having
a money-controlled government.
The primaries in Pennsylvania and
Illinois are only one of the mani
festations of the disease We must
fight it wherever it shows itself.
Must Be Regulated.
“The United States senate must
not be pennited to degenerate into
a board of directors of public util
ities or any other business. In the
states laws shoefid regulate and
strictly limit expenditures in both
primaries and election. In the na
tion the same should be true in
presidential campaigns.

CAPITAL OF
ISLES NEARLY
BLOTTED OUT
Tremors Third With

Months.
HORTA, Azores Islands Three
fourths of this city was wrecked or
damaged today by an earthquake
the extent of which was not known
this evening. Many persons were
believed to have been killed or in
jured. The area of the city most
seriously affected was in ruins tj
night.
Cable communication was unin
terrupted tonight, although the
shocks were believed to have been
general in this area.
The department instructed the
consul immediately to express the
sympathy of the United States to
the local authorities.
Capital of Isle.
Horta is the capital of Island of
Fayal in the Azores. It was a well
built town, irregularly laid out.
The last figures placed its popula
tion as G,734.
Fayal is the westernmost island of
the center group of the Azores
islands. It is a volcanic island and
reaches an elevation of over 3,000
feet. Its area is approximately 65
square miles, while the population
of the island is about 25,000. Agri
culture is the chief industry.
Worst In History.
WASHINGTON —The earthquake
which has rocked the Azores was
the severest in the history of the
islands, with heavy loss of property
and life, the American consul at
Horta Fayal, Azores, reported to the
state department today. The Amer
ican Red Cross has offered help to
the Azores if needed.
Quake Rocks Isles.
NEW YORK An earthquake
shook the Azores group of islands
in the mid-Atlantic today, the
French cable company informed the
United Press.
The French cable which goes
through the Azores group was work
ing normally today, the company
said. No report of casualties or
damage has been received in the
New York office.
Third Violent Quake.
ROME—Reports from all Italian
observatories today confirmed the
belief that the epicenter of Mon
day’s earthquake was in the Aegean
sea midway between Greece and
Asia Minor. It was the third vio
lent earthquake which had shaken
the eastern Mediterranean in the
past six months.
The second of the quakes particu
larly was damaging to the Island of
Rhodes, where several hundred
houses tumbled down and several
persons were killed.
Monday’s quake was more or less
evident along the Adriatic seaboard.
Athens Has Quake.
ATHENS—Several houses crum
bled when Athens was the center of
an earthquake disturbance last
night. Other cities such as Sparta
and Leonidon reported some dam
age.

The question of whether tli£ new
courthouse shall be planned by an
architect obtained by a nation-wide
competition or by hand-picked archi

ty bodrd late yesterday.
The committee report advised
against an open competition and
recommended that Clas, Shepard
Clas, Robert Messmer Bro. and
Alexander Eschweiler Sons, be
given a direct contract.
The fact that the Messmer firm
were the supervising architects of
Muirdale sanatorium, Wauwatosa,
which resulted in a grand jury and
the confessions of two supervisors
that they had taken bribes, while
also the fact that the Muirdale
buildings were largely built with
labor alleged to be unskilled in the
trades, and with a good deal of
labor trouble that might have been
avoided, was said to add reasons
for opposition to the three-firm
plan.
The county board committee on
judiciary and finance late yester
day voted to recommend an appro
priation of $20,000 toward complet
ing a new dormitory at the hospi
tal for the insane, Wauwatosa.
This will be added to a former ap
propriation of $75,000, which proved
inadequate.

SEWER PROTEST
AS PREMATURE
Protests against the city’s failure
to provide sewer connections in the
territory around 55h St. and Lisbon
Av., which was annxed to the city a
year ago last June, have resulted
in a survey by the health depart
ment to determine whether the lack
of sewer facilities is affecting the
health and well being of that com
munity, it was announced today by
Dr. John P. Koehler, health com
missioner.
Aid. August W. Strehlow, Socia
list, 20th ward, today characterized
the petition signed by 50 residents
of that district as a premature
protest.
Work Not Delayed.
“The city has completed the
laying of sewer mains in this dis
trict and is now at work making
the connection,” Aid. Strehlow ex
plained.
“To have completed this task in
approximately a year speaks well

lieve that the claim that there have
been unnecessary delays in this
work is hardly justifiable.
Are Rushing Improvements.

as fast as is possible but persons
living in the newly annexed terri
tory must remember that these im
provements cannot be made
immediately, and that as a general
rule, the improvements in newly
annexed territory are made long
before the residents thereof began
paying property tax to the city.”

corp of sanitary inspectors were
today detailed to call on residents
of the district and give specific in
structions as to the proper disposi
tion of sewage until such a time as
the connections can be made.

TREATMENT
The interest of and in hay fever

meeting, was demonstrated yester

allow time for those who wish to
testify to return to the city, in
formal discussion took up much of
the time of the county institutions
committee which met in the admin
istration building, Wauwatosa.
Danger In Limitation.
It was brought out that the coun
ty hospital already has a large
amount of hay fever vaccine on
hand and gave treatments during
the early part of the summer when
innoculations still had time to be
come effective for the present sea
son.

present activities against hay fe
ver, however, it was pointed* out,

are eligible to receive hay fever
treatments.
Hearing Next Week.
Under the present regulations, of
the county dispensary for providing
hay fever treatments, according to
those in charge, an applicant must
show that he is indigent. The great,
number of working men, with aver
age wages and family, are not in
cluded. Yet there are hundreds of
these latter, for whom the cost of
professional services involved in the
taking of hay fever innoculations

itive. It is to help the average man

tion is intended.

be some time next week, according
to Mr. Metcalfe.

Rood, who is fulfilling that capacity

death by lost kids, crying kids,
naughty kids, and just plain kids.

where their parents ultimately
found them. Some we sent home on
street cars.

day is an item, carfare for four
lost children, 28 cents. Many of the
little folks come in here after losing
the nickel, dime, quarter, or what
every may be the allowance for the
day’s pleasure, crying as though
they had lost a fortune.”

NORTH SHORE
TRAIN SHOWN
AT STATE FAIR
Lined up beside a stage coach of
1849 vintage, a five-car North Shore
line all-steel train, consisting of
three passenger coaches, a parlor
car and a diner, indicates to State
Fair visitors the tremendous ad
vance in transportation facilities
since that period.
Fastest in World.
The train is said to be the fastest
in the world, and can go 90 miles
an hour in actual operation. The
diner is a five-man car, with two
chefs, two waiters and a pantry
man.
The dining car facilities will be
tested both tomorrow and Thursday,
on the first day by Gov. John J.
Blaine and party, and on the second
day by Mayor Daniel W. Hoan and
members of the common council,
each party being the guests of B. W.
Arnold, assistant -general manager
of the line, at luncheon.
A Full Crew.
The rest of the train is in charge
of a conductor, a motorman and
three collectors. The train will be
put on regular service between Chi
cago and Milwaukee after the fair.
The train is in charge of George
J. Bernard, who has been in the
service of the North Shore line 23
years.
The public is allowed to walk
through the train on tours of in
spection. Talks are made by em
ployes on new methods of transpor
tation and other public utility sub
jects.

Mothers Blamed For Petting Parties
SAY PARENTS
FAIL TO TELL
GIRLS FACTS
Special Counsellor
Gives Tips on Per-
r sonal Problems.
CHICAGO —Sins of the mothers—
•ins of omission when brought
face to face with the responsibility
of directing their children into a
healthy and normal knowledge of
sex —are in a measure responsible
for “petting parties’ ’and general
license among the young people.
This is the charge made by Mrs.
Alfreda J. Howells, New York, be
fore an audience of women yester
day at the Chicago temple, speaking
under the auspices of the Illinois
Vigilance Assn.
Girls Are Advised.
Mrs. Howells, a special counsellor
for high school girls, is credited by
the association with having advised
more girls of high school age in
personal problems than any other
woman in the country. She said
she had found that girls have ap
pealed in vain to their mothers for
the advice that she gives them.
A desire to be shocking, to be in
fashion and to keep up with their
set, she asserted, leads girls to
smoke and drink. But so long as
mothers continue to smoke, it is
improbable, she said, that the young
er generation will discard the cig
aret habit. Drinking, she finds, is
more prevalent among high school
•tudents today than it was five
years ago. This condition she
blamed on the foes of prohibition
who, she said, encourage drinking
among the young to provide an ar
gument for the repeal of the dry
laws.
Drinking Has Been Cut.
“Ten years ago, however,” Mrs.
Howells said, “there were far more
high school students drinking than
there are today, but at that time it
was regarded as a perfectly normal
thing. Today they drink because
it is an adventure and a lark.”
Obscene literature and the mov
ies are at the root of the immor
ality of young people, in many cases,
Mrs. Howells believes.

LAKEVIEW, Ore.—As the waters
parted in the Red sea to allow the

of “milk and honey,” so did they re
cede at Goose lake, Oregon, to allow
the seekers of gold, in the days fol
lowing the rush of ’49, en route in
emigrant trains, to pass over its
smooth bed.
It was Indians, not Egyptians the
emigrants sought to elude. The
story of how they outwitted the In
dians by jutting away from the
original Oregon trail and traversing
i stretch of the lake bed, was told
by the settlers themselves, but
doubted.
It was in the same section that a
band of I’iutes and Modocs lay am
bushed in the lava beds a few
months afterward and massacred a
contingent at Bloody Point. Scores,
including women, were killed.
Recently the emigrants’ story has
received belated confirmataion. The
waters of the lake again receded
and where the lake once nestled a
scant sheet of not more than five
miles of water remains.
With the old floor of the lake ex
posed, traces of the rutted wheel
tracks made by the wagons and ox
cars remained, a silent legend of
the romance of three-quarters of a

MARY B. ORVIS.
STORY-WRITING
COURSE AT U.W.
EXTENSION DEPT.
Mary B. Orvis, formerly general
secretary of the Indianapolis Cen
ter of Indiana university, has
been appointed assistant professor
of English by the University of Wis
consin, and will give a new course in
short story writing in the Milwau
kee extension division, 137 2nd St.,
this fall.
Miss Orvis also will act on the
general administrative staff of the
Milwaukee district. She graduated
from the University of Wisconsin
and later received her master’s de
gree from Indiana university. She
has taught short story writing for
several years and was founder of
the Writer’s Club of Indiana.
Course in Writing.
The course in short story writing
will be given Wednesday evenings
beginning Sept. 23. It is intended
both for people who wish to gain an
idea of the principles involved in
short story writing and to those
more experienced writers who want
to improve their work through criti
cism.
The recitations will be devoted
primarily to the reading and criti
cism of stories written by members
of the class. The course is open to
anyone who has completed a univer
sity course in English composition,
or who can submit manuscript proof
of his ability to write.
Other Courses Listed.
Other courses to be given this fall
by the English department include:
Shakespeare, Browning, introduc
tion to English literature, public
speaking and English composition,
including business English.

POVERTY MAKES
HIGH MATERNAL
MORTALITY RATE
WASHINGTON—Poverty, which
is a tremendous factor in infant
mortality, also is found to be of
great weight in maternal death
rates, according to a report on ma
ternal mortality issued by the chil
dren’s bureau of the United States
department as labor, in which it
outlines a national program for
maternal mortality and morbidity
throughout the United States.
As with infant mortality, says
the report, maternal death rates in
crease as the husband’s earnings
fall, probably because of lack of
proper facilities and adequate care
for the poor mother. Color and na
tionality are also important factors
in maternal mortality. In the birth
registration area for 1921 the Ne
gro maternal death rate was 67 per
cent higher than the white rate. On
the other hand, the rate for for
eign-born white mothers was slight
ly lower than that for native white
mothers.
Highest In World.
The report, the work of Dr. Rob
ert Morse Woodbury, formerly di
rector of statistical research for the
children’s bureau, brings together
and analyzes all available material
both American and foreign, on
deaths of mothers during child
birth, and is considered one of the
most important pieces of recent re
search in the field of the bureau’s
work. Children’s bureau officials
feel that it indicates the necessary
emphasis during the coming decade
in the effort to reduce deaths
among both babies and mothers.
Maternal mortality rates in the
United States are today among the
highest in the civilized world, and
but a slight decrease in these rates
has occurred since the beginning
of the present century, Dr. Wood
bury’s report states. The signifi
cance of these facts from rs national
point of view is found not only in
the loss which this means of the
lives of women presumably at their
prime, but also in the far-reaching
effect of maternal mortality on the
infant death rate. Dr. Woodbury
points out:
Effect on Child Deaths.
“A very considerable proportion
of all deaths of infants under 1 year
of age occur during the first month
of life from causes which have their
origin in the care and condition of
mothers during pregnancy and con
finement. In the United States
as a whole it may be estimated
that approximately 100,000 deaths
of infants under 1 month of age
occur every year. Reduction in the
mortality from these causes de
pends upon improvement and exten
sion of facilities for prenatal, con
finement, and post-natal care. It
may also be estimated that at
least 100,000 stillbirths occur each
year. The same measures which
will safeguard the lives and health
of mothers during pregnancy and
labor will also tend to reduce the
stillbirth and neonatal mortality
rates.”
Dr. Woodbury estimates the total,
annual number of maternal deaths
in the United States on the basis
of 1921 birth-registration area sta
tistics to be 18,281. However, a
careful survey of sources of error
in certifications of death through
out the area leads him to the con
clusion that the true number of ma
ternal deaths is probably as much
as 12 per cent in excess of those
reported, making an estimated
yearly death toll of more than 20,-
000 women. The maternal mortal
ity rate in 1921 was 6.8 per 1,000
live births. The provisional 1924
rate was 6.6.
Some of the Causes.
Analysis of the causes of mater
nal deaths in this country shows
that the most important single
cause is puerperal septicemia, due
to infection resulting from lack of
surgical cleanliness and almost 100
per cent preventable through care
ful asepsis. Two-fifths of the ma
ternal deaths in the death-registra
tion area of 1921 were due to sep
ticemia. Among other causes, puer
peral albuminuria and convulsions
was most important, contributing

PROGRESSIVES
BEING DECEIVED,
KENT DECLARES
That the progressive people of
Wisconsin are being deceived by the
selfish individuals whom they elect
ed as true progressives was the con
tention of Herman O. Kent, Social
ist candidate for governor, speaking
at Rice Lake, Wis.
“The only way for the workers
and farmers to accomplish their
own ends and achieve a sane, con
structive government is for them to
support the Socialist state ticket,
which will work for harmony in gov
ernment and the interests of the
people,” Mr. Kent said.
They Care Little.
“All that the so-called progres
sives- are doing is laying plans to
perpetuate themselves in office.
They care but little for the people’s
welfare.
“Instead of Gov. Blaine’s conduct
ing the state government to aid the
farmers and the laborers, he has
used the gubernatorial position to
boost himself into the senate. The
same motives have prompted the
acts of other state officers.
Needs a Cleaning.
“The state capitol needs a clean
ing out, to effect the welfare of the
people, and the quicker the people
do this the better it will be for
them.
“We Socialists are not interested
in fighting the old party politicians
as individuals we are fighting the
principles that they advocate. The
Socialists are advocating the owner
ship by the people of all the things
that the people must use in com
mon.”
At Rice Lake.
The address of Aid. Herman O.
Kent, Socialist candidate for gov
ernor, delivered at Rice Lake Sat
urday night, was greeted with tre
mendous applause.
After the meeting numerous res
idents declared that they had been
fooled by the progressives and that
from now on they would vote the
Socialist ticket.
Kent cards and Socialist circulars
were taken by those in the audi
ence for delivery in various neigh
borhoods and in the shops.
Aid. Kent was optimistic follow
ing the wonderful reception he re
ceived in Rice Lake and predicted
that the Socialist ticket will carry
Barron county, as the farmers more
than ever before are leaning toward
the Socialist candidates.
Aid. Kent stated further follow
ing the meeting, that he was cer
tain that the Socialists could organ
ize a big local in Rice Lake after
the primary next week.
In Barron, Wis., the townfolk
filled Aid. Kent’s automobile with
oil and gasoline in appreciation of
the talk he delivered there. They
expressed a desire to have him re
turn to Barron at the earliest op
portunity.

Filipinos Pass Freedom Plebiscite Bill Over Wood Veto
STEP FOLLOWS
SEVERAL YEARS
OF AGITATION
Measure Will Be
Forwarded to
Coolidge.
MANILA—The bill providing for
a plebiscite in the islands on the
question of Independence was passed
by the Philippine house of repre
sentatives yesterday over the veto
of Gov. Qen. Leonard Wood. The
action was expected. The senate a
month ago took like action, and the
bill now goes to President Coolidge.
The action of the Philippine house
of representatives followed severs!
years of agitation for a government
independent of the Unite! States—
the Philippine republic. The Phil
ippine legislature, elected by the
people, has been overwhemingly In
favor of the project and has taken
many steps to forward it, some of
them being vetoed by Gov. Gen.
Wood, appointed by the president
of the United States.
Act Was Vetoed.
When the Philippine legislature
appropriated money to send a mis
sion to the United States to work
for independence, the act was
vetoed and the money was raised by
popular subscription.
Local self-government has been
extended to most of the 43 provinces
of the Philippines, the administra
tors with few exceptions being Fili
pinos.
The Moros of the southern Islands,
Mohammedans, have not lived ami
cably with the Christian Filipinos,
and frequently have expressed their
desire for continuance of the rule
by the United States, or a separate
government by Moro officials unde*'
American protection. A bill for
separation of provinces chiefly popu
lated by Moros from the remainder
of the Philippine government is
pending in congress.
Bill Up to Coolidge.
WASHINGTON—President Cool
idge will have six months in which
to act after he receives the Philip
pine independence plebiscite bill
which will be forwarded to him for
approval or veto.
The reports the president will re
ceive from Gov. Gen. Wood along
with the bill and from Carmi
Thompson, who is making a survey
of conditions In the islands, un
doubtedly will form the basis of con
sideration, but a majority of offi
cials here believe he will support
Gov. Wood’s position.
GENEVA PEACE
MEETING OPENS
GENEVA—The opening session
yesterday of the 25th universal
peace congress was featured by the
escorting of Paul Tx>ebe, president
of the German Reichstag, to a seat
of honor by a French delegate. This
gesture of reconciliation was warm
ly applauded by the 300 delegates.
The United States was represented
by Miss Jane Addams, who spoke
last night.
M. La Fontaine, vice president of
the Belgian senate, declared the
congress will fight financial and
economic imperialism as well as po
litical and military imperialism.
One proposal before the congress
is to organize a great manifesta
tion of conciliation either at Phila
delphia before the close of the ses
quicentennial or at the Acropolis in
Athens, the Forum in Rome, or the
Champ de Mars in Paris.
RICH GOLD FIND
IN NEW GUINEA;
RUSH IMPENDS
SYDNEY, Australia—Remarkable
stories are reaching Australia of ex
ceedingly rich areas of gold-bearing
territory in the upper reaches of
Edie creek in New Guinea. It is
called a second Klondyke. The peo
ple are warned against rushing into
the field because of the terrible dif
ficulties in the way of transporta
tion, savage natives and fevers. The
field is at an altitude of nearly 7,000
feet.
James Hebberd, formerly man
ager of the Sulphide corporation,
who has just returned from the
field, reporting for an Adelaide cor
poration, said the creek is a veritable
Eldorado. Judging from what he
saw, the field yields 1,000 ounces
daily, on the labor of 100 natives.
One washing of a cubic yard and a
half yielded 275 ounces of gold.
Mr. Hebberd said the area is not
a poor man’s field, as the dredging
of the property requires a large
capital investment. The occasional
flats on Edie creek do not average
more than 25 feet in width.

SLUMS STILL
SCOTCH PERIL
REPORT SHOWS
Leader Special Service.
MANCHESTER—A recent report
of the British Medical Research
council shows that the slums of
Scotland are still a greater danger
to the welfare of the workers than
low wages, writes The Manchester
Guardian.
To this extent, the report is a
powerful argument for reform, The
Guardian thinks. It gives a vivid
picture of the intolerable conditions
under which great masses of the
people still live all over Great
Britain.
“The abolition of these conditions
would do more for the wage earn
ing population than any increase in
wages.”
Give Damning Figures.
According to this report, 62 per
cent of the population of Glasgow
and 59 per cent of the population of
Dundee live in one or two-roomed
houses. There are over 40,000 one
roomed houses in Glasgow.
The report also states: “In De
cember, 1923, we found living in one
room in Glasgok a man, his wife,
and seven children, and that room
was ticketed as containing 1,200 cu
bic feet. Undoubtedly the inhabit
ants are often to blame for the dirt
they live in, but to keep clean and
wholesome a single room where
nine human beings have to sleep,
wash, eat, and drink seems little
short of impossible, and there is
little wonder that many mo hers
give up the attempt.”
Dundee is described as having an
ideal position: “Sun and air reach
the city unchecked from the south
east and west, while the sweep of
the north wind is broken by the
Sidlaw Hills, a few miles inland.”
This is what nature has done for
Dundee.
Man has treated her rather dif
ferently. “The jute factories are
scattered throughout the town, and
nearly every narrow lane is bor
dered by a high, noisy, and dusty
factory which shuts out air and sun
from the workers’ homes immedi
ately opposite but sends in jute dust
and intolerable noise. Nor do such
houses even get air freely from the
other side, as ‘backlands’ abound,
and one sometimes passes throng, i
two successive properties to reach
the third, which may abut on a
high wall.”
Score Hesitant Reporters.
In another case a man, his wife
and five children lived in one room
below the street level and facing
north. The ladies and gentlemen
who wrote the report puzzle tn Jr
heads rather inconclusively about
the problem: What is cause and
what is effect in such a case. The
Guardian refuses to waste time on
such speculations in the face of
such conditions and suggests that
the hesitant reporters should try liv
ing for six months in such a room
and then ask themselves in a cold
room whether their grandmothers
of their surroundings are more to
blame for any failure in their moral
tone.
This document has come at an op
portune time, The Guardian de
clares, for there has been a great
deal of false optimism about the
progress of Great Britain in the
matter of housing.
Even though a great many houses
have been built under the Tory
plan, it is silly to talk as if the
government had gotten over the
worst part of the job.
Problem Still Remains.
“We have scarcely touched the
slum problem,” The Guardian con
cludes. “Leeds has 33,000 back-to
back houses, of a kind condemned
by a parliamentary committee
more than 90 years ago.”
London has a shortage of decent
houses. Conditions in the poorer
sections of West Ham are getting
steadily worse. In almost all the
large British cities the state of
things can be paralleled which
came as a shock to the parliaments
of the forties of the nineteenth cen
tury.
“The slum problem is now what
it was then, the chief evil of our
social life, and there is no evidence
yet that we are going to master it.”

RESENT BRITISH
PROTECTION FOR
SCAB MINERS
PONTYPOOL, England The
miners yesterday resented the pres
ence of a large force of police, who
had been sent out to protect a “few
willing workers.”
When these men were leaving the
pits, under police protection, hun
dreds of strikers rushed at them,
hurling all sorts of missiles. The
police charged the rioters three
times and finally dispersed them. A
few persons were injured.
Rules Are Continued
LONDON—The house of com
mons and house of lords last night
voted to continue for another month
the emergency regulations in con
nection with the coal mining strike.
Because of the protest, Jack Jones,
Labor member, was suspended.
Sir William Joynson-Hicks, home
secretary, who moved the continu
ance of the emergency laws, paid
tribute to the orderliness of the min
ers, pointing out that only 64 were
arrested last month, and urging a
renewal on the grounds that the
regulations acted as a preventive.
Hit by Labor.

Leader Special Service.
COLOGNE —A Lithuanian corre
spondent of The Kolenische Zeitung
reports that the relations between
Lithuania and Poland are strained
and that the whole situation in the
border states between Russia and
Germany shows British diplomacy
feverishly at work lining up govern
ments against Soviet Russia.
This correspondent declares that
recent efforts to unite all the gov
ernments of the border states on n
common program for negotiations
with the Moscow government are in
stigated by the British foreign of
fice, and that the soviet government
has steadfastly declined to negotiate
with such a combination.
May Avoid Trap.
While the Moscow government
may avoid the trap in which a nego
tiation with a combination of Fin
land, Esthonia, Latvia, Lithuania
and Poland would catch it, there is
a possibility that Moscow will be
willing to make a joint treaty with
Esthonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the
correspondent continues.
In fact, some soviet leaders have
indicated their willingness to try
this 'experiment, moved by the con
sideration that in this way Russian
commerce would gain a wider access
to the Baltic sea and a better con
nection with Germany.
On the other hand, some soviet
leaders fear that the Rritish in
fluence is already too strong in the
Baltic states and that a treaty with
them would not prevent their join
ing Finland and Poland in an en
tente with England.
Conflict Still Endures.
The British diplomats have been
working hard to eliminate the pres
ent conflict between the Lithuanian
and Polish governments. This con
flict blocks the British efforts to
get all Baltic states into a common
anti-Russian front with Poland and
Finland.
For the present Lithuania re
mains the pivot around which all
British and French efforts against
Soviet Russia revolve. Whatever
developments may take place on the
borders of Russia, Lithuania will

back of the rumors of war prepara

but also the German. Both the
German and Russian governments
want to prevent an outcome which
would transform Lithuania into a
wall that would keep them apart.

To the Editor of The Leader:
The newspapers of a few days ago
carried stories of how two enter
prising gypsy fortune tellers were
being sought on complaint of women
who claimed a loss of money during
the “seance” as it were.
So it was that good policemen,
who are hired to give sanction to
the laws cf our land, are obliged
to keep a lookout for two women
who merely took advantage of other
women’s surprising credulity.
When a woman or a man so far
belies their reason as to glory in
mystic passings and dim lights in
the hope of learning something that
might please them, they should not
have the colossal nerve to complain
about a monetary loss.
Why will a person who is most
careful of money under ordinary cir
cumstances, fight to wrap up $25 or
SSO in a red handkerchief that the
fortune teller may hold it during
the nonsensical proceedings? And
then, after they inevitably find that
the money is gone, they raise a hue
and cry to the authorities. Evi
dently they can stand the laughter
and ridicule of those who know
them and who have no desire to
play the fool by grabbing at a peek
into the future.
Instead of fining the gypsies and
making them return the money, the
police ought to arrest the complain
ant long enough to deliver a lecture
on what constitutes foolishness.
Then dismiss the case. Maybe when
the individual loses $25 two or three
times, good judgment will topple
curiosity from the throne and the
gypsy fortune tellers will find
harder pickings. Experience is the
best teacher—experience not coun
teracted by the law.

UNITED STATES
BUYS OLOROYD
LINCOLN RELICS
WASHINGTON Thousands of
relics, intimately associated with
the life of Abraham Lincoln, came
into the possession of the govern
ment yesterday, when Col. Osborne
C. Oldroyd accepted $50,000 for the
collection which he spert 60 years
in gathering.
The check was given to Col. Old
royd by Harris Jones, assistant di
rector of public buildings and parks
in the national capital and the
transfer took place in the old house
on 10th St. which has housed the
collection for years, and will un
doubtedly be continued as a Lin
coln museum under the supervision
of the Smithonian institution. It
was in this house that Lincoln
died after he had been shot by John
Wilkes Booth in Ford’s theater
across the street.
How Collection Started.
Sixty-six years ago, when Lincoln
was a candidate for the presidency,
Col. Oldroyd, then a newsboy in
Mount Vernon, 0., began the collec
tion by gathering Lincoln campaign
literature and devoting every pen
ny which could be spared from bare
living expenses to the purchase of
other Lincoln mementoes.
In 1873 he moved to Springfield,
111., and made many valuable addi
tions to the collection. In 1883 the
late Robert T. Lincoln, son of the
martyred president, was persuaded
to rent the old Lincoln home in
Springfield to Col. Oldroyd to house
the relic and there they were kept
until 1893, when the collection was
moved to Washington.
Sought by Ford.
Hopeful that the government
would some day take it over, Col.
Oldroyd refused dozens of substan
tial offers for his collection from
private collectors, among them
Henry Ford.
When it seemed certain that the
collection must fall into the hands
of private collectors and be scat
tered all over the country. Repre
sentative Henry Rathbone, Repub
lican, Illinois, became interested
and finally succeeded in securing
the approval of congress during the
last session for a bill authorizing
the purchase at a price not to ex
ceed $50,000.

LAKE PARK EPISODE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
Your article in Saturday’s paper
regarding “rowdyism” at Lake park
concert Friday night,” was grossly
exaggerated, and I should, there
fore, like you to publish the follow
ing version of said “rowdyism.”
I, with a party of 10, attended
said concert and neither I nor any
of the others noticed any unusual
disturbance. Here and there was
some loud talking, to be sure, but
this has been done more or less at
all concerts throughout the city all
during the summer, and by the old
er as well as the younger element.
The five young men who were
arrested for alleged “rowdyism,”
with the attempt to break up the
concert, I know personally, and I
wish to state that they are as good
a set of American boys as any in
Milwaukee.
Some of them are in my house
daily and I can truthfully say that
I have never heard any of them
curse or use any profane language.
Anyone who knows them and those
in their neighborhood especially,
will give them the best of recom
mendations as to behavior.
They are purely and simply vic
tims of those circumstances arising
on the Juneau park bridge a week
ago. When the park board gave or
ders after that disturbance that any
disturbers at any concert would be
unmercifully dealt with, victims had
to be found. These innocent youths,
who had been talking a little too
loud, had to pay the penalty not
only for that offense, but for an
offense of which about one-quarter
of all those at Lake park and at
other concerts in other parks were
also guilty of.
But if anyone states that they
were rowdies who were trying to
break up the concert he is deliber
ately and falsely misrepresenting
the facts. They were only doing
what many come to these concerts
to do —chatting and talking. Each
of these boys emphatically denies
that he had been molesting anyone
or causing any other grievance of
which they are accused by tbc offi
cer who arrested him.
In order to vindicate the charac
ter of these youths I would like to
ask that any of the readers of this
paper who attended this particular
concert last Friday night at Lake
park and witnessed the arrest of
these boys and the alleged “rowdy
ism” preceding the arrest to give
me, the undersigned, in the name of
justice, their names and addresses.

GREATNESS OF
PEACE, THEME
OF DR. BESANT
CHICAGO —Dr. Annie Besant,
she who lacks but a few months of
four score years, stood up, a
straight and vigorous silhouette in
white, in the flag draped ballroom
of Hotel Sherman last night and
talked for an hour and a quarter, on
the evils of a too great orthodoxy
and the greatness of peace; on the
harm of vivisection, and, most of
all, on the need of western science
mellowing its achievement with the
eastern philosophy of brotherhood.
It was the lirst lecture which the
international president of the Theo
sophical society gave to the Ameri
can followers during this, their 40th
annual convention. And none of the
2,000 members who packed them
selves so silently in the auditorium,
corridors and galleries missed a
single syllable of the speech.
Bo Wary, Warning
Be wary, warned the white haired
woman in the white and gold tunic,
of a dangerous orthodoxy arising in
your several lodges.
‘•Be careful lest the majority im
press its views on the minority,”
she admonished, “and do not get
angry at a challenge to your belief.
When your opponent in any contro
versy becomes angry then you may
know that you are really echoing
the doubt in his own mind.”
Peace, brotherhood, international
ism—this was the threefold rubric
which the leader laid down for the
“theosophizing of the United
States.”
Hits at Vivisection.
Western science, Dr. Besant as
serted, is not always compatible
with the ideal of brotherhood; most
notably in its use of vivisection.
“For vivisection,” she declared,
“is a hopelessly immoral means to
a temporary end. It is not a way
to health, but a transient balance
of poison.”
Earlier in the day this same
quietly energetic woman of 79 years
in an address before the business
meeting had urged America to re
member that her wealthy men were
but stewards of the nation; dis
tributors, not owners.
Is Legion Guest.
Jidda Krishnamurti, Dr. Besant's
30-year-old protege, whom she and
the entire Order of the Star in the
East herald as the modern messen
ger of divinity on earth, did not ad
dress any of yesterday’s convention
meetings, but he attended parts of
all of them.
At noon, however, the Brahman
was guest of the Advertising Men’s
post of the American Legion.
“India,” Krishnamurti told the
ex-soldiers, “is looking to America
for the light, but a material one,
essentially, where India is dwelling
too much in the light of medita
tion.”

The New Court House
The agitation for a new court house has now been
going on for more than 20 years. Long before the situa
tion became as acute as it is today, there were those who
warned that it was merely a question of time when it
would happen.
The courts of the county are now distributed in four
different buildings; the district attorney’s offices are in
a fifth building; the highway department is in a sixth
building; the morgue is in a seventh building; the poor
office (a blot of shame on a wealth-glutted civilization)
is in an eighth building; the assessor of incomes is in a
ninth building.
Said a supervisor:
“Even the basement of the court house is being used
as working quarters, perhaps as unsanitary a place of
employment as there is in the city of Milwaukee. The
health department would not tolerate it anywhere else.”
There is not one office in the court house which is
adequate and fit to do the work well and expeditiously.
In recent years there have been added to the departments
of the county:
The highway commission.
The county park board.
The regional planning board.
The election commission.
The jury commission.
The civil service commission.
The civil courts.
Whenever in the growth of our city a step in advance
is contemplated, there is sure to develop an opposition
that is as unreasoning as it is obdurate. Unreasoning,
because it cannot make the most elemental comparisons,
and obdurate, because it will not be shown.
The first court house was built in 1836, when the
population of Milwaukee was estimated at 500. At that
time it was not considered extravagant to set aside one
half of a city block for court house purposes. But then
the early settlers were red-blooded pioneers. And they
had seen something more than shacks and oversized pack
ing boxes set in rows.
Today our population is over 1,000 times as large as
it was in 1836. Yet a disgusting howl goes up when a
court house site is asked for that is only four times as
large as it was in 1836.
There are counties in Wisconsin today which have
not a hundredth part of the population that the city of
Milwaukee alone has. Yet their court houses occupy
sites as large as the one on which our court house in
Milwaukee is located at the present time. And the people
of these counties would not think of calling that ex
travagant.
That is one of the baneful effects of congestion—
it thwarts vision, prowess and intellect.
The fight for location has dragged for 17 years. In
1909 the county board voted, by a small majority, to build
a new court house on the west side. In 1912 it was decid
ed, by the board, to build on the east side. That action
again was rescinded in 1913 by a bare majority.
In 1914 the county board voted to secure a site for
the court house on the west side and in 1915 the Kneeland
property, on Grand Ave., 10th and 11th Sts., was finally
secured. By this time the location of the site had become
a subject of public discussion.
Condemnation proceedings were begun and appealed
from. A year later the appeal was dismissed, judgment
entered, the money paid and deeds given. The buildings
were razed.
In 1916 an extensive tour was made by a commission
of supervisors through the United States to view court
houses, and a lengthy report was printed. For this pur
pose an appropriation of $2,000 was voted by the board.

An attempt was made to “knock out” the whole
Kneeland site proceedings on the ground that the board
had no right to vote an appropriation of $2,000 for a trip
to other cities.
The complaint was amended later by charging that
there was fraud or collusion, that the Kneeland property
is not within the county seat, and that the county board,
in selecting the Kneeland property as a site for the
court house has been guilty of such abuse of offi
cial discretion as renders the action invalid.
The case was tried before Judge A. H. Reid in 1918
and on May 6 the decision was rendered.
The county board was upheld on every contention
but the one pertaining to the appropriation of $2,000 On
this the decision says that there remains nothing for the
court to do, inasmuch as the county board, by another
resolution, directed the money to be returned, pehding
the outcome of the litigation.

The court ruled that if it were held that the Kneeland

As to the charge of fraud, the court held that “there

erty is more desirable for the new court house than the

The question of a site for the court house seemed to
have been finally settled when the civic center plans be
came sufficiently definite and pronounced to open the
whole matter again.
In March, 1921, a resolution was passed by which
the committees on public buildings and grounds and on
finance, were constituted a special committee and charged
with the duty of investigating the feasibility to place
the new court house in the civic center.
The fight was on with all its former bitterness, when
a judge burst in upon the scene with a communication:
“Gentlemen, the roof over my chamber started to
leak and resulted in badly damaging the paint on the
walls, and I think the same should be painted, etc.—
In December, 1921, the Melms resolution was intro
duced. It provided that action on the Kneeland site be
rescinded, that blocks 180 and 181 in the George Smith
addition, located in the civic center, be obtained as the
proper site, and directed the joint committee to proceed
to secure such lands.
This resolution was reported and also a minority
report dissenting. Both reports were referred to the
committee on judiciary and the district attorney.

At the January meeting of 1922, both reports were
again received and both failed of adoption by a tie vote,
which vote on the majority report was later in the meet
ing reconsidered and the report again sent to the com
mittee on judiciary. o
The Melms resolution was finally adopted on Jan. 01,
1922, with 13 votes for and 5 against. Against constant
opposition, the labors again to obtain a site were starred.
The joint committee reported that the price asked by
the owners of the land in the proposed two blocks,
bounded by State and Wells and 9th and 10th Sts., was
$754,160 and the assessed valuation $454,650. Mr. Ed
ward Grieb, who was selected the agent by the county
board, said that the land could be bought at a price less
than 20 per cent above assessed valuation.
Two tax levies of $350,000 each were resolved upon
and placed on the tax levies for 1923 and 1924.
By 1925 all of the land for the court house site ii\the
civic center had been secured, some of it at no moi e than
the assessed valuation, most of it for less than 20 per
cent above the assessed value and some had to be secui ed
through condemnation.
The final determination of this site for court house
purposes was decided in January, 1926. This fight has
taken 17 years. But we have not yet a new court house.

An architect has been selected in an advisory ca
pacity and is now busy drafting tentative plans for the
building. Four plans are in preparation which, for ob
vious reasons, cannot be discussed at this time and must
be left for a future article.
But the reality of a new court house is yet iar oil,
for an unfriendly opposition can delay the work on a
thousand propositions—always pretending to act for the
“best interests of the people.”

MANKIND DOES
BESTTHINKING
WHEN IT'S COLD
OXFORD—Mankind does its best
thinking when the weather is a little
too cold for comfort, according to
Prof. H. J. Fleure, surveying the
year's advance in anthropology be
fore the British Association for the
Advancement of Science.
“We must not argue too crudely
that man’s ‘ideal climate’ is the
climate of the region in which mod
ern man originated,” he said.
“The most we can say in that re
spect is that as his constitution
seems attuned to certain climatic
conditions those conditions are prob
ably not very far from the condi
tions obtaining in the region in
which he evolved, admitting at the
same time that quite possibly he
migrated into a region colder than
the one to which he was accustomed
and so gained, perhaps, an access of
vigor.
“Certainly man’s mental processes
are most active at a temperature be
low that of the greatest comfort
physically. Olbricht has gone so far
as to venture the suggestion that
the great mental advance to the
fully human condition of the race
probably occurred in a cold, bracing
period, perhaps one of the later
phases of the ‘ice age.’
“The conditions that make us to
day function most actively are those
of a climate with temperatures
usually varying between 70 degrees
and 20 degrees Fahrenheit, without
too long spells at either of these
limits, with enough but not too
much bright sunshine and with
variability and storms as a feature.
“Very great cold appears to have
deleterious effects mentally and
physically.”

THE CHANNEL SWIM.
Another swimmer has safely nego
tiated the English channel, this time
cutting Trudie’s record by an hour
or so. It’s getting to be a habit.
If this thing keeps up, they’ll
have to run it like a golf course.
Give ’em numbers and send ’em off
in foursomes.
Have a man in mid channel to
punch their cards.
Place wiener stands at mile in
tervals. The attendant could toss
a hot dog to the swimmers as they
passed.
It will be soon a common sight to
see people headed for the Cape Gris
Nez coast at 5 a. m. to get a head
start.
It would take a half dozen at
tendants to grease ’em as fast as
they arrived.
Greasing has a two-fold advan
tage. It also keeps the fish from
getting a good hold on their rivals.
Just think of a girl being able to
swim home from her day’s work in
Dover and back in .the morning.
If she’s late, she can tell her em
ployer she ran into a swordfish.

And then she can remove the
grease and use it on her typewriter.

Employers will get used to seeing
huge goggles loom up before them
about 8:30 a. m.
If he gets fresh she can squirt a
mouthful of salt water at him.
Boats will learn to be on time or
the passengers won’t wait for them.
The trouble is that the sailors
won’t know who is drowning and
who. is swimming the channel.

for a crew to send out a boat for
a man and then find that he doesn’t
want to be saved.

TANGIER PARLEY
BLOCKED; SPAIN
MAY WITHDRAW
LONDON—Britain’s reply to the
Spanish note inviting the former to
a conference on the status of Tan
gier was dispatched yesterday.
While couched in the friedliest
terms it is emphatic in its refusal
of the invitation. The British main
tain no useful purpose would be
served in holding a meeting on such
short notice and suggest considera
tion of the Spanish claims be post
poned until after the league of na
tions session, the primary object of
which is to admit Germany into the
league.
Misgivings were not concealed
here that Spain will withdraw from
the league following refusal of its
demands for a larger share in the
government of Tangier.
Spain to Withdraw.
The Spanish foreign minister’s
statement is taken as showing that
the cat is out of the bag, revealing
that Spain proposes to make its
participating in the league contin
gent upon the adjustment of the
Tangier controversy.
The British note points out that
France will not consider Spain’s
first two proposals, namely: inclu
sion of Tangier in the Spanish Mo
roccan protectorate or the granting
to Spain of a league of nations man
date over the territory. According
ly, Britain is unable to oppose these
views. The note suggests a third
proposal, granting Spain larger con
trol in the international zone of
Tangier, can be considered later.
In the house of commons Sir Aus
ten Chamberlain, former minister,
said Britain was willing to discuss
with Spain and France the former’s
request for a league mandate over
Tangier, but with due regard for
existing treaties He did not think
Geneva was good place for such
a oiscussioa.
Find Task Difficult.
GENEVA, Switzerland The
problem of giving Spain a perma
nent membership in. the council of
the league of nations, without di
rectly and clearly designating it as
such, is proving a difficult task.
Eminent statesemen and jurists
struggled for hours yesterday in
the committee assigned to the task
of working out the reorganization
of the council, trying to elaborate a
method whereby both Spain and Po
land could be declared re-eligible
for election as temporary members
of the council, thus virtually mak
ing them permanent.
The discussion became so in
volved over technicalities that the
matter was finally thrown Into the
hands of a subcommittee, which is
expected to find a compromise so
lution.

law was assailed by Atty. Gen.

clared that while the 6 per cent

mediately thereafter and will re
main in operation until the law is
amended or repealed.

act by which the government
turned the railroads back to the
private owners and their man
agers,” he said.

By The United Preu.
IOWA, CITY, la.—Shattered by
the loss of the backfield quartet of
Don Graham, Wesley Fry, Schir
mer and Dauber, and the line giants
—Krasuski, tackle and Griffin, cen
ter, and with star Dick Romey now
cn the list of alumni, lowa’s foot
ball team, under the directing eye
of Coach Burt Ingwerson, faces a
stiff program of reconstruction.
With Cowboy Nick Kutsch sus
pended, and attempting to regain
admission to the university through
worK at summer school, the future
of the squad largely resembles a
question mark. If announcement is
made at the opening of the season
that Kutsch is eligible, a sigh of
relief may be heard about the
world to issue from the corn belt.
Bab Kuhel, known principally In
his college days as a hurdler, but
back in the old high school days
at Cedar Rapids an all-scholastic
backfield man, may take up the bur
den of the attack if Kutsch is not
allowed to carry the ball. Both
lads are fair punters, but Graham’s
loss will be felt especially in the
booting department.
Skeeley, freshman captain in
1924, who left school, will be back
for the season; so will Don Smith,
a reserve last year. Others who
will work out for regular backfield
posts are Byers. Phillips, Flake, and
Armil, of last year’s freshman
squad.
Capt. Smith will play at end, his
old position. Brown will probably
be used to play the hole left by
Griffin, and Chatterton will at
tempt to fill Krasuski’s gap. Both
these lads jiggle the scale at more
than 200. Keel, in spring practice
looked as though he had reserved
a regular guard’s job for himself.
Rice, irregular regular last season,
should occupy Romey’s end job.

LINCOLN, Neb. Despite the
loss of such sterling players as
Tackle Ed Weir, Center Harold
Hutchinson, Fullback John “Chop
py” Rhodes, and the fleet halfback,
Roland Locke, Cfiach Earnest
Bearg of the University of Nebras
ka football team looks for a suc
cessful season this fall.
Bearg bases his hopes on 15 of
his 19 letter men returning this
fall. Although he admits that the
men who graduated last spring car
ried 75 per cent of the load on
both offense and defense, he has
sufficient confidence in these 15 and
36 new candidates who showed up
well in the spring practice sgason.
Capt. Stiner, Ashburn, Scholz and
Randall are looked upon as capa
ble of filling the tackle positions.
Howell, Beck, or Oelrich should fit
into the fullback berth. Holm and
Andrews should capably fill the
halfback jobs, while Bronson, Lin
dell and DeTeau are quarterback
candidates.
“Bunny” Oakes, Illinois line star
in 1923, and last year coach at
Tennessee, and Leo Scherer, for
mer Cornhusk er, will handle the
line coaching under Bearg. Char
ley Black, who played at Kansas
and was head coach at Grinnell,
will work with the backfield ma
terial. Rhodes, who graduated laW
spring, is to be freshman coach.

the offing,” Sibley said.

WAISTLINE
SINCE 1923
ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—Jack
Dempsey was ready again today to
show the same fistic wares that yes
terday made his followers howl with
delight.
His usual daily round of training
was to be followed, ending with the
usual brief but strenuous rounds
with his sparring partners. This
is “Saturday” in the champion’s
training camp, for Wednesday has
been picked as his day of rest.
Dough Looks Good.
This shift of the sabbath was de
cided on because Dempsey thought
he needed one days’ layoff a week
and because Sunday’s big crowds
were a financial asset too good to
miss, hence Wednesday.
Dempsey’s waistline is more than
an inch smaller than it was in 1923,
when he fought Luis Firpo in New
York.
A concern which is measuring him
for ring regalia for the Sept. 23
fight with Gene Tunney found that
he was only 33 around the waist,
against 34^4 in 1923.
“How do you explain that?”
Dempsey was asked, in view of the
fact that he weighed 194 for Firpo
and bulks 197 now.
Wrists Exceed Willard’s.
“I guess I had a little fat around
the midriff when I met Firpo,” said
Dempsey. “None there now except
a thin layer which I want to keep
on hand to work off in my training.
My extra weight now is around the
shoulders and upper arm and that’s
meat and muscle.”
Dempsey’s wrists measured 9*4
inches, as compared with a wrist
measurement of 9 inches which be
longed to Jess Willard, the biggest
man in modern ring history.

when their barn is saved from fire.
CHAPTER I.
Who Shall Talk.
When once the Silent Twins
began talking after their years of
silence they were Silent Twins no
longer. They became Talkative
Twins nd they talked and
talked and talked. They did not
give each other a chance to listen.
And as for Jack, Janet, Cousin
Clyde and Jolly Jerry, they got
all mixed up trying to keep track
of what the Twins were saying.
Suddenly Ronald Twin stopped
short, his tongue halting in the
middle of a word.
And at the same time Roland
Twin stopped short. Roland
turned to Roland.
“You have as much to tell as I
have, dear brother,” he said,
“you do your talking first.”
“No, brother,” exclaimed Ro
land, “I am sure you have more
to tell than I have. You begin.”
But Ronald would not start first
and neither would Roland. They
argued the matter, talking mope
than they had before and not get
ting anywhere in their talk.
Finally Jolly Jerry broke Into
their flood of words with a sug
gestion.
“Why don’t you draw lots to see
which will start?” The Twins
eagerly agreed to this.
The Twins had packs of cards
with which they had played soli
taire on winter nights. Jerry held
out one of these packs to them.
“The one that draws the high
est card shall begin telling what
he has seen during the silent
years,” declared Jerry. He held
the pack of cards to Ronald, who
Jerry held out one of those packs
to them.'
drew one card, not showing what
it was. Then he held the pack out
to Roland, who also drew a card.
“Let us see what you drew,”
cried Jerry. The Twins showed
their cards. Ronald had a ten of
clubs. Roland had a ten of spades.
Each was as high as the other.
Again they drew. Roland got a
Jack of diamonds. Ronald got a
jack of hearts. Still there was no
choice.
So they went on drawing, and
each time they drew a card equal
ly as high.

A Page For Women and the Home
BY DADDY
“We shall have to try some
thing else,” said Jerry finally. He
had grown tired of shutfling the
cards. “What shall it be?”
The Twins thought the matter
over. Suddenly Ronald Twin got
an idea, and at the same instant
Roland got one also. Strange to
say, it was the very same idea.,
“It is the'time we feed the wild
partridges,” they cried together.
“The partridges are the shyest of
birds, but they have grown to
love us, as we feed them grain
every day at this hour. We will
feed them now, and the one to
whom the first partridge comes to
eat out of his hand shall begin
first to tell the things he learned
in his silent years.”
The children were glad of this
suggestion. They were keen to
see the Twins feed the partridges.
Never had Jack and Janet been
able to get near one of these timid
birds.
Each Twin got a handful of
grain. Each went into the edge
of the woods. The children fol
lowed, hiding in the bushes.
Each Twin made a little cluck
ing noise. There was silence in
the forest. There was stillness,
too. Suddenly a partridge ap
peared in the trail. And another
partridge, and another, until there
were a dozen of them. Slowly and
warily they neared the Twins.
One partridge stepped out ahead
of the others and pecked at the
grain in Roland’s hand. But at
the very same instant another
partridge pecked at the grain in
Ronald’s hand. Neither Twin had
won. Again the contest was a tie.
“My goodness!” exclaimed
Janet impatiently. “It must be
awful to be a twin. Neither can
win from the other. They
wouldn’t have much fun playing
games with each other.”
And Jack and Clyde agreed
that seemed true.
How Jack breaks the tie will be
told tomorrow.

BY WILLIAM BRADY, M. D.
WELL WOMEN MAY BATHE.
At one time or another nearly
everybody is bound to be over
taken, I suppose by old fogyism.
Had a narrow squeak myself re
cently when I was launching one
of my mean cracks at the mutila
tion known as bobbing the hair;
I coupled that with a veritable old
fogy condemnation of basketball
contests played in public by high
school girls. One high school girl
player knocked me for a string of
Woolworth beads by asking me
what the objection was, and I
squirmed and blushed —I am glad
to say I blushed, or at any rate
I felt that way—and had to ad
mit that I was condemning a per
fectly proper athletic activity
merely because I happened to
know of instances in which high
school girls had abused the privi
leges and freedom from restraint
which basketball games in other
cities gave them. I have formally
apologized here for that bit of old
fogyism, and I now repeat that
in my judgment basketball is a
fine game for high school girls,
and interscholastic or interclass
contests in public are quite as
commendable as are debating or
singing contests. I hope I shall
have no more such spells of old
age—and I hope my young friends
will keep an eye on me and see
that I be myself in future.
This season, I think, there have
been 10 times as many inquiries
from girls and women about the
imaginary risks of going in swim
ming or taking baths in the course
of the menstrual period than I
have received in any previous
year. I interpret this as a sign of
awakening—the light is beginning
to break through the mists of su

Love Madness
BY CLAIRE FOMEROYE
Mutual Confessions
There seemed a dearth in the
conversation after Jay Vannah
had told Gloria that it was his
intention to go away forever.
There seemed nothing left to talk
about.
“Of course, Gloria, I shajl see
you before I go,” he said a little
vaguely. “My steamer leaves
New York Saturday.”
Gloria managed to speak calm
ly and their good nights at the
door seemed commonplace. Cer-
tainly Gloria did not feel the calm
and self-possession she pretended.
The light in the dining room
was extinguished and she as
cended to her room. The door of
Evelyn’s room was closed but the
sharp streak of light on the thres
hold indicated that she had not
turned in for the night. Gloria
paused before her door for a mo
ment with the thought of speak
ing to her. But she passed on to
her own room.
As Gloria West slowly un
dressed she tried to bring the dis
ordered thoughts and ideas of her
mind out of chaos. She tried to
adjust herself to the extraordin
ary denouement into which the
Vannah affair had resolved itself.
At one moment she seemed to pic
ture herself one of the leading
actors in this incredible drama
and at another moment she felt
herself apart from the scene, an
outsider, viewing it all through
the eyes of a mere spectator.
Vannah tonight had seemed so
wistful and so dependent. She
wondered if she had given him
the crumb of comfort of which he
had obviously been in search
when he had sought her out. She
wondered if he had had a more
definite object in view in coming
to her than that which he had
expressed, some more vital pur
pose which he had not mustered
the courage to reveal. She won
dered if she had seemed cold and
disinterested and thus blocked his
confidence.
“Gloria I”
Gloria roused herself from this
profitless reverie as she heard
Evelyn calling from the passage
way.
The new member of the family
was standing in her nightgown
outside her door.
“I’d like to talk to you for a
few minutes, Gloria.” she whis
pered softly. “May I?”
“Of course, dear. I’ll come over
to your room.” Gloria tucked her
self into a negligee and joined
Evelyn in her room.
The girls made themselves com
fortable, sitting cross-legged, in
Indian fashion, on Evelyn’s bed,
and in guarded whispers melted
into a state of mutual confidence,
both eager but hesitant to con
fess the true problem with which
they were confronted. It was not
strange that these two girls were
swept so swiftly into a rare af
finity, for there could not have
been two whose characters were
so different, whose philosophies
were so radically apart And
bound by this peculiar tie of sym
pathy their intuitiveness had been
sharpened to an almost uncanny
degree. Gloria had quickly pene
trated the attachment existing be
tween Carson Brooks and Evelyn
and while she may not have been
conscious of her feeling, she was
instinctively inspired to further
their romance until it had arrived
at its logical peak. Evelyn, on
the other hand, grown wise by her
exciting experiences of the past
few weeks, had weighed Vannah
anew and had discarded the ro
mantic and juvenile illusions
which she had built up about him
in her mind. So it was that
Gloria and Evelyn presently found
themselves to be deep in the de
tails of their naive confessions,
as natural and as honest with
each other as if they had been
the closest of friends for years.
Indeed, Gloria found it much
easier so be honest in discussing
her feeling for Vannah with Eve
lyn than she had ever been in
thinking about it herself. And
Evelyn discovered that it was
perfectly natural for her to speak
of being in love with Carson
Brooks, something she had never
put into her concerete thought be
fore.
“But I suppose it all has to end
this way,” sighed Gloria wist
fully. “Jay is probably sick of
the sight of women. And you
couldn’t blame him.”
“He wouldn’t have come to see
you tonight if he didn’t care—a
lot,” replied Evelyn with a quaint
little air of authority. “Men who
are going away forever don’t come
around like that unless they mean
it.”
Gloria stirred restlessly and
made a peculiar hopeless gesture
with her hands.
“Jay probably thought that he
owed it to me to say goodbye,”
said Gloria sadly.
“But it isn’t Jay who owes me
anything, but I who am indebted
to him. I’ve never known a man
so fine and so true and so honor
able. And, of course, he has his
weakness, too —he wouldn’t be so
wonderful if he were not also
likely to do foolish things.”
“What a pity it is,” murmured
Evelyn thoughtfully, “that Van
nah doesn’t know that you love,
him. Gloria,” said Evelyn
suddenly,’ “would you marry Van
nah if he asked you to?”
An unbidden tear welled into
Gloria’s eye and she brushed it
away angrily.
“He did ask me —once —before
his wife died.”
Evelyn was shocked into si
lence. Try as she might she
could not reconcile jo her mind
that Vannah could have been so
cruelly fooling her at the same
time he was paying furtive at
tention to Gloria West. The fine
idol of the man which had come
into being in her mind wavered.
“I guess the best thing for both
of us to do is to forget about such
things and strike out on our
own,” said Evelyn with a little
grimace.
Gloria gave a little cry of sur-
prise.
“But you’re all right, Evelyn,”
she put in quickly. “I know that
Carson will ask you to marry
him, now that all the worry and
uncertainty is gone.”
Evelyn shook her head despond
ently.
“Just can’t be done,” she
laughed flippantly, but the brood
ing in her eyes belied the light
ness of her words. “You know
Carson isn’t earning enough to
look after himself decently. And
besides” —a tear in her voice—■
“he’s never asked me.”
“Don’t you fret about that part
of it,” reasoningly from Gloria.
“He’s going to ask you—l feel it
in my bones. And besides, I’m
going to let you in on a secret.
Carson’s dining in state with Mr.
Bigelow tonight. And it isn’t
merely a dinner of soup and fish
down to the black coffee. It’s
big.”
“What do you mean, big?”
“Mr. Bigelow’s going to do
something splendid for Carson,”
replied Gloria. “He’s been awfully
pleased with what Carson has
done lately. Why, this case has
just been the making of Carson.
He’ll have money enough, don’t
you fear.”
The steady buzz and rumble of
the girl’s conversation had finally
crept in to Mrs. West. It must
have been three o’clock.
“For goodness sake, girls, do
go to bed and get some sleep,” she
commanded, drowsily. “You’ve
got to get up for breakfast and
it’s most dawn now.”
And the two girls exchanged
startled glances. Sure enough,
they had been chattering away for
hours. There was a sweet note of
sympathy and complete under
standing between them as Gloria
went out of Evelyn’s room on her
way to bed.
“Will you get up in the morn
ing as early as I?” asked Gloria.
“I’m a poor working girl, you
know and have to have breakfast
at half past seven.”
“Will I?” exclaimed Evelyn
with an expression of mock in
dignation. “I’ll tell the world I’ll
get up. I’ve got to find a job.”

DISHES WITH CURRY.
Curry is a flavor that when it is
liked is enjoyed very much and
when it is not, or not well prepared,
“it is horrid.”
Always cook curry with the ingre
dients of the dish when possible,
not idd it as a seasoning at thu
last.
In the Orient there are over -M
ways of preparing this condiment,
and only there do they serve it in
perfection. Curry is not always
blended alike; different, places pre
pare different powders. It is like
mincemeat and fruit cake, and
mother’s pickles; we like the kind
we are accustomed to use.
Chicken Curry.
Cut up a plump young bird and
fry brown in olive oil. Remove
from the frying pan and place iu
the oven. Mix two tablespoonfuls
each of flour and curry powder,
then add gradually one cupful of
any well-seasoned stock. Fry two
sliced onions in hot fat, add the
prepared stock, cook five minutes,
then turn in the chicken. Co nr
and simmer 15 minutes. Serve hot
wilth boiled seasoned rice. If the
sauce seems too thick add more
stock.
Curry of Succotash.
Take two cupfuls each of fresh
lima beans and cooked corn, or ;wo
cans of each. Heat until hot and
season well, then heap on a flat
dish, cover with curry sauce and
serve with potato croquets.
Curry Sauce.
Simmer two tablespoonfuls of but
ter, one large onion finely minced,
then add one tart apple chopped,
cooked three minutes, add one-half
cupful of highly seasoned stock and
cook gently for five minutes; add
another half cupful of stock and
one cupful of milk into which a
dessert spoonful of curry has beeO
stirred; let all boil up once, then
press through a sieve, return to ths
fire and thicken with a tablespoon
ful of flour and one of butter for
every cupful of the liquid. Srir
until it thickens and season well
before serving. This makes a mild
curry sauce, and a good one to
practice on.—Nellie Maxwell.
Potato Waffles.
Three medium potatoes, one tea
spoon butter, two teaspoons baking
powder, cne teaspoon salt, one-half
teaspoon soda, one egg. Beat egg
lightly, add milk, shortening, sugar,
salt and flour. Beat smooth and
add water. Sift baking powder
into batter, add soda dissolved in
a teaspoon of water. Add to batter
and mix well. Do not stir any
more. Pour batter into a pitcher
and then into the center of a
waffle iron, filling half full. Spread
quickly, close and turn iron, cook
two minutes. Turn and cook one
minute.
Huckleberry Pudding.
Two cups flour, one-half cup mo
lasses, one-half teaspoon salt, one
half cup sour milk, one-half tea-
spoon soda, two tablespoons mdted
shortening, one-fourth teasp^
mixed spice, one heaped cup chopped
huckleberries. Mix as for ginger-
bread. Spices may be cinnamon,
nutmeg, cloves or ginger. Pour in
greased mold. Steam one to two
hours. Serve with sauce.
Sausage With Bananas.
Shape pork sausage meat into lit
tle rolls, place them in a frying pan
with just enough water to cover
and let boil one minute. Drain off
water and frey the sausage until
crisp over a quick fire. Remove
from pan and keep in hot place.
Peel three or four bananas and slice
length-wise. Put a small piece of
butter into pan in which sausages
were cooked and all bananas. Fry
them over a hot fire until hot
through. Pile the bananas in the
center of a hot platter and arrange
the bananas in slices around the
edge. Garnish with parsley.

morial Institute.
Every man and woman, even ev-
very child 10 years old, knows that
|n ordinary life emergencies arise,
which are urgent, requiring instant
attention. When the house is on
fire they know that action must be
taken at once or with the least pos-
Fible delay. They can see the fire;
they know from experience that
failure to act means loss of the
house.
The same individuals who act so
promptly, so intelligently in ordi
nary emergencies too often show
utter lack of intelligence in their
action when confronted with an
emergency surgical condition in
themselves or in the family.
They want to wait; they want to
confer with a far away spouse or
parent. In other words they defer.
They use none of the intelligence
displayed by the most ordinary in
dividual in case of fire. They will
wait till tomorrow or until after the
wedding.
They question secretly the diag
nosis of the most learned physi
ians and surgeons, and place their
n conclusions in opposition to
4 ose of the most skillful diag
nostician. They do not believe they
have appendicitis or a perforation
or an internal hemorrhage or in
testinal obstruction; it doesn’t feel
quite like what they think such a
condition ought to feel.
Hense procrastination in urgent
surgical conditions accounts for a
neat percentage of the total mor
tality. In acute appendicitis the
death rate should be not more than
one in 1.000 if the operation is done
before the appendix ruptures. It is
at least 50 in 1,000 if rupture is
allowed to occur.
Surgical skill cannot alter this
discrepancy; it can be altered only
by the patient accepting the opera
tion at such time as will offer him
bent result*.
That afternoon, however, bot
with the shadow of that next week
on their minds, redoubled their ef
forts to please—and in their over
anxiety, of course, only failed the
harder. It was the same story
throughout that all too short week
as it slipped by on reels of wind.
On the day that marked the six
tieth since first they arrived upon
the Amalgamated lot full of great
dreams and high ambitions, Cam
eron summoned both to his office
early in the afternoon.
