him, Cameron swung from his desk
and came to the point.
“As you know, of course, the con
tracts under which the Amalga
mated Studios brought you here
expire today. I’m sorry to tell you
that we have no more steady work
for you and will have to remove
your name^ from the payroll to
day.”
“Oh,” cried Betsy, “then we’ve
we’ve failed? Our tryouts were un
successfid
“Yes,” said Cameron bluntly.
Hal felt the hot color of disap
pointment burning in his cheeks;
but his primary sorrow was not
for himself, but for Betsy, whose
eyes glistened with tears.
“I tried my best,” she lamented.
“I wanted so much to —make good.”
“And so did I,” said Hal, think
ing of how his mother and his sis
ter would take the news of his
failure; and all the good friends in
Centipede who had seen him off,
who had worked hard to gain votes
for him so that he could have this
chance. He had failed their faith.
That thought alone made him sud
denly stubborn, made him forget his
common sense declarations about
going home if he failed. “And I’ve
been working right along,” he said
doggedly, “without any kicks lately.
What’s the matter with what I’ve
done, anyhow?”
“You’ve worked, it is true. But
you haven’t shown anything that
convinces us we ought to keep you
on the regular payroll. That, of
course, is an arrangement we make
only with stars and the very best
second string of talent. Of course,
if anything comes up where we can
use either of you—we’ll be glad to.
But you’ll have to take your
chances with the other 12,000 now.”
No matter how much humans are
prepared for death or failure, the
shock of the actual occurence of
either of these rawest experiences
of life is never any the less. Betsy
and Hal, although they had talked
it over and were prepared for the
possibilities, looked at one another
in dismay now that they suddenly
realized to the full that they were
cast adrift on the teeming sea of
Hollywood’s extras.
“Of course,” said Cameron, more
kindly now, for he, better than any
one else, realized just what these
two were up against, “under the
contract you get your fare to your
homes paid to you in cash at the
expiration of the agreement. There
fore, my frank and earnest advice
to both of you is to go home at once
and leave acting in the movies to
those who have the genuine talent
and the elastic hearts that are nec
essary. For, an I’ve told you both
before, ambition and hard work
alone won’t get you very far in this
business. You two are just kids. I
like you. Everybody around here
who has come into contact with you
likes you, and is interested in you.
So, while it’s not usual for me to
step out of my job and talk like a
Dutch uncle to would-be stars in
this way, I’m doing it because I
don’t want to see happen to you
what I’ve seen happen to so many
others.”

WHERE THE MOSQUITO
FORGETS TO STING.
About six hours by steamer from
Venice, I came to the beautiful
Brioni islands, a small group off
Pola in the Adriatic sea. Of all
the pleasant places on the Istrian
coast, I think this spot must be
claimed as the finest for a holiday
and rest. It is different from most
resorts. On the largest island, which
is the real resort, there is no village,
simply round the lovely harbor
stand the hotels and the casino; yet
the island is complete with every
comfort as much as if it were next
door to Naples. The irregular
coastline is wooded down to the wa
ter’s edge and the avenues away
from the shore are flanked with
palms and semi-tropical plants. The
ruins of a Roman villa testify to the
fact that it has been loved for a
holiday for 2,000 years. There are
also the remains of a basilica arena
and arches. Its beaches are a de
light to children and to bathers and
if there are mosquitos here, they
forget to sting, for there has never
been anyone stung on the Brioni
Islands yet.

It’s a case of who’s who and who
cares over at the Palace theater this
week. The cards at either side of
the stage drop as per custom about
every 15 minutes to announce a new
act, but that doesn’t mean any
thing, as the actors and actorines
don’t believe in signs. Which all
goes to make up a hodge-podge of
fun and a rather unusual amount
of dancing. The settings are smart
and the prettily costumed girls
passing fair.

Will Ferry, alias The Frog, opens
the show in a different atmosphere
than has been his custom. Then,
too, the octet of young women make
their first appearance, and all but
ruined our regard for them by try
ing to warble en mass». And they
weren’t dressed like frogs. But
Ferry is his usual clever supple self
and is up to snuff.
Bud and Jack Pearson show
flashes of good dancing both in
their first appearance and in the
closing revue.
The girls and a charming scene
in front of a millinery establish
ment help Kraft and Lamont in
their little skit, Put Up the Lights.
You can't help but enjoy this act,
even though the gentleman’s ac
tions seem more or less silly at
times. But be works hard and is
blessed with an entertaining part
ner and the above mentioned girls,
strikingly costumed as a “sports
eight.”
Perhaps the two who were en
joyed the most —as they momentari
ly stopped the show —were Lewis
and Sargent, and they sang so well
that it would have been hard not
to like them. Both play various
stringed instruments and use a cou
ple of good voices to put over sev
eral astonishingly new and peppy
songs. It turns out that they are
the son and son-in-law of “Papa”
Cameron and as such play an im
portant part in the next act, which
is always enjoyable. For who has
not laughed time and again at the
sally: “Son, do as papa tells you
or papa’ll bruise yau.” And Mr.
Cameron, Sr., has always faithfully
promised to shoot “all three.”
Of course the London, Paris, New
York revue is the big thing of the
evening and is staged with regard
to proper choice of scenery, lighting
effects and costumes. The Prince of
Wales is the central figure in the
first scene and gives way to a
French artist in the second. The
final —a traffic scene on Broadway
—is exceptionally clever, even
though some of the girls’ headlights
were out.

Canning Green Beans.
Dear Editor: The following re
cipe is so simple that a child could
follow it, but I have never lost a
can in using it. First gather,
string and break nice tender green
beans. Wash them through several
waters until clean. Pack beans in
one quart fruit jars and fill to top
of jar with cold water. Add one
teaspoon salt. Put jar rings on and
screw lid down half way. Next
take an ordinary wash boiler and
lay flat strips of wood in bottom of
boiler so the bottom of the jars
won’t touch the boiler. Cover the
jars with water Bring to a boil
and boil hard for three hours. Re
move from stove and seal while hot.
You will never fail to save your
beans if you use this method.

about and inside the log church
upon a bright hot Sunday.
“Look! I do wish you would
look at that!” Sist’ Beveridge
ejaculated in a groaning whisper,
eyes fast to the window. She
weighed 200, “raised the tuno”
regularly, and led in prayer meet
ings to beat anybody. “No! 1®
won’t see that little fool preacher.
Like's, not he’s off flshin’—said
hisself he always wanted to go
days like this. But Polly-Anu
Huelin, all by herself, has rid
in, past the horse-block on to the
furthest hitch-tree, flung her brb
die over a swingin’ limb—an* slid
down, ’thout waitin’ for any
man’s helpin’—”
“What of it? She’s a Huelin—
like’s not her ma’s gig is half a
mile behind her,” Sist’ Mason, her
gossip, returned placidly.
Sist’ Beveridge snorted: “You
needn’t be takin’ up fer that gal
—she’ll never more’n say scat to
your son Joe again—her mind’s
plum sot on that fool little preach
er.”
“I doubt it —but shoe’s she
wants him, she’ll git him—that’s
her way,” the gossip chuckled
amiablv.
Up went Beveridge’s hands—
came sibilantly from the watcher:
“There he comes—the preacher—
full gallopin’—straight to Polly-
Ann’s tree. Lawsy! He don’t
more’n nod to her. Her back’s co
him—makin’ out she’s waitin for
her ma. I made shore they’d
come in together.”
The Huelins were distinctly
what the blacks called “quality
white folks.” Also foremost in
every good work. The crucial dif
ference in their religious beliefs
made no rift in family life. Rath
er it bred a tolerance as rare as
it was beautiful. The squire was
courteously hospitable to all min
isters—it had gone hard with him
to say to young Headly: “Ton’ll
understand why I say don’t
show yourself too friendly with
us. Your church people will re
sent it. I’m sorry-—you’re of our
own sort—then, too, you’ll be a
fine measure of a man for my
Polly—after a while.”
Only that—but Headly under
stood. Marian was no more for
him than for her humble slave,
Joe Mason. Hard! How hard he
had not dreamed, until the inner
sense constrained him to pass her
in silence—unless his eyes spoke.
Did they? He wondered dully,
the while he strove manfully to
give heart and soul to the work
in hand. He loved it—best of
anything, he tried to tell his con
science. Vainly! Yet there listen
ing felt awed. He spoke as
through lips touched with holy
fire, His words cut deep, stung,
stirred, until listeners fell to
weeping, praying, at last shout
ing loudly their joy in the glory,
the goodness of God. Madame
Huelin led the shouting—she who
was normally so shy, so sweetly
silent, a very white rose of wom
anhood. Though her husband
never listened to a sermon, he
came always to take her home
after service. Thus in the height
of her ecstasy she saw his face
outside the door and darted down
the aisle, crying clearly: “Jamie!
I’m seeing heaven—but—if yen
won’t come there I’ll go with
you—”
With her last words madame
had sunk to her knees—to the
floor—lay there breathless, white
and still as death.
A week later she was almost
herself. Marian had hardly left her
throughout the first days. Now
she was sleeping the clock round,
unheeding that her father sat
deep in conclave with Headly.
At last the squire asked, with a
hard breath: “Son, how did it
happen? You didn’t do it—
it was possession—something In
you beyond the power of mere
mortal. Was it, think you, of
God—or the devil—you believe la
them—l do not.”
“Neither, sir! Headly an
swered, his head low-bowed apoa
clasped hands. “Nothing more
than the outreach, the agony of
love—love denied. It was a man
choosing between his heart and
his soul. I may be vain, *nt -i
might win your daughter in spite
of you. He happiness would be
the price. She does not love me
—yet—only cares for me fantas
tically because I’m different. Bk
she won’t forget me quite—not
even when the true love comes.
You—you—’ll say goodbye for
me—l don’t dare. I’d die to make
her happy—this is harder a lot.”
“You you shan’t go,” the
squire said tremulously. “Take
her —with my blessing. I may be
cloudy-minded about God—but I
know a man when I find one.’’

TWELVE
TARIFF REVOLT
TAKING SHAPE
IN MIDWEST
CHICAGO —There are signs of a
new economic and political revolt
in the middle west agricultural
states. Except among the more
radical agriculturists and poli
ticians the demand for some kind of
government price fixing or subsidy
on grains is subsiding, writes O. A.
Mather in The Tribune.
One hears little of strong demand
for such measures as the McNary-
Haugen bill in Kansas and Ne
braska, although it still persists in
lowa-
But a different line of economic
and political thought is developing
that may be more difficult to
assuage and is likely to cause the
Republican party considerable trou
ble in the forthcoming national cam
paign. This is the tariff. From de
manding higher prices for his prod
ucts the middle west farmer is turn
ing to a demand for lower prices for
the things he buys. But let a Ne
braska farmer-banker-politician give
the argument.
“The demand for some sort of
price fixing for the chief agricul
tural products was born out of des
peration,” this farmer said. “With
the unfortunate results of land spec
ulation passing, and with better
crops, this demand is growing less.
A great many farmers did not re
gard the price fixing proposals as
sound economics.
“But the disparity between what
the farmer has to sell and what he
buys still remains, and we are think
ing there may be another and eco
nomic method of remedying this
spread. We see industrial wages
about double the pre-war rates and
we see industrial corporations mak
ing excellent profits, often the
largest in their history. But we also
see a much smaller appreciation in
farm produce prices.
“If a lowering of the tariff will
produce greater equality between
the industrial population and the
agricultural workers we want the
tariff lowered. We want to buy our
manufactured articles cheaper.
Won’t Flood Country.
“We have begun to realize that
the high wages in industry and the
high prices for manufactured ar
ticles do not return to the farmer.
The workman whose income is dou
bled doesn’t eat twice as much as
he did before, neither does he wear
twice as many clothes.
“Frankly, we believe that indus
trial wages and profits can be mod
erately reduced without any lessen
ing of the demand for and consump
tion of farm products. If a lower
ing of the tariff will bring about
some lowering of prices of the mer
chandise that the farmer must buy
we are going to demand that the Re
publican party promise such re
vision.
“It is old stuff for us to be told
that a lowering of the tariff will
flood this country with foreign
goods and wreck our industries. We
see our exports of manufactured
goods constantly expanding in world
competition and our exports of food
stuffs constantly diminishing.”

EGYPT TAKES
STEPS TO AID
ITS FARMERS
WASHINGTON The Egyptian
minister of agriculture is sponsor
ing a movement for the creation of
agricultural co-operative societies
on a solid financial basis so that
they may not suffer from a change
of government, according to a re
port to the department of commerce
from Assistant Trade Commissioner
William D. Mann, Alexandria.
The minister stated before a re
cent session of the house of deputies
that about £1,000,009 would be re
quired to finance the scheme and
that the government would be called
upon to open the credit.
Foreign Trade Dependent.
Egypt’s foreign trade, and to a
large extent its financial position, is
said to be almost entirely dependent
upon its agricultural situation. The
maintenance of stabilization in agri
cultural conditions is, therefore, es
sential to the country’s general eco
nomic welfare.
It was with this fact in view that
a movement for the organization of
agricultural co-operation was first
started some 20 years ago. How
ever, although the movement had
considerable popular support, it has
heretofore failed to succeed because
of difficulty in securing funds.
To Study Situation.
The recent proposal of the mini
jter of agriculture would give Egyp
tian co-operative financial security
that they never before have had
by the appropriation of £1,000,000
to be drawn from the government’s
reserve fund.
It has further been recommended
that the government Increase its en
dowment fund by allocating to it a
part of the proceeds of the cotton
tax, which at present produces an
annual revenue of approximately
£2,000,000. A committee has been
appointed by the ministry of agri
culture to study the various phases
of the situation and to perfect the
plan for government endowment of
co-operatives.

U.S. SHIPS TEETH
AND PEANUTS
In the consideration of the wide
range export and import figures
necessary to denote the progress of
the foreign trade of the United
States, it is very easy to overlook
the smaller shipments of a multi
tude of commodities which annually
find their way from the American
factories to the markets of the
world.
The publication of the depart
ment of commerce which describes
statistically the progress of Amer
ican foreign commerce reveals the
fact that foreign purchasers come
to the American manufacturer for
false teeth as well as for automo
biles and for corsets as well as for
iron and steel products.

1925, the total exports of teeth from
the United States numbered 29,412,-
243, and were valued at $1,286,838.

worth $2,961,126 were dispatched
into the shops and homes of foreign
nations.

$392,241 performed their share in
amassing the total volume of Amer
ican exports during the past fiscal
year; American exports of phono
graph records, numbering 4,937,388
and valued at $1,949,999, contrib
uted to the satisfaction of the mu
sical demands of foreign ^buyers,
while $1,441,348 worth of American
rouges and other cosmetics answered
the year’s demands of foreign wom
en for toilet preparations.

EXPORT TRADE
DRIVE LAUNCHED
WASHINGTON—A move to build
up America’s annual export trade
with Europe got under way today
with the departure of Dr. Julius
Klein, director of the bureau of for
eign and domestic commerce, to con
duct a sweeping economic survey
abroad.
Dr .Klein will sail from New York
tomorrow on a journey which will
take him to 27 European cities be
fore his return to this country.
“Europe, with imports from the
United States averaging well over
$2,999,900,099 annually during the
last four years, and with receipts
from this country totaling $2,694,-
999,009 in 1925, is by far the world’s
largest market for American goods,
the department said.
“The largest proportion of the 2,-
999,099 queries which the depart
ment of commerce is now receiving
every year from business men who
wish to sell their products abroad
concerns the countries of Europe.
“The prime purpose of Dr. Klein’s
trip, therefore, is to assure to Amer
ican business the continued receipt
of timely and practical trade infor
mation by the department from the
29 trade offices which is maintained
in Europe.”
Ripley Stock Censor
Idea Regarded as
Radical By Hainer
WASHINGTON—Bayard T. Hain
er, chief counsel for the federal
trade commission, today character
ized as “too sweeping” Prof. Wil
liam Z. Ripley’s proposal that the
federal trade commission can and
should require corporations whose
stock is traded in on the New York
Stock Exchange and widely held-by
investors throughout the country to
publish financial statements yearly
that are a true index of the worth
and earnings of the company.
“Congress did grant the federal
trade commission broad authority,”
Mr. Hainer declared.
“But the language of the federal
trade commission act must be read
in conjunction with the commerce
clause of the constitution and the
courts consequently have circum
scribed the commission’s visitorial
power over private corporations to
activities of an interstate commerce
character.”

SERVICE TO BE COMBINED
The postmaster general says airmail cannot be made
to pay its way unless the planes carry passengers as well
as mail.
That seems reasonable. The railroad passenger trains
carry mail incidentally. Airplanes could do likewise. To
make them pay by means of mail alone the charges would
have to be very high. And that would react, for the send
ers would use the telegraph instead of airmail, since the
telegraph is speedier and if the charges were about the
same they might as well use it or send by ordinary mail.
But the government is mistaken in turning the whole
matter over to private contractors. It has spent much
money to develop airmail, has made experiments which
were bound to be a monetary loss, but which are of much
value as experience. After having done this, it proposes
to pocket the loss and turn the air service over to private
owners to make money out of, as they undoubtedly will
when they combine mail and passenger service. In some
cases they are doing it now.
Why should not Uncle Sam do that himself?
There is no answer except that it is not the old party
way. The old parties always play into the hands of pri
vate capital. They pour out the public money for things
that do not pay, and they let private owners have the
things that do pay. That is a policy that must be changed.
But you’ll have to vote for Socialist candidates if you want
to change it.
If you don’t believe it, read this from the postmaster
general’s statement, “We ordered 50 new planes of the
very best type, 18 of which have already been delivered,
and which are coming at the rate of three a week. They
are designed to carry mail only, for obviously the govern
ment is not going into the passenger business.”
Why not?
Vote the Socialist ticket and show him.
EMPLOYERS’ DECEIT
Employers of the “open shop” variety, and particular
ly the Milwaukee organ of the slavery in employment
contingent, try to kid the people with the notion that em
ployers in America prefer to pay high wages and therefore
no labor unions are necessary to jack wages up.
This is pure poppycock. A mere handful of employ
ers have been wise enough to know that they get better
work by paying higher wages. The rest—the vast major
ity of employers—always keep wages down just as far as
they can. They never raise wages unless they have to.
Occasionally economic conditions compel them to do sc.
Usually a trade union compels them to, either directly
or indirectly.
The nonunion men always reap some cf the advan
tages of unionism. The unions force better wages and
conditions in some industries. In this way, they better the
condition of the whole working class, for they pull the non
union workers up after them. The nonunion men do not
get as good a deal as the union men, but they get a far
better deal than they would if there were no unions.
Thus the nonunion men get something for nothing.
They get part of the benefits of unionism without paying
any of the dues or doing any of the work of the unions.
How can they be satisfied to occupy this parasitic attitude?
It is about the same as accepting charity. Wherever eli
gible they should join the unions and do their share. This
is not only the self-respecting thing to do, but it will bring
them higher wages and better conditions.

A GOOD EXAMPLE
The net earnings of the Canadian National Railways
—the system owned and operated by the government—
will be about $40,000,000 this year, if the present pros
pects pan out. Some of the papers grudgingly admit that
government ownership is succeeding.
These papers do not fail to point out that there are
many charges against the system, old interest charges.
But they neglect to say that these charges are due to the
miserable failure of private ownership previous to the
time when the government took the road over. They also
neglect to say that the road was bankrupted under pri
vate ownership, that it was in such a terrible condition
that it could not continue to operate, and that the govern
ment took it over by sheer necessity in order that the
people living along the line of the road might not be utter
ly deprived of railway service.
The system was taken over when the conditions were
about the worst possible. The government has operated
it with splendid success. Part of it runs through sparsely
settled territory where it is difficult to make it pay, but
where the settlers need it badly. Yet as a whole it makes
a fine success financially, and sets an example for Uncle

WHERE GERMANY MEETS FRANCE^
The champions of the German republic probably
take a greater interest in the fall of the French franc than
any other section of European life.
It is just as essential for German as for French in
dustry that the franc should be restored to some stable
relation on a gold basis.
A few German speculators may get an easy rake-off
from the juggling of big bankers with the franc, but
German industry as a whole suffers, because German ex
ports to France are more and more reduced in proportion
as the fall of the franc disorganizes the French markets.
The total internal debt of France today amounts to
about 300 billions of francs, and very little of this can be
covered by the repayment of money which France loaned
to other European countries. The money which is ex
pected from the French share in German reparations has
already been spent in the reconstruction of the devastated
regions.
Taking the domestic and foreign debts of France to
gether, she owes about 600,000,000,000 paper francs. If
she has to pay interest on this enormous sum with francs
far below the pre-war gold value of the franc, she will re
main the slave of foreign bankers, until the Socialist par
ties of Europe can make an end of private banking. The
British and American debt settlements to which all French
parties object, would keep France at the mercy of foreign
bankers until the year 2,000.
The enormous size of the French debts would make
this debt problem insoluble for the old party statesmen,
even if the whole military budget of France were wiped
out. It is desirable, of course, to make an end of militar
ism, but the French debt problem would not be essentially
altered by the cancellation of the military expenses. They
amount to only one tenth of the total burdens of the
French government.
The most bothersome and dangerous debts are the
short term and the floating debts, and these keep the
French government at the mercy of foreign gamblers,
who hold about 50 to 60 billions of gold francs. Unless
the French government can buy back the controlling share
of this emigrated money, French politics and business will
be at the mercy of foreign bankers.
To the extent that German industry suffers, the Dawes
plan is menaced, so that the British and American insist
ence upon the collection of the uncancelled part of the
war debt adds to the already enormous difficulties which
stand in the way of the Dawes plan. It is certain, under
these circumstances, that the British and American gov
ernments will soon have to revise their attitude towards
French finance, and to reconsider the Dawes plan.
This will have to be done some time before the next
presidential elections, and how the Coolidge government
and the Republican and Democratic world court senators
will manage this, will be interesting to watch.
While French and German economic intereSts will be
drawn more and more closely together, with political ef
fects which cannot be very agreeable to the imperialists
of England, Spain and Italy, the old parties in the United
States will invent new ways to fool the small American
taxpayer, bank depositor and voter. k
Of course, no old party statesman will suggest to tax

AMERICAN MONEY IN EUROPE
American capitalists have invested several billions of
dollars in Europe since the end of the war. Will this
money speed up or hold back the development of Europe
towards Socialism?
The people who invest this money have an answer
ready. They don’t bother their heads about Socialism.
So far as they know, there is no such thing as a develop
ment towards Socialism. It is all a dream of hairbrained
radicals who don’t amount to a hill of beans.
Our investors in Europe have a severe lesson in social
science coming. European labor unions don’t vote the
old party tickets any more. European farmers and little
business people also fall away more and more towards the
political left.
The more money American capitalists invest in,
Europe, the more the capitalists will want to speed up the
work, in order to extract extra profits and keep their own
high enough to suit their pleasure or vanity.
Monopolies will take on a more and more internation
al hue. The European workers will get more and more
determined to throw off foreign rule and with it the rule
of domestic capital.
We would rather see American capitalists invest their
money in the United States and make this country fit for
heroes to live in. But if they prefer to pay Europe a high
price for a thorough education in Socialism, instead of
learning it at home in a more pleasant and orofitable way,
we shall have to be satisfied.

gun. The mere fact that only 38

ada, supported the president. Von

reservations.

SHOT, IS REPORT
MANVILLE, R. I.—Five persons
were reported shot, one seriously, by
state police in a clash last night
with striking operatives of the Man
ville-Jenckes Co., and sympathizers
over possession of the bridge con
necting Manville with the mill. The
plant is a cotton mill.
Col. Everitte St. J. Chaffee, com
manding the state police, asked Adjt.
Gen. Cole for assistance, and late
last night a picked detachment of
35 men from the 103rd field artil
lery was ordered to Manville by
Adj. Gen. Cole.
The trouble began Sunday night,
when the mill was stoned and an
attempt was made to fire it. The
disorders continued yesterday and
last night.
Last night the crowd assembled
at the bridgehead and taunted the
troopers with abuse and stones. A
sympathizer tried to force his way
across the bridge and was thrust
back.
A little later the troopers fired
their first volley from revolvers and
one man was carried away. Shortly
afterward another man was shot.
Later the troopers fired another
volley of six or seven shots, one of
which struck a boy in the leg. An
other person, a man, is reported to
have been hit also.
The troopers were aided by more
than a score of deputy sheriffs.

FARMERS GET
LOW PAY FOR
HARD LABOR
Tens of thousands of people in
Wisconsin are working for less than
5 cents an hour because they are
still using mediaeval methods In
modern times.
That is the startling message
projected by the unique exhibition
of the Wisconsin committee on the
relation of electricity to agriculture
on display in the educational build
ing at the State Fair.
To visualize the message, a con
test between any man and a one
half horse-power utility motor is
staged any time some skeptic
“wants to be shown” the truth of
the assertion. A pump has been
placed between two tanks. The
motor pumps water into one tank
and the skeptic pumps water into
the other. The one who pumps the
W’ater faster than the other wins.
The motor always wins.
“A man working hard will pump
about 180 gallons in one hour,” said
W. C. Krueger, University of Wis
consin research student, who is in
charge of the exhibit.
“The motor will pump 300 gal
lons an hour and will keep it up all
day.
“Anyone who is doing work which
an electric motor can do is working
for less than 5 cents an hour and
at the same time is doing very much
less work than the motor performs.”
The exhibit shows a modern farm
kitchen, the farm yard and a dairy.
The kitchen is equipped with elec
trically-operated range, water heat
er, dish washer, refrigerator, iron,
vacuum cleaner, fiber scrubber, pol
isher, exhaust-ventilator, window
fan, and other electrical appliances
for the farm.
Wine Is Preserved
For 1,600 Years
BERLIN, Germany—A bottle of
wine reputed to be the oldest in
the world is a special attraction of
the wine section in the historical
museum at Speyer.
This ancient relic of a hard-drink
ing age is over 1,600 years old. It
is a mixture of wine and honey,
almost two-thirds of which Is still
in the liquid state.
The bottle was found in a grave
dating from the year 300 A. D.
Originally the contents were sealed
with oil which in the course of many
centuries has become gummed up.
w’hereby the precious beverage has
been preserved.

Adjournment of the John Doe
proceedings in district court where

of conduct of city officials and the

saloonkeepers to obtain renewals of
saloon licenses, has been taken until
Friday, it was announced today.

today. To, permit employes to at

Milwaukee day, there will be no ses

Miss Clarkson Hides.
The John Doe proceedings, if not
concluded Saturday will be contin
ued Wednesday. No court sessions
will be held Monday, Labor day, or
Tuesday, primary election day.
According to a report furnished
Asst. Dist. Atty. George A. Bowman
by detectives, the whereabouts of
Miss Mary Clarkson, president of
the Federated Church Women, who
has been sought as a witness for
more than a week, is being kept
secret.
Officers of the federation, it is
said, at first reported that Miss
Clarkson was “on vacation,” and
that they did not know her where
abouts. Yesterday, however, de
tectives reported that they knew
where Miss Clarkson was, but
that they would not tell.

LAST MONTH WAS ONE OF SIX
DRIEST AVGUSTS SINCE 1871
August was one of the six driest
Augusts since 1871, according to the
report issued today by W. P. Stew
art, weather forecaster.
The five other driest years dur
ing that period were 1878, 1883,
1894, 1902 and 1917.
Precipitation amounted to 0.65 of
an inch, while the normal is 2.82.
While there were 15 partly cloudy
and nine cloudy days there were
only five days on which it rained
sufficiently to make a record. It
never rained more than one-fourth
of an inch at a time.
August also has been warmer
than usual. The highest tempera
ture was recorded Aug. 28, with 97.
which was also the record for the
entire summer, and the lowest was
on Aug. 8.
BLOCK RAID ON
COUNTY PURSE
FOR $150,000
Blocked by Socialist and nonpar
tisan supervisors who refused to
permit the county treasury to be
raided for $150,000, the plan of non
partisan supervisors to purchase a
county airport was sent to a com
mittee for consideration late yester
day by the county board.
The proposed purchase of another
county airport at Hamilton field,
south of the city, near Lake Michi
gan, and the resolution that $150,000
be appropriated for the purpose led
to a stormy debate lasting for an
hour.
“Stampede” Play Fails.
The effort of Supervisors Hugo
Franke, Albert Foster, Eugene War
nimont and George Herrmaiiß, non
partisans, to force the measure
through, was characterized by So
cialists as a “a high-handed attempt
to stampede the board.”
The county has been maintaining
an airport at its park on the Lisbon
road. A move to turn this into a
golf field and obtain another site
resulted in a communication pur
porting to come from the county
park commission, and signed by W.
R. McGovern, president, asking tor
money to buy the Hamilton field.
This had been preceded by several
communications from the commis
sion, signed by its secretary, C.
B. Whitnail.
Supervisor Frederic Heath, So
cialist, started the fireworks by
challenging the validity of the Mc-
Govern communication. He refut
ed a statement by Supervisor
Franke that the park commission
had directed McGovern to send in
such a communication, and said
newspapermen had told him they
had found no such meeting had been
held.
McGovern was a silent auditor to
this controversy, occupying a scat at
the rear of the chamber.
Tucker Takes a Hand.
An attempt was made by Super
visor Warnimont to excuse the Mc-
Govern letter by saying that Whit
nall had sent out letters to the
public not sanctioned by the com
mission, and he joined with Super
visors Franke and Foster in de
claring that the board must act at
once or the city would forever lose
its place in the air mail game.
Supervisor Herman Tucker, So
cialist, scored the supervisors for
trying to rush through such an im
portant expenditure of money with
out committee action, and moved
that it be sent to committee.
Supervisor C. C. Jacobus, non
partisan, cautioned his fellow par
tisans against denying members the
right to look into the matter.
Supervisor James P. Sheehan, So
cialist, said he considered it nervy
to try to force the board to vote
thousands of dollars for a new and
unknown project by a wave of the
hand.
“One hundred and fifty thousand
dollars may seem small to some
members, but I don’t see it that
way—and I don’t believe any sound
business man expects it of us,” he
said.
A motion by Supervisor Foster
to adjourn for 10 minutes to go
through the form of holding a com
mittee meeting was lost, 7 to 12,
and after further sharp debating
the Tucker motion was finally
adopted, 12 to 7.

farm homes and dairies in the
counties we serve,” announced S. B.

CLUB WOMEN
ATTACK BLAINE
PARDON RECORD
Using his own reports to the state
senate as substantiation of their
charges against Gov. John J.
Blaine’s pardon record, particularly
with reference to leniency shown
criminals convicted of crimes against
women and children, prominent
Milwaukee club women at an in
dignation meeting in the Martin ho
tel, yesterday, began a campaign
to bring this record before the
motheis of the state.
Taking the governor's own re
port, the club women revealed that
the chief executive during the four
year period ending in January,
1925, pardoned or commuted the
sentences of 500 criminals from
state institutions for felonious of
fenses, and pointed out that only
128 were recommended by the trial
judge or prosecutor for pardon.
To counter campaign assertions
of Gov. Blaine that he released
only 396 convicts in live years, the
club women will issue a compila
tion of his senate report showing
the number of pardons and commu
tations, including the number of re
leases granted those whose crimes
were against women and'children.
A letter was ordered drafted by
Mrs. F. J. Rucks incorporating this
public record of Gov. Blaine’s par
dons for distribution to club women
of the state.

BERLIN The London corre
spondent of The Berlin Vorwaerts
Writes that the British government,
by attempting to force the miners
into submission through the starva
tion of their women and children,
has suffered a great loss of respect
among the British voters.
The action of the Baldwin gov
ernment is no longer decent, the
correspondent continues. The only
reason why Baldwin’s letter to
America has not caused an even
greater protest is that the capital
ist press of England has suppressed
as much as possible the real truth
about the condition of the miners.
Government Will Suffer.
The correspondent believes that
the Tory government of Great Brit
ain will not succeed even with such
methods. The British miners have
once before stood the brunt of a
strike which lasted over a year.
Methods which might break other
labor organization have little effect
on the British miners.
In the present case, the judgment
of experts about the probable dura
tion of the war proved just as un
reliable as that of those who pre
dicted a quick and short world war.
'‘But even if the miners should
break down under the pressure of
want,” the correspondent concludes,
“the government will have no rea
son to feel elated over the outcome.
“Aside from the fact that the
government has wrecked every
chance of polling a large Conserva
tive vote in any district with a
large industrial population, it also
has created such a vast general
wave of dissatisfaction that Bald
win and his friends face a very dis
mal perspective in the next years.”
Should Contribute Freely.
Vorwaerts comments on this re
port: “The German workers can
see from this report that it is very
urgent that the lists for the sup
port of the British miners should
be generously subscribed.”
Reports from England indicate
that the government is beginning to
feel the pressure of public opinion
as much as the miners feel the
weight of want
The general sentiment among the
miners and among the British work
ers generally favors the idea that
the mine owners and the govern
ment will not succeed in breaking
the miners and forcing lower wages
and longer hours on them.

WE WANT TO
PAY U.S, DEBT,
RUSSIA SAYS
CHICAGO—“We are prepared to
make the first move towards settle
ment of the former Russian debts
to the United States, but are un
willing to do so without assurance
that they will agree to receive our
debt funding commission,” was the
statement made by a high official
“spokesman” of the soviet foreign
office to the foreign press repre
sentatives yesterday, according to a
copyrighted New York Times story
appearing in The Tribune.
Anxious to Meet.
He continued:
“The American government has
refused to deal with us until we
undertake to meet the Russian ob
ligations to America. We are
anxious to do so in order to put the
business relations between the two
countries on a firm footing.
“We authorized certain Ameri
cans to make that known to the
American government. Why doesn’t
the American government say it is
willing to receive our commission?
“We don’t make political recog
nition or a new American loan a
preliminary condition for opening
debt discussion. We have stated as
plainly as possible that we are
ready to pay to the measure of our
capacity. What prevents the Amer
icans from giving us a hearing?”
Cites Kerensky Loan.
In reply to a question the spokes
man said there was no reason why
recognition by Russia of the Ke
rensky loan should involve recogni
tion of other obligations, adding:
“Any debt can be recognized with
out involving all of them.”
He said also that claims of pri
vate American citizens come with
in the province of the debt fund
ing commission, as well as debts to
the United States government.
[MILWAUKEE NEWSPAPER WOMAN I
I VISITS BRITISH LABOR SCHOO!]
[The following account of the
British Labor scliool at Easton
Lodge, Dunmow, England, is con
tained in private letters from
Mrs. Doris Berger Welles to her
parents in Milwaukee. Easton
Lodge, the palatial residence of
the Countess of Warwick, has
been annually lent to the use of
the Labor school by Lady War
wick since she became a Socialist.
Other letters from Mrs. Welles on
the British coal strike and the
Labor party in England and Scot
land will follow.—Editor.]
Easton Lodge, Dunmow, England.
Aug. 3, 1926.
Nothing I can write will tell you
quite all about this lordly mansion
of Lady Warwick. Therefore I shall
just say that we are here, in the
most gorgeously furnished building
I’ve ever seen —that our windows
look over miles of park garden, that
the library is furnished from floor
to ceiling with the most ancient
books—that’s ont telling it. I’d bet
ter do it in some sequence.
We landed about 10 yesterday
morning and were met by Thomas
Oswald Moseley’s secretary—a dap
per and earnest young fellow—
whom I guessed at once to be Mos
ley’s secretary because his face wore
a somewhat puzzled look, while the
others on the dock looked eager.
Quaint Old England.
It was frightfully exciting. Lon
don, huge and gray, and girded with
iron, first—then picturesque and
lacy with Gothic buildings in West
minster, and quaint and ancient
where the Mosleys live at 8 Smith
Square, in a house more than 200
years old, and exquisitely furnished.
We all went out to lunch. And
later walked past Buckingham pal
ace, down to Piccadilly Circus and
Leicester Square—old London thor
oughfares—and finally took the
train for the Labor school at Easton
Lodge, Dunmow, where we are now.
We were terribly tired, but even
so, the train ride was fun.
We passed nice little vine-covered
stone houses, thatch-roofed, and set
in gardens. The Mosleys met us. So
cordial they were, and warmly
friendly, that we miraculously lost
all tiredness. We drove from the vil
lage, which is about four miles
away, along a very pretty English
countryside, to the park gates—and
then miles to the most enormous
mansion, surrounded by gardens and
pools and rose arbors and tennis
courts and endless things of beauty
which outdo the wildest painted
stage scenery I’ve ever seen.
Most Entrancing Gardens.
Our room is on the top floor,
looking out on these most entranc
ing gardens, the end of which we
cannot even see. But there’s
scarcely time to tell about them
rose-covered columns, yews cut like
sentinels, thatched summer houses,
vine-covered, built up in great
trees, little surprising nooks fitted
with stone seats, sunken gardens,
bursts of the brightest flowers
around corners, formal beds stud
ding acres of close cropped lawn,
paths leading through wildish
places.
I’ll tell you about the mansion,
any room of which is larger than
your entire house.
It is somewhat like the white
house in Washington, but the rooms
are much larger and fuller and
more gaudy.
I don’t even now (and it’s 24
hours), know how many rooms
there are—but the staircase is a
broad green and gold affair'', with
mirrors for walls and divans on
every landing, which you may have
seen the like of in the movies—but
I doubt it.
Movies Are Outdone.
In fact, I’ve never seen anything
half so exquisite as the gardens—
not even in the movies. All the
luxuries of centuries are collected
in the house, and the gardens seem
to have been tended for almost for
ever, since the Warwicks are an
old English feudal family, closely
allied with British royalty, which
reminds me that the butler re
ferred to the Countess of Warwick
as “her ladyship” this morning,
and I felt too utterly as If I were
in the theater.
The General Strike.
As to the Labor school—
Pat Dolan, of Clyde, Scotland, is
manager of the school (“the dicta
tor,” he calls himself) this fort
night, of which we missed one day.
Mr. Dolan is a witty and charm
ing fellow, who seems well loved,
even by those who do not agree with
him.
I brought him papa’s regards.
Fenner Brockway is hero (he is
the secretary of the Independent
Labor party) and last night Phil
lips-Rice gave the lecture, which
was on The General Strike. He
gave an historical survey, showing
that the general strike nas never
been successful when it was waged
over a purely ecomonic issue, and
proved that it was most effective
when it was tied up with some po
litical demands.
There was much agitation among
the 60 students who, though they
were courteous as to the academic
value of his speech, had expected
him to talk about the general
strike of May.
Mosley Calms Discussion.
It seems that the Labor party—
or at least the younger members

are very resentful of the trades
union leaders who called off the
strike, without even the guarantee
of no penalties for the workers.
And there was a good bit of ex
cited condemnation aimed at the*
leaders in general, including and
especially, J. Ramsay MacDonald.
Then T. Oswald Mosley rose. In a
persuasive and yet dominatingly
logical way, he urged “wars usually
are not won or lost in one great
clash.” That the mistake made by
the Labor party was its failure to
demand a general election last year
—backed by the threat of a general
strike.
He argued, that if the Tories had
denied them a “general election”
on the important issue of wages,
after Baldwin had said “every work
er in England must expect a reduc
tion of wages”—then they would
have had an issue near and dear to
the hearts of liberty-loving English
men—their old established constitu
tional right to an election.
And with such an issue, well ad
vertised previously in lectures,
pamphlets and the press, the work
ingmen might have expected more
from the strike.
Mosley Next Labor Premier.
The effect was miraculous.
All of the dissension was swept
away, and there were cries of “Hear,
hear” (which is an Englishman’s
way of expressing approval) and
much stamping of feet and applause.
And they say it’s always so.
I tell you, “Tom” Mosley—as he
is atfectionally called by the work
ers, may be the next premier (La
bor) of England. He is already rec
ognized as a leader. Chamberlain
has declared he will not run against
him, and he (Mosley) thinks that it
is a dead sure thing he will win a
seat again in the house of commons
at the very next election.
This morning Barnes, a co-opera
tive member of parliament, talked
on the Co-operative movement. It
was tremendously, learned, and the
most inspiring lecture of that kind
I’ve heard in a long time. His plea
was that the Labor party and the
trades unions and the co-operatives
all work together for Socialism.
He said—but I shall write that up
for The Leader, and you’ll see it
there later. Everyone pronounced
it the most authentic and complete
analysis of the co-operatives.
Will Be MacDonald’s Neighbor.
Tonight there is to be a lecture by
some German delegate from the So
cial-Democratic party of Germany,
tomorrow a discussion of the future
program of the British Labor party,
a continuation of the analysis of the
tactics in the general strike, a talk
by Prof. John Maynard Keynes—
former economist and author of
The Economic Consequences of the
War. For Friday they plan a trip to
Oxford and Cambridge.
Another day a visit to H. G.
Wells’ home—which is just next
door (beyond the park). Mr. Wells
isn’t at home—only his wife.
Later Cynthia Mosley says she
means to drive us to Scotland, stay
ing two nights with her relatives, en
route, and also arranging a big
miners’ meeting, on the way. In
Scotland, we shall live at the sum
mer home of the Mosleys—next door
to Ramsay MacDonald. And after
that the Mosleys talk of taking me
to motor all over the continent.
Tennis on Wells’ Court.
Aug. 5, 1926.
Lady Cynthia is the most gracious
of hostesses, the most charming by
far, of all the persons here.
Yesterday Mr. Mosley and my
husband (Colin G. Wells) and John
Strachey and I went over to play
on H. G. Wells’ court.
The Wells’ house is charming—
vine-covered red brick with a bright
gay garden and park, where “Mr.
Brittling saw things through.” John
Strachey is the editor of The Social
ist Review. The Miner, and the
author of several pamphlets. He’s
very young—the son of John St. Leo
Strachey, editor of The Spectator.
Evenings there are songs, usually,
and Scottish dances, led by Pat Do
lan.
Which reminds me, papa, Pat
adores you.
And Cynthia Mosley the other day
at table said you -were the only
American Socialist who meant any
thing. Do you remember the con
troversy about war guilt and the
pact of Versailles at the Interna-

300 DROWN AS
RUSSIAN SHIP
SINKS AT PIER
CHICAGO About 300 persons
were killed when the Lenlngrad-to-
Cronstadt steamer Buryvestnik
rammed a pier late Sunday night
and sank in 15 minutes amid ter
rible panic, according to the esti
mate of the steamship company, a
copyrighted New York Times story
appearing in The Tribune states.
Officials say the company sold 583
passenger tickets, whereas the num
ber saved was under 300.
The soviet government has named
two commissions to investigate and
fix the blame for the disaster. If
anyone is found at fault severe pen
alties will be inflicted.
Ship Was Overloaded.
The night was pitch dark and the
little vessel overcrowded with holi
day crowds Cronstadt officials,
sailors, dock workers and families
returning from a week-end at the
former capital.
There was one small lifeboat, 172
cork vests and 55 life belts to accom
modate all the crowd. The spot was
deserted and as the vessel slowly
slid, bow foremost, down to the bot
tom, 30 feet below, the frantic crowd
on deck was left to sink or swim,
except for a few lucky ones who
clung to the funnel and the masts.
Scores perished miserably below,
unable to escape from the restaurant
or private cabins, one of which was
occupied by the wife and two chil
dren of the captain.
Has One Hero.
Apparently few at first realized
the danger, and when the ship sud
denly began to sink the sudden
panic became uncontrollable. On the
other hand, the conduct of a sailor
on the Russian battleship Marat
throws a ray of heroic light on the
dark picture. As soon as he felt the
shock he dashed to the engine room,
buffeting his way past the terrified
engineers and firemen, and turned
off the steam cocks, averting an ex
plosion of the boilers.

INDIAN HISTORY
SANTA FE, N. M.—Field work
at the ruins of the Pueblo Indian
village of Pecos, in northern New
Mexico, has been resumed for the
summer by Alfred V. Kidder, field
director of the department of
archaeology of the Phillips Andover
academy of Massachusetts.
During the period of 11 years Dr.
Kidder has been exploring and ex
cavating the site which was occu
pied for centuries by the prehistoric
Indians and abandoned by their de
scendants only in modern times.
Piece by piece, as if matching
fragments of a broken pottery bowl,
Dr. Kidder is patching together the
unrecorded history of the early
occupants of Pecos. He finds the
skeletons and mortuary offerings in
the rubbish heaps which border the
village mound so stratified as to in
dicate the development of the arts
and industries of the community
from the earliest times. The site is
so large that only a small portion of
the ruins has been cleared in many
seasons’ work. It is owned by the
state museum of New Mexico.

BREAD, WATER
BY TOMORROW
TEKMAH, Neb.—Today is a feast
day at the homes of Bay Carson and
Thomas Nelson, young farmers who
must serve a jail sentence on a
bread and water diet for having
-violated the prohibition law.
Ham and eggs in bounteous
fashion was the breakfast menu for-,
both homes. There was a breakfast
food and plenty of coffee. The
bread was buttered.
Chicken and Corn.
Carson at noon will have chicken,
corn on the cob, potatoes and des
sert.
Nelson will have a large and thick
steak and the usual vegetables
which go to make up a meal. Pies
feature the menu at Nelson’s home.
This may be the last time in 20
days that the two will have a chance
to eat anything more than unhut
tered bread and cool sparkling
water. The supreme court mandate
ordering them to start serving their
sentence is expected to arrive to
morrow and the two will both go to
jail at that time.
They Won’t Starve.
“We’re going to fill up today.”
Nelson said. “A farmer doesn't
build up much of a waist line and
we’ll probably need a reserve when
we get to eating nothing but bread.”
“They won’t starve in jail,”
Sheriff W. D. Smith said today. “I
will see that there is a plentiful
supply of bread on hand at all
times and they can have all the
water they want to drink.”

CURFEW RINGS
IN CHICAGO, BUT
FEW DISOBEY
CHICAGO Curfew rang last
night at 10, establishing a new era
in Chicago with the beginning of
the enforcement of the old law keep
ing children off the streets at night.
A checkup at midnight by police
a’l over the city brought forth re
ports that itith few exceptions the
curfew was obeyed—children under
16 not being found away from their
homes alone.
Policemen Joseph Scott and E. J.
Rumps of the East Chicago Ave.
station came upon three youngsters
about 11.
To them the policemen explained
the new order, a revival of the an
cient custom of ringing a bell at the
curfew hour, anl told them that
henceforth they must be home be
fore 10. Then the policemen ful
filled their duty by escorting the
boys to their homes and notifying
their parents. The boys were Albert
and Joe Greenman and John Spat
fora.
Subject to Fine.
The police were ordered to ques
tion any children found unescorted
after the forbidden hour and send
them home. On a second offense,
under the ordinance, the parents
will face a $5 to SIOO fine and the
child the juvenile court.
“Youngsters must do their petting
hereafter in the parlor at home,”
said Chief of Police Collins. “Not
that we want to be old fashioned
and violate personal liberty, but
simply as a common sense measure
to check dangers to themselves.
“The worst of the moron crimes
are committed against young girls.
It is too late to save them after
they are picked up or kidnaped. The
police are getting the guilty men,
but that doesn’t help the girl after
the affair is over.”
A similar statement came from
Chief Le Roy Davidson, who is di
recting the curfew campaign along
the county highways.
Protection Is Needed.
“Girls with parents or members
of their families or on their way to
and from work will not be mo
lested,” he said. “But we are try
ing to protect them from unscrup
ulous men. Many don’t realize what
an apparently innocent automobile
ride may lead to. If their parents
won’t stop them, we will.”
Although the order to the city
police did not go into effect until
last night, the county curfew—which
applies to girls under 18 after 10:30
p. m.—was sounded early yesterday.
More than a score of girls were
caught and warned that the next
time they will go to the Juvenile
Detention home. Their parents
were notified.

THE LEAST OF THESE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
While a 15-year-old child, alert
and capable of understanding every
thing said about her, stood before
the judge’s bench in juvenile court
last week, officials calmly discussed
whether or pot she had a residence,
and what institution might be in
duced to take her for the next few
years.
Her mother and father were from
North Dakota. But her father had
died and her mother had taken her
to lowa, where she abandoned her
and ran off with a second man.
The Wisconsin Home society, Mil
waukee, has taken care of her for
several years and now, because she
does not seem to fit into the several
homes they have tried her in, it
appealed to the state to take her off
its hands temporarily.
There is nothing bad about the
girl, it was declared. She just is
restless, likes to move from place to
place, and hence rather takes satis
faction in dissatisfying her succes
sive employers.
Far from the worst type of child,
certainly! Yet she stood there,
homeless, without parents, and
heard the state debate and reject
this after that institution as one
which would not want her.
An official of one state institution
even insisted that she was not a
citizen of Wisconsin, and hence not
legally a recipient of its protection.
Even though the Home society, in
corporated under the laws of Wis
consin, was her legal guardian, and
its main officers here in Milwaukee,
said this official, the girl must not
be considered a Wisconsin citizen.

than those in the city, but only 45
per cent expressed a preference for
rural teaching.

FREED BY COURT
Edward Hacker, town of Gran
ville, who has been held on a charge
of manslaughter since July 28, when
the bus he was driving was struck
by a North-Western road train near
Fondy station and four passengers
were killed, was freed in district
court yesterday.
Hacker’s case was dismissal by
Judge Michael Blenski on the
ground that there was insufficient
evidence to convict him.
Leo Cappan, 1554 2Gth St., who
was driving an automobile immedi
ately behind the bus when the acci
dent occurred, testified that the bus
had not been exceeding a speed of
15 miles an hour.
Charles Campbell and Peter Wei
rich, both living at Adams, Wis.,
who were the engine crew of the
passenger train, admitted that the
train was going at a speed of about
50 miles an hour and that the bus
was not going much faster than 15
miles an hour.

My European
Excursions
By Eiwta Bobart Petro
HUNTING IN IRELAND.
The Irish have a “crack” to the
effect that “the English love to hunt
in Ireland,” but in these happier
days it has lost its tragic reference.
Sportsmen, however, still cross the
little channel to follow the hounds,
and judging by the number I saw
there in the spring they evidently
come with enthusiasm and are wel
comed heartily. This year the Ameri
cans were also in evidence. Bective
house, near Navan, once the resi
dence of John Watson, who for
many years before his death was
master of the Meath hounds, has
been recently purchased by a group
of Americans Interested in the Irish
hunts. It will act as a clubhouse
for visiting Americans, who will
hunt with the Meath hounds, and
fine bloodstock is being secured to
make first-class seasons. It is a
lovely view that I obtained from
the house, its gardens overlooking
the River Boyne. I should imagine
that there are scores of houses in
Ireland that could be similarly de
voted to American club purposes, for
the hunting in this little country is
unusually good.

WATER RATE
MAY BE FIXED
Fixing of Milwaukee’s future wa
ter rate probably will be the result
of the action started late yesterday
before the state rail commission at
Madison.
The present Milwaukee rate has
been filed with the commission with
a request that it be kept in force.
The commission has announced that
it will hold a public hearing to de
termine the sentiment of the people
on the present rate.
The action is the result of the re
cent decision of the supreme court
to the effect that the city cannot fix
its water rate except with the ap
proval of the commission. The pres
ent rate, fixed by the common coun
cil, never has been approved by the
commission.
A date for the public hearing will
be announced within 10 days, the
commission announced late yester
day.

HERITAGE OF
BADGER STATE
CHICAGO—The greatest heritage
Wisconsin had was its forests, and
one thing that appears passing
strange to'the observer is that, with
all the decades of talk about con
servation and progressivism, the
state has done so little towards re
forestation, writes Arthur Evans in
The Tribune.
Lumber men say, in fact, Wiscon
sin, which once led the world in
lumber output, has done practically
nothing to promote tree growth on
the cut-over lands, except for a
nursery station here and there.
What is left of the virgin forest
cover is vanishing at a rate that is
appaling to tourists, who have the
habit of the north woods for vaca
tions, and the higher the taxes rise
on timbered lands the faster it is
logged to escape still higher taxes.
End Is Seen.
One leading lumberman says that
at the present rate of cutting Wis
consin will see its stands of com
mercial timber all finished within
15 years and nothing will be left
but lumber from the farm wood
lots. x
The lumber interests say waste
anj> denudation might be retarded
by a severance tax law that would
permit taxes to pile up and be paid
when the timber is cut. Taxes on
standing timber are running 20 to
25 cents a thousand. Records on
one extensive tract show in 1919
the taxes ran at the rate of .$22 for
40 timber acres. This year they
are s9l.
“It means it will be cut quickly,
regardless of waste and the mar
ket,” said the lumberman. “It will
be logged to escape the growing tax
burden. Hold it 10 years and see
how it would pile up. Thus the tax
system promotes waste of the for
est. Similarly it remove and in
centive for reforestating cut-over
lands. We just let tne denuded
land take care of itself.
Would Be Different.
“Start growing trees and it would
be taxed as timber bearing land,
and as it takes 40 or 50 years to
grow a crop of trees, you can see in
50 years the taxes might be more
than the crop is worth. If taxes
could be paid when the timber is
cut, as in Massachusetts and Arkan
sas, it would be different.”

JULY FIGURES
BEST SHOWN
DURING YEAR
New High Traffic
Record Expected
in 1926.
For the second month this year
class one railroads of the United
States report earnings on the rate
of making property investment of
over 6 per cent, July earnings estab
lishing a record for that month both
in gross revenues and net operating
Income. July figures also are the
highest reported so far this year.
The first 78 carriers and systems
report a total net operating income
for July of $104,850,000, compared
with $85,041,000 for the correspond
ing month last year, an inrcease of
$19,809,000. In June of this year
these same roads had a net of $96,-
664,000.
Show 6.4 Per Cent Gain.
On the basis of roads so far re
porting the aggregate July net for
all class one carriers should approxi
mate $122,000,000, compared with an
actual net of $99,402,735 for the cor
responding month last year, and
$107,335,054 for June of this year.
Such results would represent July
earnings at the annual seasonal rate
Of 6.61 per cent on the rate making
valuation taken at $21,175,000,000 at
the close of 1925. This compares
with a rate of 5.56 per cent in July,
1925, on a valuation of $20,500,000,-
000 at the close of 1924, and a rate
of 6.18 per cent in June of this year.
Gross revenues of the reporting
roads aggregate $490,934,000, com
pared with $461,473,000 a year ago,
an increase of 6.4 per cent.
Sees New Record.
On the basis of the net operating
Income for July, as estimated above,
the net for the first seven months
of the present year will approximate
$616,800,000, this being at the an
nual rate of return of 5.76 per cent
on the valuation, compared with an
actual net of $537,165,541, or an an
nual rate of 5.19 per cent for the
corresponding period last yepr, and
5.57 per cent shown for the first
half of this year.
It also appears likely that this
^ear will set a new high record in
traffic. (Railroad mi& predict there
will be at least 27 “million car”
Weeks, thereby' bettering last year’s
record of 20 such weeks. The esti
mate is gained by adding the 1,000,-
000-car weeks to date this year to
the number recording in the remain
ing period of last year.
New Scheme for
Focusing Headlights
ST. AUGUSTINE, Fla. A new
taethod of adjusting headlights on
automobiles which obviates the
•icessity of waiting for darkness
has been put in operation here.
Working on the principle that if
the lamp in the headlight is proper
ly focused the light beams from it
will travel in parallel lines, two
steel plates, with a circle of small
holes bored in them, are mounted
parallel to each other, eight inches
apart oh .the headlights.
If the beams of light which pass
through the holes register upon the
holes of the outer plate as viewed
upon its inner surface, the head
lights are in focus.

AUGUST MEAT
TRADE BETTER,
REPORT SHOWS
CHICAGO—A review of the live
stock and meat situation during the
month just closed, issued today by
the Institute of American Meat
Packers, states in part:
“Conditions in the wholesale meat
trade during the month closed to
day showed some improvement as
compared with the preceding month.
Trade in pork products lagged dur
ing the first part, but later showed
substantial improvement. The beef
trade, which also was rather dull
during the first part, improved
toward the close.
“A feature of interest in the fresh
pork trade was the widening of the
price difference between light and
heavy loins to the point where the
heavy loins wholesaled at only about
half the price of the lightest.
“Picnics, especially those of heav
ier weight, declined substantially,
and the demand is improving at the
lower prices. Picnics weighing
from 8 to 10 pounds are wholesaling
now for about half the price per
pound of skinned hams weighing
from 14 to 16 pounds.
Since September and October are
months in which the consumption of
picnics ordinarily is largest, the
present market situation should be
of timely interest to consumers.
“The export trade in pork prod
ucts was of fair dimensions for this
season of the year. The lard trade
was of fair proportions for this
period of the year.”
Too Many Books,
Too Many Graves,
LONDON, England There are
too many books and too many
graves in the world, says Prof. J. F.
Thorpe, F. R. S., organic chemistry
expert.
“Civilization appears to be con
fronted with two ever-growing prob
lems —the increase in its cemeteries
and in its libraries” —the professor
declared in his presidential address
to the chemistry section of the Brit
ish association at Oxford. “The
former, no doubt, will be solved by
cremation. Is it too much to hope
that a judicious exercise of this
method may also be applied to our
libraries?” Prof. Thorpe asked in
the course of his address. “When it
is remembered,” he added, “that
there are some 23,000 scientific
periodicals published throughout
the world, the mind stanils appalled
at the prospects which will confront
civilization even in so short a time
as 100 years.
“The space occupied by our ever
increasing libraries must cause
alarm to those who contemplate the
possibilities of the future.”
School Books to
Contain U. S. Flag
TOPEKA, Kan. Every pupil in
the public schools of Kansas will
see Old Glory daily next winter,
even if the school may be too poor
to buy a new flag.
The first page of each of the
1,000,000 volumes published at the
state printing plant this year will be
devoted to a picture of the Amer
ican flag. The picture appeared in
several editions of state texts last
year, but it will be found in every
book this year.
Insertion of a full-page reproduc
tion of the flag in colors was sug
gested to the state printer by the
Americanization committee of the
Kansas American legion.

Save Norman Abbey,
Americans Plead
MALMESBURY, England—What
remains of Malmesbury abbey, an
historic Norman ruin, now serves as
the parish church of this village, a
flourishing commercial center in the
middle ages. The ruin is in need of
immediate repairs, if the structure
is to be saved. The parish is too
poor to bear the expense and the
vicar has inade an appeal to Amer
icans, as the neighborhood is closely
associated with the history of the
Washingtons. Lawrence Washing
ton was one of the two members of
parliament-elected from Malmesbury
in 1661.

BEAN VITALITY
IS MEASURED
CHICAGO —Having succeeded in
measuring the vitality of hundreds
of unsprouted bean seeds by means
of a delicate vibratory machine, Dr.
Lulu F. McManis and other mem
bers of the American Electronic Re
search Assn, are making tests of
other plant life with the aim of
placing agricultural planting on a
more scientific basis, it was an
nounced today by Dr. E. E. Murphy,
secretary of the department of edu
cation of the association.
Seed experiments are now be’.ng
carried on with wheat, corn and
oats. Agricultural colleges and as
sociations are watching the tests
with keen interest.
Dr. McManis, who is credited with
original research work in seed se
lection, tests only one seed at a
time, but hopes eventually to evolve
some means of selection on a quan
tity basis, thus making the method
commercially practicable.
The tests are being carried on
with the aid of an Abrams diag
nostic machine, originally developed
to measure the vibration given oiT
by diseased tissue in humans. Work
ing on the accepted scientific theory
that everything in nature gives off
its own specific rate of vibration,
Dr. McManis dissected some un
sprouted bean seeds and measured
their vibrations, thus getting the
key to their vitality or energy.
Further data on the seed experi
ments, will be given at the annual
convention of the association in Chi
cago beginning Sept. 19.

British Steel, Iron
Show Effects of
Coal Situation
LONDON —Many trades in Great
Britain have carried on with con
spicuous success despite the strike,
but statistics for July emphatically
confirm all that has been said as to
the disastrous effect upon the iron
and steel trades.
In April the high iron output was
539,100 tons, reduced in May to
88,000 tons, in June to 41,800 tons
and in July to 17,900 tons. At the
end of last month only eight fur
naces were in operation against 147
on the eve of the stoppage.
The figures for steel ingots and
castings are not quite so bad, prob
ably because a certain number of
electric furnaces have been making
steel. In April the output under
this head was 681,000 tons, in May
45,700 tons, in June 34,500 tons and
in July 32,100 tons.

in Paris, it was suggested that the
members of the team could be given
first class cabins. This, however,
would mean that the team would
have to be held to the bare minimum
and the number of officials and
coaches would have to be reduced in
the same proportion or it would take
the Leviathan to keep them all sat
isfied.

Here’s Benny Friedman, all-Amer
ican quarterback 7 in 1925 and cap
tain of this year’s University of

team. The Wol
verines had won
derful success on

enny will be

uff again aug
urs well for the

A brief account of the first half
minute of the Michigan-Wisconsin
game at Madison last October will
give you an idea of Friedman’s ca
pabilities. Doyle Harmon kicked off
for the Badgers and it was Michi
gan’s ball on its own 40-yard line.
Wisconsin naturally expected a run
ning play, but they didn’t know the
Wolverine quarterback.
Benny took the ball from center in
a short punt formation and shot a
30-yard pass to Gregory, who ran
the remainding 30 yards to a touch
down. Friedman then kicked the
goal for the extra point, and Doyle
Harmon kicked off again—this time
right into the hands of Bennie
Friedman. All Benny did was to
run 80 yards through the whole
Badger team for a touchdown and
then kick the goal! And just 37
seconds of play had elapsed! Wis
consin was getting acquainted with
Benny now.
That’s the way it went all year,
with Friedman probably having a
hand in more touchdowns than any
other player in the country. Only
in the Northwestern game, which
was played under the most adverse
weather conditions, did he fail to
play bang-up football. As a field
general, this 20-year-old lad is un
surpassed. Coach Yost is praying
that some day he will get another
one like him.

wallop heavy enough to rock Jack
Dempsey to sleep and take away his
heavyweight crown, is a matter of
discussion, but there is no denying
that Gene carts away all the honors
of a screen actor when "stacked
against the champ.

ously in his screen serial, which was
filmed by Pathe and is now show
ing at the Empress. There is at
least one knockout per reel in the
Tunney film, The Fighting Marine,
and while there is some loving in
which Gene figures as the heavy
sweetheart of Marjorie Gay, the
film unwinds for 20.000 feet with
the runner-up for the heavy crown
doing a kissing act just once, and
that in the final reel.
Gene likes to use his fists and not
his lips and therefore he cut all but
one kiss from the film. However,
he fights for the girl and cuddles
her—and to say the least Gene is a
“hot lover” and a rip roaring fightei
—even though he starts the film as
a newspaper reporter out for ad
venture, which he finds in the ma
rines.

race. The world champions were
completely stopped by Bill Sherdel

discarded to the minors at least a
dozen times this summer, had the
honor of pitching Rogers Hornsby’s
outfit into the lead. Starting his
second game of the season, his first
since last April 30, he held the
Pirates to three hits.

hoisted them into the lead with a
rally in the seventh. Bottomley
opened the seventh with a walk and
Bell sacrificed. Hafey’s single to
right put Bottomley across with the
tying run. O’Farrell singled to
right, sending Hafey to third, and
Thevenow slammed a line single to
center, scoring Hafey with the win
ning and first place run.
The Cardinals routed Lee Mead
ows with a base hit shower in the
opening game. Les Bell featured it
with his 16th home run in the third
inning with one on. Chick Hafey
also hit into the left field seats. The
only run against Sherdel was Cuy
ler’s homer into the bleachers.

As Carson Brooks shaved that
evening, preparatory, to dining
with Mr. Bigelow, he found his
hand unsteady and he was tired.
It was the natural let-down from
the high tension to which his
nerves had been tuned during the
exciting weeks that the Vannah
case had occupied him. He guessed
that the firm was about to offer
him some reward.
And yet Brooks found himself
dissatisfied with himself. It was
true that the Vannah case was a
completed episode so far as the
Interest of the office was con
cerned. But what about his in
terests?
Mr. Bigelow greeted him with
warm and unaffected cordiality at
the club and Carson found him
self seated opposite his employer
at a quiet table tucked away in
an alcove of the grill room.
The dinner was excellent and
Mr. Bigelow’s hospitality alto
gether charming. The men talked
as friends, as intimates, and with
out suggestion that they were em
ployer and a hired drudge, for the
life of a law clerk at $25 a week
is conceded by the employer and
the employe to be a turn at
drudgery. It is the dull and tire
some apprenticeship of a shrewd
profession.
“My boy, I’m not going to tell
you any further how delighted I
am with your success in the Van
nah business,” said Mr. Bigelow
beaming. “I'm proud of you and
I’ve been wondering all day what
there is I can do for you by way
of a deserved re Ward.”
Carson grinned appreciatively
and renewed his attack on the filet
mignon Marsellaise before him.
“I’m not looking for any re
ward, Mr. Bigelow’,” he said boy
ishly. “I would like to have the
lawyers around town know that I
had something to do with the case,
though—it would help me get a
name.”
“That’s what I’m getting at,
Brooks,” agreed Mr. Bigelow*.
“I want to keep you with us,
but you know we are a small
office and for twenty years a man
aging clerk has been all we’ve
needed. It was in our office that
John Wellington started as a
clerk at $lO a week. That was
more than 15 years ago And
now, I daresay Wellington’s
smallest fee would be SIOO,OOO.
Yes, there is great opportunity
for you but I swear I can’t make
up my mind whether it lies in our
Armor elsewhere.”
Carson Brooks, at the moment,
felt that he would be satisfied to
remain under the mentorship of
this splendid, kindly old counsel
lor for the rest of his life, the old
boy seemed so genuinely proud of
him.
“I’m sure I’d rather stay with
you,” he said positively.
“Thank you, Brooks,” said the
old man quietly. “Well, then let
us say that for the balance of the
year you shall receive SSO
a week. I believe that after the
New Year there will be some
change in the partnership. Judge
Frost has been dead a great many
years now and I doubt if his name
should continue to be used. It
doesn’t seem quite fair to the
judge.” The blue smoke
ascended from the tip of his cigar
in curious curls and he watched
them intently. He was brought to
himself by the appearance of a
silver urn of coffee. “Perhaps
you might become a partner next
year.”

pulled himself up a rung on the

taking a pint of water/with a tea
spoonful of salt dissolved in it each
morning half an hour before break
fast, in a case of rheumatism? (F.

Answer—lt is a healthful habit to
drink a pint or less of water on rising

vise you to omit the salt. The reason
for the remarkable benefits some suf
ferers from illness ascribe to such a
practice Is mainly coincidence —the ill
ness passes while the habit is in
dulged, and sometimes the fact that
this habit insures at least part of the
water which every one should drink

much water as they should. From

required in health. Of course a good
part of this is taken in or with food.

glass of cold water before or in the
course of each meal, between meals,

The Hot Fire Fly.
The children were eager to
hear the stories the Silent Twins
had to tell. And the Silent Twins
were just as eager to tell the

cide which should begin first.
Then Jack hit upon a plan.
“Why not run a race?”>he sug
gested. “The one who crosses the
mark first shall tell the first
story.”
The twins agreed to this. Jack
and Clyde marked out a course.
Janet started the race. “One, two,
three Go!” she cried.
Away went the twins at the
very same instant. They raced
along side by side. Their stride
was as regular as that of sol
diers on parade. Each stride
took them an equal distance, and
each stride was taken at the same
time. They crossed the mark
with their noses even.
“Try again,” said Jack., And
now he had another scheme. He
whispered it to Clyde.
And so when the Silent Twins
raced again, and went on their
way stride for stride, Clyde
bumped into Ronald and delayed
him. At the same time Jack gave
Roland a push and sent him
across the winning mark.
“Hurrah 1” shouted .Ronald, not
getting a bit angry at having his
brother win in this way. “Roland
shall tell the first story.”

fierce as darkness falls, possibly
because they are cowardly like
wolves and like to prowl in the
dark.
“But there is one bird that
doesn’t go to bed with the others.
It is Squeaky Night Hawk. He
is fond of mosquitoes—not in a

Lucretia Goddard Bush, 17, daughter of Henry S. Bush,
Boston banker, will make her debut in opera, Oct. 1, at the

Chorus Girl Suing
Irish Baronet
Alice Harris, chorus girl, has filed
a SIOO,OOO breach of promise suit in
Chicago against Sir Maurice Fitz
gerald, Irish baronet
“I met Sir Maurice in Montreal in
1923,” Miss Harris explained. ‘’He
courted me violently took me to
parties and cabarets and finally pro
posed marriage. He said he was
suing his wife for divorce and would
marry me as soon as a decree was
granted. But the decree seemed a
long time in coming.”
Miss Harris said that as a pledge
of his good faith, Sir Maurice gave
her a ring which had been a family
heirloom for three centuries. The
ring would have been awfully good
evidence in the suit, she said, but
unfortunately she lost it Monday.

Berlin newspapers, commenting on
the visit of Geraldine Farrar, recall

former royal opera house and tne
many rumors that connected her
name with that of the former crown
prince. Miss Farrar made the trip
from Munich to Berlin by airplane,
accompanied by her father and a
woman friend.
