Mary Pickford Does Not Smoke.
In an interview she gave yester
day to Chicago newspaper men,
Mary Pickford disclosed that she
does not smoke cigarets because she
has never felt the need of it. Pola
Negri’s grief over Valentino ap
peared very real, Miss Pickford
said. Douglas Fairbanks attended
to business affairs while his wife
toured the city. They left for
Hollywood last night.
Patsy Ruth Miller Victim of
Breakdown.
Due to a nervous breakdown,
Patsy Ruth Miller was not able to
report for work on What Happened
to Father, which was scheduled to
commence this week at the War
ner Bros, studio in Hollywood.
Work on the production has been
postponed until later in the season.
Miss Miller has been working stead
ily for the past several months in
So This Is Paris, Broken Hearts
of Hollywood and as the female lead
with George Jessel in Private Izzy
Murphy. After a complete rest,
Miss Miller will return to work.
Eddie Lyons Dead.
Eddie Lyons, of the team of
of Lyons and Moran, motion
picture comedians, died last
night in the Bishop sanitarium,
Pasadena, Calif. Lyons was a na
tive of Beardstown, 111. He left his
home town when 17 years old as a
“barnstormer.” His first big part
was in Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage
Patch, played in the old Marlowe
theater, Chicago.
No “Hell” for English Actress.
May Moore Duprez, English ac
tress, was given an ovation last
night in a London theater when she
circumvented the expression, “You
go to hell,” called for by the
script, with a polite, “You may go
wherever you like.” Press agents
had worked the audience up to a
state of expectancy, announcing
that the actress had declared she
would not say the word.
Open Production on Biblical Film
With Ceremony.
Representatives of 10 different re
ligious faiths gathered the other
day at the Cecil de Mille studio,
Culver City, Calif., to participate
in a ceremony preceding the opening
of production on The King of Kings,
a film designed to picture the life
of Christ. H. B. Warner, English
actor, portrays the title role in this
production, while Jacqueline Logan,
as Mary Magdalene: Joseph Schild
kraut, as Judas; Rudolph Schild
kraut as Caiaphas, and Ernest Tor
rence as Peter are other prominent
players in the cast.
Mountain Girl of
South in Movie
Only the primitive people of the
mountain fastnesses of the south
appear in Stark Love, a picture
which Famous Players-Lasky an
nounces for release.
A 16-year-old mountain girl, Helen
Mundy, played the principal femi
nine role, and a young man, Forrest
James, the male lead.
There are no feuds, no revenue of
ficers, no handsome stranger from
the city. It is a story based on con
flict between father and son for the
love of a girl.
Most of the picture was made in
the mountains of North Carolina at
a point 130 miles from 21sheville.
Automobiles could go as far as Rob
binsville, N. C., which was 12 miles
from a railroad. Horses and mules
were used to go another 14 miles
in the mountains. To make the lo
cation accessible, three weeks were
spent in blasting rocks. In this
work the mountaineers refused to
lend assistance, and the laborers
were guarded by two deputy sheriffs
to protect them in case of a hostile
demonstration.
Walthall in De Mille Picture.
Henry B. Walthall has been
signed for a featured role In A
Fighting Love, which will star Jetta
Goudal at the De Mille studio un
der the direction of Nils Olaf Chris
ander, Swedish director. Chrisan
der, who hails from the old UFA
where at one time he was Pola Ne
gri’s leading man and later director
general of the Berlin plant, makes
his American directorial debut on
this production. Victor Varconi,
who scored so convincingly in The
Volga Boatman, will play the male
lead in support of Miss Goudal.

and others of various shapes and
sizes. They are light in weight,
but large enough to really build
small houses, and other structures
that the children plan.

THE LUSCIOUS PEACH.
No more delicious dish for dessert
can be served than one of sliced
peaches with cream and sugar.
When peaches are plentiful one likes
to vary the method of serving.
A most appetizing pie may be
made by baking a rich crust and
when cold fill it with sliced peaches
well sugared; cover with sweet
ened cream, whipped.
A bird’s nest pudding Is another
way of serving a peach pudding.
Slice the peaches (those not too
ripe may be used for this dish),
cover with a rich biscuit batter and
bake. Turn out inverted on a large
plate, sprinkle with sugar, dot with
butter ^nd a sprinkling of nutmeg if
liked and serve cut into pie-shaped
pieces.

cupful of dry bread crumbs and
let stand five minutes; add half
a cupful of sugar, the well-beaten

Heap thinly sliced peaches well
sweetened over the top and cover
with a meringue made of two egg
whites and three tablespoonfuls of

Peaches With Rice.
Cook one cupful of rice until ten
der, adding milk at the last of the
cooking; season with butter, add
sugar to sweeten, then pour into a
hollow mold. When ready to serve
unmold and fill the center with
sweetened sliced peaches. Serve
with sugar and cream.
Peach Chutney.
Peel three pounds of peaches, put
them into a saucepan with a pint
of mild vinegar, cook until tender.
Pound in a mortar four ounces of
onion, two ounces of garlic, five
ounces of fresh ginger root; add the
peaches, six ounces of raising, one
ounce each of white mustard seed
and chilipeppers, and six ounces of
sugar. Simmer for 10 miniites, add
ing more vinegar if needed. Bottle
for winter use. This is especially
well liked by the English, though
they use apple instead of peaches.—
Nellie Maxwell.
Fruit Salad Dressing.
One-quarter cup of pineapple
juice, cup lemon juice, 2 eggs,
cup sugar, 1 cup whipped cream.
Beat eggs, add sugar, pineapple and
lemon juice. Cook in double boiler,
stirring until thick, then set aside
to cool. Whip the cream and »tir
into mixture just before serving.
This dressing is lovely with a
fruit salad, which may be served
either for luncheon or as a dessert
for dinner when the men of the
house do not care for a regular des
sert.
Watermelon Sherbet.
One tablespoon gelatine, one
fourth cup cold water, four cups hot
water, two cups water, one cup or
ange juice, two cups watermelon
cubes. Soak gelatine in cold water
for five minutes. Make syrup by
boiling hot water and sugar 10 min
utes and add soaked gelatine and
orange juice. Strain, chill and
freeze to a mush. Then add water
melon cubs and let stand one hour.

State Tax Boost
Reported By Kearney
In answer to Gov. Blaine’s conten
tion that taxes are relatively no
higher than they have previously
been, Thomas AI. Kearney, Demo
cratic candidate for United States
senator, at the South Side armory
last night showed the following in
creases in the expenses of state de
partments, commissions and bureaus
since 1900:
Departments headed by attorney
general, 700 per cent; department of
agriculture, 5,000 per cent; tax com
mission, 2,000 per cent; industrial
commission, 1,500 per cent; health
department, 2,500 per cent; dairy
and food departments, 1,000 per
cent; railroad commission, 3,000 per
cent; conservation commission, 500
per cent; state board of control, 500
per cent, and library commission,
1,000 per cent.
Air. Kearney reminded his hearers
that Wisconsin as a state was or
ganized by the Democratic party in
1849, and that less than 25 appoint
ive offices were allowed in state
government then. He said that now
5,000 such appointments are made
by the governor or the men he has
set at heads of state departments.

a communique signed by the min
ister of the interior which said that
4,000 houses had been destroyed and
that many families were without
food, in and about Horta. The dam
age was likely to amount to “mil
lions of dollars.”

out the island of Fayal and with
special violence in Horta, according
to the communique. “The popula

tetanus had been taken by the local
government.

nounced that almost the entire city

itance taxes led by Secretary of the
Treasury Andrew W. Mellon, was
voiced by Atty. Gen. Herman L.
Ekern, the Progressive Republican
candidate for the gubernatorial
nomination, in a speech nere today.
Ekern declared that “there is no
more ju§t tax than the Income tax
and the inheritance tax.” He as
serted that he favored such “ad
justment of the taxes as will give
the greatest possible reduction in
taxes upon the property of the home
owners, farms and other property
which now bears a disproportionate
burden when income returns from
the property are taken into ac
count.”
The attorney general cited the
wiping out of $5,000,000 of 1925
state taxes upon property as the
result of the tax law passed by the
last legislature as an instance of
fair tax adjustment and reduction.
He pledged himself to a continuance
of the policy of reducing property
taxes.

Long Island, N. Y.,
Has Horse Thief
HEMPSTEAD, L. I.—There is a
horse thief on Long Island. When
Edward Wilson reported the loss
of his horse to police headquarters
here old-timers in the department
scanned the records and found that
it was 15 years since a horse was
stolen here. Nothing but automo
biles now, they said.
There was a time, though, when
truck farmers hauled all their sup
plies all the way to New York in
carts and wagons. In those days
horse thefts were not as infrequent.
But there is a hor.se missing now.
Wilson’s white horse, with a star in
its forehead, disappeared from Wil
son’s stable recently and no trace
of it has been found.
Bedbug Battle ‘Hero 9
Mounts His Victims
TOPEKA, Kan.—A bottle of bed
bugs, mounted and stuffed, has been
added to the collection of Flora and
Fauna of the State of Kansas, by an
irate traveling salesman, who had
been stopping at a western Kansas
hotel.
When the bugs interfered with
his slumbers, the salesman caught
and bottled them and sent them as a
present to State Hotel Commissioner
Phil Zimmerman, to be added to the
Kansas collection.
“Travelers need state aid to bat
tle these fierce animals.” was the
comment that accompanied the do
nation.

A FORECAST BASED ON FACTS
When Annie Besant makes forecasts of the future
along lines wherein we are not informed, we treat her
views with the respect due to one who has done a great
deal for forward-looking ideas—as witness our remark^
on Krishnamurti—but when she speaks of the past and
praises Woodrow Wilson, she enters into a field where we
are better posted than she is.
According to a Chicago paper stye said in an address
that two great examples of peace, brotherhood and inter
nationalism were Abraham Lincoln and Woodrow Wilson.
Of the latter she said, “But he will be honored by genera
tions hence who will live in a time when war will be
outlawed.”
On the contrary he will be execrated by generations
hence—provided they execrate anybody, and provided they
know the truth about Wilson.
He led the United States into an unnecessary war
which cost this country the lives of more than a hundred
thousand youths. It also cost this country directly and
indirectly not less than one hundred billions of dollars.
It also prevented the “peace without victory” concerning
which Wilson had prated, and brought on the frightful
condition in which Europe has found itself since the war.
Where is the peace, brotherhood and internationalism in
all this?
During the war, Wilson fathered the conscription of
men to fight. He also fathered a most infamous espionage
act under which thousands of peace-loving citizens were
hounded, and many of them arrested and sent to prison.
Conscientious objectors were persecuted. Everyone who
worked for peace was considered a traitor. Newspapers
that stood for peace were persecuted and many of them
utterly destroyed. Where is the peace, brotherhood and
internationalism in this?
At the close of the war Wilson went to Paris carrying
with him 14 high-sounding, but largely meaningless points.
At Paris, he allowed the wolf and the tiger to flatter him
into relinquishing all the good he stood for, and the tragic
“peace” of Versailles was the result. Where is the peace,
brotherhood and internationalism in this?
It is hardly probable that future generations will be
ignorant of these things—and if they are not ignorant of
them, their opinion of Woodrow Wilson will be quite the
opposite of that which Mrs. Besant thinks. This forecast
of ours is based on facts. It cannot go astray unless the
people of the future admire bad judgment, vanity, egotism,
tyranny and warfare. If the people of the future are as
good as, or better than, the people of the present, our pre
diction will unerringly be fulfilled. It will certainly be
fulfilled if future generations “live in a time when war
will be outlawed.”
HELP THE BRITISH MINERS
The British mine owners and their governmental sup
porters are brutally trying to starve the miners into sub
mission. Baldwin gives out the statement that there is no
suffering among the miners, in an effort to keep Americans
from contributing to their support. Ramsay MacDonald
says the opposite—and we know which of them to believe.
When a conference between the owners and the rep
resentatives of the men took place a short time ago, the
owners merely asked the men if they were ready to sur
render. Of course no negotiations can be had on that
basis. The owners also felt encouraged because they found
the men hungry when they gave them tea before the con
ference.
Isn’t it a wonderful system where bloated owners are
gratified to find the workers*hungry? The miners and the
Labor party would eliminate the useless private owners if
they could, and have the mines owned by the nation. The
winning of the present strike, while it probably would not
result automatically in public ownership, would neverthe
less help vastly in gaining that object.
The dispatches say that the miners watch eagerly for
the reports of aid coming from other countries, and that
they cheer these reports.
This shows they need the money for the support of
their wives, their children and themselves, while holding
out. It shows also that they realize the international soli
darity of labor.
Do we realize it as much as they? Do we realize that
an injury to one is an injury to all? Do we realize that
a defeat for the British miners would be a defeat for
labor everywhere?
The American Federation of Labor is doing one of the
most admirable things it has ever done, in gathering funds
to aid this strike. Milwaukee labor is always at the head
of the procession, and it must keep at the head by contrib
uting generously for this cause. Send contributions to
Frank J. Weber, Secretary Federated Trades Council, 302
Brisbane Hall.
RIDICULOUS JOURNALISM
At the Valentino funeral, arcording to the papers,
Mary Pickford sobbed and wore a small black straw hat,
a black georgette, a white lace collar, and a string of
pearls. Other stars wept and wore clothes not quite so
well inventoried. Why didn’t the papers say Douglas
Fairbanks sobbed and wore a coat and vest and trousers?
They missed a great opportunity to make journalism
more absurd than it already is.

ness and make political enemies of former allies.
Baker excoriates the folly that first imposes a heavy
tribute on friend and foe and then puts every obstacle
in the way of their ability to pay the tribute. He is also
outspoken against the silly heads who continually demand
the political and economic isolation of the United States
in the day of universal international relations.
“In the modern world, industrial nations are so in
tegrated, by mutual investment and by trade relations,
that political isolation is an illusion,” Baker writes.
“The overseas investments of the people of the
United States now aggregate perhaps eleven billions of
dollars and we are investing annually overseas at the rate
of a billion a year. v
“As this goes on, our interest in world peace becomes
more and more insistent. Where our treasure is there
our hearts will be.
“We can maintain the form of political isolation but
the fact is that we are daily becoming not merely en
tangled, but interwoven economically into the world
fabric.
“Our enormous wealth demands this avenue of op
portunity, our industries must have access to the raw ma
terials of the world, our producers must have a world
market, and these necessities are of reciprocal advantage
to us and to the rest of the world.”
And again: “Every country in the world has had
the experience of a vast and hopeless debtor class and has
realized that every so often it is necessary to wipe off the
slate and start afresh as in the scriptural year of the
Jubilee. This releases the energies of men, restores hope,
cures political disorder and gives life a fresh start. The
anology applies perfectly to the present international
situation.”
So far, so good. It has taken Baker eight years to
see what we predicted in 1917, before Baker’s boss took ua
into the World war and wasted American lives and money.
The remorse comes a little too late, but it is better than
the stubborn folly of certain old party statesmen who still
nurse the war mentality and war stupidity.
Nevertheless, Baker and his friends have a lot more
to learn. We will continue to predict, as we have her
tofore, that in those respects in which our hundredX
centers are still stubborn, they will also follow in the ste^.
of The Leader by and by.
It is all right to cancel the allied war debts and reduce
German payments under the Dawes plan. But it is not
enough. The mass of the American wage workers, farm
ers and little business people will still have to bear
Europe’s unpaid war burdens after Baker’s plan has been
adopted. The American and European consumers will
still face increased production with decreased buying
power.
It is all right to admit that America is economically
interwoven with the rest of the world, but it is a long way
from this admission to that reciprocity which will permit
Europe to do over here what American government agents
do in Europe. It is still a long way from that economic
conference of nations which will lead to real international
co-operation.
The House of Morgan has learned only a small part
of its lesson. It needs statesmen with an international
outlook, but the American people need statesmen that will
do for them what the old parties have so far done only for
Morgan.
The cancellation of the Versailles treaty and Dawes
plan will be futile, until it is followed by a cancellation
of the private banker’s power over the public life. We
predict that this, too, will come in due time and that the
Morgan policies will hasten its coming.
EUROPE STANDS PAT
Georges Clemenceau, the Tiger, gloats over his letter
to President Coolidge and repeats that France will never
accept a Dawes plan for itself. Dictator Mussolini tells
the big bankers the same thing for Italy. They want to
raise new loans for the French and Italian governments
and know that they will have to keep this up indefinitely.
They want the public debts cancelled, but nobody has th
courage to tell them that even most of their private clairft.
on Europe will have to be cancelled sooner or later.
Europe stands pat for the present on its refusal to
pay tribute till the year 2,000 on public debts to America.
In a little while the big European governments will also
tell Wall Street that private debts to America must be
cancelled. But that will not prevent British and French
bankers from insisting that Soviet Russia must acknowl
edge its obligation to pay Kerensky’s war debts and the
private loans made through unofficial channels.
A change is coming soon, however. The middle and
working classes over there will start a new deal. The
American middle and working classes will follow the
European example.

CHICAGO—The middle west—
that section which includes central
Illinois, lowa and Nebraska —today
was checking up the loss from the
heaviest rains of the season.
One man was killed and two
others injured in the storms. Eve
rett Dent was struck by lightning
while at work near Valley, Neb., and
killed. A fellow workman was in
jured. Another man was injured
in Omaha, when lightning struck a
power house.
Rains Are Heavy.
The rains, starting 24 hours ago,
averaged from two to eight inches.
In some places the rains reached
near cloudburst proportions.
Galesburg, near Peoria, received
the most serious damage' from the
storm. Railroad tracks were washed
out, rivers and small creeks left
their banks, streets were flooded
and many basements filled with
water.
Earlier reports of many persons
being homeless in this district were
denied today at Galesburg Many
families were marooned for several
hours yesterday following an eight
inch rain, but were able to return to
their homes later.

Railroads in the vicinity of Gales
burg and Peoria were the heaviest
losers. It was impossible to check
up on the damage, but estimates
placed it at between $500,000 and
$1,000,000 in each of the cities.
Trains in Nebraska were operated
on slow schedules and trans-conti
nental tourist trains were forced to
re-route 150 miles through Sioux
City and Ames, la., in order to
reach Omaha.
Three washouts were reported
near Vail. Neb., while several others
were reported from north of there.

STILL IN COMA
MARTINSVILLE, Ind.—The con
dition of United States Senator Wil
liam B. McKinley of Illinois who

night last night, remained un
changed today, according to his
physician, Dr. R. P. Egbert. Dr.

ability to survive the attack of
rheumatism from which the senator
has been suffering since Aug. 18 at
a sanitarium here.
After rallying late yesterday

sive periods of depression greatly
weakening him and attendants
feared that his heart would be un
able to withstand the strain.

abled him to survive the night, the
doctors said. McKinley had spent
hours in the gymnasium and on the
golf links during his 22 years in
Washington as congressman and
senator.

nomic independence by the Filipinos

withdrawing from the islands, but

ippine islands we want independ

Camels Lived in
Florida 1,000,000
Years Ago, Belief
WASHINGTON—A camel that
lived in Florida 1,000,000 years ago,
more or less, and that is different
from any other branch of the camel
tribe, is at last about to be christ
ened. This nameless orphan was
discovered at Melbourne, Fla., re
cently by Dr. J. W. Gidley, curator
of vertebrate paleontology of the na
tional museum.
The bones indicate that the Flor
ida camel had long, slender legs and
should have been a fast runner. It
was a little smaller than the old
world camels and a little larger
than the guanacos of South Amer
ica. Presence of this desert animal
in Florida is taken by Dr. Gidley
as an indication that Florida may
have been more dry and desertlike,
in patches at least, than today.
The new genus of ancient Amer
ican camel is being compared with
fossil bones of other better kown
kinds by the paleontologist. There
have been a number of kinds of
camels in this country as far back
as the eocence period of geological
time, which means 40,000,000 years
or even longer, according to recent
estimates of the earth’s history.
Some of the prehistoric specimens
had long legs and some had short
legs, Dr. Gidley says. Some had
long necks and some short. Some
were like the old-world camels, but
bigger, and some were like strange
little colts, no larger than a big,
long-legged dog.

damaged.

visitations.

houses had been destroyed.

MEXICO CI T Y—President
Calles’ address at the opening of
congress, and a firm statement
issued by the Mexican Episcopate
almost simultaneously, indicate a
deadlock in Mexico’s religious
crisis, observers here said today.
Speaking before congress yes
terday Calles mentioned the tran
quility and progress in the nation,
and emphasized the efforts of the
government to obtain strict com
pliance With the constitution and
laws.
Referring to foreign relations
he justified the oil laws and other
laws which have occasioned diplo
matic correspondence. All legiti
mately acquired foreign rights
would be protected, he said, add
ing that “foreign suggestions are
unnecessary.”
PAUL SMITS, N. Y.—Hope is ex
pressed by the Knights of Colum
bus that the Washington govern
ment can use its good offices under
international law to ameliorate con
ditions in Mexico, but does not ask
intervention, James A. Flaherty of
Philadelphia, supreme knight of the
order, informed President Coolidge
yesterday.
Accompanied by members of his
supreme council, Mr. Flaherty
came to the summer white house to
discuss details of the recent resolu
tion adopted by the knights at Phil
adelphia seeking American govern
ment protection for Catholic
churchmen in Mexico.
The delegation let it be known It
Is not asking the withdrawal of rec
ognition by the United States of the
Calles government or the lifting
of the arms embargo.
Cal Was Kind.
No statement was made on be
half of the president after the con
ference, and there was no indica
tion of a change in his policy of
“hands off” in the religious dispute
Unless American citizens are in
jured in person or property in Mex
ico. Mr. Coolidge was said by the
delegates to have been “most kind
and patient” in hearing their views.
Mr. Flaherty said he brought do
list of outrages against Americans
in Mexico to show the president, ex
plaining that the state department
was intimately in touch with that
phase of the situation.
Mr. Flaherty attributes present
conditions in Mexico to a great ex
tent to policies pursued toward that
country by previous American ad
ministrations. t
Made Stand Plain.
In a formal statement made after
the conference Mr. Flaherty said:
“We made it plain to the presi
dent that the Knights of Columbus
are not seeking for intervention.
However, we did present to the pres
ident the views of the order and en
deavored to make It plain that from
our viewpoint the present situation
in Mexico is the result of the atti
tude by this government as repre
sented by previous administrations
in connection with Mexican affairs,
in that Mr. Calles is the successor
of the Carranza and Obregon re
gimes.
“Carranza owed his position in
Mexican affairs to the support and
co-operation given to him by this
wctfiiment. During the adminis-
-don of Mr. Obregon this govern
uent supplied him with arms and
munitions of war, including mili
tary airplanes, at the same time
placing an embargo,upon the ship
ment and delivery of arms to Mex
ico.
Let Troops Through.
“Also, for the first time in the
history of this government, it per
mitted the transportation and pas
sage of armed military forces of
another government across Amer
ican territory when it permitted
the troops of Obregon to pass from
Nogales to El Paso for the pur
pose of suppressing a revolution.”

CALLES OFFERS
OLIVE BRANCH
ON LAND LAWS
CHICAGO—A disposition to fit
the policy of the government to the
necessities* of all parties affected
by the recent land, oil and religious
laws, should experience show a
change necessary, was the outstand
ing feature of President Calles’ mes
sage to the Mexican congress last
night, says a copyrighted dispatch
from Mexico City to The Tribune.
The president reiterated the state
ment made on previous occasions of
his determination to uphold the con
stitution, laws and dignity of the
nation, but asserted a willingness
to change even the constitution
should experience and necessity call
for that.
Referring to the oil situation, the
president said that after represen
tations on the part of the United
States government and diplomatic
crossfiring the question finally has
reached a point where all parties
apparently are satisfied.
A Diplomatic Controversy.
“The promulgation of laws and
regulations thereof concerning pe
troleum caused diplomatic repre
sentations by the United States gov
ernment, originating in a contro
versy of a diplomatic chaiacter, in
which the American government
submitted statements showing that
interests of American citizens in
Mexico have been injured and
asked for modification of some of
the provisions of the law,” President
Calles said.
“Tae Mexican government an
swered by sustaining the right to
issue said laws and regulations, not
only because the regulations were
ordered by the constitution, but be
cause their enactment and enforce
ment could not affect rights legit
imately acquired.
“My government has followed the
policy of its predecessors in power.
It was necessary to define precisely
our right to legislate and protect
the interests of our country
“If in practice, however, the gov
ernment should find the application
of these laws does not conform
to its policy and to the attitude and
aims of Mexico, or if experience
suggests modifications in accord
ance with justice and equity, the
president will initiate such modifi
cations in accordance with the con
stitution.”
Church “Needlessly Alarmed.”
Senor Calles devoted much time
to the church situation.
“The palpitating question which
has aroused the interest of foreign
countries out of all proportion to
what has been done in our country
has been created by the clergy,
which has always been rebellious
against the institutions of the re
public,” he said. “Seizing a moment
which they thought propitious for
their ends, the priests have dis
avowed the constitution and the
laws based thereon regulating the
exercise of religion.
“There is nothing at the bottom
of the so-called religious problem.
Neither your president nor the de
partment of the interior made
changes which should alarm
churches and congregations. Ar
ticle 130 of the constitution and the
reform laws had only the appear
ance of a declaration of principles
and were without expression of co
ercive measures.”

CZECHS, SLOVAKS
URGED TO MAKE
USE OF BALLOT
Declaring that one of the greatest
privileges which any foreign-born
citizen acquires with his second
American citizenship papers is that
of taking a hand in choosing the of
ficers of this country, John V. Kla
bouch, speaking over the radio last
night in behalf of the League of
Women Voters, urged his fellow
Czecho-Slovakians, in their own lan
guage, to go to the polls and vote
during the coming elections.
“You, my fellow countrymen,
came to America to enjoy its per
sonal liberty, better living and work
ing conditions, educational advan
tages for your children and the add
ed privilege of taking a direct part
in choosing your executives. It is
your solemn duty to exercise this
last privilege,” Mr. Klabouch said.
“By the power of your ballot you
help to choose men who either do
or do not represent the ideals of
this nation.”
Mr. Klabouch further urged the
Bohemians of Milwaukee to find
out just what type of men are run
ning for offices, by following the
newspapers, radio and public party
platforms, and the accomplishments
of the men in public office, conclud
ing with this appeals to the Czechs’
innate love of politics:
“You men and women of Masa
ryk’s blood and vision, do not slack
en now, when the need for your
votes is so urgent.”

FEW SAILING
SHIPS REMAIN
ON HIGH SEAS
BY A. W. V. KING.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
SYDNEY Romance went from
the seas, say the old seadogs, with
the deep-sea sailing ships.
If that is so, there is mighty little
romance left to be garnered under
the Red Ensign of the British. There
are now only four British deep-sea
sailing ships—the full-rigged ships
Monkbarns and William Mitchell,
the barque Kilmallie, and the four
masted barque, Garthpool—and all
of them were in Australian ports
within the last year or so.
A fifth, the Garthneill, recently
was sold to an Adelaide firm as a
store ship, after waiting fruitlessly
for eight months in Melbourne for
a cargo.
It was a sad end to a sentimental
journey which had already cost her
owners, the Marine Navigation Co.
of Canada, many thousands of dol
lars.
In May last year she arrived in
England with a cargo of nitrates
from Chile, showing a heavy loss on
her two-years’ voyage round the
world. She was about to be broken
up when her owners yielded to senti
ment and sent her out on a last voy
age. If it did not return a profit,
she was to be broken up, but no
amount of sentiment would procure
her a cargo, and she arrived ii.
Australia, never to return.
The loss of keeping her idle In
commission could not go on forever,
and she was sold for the proverbial
song.
The Garthneill, then the Inver
neill, was launched at Glasgow
(Scotland) in 1895. She paid her
way for more than 20 years, and in
1919 had her greatest fight against
wind and waves. She left Melbourne
in June, 1919, in ballast for Bun
bury, on the southern coast of west
ern Australia, to pick up a cargo of
hardwood for South Africa.
Beaten By Waves.
Seven weeks later a strange
barque was reported off Sydney. It
was the Garthneill, coming back
from a losing fight with the storm
devils of the Great Australian Bight.
After refitting another attempt to
make westing failed. Then the
master, trusting to providence that
the westerly wind would hold, de
cided to take the route via the Horn
and Cape Good Hope in order to
reach Bunbury in time to keep his
charter.
The west wind respected the brave
man in charge of the Garthneill,
and two and a half months after
leaving Sydney, the Garthneill ar
rived at Bunbury, after traveling
nearly round the world to reach a
port barely 2,000 miles from her
starting point.
Since then cargoes have been dif
ficult to secure, and slowly the
Garthneill has dropped out of the
race with progress, a defeated war
rior of the seas.

Wall Street Demands

WASHINGTON —Resumption of
relations with Russia appeared a
step nearer today when it became
known the United States is willing
to talk business with the Soviet on
the debt problem.
In the absence of President Cool
idge and Secretary Kellogg, official
comment was withheld, but it was
learned on high authority that the
United States will receive a mission
from Russia to discuss her debts
and claims, should it materialise.
Big Biz Wants It.
Whether recognition would grow
out of such a meeting was a matter
for conjecture, but the state de
partment all along has held the debt
and claim question to be the main
barrier.
Russian propaganda, which the
government claimed was designed to
undermine American Institutions, Is
no longer in the way, it was in
timated.
“Big business” in Wall Street has
launched a campaign to secure rec,
ognition and now is pouring mil
lions into Russia.
The preliminary conferences, if
held, 'will concern only the debt.
Exceeds Halt Billion.
The Russian debt, private and
public, exceeds half a billion dob
lars. The treasury advanced $192,-
000,000 to the ill-fated Kerensky
government, which with interest
amounts now to $265,000,000.
There are claims of Americans
for about $400,000,000 for property
seized or destroyed, $86,000,000 cf
cardist bonds, an $11,000,000
bond issue by the National City
bank and two by J. P. Morgan Co.
for $75,000,000.
Eight Community
Trout Hatcheries
Acquired By State
MADISON— With six old Wis
consin trout hatcheries each year
turning 15,000,000 speckled trout
into Wisconsin waters, eight new
hatcheries are being developed by
the, state conservation commission
with an additional capacity of be
tween 6,000,000 and 7,000,000, and
prospects are for a greatly en
larged production, Elmer S. Hall,
state conservation commissioner,
announced today.
With the exception of the Han
son hatchery, three miles from St.
Croix Falls, which was leased by
the state last spring for 10 years,
the new hatcheries were given to
the state by the people of local com
munities who are interested in fish
culture.
The new community hatcheries
given to the state for the raising
of trout are located at Westfield,
the Little Langlade county, the
Douglas county, the Crystal Springs
hatchery, Langlade county, the
Stevens Point/ Nekoosa, Marinette
and Sparta hatcheries.
“Wisconsin has 7,000 miles of
trout streams, practically all of
which are expected to be reached
with the new peak production of the
speckled game fish,” Hall declared.
Bread, Water Diet
For Bootleggers Is
Defended By Judge
TEKAMAH, Neb.—County Judge
Orville Chatt, who has come into
national prominence by imposing
bread and water sentences on Ne
braska bootleggers, undertook yes
terday to defend his drastic meas
nres.
“Bootleggers are a bad lot,” he
said; “the worst type of criminal we
have to deal with, and I believe it is
the duty of judges to give them all
the punishment the law allows.”
No prisoners in jail for any other
crime, however heinous, get the
bread and water treatment.
The bootleggers, both farmers,
served seven days of their bread and
water sentence a year ago before
obtaining habeas corpus writs for
an appeal to the supreme court. On
the basis of that experience they
don’t believe they will survive the
two 20-day diets, which are to be
separated by 20 days of regular
prison fare. They view it as a death
sentence.

picnic.

100 DEAD AFTER
8-HOURBATTLE
IN NICARAGUA
MANAGUA, Nicaragua—A severe
defeat is said to have been .inflicted
by government forces on a revolu
tionary force near Coseguina, on
the western coast near the Gulf of
Fonseca.
The battle, described as the
bloodiest of, the present revolution,
lasted eight hours. The government
losses are placed at 60 killed, and
the rebels’ at 40. The number of
wounded has not been determined.
U. S. Gunboat at Scene.
Col. Marcos Potosme of the gov
ernmental forces was made a gen
eral on the battlefield for his ex
ceptional bravery.
On request of Pr6sident Clamorro,
the American gunboat Tulsa started
for Coseguina to take the wounded
to Corinto. Few doctors were at
tached to both sides and it would
require a week or more to carry the
wounded over the mountain trails
to the hospital in the town of Cbi
nandega.

To Sell Ships of
U. S. Fleet Only to
Americans, Claim
NEW YORK—No hasty disposal
of government ships is contemplated,
according to Brig. Gen. A. C. Dal
ton, president of the Emergency
Fleet corporation.
“They will be disposed of to
American flag owners only, as it is
made clear that they must be op
erated by private owners on trade
routes essential to the maintenance
of American overseas commerce,” he
said. “They must be operated un
der the American flag.”
Gen. Dalton yesterday accom
panied T. V. O’Connor, chairman of
the shipping board, to the pier from
which the George Washington of the
United States line sailed for Ply
mouth, Cherbourg, and Bremen. Mr.
O’Connor sailed on the vessel for a
survey of shipping conditions abroad.
Mr. O’Connor, in speaking of the
sale of the ships, said:
“My position is that these vessels
are to be sold only to an American
company under a 10-year guaranty
of operation under the American
flag.”

Leader Special Service.
MEXICO CITY Prof. Beteta
Quintana, in a recent address to the
summer school of the national uni
versity of Mexico, here, told an au
dience composed largely of Ameri
can students that the present trou
ble between the Calles government
and the Catholic hierarchy is due to
an attempt of the latter to evade
the constitution of the nation and
to resist its application to ille
gally held church property.
“Since 1857, all churches, monas
teries, etc., and lands connected with
them have been the property of the
nation,” Prof. Quintana said. “The
government has asked the priests
administering this property to com
ply with the penal code of the con
stitution and to register with the
municipal authorities, so that the
government responsible for national
property may know who are the
direct keepers of it.
Will Uphold the Law.
“Officials and priests of the Ro
man Catholic church have refused
to do this, although the few min
isters of other creeds have com
plied,” Prof. Quintana continued.
“The constitution in Mexico does
not represent the feeling of all the
people in Mexico, but it does rep
resent a century of fighting in Mex
ico. The present government is
obliged to see the constitution re
spected.
“The Catholic clergy were persist
ent. The government, therefore,
could only say: ‘According to the
law, church property belongs to the
nation. If you, the priests in
charge, leave the cathedrals and
chapels, we are obliged to protect
them ourselves in our own way.’
“The municipal authorities then
appointed committees of neighbors,
who, after inventory had been tak
en, guard the churches so that they
may be kept open to the public.”
Indians Are Majority.
The majority of the Mexican peo
ple are Indians with different de
grees of culture than the whites and
mixed races, Prof. Quintana ex
plained. The majority are also
Catholics and don’t want any
other religion. But the various rev
olutions in Mexico have j&rred the
Indians loose from their old ideas.
“Being an Indian in Mexico is
not so much a question of blood as
of standards of civilization,” Prof.
Quintana pointed out. “During
each revolution, more Indians join
the armies, leave their limited tri
bal areas in the mountain fastnesses
and get a better idea of their coun
try’s vastness and wealth.
“In army life, they come in con
tact to a certain extent with mod
ern civilization. Being very adapt
able, they naturally take to the new
ways of life when not forced into
them.”
Races Will Co-operate.
The Indian and other races and
their mixed offspring must all learn
to co-operate in Mexico and adjust
their different civilizations to one
another, Prof. Quintana concluded.
It is part of this adjustment that
the Mexican government is now
forced to take up the challenge of
the temporal power of the Roman
Catholic hierarchy.
Although 90 per cent of the Mex
ican people are Roman Catholics
and do not want the clergy to aban
don them, they are equally deter
mined to back President Calles in
enforcing the national constitution.
Peace in Mexico requires that the
spiritual mission of the church
should not be subordinated to the
attempt of the hierarchy to use the
properties of the church as an as
set for political intrigues.

CHICAGO—Famous Englishmen
today were reading the pages of
The World of William Clossold, to
discover what part they play in
that imaginative world just created
by the novelist, H. G. Wells, says a
copyrighted story reprinted by The
Tribune from The New York Times.
The first book of Mr. Wells’ three
volume novel was published yester
day.
Since Mr. "Wells announced sev
eral months ago his intention of
introducing real people into the
novel the interest in it has been
whetted. Today London newspa
pers devoted columns to the new
book, which, one writer describes

ously outspoken about birth control.

Lenin.

looks upon life in his latest novel

secutiveness of a London or New

“Czarism in New Dress.”

PARIS—Le Quotidien, the organ
of the left wing of the French Radi
cal party, ridicules the eternal cry
for economy witli which every new
premier meets the demands of the
government employes for an adjust
ment of their wages to the rising
cost of living.
This cry for economy has devel
oped a regular ritual through which
every new cabinet has to run re
ligiously, Le Quotidien laughs.
“The bead of the government calls
his cabinet ministers and tells them
emphatically: ‘Gentlemen, each one
of you must cut down the expenses
of his department,’ Le Quotidien
describes the performance.
Ceremonies Don’t Help.
“The ministers ask: ‘Where can
we economize?’ The chief retorts:
‘lt’s up to you. Cut all expenses
that are compatible with the proper
performance of your services.’
“Fine,” comments Le Quotidien.
“All this is necessary is to distin
guish between expenses that are
and that are not necessary for the
proper performance of the minis
terial duties. So one problem
raises another.
“The ministers call their depart
ment chiefs and subchiefs and tell
them emphatically to cut expenses.
These subofficials know the refrain
to this order so well that it does not
excite them at all.
“They smile at each other, then
they cut and grumble and complain
that they are depriving themselves
of vital forces.
Bluff Continues Longer.
“Several months pass,” Le Quoti
dien continues. “The items which
have been cut out of one budget re
appear in the next one, in the shajie
of a fine batch of supplementary
credits.”
Public opinion has learned to see
through this bluff, Le Quotidien
thinks. If any real economies are
desired, the high officials of the
government should realize that they
must understand the practical ways
of achieving them.
The fellows on top don’t know
where the waste is/ They look down
from the top. The waste can be seen
only by looking up from below.
The rank and file of the govern
ment employes know where the
leaks are. These employes need an
improvement of their condition.
The government could easily make
it worth their while to tell the high
erups where the leaks are. But so
long as the high functionaries like
bluff better than performance, noth
ing ca;« come of such antics.

IDEAL KITCHEN
GIVES VISITORS
A REAL THRILL
Do you want to get a real thrill,
seeing just' how easily you can pre
pare a meal and do up the work
afterward?
Then visit “The Ideal Kitchen” in
the Women’s building at the State
Fair. Miss Wealthy Hale, head of
the dietetics kitchen of the Univer
sity of Wisconsin Home Economics
extension service, demonstrates
every day this week just how it can
be done.
Machines now exist, Miss Hale
says, which will perform every
mechanical operation of the kitchen.
Her exhibit shows what equipment
the modern kitchen should have,
and how that most important room
in the house should be arranged for
maximum efficiency.
Men Are Interested.
“Our dish washing machine at
tracts the greatest interest among
spectators who crowd about—espe
cially among the men,” Miss Hale
said.
“Men must realize the drudgery
of washing dishes (perhaps they
have had to assist too many times)
because scarcely a man passes our
booth who does not stop and ask
questions about the dish washing
machine.”
An electric refrigerator, a kitchen
cabinet flanked 'with utility closets
for both dishes and food, and a ma
chine called the kitchen aid are
among the luxuries which the mod
ern housewife may have in her
kitchen. The latter whips, stirs,
cuts, chips ice, freezes slices or
strains, depending on the particular
appliance used, Miss Hale says.
How to Save Steps.
In arranging a kitchen for maxi
mum efficiency, she points to the
ice box, the range and the dish
washer near the dining room door,
to save steps. The latter must also
be near the sink, as it gets its wash
ing water from the sink faucet and
the dirty water flows back into the
sink from the machine.
The kitchen work table is placed
between range and machine for
whipping. It should always be as
nearly centralized as possible, Miss
Hale points out.

AUGUST STATE'S
HEALTH PERIOD
MADISON—Which is Wisconsin’s
most healthful month? This is an
swered by the state board of health
in its quarterly bulletin just pub
lished, which asserts that, judging
from mortality alone, June, July,
August and September hold this fa
vorable claim. These months have
fewer deaths than any other season
of the year.
This was not always the case, ac
cording to the board. Before people
knew as much about keeping well as
they do today the hot summer
months, particularly July and Au
gust, took the largest toll. That was
the period when digestive disurb
ances, mainly enetritis in infants
and typhoid fever, kept physicians
busy. Today the summer months
are comparatively healthful and the
death rates low.

Congressional Probe of Drys* Shoot to Bill Order Likely
HAIR TRIGGER
ENFORCEMENT
STIRS SOLONS
Another Man Slain
By Dry Raiders at
Tacoma.
WASHINGTON— Possibility of a
congressional investigation into the
“shoot to kill” prohibition enforce
ment policy which protects the kill
ers against prosecution for murder
or manslaughter is enhanced as a
result of the killing of another man
by dry raiders near Tacoma, Wash.
As in a score or more of similar
cases throughout the country dur
ing the last two years, the agents
accused of murdering an alleged
moonshiner at Orting, 18 miles from
Tacoma, were granted federal court
protection against trial in a state
court. The United States district
attorney has announced he will ex
ert himself to prevent their indict
ment by a federal jury as murderers
and will appear to defend them if
an indictment is obtained.
None Is Punished.
In the 22 months, which ended on
April 30. last, 38 citizens were killed
by prohibition agents and although
many of the latter were indicted for
murder or manslaughter in state
courts, not one of them has ever
been punished.
In each case, federal district at
torneys have induced United States
courts to assume jurisdiction, halt
ing the state prosecution and in
many instances obtaining the re
lease of the slayers.
James E. Jones, director of pro
hibition, refused to discuss the
Washington case today and he re
fused to say how many more citi
zens have been killed by agents
since April 30, although he was
quite willing to make public a list
of prohibition agents killed in af
frays with alleged moonshiners or
bootleggers—the attitude he main
tained when appearing before the
house appropriations committee last
year.
Will Guard Slayers.
TACOMA, Wash. —“Any man who
gives aid to a United States revenue
officer in enforcing the law is en
titled to the same protection that
the officers themselves are af
forded,” said United States Attorney
Thomas P. Revelle of the western
Washington district. He said that
the Rev. George A. Seeley, pastor of
the Orting Free Methodist church,
who is out on $5,000 bond on a first
degree murder charge as the result
of the killing of a fugitive during
a raid on a still, will be given pro
tection with the three federal pro
hbition agents with whom he was
arrested.

To the Editor of The Leader:
I was interested in finding out
the other day that the weekly notes
on child welfare taken by the Unit
ed States children’s bureau show in
dividual differences in great num
bers but very little difference in the
curve of intelligence scores as be
tween races and nationalities. This
test was made at Ellis island and
25 nationalities were represented.
This breaks down the last preju
dice against the mentality and
hereditary disadvantages under
which many of us once thought the
foreign child labored.

not the group differences, with
which we must be concerned if we
wish to deal properly with child
psychology and make childhood a
better time to live in.

“MOOI HOLLANDE.”
The scenery of Holland is very
generally the loveliness of the plain
and lowland. In parts of Gueldres
and Limburg miniature mountains
and woods do present a picturesque
landscape. This is specially true
around the heights of Arnhem, in
the woods of Het Loo, on Holland’s
one mountain, the Wisselschebosch.
On the boundary between Limburg
and Germany tbere is a range of
hills for the eyes only of the Nether
landers, for they belong to Germany.
Despite the .flatness however, the
attractiveness of the country has
never been questioned. The absence
of the sensational scene and the ab
normal landscape, centers attention
on listening to an anthem of little
harmonizing sounds which create a
fresh ideal of beauty. It has made
the Dutch so love their country, that
many of them never leave it. To
adventure away into the next prov
ince is often called “going abroad”
so far does it seem. The whole na
tion is dominated with a quiet con
tent with its quaint beauty, which
explains why the folk here often
refer to their country as “Mooi Hol
lande,” —“pretty Holland.”

CHICAGO—Jiddu Krishnamurti,
Hindu mystic and prophet of theo
sophy, garbed in the white tunic
and turban of his race, bade his
last public farewell to Chicago last
night before an audience of 2,200
theosophists and their friends who
crowded into the grand ballroom
of the Hotel Sherman to feast upon
his words and a vegetarian banquet
heralded as “the largest meatless
feast ever served in America.”
The banquet, which consisted of
300 dozen scrambled eggs, mush
rooms, fruits, vegetables, and ice
cream, brought to a close the four
day international theosophical con
vention. Plans are now under way
to have the convention held here
again next year.
Humor Great Quality.
While in Chicago he has been
greatly impressed with the humor
and gayety of the people, Krishna
murti declared, and humor is the
greatest of qualities, he said. It
helps us overcome the difficulties
and tragedies of occidental life,
where noise and confusion make
contemplation almost Impossible.
“But as long as you are happy
you are really spiritual,” he said.
“You are approaching that serious
joyousness which is above all things
and alone eternal.”
As he spoke, those 2,200 people
hung upon each word, waiting to
hear a repetition of the mystic mes
sage he is said to have given last
year. But they waited in vain. For
Krishnamurti declared it Is “too
stuffy, too crowded and noisy” in
Chicago for the receiving of a great
manifestation.
Too Stuffy for Message.
Divine gifts manifest themselves
in solitude and contemplation, he
said, and he indicated that the Chi
cago atmosphere contained too
much static to receive a message
from the other world.

fy^EO P. FLYNN, a manager of several ring champions, comes oiH^
Ito sav he has compiled a list of the greatest champions of a
Lyj time.* Leo may have been totally unbiased in his selection
but it would seem to a great many boxing fans that I lj nn baa
erred several places in compiling his choice. He heads the list
with Jack Johnson as the greatest of heavyweight champions. Johnson
was probably a great heavyweight, but it would seem to a great many
who have seen Dempsey in action that the present title holder should
come in for consideration when the greatest of heavyweights is mentioned.
Dempsey isn’t the most popular champion we ever had, hut there
is no mistaking the fact Jack has left a long string of knockout
victims behind him. The present champion crowned every good contender
when he was coming up and when he felt inclined to tight for a
living.
The only contender he hasn’t met
and defeated is Harry Wills. At
the time Dempsey w’as climbing the
ladder to pugilistic fame 'Wills was
only an obscure heavyweight who
was having trouble with the third
raters and has-beens.
Sam Langford, long past his
prime and half blind, toyed with
Wills in a number of bouts right
up to the time of Sam’s retirement
because his failing eyes made it
difficult for him to find his way
into the ring.
Even though he hasn’t met Wills
there is not one type or class of
fighter whom Dempsey has not met
and defeated. Jack has beaten
clever boxers, tough fighters and
hard punchers with the same result
and a glance over his record would
cause one to believe Dempsey was
greater than Johnson.

The light heavyweight class is
topped by Bob Fitzsimmons, and
judging from the stories the old
timers tell, Leo has this one right.

The same is true in the middle
weight division, where Flynn picks
Billy Papke as the greatest, of the
class. However, Harry Greb is a
pretty tough bird and has furnished
a lot* of trouble for everyone in his
class and a few heavyweights as
well.
Flynn picks Tommy Ryan as the
great of welterweights. Jack
Kearns would probably say Mickey
Walker, but he couldn’t prove It.

PHILADELPHIA Philadelphia
was talking Gene Tunney today. A
few days ago Jack Dempsey was
on everyone’s lips, but since the
challenger’s whirlwind visit to the
scene of the fight here yesterday,
comment has shifted to the former
“Devil Dog.”
Yesterday was a stiff training
dav for the Greenwich Village boy.
A hundred United States marines,
former buddies at Soissons and the
Argonne, were on hand with thou
sands of Philadelphians to greet
Tunney on his arrival from Strouds
burg, Pa., his training headquar
ters.
When the crowd swarmed around
him the marines formed a hollow
square about him. They were
pushed aside by the cheering mul
titude and Gene had to duck his
head and fight his way out. He
did it.
A triumphant parade was made
from city hall to the Sesqui exposi
tion grounds where Tunney looked
over the stadium.
Thousands of ticket orders poured
into the office during the day.

THE RISE OF RICE
In August, 1915, the Petersburg
club of the Virginia league sold a
promising young right-handed pitch
er to the Washington Senators for
BSSOO. He worked
in four games for
the Nationals that
year, and the
following season
was converted into
an outfielder, in
which position he
has played ever
since, except in
1918 w'hen he fig
ured that there
was something
else more impor
tant than base
ball going on in
Tea; Murray. the W orld.
The player was Sam Rice, the
hard-hitting Hoosier, one of the
best all-around players in the
American league.
Sam, whose real name is Edgar
Charles Rice, is now in his 35th
year and this is his 11th season
with Washington, yet he appears to
retain the great natural speed and
the keen batting eye which have,
made him so valuable to the Sena
tors. Watching Rice play, you get
an impression of cool-headedness,
reliability, and dazzling speed, and
a glance at his record adds to the
opinions formed from seeing him on
the diamond.
Sam’s major league batting av
erage, including 1925, is .323. This
j ear he is hitting around .350,
which was his last season’s mark.
He steals about 25 bases each year,
and in 1920 was the leading sack
pilferer of both circuits with 62 to
his credit. In the last three full
seasons, he has been in the select
class of those who have scored more
than 100 runs, and in 1924 and
1925 he corralled considerably
more than 200 hits. He seems to be
well on his way to score 100 runs
and get 200 hits this year also, and,
as usual, is one of the leading base
stealers.
In 1924, Sam set a record by be
ing at bat nine times in a single
game. His performance in the
world series last year was of the
highest order, for, besides batting
.367 in the seven games, he made
17 putouts in the outfield, turning
in some truly remarkable catches.

Love Madness
The coming of a new day found
Gloria West the prey of conflict
ing emotions. Try as she might
she could not resign herself to a
return to the placid life which had
been her lot before Jay Vannah
had invaded her heart. Gloria
was not temperamentally of a
sentimental mould. She was so
phisticated because of her intelli
gence and;not because of her ex
periences.
She revolved in her mind the
events of the past few weeks and
although she realized the impos
sibility of changing the course of
these events, something within her
whispered that fate could not be
so unjust and so cruel as to per
mit Vannah. to fade out of her life.
For the first time, perhaps, Gloria
realized that she loved Vannah so
fully and so completely that no
matter what happened she would
never give up loving him. This
conviction had been born in her
mind by her frank admission of
her love during her midnight con
versation with Evelyn Waye.
Gloria bad never had a sweet
heart. She had never even “kept
company” with any boy. No, she
was not sentimental and she was
not manifestly emotional She
wondered now if he might not be
cold and immune against the con
ventional inspirations of love.
How easy it would have been for
her to have changed the course of
events of Jay Vannah’s visit last
night. She wondered if she had
been stupid and by her indiffer
ence discouraged some definite
plan he may have had to propose
to her. Vannah had told her once
that he loved her and that was at
a time when he had no right to
express his love. Yet he had done
so and she had listened. What had
happened that now he was free, he
kept silent?
She realized, in a sort of panic,
that within two or three days
Vannah would be gone out of her
life forever. She did not become
theatrical and picture herself a
deserted Miss Innocence, nor as
the abandoned heroine. In spite
of a heavy heart and a bewildered
mind, she managed to keep her
sense of perspective. She comfort
ed herself with the thought that
a girl who is disappointed in love
isn’t necessarily condemned to
heart-break. Hearts, Gloria knew,
are not broken so easily and time
heals all wounds.

and she was the same girl, in out

ened out and, by George, it’s go
ing to be a job. Such a man, such

been to us. Well, it’s all over now
and I imagine it will be many a
long day before we see him again.
He’s going away, you know, go
ing to South America.”
Gloria’s face was a model of
composure and her voice was cool
and impersonal.
“That’s a long way,” she said
and instantly realized the stupid
ity of her remark.
’‘lt’s probably the best thing he
can do,” observed Mr. Bigelow
sagely. “He’d never be content
here again. Fact is, though, I’m
afraid Vannah won’t find the
wilderness so attractive as he
thinks. He’s used to crowds and
lots of friends and gay surround
ings. Now he’s going to buy half
interest in a vast plantation
down there in the Argentine.
Hundreds of miles from a railroad
—half a dozen white men and not
a white woman within a day’s
journey. “I don’t believe Vannah
will stick it, not for long.”
They were busy all day, cata
loguing Vannah’s investments and
listing the securities which he
would also leave behind in the
trusteeship of his lawyers. Van
nah had refused to make any
disposition of the big white house
in which he was born and in
which he lived, off and on, all his
life up to the night on which his
wife had met her death.
“Funny thing about that too,”
Mr. Bigelow remarked to Gloria.
“He wants it left standing just
as it is. Has instructed me to put
a caretaker in and to never allow
anybody to visit the house. Wants
it to just rot into dust and decay,
it seems.”
“Perhaps it is a sentiment of
his boyhood life there,” suggested
Gloria softly.
Mr. Bigelow arched his eye
brows.
“Sentiment? Jay Vannah senti
mental about his boyhood or any
thing else?” he smiled. “Hardly.
Jay Vannah is sentimental about
nothing but dogs.”
They reached the end of their
task at last. Vannah’s fortune
was close to $3,000,000 and more
than half of it in securities which
Mr. Bigelow intended to turn into
negotiable paper at the bank next
day.
“It’s a lot of money, isn’t it,
Miss West?’
She agreed listlessly.
“Well, he’ll take along a million
of It for his white elephant,” com
mented the old man.
“Why, white elephant?” asked
Gloria innocently.
“He’ll never make a go of it
down there, I tell you,” insisted
Mr. Bigelow testily. “Jay Van
nah’s not the type of man for an
austere life, an exile from the
gayeties of the world. He would
get along better in a monastery,
than in this isolated place where
he will have no interests and no
way of gratifying his taste for
pleasure, for companionship. Now,
if he were happily married, things
would be different.” The old
lawyer shrugged.
“But he’s not and not likely to
be.”
The pity of it!
That was all Gloria could think
of as sho went home wearily after
the day’s work was done, the sheer
blinding pity of it.
She knew that Vannah was de
liberately exiling himself in self
punishment as if he still believed
himself guilty of the tragic end
ing of his wife.
Fully realizing the futility of
hoping that there might be at
least a respite, Gloria still hoped.
Perhaps something would happen
to delay him, to postpone this mad
excursion. That was what her
heart prompted, but her intelli
gent mind bade her hope no more.

ever, a stray wolf would come

keep close watch until we got a
chance to trap it or shoot it.
Such a stray wolf was the Great

KING VIDOR, DIRECTOR OF BIG
PARADE, IS MAN WHO LISTENS
Some 12 years ago in Texas a
boy in his late ’teens set out to
write, finance, direct and act his
own motion pictures. They were
minor comedies ami did not make
a noticeable impression. His Texas
friends and relatives said that he
was wasting his time. Nevertheless,
this Texas boy’ has directed what
many critics claim to be one of the
really great pictures of all times—
The Big Parade.
King Vidor, in his picturization
of Laurence Stallings’ story, to be
shown at the Davidson next week,
has placed upon the screen one of
the most dramatic, human and lov
able stories ever filmed. Those who
have witnessed King Vidor’s treat
ment of this screen story, have
hailed his efforts as the zenith of
motion picture direction.
King Vidor was born in Galves
ton, Tex. His father, a lumber
manufacturer, wanted him to follow
that business. After his schooling
at San Antonio and up north at
Tome institute the initial steps to
ward becoming a lumber king did
not interest the young man and he
organised a “one-man” moving pic
ture company which proved a rath
er costly experiment to his father
and himself. However, he did dis
cover two very capable actresses in
Florence Vidor and Corinne Grif
fith, who appeared in these initial
pictures.
Finding that his comedies had
but a limited appeal King Vidor
went to Hollywood in 1915. Then
for three years he worked at sev
eral studios as cameraman, assist
ant director and actor. Then came
the chance to direct his own pic-

EVERYDAY GOOD THINGS.
For a delicious breakfast bread
you might try the following:
Sally Lunn.
Mix at night one cupful of milk,
two eggs, two tablespoonfuls of but
ter, one teaspoonful of salt, one
tablespoonful of sugar and four cup
fuls of flour with one-half cupful of
good yeast. Cover closely and put
to rise, giving plenty of room for
rising. In the morning beat well,
turn into greased muffin pans and
set to rise an hour, then bake in a
moderate oven.
Tongue on Toast.
This is another good breakfast
dish which uses the rough pieces of
boiled tongue. Mince the tongue,
adding a bit of onion juice, nutmeg,
salt and pepper, a tablespoonful of
chopped green pepper. Prepare a
rich white sauce, using half milk
and half broth with the tongue, add
ing two tablespoonfuls each of flour
and butter cooked together. Sweet
cream may be used instead of milk,
omitting the milk and butter; add
the tongue and pour over squares of
buttered toast.
Gateau a la Africaine.
Beat three eggs, add three-fourths
of a cupful of sugar and the same
of flour. To the beaten yolks add
the sugar, beat well, add the flour
and beaten whites, stirring lightly,
add flavoring, and bake in patty
tins. When cool remove the centers,
fill with whipped cream sweetened
and flavored and put together in
pairs. Cover with chocolate icing.
Welsh Rarebit.
Cut one-half pound of cheese into
bits, put it into a saucepan, scald a
pint of milk, add a beaten egg to
which has been added two table
spoonfuls of flour and one-half tea
spoonful of salt. Let this mixture
cool, stirring until smooth, then pour
the milk into the cheese and beat
vigorously with an egg beater. Sea
son to taste with cayenne pepper
and serve on hot buttered toast or
large crackers which have been
browned and buttered lightly.

artistic effect of a meal and it is
often easier than getting the meal
all on the table at once; however,
without a maid, this is not always
convenient. —Nellie Maxwell.

Frederick Stock Is
Praised in East.
Frederick Stock, conductor, Chi
cago Symphony orchestra, which
will again be heard In Milwaukee
next season, has been winning
laurels in the east, first in the
Stadium Concerts, New York, and
then at the Sesquicentennial at
Philadelphia. One of the leading
Gotham reviewers summed up his
estimate of Mr. Stock as follows:
“At the conclusion of his one w’eek
of guest appearances, it is possible
to pronounce Frederick Stock one of
our foremost conductors. He is
classically sound, admirably rou
tined, a musician to bis finger tips,
and an artist. He indulges in
nothing which is of a superficial or
artificial character. Showmanship
is not for one of his serious char
acter. His approach to his task is
that of one respecting his place and
its requirements, and proceeding ac
cordingly. And there w’ere two out
standing characteristics in the
Stock conducting: he made the or
chestra ‘sipg’ and he rarely inter
rupted the smooth and regular flow
of the phrase line.”
CONGO GORILLAS FILMED.
Ben Burbridge, Jacksonville,
Fla., big game hunter, has just
emerged from a two year hunt in
the jungles of the Belgian Congo.
With him he has brought The Gor
illa Hunt, the only motion picture
ever made of these giant ape-men
in their native environment. Not
only did Burbridge make “movies”
of these “missing links,” but he
captured four of them alive, and
in self-defense shot a huge mon
ster weighing 450 pounds and
standing over six feet in height.
No Screen Stories Wanted by Har-
old Lloyd From Outsiders.
Harold Lloyd Is not in the market
for stories!
For the benefit of the scores who
every month write him asking if
he would consider a scenario, or
story idea, Lloyd let it be known
again that he maintains his own
staff of writers, and will not con
sider material from outside sources.
The way Lloyd works in his com
edy production makes it almost an
impossibility for an outsider to de
velop material that would be suit
able for his reproduction on the
screen. Lloyd never works from a
script, but develops as his picture
progresses, the main idea or theme
selected for the basis of his story
or plot.

took place recently when Hal Mohr,
chief cameraman for Erich von
Stroheim, and Claire Del Mar, ac
tress, were married on a set in Von
Stroheim’s present picture, The
Wedding March.

For a long time past the term
“nervous breakdown” has been
used to cover a very great variety of
ills associated with the nervous sys
tem.
It is a rather pleasant but mean
ingless diagnosis that often glosses
over more or less serious diseases
of the central nervous system. In
fact, it is used so loosely and so
generally that it is a term that
covers alomst all the ills flesh is
heir to, ranging from simple fears,
up to and including a.- serious a dis
ease as general paresis, an organic
disease of the brain, fatal in its
termination, unless early and inten
sive treatment is started.
There is always a cause for nerv
ousness. Sometimes that cause is
entirely the result of an impaired
physical condition; .‘or example,
goitre or anemia. At other times, it
is due to some physical cause such
as fear or a morbid feeling of in
feriority.
Two groups of cases are often hid
den under the term “nervous break
down.” One is the psychoneuroses,
those functional disorders of the
nervous system often having a psy
chis cause which can be remedied, if
not entirely removed. In the other
group are those more serious men
tal states leading to mental diseases
of great severity, such as dementia
praecox, a mental disease developing
about the adolescent period and
tending to progress toward great
mental deterioration.
Every year more than 50,000 new
patients are admitted to the mental
hospitals in this country. If that
rate does not diminish—and there
is very little present evidence that
it is diminishing—there will be ad
mitted to these hospitals, within the

Too Much Rain Damages Cotton, Corn and Potato Crops
TOBACCO YIELD
IS BENEFITED
BY MOISTURE
Sugar Beets Report
ed in Excellent
Condition.
BY JOSEPH F. WASNEY.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
WASHINGTON Unfavorable
weather conditions in recent weeks
have seriously retarded many crops,
leaving farmers uncertain what
their yields will be, reports to the
agricultural department showed to
day.
Rain in the latter part of August
rotted potatoes in some sections,
hampered the maturity of corn and
flooded low land cotton fields. The
drenched soil also prevented farm
ers from plowing land for winter
wheat crops.
Spuds Do Well.
Potatoes are doing well in the
northeast but in the middle At
lantic states and Ohio valley rains
have caused “wet rot” among the
tubers. Too severe moisture also
damaged the late tomato crops, re
ports to the department said.
Tobacco and corn were the only
crops benefited by rains. The corn
crop, however, has now had suffi
cient moisture and needs dry warm
weather to hasten maturity.
Cotton Is Fair.
Sugar cane in the south and sug
ar beets in the west were reported
In excellent condition and a big pro
duction of these crops was fore
cast.
Cotton was reported as making
fair progress, though hampered by
too much rain. The rains in Texas
have caused an increase of boll wee
vil damage.

September and the fourth quarter
of the year at the unusually favor
able rate which marked the summer
months, the weekly reviews of the
industry indicated yesterday.

week in respect to mill operations,
as well as prospective demand, have
been more defintely favorable,”
Iron Age asserts.
See Larger Operations.
“A gauge of the high August rate
of steel production is furnished by
I our pig iron statistics gathered on
the last day of the month. Pro
ducers’ figures from all the furnaces
in the country, with Aug. 31 esti
mated, give a total of 3,196,190 tons,
or 103,103 tons per day, against
3,223,338 tons in July, or 103,978
tons a day—a falling off of but 875
tons a day, against 3,866 tons in
July.
Furnaces in blast Sept. 1 num
bered 214; Aug. 1 there were 216.
Leading steel producers are now
counting on larger operations in the
next 60 days than they were willing
to predict in the lull that came in
mid-August.

earlier than in 1925. Fall consump
tion of steel for automobiles will ex
ceed last year’s and structural mills
see more fall business ahead than
was indicated 30 days ago. Chicago
district steel mills report shipments
in June, July and August 50 per cent
greater than for any like period in
their history, while production aver
aged 85 per cent of Capacity.

ished steel composite prices remain

cents per pound for 11 weeks. Both
were 1 to 2 per cent lower a year
ago.”

French Smokers
Roll Their Own
PARlS—Twice as many hand
rolled cigarets are smoked in France
as machine made by the state fac
tories, the totals for last year being
10,600,000,000 state-made as against
22,000,000,000 self-made.
This is explained by some smokers
as a reflection on the defective man
ner the state turns out its cigarets,
but it also is greatly due to the
economy a smoker finds in rolling
his own cigarets.
The commercialization of the to
bacco trade in France, which the
Poincare government is introducing,
will no doubt try to change this
state of affairs and bring France
into line with other countries where
the number of machine-made cigar
ets sold is at least double that of
hand-made.

CHICAGO Bankers, traction
representatives and city council
traction officials yesterday took two
steps which it is believed will pro
duce results vital to a solution of
Chicago’s transportation problem.
The first was almost complete
agreement on a plan of consolidation
of the elevated, surface lines, motor
busses and the subways—when the
latter was built.
The second is that the proposed
new traction ordinance should pro
vide that an indeterminate fran
chise be issued by the city instead of
the state.
The representative further dis
cussed a scrvice-at-cost proposal, to
be governed by ordinance and based
on a reasonable rate of return to
the companies, such return to be
fixed by proper authorities with
power to change as conditions re
quired.
The surprise of the meeting was
the favorable attitude of the trac
tion officials and bankers on a city
issued franchise. The concession, it.
is explained, does not mean that the
traction executives will find govern
ment by a city commission accept
able to them, but members of the
local transportation committee are
convinced it will virtually bring
about municipal jurisdiction over
the utilities.

Burlington Road
Is 76 Years Old
CHICAGO—On Sept. 2, 1850, a
second-hand tea kettle engine, pull
ing a coach and two freight cars,
made the initial trip over the then
Aurora branch railroad, a 12-miie
stretch of track connecting Aurora,
111., with Turner Junction, now West
Chicago.
Today is the 76th birthday of that
same railroad, the 12 miles of track
has grown into almost 12,000, and
the engine, coach and two freight
cars that set out on the original
trip have grown to 75,000 -units of
equipment.
The railroad is the Chicago, Bur
lington Quincy, and the desk of
its president, Hale Holden, yester
day was piled high with congratu
latory telegrams.

WASHINGTON Figures made
public by the bureau of internal
revenue show that tax collections
during July—the first full month in
which all provisions of the new reve
nue act were in effect —were $104,-
369,095, a decrease of $21,497,594
from July of 1925.
The capital stock tax was the last
item of the act of 1924 to be re
pealed, being replaced by an in
crease in the tax on corporations.
Income Tax Receipts Gain.
The bureau’s record showed re
ceipts of $50,551,730.13 from income
taxes, a gain of $15,598,511.47 over
July of last year, but miscellaneous
taxes fell off $37,096,105.42, as com
pared with July, 1925. The figures
for July on miscellaneous receipts
were given at $53,817,365.10, as com
pared with $90,913,470.92 for July
last year.
Of the total income tax pay
ments, $34,940,126.07 was from cor
porations, and $15,611,604.06 was
from individuals. The division of
income tax receipts for July, 1925,
was $23,148,058.10 from corpora
tions and $11,805,160.56 from indi
viduals.
Estates Pay $4,768,524.
Estate taxes yielded $4,768,524.45
in July as compared with $7,628,-
346.08 in July, 1925. The tobacco
tax brought in $32,123,606.69, a de
crease of $1,098,425.16 from July,
1925. The tobacco taxes included
$2,019,291.91 on large cigars, as
compared with $3,755,266.66 for
July, 1925; $24,540.99 for small ci
gars, as compared with $55,685.37
in July, 1925; $23,883,225 96 for
small cigarets as compared with
$22,836,908.59 for July, 1925; $544,-
154.46 on snuff as against $551,-
406.36 in the corresponding month
last year, and $5,612,791.77 on chew
ing and smoking tobacco as against
$5,866,148.52 for July, 1925.
The taxes on automobiles and mo
torcycles—the tax having been re
pealed on trucks and wagons—was
$7,271,936.86 last month. For July,
1925, the collections totaled $12,332,-
971.60, but the rate was higher un
der the revenue act of 1924.
Club Dues Taxed.
A total of $19,164.96 was yielded
the government from the new tax
on cereal beverages.
Athletic, social and sporting dub
dues were taxed to the amount cf
$764,986.68, while in July, 1925, the
same tax produced $754,039.28.

FINO HEARSE
RUM STOCKED
DETROIT, Mich.—The suspici
ously inquisitive eyes of a highway
police lieutenant alarmed what,
purported to be a funeral cortege
here and afteh the mourners fled
r ^ly from the procession the
se and other cars were found
pocked with liquor.
.squad of police was making its
y along an outlying road toward
^corse, a rum-running base, when
it rounded a curve in sight of the
funeral procession. The unusually
loud manifestations of grief which
came from the cortege attracted the
attention of the lieutenant In
charge of <he squad, he said.
Driving to the head of the line he
glanced casually at the hearse driv
er. As he gazed at the man the
driver became nervous, faltered
and then jamming the brakes leaped
from the machine and fled. To the
astonishment of the officers the
mourners immediately began pour
ing from the cars in the rear and
fled in all directions.
An inspection of the hearse re
vealed instead of a body 50 cases
of beer. The other cars were like
wise loaded with contraband.

Spain’s Seat Vacant.
BY FREDERICK KUH.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
GENEVA—When the league coun
cil met today with Foreign Minister
Benes of Czecho-Slovakia presiding,
the conspicuous absence of the
Spanish delegate increased appre
hension that yesterday’s rejection of
the Spanish claim for a permanent
seat on the council would hasten
Spain’s withdrawal from the league.
Informed observers believe that
Madrid will await both the council’s
and the assembly’s formal confirma-
tion of refusal to give Spain a per
manent seat before actual with
drawal, however.
