QUEEN VICTORIA
GIVES CORNET
TO KANSAS MAN
M’PHERSON, Kans.—ln a com
fortable Kansas home here reposes
a silver cornet, the gift of Queen
Victoria to Harry Hapgood. Only
one other like presentation was
made by Queen Victoria during her
reign, and that was to Bugler Dunn,
Boer war hero, to whom she gave a
silver bugle.
Hapgood, of a musical family, be
gan playing a cornet at the age of
8, was a member of the famous Dis
patch band of Kansas, served with
several circuses and in 1891 went
to Morrison, Wales, where he joined
the grand Victorian army band.
The grenadier guards, to which
the band was attached, had its bar
racks in St. Janies palace in Lon
don and the bandsmen came in con
tact with members of the queen’s
household. Queen Victoria took a
personal interest in her musicians,
as did the Duke of York, now
George V.
When Hapgood, after several
years of service, resigned to return
to America, the queen at a public
gathering presented him with a sil
ver cornet with a suitable inscrip
tion.

FARMERS TRY CASTOR OIL
Out in Montana some of the farm mortgages are com
ing due and the farmers are unable to pay. The money
lenders, in Minneapolis and St. Paul, have had what they
undoubtedly consider a cute idea. They have been fore
closing the mortgages previous to the harvesting of this
year’s crop, so that the farmers lose the land and the crop
too.
But, one recent event makes them go a little slow, or
at least makes the local officials not very keen to carry
out the orders.
When a deputy sheriff went to take possession of a
certain farm, a group of neighbors gathered and remon
strated with him. As he was about to insist upon fulfilling
his mission, they seized him, poured a pint of castor oil
down his throat, and sent him home. See how far the
influence of Mussolini has spread?
But that is not the whole story. The loan company
brought an injunction suit to prevent the farmer from
removing any of the crop from the farm. The trial of the
injunction was set for a certain day. In the meantime
about 150 farmers from all around, and their wives and
children, gathered at the farm. The women brought the
eats along. The men cut and thrashed the farmer’s wheat.
Then everybody had a big feed which the women had laid
out on the ground, after which the men hauled the wheat
off the farm so it would not be there if the injunction
should be granted. When the trial day came, inasmuch
as there was nothing to enjoin, the judge dismissed the
case.
This little incident indicates the way the farmers
feel. It is reminiscent of Populist days, for the mort
gage evil was the big thing in those times. Nowadays
there are lots of mortgages, but the low price of farm
products seems to be the main thing the farmers object to.
If they would collectively transfer the spirit of the above
incident into the ballot box, by voting the Socialist ticket,
they could solve their problems without the use of castor
oil.
I SHALL THE UNITED STATES BE
MADE A PHILIPPINE COLONY?
The people of the Philippine Islands are clamoring
for self-government these days, and Cal Coolidge and the
other old politicians deny them that boon. They assert
that the Filipinos are not yet capable of self-government.
Cal and his cohorts have this thing turned wrong end
to. It is the American people who are not yet capable of
self-government. They don’t take any interest in their
own government, but let the Coolidges and the Mellons
and the Wall Street bankers run it—and what they do
to the people is a-plenty. As Americans do not know how
to run America, why should they assume that they knew
how to run the Philippines?
On the contrary, would it not be a good idea for the
United States to relinquish its independence and turn it
self over to the Filipinos for government? Since the Fil
ipinos are interested in their own government, they prob
ably would be interested in ours too if we were a Philip
pine colony. We recommend this idea to the consideration
of all American men and women who do not vote, or who
vote for old party candidates.
MONEY HAS BEEN TALKING FOR
QUITE A WHILE
Young Teddy says we must not have a money-con
trolled government.
What does he think we have now?- Is he so naive as
not to know that we have a money-controlled government,
and that we have had such a government for many years?
Certainly the expenditures in the Republican pri
maries of Pennsylvania and Illinois are disgraceful.
But they do not heap any worse disgrace upon the
Republican party, for the simple reason that the Repub
lican party is already so deep in disgrace, in the eyes of
decent people, that it cannot get any decree. The idea
that the Greedy Old Party could make itself any more
disgraceful is preposterous.
STOP DIVIDING UP
Arthur Brisbane says that whatever other defects
Americans may have, they cannot be accused of dividing
up.
Wrong again. Dividing up is what Americans do
nothing else but. The mass of Americans, we mean, not
the few. The masses divide up with the few. The stocks
and bonds of the industries are chiefly owned by a small
minority of parasites who do nothing whatsoever to earn
th* billions of dividends and interest. The masses do
the useful work, and, instead of getting the whole benefit
themselves, they divide up with these parasites. This is
one of the principal objections which the Socialists make
against the present social system. We Socialists want a
system in which the industrious will not be compelled
to divide up with the idle.

BANKERS AND POLITICIANS
The differences among American bankers over the can
cellation of allied war debts and the reduction of Ger
many’s payments under the Dawes plan show how little
the big men of capitalism know about the natural work
ings of their own chaotic system.
Even those bankers who see that American business
today is woven into the pattern of international business
do not understand that much more than a correction of
the mistakes of war and after-war finance is at stake.
The old party editors are even more stupid in their
discussion of Newton D. Baker’s demand for cancellation.
They keep their eyes glued on the fact that he was a Wib
son Democrat. They speculate in tedious articles about
the Democratic and Republican politics of this matter,
as if the problem had more political than economic sig
nificance.
But when Baker now tries to undo what he helped
to start under Wilson, and when he can quote Andrew
Mellon against Coolidge to support his own revised po
sition, it must be evident to even a casual thinker that this
problem far transcends the limits of the Repodemocrati:
corral.
How can anybody expect the Republican and Demo
cratic statesmen to do anything practical about this
muddle, when the big business leaders themselves don’t
know from one year to another what to do about it?
About seven years ago, the press of the big bankers
everywhere spread the silly idea that Germany could pay
for the whole cost of the war which exceeded the total
value of all personal and public property of the German
people.
It took five years after that to convince the big bank
ers that they had tried to bite off their own noses to spite
their faces. They forced the British, French and Italian
bankers to revise the Versailles treaty to the extent of
accepting the Dawes plan and settling their war debts on
a 62-year basis.
Two years later we find them still retracing their
steps, after several efforts to revise the Dawes plan with
out revising the whole war finance. And we are still about
two years away from the date on which the Dawes plan
is supposed to go into full effect.
In all these amendments to foolish treaties and plans,
the big bankers never bothered their heads about the ef
fects of their blundering on the middle and working
classes, or even on the industrial capitalists. Only to the
extent that these injured classes protested and were able
to make their protests effective, did the big bankers amend
their play, but even then only with the same hit-or-miss
methods that have been characteristic of their whole
career.
It is not a matter for much wonder or surprise, then,
that the old party statesmen have simply played with
this problem. The big business men were never willing to
have the statesmen do anything effective about it. They,
are rather satisfied with a man like Coolidge, who lets
matters slide and waits for them to settle themselves.
But now the middle and working classes of Europe
are getting up their dander. That bothers both big busi
ness and old party statesmen terribly. It was all right
let things settle themselves, so long as others had to sb.
But when the common people begin to take a hand in k
settlement, the policy of letting things slide has to make
way for a policy of the iron hand, and that hand never
builds better than it destroys.
OUR IMPERSONAL ATTITUDE
We hear some people sighing now and then for a re
turn of the good old journalism that wielded a brilliant
pen and denounced public characters with a virulent array
of blistering epithets. We are asked occasionally, why we
do not,follow that style and rip leading statesmen or
business men up the back with such personal excoriations.
The answer is: We study men in relation with their
conditions. The leaders of capitalism are in our opinion
as much the creatures as the makers of their society. We
know that personal attacks do not change conditions, and
we consider it foolish to attack persons for being what
they must naturally be as a rule under prevailing condi
tions.
The great statesmen of capitalism have proved them
selves very small, because it does not pay them to be great
in the sense of sacrificing their personal fortunes for the
good of impersonal mankind. And we don’t blame them
much, because mankind in the mass has always crucified
those who were more interested in the general welfare
than in their own fortunes.
For this reason we attack men for being represen
tatives of a bad system rather than for failing to be better
than their system. Do away with private ownership of
public life, take away from individuals the power to get

For the first time the books

The Chicago Sanitary Dis
trict Board is a commission
which is supposed to have
charge of Chicago’s sewage
problem. It is, however, really a
political body devoted to lower
ing the levels of the Great
Lakes by taking water out of
Lake Michigan to wash Chi
cago’s sewage down the Illinois
River—so that wealthy Chi
cagoans will not have to pay
taxes to build sewage disposal
plants.

The accountants show that in
1923, 1924 and 1925, $1,606,400
was spent by the Sanitary
Board in the lake levels fights
opposing Milwaukee and other
Great Lakes cities that were try
ing to protect their harbors
against the Chicago water steal.
Five hundred twenty-two
thousand two hundred sixteen
dollars of that money went
in fees to special engineers and
attorneys —$247,787 went for
traveling expenses, meals and
‘entertainment”; $140,683 went
for publicity and advertising,
and $624,875 for pay rolls.
’These pay rolls contained a
list of 43 Illinois legislators,
Chicago politicians and rela
tives of politicians who received
over a quarter of a million dol
lars.
The audit also shows that a
large number of employes were
added to the pay rolls a few
weeks before each election in
1924 —and were laid off a few
days after each election.

Interesting to Milwaukeeans
is the fact that T. Chalkley
Hatton, chief engineer of Dr.
Bading’s Sewerage Commission

appointed for life by legislative
enactment in 1913 —received
the sum of $10,885.50 from the

Mr. Hatton, Milwaukee’s en
gineer, signed a so-called “re
port” as a result of his being
hired by the Chicago people—
this report helped Chicago in
its fight against Milwaukee.

honesty by the Chicago Sani
tary Board forces The Chicago

GENEVA The United States
senate’s world court reservations
have come under fire of the British
dominions with Sir George Foster
of Canada and Sir Francis Bell of
New Zealand as critics of the con
tested sth article.
The strongest attack came from
the American continent rather than
Europe as the conference of signa
tories of the statute of the perma
nent court of international justice
debated the article.
They were made despite Eng
land’s warm support of the Ameri
can reservations.
Attack by Canadian.
A possibility in the problem pre
sented 1 by the senate reservations
has been advanced by Foreign Min
ister Osten Unden of Sweden. He
declared that .he could not see how
it would be possible to grant the
United States the sweeping right re
quested in the fifth reservation, but
suggested that the conference itself
make reseravtions, namely, accept
ance of the United States’ adherence
to the court, provided that the res
ervations did not cause trouble, but
that, should trouble develop, the sig
natories would withdraw acceptance
of'the United States.
In a caustic address Sir George
Foster pictured the situation which
would arise were the reservation ac
cepted.
He said it must then constantly
be born in mind that whenever The
Hague court was asked to give an
advisory opinion its first duty would
be to ascertain whether the United
States was interested.
Danger in Delays.
This information he emphasized,
was available only from the United
States itself, and not from some
designated source in the United
States. Hence, he said, it must
first be decided what constitutes
the United States in this case.
After the court had received its
statement from the United ^tates,
that it was interested, he continued,
the court did not have the right to
decide whether the claim of the
United States was just. He said
that as a result of this the reserva
tion would mean the utmost delay,
which in certain cases would be
fatal. He declared that, the whole
experience of the league demanded
the necessity of quick decision and
action.
Sir George expressed himself as
willing to go to any extent neces
sary to assure the United States
equality, and said he was certain
that if the United States found that
it had asked more than equality the
question could be discussed “man to
man” fashion and an adjustment
could be reached.

tered the grounds shortly after 8:30

wife.

decided that a dead man was better

employed to take charge of his

see that his body was cremated.

could find a certain letter addressed

JEWS OF CITY
WILL OBSERVE
ROSHHASHANAH
Milwaukee Jewry will open the
Jewish holy season with New Year’s
services, Wednesday night. Rosh
Hashanah, or New Year’s, occurs
earlier this year than usual.
In the Jewish tradition the Rosh
Hashanah marks the anniversary of
the creatiofi of the world, supposed
to have taken place 5,687 years ago.
Arises at Dawn.
In order to prepare for the solemn
holy season, the orthodox Jew for
some days before the New Year’s
day arises at dawn and repairs to
the synagogue where penitent pray
ers are intoned in a special mourn
ful chant.
The early morning services con
tinue during the 10 days immediate
ly following the New Year’s day,
until the day of atonement.
The Jewish people throughout the
world will celebrate the annual Day
of Atonement, or Yom Kippur, Sept.
18. It will be ushered in the eve
ning before with a solemn service
in all synagogues and will be de
voted to prayer and fasting. A
memorial service in honor of the de
parted will be held during the day.
Is Well Observed.
The Day of Atonement is an an
cient institution, dating back to
early Bible times. It is observed by
all loyal Jews whether reform or
orthodox, through total abstinence
from business occupations as well
as from all food, drink and carnal
pleasures.

CHARITY GOODS
PROVIDE WORK
FOR HUNDREDS
Transforming $55,000 from char
ity to self-respecting wages last
year; the Milwaukee Goodwill In
dustries, the headquarters of which
are at 360 Grove St., gave employ
ment to hundreds of aged, needy
and crippled individuals throughout
the city and in 600 different ways

pursue a trade, it is brought out at
the Goodwill booth in the Educa
tional Bldg, at the State Fair.

thropy and two of those who have

stant attendance at the booth dem
onstrating how they now are able
to earn a livelihood.
Edward Rausch is blind. But he
learned to do many things at the
Janesville state school for the
blind. And he works every day as
an employe of the Goodwill Indus
tries weaving rugs.

noons in the booth at the fair paint
ing Christmas cards, the sale of

surmountable affliction.

mending old furniture, cutting up

Northwest Airways, Inc., was
granted a corporate charter by the
Michigan secretary of state today
and authorized to operate airplanes
between Detroit and St Paul.
This is understood to be the or
ganization, which, with the financial
backing of Henry Ford, is to bid
on the Chicago, Milwaukee and
Twin Cities air mail route recently
abandoned by Charles Dickinson,
Chicago contractor.
Bids Due Tomorrow.
W. A. Kidder and J H. Brlttin,
Minneapolis, also are interested in
this concern.

opened in Washington tomorrow and
it already has been intimated that
the conditions under which the Ford
organization is prepared to operate
the line will be so low as to make
it a certainty that the contract will
be awarded to it.
Legal Status Doubted.

state public utilities commission and
the state securities commission.

$300,000 worth of stock to individ
uals who have already subscribed
and it had not been decided which
of the two commissions has jurisdic
tion.

WASHINGTON —For the 10th
time in the history of the United
States, the senate will try a federal
official upon impeachment charges
when it meets Nov. 10 to consider
the evidence against George W. Eng
lish, federal judge of the eastern
district of Illinois.
English was impeached last ses
sion by the house of representatives
upon recommendation of its judi
ciary committee which found the
jurist guilty upon five counts. He
was charged (1) with tyrannically
and oppressively disbarring two at
torneys, coercing a jury and threat
ening freedom of the press; (2) mis
demeanor in office in handling
bankruptcy cases; (3) extension of
partiality and favoritism to a sole
referee in bankruptcy; (4) corrupt
and improper control of the deposit
of bankruptcy and (5) that he has
treated members of the bar coarsely,
indecently, arbitrarily and tyran
nically.
Meets Month Earlier.
Preliminary details of the in
volved impeachment procedure were
complied with during the last ses
sion of the senate and all prepara
tions have been made to begin the
actual trial when the upper house
reconvenes a month before the regu
lar session in a special session
called for that purpose.
The senate will be turned into a
court for the trial. Vice-President
Charles G. Dawes will preside but
the 96 members of the senate by
their votes will act as judges. The
house of representatives has ap
pointed members to act as prose
cutors of the impeachment charges
and English will be represented by
his own attorneys.
A notice already has been issued
to English to appear on the opening
day of the senate ready for trial.
Only nine federal officials in his
tory have been tried by the senate,
six of them judges. The only three
convicted were judges: John Pick
ering, judge of thd New Hampshire
district court who in 1803 was held
guilty of drunkenness and disregard
of the statutes and dismissed from
office; Robert W. Archbald, com
merce court judge, who in 1912 was
found guilty of corrupt collusion
with coal mine owners and railroad
officials and dismissed from office
and West H. Humphreys, Tennessee
district judge, who in 1862 was vot
ed unlawfully acting as judge of the
confederate district court and re
moved.
One Was President.
Others tried include Senator Wil
liam Blount, Tenn., charged with
conspiring to wage war with Spain

WASHINGTON—Members of la
bor organizations all over America
are being asked by the American
Federation of Labor today to “give
to the limit of their ability” to pro
vide food and clothing for the suf
fering families of striking Britisn
miners. Despite reports of the Brit
ish government that no suffering is

reached the point where suffering

tense.
Give Chief Free Hand.
LONDON—Late tonight the min
ers* delegates’ conference, in session
here, resolved by a majority of 330
out of 2,000 votes, to authorize the
executive committee to “take neces
sary steps to submit proposals for
setting up a national agreement for
the mining industry.” The vote of
the delegates represented about BGO,-
000 miners in favor of negotiating
a settlement, and 225,000 against.
It is significant that the resolution
is free from reservations respecting
hours and wages.
While the decision represents the
most material approach the miners’
federation yet has made toward
peace, It still clashes with declara
tions of the owners that they cannot
negotiate a settlement as a national
body, being determined on district
settlements. The executive commit
tee of the federation Is expected to
get In early touch with the govern
ment following tonight’s decision.
Hajnacki Urges
Poles to Do Their
Part Primary Day
Recalling how desperately people
of other nations have fought and
bled for citizenship and personal
liberties, Leo Hajnacki, speaking in
Polish over the radio in behalf of
the Milwaukee County League of
Women Voters, last night, urged the
people of his nationality to vote at
the coming primary.
“The French, Russian and Amer
ican revolutions were fought to
throw off the yoke of an oppressive
nation —to acquire the right of suf
frage,” he said.
“The privileges of citizenship re
quire in return the performance of
the duties of citizenship, the most
important of which is the duty of
voting.”

was the horror of the soldiers in

among the duties of France’s sol
diers when Minister of War Paul
Painleve perfects his new plan, an
nounced yesterday.

not to peel potatoes,” M. Painleve
says.

ask for bids for thousands of vacu
um cleaners, electric potato peelers,

massage. But civilians will operate
these machine in the barracks.
Top sergeants, under the new
plan, will be selected by civil serv
ice examinations.

THIS SUMMERLESS SUMMER.
To the Editor of The Leader:
There has been so much comment
during and following the heated
spell of July and early August on
the failure of an alleged forecast
that 1926 would be summerless, that
I would like to furnish you the
facts.
No one has made any forecast
that either this year or next year
would be “summerless.” For three
years past I have made forecasts
that the crop season of 1926-1927 in
the southern hemisphere and the
crop season of 1927 in the northern
hemisphere would witness a return
of the conditions of 1816, the his
torically famous “year without a
summer.” That title was given to
the year by English papers in 1816
and adopted in America. It has
been used by me because it was the
title of the year, just as I would
refer to George Washington as
“The Father of His Country,” with
out charging promiscuity.
To illustrate: Over the whole
northwestern section of 4he United
States and Canada south to the
Ohio and Potomac rivers, there
was a snowstorm June 17-19, 1816,
followed later by freezing tempera
tures and ice the night of July 4
and during the first week of Au
gust. Yet there were intervals of
warmth. What would be the ef
fect on all crops—corn, wheat, bar
ley, oats, potatoes and vegetables
generally—to have a repetition of
that weather on approximately the
same dates in 1927? Would it not
be disastrous? Would it not re
quire the war powers of the govern
ment fully exerted to avert famine?
Remember, the same type of weath
er occurred quite generally all over
Europe and into Asia in 1816, ex
tending into North Africa and the
West Indies. The records are in
sufficient to indicate how far it ex
tended into the unsettled west of
North America.
The markets are just discovering
what I had forecasted many months
ago, that the world is even now fac
ing a grain shortage approximating
a billion bushels. This includes
wheat, rye, corn, barley and oats.
In the United States, east of the
Mississippi, tens of millions of bush
els of winter wheat unthreshed on
Aug. 2U were sprouting in the
shucks from incessant and heavy
rains.
1 enclose evidence in confirmation,
calling attention by portions of the
articles in question that what I
meant was violent swings from
heat to cold, from droughts to floods
—in other words, the wrong weath
er at the wrong time, the so-called
"averages” of temperature and rain
fall could be normal.
The Dearborn independent, April
7, 1923: “Weather history justifies
the statement that variations which
affect future conditions, like ex
tremely dry weather on the Western
plains and a thin Canadian snow
cover, continue to a grand climac
teric of abnormality, which in
America takes the form of a nation
wide drought, or a repetition of that
extraordinary year, 1816, ‘The Year
Without a Summer.’
“In either form, the probabilities
are for a continuation of the freak
weather of 1920-1922, until, perhaps,
1926-1927, the period for the recur
rence of the great 55.8 year cycle
of maxima of sunspots and Aurora
Borealis.”
This statement was made in more
extended form before the committee
on agriculture of the house of rep
resentatives on Feb. 6, 1923, and ap
pears on pages 160-170, document of
.he house committee on agriculture,
67th congress, third and fourth ses
sions, published under the title,
“Stabilizing Prices of Farm Prod
ucts,” (with particular reference to
page 169).
American Agriculturist, June 28,
1924: “I again sound the warning
that the years 1926-1927 threaten
grave disaster to the grain crops of
the whole world.”
Bulletin, Sept. 4, 1925: “I have
no hesitation in advising the most
extensive planting of winter wheat
and rye which can be undertaken.
The world is too near the danger
years of 1926-27 not to exert every

mony.

which is that of her millionaire
father.”
Berlin could not be reached today
to confirm the report.

CHICAGO MOVIE
THEATERS FACE
MUSIC STRIKE
CHICAGO—Strike orders will be
issued to all musicians employed in
Chicago motion picture and vaude
ville theaters Sunday night, after
performance, unless the theater
managers grant the wage increase
and working hour demands of the
players, James C. Petrillo, president,
Chicago Federation of Musicians,
declared last night.
May Be Nationwide.
That the walkout may become na
tionwide was indicated in a dis
patch from Seattle, where the
Orpheum theater manager an
nounced that a general strike of mu
sicians had been called in all the
aters of the Orpheum vaudeville cir
cuit by Joseph Weber, international
president of the union. The strike
order was issued, it was asserted, in
connection with a walkout of mu
sicians in San Francisco.
Yesterday members of the Ex
hibitors’ Association of Chicago met
to discuss the situation.
On adjournment it was announced
by Jack Miller, the association’s
business representative, that theater
managers are willing to grant the
musicians a wage increase, but in
sist on the right to adjust certain
working rules.
Miller said the managers also are
willing to submit the controversy to
arbitration, but that this method of
adjustment was rejected by Petrillo.
Where They Differ.
The union is demanding a wage
boost from $82.50 to SB6 a week, an
increase in rehearsal rates from $2
to $4, a rest period of 20 minutes in
stead of the present 15 minutes, and
a reduction of the Sunday seven
hour day to six hours to correspond
with the weekday schedule.
Motion picture theater managers
want to reduce the working shifts
from six hours to five and a half
hours on week days, the extra time
to be added to the Saturday and
Sunday schedules. Vaudeville man
agers claim they should be entitled
to the privilege of discharging mu
sicians at any time during the sea
son. Union rules specify that once
a musician is hired beyond the two
week period he shall continue in
that employment for a full season.

MEXICO CITY Business men
of Mexico fear enactment of a new
labor law.
The new session of congress,
which began last night and contin
ues to Dec. 31, is expected to con
sider the labor bill, which passed
the chamber of deputies last year.
The bill, viewed sympathetically
by the government, requires employ*
ers to share profits with employes
and prescribes workmen’s benefits
required of employers.
Some business men have said
these requirements would force them
to close. Official reports were
made to the United States last
year that the measure would harm
American business interests more
than the alien land and petroleum
laws.
No Burden, Claim.
Business in Mexico was bad be
fore the religious crisis began, and
It has been affected further by
the economic boycott.
Labor leaders deny the law will
be unjustly burdensome.
If congress fails to enact the bill,
organized labor may try to have the
president promulgate it. Soma of
its provisions are:
Employes’ committees are em
powered to examine employers’
books and fix amount of profits to
be divided with workmen.
Employers must pay minimum
wagos determined by workmen's
committees.
Eighty per cent of the employes
of every concern must be Mexican
citizens.
Provide for Injuries.
Workmen’s compensation for in
juries is provided for.
Employers are required to depos
it with the government such sums
as the president may require to
guarantee fulfillment.
Mexico’s new chamber of depu
ties was condemned as “illegitimate”
yesterday in a manifesto signed by
deputies belonging to the coalition
or regional party.
The manifesto declared the cham
ber was organized and installed in
office through the employment es
the national army.
The signatures on the document
Include that of Francisco Labastida
Izquierdo, a close friend and polit
ical associate of former President
Obregon.

SEE THE VIKING SHIPS.
I suppose it is natural, but every
time I bring friends to Norway they
ask, “Where can we see the Viking
ships?’’ They seem to be as im
portant a lure as the little Edel
e’ flower in Switzerland, or the
om in which the little princes
were murdered in the Tower of
London. And why not? You can
not see Vikings or their ships to
day and they are as fuL of interest
as anything else in this northern
kingdom. Prof. Gustafson says:
"The most noteworthy objects in
Oslo are beyond all question the
venerable relics from the days of
the Vikings. Neither within nor be
yond the frontiers of Norway can
we find other vessels preserved
from the ]>eriod when the Norwe
gian Vikings set forth with their
fleets and visited the coasts of Eu
rope, Iceland, Greenland and even
reached the shores of North Amer
ica, which continent they were the
first to discover.” The vessels to
day are eared for by the University,
the Gokstad and the Ostberg ships
being the most interesting.

POINCARE AS A
PACIFIST HARD
PILL TO TAKE
Leader Special Service.
PARlS—Premier Poincare in the
role of a pacifist is such an unusual
and paradoxial sight that a great
many journalists of Europe find it
almost incredible.
It is noted as a fact, however,
that parliament and the various
government committees have really
speeded up their work since Poin
care took hold of the state machine.
A great deal of comment is de
voted to the remarkable change of
roles which took place since the
Briand-Caillaux cabinet tried to get
the sanction of parliament for a
debt funding plan with the United
States.
Roles Are Changed.
At that time, Poincare, Tardieu,
Bokanowsky and Marin were bit
terly opposed to the acceptance of
the Mellon plan. Now the first
three, in control of the government,
are anxious to put over what they
fought in parliament, whereas
Marin, the leader of the reaction
aries in parliament', still hangs
back.
On the other hand, Herriot has
also abandoned what he once
preached so vehemently.
It is expected that the Marin re
actionaries will also give in to Mel
lon, later on, perhaps when the
French parliament convenes after
the vacations.
A great deal of satisfaction is ex
pressed in various quarters over the
fact that the advent of Poincare to
power has not prevented the conclu
sion of a French-German commer
cial treaty.
French Favor Accord.
For the last two years,' the ne
gotiations between the German and
French governments over this com
mercial treaty dragged along incon
clusively. Now the thing is done,
and even the press close to Poin
care expresses satisfaction.
Le Matin even writes that the
French-German treaty opens the
way to an economic Locarno pact.
This is certainly due to the pressure
of public opinion which has become
more and more insistent upon more
cordial relations between French
and Germans.

WORLD PEACE
CONGRESS HAS
HUGE MEETING
Leader Special Service.
PARIS—A great peace demonstra
tion was recently staged under rhe
auspices of the world peace con
gress in one of the big theaters here
with the collaboration of the inter
national labor bureau of the league
of nations.
Arthur Fontaine, president of the
board of management of the inter
national labor offfice, opened the
demonstration with an address, in
which he said that the distinction
between the former allies and their
enemies has no longer any meaning.
Today men and women of all na
tions are united in a nation of
peace, he declared^ Francesco Nitti,
former premier of Italy, pledged
himself again to the cause of peace
and recalled that his first official
act at the head of the Italian gov
ernment had been to avoid a war
with Soviet Russia.
Recalls Georgian Raid.
Nitti recalled that the allies had
tried to persuade him to attack
Soviet Russia through Georgia. He
had refused in spite of bitter press
attacks on himself. Two months
later events had proved him right,
for the Bolshevists had marched
into Georgia and driven the allies
out.
Pointing to Switzerland, which
succeeded throughoiut the World
war in maintaining its neutrality
with a population consisting of Ger
mans, Frenchmen and Italians, Nitti
prophesied that Europe would es
cape war, if it would form a federa
tion like the Swiss.
Before the war, Nitti said, there
were 25 states in Europe. Now there
are 35. New tariff fences have been
erected everywhere. They must be
taken down, in the interest of peace.
Defends Popular Democracy.
Democratic liberties are essential
for the maintenance of peace, Nitti
maintained. Even a bad parliament
is better than none. Peace cannot
be kept when dictators rule nations.
Of course, Nitti said with sar
casm, dictators are welcome at first
to certain circles, but they are a
confession of political incapacity.
Gen. Perrau, of the French army,
also denounced war and war psy
chology. He would not hesitate to
choose a man like Pasteur, who
saved human lives, if asked to
choose between him and a mass
killer like Napoleon.
Mr. Bergstraesser, member of the
German reichstag.^said that one of
the best ways to promote peace is
for nations to respect one another.
Every nation contributes something
worth while to the common evolu
tion of civilization.
Enemies Must Unite.
All nations suffered from the war,
Bergstraesser pointed out. All have
now the same interest in undoing
the evil work of hatred and de
struction.
Not only the walls of hatred, but
the tariff walls must be taken down.

TROOPS LAND TO
PROTECTYANKS
IN NICARAGUA
WASHINGTON With arrival
today of the United States S. S.
Rochester at Bluefields, Nicaragua,
American interests will be doubly
guarded when government troops
and revolutionists battle for control
of El Bluff across the harbor.
The city of Bluefields was de
clared a neutral zone several days
ago by the U. S. S. Galveston, and
now is occupied by marines and
bluejackets. The United States, how
ever, is taking no part in the dispute
but is protecting interests of Ameri
can citizens.
Yanks Are Ready.
An additional 500 marines and
bluejackets will be held in readiness
by the Rochester, should the fight
ing spread into the neutral zone, the
navy department said. Skirmishing
is reported to have started already
in the vicinity of El Bluff.
Several hundred Americans are
said to live inland near Bluefields
and have large property holdings.
No deaths have been reported in
that vicinity, but two Americans are
believed to have been killed at
Brangman’s Bluff, 120 miles up
the coast.
El Bluff Is Sought.
After two weeks of fighting revo
lutionists are said to be in control
of the northeastern coast. Their im
mediate objective is El Bluff, the
strategic point which overlooks the
harbor of Bluefields.
Government troops are said to be
in possession of the stronghold
which was bombarded last week.
Quiet prevails on the west coast,
according to official reports, after
the engagement at Coseguinea, in
which more than 100 were killed
and an equal number injured. The
U. 8. S. Tulsa, which has been sta
tioned on the west coast, is convey
ing the wounded to relief stations
at Corinto.
Economic and technical progress are
best promoted by free trade.
In Europe, one of the greatest
steps in the direction of promoting
peace would be a close union of
France and Germany. The present
co-operation between French and
Germans for peace was a tremend
ous progress compared to the Ver
sailles decree in 1919.

SHAW PREDICTS
WORLD DEVOID
OF ALL SOCIETY
LONDON Bernard Shaw
sketches a misanthropical world
devoid of neighborliness in the out
line of a Fabian society lecture he
intends to give next winter
In the synopsis of his lecture
Shaw writes:
“Among the visions of the future
in which our men of letters have
occasionally indulged is one by
Rudyard Kipling. In it he fore
casts a state of society in which the
first concern of each household is
that it shall not be overlooked.
“Like the Boers, the inhabitants
of each house insist that no neigh
bor’s house shall be visible from
their windows. They surround their
houses with electric hedges to shock
off callers. They resent even the
harmless and necessary postman,
and are furious when an airman
trespasses on their sky.
“This, if only one side of life, is
a real side. Modern science encour
ages it.
“Formerly we did not dare to let
ourselves know that man is a de
testable^ animal. Having to asso
ciate with him willy-nilly, we have
had to make the best of him. When
exceptional persons like Shakes
peare and Swift called him an
angry ape and a yahoo we had to
rebuke their pessimism. But that
we secretly agreed with him can be
doubted by nobody who has seen
the scowl of murderous hate with
which the occupants of a railway
carriage, especially a second-class
carriage, receive the stranger whose
valises claim the unoccupied seat.”

PASSAIC, N. J.—With the char
tering yesterday of Passaic Local
No. 1603, United Textile Workers
workers of Passaic and vicinity,
who have waged a heroic battle for
•he last 32 weeks against the tex
?le barons, became affiliated with
:he American Federation of Labor,
thus fulfilling one of the major
aims announced from the beginning
of the strike by the former leader
ship.
With the continued backing of
the American Federation of Labor,
which, now that the strikers have
been admitted Into the United Tex
tile Workers. will be intensified a
thousand-fold, the strikers expect
to bring their 224-day strike to a
speedy and victorious close.
To Ask Probe.
Henry T. Hunt, vice-chairman of
the Lauck committee, through
which the American Federation of
Labor affiliation was negotiated,
said yesterday that the work of the
committee was not yet ended, as it
had been asked by the United Tex
tile Workers to collaborate in fur
ther negotiations with the mill own
ers.
Mr. Hunt also said that the work
of organizing a general committee
of 100 to promote a congressional
investigation of the textile industry
with special attention to tariffs and
wage scales, will be proceeded with.
“I would advise the textile bar
ons to put their house in order be
fore this investigation,” Mr. Hunt
added, “as they are in no position
to go before the public now.”
He pointed out as an absurdity
the 74 per cent protective tariff im
posed on the American consumer
through the tax on imported textile
goods, which, he said, combined
with the miserably low wages paid
their workers, enables the Ameri
can textile manufacturers to make
100 per cent profits.
The new charter is dated Aug.
30, and 4,500 of the 8,000 union
cards are ready for distribution in
Passaic as soon as the executive
committee of the strikers goes
through the formality of accepting
the charter from the ijauck commit
tee, to whom the charter has been
turned over by the United Textile
Workers. Eight thousand strikers
have enrolled so far, but the lines
are still, long at 743 Main Ave., and
it is confidently predicted that over
12,000 will enter the new American
Federation of Labor union.
Weisbrod Steps Aside.
Albert Weisbrod, the organizer of
the strike and leader through the
last seveh months of heroic strug
gle, will step aside as soon as the
strikers accept, the charter of the
United Textile Workers in accord
ance with Lis promise during the
early negotiations when the United
Textile Workers demanded his
withdrawal from the strike as the
basis of their acceptance of the
strikers into a local. Weisbrod for
the last several weeks has been ral
lying the strikers to the United
Textile Workers and doing every
thing in his power to keep their
ranks Intact and turn over a 100
per cent strike to the union. In
this he has fully succeeded, and the
strike today is still a 100 per cent
strike
$5,904,774 Paid to
U. S. By Germany
Under Dawes Plan
WASHINGTO N—The United
States has received from Germany
on account of reparations under the
Dawes plan, which has just conclud
ed its second year of operation, $5,-
904,774, it was announced at the
treasury yesterday.
These payments apply to the
credit of the mixed claims commis
sion which is engaged in adjudicat
ing all claims of American citizens
against Germany growing out of the
war.
S. Parker Gilbert, agent general
for reparation payments, found it
possible to make practically all of
this country’s receipts from that
source by transfers of cash, in con
tradistinction to France, Belgium,
and some of the other allied nations
which receive the greater part of
their payments through “deliveries
in kind.”
Payments on account of the cost
of the army of occupation will start
with the third Dawes plan year,
which began Sept. 1. On account of
the larger suras which Germany will
be called upon to pay from now on
it is believed that the real test of the
Dawes plan will come during the
next year.

WASHINGTON—During August
the public debt was cut by $88,000,-
000, bringing the total reductions
for the last year Yo almost $1,000,-
000,000 and leaving the gross debt
at $19,534,371,300.
Most of the August reduction was
accomplished through the retire
ment of third Liberty loan bonds on
which the treasury is now applying
money from the sinking fund. These
bonds fall due in 1928, and $2,393,-
936.000 remains outstanding.
The net balance in the treasury
was cut during the month, however,
from $218,237,000 to $147,569,310.

Ten Government Operated Warehouses Urged For Farmers
WOULD ERECT
STOREROOMS
ON MISSISSIPPI
Barge Lines Would
Furnish Cheap
Transportation.
WASHINGTON —Construction by
the federal government of a series
of eight or 10 great terminal grain
elevator® at the principal railroad
crossing points on the Mississippi
river is under consideraion by Pres
ident Coolidge and members of his
cabinet as one of the major items
in the administration’s farm relief
program, it was learned yesterday.
The plan was proposed to admin
istration leaders by the board of
advisors of the Inland Waterways
corporation as a means of making
available to the grain producing
farmers of the west the cheap trans
portation provided by the barge
lines on the Mississippi river.
Operates Under Bond.
The proposal of the waterways
board provides that the elevators
shall be operated by the depart
ment of agriculture as bonded ware
houses.
H. W. Seaman, Chicago member
of the waterways board, said that
until recently he had been of the
opinion that rather than have the
government operate the elevators
under some duly guarded agency,
it would be better if they were to
be privately owned and operated, or
built by the government and then
leased to private interests —rail-
road, co-operative, or professional
warehousemen —but in any event
that their operation should be su
pervised by the government.
One Project Job.
“In the light of existing condi
tions inthe grain belt,” Mr. Seaman
said, “I have come to the conclu
sion that if the farmer is to obtain
the prompt and permanent relief
to which he is entitled, including
the low cost barge haulage, then
under all circumstances it will be
best if these public elevators be
built, and, for the time being at
least, be operated by a government
al agency that would function pref
erably through a division of the de 4
partment of agriculture.
“Another imperative reason for
the need for each and everyone of
these six or eight big storage ele
vators is that collectively they will
inswer but the one single purpose,
md consequently the job should be
undertaken as one project. Nego
tiations with the various railroads,
or with the as yet more or less em
bryonic farmers’ co-operative or
ganizations, would entail the loss of
too much time. Once built, how
ever, and their usefulness fully
demonstrated, they could then in
due time, if found expedient, be
transferred to private ownership or
operation.”
Take Over Elevators.
The Mississippi river, Mr. Sea
man said, has always been a power
ful factor in the regulation of trans
portation costs and it is essential
to the farmers of the west that the
‘river be opened up to their prod
ucts through the erection of river
bank elevators.
“The co-operative farmers’ asso
ciations are taking over the coun
try elevators,” he went on, “and
they are very properly looking for
the provision of complimentary ter
minal storage, free from the control
of either carriers or grain buying
houses. These interests are de
manding public elevators. They re
quire great storage reservoirs at
strategic locations, which will act
as concentrating points to which
their grains may be forwarded as
the interior elevators become con
gested.”
Rail Crossing Handy.
The rail crossings on the Missis
sippi were the logical locations for
the elevators, Mr. Seaman assert
ed, pointing out that from here the
grain may go to local mills or
moved up to Minneapolis or east
ward; it may go on to the Great
Lakes at Chicago, or down the river
to tidewater at New Orleans; corn
and oats may be moved down river
to complementary elevators at St.
Louis, Cairo, Helena. Memphis,
Vicksburg or New Orleans for
transshipment to consumers in the
southeast and southwest.
“These storage elevators will
thaw out, as it were, the grain
equipment periodically frozen when
thousands upon thousands of box
cars are massed at Baltimore and
other seaboard terminals awaiting
boat movements,” Mr. Seaman con
tinued.

NICKEL PLATE
MERGER SEEN
BY FINANCIER
NEW YORK —News and views on
general conditions continued cheer
ful yesterday. George F. Baker,
veteran chairman cf the First Na
tional bank of New York, returned
from Europe optimistic regarding
the country’s prospects. He inti
mated he does not expect the United^
States Steel corporation to do any-'
thing in the way of extra disburse
ments for the stockholders in the
immediate future, but he said the
advance in New York Central stock
shows the “public is beginning to
appreciate true values,” and he said
he expects the Nickel Plate railroad
merger to go through.
Steel Shipments Up.
“Railroad securities now are on
the point of being best fitted to be
safe investments for the average in
vestor,” Prof. W. Z. Ripley of Har
vard, who drafted a comprehensive
plan of railroad consolidations for
the interstate commerce commission,
said yesterday.
“Railroads have uniform account
ing methods and full publicity of
reports. They are operated at the
highest efficiency in their history
and are financed on a sound basis.”
Bank Clearings Down?
Shipments of steel by independent
companies in the Youngstown valley
during August established new high
records, with indications that the
volume will be surpassed in Septem
ber. On the other hand, President
Lamont said that the American
Steel Foundries Co.’s steel plants
are operating at about 50 per cent
of capacity and business is very
quiet.
Bank clearings at 126 cities of the
United States for August, as re
ported to Bradstreet’s, aggregated
$39,148,487,000, a decrease of 9 per
cent from July. A seasonal reac
tion, but a gain of 5 per cent over
August last year. Clearings for the
eight months of 1926 were $343,-
683,770,000, a gain of 5.1 per cent
over a year ago.
Coal Shows Gain.
Coal consumption for July totaled
37,424,000 tons, an increase over
June of 1,883,000 tons. Sustained
activity in most lines of industry is
held responsible for the enlarged
fuel demand. Bituminous produc
tion gained in July, the output for
the month being 43,472,000. Anthra
cite fields showed a drop of 5.7 per
cent from the previous months.
New Incorporations
Jump in August
NEW YORK—There were 652
new enterprises, each with a capi
talization of SIOO,OOO or more,
chartered during August with an
aggregate capital of $505,769,900,
according to figures compiled by The
Journal of Commerce. This repre
sents an increase over the preceding
month when capitalization totaled
$454,865,100, but shows a decline
from the corresponding month a
a year ago, which had a total of
$972,734,000. Textile, oil and gas
firms showed the greatest increase.

$473,420,230; last year it was
$412,643,914. Adding the totals of
real estate and personal property
valuations and multiplying by two,
the board arrives at the real valua
tion.

TORRENT HITS
CANADIAN GRAIN
WINNIPEG, Man. With the
hopes of the grain growers that this
wheat crop of western Canada
would total 400,000,000 bushels, with
100,000,000 from Alberta, a tremen
dous rainfall hit the northern part
of that province today. It is said
to be the heaviest in history. Every
river in the northern and western
part of Alberta is rising and cloud
bursts are reported from many sec
tions. The harvest has been set
back several days at the most crit
ical time.
Many thousands of dollars’ worth
of flowers were destroyed on the
eve of flower shows in larger cen
ters.
Rivers west of Calgary and Ed
monton are raging torrents, bridges
are being swept away, and ship
ments in coal mines -are at a
standstill owing to washouts on
railways. In Manitoba there has
been little rain and wheat thrash
ing is going ahead.
Every indication is that the yield
in western Canada will be greater
than the government report of Aug.
1 by 70,000,000 bushels.

Illinois Central road, yesterday was
retired under the system’s pension
plan.
Mr. Brennan had been chief coun
sel for the Illinois Contral for 30
years and has been practicing law
in Illinois since 1879. He announces
that he will conduct a private prac
tice.
The veteran lawyer is succeeded
by Vernon W. Foster, Chicago attor
ney for the road, who began as sec
retary to the auditor of passenger
receipts. His age is 45.
EXPECT 50,000
AT STEEL SHOW
CHICAGO —The world’s largest
industrial exhibition will be held at
the municipal pier, Chicago, Sept.
20 to 24. More than 50,000 persons
are expected to attend the eighth
annual steel and machine tool ex
position to be held in conjunction
with the convention of the Ameri
can Society for Steel Treating.
More than 80,000 square feet of
space will be required by the 350 or
more exhibitors. The entire pier,
2,280 feet long, has been reserved
for the exhibit.
An elaborate program has been
prepared for the convention, in
cluding technical papers prepared
by authors well known in metal
lurgical fields of America and Eu
rope.
Municipal pier is a busy place this
week in preparation for the big
event. More than 25 carloads of
machinery have been received.
The annual banquet will be held
in the ballroom of the Drake hotel
Sept. 23, 6:30 p. m. Certificates of
honorary membership in the Amer
ican Society of Steel Treating will
be given E. J. Buffington, president
of the Illinois Steel Co., and Charles
M. Schwab, chairman of the Bethle
hem Steel corporation. E. H. Gary,
chairman of the United States
Steel corporation, will be unable to
attend the convention.

LESS INTEREST
IN HISTORY;
BLAME WRITERS
NEW YORK—History is not get
ting proper attention from the read
ing public, the American Historical
Assn. declares in a report pub
lished recently.
To find out what H wrong with
history, the committee on the writ
ing of history of the American His
torical society reports it called a
consultation of Dr. J. Franklin
Jameson, managing editor of the
American Historical Review, and
Ellery Sedgwick, editor of The At
lantic Monthly.
The recorded opinion of Dr. Ja
meson, director of the department of
historical research of the Carnegie
Institute, was that historians do
not write well enough tn compete
with story tellers for public atten
tion.
“As to smoothness of expression
and consequent ease of reading,” Dr.
Jameson said, “it often seems im
possible that the writer can have
read a single paragraph aloud. It
is possible to maintain —and it has
been done—that history has no bus
iness to be either interesting or at
tractive; but it is not possible to
maintain that austere position and
at the same time complain that
what we write has no effect upon
the public mind.
Lack General Culture.
“What is the reason for these de
ficiencies?” Dr. Jameson continued.
“Mainly, I think, that many of those
who undertake the writing of his
tory enter upon it with too little of
general or literary cultivation, and
this is largely because of the habit
of specializing prematurely.”
Mr. Sedgwick, editor of The At
lantic Monthly since 1909, recorded
his opinion as follows:
“Interest in history has undergone
a long and'slow decline. The rea
son is not inherent, for there has
certainly never been a time when
the lessons of history called for so
wide an application. It is the his
torians themselves who seem at
fault. They have catalogued and
dissected and subdivided history in
a way repugnant to normal human
Interest.
Terrify Ordinary Man.
“Great historical enterprises,
such as the Cambridge History,”
Mr. Sedgwick continued, “are writ
ten by a small and read by a large
group of specialists. The ordinary
man feels the terrifying complexi
ties of the subject and knows that
to master it in any degree he must
wade through a whole series of vol
umes. He craves the things—a gen
eral synthesis whereby he may try
at least to see history steadily and
whole, and the return of that old
fshioned preoccupation with the
leaders of the race which used to
etimulate the imagination and give
the personal note which most of us
still desire.
“Whatever the learned historlal
may say, a good book like Wels’
Outline of History has been a very
great stimulus to the study of his
tory. Yet Wells does- not give
those individual Imaginative por
traits which once drew the world
to Macauley and Carlyle. I be
lieve, therefore, that we need more
general histories in which the cur
rent of narrative flows continu
ously through some considerable
period; and second, biographies in
scale.
Suggest the Realities.
“Speaking for The Atlantic, I
may say that I incline distinctively
toward the publication of original
and racy documents—the story of
a Quaker in the Revolutionary war,
the record of an early journey
across the plains, anything of a
private and conspicuous sort which
might suggest from its character
the realities of other times. Per
haps I should lay special stress
upon the desirability of publishing
important extracts from diaries.
There is nothing like a personal
journal for giving a reader at once
a sense of the individuality of the
writer and a conviction that the
views he expresses are absolutely
unvarnished.”
The statements of Mr. Sedgwick
and Dr. Jameson are appended to
the report of the American Histo
rical Assn.’s committee on the Writ
ing of History, composed of former
Ambassador Jean Jules Jusserand,
Prof. Wilbur Cortz Abbott of Har
vard, Charles W. Colby and Prof.
John Spencer Bassett of Smith
college.

SAYS ENGLAND
FEARS OPINION
OF 11. S. ON INDIA
CHICAGO American public
opinion is the only public opinion in
the world that England cares for,
according to Dr. Annie Besant,
world leader of the Theosophical
society, who yesterday spoke on con
ditions in India in her first public
lecture here, following the close of
the society’s convention.
Dr. Besant spoke from the plat
form of the Studebaker theater,
which was jammed to the doors and
with an overflow crowd on the
stage.
Makes Us Responsible.
“If you would realize that Eng
land cares only for your opinion,”
she went on, “I could say that you
are responsible. for conditions in
India.
“My position is not to prove to
you that India has the right to rule
herself, but to ask you if England
can prove her right to rule India.
I charge that while Britain’s rule
is efficient in railways, posts and
governments, it is monstrously in
efficient in the matters of the wel
fare of the people.
Tells of Conditions.
“For"instance, 40,000,000 of peo
ple pass through life with only one
meal a day, and 78 per cent of the
children are suffering from diseases
caused by malnutrition.”
Dr. Besant and a group of In
dians have prepared a Common
wealth of India bill, which has been
taken up by the Labor party, which,
she says, will be the next party in
control in England, and will be
placed by them before the next
parliament.

LABOR DAY
THE MILWAUKEE LEADER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 3,
The perfect time for a beach
party is the late afternoon and
early twilight. It is then, after the
heat of the day has subsided and
the calm of evening has descended,
that the camp fire burns clearer
and the odors of food cooked out
of doors smell more alluring. There
is nothing more satifying than the
faint aroma of coffee wafted across
the still air to a group of people
who are resting after the walk to
the beach and the exertion of gath
ering wood for the fire.
It is moreover the signal to gath
er up cup and spoons and to open
the lunch basket which may pro
vide the supper all prepared or the
makings in the form of bacon and
rolls, or some other favorite food
that can be cooked quickly over the
fire.
For a small crowd, the latter type
of lunch is usually preferred, as
preparing and cooking the food Is
part of the fun. Among the stand
ard dishes are broiled steak or
bacon, cooked either on pointed
sticks or on a wire rack placed
over the coals and eaten sandwich
fashion between halves of buttered
buns.
For a change, however, toasted
cheese sandwiches with fried
bacon, and small whole tomatoes
form a good combination. Slice the
loaf of bread at home, packing it
back in the original waxed paper.
Also slice the cheese thinly. To
make the sandwiches, place the
cheese between two slices of bread,
skewer them together firmly with
toothpicks provided for the purpose,
and toast the outer surfaces by
holding over the fire on a stick.
A dessert which is easy to make
and which is usually a great favor
ite, is a French pancake. It con
sists of a very simple batter that
can be prepared at home in a few
minutes and carried to the beach
in a glass jar where it is cooked
in a skillet heated over the coals.
A recipe is given below for this
dessert as well as for picnic tarts
which will serve in its place if the
hostess prefers a ready to serve
sweet.
Taffy Tartlets—Two cups brown
sugar, two tablespoons shortening,
four teaspoons cold water, two eggs,
two teaspoons vanilla.
Beat eggs, add sugar and vanilla.
Then add water and melted shorten
ing. Mix well. Pour into shells
and bake in a moderate oven (375
degrees F.) until firm.
Shells—One and one-half cups
flour, one-half cup shortening, one
half teaspoon salt, cold water.

French Pancakes —Two eggs, two
teaspoons baking powder, one tea
spoon salt, one cup milk, one cup
flour, one tablespoon melted short
ening.
Sift together baking powder, salt
and flour. Stir in eggs, milk and
melted shortening. Beat until
smooth. Pour into grease griddle,
making each cake about five inches
across. Cook until nearly done,
then turn and brown other side.
Cake should be very thin, spread
jelly roll and dust with powdered
sugar.
WHAT IS GOOD
PASTRY?
To make good, flaky and tender
pastry is an accomplished art, and
it is more often said that pies are
of poorer quality than any other
baked food.
Tfie less the dough is handled the
crisper, more tender and lighter
the crust will be. To have pies
which fairly melt in your mouth,
you must be light of hand when
working with the dough.
To have a light pie crust, a small
amount of baking powder added im
proves the texture. If you want a
crisp, tender crust, add only
enough cold water to hold the in
gredients together, for it is too much
liquid which results in a tough
crust. The large amount of fat
acts as a liquid during the baking.
Flaky pastry results when the
fat is cut into the dry inugredients
and left in large pieces instead of
cutting in small ones. Then when
the dough is rolled there are layers
of flour and fat.
Many housewives make the mis
take of cooking their pies too
quickly and at too high a temper
ature. When baked this way pas
try is difficult to digest. Fats that
are heated to a high temperature
recompose and are less readily di
gested, and for this reason they
should be baked more slowly.

CINCINNATI Immigration Di
rector Thomas today received a

The Labor Day Picnic
The coming of Labor day means
the beginning of school and an end
to the many picnics and outings of
the summer months. Since Labor
day is often regarded as the last
holiday of the picnicking season, it
should be made the outstanding out
ing of the summer to be pleasantly
remembered during the long winter
days when the snow has covered all
the picnic spots.
Many families rent a cottage at
some interesting lake for these
three days and let the children
romp in the open while they swim,
golf or rest. This, to me, is an ideal
way to spend Labor day, since this
day was made a holiday especially
for the working people to enjoy.
But, no matter whether you rent a
cottage or pack your lunch and go
into the woods just for a day and
return home at night, the lunch
still must be a picnic lunch and
planned as such. A camp fire al
ways adds to the coziness of a meal
in the open and is so thoroughly
enjoyed by the children. So why
not pick out a place where you may
safely build a camp fire for this
last outing?
Sandwiches are usually the foun
dation of the picnic lunch and with
a camp fire, very delicious’ hot
sandwiches may be made of ham
burger, wieners or steak. The steak
may be cut into pieces about four
inches square and broiled on the
end of long sticks over the fire. It
is very delicious cooked in this
fashion but quite expensive and the
hamburg or wieners taste quite as
delicious when everybody is eating
them out in the open.

HT SEEMS that the current pennant races have failed to develop
an outstanding club, a real machine that could be rated on a
par—or somewhere close to that point—with some of the old
combinations still fresh in memory. There are the Yankees,
of course, a better-than-average ball club, but still not to be
compared with the old-time outfits. We’re speaking of the old Cubs, the
old Athletics and the pennant-winning Giants of Matty's time. Perhaps
there have been better ball clubs than these were, and, then again, per
haps not. But there never was a club that carried more names that are
still remembered than any of these three.
Take the old Cubs —Frank Chance, Three-Finger Brown. Frank
Schulte, Johnny Evers, Joe Tinker, Johnny Kling, Artie Hofman and
Jimmy Sheckard, just to name a few. There was a team covered with
color, dash and action, a team of mechanical skill and brains.

And then came the great Mack
machine—with Barry, Collins and
Mclnnis, taking up where Tinker,
Evers and Chance left off. It
would be out of order to break
off here without mentioning the one
and only Home Run Baker.
That old Cub crew found Coombs,
Bender and Plank just a little too
much to handle through a short
series. It’s doubtful if any one
team ever carried greater boxmen in
its prime than the Colby Carbine,
the Chippewa Chief and the Gettys
burg Gatling.
It may be that in years to come
another great club with the same
pitching strength will happen along,
yet—
But with all of this the Mackmen
of that regime were second to the
Cubs of Chance in vivid color and
dash. There was a club.

These clubs held the baseball spot
light from 1906 to 1914, winning
eight pennants and five world series.
They are to be rated among the best
of all time with the famous Orioles
of the 90’s and the Boston team that
included Tenney, Lowe, Long and
Collins.
This quartet of clubs, beyond
question, is the richest in tradition,
strongest in achievement and great
est in achievement and greatest in
memory. It may be a long time
before another team comes along to
join in the march down through
the years.

OFFERED BIG
PRICE TO ROB
JACK OF TITLE
ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—“l was
offered a fortune to ‘steal’ the
world’s championship from Jack
Dempsey in 1023,” was' the aston
ishing statement made yesterday by
Jimmy Dougherty of Ridley Park,
Pa., who refereed the encounter be
tween Tom Gibbons and the cham
pion at Shelby, Mont.
“After I was named referee of
that fight,” Dougherty continued,
“a man came to me and said if I
would award the decision to Gibbons
on a foul or in any other way he
would give me a sum of money that
was enormous. I laughed at him
and told him to go to hell. I didn’t
see him again until I arrived in
Shelby. He was there then.
Proposition is Renewed.
“He renewed the proposition and
nearly doubled the original offer.
My answer was the same. Then he
offered me a lot of money If I would
agree to at least call it a draw if
both men were on their feet at the
end. I refused him.
“I knew what his game was. He
was the tool of a big gambling gang,
and if I had agreed to his proposi
tion they would have made a big
cleanup by taking the short end and
backing Gibbons.
“I have told this story before—
but only in confidence. Today I
am telling it straight. Dempsey told
me I was not his friend, and it
made me mad.
Friendly to Dempsey.
“I want the world to know that
I proved my friendship for him in
3923 by refusing to sell my decision,
which would have deprived him of
the title and knocked him out of his
chance to get that $470,000 for fight
ing Firpo.”
Dempsey and Dougherty were
friends as long as the Dempsey-
Kearns alliance lasted.

Death Comes to Ben
Welch, Comedian
Ben Welch, 52, veteran burlesque
and musical show comedian, is dead
at the Kings Park, L. 1., hospital,
where he was taken Aug. 25, suffer
ing from bronchial pneumonia,
Welch, who refused to leave the
stage when total blindness overtook
him at the height of his career, had
been in poor health for the last four
years, but he insisted upon filling
his numerous vaudeville contracts.
The comedian, internationally
known for his Yiddish characteriza
tions, began his career in a Hoboken
burlesque house at $1 a performance
and rose to a salary of $50,000 a
year. He appeared here last at the
Palace two seasons ago. He had
been a frequent visitor here previ
ously.

ranean sharks. The operatic feet

ANNEXATION OF
BIG TRACT ON
2ND TRY SEEN
Annexation to Milwaukee of a
1,700-acre tract with its 700 resi
dents appears likely, it was an
nounced today by George A. Alt
peter, head of the city annexation
department.
Includes Lincoln Park.
The tract in the town of Milwau
kee, including Lincoln park, is
bounded by the north city limits,
27th St., Silver Spring road and the
North Western road, appears to be
scheduled for annexation as the re
sult of the recent meeting of resi
dents and property owners in the
district, in which 154 of the 320
signed a petition requesting annex
ation.
The petition will be presented to
the common council Sept. 13.
The tract is the one which the
city attempted to annex two years
ago. At that time, however, de
spite the fact that every resident
and property holder living therein
was in favor of annexation, a large
manufacturing concern in the dis
trict owned so much land with such
a large valuation that it was able
to block the annexation.
Situation Is Altered.
With the building of approxi
mately 150 homes since that time
the property valuation of the small
holder has increased to the point
where they can now defeat the
manufacturers, according to Mr.
Altpeter.

What Old Party Politicians Say
PROGRESSIVES
SUPPORT DEM.
—SCHAFER.
Congressman John C. Schafer,
speaking at Sheboygan yesterday,
made the following statement:
“In the wet territory, the Madi
son ring candidates have been car
rying on a whispering campaign,
telling the voters who are in favor
of modification of the Volstead act
that Zimmerman is an Anti-Saloon
league candidate and that Ekern is
in favor of modification.
“We all know that there is no
man who is politically or personally
drier than Mr. Ekern, but even
granting him to be as wet as he is
claimed to be in wet territory, what
would he do to amend the federal
prohibition law which two wet gov
ernors have not done during the
last 12 years.
“Do not be confused by this whis
pering of the Madison ring crowd
and their cohorts. If you want the
Volstead law amended, look to your
federal officials and your members
of congress.”
“The campaign edition of Labor
issued Aug. 21, hundreds of thou
sands of copies of which are being
circulated in Wisconsin, states
when indorsing Charles A. Kading
for congress in the 2nd district that
he ‘has an excellent record as a
public official and always has been
a La Follette progressive.’ The
voters of Wisconsin well know that
the editor of Labor has been fur
nished with incorrect information,
for Mr. Kading has repeatedly been
elected to office on the Democratic
ticket, and ran for attorney general
in 1914 on the Democratic ticket
with Mr. Karel, who was the Demo
cratic candidate for governor. The
progressives, including members of
the Madison ring slate, branded the
Karel-Kading ticket as reactionary,
and carried on an intensive cam
paign against them.
“The campaign edition of Labor
also states, referring to Theodore
Dammann, who is now paraded as
the only progressive candidate for
secretary of state, ‘while a progres
sive leader in Milwaukee for many
years, has never held public office.’
This assertion is also incorrect, as
the citizens of Milwaukee county
well know that Mr. Dammann did
hold public office, and was elected
county treasurer in 1912, 1914 and
1916, and defeated in 1918.
“This same Mr. Dammann was
not progressve enough to receive
the indorsement of the late Sena
tor La Follette in 1924. At that
time the senator indorsed Fred R.
Zimmerman, and stated, ‘I have
known Fred Zimmerman for 20
years and he has always been right.’
Notwithstanding the indorsement of
Zimmerman by the late senator,
Theodore Dammann ran against
Zimmerman and is quoted as hav
ing said, ‘What the do we care
for La Follette?’”

Told By Lenroot

day that his successful efforts to

ers of Wisconsin than all the rad
ical promises that have been made

m investigation.”

Walton Disciples
In Weekend Rush
To Trout Streams
More than 200 Milwaukeeans have
made reservations for the fisher
man’s special, leaving today, 8:25 p.
m., over the Milwaukee road for
northern Wisconsin, and over 400
are expected to ride the same train
tomorrow night, according to J. C.
Prien, passenger agent.
It will be necessary to run the
train in two sections both nights,
Mr. Prien said.

one more day to the week-end vaca
tion, is the argument which will con
vince local Waltonians to hie them
selves to the trout streams, Mr.
Prien said.

Wisconsin Rapids, Wausau, Merrill,
Tomahawk, Trout Lake, Boulder
Junction and other lake and resort
points.

Daggett Appeal
MADISON, Wis.—Appealing to
all voters who wish to see “con
ditions at Madison changed,” H. B.
Daggett, chairman of the Repub
lican executive committee, in a
statement made public today urged
support of Charles B. Perry, Repub
lican candidate for the nomination
for governor, because “Perry is a
Republican. He belongs to neither
lunatic fringe of reactionary or
radical.”
“I appeal for support of Perry
first and foremost because of his
record and standing,” the statement
says. “He was one of the leaders
in the most courageous fight ever
put up in the Wisconsin legislature
against the present system of tax
ation.
“He has led the fight since 1911
against the initiative and referen
dum, and to his efforts as much as
to any other person is due the credit
for stopping it before it reached the
stage where it was about to be
come a menace to certain rights
still retained by the people.”
Zimmerman Gives
Reasons for High
Office Expenses
Explaining that the cost of ex
ecuting the new title license fee
law, in operation this year for the
first time, naturally has increased
the cost of operating the depart
ment over a given cost for the year
preceding, Secretary of State Fred
R. Zimmerman declared here in c
campaign speech last night that
“charges by the Madison ring can
didate for secretary of state that
the cost of conducting the affairs
of the department have increased
without good reason are absolutely
false.”
“The added cost of new machin
ery to take care of the mechanical
end of the administration of this
new title license fee law is a cost
which will occur only the first
year,” Zimmerman said, “because
the same machinery can be used
next year and years following.
“The title law, which was passed
by the last session of the legisla
ture, almost doubled the work of
this department and is responsible
for the increased cost of adminis
tration over 1924.”

Wets and Drys
Declaring that he stands on the

ture and assailing candidates who
are “wet in wet territory and dry
in dry territory,” Senator Ben Get
telman last night spoke at a meet
ing of voters of the fifth district,

Get Out the Vote,
Plea of Levitan
MENONONEE FALLS, Wis.—
Stressing the importance of Wis
consin’s primary election this year,
State Treasurer Solomon Levitan,
in an address here last night, urged
his listeners to vote next Tuesday.
“Vote, no matter whom you vote
for. but vote,” Levitan said. “It
is a sad commentary on American
interest in public affairs that so
few take the trouble to go to the
polls on election day. It is because
such a comparatively small per
centage of those eligible to vote go
to the polls that public affairs are
left to the politicians.”
8 KILLED IN
GAR COLLISION
PROBE STARTED
MONROE, Mich.—ln an effort to
fix responsibility for the head-ton
collision of two interurban cars
here late yesterday, resulting in the
death of eight persons and injury of
25 others, officials of the road and
county today planned to closely
question William Owen, veteran
motorman of the southbound car.
Hit on Curve.
The two cars of the Detroit, Mon
roe Toledo Shore line came to
gether on a 2,000-foot curve while
traveling at approximately 40 miles
an hour, according to witnesses.
According to one official Owen
has been accused of attempting to
make up lost time, and failure to
make a scheduled stop at Pine Sid
ing to await the other car. He
jumped and escaped with minor in
juries, going to his home at To
ledo.
Two Men Killed.
CUMBERLAND, Md.—Two rail
way men were killed and two were
injured in a collision between a
Baltimore Ohio passenger train
en route from New York to Chicago
and a freight train near Foley, Pa.,
last night. As far as is known no
passengers were injured.
The dead men are "Wilkie Collins,
engineer of the passenger train, and
R. L. Albright, fireman. A fireman
and a brakeman of the freight train
were injured.

JANESVILLE, Wis. Declaring
that the law makes “the secretary of
state sole judge of whether a license
shall or shall not be granted to a
non-recommended detective agency.”
Atty. Gen. Herman L. Ekern, speak

Madison Newspaper
Sees Progressive
Support for Melms
MADISON—La Follette progres
sives may endeavor to defeat Con
gressman John C. Schafer, who
bolted the La Follette-Ekern ticket
to back Zimmerman in the 4th dis
trict, by throwing their support to
the Socialist candiate for congress
in the 4th district, E. T. Melms,
or by thrusting forth an independent
after the primary, writes Ruben
Levin in The Capital Times.

politicians now in Milwaukee,
Schafer’s home, for the State Fair.

upon Schafer for his sudden shift to
Zimmerman, though he had been
standing high in the La Follette cer
cles.

delighted with the situation. They
will gain whether the La Follette
progressives back Melms or put
forth an independent. Since Melms
gave Schafer a hard fight in 3922,
it is likely that victory may be in
his grasp.
However, if Zimmerman should
break through as a winner Tuesday
and the election, Congressman Scha
fer will find himself in a fortunate
position, and may become a candi
date for United States senator in
1928, it is predicted.

LARGEST BOAT
ENDS EXCELLENT
TOURIST SEASON
The Christopher Columbus, larg
est passenger boat on clear water,
which carried more than 2,000 pas
sengers daily in its trips between
Chicago and Milwaukee this sum
mer, will drop her anchor Monday
night, concluding one of the most
successful tourist seasons in the
Goodrich line’s 75 years of business,
according to Charles L. Dunlop,
Milwaukee passenger agent.
The daily service to Chicago will
be continued throughout the year by
the Illinois and the Wisconsin, but
the excursion boat season closes
Labor day, Mr. Dunlop said.
During the summer, the 12 boats
on the Goodrich line have carried
more than 1,000,000 passengers, he
said.
The Theodore Roosevelt, recently
purchased by the Goodrich line, is
being entirely rebuilt.
Other changes, additions to equip
ment and service will be made be
fore the 1927 tourist season opens,
according to Mr. Dunlop.
