WATCH YOUR STEP NEXT TUESDAY
Because there is a pre-primary scrap in the Repub
lican party of Wisconsin over candidates, that party re
ceives much publicity at the hands of the newspapers.
Don’t let that fool you into thinking that the Repub
lican scrap is important, that there is any difference be
tween the candidates, or that you should vote the
Republican ticket at the primary.
It is only a sham battle. The candidates try to hang
onto the coat-tail of the late Senator La Follette, but they
have all abandoned him for the purpose of boosting their
own selfish interests and ambitions. There is not the
slightest choice between these self-seekers. They all rep
resent capitalism and economic chaos. Not one of them
has a constructive program to offer, nor the will or wis
dom to carry it out if he had.
The Socialist candidates, on the contrary, offer a
carefully thought-out program. It has been published in
The Leader and printed in leaflet form. You have read
it and you know that it is an honest, constructive pro
gram for the betterment of the conditions of the people.
You also know that the Socialists have always been
true to the interests of the people in the past. They are
not forever engaged in pushing their own selfish interests.
Neither are they hazy and chaotic in their thinking on
public questions, as the so-called progressives are. The
Socialists know what they want and they go about doing it
when they are elected.
When you go to the polls next Tuesday, vote for all
of the Socialist candidates. Give them a big boost on that
day, and thereby help them to win on election day in
Nevember.
AN ADMISSION AGAINST INTEREST
Although we are living under “Coolidge prosperity,”
Cal’s own department of labor officials have discovered
that poverty is an important factor in the high rate of
deaths among mothers and infants.
It does not take an investigator to tell that. We
found it out years ago without the aid of statistics. Any
body with eyes in his head and a heart in his breast could
find it out by walking through the poorest sections of the
cities. He need not go into the houses at all, for if he has
any sense he can reach the logical conclusion that families
living in such places must have the hearse visit them more
often at times when the stork arrives than would be the
case if they lived in a better environment.
Nevertheless, it is well to have the statistical and of
ficial corroboration. Especially when it comes from a de
partment of a Republican administration which is always
trying to make the people believe that wonderful prosper
ity exists. You know the old legal rule that admissions
against interest are very weighty as evidence. It is against
the interest of the Coolidge administration to admit that
poverty is an important factor in maternal and infancy
mortality. This makes the admission more weighty.
But what of it? Well, there is a primary coming.
Vote against all Republican candidates—and vote for all
Socialist candidates—and you will be voting against pov
erty and for genuine prosperity.
THOROUGHLY FLEECED
The farmers are certainly getting it in the neck.
The department of agriculture reports that the purchasing
power of farm products is at the lowest level it has occu
pied for about two years.
In other words, the amount of money for which farm
products sell will buy less of the necessaries of life than
at any time since two years ago—and it would buy pre
cious little then.
This, at a time when Republican politicians are broad
casting the assertion that the farmers are coming into
their own and all they need is to be let alone. Surely, all
they need is to be let alone—if their highest ambition is
to become flat financially and have mortgages and the
bankruptcy court take possession of what little property
they have. “Let’m alone an’ they’ll all come home a-wag
gin’ their tails behind’m”—but thoroughly fleeced.
The above report is another admission against in
terest —and another reason why farmers should vote the
Socialist ticket straight.
Minnesota is supposed to be a radical state, but there
are more marriages asd less divorces in that state—an
unusual condition nowadays. As announced by the de
partment of commerce—Mr. Hoover, at the head of that
department, seems to be interested in everything under the
sun —there were 23,654 marriage ceremonies performed in
Minnesota in 1925 as compared with 23,204 in 1924—and
there were 2,673 divorces granted in 1925 as compared
with 2,803 in 1924. This makes an increase of 1.9 per
r«nt in marriages and a decrease of 4.6 per cent in divorces.

BY JAMES ONEAL.
We imagine that Judge Gary of
the steel trust and some others of
his type get a “moral thrill” out
of the Crime Commission which
they have inspired. They are very
much concerned aoout the increas
ing spread of crime. It does not
occur to them that the petty crim
inals may often be trying to imi
tate big ones who have taken the
precaution to legalize their trade
and make it respectable. It is
no accident that crimes are on the
increase since the end of the
World war, for that crusade was
crime enlarged on a world scale
and had for its object pilfering
other people’s property.
It might be well for the various
commissions investigating crime
to go back to the first half of the
18th century and investigate the
causes of piracy which was then
rampant. The slave trade had be
come the greatest business in all
history. Christian merchants had
ships specially designed for the
traffic and raided Africa for Ne
groes” to be sold in America and
the West Indies. This criminal
practice had the sanction of gov
ernments which often chartered
companies to engage in the trade.

This was also a period of whole
sale confiscation of the common
lands at home which had served
the masses for generations. The
workers were ousted and turned
adrift on the highways and the
lands became booty of favorites
of the ruling classes. Lands
abroad were also taken by force
and the natives reduced to servi
tude to alien masters. The high
seas became a theater for raids
and often privateering came so
close to piracy that one could not
be distinguished from the other.
Selling shoddy fish to natives and
watering rum for increased prof
its became notorious. Need it be
surprising that in the American
colonies the merchants became
smugglers and increased their
fortunes by cheating the customs?
All this was in the early days
of capitalism, the system which,
by force and fraud, accumulated
large forms of capital to be
turned into a source for further
robbery of disinherited laborers.
The naked cynicism and greed of
the ruling classes of the period
made its impress upon many oth
ers and crime became rampant.

“Damn ye,” said Bellamy, “you

Men have made for their own
Security. They rob the Poor

more than a mere wage dispute
between organized labor and cap
ital. It is capitalism on its death
bed struggling for a prolonged
lease of life.
Coal mining in Britain has
reached such a stage that it is no
longer possible to pay the miners

capitalist and a royalty to the
landed aristocracy of old England.
The struggle has now developed

mining shall be socialized or the
standard of living of the workers
be lowered in order that capital
ism may be prolonged.

solidly arrayed against the work
ers in this fight, and if the min

OLD DIPLOMACY PLUNDERS AG AU
The foreign diplomacy of leading European govern
ments is as two-faced now as it ever was before the war.
Every government has made treaties of friendship with
others and then turned right round and made military
pacts against its friends.
The fruit of this blundering and double crossing is
now visible in Geneva, where the question of Germany’s
admission to the league of nations is once more on the
order of business.
The Spanish and Italian governments, ruled by
dictators, want to make Germany’s admission to the league
dependent upon their own imperialist ambitions.
The tangled web of these ambitions extends from
Gibraltar to Constantinople and Suez. It is used by the
dictators to fish in the troubled waters of the growing
conflicts between French and British interests.
The Spanish-Italian treaty and the French-Rumanian
treaty, both made just before the league meets to debate
Germany’s admission, mark the two crooked hooks upon
which the diplomats hang their intrigues. The British
attitude in this matter is just as two-faced as the French,
British, Russian and Italian was towards Germany be
fore the war.
If any one wants to believe the usual diplomatic de
nials of ulterior and sinister aims, he ought to ask: Then
why make such treaties at all? The evident object of the
Spanish-Italian treaty is to cripple the French navy in the
Mediterranean. The equally evident object of the French-
Rumanian treaty is to line Rumania up with Jugo-Slavia
against Italy.
In the league meeting at Geneva, Mussolini will then
back Rivera’s demand for making Tangier Spanish.
Rivera will back Mussolini’s demand for a piece of French
Tunis and for ignoring the Abyssinian protest against the
Italian-British division of its sovereign territory.
The treacherous attitude of the British Foreign Min
ister Chamberlain towards France in Morocco, Syria and
Abyssinia has produced an equally treacherous French
attitude. The French diplomats have tried to win Ibn
Saud, the leading Arab chief, away from the British, and
to use him and the Kemal Pasha government in Turkey as
buffers against the British in the Near East.
French diplomats will also back the Abyssinian pro
test against British and Italian designs. Recent French
concessions to German business in African colonies and the
rapid formation of French-Belgian-German pools in basic
industries have been hastened by the latest international
intrigues.
The British have thwarted Mussolini in Albania and
Greece, but backed him in Abyssinia. They backed Rivera
in Morocco, but oppose him in Tangier. They have backed
and filled in their attitude towards Germany, France,
Greece and Turkey. They keep Finland, the Baltic States
and Poland in suspense by plots against Soviet Russia.
Chamberlain has played pingpong with Egyptian,
Arabian, Persian and Turkestan chiefs, until the name
of British diplomacy in the Near East is synonymous
with deceit.
Under this cloud of rascalities, the German republic
knocks once more at the gate of the league and offers to
take her seat in the so-called parliament of nations which
is in fact only a committee of governments that mutua 1
distrust and cheat each other. And the German rejftC
being still a capitalist concern, has as many secret axes
grind as the other powers.
OUR MONROE DOCTRINAIRES
The pose of naive innocence which our Monroe doc
trinaires always assume when their attitude oward the
league of nations is discussed does not fool European dip
lomats, although it still leads many American voters by
the nose.
European statesmen are quick to tell our naive Nellies
that no European power nowadays plans any conquest
of any American state, but to pretend that the Monroe
doctrine forbids European powers to look after their
legitimate business interests in American states is dis
honest.
So it is, but European statesmen are not honest, either,
when they pretend that American statesmen cannot prop*
erly attend to American interests in Europe without join
ing the league and world court.
This sly pose of European statesmen does not inspire
any better confidence when it is imitated by certain Euro
pean Socialist leaders, who never tire of lecturing Ameri
can Socialists on the duties of international solidarity.
If solidarity meant that we must agree with every per
sonal opinion of European comrades, no matter how in
jurious to the American Socialist party, we would be in
a bad way.
THE MANIA TO POSE
Even though Zinoviev has been shelved for the pres
ent, the International Press Correspondence still is the
stage upon which all the bad actors of Communism grat
ify their incurable mania to pose.
We note in a recent issue of this strutting sheet thr
Lord Birkenhead, Tory secretary of state for India,
believed by the Russian Communist leftwingers when hw.
claims that he is carrying out Ramsay MacDonald’s policy
in East India.
The ghost dancers of Communism don’t see anything
funny in their readiness to believe any nonsense that a
Tory spouts against a Socialist. But they get raving mad,
if the same Tory lies about a Communist.
In the'same issue Bela Kun, former Communist czar
of Hungary, announces grandiloquently another grand
war for the revolution against the Horthy dictatorship.
It’s another pose, that’s all.
Instead of gratifying their mania to pose, the Russian
leftwingers had better straighten out the kinks in their
heads and stop the impending split in the Russian Com
munist party.

The Real Color of Gold
STRICTLY speaking, gold is not yellow in
color. It merely appears so, but, being a
metal and generally with a bright surface,
it acts as a reflector and throws back quite a lot
of the white light that falls on it.
This reflected white light, which is not part
of the color of gold, dilutes the metal’s real
color, making it appear yellow. The real color
of the gold, metallurgists say, is a deep orange,
entirely different from the familiar yellow.
But this precious metal has other colors as
well as yellow and orange. Ground into a fine
powder pure gold becomes ruby red. Every
body has seen this ruby color at one time or an
other, though they may hot have been aware
that it was the color of gold they were looking
at. It is seen in the rich ruby glass used for
photographic dark-room lamps, the minute par
ticles "of gold added to the glass imparting their
deep color.

How Queen Bees
Duel to Death
WHEN a hive_ of bees becomes over
crowded, they swarm. That is, a great
army of anything up to 50,000 bees will
leave their original home to start another colony
elsewhere. Although so many leave, there will
probably be quite as many left behind, although
they are without a fertile queen, for she left with
the swarm.
It sometimes happens that when a hive is ready
to swarm, the weather becomes so inclement that
it is impossible for them to leave. Inside the hive
the queen cells have been built, and each con
tains a living princess ready to emerge. But day
after day the rain comes down, or cold winds
prevail, so that the old queen cannot lead her
thousands of followers out into the sunshine.
“The time is ripe for the young queens to
leave their cells, and if all should come out with
the old queen still in the hive chaos would result,
for if two queens meet they immediately fight,”
writes Oliver G. Pike, F. Z. S., in London Tit-
Bits. “But these far-seeing creatures will not
allow any, such thing to occur. Should the
weather still remain cold, the cradles of wax
are torn open and the young queens are slaugh
tered by the worker bees.
“However, before they do this they seem to
have a lingering hope that the weather will
change in their favor. When the young queens
begin to bite through the waxen end of their
cells, the cell-builders hurry to the scene and
quickly seal up the holes. Thus we see a remark
able incident. The queens inside are trying to
escape, but the workers, knowing the mad tumult
that would ensue if their exit were allowed, take
care to prevent it. As quickly as the imprisoned
creatures bite away the wax, they seal up the
breaches.
“But at last a favorable day arrives, and the
sun shines into the hive. It is a sign of hope to
the bees; a state of excitement runs through the
whole colony. The swarm goes out, and directly

“It is a common complaint of sedentary
workers that at the end of their day’s routine
they are too tired to exercise. This feeling of
fatigue is not due to long hours of physical
activity but to stagnation and passive existence
with a backing-up of fatigue poisons from over
loaded stomachs and intestines, and an over-ex
penditure of mental effort.
“A stirring up of the general circulation by
exercise, to the point of moderate perspiration
and sweating out of these poisonous materials,
will help to clear the system of this feeling of
lassitude. Moderate exercise stimulates the kid
neys and affects favorably every organ and tis
sue in the body. The oxygen in the air replaces
the poisonous excretions with which the blood is
loaded, and the tissues are nourished and feel the
tonic effect.
“Sound sleep and moderate exercise are the
two best foes of fatigue poisons. It seems to be
a difficult thing to arrange the daily program so
that these two important and health-giving fac
tors should have sufficient consideration. It is
so much easier to whip up the nerves and flag
ging energies with stimulants. In themselves
these may not be injurious, but by masking the
feeling of fatigue and depression, they lead the
individual into a feeling of false security, so that
the real causes do not get proper attention and
go on contributing their quota and daily dose of
poisons until damaged kidneys, nervous break
downs and severe anemias result.
“Remember that sound sleep and moderate
exercise are the two first steps to take in con
quering this difficulty. Stuffing with whole
some nourishing food will not cure a sense of
fatigue and debility if the food tube is clogged
and the blood stream saturated with the poison
ous end products of digestion and tissue waste.

By MARY MARSHALL
WHEN a girl makes her plans to go away to school or col
lege, her wardrobe seems a thing of great importance.
Never again will any collection of clothes—save the
bridal trousseau —need to be chosen with such care and fore
thought. When you see the young schoolgirl or the sub-fresh
man shopping and planning and contriving to assemble just the
right sort of clothes and accessories for the autumn, you may be
inclined to be amused —that is if you are a cynical middle-aged
sort of person with a condescending attitude toward social activi
ties of college life.
“How silly to go to all that trouble and expense,” the
middle-aged sort of person says. “For after all college teas and
boarding-school dances are not real social events. A girl goes
to college to develop her intellect. If she does not do that she
had much better stay at home. Time enough to play the social
game after school and college days are over—time enough then
to think about clothes.”
However, to a very great many
girls school and colege Is the only
or most Important social introduc
tion available. College dances and
parties are to most who attend
them really quite important and
smart affairs. Friendships that last
a lifetime are formed then, social
contacts are made —and needless to
say clothes play an important role.
Start With Coat
In planning the school or college
wardrobe it is a good idea to start
with the coat—because this is
usually the most expensive single
garment. There is still a strong
contingency of collegians in favor
of the fur sports coat, but It is no
longer one of the requirements for
college entrance. You needn’t have
a racoon coat on the campus this
autumn, in fact, you needn’t have
a fur coat at all. Fashions have

Suits Ideal
The two-piece tailored cloth suit
once seemed an ideal costume for
the college girl. Freshly laundered
blouses gave it a fresh aspect.
Just why it is that American
women are so much less inclined
to revive the suit at present than
French women it is hard to say—
or rather from the American point
of view it is hard to see why the
French have been so glad to re
adopt the suit. The short-waisted
appearance produced by wearing
the suit skirt with a tuck in
blouse, sans the suit jacket, seems
most unattractive to most girls
here. They find the shortened
waistline rather to their taste jn
an evening frock—but certainly not
when produced by a separate blouse
and skirt.
The girl who does not want to
follow the beaten track in her
school wardrobe really should in
clude a smart little suit. She will
find it a most useful street and in
formal afternoon costume.
Girls Like Jumpers
Whatever^the fate of the jumper
for general wear, it remains secure
in the estimation of schoolgirls.
And they like the real two-piece
jumper and not the one-piece frock
in two-piece jumper effect of the
sort that some of the French dress
makers are making this autumn.
Usually the skirt of the jumper is
mounted oin a silk top. For in
formal afternoon or everyday wear
you may like one of the new wool
crepe jumper frocks, made with a
comfortable collar line, long sleeves
of course and skirt showing pleats
at the front. Some of the new
wool-jersey jumper frocks are at
tractive, and for warmer wear
there are jumper frocks of tweed.
Plaid velveteen in rich shades of
blue and green or tan and brown
is sometimes made into a jumper
top, worn with a wool skirt of plain
harmonizing color.
For evening clothes the college
or schoolgirl has not very great
need at this time of the year. Eve
ning activities do not usually begin
until after the Thanksgiving vaca
tion possibly not until after
Christmas. One or two dance
frocks is all that most girls would
need for the time being and if
strict economy is necessary a girl
could probably manage without an
evening coat —using a fur-collared
autumn or winter coat on the rare
occasions when one is necessary.
But the little evening frocks must
be well made and dainty. A simple
flare-skirted crepe de chine in one
of the vibrant evening shades will
answer many requirements and for
the one really dress-up evening
frock at this time a very simple
velvet dress would be a good
selection.
And don’t forget a warm negligee
or two. Simple but not too man
nish wrappers of gay striped flannel
are looked upon with approval in
the dormitories.
PAJAMAS REPLACE TEAGOWNS
LONDON
The time-honored teagown has
at last been shoved aside in Eng
land, and it has given way to the
pajama suit. It is now a matter
of course for an English hostess to
receive her tea-time guests in
pajamas if she likes. They are
considered much more appropriate
for this purpose than the old-time
sort of teagown, all frills and
flounces. Some women wear pa
jamas to match the cushions and
hangings of their rooms and the
interior decorator who works out
the color scheme of the room fre
quently is commissioned to design
a number of pajama costumes that
will harmonize with the surround
ings.

terce Grizzly Has
Lair In Mountains
In the caverns of the Rockies
and the Sierras the grizzly bear,
like many a bold human bandit,
has his lair. He’s proud of his
reputation as the most dangerous
and most hunted wild animal in
North America.
When the shadows fall over the
valley below, the grizzly creeps
down out of his mountain fastness
and steals out on the ranches to
pounce upon the choicest of the
cattle. He’s a blood-thirsty _ ter
ror, for often he kills an animaL
sucks its blood, and then is on
after another victim. He can kill
a bull with one stroke of his pow
erful paw, and, if he likes, he is
strong enough to carry it off with
him to his mountainous lair.
He isn’t particular about his
.food, though, and will eat anything
from a cow to ants and crickets.
He even dines on watermelons and
raw potatoes, and he is never hap
pier than when licking his paws
dripping with stoler honey, while
the angry bees swarm about him
and try to sting through his ar
mor-like hide.
The grizzly bear is a thoroughly
bad character. He isn’t even good
to his own family. He never plays
with his little cubs, like most bears,
but will cold-bloodedly desert them,
or even kill them. His poor wife
•does all the looking out for the
children and will fight desperately
to protect them.
Clumsy as he looks, the big fel
low can travel very swiftly away
from danger. He is always on the
watch and has such a keen sense
of smell that it is hard for hunters
to fool him with traps or even to
get a glimpse of him. One fa
mous old grizzly was hunted for
fifteen years before any one was
able to get a shot at him.
SKILL NEEDED IN HAND TENNIS
WHICH IS PLAYED ON SIDEWALK
How would you like to hold a tennis tournament on your front
walk or in your back yard? You can do it if you play hand tennis,
which furnishes all the thrills of the real game without either a
racquet or a big court.
First of all, lay out a small court, which should be about 15
by 8 feet, or smaller if necessary. You can mark this out with chalk
on the sidewalk or a garage or basement floor, or with tape upon a
smooth piece of lawn. Mark it so that it looks like a regular court,
with alleys not wider than 12 inches.
A line drawn across the middle of the court will serve as the net,

The ball is served with the open hand, and must land in the proper

and the server may serve again.
The regular rules and scoring of tennis are used for this game.
Cuts, lobs, slices and backhand strokes may all be executed with the

hand during the entire set, a change of hands not being allowed. Both
doubles and singles can be played.
Hand tennis requires a great deal of speed, and it is possible to
develop lots of skill at the sport. One excellent way of scoring a point
is to allow a served ball to hit the hand so that it will be deadened,
and the return will land on the other side of the net line without
bouncing. Tournaments to find the champions of your “gang” will
be interesting, and in tournament play, of course, a referee should be
chosen to determine whether strokes are good or bad.

This week we have the stories of

read. One is a pony and the other
is a dog. Do any of the other
readers of this page have pets that
have won prizes?

Asia Carringtom of Bloomington
Springs, Tennessee, has a little
black pony whose name is Charlie.
Asia has taught him to “shake
hands” with his foot. Charlie is a
“wonder” pony. He can bridle
himself and is able to dance when
he hears music. Asia says that
she is the only one who can catch
him and he will not perform his
tricks for anyone else. She thinks
that Charlie is the best pet any
boy or girl could have, and others
agree with her. Charlie is not
only a “wonder” pony and able to
do so many tricks, but he is also
a prize winning horse. He has
taken the first prize at three dif
ferent fairs. He has also won
prizes for the exceptionally good
tricks which he can do. Asia says
that she is very proud of him and
would not sell her pet for “thou
sands of dollars.”

Jack O’Connor of Salt Lake City,
Utah, has a white airedale dog that
won the second prize in a recent
dog show held in that city. This
dog is a very good jumper, too.
Jack entered him in the racing
contest and he ran 210 yards in
two and one-half minutes. That is
“some speed.” Jack is right when
he says that he is a lucky boy to
have such a splendid pet.

Another Labor Day!
What does it signify in our
So far, very little in
deed —because it really was a
gift of the American capitalist
class to the American labor
movement when that movement
was very small and just begin
ning to assert itself. Labor Day
under these conditions was sim
ply meant to be a holiday some
what similar to the one that the
ancient Romans used to give
their slaves once a year.

Modern conditions and hu
man progress, however, assert
themselves.
And the growth of the labor
movement the world over is un
doubtedly the most outstanding
fact in the world today. Just
look at England, Germany,
France and the Scandinavian
countries.
There can be no doubt that
the capitalist system is bound
to disappear some day as other
barbaric, economic epochs of
the past, feudalism and chattel
slavery, have disappeared. The
change is to be brought about
gradually and by the use of the
ballot in the democratic coun
tries of Western Europe and
America. And from this point
of view the various election
days are and ought to be in
every civilized country the real
Labor Days.
Please, remember this!
Again we say to our readers:
Stay out of the primaries of the
Republican party, and of the
Democratic party for that mat
ter. Bv “mixing in” you are
simply borrowing trouble.

the present day is a Stalwart-
La Follette-Progressive-Stand
pat witches-calderon brewing
hellish mixture for the voters of
the state.
And as for the Democratic
party? Why disturb the dead?
Stay in your own primary—
and vote the straight Socialist
ticket!
Most of the candidates for
the state offices are running as
“Progressive Republicans,” and
practically all of the county can-

aim the same title.
And why not?
The La Follette “Progres
sives” have for many years
masqueraded as “regular” Re
publicans—that it is only natur
al for the regular Republicans
to masquerade as Republican

continuous activity of the So
cialists and other “radicals”

Clear Path for Germany.
GENEVA—The League of Na
tions council, in secret session to
day, decided unanimously to recom
mend to the assembly the creation
of a single permanent seat on the
council for Germany, thus over
coming what was presumably the
last obstacle to Germany’s admis
sion to the league.
The council also decided to rec
ommend the creation of three new
non-permanent seats.
The resolution regarding the in
crease in the number of non-perma
nent seats is understood to give full
satisfaction to Poland, as it is
highly likely that she will obtain
one of the three available seats.
It is understood that China also
will be seated.
Ex-Husband of
Dancer Seeking
Child at Taliesin
BARABOO, Wis.—A hearing is
scheduled in court hero today on a
writ of habeas corpus by which
Vladimir Hinzenberg, divorced hus
band of Olga Milanoff, Russian
dancer, seeks to obtain custody of
their 9-year-old daughter, Vetlana.
Hinzenberg and his attorney ob
tained the writ yesterday and pro
ceeded to Taliesin, the country home
of Frank Lloyd Wright, internation
ally known architect, near Spring
Green. The writ was served upon
the caretaker and a young archi
tect at Taliesen, who will appear
in court today.
It is expected they will be ques
tioned in an attempt to ascertain
the whereabouts of Mme. Milanoff,
who has been Wright’s companion
and housekeeper since her divorce
from Hinzenberg, and of her child,
who has been at Taliesin with her.

PRESIDENTIAL
CANDIDATE TO
BE PRESENTED
Episcopate Plans
Long Struggle With
State, Belief.
MEXICO CITY Presentation of
a church candidate for the presi
dency in the elections scheduled for
two years hence appeared today to
be the most probable course of the
Catholic church in seeking reform
c" the religious law.
It is becoming more and more
obvious that the episcopate is pre
paring for an extremely long
Struggle with the state to regain
what the church considers to be its
constitutional rights.
The struggle probably will involve
municipal, state, and federal politics
before it is ended.
Break All Precedents.
Replying to President Calles’
statement before congress when that
body convened, the episcopate said
that the government’s actions had
been unconstitutional and “smelled
of Bolshevism.”
The bishops broke all precedents
since the death of Juarez, more than
half a century ago, by criticizing the
massage of a president to the peo
ple on the opening of congress.
Cannot Make People Over.
In reply to President Calles’
statement that no part of the laws
or presidential decree should cause
alarm to right-minded Christians,
the bishops counter with tne state
ment that he has made life for the
Catholic church impossible and the
additional laws issued by the va
rious Mexican states have taken all
the liberty from the Catholics.
“President Calles is mistaken
when he would ‘change completely
the life and government of the peo
ple,’ for it cannot be done cither in
a day or over a considerable time
by legislation, for the reasons that
laws do not make and unmake peo
ple,” says the episcopate statement.

OUTLINES PLAN

REFERENDUM
Leader Special Service.
LONDON —The Daily Herald re
ports the following interview with
J. P. Jones, member of the upper
house of Victoria and a member of
the last labor government of that
Australian state, for the purpose of
giving a clear idea of the present
referendum issue in Australia.
The present anti-labor government
of Australia has submitted to the
voters two main proposals, Mr.
Jones explained. The first is an
amendment to section 51 of the fed
eral" constitution with the object of
giving wider powers to the federal
government with regard to wages,
hours, conditions of labor and other
industrial and commercial matters.
The second proposal aims to give
the federal government power to
take special measures in case of
strikes.
Hate Labor Success.
“The motive behind these pro
posals is to be found in recent in
dustrial events in tbe common
wealth,” Mr. Jpnes declared. “First
there was the seamen’s strike. Mr.
Bruce, the federal head, found that
the existence of labor governments
in five of the six Australian states
handicapped his frenzied attempts
at strike breaking, arresting and de
porting strike leaders, and so on.
“The other proposal is due to the
success of the labor movement of
New South Wales in enforcing the
44-hour week in spite of .legal ob-
ticles, smuggled into various news
papers, have the object of destroy
ing the Socialist party. We declare
that nobody will succeed in destroy
ing us.
“We want a clean party. We
don’t want anybody in our party
who does not live up to the party
principles or who is tainted by some
scandal. We want our party to be
strong, in the interest of tne work
ing people, of the nation and of
the republic.”
Convention Will Decide.
The national 'executive of the
Czecho-Slovakian Socialist party de
cide to call a special meeting of
the national committee for Sept.
18 and a special convention of the
party for Sept. 19, for the purpose
of clarifying the internal situation
in the Socialist party.
A meeting of delegates of the Pil
sen district of the Socialist party
indorsed the position of Senator
Klofach. Pravo Lidu, the central
organ of the Czecho-Slovakian So
cialist party, demands an early
convocation of parliament and
points out that a special study of
the budget is necessary, which will
require a good deal of time. If par
liament is not convoked until Oct.
15, the lower house would have only
six weeks and the senate 14 days
for the discussion of the budget.

“Defeated by the solidarity of the
workers, the employers have ap
parently exerted pressure on Mr.
Bruce to intervene on their behalf,”
Mr. Jones said.
The Australian labor movement is

proposal, Mr. Jones went on, but
there is some difference of opinion

This arises from the fact that the

Mr. Bruce wants to give complete

agrees that the government should
have power to deal with industrial
problems, even with trusts and
pools, but it does not like to let
irresponsible judges wield such
power.
Must Oppose Reaction.
The leader of the federal Labor
party, Mr. Charlton, with the ap

tralian Labor party, tried to secure

amend the first proposal in such a
way that the Democratic control of

guarded. But owing to the anti
labor majority in the federal con
gress, this effort was only partly
successful.
The Australian Workers’ Union
is conducting a vigorous campaign
the proposals with the sup
port of the Labor parties of New
South Wales, Queensland and
western Australia. It is hoped to
defeat the referendum, because :lt
will require a majority, not only of
the 3,000,000 federal electors, but
also of the states.
Of course, the Labor party is in
principle for a referendum to settle
such questions, but it is opposed to
the form in which the present pro
posals have been put to a referen
dum.

Confession By An
other Absolves Two
of Slaying-.
BOSTON—The respite granted by
Gov. Fuller and the executive coun
cil to Celestino F. Madeiros, sen
tenced to be executed next week for
the murder of an aged bank cashier
at Wrentliam, has aroused new in
terest in the case of Nicola Sacco
and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, and their
petition>for a new trial.
Confession Clears Them.
Although Madeiros has made a
confession which is alleged to have
absolved Sacco and Vanzetti of the
South Baintroe pay roll robbery and
murder of April 15, 1920, mystery
surrounds the nature of Madeiros’
statement and the affidavits of his
associate, some of whom are in state
prison.
The confession is understood not
to be the strongest of the conten
tions which William G. Thompson,
counsel for Sacco and Vanzetti, will
make in argrulng the motion for a
new trial. The hearing on the mo
tion will open before Judge Thayer
at Dedham, Sept. 14.
Has New Evidence.
Judge Thayer presided ht the
trial of Sacco and Vanzetti in the
summer of 1921 and also at the
trial of Vanzetti in June, 1820, at
Plymouth, for an attempted pay roll
robbery there. There is said to be
in the possession of defendant’s
counsel evidence never before pre
sented, for eye-witnesses of the
South Baintree crime, known to the
government soon after the affair
of more than six years ago, but un
known to the defense until two
months ago.

WIN RIBBONS
Hot partisanship developed last
night at the horse show at the State
Fair.
Many of the mounts have shown
In former events during the week,
and riders also have become famil
iar, winning differing degrees of ad
miration last night from the reg
ular fans, who showed their prefer
ences in bursts of applause that lent
real enthusiasm to the spectacle of
thousands of dollars’ worth of fine
aorseflesh performing in the tan
>ark ring.
Milwaukee was again well rep
resented when the ribbons were
awarded. The boy and girl class
pras taken entirely by Milwaukee
ms, Philip Schandein, son of Emil
Schandein, 190 Prospect Ave., rid
ing with Dorothy Teshan, winning
the blue ribbon, Both are students
at the Berg Riding academy and
rode academy horses.
Spanish Dictator
Removes Danger
Of Army Revolt
MADRl£>—The chief cause of the
revolutionary danger in Spain was
removed yesterday with the accept
ance by discontented army officers
>f the government’s offer of a com
promise, putting an end to the feud
between Dictator Primp de Rivera
ind the juntas that disrupted army
liscipline and threatened revolt.
The officers’ groups decided to be
latisfieu with the government’s as
surances that it will not order pro
lootions except in cases which are
recommended by fellow officers of
the man in question, although it re
fused to cancel the trouble making
regulation.
National feeling is aroused by the
Tangier situation, and this strength
ened Gen. de Rivera’s hand and led
the officers to accept the compro
mise for the sake of national pres
tige and to scotch rumors of im
minent revolution.

SEPT. 4, 1926.
Pioneer Settler Guided
Prairie Schooner Train.
Marcus Whitman, a missionary,
had Just made a trip east, across
the western plains, with only two
other men, and had arrived safely
back at the settlements near the
Mississippi river. Everywhere he
went people crowded around to hear
of his trip through the Indian coun
try, and of the land, far away on
the coast of the Pacific, from which
he had come.
“It is a rich and fertile country,”
he said. “The part of the country
in which I Stayed is called the Ore
gon. There is much land there for
settlers to take up. I am going
back. Why don’t you join me?” So
he went around, trying to interest
people In settling the new country.
When he returned he guided a
large train of prairie schooners
across the plains clear to the Walla
Walla valley in the far west. It
was the first large emigrant train
to cross the continent.
Marcus Whitman, born Sept. 4,
1802, was killed by the Indians, in
his tiny settlement, but he is re
membered, especially on the western
coast, for being a leader in the set
tling of what Is now the state of
Oregon.

Suitor of 70, Kills
Woman; Ends Life
LEXINGTON, Ky. A telephone
operator was slain yesterday by her
70-year-old suitor, who later com
mitted suicide. The killing followed
a quarrel over the size of the stone
in a diamond ring. Kelly C. Kirt
ley, wealthy restaurant and hotel
man of Charleston, W. Va., fired a
bullet Into the brain of Miss Mil
dred McDaniel, 26, of Brooklyn, N.
Y., while she slept in a hotel here.
He then entered the bathroom and
shot himself twice, dying before
help could be summoned.

BANDITS’ SLIP
FATAL; 1 DEAD,
ONE ARRESTED
BRECKENRIDGE, Minn. The
failure of two bandits to count the
number of victims before them
proved fatal to one and resulted in
the arrest of the other.
The men walked into a poolroom
in the business district here Fri
day night, whipped out revolvers
and lined up the bartender and 14
patrons against the wall.
Some Slip Away.
First they went through the cash
register and emptied it. Next they
started to search their victims.
While the search was being made
carelessly, a half dozen of the pa
trons slipped out of the line one by
one and escaped through a side doOr.
The bandits did not observe this
and continued to take their time.
Then Bullets Fly.
The escaped patrons ran to Po
liceman Casper Scott, who entered
the poolroom. Just as he stepped
across the threshold, he began shoot
ing and one of the bandits fell dead.
The second bandit dropped his
gun whirled 'a patron in front of
himself and behind this human
shield was protected from the bul
lets. He surrendered immediately,
but refused to talk.
St. Louis Has Its
Own Sesqui Expo
For Next 15 Days
ST. LOUIS—The Greater St.
Louis exposition, commemorating
150 years of American independence
and industrial progress, opened
here today.
Those fostering the exposition,
which will continue until Sept. 19,
have bent every effort to place it
on a par with the 1904 world’s fair
here. Te scene of the exposition is
Forest park, close to the world’s fair
site.
With elaborate dedicatory cere
monies the exposition was thrown
open to the public today. There are
more than 600 industrial displays on
the grounds.
A corps of artists has been work
ing for months to prepare- the
grounds for the exposition. Dis
tinguished visitors who have been
invited to be present include Presi
dent Coolldge, President Calles of
Mexico, and Gen. Willmington of
Canada, as well as the governors so
12 states in the Mississippi valley.
Secretary of Labor James J. Davis
will participate in the exposition’s
Labor day program Sept. 6, and
Secretary of W'ar Dwight Davis will
be the principal guest on Military
day.
Preparations have been made for
the entertainment of 1,000,000 visi
tors from all parts of the nation
during the 15 days which the ex
position will be in progress.

CONGRESS WILL
ACT ON SHOALS
PLANT DISPOSAL
BY PAUL R. MALLON.
Staff Correspondent
The United l’ress
WASHINGTON—For seven years
congress has been fighting over the
disposal of the $105,000,000 power
dams built by the government on
the Tennessee river at Muscle
Shoals, Alabama, during the war.
The climax of the long battle which
involves needed low priced fer
tilizer for farmers and the cost of
electricity for homes and commer
cial purposes in the south is to be
reached at the coming session of
congress.
The special joint congressional
committee appointed by congress
itself to find a solution of the per
plexing problem has proposed to the
senate that the project be leased
to the Alabama Power Co. and a
dozen associated southern power
companies.
A strong opposition is growing to
the measure. Senator Norris, Re
publican, Nebraska, advocate of
government operation of the prop
erty, who has in the past prevented
acceptance by congress of any of
the leases proposed, is planning an
other strenuous fight.
The view of the opposition is set
forth by Representative W. Frank
James, Republican, Michigan, who
in a minority report of the joint
committee stated: “These bidders
have shown by their actions that
they are interested in avoiding fer
tilizer responsibilities just as far as
they possibly can, and when, like
Greeks bearing gifts, they come
here offering a price for the power
that is greater than a reasonable
return to the government—a price
which would have the effect of de
liberately making fertilizers less
saleable and deliberately releasing
moro power for their own purpose.
I fear them, for I have no confi
dence in their good faith.”
War on Lynn, Mass.,
Teachers Who Smoke
LYNN, Mass. Mayor Ralph S.
Bauer has declared war on eigaret
smoking by Lynn teachers, both men
and women. In a statement yester
day he announced that, they must
make New Year’s resolutions to
abandon the habit or resign their
positions. He will offer a resolution
to this effect before the school board
and admits he expects to have some
difficulty in passing the order.

Holds State Costs
Less Than A verage
Of Entire Nation
LONE ROCK, Wis.—Wisconsin’s
government costs less than that of
any neighboring state and less than
the average of the nation, Alvin C.
Reis, Madison attorney and former
ly assistant attorney general, de
clared here last hight in an address
of 11th hour answers to critics of
the Madison ring.
Reis quoted government census
statistics to show that the per cap
ita figure for annual operation of
state government for Wisconsin is
less than neighboring states of
Michigan, lowa, Illinois and Min
nesota.
“Not only is Wisconsin’s govern
ment costing less than throughout
the country, but the percentage of
increase in the past 10 years has
been less,” Reis declared.

stroy the workers’ rights. The bat
tle has been fierce and the sacrifice

holding tight against every attack.

will nurse and develop good will in
industry and that a spirit of real
fellowship may take the place of dis
trust, misunderstanding, and bitter
ness.

Kept Bail Money,
Charge; Is Sued,
Suit was instituted in circuit
court yesterday against Atty. Ed
ward T. Curley for the return of
mopey given him by a client for
bail which, it is alleged, he con
verted to his own use.
Citrley last March was convicted
of larceny as bailee and sentenced
to two weeks in the house of correc
tion as the result of a complaint
made by Jennie Keller, the client,
that he had misappropriated .$750
of her money. The action today is
brought in the name of Jennie
Schuster.
The complaint states that Cur
ley was given the money July 35,
1925, by Jennie Schuster to deposit
as bail, after she had been arrested
on a criminal warrant. Curley’s
contention was that the money was
given him as a fee for defending
the woman.

BRITON CHARGED
WITH SLAYING
BARES TRIANGLE
CANTERBURY, England-
Charged with the murder of Thomas
Derham, Alphonse F. A. Smith,
grandson of Hugh Ryan and Sir
Frederick Smith, Canadian railroad
magnates, from whom he inherited
great wealth, was committed last
night for trial at the next court ses
sion. Derham also was a member
of a well known British family.
The pronouncement was given on
the completion of the evidence at the
arraignment of Smith, whose com
ment was: “I have nothing to say
except that I am not guilty.”
Smith’s counsel argued that the
evidence did not warrant committal
except for manslaughter. The de
fense apparently will he that Smith
Intended to commit suicide and that
in a struggle with Derham a shot
Intended to end his (Smith’s) own
life killed Derham.
Lured Victim Charged.
The prosecutor charged that
Smith actuated by fierce jealousy
of Derham, lured him to the Smith
villa, Stella Maris, Aug. 12, with a
telegram signed in the name of Mrs.
Smith, the former Catherine White,
and then shot him.
Derham went to Smith’s villa, the
lawyer said, and found the husband
and wife both there. The alterca
tion broke out in the drawing room.
Atty. Cohen, the prosecutor, in
dicated that the two men had been
friends. Derham, who was separat
ed from his wife, became a frequent
visitor at Smith’s villa and Smith
appeared to become acutely jealous
of his friend’s association with his
wife.
The prosecutor read the letter
written by Smith and intended for
his wife, which might be constructed
as indicating he intended to committ
suicide rather than kill Derham.
The letter addressed to Mrs. Smith
never was delivered to her, but was
handed unopened to the police by
Smith when he was arrested. It
reads in i>art:
Gives Letter to Police.
“My dear, dear girl: This prob
lem can be solved in one way, re
moval of your lover, Derham, or my
self.
“His pursuit of you—a young
married woman with three children,
babies, and a little money, knowing
In full that marriage (he being al
ready married), was impossible—
and is a despicable, damnable thing.
“Nor are you much less to blame,
with your constant lies and the en
listment of your reputable friends
to cover up your affairs.
“I cannot forget while I live, and
cannot go on supporting this great
enemy of mind and heart. May God
forgive me for what I am about to
do and may God forgive you, the
cause of it all.
“As for your man, you will al
ways have this between you, and if
you can go on after it, there are no
sentences in the language which
could be constructed to express what
you both are.”
Increase Faculty
And Curriculum
Of Music School
The Wisconsin Conservatory of
Music, 440 Milwaukee St., continu
ing the high standard of work which
caused the National Association of
Schools of Music and Allied Arts
to name it as one of the 23 charter
members of that association, when
it was organized two years ago, has
added to its curriculum and faculty
to keep up with the high standards
anticipated by the organization.
The fall term begins Thursday.
The entire course of study has
been reorganized, the semester hour
being made the basis of credit, and
nine new qualified teachers have
been added to the teaching force,
leaking i. faculty enrollment of 104.
The new fall term catalog of the
School, more interesting and Instruc
tive than any of its predecessors,
has just been published.

ONE DAY AT AARHUS.
Having ordered a carriage the day
before by telephone I proceeded to
Agri and thence over Mols Bjerge,
enjoying every moment the land
scapes where the numerous heather
covered hills are crowned by scores
and scores of barrows, the last rest
ing place of the Vikings. Soon we
arrived at Femmoller. the Five Wa
termills, with its good hotel. Thence
to Kalo and a visit to the ruins of
the old castle on the peninsula. In
this old royal castle Gustavos Vasa
of Sweden was onee a prisoner.
From Valo we drove to the famous
castle of Rosenholm, the ancient
home of the Itosenkrautz family,
and after asking permission, were
allowed to see some of its fine in
teriors. From Hornslet station
near by, I got the evening train
back to Aarhus, quietly brimming
over with the calm of the passing
countrysides and the thoughts of
the past which ruined castles and
ancient burial mounds wash as eve
ning tides into the mind.

THE MILWAUKEE LEADER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 4, 1928
URGES GERMAN
CAPITAL COPY
U.S. LABOR IDEA
DRESDEN, Germany—Two thou
sand German manufacturers from
every branch of German industry,
assembled here yesterday, were told
by government leaders and their
own chiefs that while Germany has
ascended from the depths of its de
pression, business still has a long
way to go before the country will
have achieved prosperity. The man
ufacturers are attending the annual
convention of the National Associa
tion of German Industry.
A point brought out emphatically
was that the reparations burden im
posed by the Dawes plan cannot be
borne by Germany in the long run.
Drop Petty Discords.
Dr. Carl Duisberg, head of the
huge German dye trust, who has
just completed a tour of the world,
studying industry, urged the work
ers and employers to drop their pet
ty discords and copy after American
industries, which, he said, have
achieved a prosperity never known
in Europe.
He demanded that the American
system paying the workers for
the value of work done be adopted
in Germany.
The tenor of the discussions was
summed up by Dr. Reinhold, minis
ter of finance, who said:
“Endless difficulties still stand in
the way of our complete economic
recovery. There can be no question
of a favorable financial position at
present. But if it is being optimis
tic to believe in Germany’s future
prosperity, then I am an optimist.
Still In Tunnel.
“Germany is still far inside the
black tunnel of our frightful eco
nomic distress. But I think that
now we can vaguely see the first
faint glimmering of dawn at the
end of the tunnel—the first dim
sign of our ultimate liberation and
restoration. To get out of the tun
nel, however, untiring hard work
will be imperative for a long time
to come.”

creasing the productivity of rural
districts.”

YOUTH WINS
RADIO FAME IN
A. P. ORCHESTRA
Shortly after the close of the
World war a young man appeared
'at the offices of the American con
sul in Constantinople and asked if
he could obtain information con
cerning his parents.
To a group of interested auditors
he unfolded an amazing tale of ad
venture and privation. Upon the
outbreak of the war he had enlist
ed in the Russian army and for
three and a half years was engaged
in actions on the Russian front.
Then bame the Russian upheaval
and his capture by the Bolsheviki as
a soldier of the czar.
The narrator then told his hear
ers that he put into effect a care
fully matured plan to escape and
work his way down to the Golden
Horn.
Tucked under his arm was a vio
lin case. The young man opened the
case, and there lay a violin and
equipment in perfect
despite his trying experiences. Then
he played, and won the hearts of
his hearers. They finally established
communication with his parents,
who, in the meantime, had departed
for America. Funds were sent for
his passage and the young refugee
arrived in New York.
In a few months his art in inter
preting the songs of his native land
attracted widespread attention. He
was engaged to play at exclusive
restaurants, at resorts and before
private gatherings.
Then one day representatives of
The Great A. P. Tea Co., in sarch
of radio talent, heard this young
Russian and a group of his com
patriots who he had gathered about
him.
Today millions know him as
Harry Horlick and his group of mu
sicians as the A. &P. Gypsies. Early
in September his beloved violin, that
survived so many vicissitudes, will
again be heard over WEAF and a
group of other stations, when the
A. P. Gypsies will resume their
hour of broadcasting.

with high expectations, because the
patter on its wrapper says that it is

as a mere confession of ignorance,

really comes out of Yassar, we cer
tainly want to know it. So we
went into this volume with an ener
getic enthusiasm equalled only once
in our long life, when we fell for
the witching words of a mining
partner and dug out half a moun
tain in the frenzied search for an
alleged gold pocket.
After reading the book, we felt
about as we felt then, having dis
covered that the gold pocket which
was really mined was not the
mountain’s, but our own.
If we tried to place Prof. Drake
in ,the light of his own theory, we
might believe that he was a duck.

so-called realists who arrive at the
conclusion that very little in this

a but, if, however, nevertheless, etc.
to his positive assertions and al
ways leaves his readers with a
doubt.

rior to his realist friends in Eng
land, who, like Bertrand Russell,
Whitehead and Broad, emphasize
the objective existence of the
things which the mind reflects. He
calls himself a monist realist and
insists that some things are only in

uses this simple and undeniable)
fact which has been noted by phi*
losophers as far back as the mind!

Plato’s and Aristotle's types for in
dividual forms were real or im
aginary, so Prof. Drake quarrels
with Prof. Broad about the puzzle:
To what extent are ideas subjective
without objective types and to what
extent are reflexes of real ob

he fancies that this -gives him an

men wondered whether matter could

evolution from Cartesius, Spinoza
and Leibniz via British skepticism
and French materialism back to
Kant and Hegel, and the backward
development from Darwin, Haeckel,

CHICAGO—The plight of the
farmer is the only blight on the
prosperity of the United States, in
the opinion of Otto Kahn, interna
tional banker and patron of the
Arts, who was in Chicago yesterday.
His interests in Chicago converge
tipon the Ravinia opera, where he
was the guest of honor last night,
but he was cornered in the Drake
hotel yesterday long enough to ob
tain his ideas on business, the stock
market and international finance.
Plea For Farmer.
Mr. Kahn turned to the subject of
-'American business and became
glowing in his enthusiasm of cor
porate prosperity, but rather glum
in consideration of the agricultural
side of the picture. “Business,” he
said, “should address itself very
seriously to the problem of what
can be done to give the farmer a
larger share of the prosperity in
this country.
“I am not in sympathy with the
common view that the farmer needs
no help or that he is prosperous.
This complaint that has been com
ing from the farm regions for the
past several years certainly is not
a discontent without foundation.
These millions would not complain
if they did not have a grievance.
Just what the solution is I cannot
eay because I have none to offer
myself. But I am sure that one
could be found if the responsible
men of judgment and knowledge in
the matter could be forced to find
a way out.
Need Drastic Tactics.
“I rather think the way to find
a solution would be the one adopt
ed by Senator Aldrich at the time
when he was wrestling with Amer
ican currency problems. Bankers
would not agree and there was a
great divergence of opinion on the
subject. Senator Aldrich took, I
believe, a half dozen of the out
standing bankers on a boat to an
island off the American coast, pre
sumably on a pleasure-business trip.
"When they reached the island he
eaid: ‘Now gentlemen there is no
means of return except by my boat.
You will not return until you have
prepared a report on the subject
unanimously agreed upon.’ In a
few days they had a unanimous re
port on the solution of the currency
problem and that was substantially
the foundation for our present fed
eral reserve system.
“If we could adopt the same tac
tics in approaching the farm ques
tion I have, no doubt we would find
i n answer to the question and ws
Jainly should try to at least.
Sees No Inflation.
Reverting to the high grade of
business activity in the United
States, Mr. Kahn stated he had seen
no sign of inflation. “In fact,” he
continued, “American business men
on the whole have shown remark
able restraint in not letting pros
perity run away with them. I look
for this condition to continue, al
though not, of cours,*, indefinitely
because the laws of reaction still
are in force.”
Mr. Kahn would not say much
'about the stock market situation
beyond the fact that it is discount
ing the large profits of American
business. “The stock market al
ways discounts,” he said, “and I do
hot think that it has run ahead of
the business activity as some per
sons seem to believe. The stock
market cannot run counter to tne
great business currents. The popu
lar idea that any group of men can
manipulate the market is all wrong.
They can force one or two stocks
up, but the main trend of the mar
ket represents the opinion of all the
people of the country on future
busitess.”

UP IN CANADA
MONTREAL—GeneraI trade con
ditions are reported good In Quebec,
Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Brit
ish Columbia and fair in the other
provinces. Mining activity continues
at a high rate in northern Ontario
and Quebec and a new record In
gold production is predicted for this
year. The Canadian automotive in
dustry slackened its production
somewhat In July.
Great Britain.
With about 40,000 miners back at
work, about 200,000 tons of British
coal are being produced weekly,
while foreign coal is now coming
into the country at the rate of 1,000,-
000 tons a week. The number of un
employed other than coal miners
was 1,580,500 Aug. 16, as compared
with 1,594,200 Aug. 9.
Norway.
There has been recently a de
crease in Norway’s import surplus,
owing to well sustained exports and
reduced imports, the latter result
ing from the depression in industry
and commerce. The Industrial situa
tion is still stagnant, and continued
lew domestic demand prevents Nor
wegian interests from expecting an
early improvement. Unemployment
now totals about 30,000.
Sweden.
No prpnounced changes have oc
curred in the general economic and
financial situation In Sweden re
cently and basic factors apparently
indicate continued favorable devel
opment. Wholesale and retail prices
have shown a slight decline. Iron
ore exports have decreased and the
lumber market is quiet.
Industrial depression and high un
employment are still dominating
features in Danish economic life.
There are some bright spots, how
ever; the Danish merchant marine
is well occupied, owing largely to
the increased coal carrying trade;
harvest returns indicate a normal
yield, and the exchange rate re
mains stable. Unemployment is in
creasing.
Germany.
July foreign trade again showed
an adverse balance, imports amount
ing to 949,000,000 marks and exports
to 823,000,000 marks. As in June
the increase in the value of imports
was largely based upon important,
purchases of grain, flour and meat
in anticipation of the tariff in
creases which became effective
Aug. 1.
China.
The trade outlook in China con
tinues unfavorable. Military opera
tions continue in the Hankow dis
trict and there are no prospects of
a definite settlement of the *North
China political situation.
Brazil.
There are slight evidences of im
provement in the Brazilian situa
tion. Trade, however, continues dull
with only careful buying for imme
diate needs.

French Revenue
For July Jumps
NEW YORK—French government
revenue from all sources in July,
1926, not including the receipts of
the postal administration, which are
carried to a separate budget, totaled
3,661,106,700 francs as against
2,404,18,400 francs in June, 1926,
and 2,534,068,000 francs in July,
1925.
The increase of 1,127,038,600
francs over the preceding year is
due to increased taxes enforced by
the laws of April 4 and April 29,
last, and by the increase in indirect
taxes, many of which are assessed
ad valorem and consequently grow
larger with the higher prices.
According to official figures re
ceived by the Bankers Trust Co. of
New York from its French informa
tion service, out of the above total
of 3,061,106,700 francs exceptional
resources accounted for 77,468,100
francs, of which 45,396,100 francs
were produced by the tax on excess
war profits.

Week 9 s Commercial
Failures Decline
NEW YORK —The number of
failures in the United States in
creased slightly this week, totaling
377. This is 11 more than the num
ber reported to R. G. Dun Co.
last week and compares with 331
defaults a year ago.
Fewer insolvencies occurred this
week than last week in the east
and on the Pacific coast, but these
reductions are more than offset by
increases in the south and in the
west. Of the current week's fail
ures, 221 had liabilities of more than
$5,000 in each case, which contrasts
with 190 similar defaults last week
and 169 a year ago.
Canadian insolvencies this week,
numbering 34, show a decrease from
the total of 48 reported to R. G.
Dun and Co. last week. A year ago
the number of failures in Canada
was 32.

MIDDLE WEST
EXPORTS GAIN
CHICAGO—Market increases In
the export trade from Chicago and
the middle west during the
years are revealed in a report is
sued yesterday by the domestic and
foreign commerce committee of the
Chicago Association of Commerce.
The greatest increases during this
period are shown to have taken
place in the trade with South Amer
ica and Oceania, which has grown
over 200 per cent since 1922. Trade
with Venezuela, Argentina and Bra
zil, particularly, showed large gains.
Exporters from the middle west
held their own in trade with China
and Japan and registered increases
of 100 per cent In their commerce
with other countries of the Far East.
Trade with South Africa also dou
bled during the five-year period.
Every continent shared in the in
crease except Europe.
Steel Trade Awaits
Official Figures;
Prices Hold Steady
CHICAGO Official figures on
the production of steel ingots in Au
gust are awaited eagerly in the
trade as well as reports of sales
and shipments for the last month.
The official figures will be out in
about a week.
Unofficial reports are that August
production by all companies was
larger than June or July. Some re
ports are that August output aver
aged 82 per cent of capacity. The
Steel corporation averaged between
87 and 88 per cent in the last month
and the present output is reported
slightly above this level.
The trend of prices generally is
upward, but no definite policy on
bars, shapes and plates has been an
nounced.

HUGGINS MAY STAND
PAT ON PRESENT
LINEUP NEXT YEAR
By The United Tresi.
NEW YORK—Miller Huggins, of
all the major league managers, can
face another season with less worry
than his rivals. The manager of
the prospective American league
champions is perhaps the only pilot
in the major leagues who is not
faced with the necessity of a reor
ganization.
Strange things can happen in one
year when the luck breaks. This
time last season, instead of being
out in front, the Yankees were firm
ly established in the second divi
sion and there seemed to be little
hope for the future.
Fills Bad Hole.
The Babe wasn’t doing any too
well, the pitchers weren't going and
there was a huge hole in the mid
dle of the infield. Huggins knew
that he had to find a shortstop and
a second baseman and luck was
with him. He found Tony Lazzeri
and Mark Koenig and they meant
the difference between the second

TUNNEY TAKING
IT EASY IN
TRAINING
STROUDSBURG, Pa. (United
Press) —For the first time since es
tablishing his training camp here,
Gene Tunney was to work out with
his sparring partners today. A large
crowd of spectators from among the
persons here for the week-end was
expected.
“I am going along easy,” Tunney
said. “I am in condition to enter
the ring with Dempsey today, so
I am not going to take any chances
of over-training.
“I shall box only three days a
week, but not nine rounds a day.
Then I’ll take it easy the rest of
the time, hiking over the mountains
and playing golf.
"That will keep me razor-fine,
just as I want to be when I get in
there and win that title.”

‘SOMETHING FOR NOTHING' PROVES
POOR SUMMER CONCERT POLICY
BY PHRYGIAN.
NEW YORK —Request programs
are so frequent that we do not stop
to inquire at whose request they are
played. When they are legitimately
gathered there is still question if
they ure representative, because
most people only believe in asking
for things they need, and not many
of them really need a Beethoven
symphony.
However, the New York Philhar
monic has made it a yearly custom
to have its summer listeners pick out
the last program of the season.
There has never been any startling
choice and it has always been the
solid type of music that appealed
most. It used to be "Wagner,
Tschaikowsky and Liszt year after
year. But those of this year’s audi
ences who had the energy and initi
ative to fill out little slips of paper,
asking for what they wanted most,
decided as follows:
Tschaikowsky: Pathetique Sym
phony.
Richard Strauss Don Juan.
Johann Strauss: Tales of the
Vienna Woods.
Tschaikowsky: 1812 Overture.
The two Strauss numbers repre
sent a definite breaking away from
tradition for two reasons; First, for
the conservative type that votes for
request programs, Richard Strauss
has to date been a newcomer and a
revolutionary. Don Juan in con
struction and interpretation is out
of the ordinary. Second, the com
positions of Johann Strauss have al
ways been thought nice diversion,
but as symphonic music—well, you
know.
Furtwaengler Started It,
If these changes in choice could
be called a trend, and if such trend
could be interpreted, one might say
that audiences are less limited in
their desires. They like variety and
a little more charm than can be had
from a diet of strictly classical com-
X»osers. Johann Strauss has had a
real vogue in New York this past
season, begun by the German con
ductor, Furtwaengler. Johann was
not always strong on orchestration,
nor a master at development, but his
tunes carry their own impetus.
The omission of Wagner from
the program should not be counted
as a serious failing in taste. His
name appeared so often during the
regular season that the audience got
him with or without request. The
omission will undoubtedly be cor
rected by nevt year.
It might be interesting to note
what other numbers received exten
sive popular support. Beethoven’s
Fifth Symphony was the -second
symphonic choice, followed by the
Eroiea, the Tschaikowsky Fifth,
Schubert Unfinished, Beethoven’s
Ninth, Cesar Franck, Dvorak’s New
World, Brahms’ Fourth and First.
Leonore and Tannhauser were of
course included in the list of popu
lar overtures.
This request program brought to
a close the outdoor season of the
Philharmonic orchestra. No records
were broken, but the fact that an
orchestra can find enough people in
terested to keep summer concerts
going nightly for eight weeks is in
itself always a record. The resume
made by the orchestra shows Wag
ner a leading light, followed by
Beethoven. Tschaikowsky, Brahms,
Richard Strauss and Rimsky-Kor
sakoff.
Goldman Modesty.
There is very little in character
to distinguish the summer from the
winter concerts, except the strict ab
sence of important soloists. There
is no longer the sharp division in
taste that used to separate the two
series. All the latest numbers of
the previous winter appear now dur
ing the summer, and none of the
conductors makes any effort to keep
his programs within the not too
heavy class. Among other things
the outdoor concerts had Casella’s
Italia, Respighi’s Pines of Rome,
Stravinsky’s Rites of Spring and
many other pieces that can still be
classified as novelties.
Strange as it may seem the sea
son of music by the Goldman band
also came to a close this week, and
it also discovered that its leading
composer was Wagner. Tschaikow
sky was a close second, and other
classical composers, Bizet, Liszt,
Beethoven and Verdi were at the
top. Mr. Goldman did not forget
himself, and railked right alongside
the leaders with 20 different per
formances of his works. Mr. Gold
man writes attractive marches at
times, but he ought to be more
modest in their use. They have a
striking similarity to each other in
many ways and sound suspiciously
mathematical. His programs were
otherwise exemplary.
This comparison of the band and
orchestra series leads one to ques
tion whether one dqes not interfere
with the other. They play a good
deal of the same music. But there
are several factors which work to
bring a different clientele to each.
For one thing the Goldman con
certs are free and a free concert
will always attract a less eager
crowd than one where admission is
charged, even if it is as little as
the quarter collected by the' Phil
harmonic for some of its seats.
Then again, a number of people
who enjoy Wagner as the band
plays him might not like him so
well from an orchestra. A band is
not designed to render subtle effects
and its tone color is mostly limited
to the possibilities of the brasses.
For that reason the 1812 Overture
is as much a favorite with the
bands as the orchestras. It has
flaring color without much variety.
The attempts of band leaders to
raise the standard of their reper
toire has met with a measure of
success, but we believe that to the
band audience the real things are
still the marches and the man who
lpads.

JACK, THE TIGHTWAD.
BY H. IRVING KING.
Our friends and acquaintances
form a jury before which we are
perpetually on trial, and their ver
dict is generally a just one, how
ever much we may protest against
it. The verdict In the case of John
M. Codington was: “Jack would
be a first rate fellow —if he wasn’t
such a tightwad.” Jack had not
made muclj money himself—his
forebears had done that. But it
was working for Jack, and he saw
to it that it worked. There were
no vacations, or eight-hour days
for Jack’s dollars.
So when it got about that Jack
Codington was engaged to Elsie
Capron people laughed and won
dered, and even sneered. “Well,
that would be a match!” said one.
“Elsie Capron! She’ll make his
money fly for him.” And another
said: “What can Elsie be think
ing of? He’ll half starve her and
never let her have a decent dress

to her back.” While still a third
opinion—and this was the one
generally held by the men—was
that Elsie’s father, Cyrus, was at
the bottom of it all, using his
daughter as a bait to try and get
some of Jack’s hoarded wealth
coming his way to help him out
of the financial difficulties in
which, rumor said, he was in
volved.
This added greatly to the sus
picions of Mr. Caprou’s solvency.
None but a desperate man would
ever undertake such a desperate
enterprise. Elsie knew what was
being said; Jack knew, and Cyrus
knew.
Elsie was greatly annoyed;
Cyrus chuckled over it aud didn't
mind it a bit; Jack brooded over
it. For the first time in his life
he had a real case of introspec
tion. Between him and Elsie there
had been no financial thought.
Eros had knocked Mammon for
the count. With her Jack’s penuri
ousness was merely prudence.
Still she did wish that he would
commit some act of covert gen
erosity, “just to show the people.”
First she thought she would hint
at something of the kind to Jack.
Then she thought she wouldn’t—
he might think she believed the
things people said about him.
Once she thought of asking Cyrus
if he really was in financial dif
ficulties—but she knew too well
what he would say. He would tell
her to “mind her own business.”
Altogether, Elsie was about as un
happy as a girl can be who Is still
on good terms with the man shs
loves and to whom she is engaged.
As for Jack, the sufferings he
endured from his attack of intro
spection were something awful.
No one who has not had an acute
attack of the same kind can real
ize what he went through. He
had known, of course, before this,
that he was generally regarded as
a “tightwad”; but it had not both
ered him at all. Now it did, for
a great fear was upon him that
Elsie had come to look upon him
as others did.
One of Jack’s first moves after
his transformation was to visit
Mr. Capron in his office. “I have
heard—that is, there is a rumor,”
he began in an embarrassed man
ner, “that you are in financial
difficulties, Mr. Capron. I have
come to say that if I can be of
any assistance my fortune is as
your service.”
“Ha! ha!” laughed the old man,
“that’s a good one! So I am in
financial difficulties and Tight
wad Codington is ready to loosen
up! Who’d ’a’ thought it! My
dear young man, I am no more in
financial difficulties than you are.
There’s a gang been after my scalp
and thought they bad it, but I've
been playing possum on them. I
helped spread those rumors of
financial decrepitude myself—it
worked in with my plans. I
caught ’em napping and have just
given orders to my brokers which
will make, that gang of high
binders come across with several
hundred thousand dollars before
the exchange closes. Thank you,
just the same. I’ll tell Elsie about
your offer; it will tickle her.”
Reaching the office building,
which he owned and where he had
his headquarters, Jack gave Tony,
the bootblack in the lower hall
way, 50 cents for shining his
shoes and told him to keep the
change. Under pretense of a de
layed Christmas present he be
stowed $5 on the elevator man
who took him up. He sent for the
janitor to come to his office and
told him to announce a 10 per cent
rAise in the pay of all the em
ployes of the building. An im
promptu meeting of the employes
was held and grave doubt* were
expressed as to Mr. Codington’s
sanity,
“Aw, ’tain’t nothin’,” said Tony,
the bootblack; “the guy’s goin’ to
git married—that’s all.”
That night Jack appeared at
Elsie’s with a bouquet of orchids
and a five-pound box of candy.
“Oh, you dear, old Jack,” cried
Elsie, “father has told me all
about your offer. I always knew
those horried people lied when
they called you a tightwad.”

MADISON—The state board of of
normal resents derided late yester
day that Dr. M. A. Bussewitz, re
cently dismissed from the fa ulty
of Milwaukee Normal school by
President Frar k E. Baker, will be
given a chance to file a formal
answer to the charges.
President Baker charged Dr.
Bussewitz with inefficiency as the
school’s medical advisor; that he
filed incomplete class schedules
with the registrar; that he never
made one constructive suggestion
for the improvement of the school
system; that he required too much
pratice teaching of his students and
that not more than 58 of the per
sons taught by Dr. Bussewitz were
actively engaged as teachers.
All of President Baker’s charges
were denied by Carroll G. Pearse,
former president of the school.
The decision of the regents will
be announced following the filing
of Dr. Bussewitz’s answer.

This point in the whirligig of time finds labor strug
gling forward against odds as usual. It has its ups and
downs, and the present is not one of the ups, but it
keeps going upward in the long run. That is the
couraging feature. Anyone can stand an occasional slump
if he knows he will on the whole keep going ahead and
gaining ground.
Passaic is one of the lively spots m the American
labor movement at present. The strike has been taken
over by the American Federation of Labor, which, it it
is wise, will pour in whatever amounts of money is neces
sary to maintain the strikers and win the strike. The way
will then be open for the organization of the entire tex
tile industry. That’s why the bosses are fighting the
The garment workers have won victories, and other
unions have settled disputes on creditable terms. There
have been decreases of wages in some lines. The com
pany union movement has spread. It constitutes one of
the worst enemies of the legitimate labor movement at
the present time, and it calls for all of the wisdom and
ability there is in the movement.
Labor fell down pitiably on the organization of the
new political deal in 1924. There was no excuse for this
except lack of good sense on the part of the leaders and
the languor of the rank and file. However, labor is not
left without a political movement. The Socialist party
is the party of labor. It will carry the banner, and when
ever the occasion is ripe it will aid in the formation of a
labor party unless the Socialist party sooner sweeps the
field. In the meantime it is the duty of all workers, male
and female, to vote the Socialist ticket.
Our brothers in England have the miners’ strike on
their hands. It affects the interests of labor the world
over, and it must not be permitted to fail. The American
workers can help greatly to win the strike, by aiding it
financially. A good way to celebrate Labor Day would
be to make a contribution for that strike. Send it to
Frank J. Weber, Secretary, Federated Trades Council, 302
Brisbane Hall.
A LITTLE MORE PEP, PLEASE
Why should President Green of the American Fed
eration of Labor speak approvingly of military training,
as reports say he did?
It is nice to be agreeable, out it can be carried too far.
Labor wants to get along peaceably, but it wants to ad
vance peaceably, not to backslide.
Samuel Gompers went along during the war. He did
more than that —he called the labor chieftains together in
March, 1917, and mapped out a program for active par
ticipation in boosting the war.
Some think Samuel did this because he was born in
England and was prejudiced on the allied side. Others
think he did it because he really believed it was a war to
end war, and a war for democracy—but it hardly seems
likely that so astute a man could have been thus taken in.
Others think he did it in what he considered a long-headed
move to boost the labor movement.
If he had the last-named end in view he made a fear
ful mistake. The union movement secured hosts of new
members during the war, and seemed to be swimmingly
successful, but it lost most of them after the war. It
has less vitality, less pep, less fighting power, at the pres
ent time than before the war. If Gompers thought his sup
port of the war would be a gain for unionism he guessed
most absurdly wrong.
The cue of the A. F. of L. was to oppose the war from
start to finish. By so doing, it would have brought a storm
of criticism upon itself at the time, but it would have saved
its soul, and it would have been much stronger today.

A vote for any old party candidate is a vote against
