workers can put up.
Big business everywhere is now divided about the
best method of dealing with Labor. Some favor a Fascist-
Monarchist combination and a fight to a finish. Others
prefer constitutional government and a policy of concilia
tion.
Because big business is divided, a united Labor and
Socialist international can defeat the Fascist plotters by
seeking points of contact with those big business leaders
who see that a social transformation is inevitable. It is
possible to devise ways and means between them and for
ward looking Labor for a constructive social program.
International labor unity is essential for this.
Efforts to this end are promoted by the Amsterdam
and Zurich internationals with promising prospects. The
trade unions and Socialists of the following nations are
already working together: Great Britain, Sweden, Fin
land, Denmark, Latvia, Holland, Belgium, France, Ger
many, Poland, Czecho-Slovakia, Austria, Hungary, Spain,
Switzerland, Italy, Jugo-Slavia, Rumania, Bulgaria, Ar
gentina, Canada, South Africa, Palestine and Japan.
These represent over 49 per cent of the world’s trade
unions with a total membership of about 18,000,000.
They are affiliated with the Amsterdam trade union in
ternational which works in harmony with the Socialist
international. The total membership of these two inter
nationals is about 40,000,000.
The next strongest group of trade unions is composed
of the Pan-American Federation of Labor, of which the
American Federation of Labor is the strongest body. It
includes the Mexican, Central American and Brazilian
trade unions. The trade unions of Australia and New
Zealand are also outside the Amsterdam trade union inter
national. This independent group of All-American, Aus
tralian and New Zealand trade unions, together with simi
lar unaffiliated bodies in other continents, represents
about 24 per cent of the world’s trade unions. While not
affiliated with the Amsterdam and Zurich internationals,
this body keeps in touch with them. Its total membership
is about 9,000,000.
The third group of trade unions are the Russian Com
munist unions and their sympathizers in all countries.
They represent about 21 per cent of the world’s trade
unions and are affiliated with the Moscow international
Total membership about 6,000,000.
The fourth group of trade unions are the so-called
Christian or Catholic unions. They represent about 5 per
cent of the world’s trade unions. Total membership about
2,000,000. The remaining 1 per cent is made up of the
anarcho-syndicalist bodies. Total membership about
400,000.
It is evident then, that a co-operation between the Am
sterdam and Zurich internationals, aided by the Pan-
American and Australian group, will unite 73 per cent
all organized workers for international action. F(\
present, local conditions prevent such an internatioi.
union. But in proportion as capitalism puts them all be
fore the same problems, they will be found working to
gether, even if they are not affiliated with the same
international bodies. This drift will force also the Russian
and Catholic unions and their sympathizers in other coun
tries to seek the support of the stronger bodies and to
modify their policies accordingly.
THEY WILL COME TO IT LATER
The Coolidge administration naturally refuses to ac
cept the advice of the Wilson Democrat Newton D. Baker
and to commit itself frankly to a cancellation of the allied
war debts and of the Dawes plan. But they will come to
the same end, just the same, even if they get around to it
by covered and devious methods.
The Dawes plan itself provides for partial cancella
tion at any time when German payment should disturb the
international exchanges. If it should become necessary
to resort to this way out, it will be easy enough to stage a
little international panic.
Protective tariffs are another way of making it im
possible for the European industries to earn the money
for the payment of allied war debts and of the Dawes
reparations. And so long as the high tariff crowd or the
gold Democrats rule in Washington, this method of can
celling war debts and stopping Dawes payments by mak
ing them impossible will always be ready at hand.
Cancellation by honest or dishonest methods will be
the natural outcome, especially when the middle and work
ing class in Europe and the United States get enough
sense and power to smash the Morgan policies.

from further embarrassment with the help of Senator

Staff Correspondent
The United Press
GENEVA —Final vote upon the
report of the committee which con
sidered and approved Germany’s
admission to the league of nations
probably will be taken tomorrow,
it was announced today when the
seventh assembly of the league ad
journed for the day.
The constitutional committee of
the league also will report on the
plan for reorganization of the coun
cil tomorrow, and it was expected
that a final vote would be taken on
that, too.
The Canadian delegation to the
league met secretly today and de
cided temporarily to abandon its
claim for a semi-permanent seat on
the league council.
“For the present, Canada will not
press her claim to a council seat,”
Sir George Foster told the United
Press, “although she will reserve
the right to put forward such a de
mand in the future.”
This decision, naturally, does not
commit the other dominions, which
retain liberty of action. But, since
Canada was considered to be the
most prominent potential candidate
for the council among the British
dominions, her abstention from the
scramble for a council seat evoked
the belief that all the dominions
would refrain from urging similar
claims during this session. With
Canada, it was understood hereto
fore that Australia might become a
strong contender for a seat. The
sentiment of the dominion delegates
indicated that they must be reck
oned among the future claimants
for direct representation in the
council.

Quick Raises Laughter.
State Senator William F. Quick
raised laughter and applause when
he told of visiting an insane asylum
and being shown the room where
crazy murderers were kept. There
was only one guard over them.
He asked the guide how one man
dared to stand guard over such a
collection of bad actors, and was
told that there was no danger, that
if those inmates had had sense
enough to organize they would not
be where they were.
“What do we organize for?” he

“To get a simple and easy living.

Wall Street. We are engaged in
the struggle for existence, every one
of us, and we are in the struggle to
get food, clothing and shelter.
“We cannot escape that struggle,
but the way we get our food today
is vastly different from the case of

ciety. Organiaztion brought us out

the store taken from the people.

dollars.”

whether the many who produce the
food should decide.

THREE
FEDERAL RISK
PROTECTION FOR
400,000 SOUGHT
NEW YORK—Efforts during the
present year to extend the protec
tion of accident compensation laws
to large groups of wage-earners not
yet included have centered chiefly
in two bills that have been advanced
to a place on the calendar of con
gress, according to a statement just
issued by the American Association
for Labor Legislation.
One measure is the Cummins
Graham bill to provide federal acci
dent compensation for longshore
men, ship repairmen and other har
bor workers. The other is the Fitz
gerald bill to provide similar pro
tection for wage-earners in private
employment in the District of Co
lumbia.
Over 400,000 Affected.
“These bills, covering more than
a third of a million workers,” the
association states, “aim to close
up a conspicuous gap in American
accident compensation legislation.
Labor in all of the states, except
six in the non-industrial south, now
enjoy the benefits of compensation
laws. Yet the wage-earners in the
District of Columbia who meet with
accidents and the longshoremen in
the various ports of the country who
suffer work injuries while aboard
the vessel have no remedy except
costly and uncertain lawsuits. Con
gress alone has power to provide
the urgently needed protection,
which is urged by social service or
ganizations, compensation officials,
organized labor and progressive em
ployers. This legislation is now
squarely up to congress for final
action at the December session.”
Reports Are Unanimous.
Both judiciary committees of con
gress have unanimously reported
in favor of the harbor workers’ bill
and the senate passed it in June,
according to the statement, while
the District of Columbia compensa
tion bill was favorably reported by
the house committee in April for
the third time in five years.
“In two states accident compensa
tion is an immediate issue,” says
the association. “The Missouri
workmen’s compensation act of 1925
has been held up for a referendum
vote and will be voted upon in the
November election. It is supported
by both organized labor and the
state association of employers. In
Florida a workmen’s compensation
bill will be presented to the next
legislature with the backing of la
bor and of employers who see in
creased need for this legislation as
a result of recent industrial activity
in building construction.”

THE PLAYGROUND. I
The playground in the
United States, had its begin
ning in the city of Boston
40 years ago. Not that
Boston had a vision of di
vine light, but the growth of
modern industry and com
merce in a city of kinky
lanes, crooked streets and
blind alleys, simply rode
roughshod over the rights
of the child.

In Milwaukee the move
ment started much later.
The subject of playgrounds
appears in the proceedings
of the common council for
the first time about 20 years
ago. And the first play
grounds were obtained in
the 20th and 21st wards in
the north and northwest
sections of the city.
Incidentally, those wards,
together with others on the
west and south sides, had
experienced a political up
heaval in 1904.

It was at the time of the
advent of the automobile
which made the streets a
death zone—unfit to be used
by children for play.
Those were hard days for
the child, bubbling over with
life, and for youth as well.
Property owners were in
wrath over windows broken
by stray balls. The "good”
citizen was indignant over
the dance hall, poolroom
and street corner gang-
Automobile drivers kicked
over the kids running free.
"Always in the way,” was
sung in the show houses. An
obliging city government
forbade playing on the
streets and congregating of
numbers at the corners and
the watchful eye of the
"law” was everywhere with
its peremptory "Move On”
and a club to enforce the
command.

Nowhere was there a
kindly "Come, play, laugh
and sing.” Oh yes, there
were those buildings with
inscriptions—suffer the little ones to come—but the
buildings were locked and on the grounds around these
buildings were signs ‘Keep off the grass—or "Please.”
In 1908 a mass prayer (petition) signed by many
children of Milwaukee, was sent to the common council:
"Please give us playgrounds!”
Since then the subject of playgrounds has become a
matter of constant attention by the common council.

After securing the first playgrounds in the north
and northwest of the city, the south side also asked for
consideration and rightfully so because the congestion in
that section was more prounounced than elsewhere.
By 1910 the agitation for playgrounds had gathered
momentum. Civic clubs, advancement associations, social
and political organizations took up the cause of room
for play.
As an expedient, streets were blocked to traffic for
certain hours of the day, to give the children safe places
to play, and vacant lots that were available were put into
use.

The park board set aside space in the public parks
and provided equipment for play.
The department of public works supplied help and
machinery for plotting the grounds.
In a number of cases alleys and even streets had to
be closed which can be done only by action of the
common council.
A bond issue of $1,000,000 has been voted by the
people of Milwaukee, to be used for the purchase and
equipment of playgrounds.
How widely the need for playgrounds was felt can
be gathered from the fact that only little opposition was
met and this came only from a few who feared injury
to their property.

By 1925 there were in use under the control of the
extension department of the Milwaukee public schools
25 playgrounds.
At first the grounds were in the care of the depart
ment of public works. The department might be able
to do the rudimentary work, but it had no means for
planning or beautifying the grounds.
Bare grounds are poor playgrounds. Equipment
was purchased for some grounds, while others were bare
for years. The grounds were transferred to the park
board.

This board had little means for planning and beauti
fying and no money for planning and supervising the use
of the grounds.
The school board also had grounds around its school

By 1925 the board of public land commissioners,
which, in its plans, never omits to provide for recrea
tional, social and playground needs, had made a thorough
study of the situation and reported its recommendations
to the common council.

It recommended a definite control and maintenance
of the playgrounds as follows:
(a) The school board shall maintain the play
grounds.
(b) A budget provision for maintenance of the
playgrounds.
(c) An expansion of the school board facilities.
For 1926 the estimate of cost, for 48 playgrounds
covered by the report, was given at $39,200. In addition,
a contingent fund was recommended.
The recommendations of the land commissioners
were, in the main, adopted by the common council and
today the school board is responsible for the maintenance
and supervision of such playgrounds as are finished and
ready for use.

The playgrounds are now under the supervision of
the very able head of the extension department, Miss
Dorothy C. Enderis, assistant to the superintendent of
schools.
An idea of the need of these playgrounds can be
gathered from the report on playground attendance dur
ing the vacation months of July and August, 1925. The
figures for 1926 are not yet available.
In those two months, 73,027 boys and 53,933 girls
attended in the forenoon; 106,415 boys and 99,200 girls
attended in the afternoon, and 157,607 boys and 64,864
girls attended in the evening.
This makes a total of 337,049 boys and 217,997 girls,
or a grand total of 555,064, who availed themselves of
the opportunity for clean and wholesome play and rec
reation.
The increased number in the evening shows that
many children who are at work in the day time get the
advantage of evening play when the grounds are brightly
illuminated.
And while our children are at the playground,
playing under the care and kindly direction of super

Mussolini's Attempt to Grab Albania Blocked by Europe
USED PISTOL TO
PUSH PLAN FOR
PROTECTORATE
Duce Offered Gold,
Arms to Fight
Serbs, Claim.
LONDON—FuII official details of
a carefully concealed story of Pre
mier Mussolini's attempt to grab
Albania as an Italian protectorate
have come to light.
Official documents show conclu
sively that Premier Mussolini’s min
ister, Count Aloise, went June 27 to
the president of the Albanian repub
lic and literally leveled a pistol at
him, demanding his immediate con
sent to placing Albania under an
Italian protectorate.
Economically Albania is entirely
dependent upon Italian banks, to
which it is engaged by customs liens
and a financial mortgage, but this
new political demand bowled the
Albanian president off his legs.
Offered Gold, Arms.
He immediately summoned the
foreign envoys to Albania to a con
ference at his residence, where he
reported the statements made by
Count Aloise. The Albanian presi
dent said that Italy demanded the
transfer of foreign representation of
Albania to Italian diplomacy. If
this demand was accorded, Premier
Mussolini offered a large sum of
gold and full equipment for the Al
banian army against Serbia. If it
was rejected, Count Aloise threat
ened an Italian occupation of the
port of Valona and other sanctions.
President Ahmed Zogu informed
the diplomats that he rejected the
ultimatum and that Count Aloise
left in a dudgeon, departing for
Italy aboard a destroyer which was
lying at his disposal in the harbor
of Durazzo.
The Albanian government rushed
troops to defend Valona and sus
pended all Italian military instruc
tors.
The foreign diplomats, in great ex
citement, wired the news to their
governments, and Britain and Ser
bia immediately took steps to elicit
the truth of the incident and to pro
tect Albania against Italian inter
ference.
Explanation Was Asked.
The Serb war minister even sent
advance mobilization notices to the
army, while the British ambassador
immediately visited Premier Musso
lini, confronting him with* a cate
gorical demand for an explanation.
Premier Mussolini asserted that
the Albanian president was an abso
lute liar and that Count Aloise
never presented any such demand,
much less an ultimatum, and that
the only thing Italy demanded was
the signing of a pact of nonaggres
sion or similar existing ones of in
ternational practice.
Officially, this closed the incident^
and the governments interested
have kept close mouthed silence.
But ft is most significant that Brit
ish cruisers were ordered to Al
banian ports immediately after the
Incident and were afforded an en
thusiastic reception by the author
ities and population.

CAPE TOWN, South Africa—On
the even of sailing for the imperial
conference in London, Prime Min
ister J. B. M. Hertzog last night
in an important speech emphasized
South Africa’s independence and
fiercely attacked those who desire
the Union Jack as the South African
flag.
“I shall urge at the imperial con
ference that necessary steps be
taken so that our national status
shall equal that of Great Britain or
other commonwealths and our title
to international recognition can be
published.”
Gen. Hertzog attacked the Sons of
England society and also the em
pire group of Natal, emphasizing
that they are using the Union Jack
for political purposes.
“To deny us, who are citizens of
the UnJon of South Anka, the
right to have our own flag not only
is unreasonable but selfish and
mean,” he said. “It is an insult
to every individual who has national
self-respect.”

BRITISH LABOR
MEETS TO ASK
IMPROVEMENTS
BOURNEMOUTH, England
Unity in a common organization of
trade unions of all countries, a
minimum wage scale and a maxi
mum working week of 44 hours
were the principal demands of reso
lutions presented at the annual
meeting of the trades union con
gress, which opened here today.
More than 1,000 delegates, repre
senting all of the national British
unions affiliated with the trades
union congress, attended.
One of the principal resolutions
presented to the congress for adop
tion was made by the iron and steel
trades federation, which proposed
an international wage convention
to consider a minimum wage scale
as a necessary corollary to the 48-
hours convention.
They declared that the British
government should prohibit the im
portation of competing goods into
Great Britain produced in foreign
countries under conditions harmful
to the worker. The resolution is
particularly directed against some
of the so-called cheap labor in
oriental countries and countries
where the sweatshop prevails.
Another resolution called upon
the trades union council to agitate
for the ratification of the Washing
ton convention on hours of indus
trial employment.
Several resolutions dealing with
the payment of wages on regular
yearly national holidays were pre
sented.
The Amalgamated Society of
Tailors and Tailoresses voiced a
protest against the growing ten
dency in the garment trade to have
workers take their labor into the
home. They demanded that the
council place the situation before
the home secretary with a demand
that legislation be passed forbidding
garment workers from working un
der such conditions.
The Engineering union proposed
definite powers for the general coun
cil as follows:
To assist unions or alliance of
unions contemplating entering upon
a struggle for the improvement of,
or in defense of,, the conditions of
their members, by taking over the
direction of the struggle.
To have power to levy all or part
of the affiliated unions.
To call a stoppage of work by
affiliated organizations.
The building workers unions, how
ever, apparently deploring the re
sults of the recent general strike,
presented a resolution making a
complete ballot and full discussion
of the points at issue necessary be
fore a general walkout could be
called.

formation has reached the public
about the contents of the recently
concluded French-Rumanian treaty.
About the only informatior given
out by the government in a round
about way is that the treaty is
made for 10 years and provides for
the arbitration of all differences
between the two governments.
The newspapers who are close to
the government give out that the
text of the treaty cannot be pub
lished until it has been placed be
fore the league of nations for regis
tration, but that it contains 21 arti
cles setting forth the details of ar
bitration. 1
Want Russian Pact.

cles appearing in the Rumanian
government press that the Avarescu
government wants to exert pressure
on Soviet Russia with a view to
having Moscow government ac
knowledge Rumania’s right to Bes
sarabia.
Some papers claim that this is
quite in accord with the Locarno
spirit, whereas the Russian soviet
press hints that it would have been
better to show some Locarno spirit
before taking advantage of Russian
disorders and war to steal Bess
arabia from Russia.
It is claimed that this treaty does
not pledge France to the defense
of Rumania in case of a dispute
with Russia over the Dniester fron
tier. Bu.t as this would involve
also Poland, which has a military
treaty with Rumania, this claim
may be taken with some reserve.
Makes Easy Promise.
Some Austrian papers say ‘hat
France promised Rumania to induce
Mussolini to guarantee the Dnies
ter frontier. If this is true, it
means very little, because any in
fluence of the French government
over Mussolini in such a question
would be negligible.

cause the treaty between France
and Russia will have the effect of
making Jugo-Slavia stronger in its
resistance of Italy. For this rea
son Mussolini cannot find much
pleasure in this French-Rumanian
pact.

closer relation between Rumania
and Italy would necessarily mean
a cooler sentiment towards France.
On the other hand, it is pointed
out that the Rumanian government
received a loan of 200,000,000 lire
from the Italian government a
short while before the conclusion
of the treaty with France.
Wonder About Effects.
Thinking these things over, some
editors ask: Did Mussolini know
that this French-Rumanian treaty
was being concluded when he
agreed to loan the Avarescu govern
ment 200,000,000 lire? Did he know
it while A aresuc was on a visit
to Rome?
Some Rumanian editors are in
clined to think that an understand
ing between the French and Italian
governments about their mutual re
lations to the Rumanian and to the
Dniester border is possible.
These editors base themselves
upon a recent statement of Foreign
Minister Mitilineu, who held out
the hope of a similar treaty be
tween Rumania and Italy.

BOURNEMOUTH, Eng.—British
trade unionism reaffirmed its inten
tion to continue to use the general
strike as the workers’ weapon and
declared nationalization is the
remedy for the coal mine trouble
yesterday at the opening here of the
58th trades union congress, attended
by more than 700 delegates.

be drawn from the general strike

ists.
LEAGUE MEETS;
SETS SCENE TO
ADMIT GERMANY
CHICAGO —Under the blazing
rays of batteries of high powered
arc lights, located by movie opera
tors to film the proceedings, with
many powerful, squeaky loud speak
ers to broadcast the orator’s words,
the seventh assembly of the league
of nations convened here yesterday,
says a copyrighted dispatch from
Geneva to The Tribune. The meet
ing, which unless some new hitch
arises, will be marked by the ad
mission of Germany, was dimmed
a bit today by the absence of the
delegates of Spain and Brazil, who
have bolted.
Paderewski in Gallery.
A brilliant galaxy of spectators
jammed the galleries. Mrs. Wood
row Wilson in a black cloche hat
and black fur trimmed manteau sat
in the front row, with Miss Belle
Baruch, daughter of the New York
banker, Bernard Baruch, and Ig
nace Paderewski, famous pianist,
and his wife. Senator Swanson,
Congressman Stephen Porter, and
Maharajah Kapurthals, with the
royal emerald earrings, also were
present.
Edouard Benes, foreign minister
of Czecho-Slovakia, as chairman of
the council, presided until the as
sembly elected M. Nintchitch, for
eign minister of Jugo-Slavia, as
president. M. Benes, in a long
speech, told the world not to get
discouraged because of she slow
progress with which the league is
handling its important problems.
Harsh and Unkind.
“It is harsh and unkind for pessi
mists to say that our six years’ ef
forts have yielded meager results.
Disarmament cannot now be solved
in its entirety, but we propose to
accomplish the first stage and reach
an intial international agreement
limiting preparations for war, how
ever limited the restrictions may
be.”
He said the admission of Ger
many would give the league new
prestige. Then he shed a few tears
over the “departure, to our sorrow,
of some states which were dearest
to us,” meaning Spain and Brazil,
who quit when denied permanent
seats in the league’s council.

WASHINGTON—In spite of at
tempts by congress to check the is
suance of propaganda, a flood of
literature of varous kinds, printed,
mimeographed, and typewritten,
continues to emanate from the dif
ferent government departments.
Departments press agents, usually
disguised under anothed title, seek
to make reporting easy for news
paper correspondents as well as to
get across to the public some
achievement of a government
agency or official. Sometimes the
material gets into the newspapers.
Just as often it goes into the waste
basket. One or two good sized waste
baskets can be filled daily with the
matter coming into the office of a
Washington correspondent.
Important news developments in
Washington usually are not press
n gen ted, notwithstanding the im
pression that might he given by the
quantity of material coming from
the departments daily. The cabinet
members, in their daily, seml-week
ly, or weekly conferences with the
press, distribute their information
first hand without the aid of pre
pared statements.
Press agenting by the government
reached its peak during the war,
during the regime of the committee
on public information. Nearly all
the departments were obliged to dis
tribute their news material through
that committee, which was a highly
organized body with news, propa
ganda, photographic, foreign lan
guage, and other divisions.

Total Indebtedness of 48 States Doubled in Eight Years
$5.01 INCREASE
IN PER CAPITA
SUM REPORTED
Bonds Issued in 1925
Were Mostly for
Highways.
WASHINGTON—Per capita expen
ditures and per capita indebtedness
of the 48 states more than doubled
during the period from 1917 to 1925,
according to a summary of financial
statistics of all the states issued
yesterday by the department of
commerce.
The per capita expenditures for
the maintenance and operation of
the general departments of the state
governments went up from $4.19 per
capita in 1917 to $9.20 per capita
in 1925. The figure was $9 in 1924.
The per capita net indebtedness
mounted from $4.93 in 1917 to
$11.12 in 1925. It was $10.64 in
1924.
Bonds for Highways.
Twentysix states effected a de
crease in their indebtedness in 1925,
but the aggregate increase in the net
debt of the 48 states last year was
$118,683,000. The total indebted
ness at the end of last year amount
ed to $1,251,702,639. Bonds issued
during 1925 were chiefly for high
ways.
The total revenue receipts of the
state governments sos 1925 were sl,-
485,242,240. This was $373,703,981
more than the total payments of
the year exclusive of the outlay pay
ments for permanent improvements,
but $129,319,990 less than the to
tal payments including those for
permanent improvements. In only
17 of the states was there sufficient
revenue to meet all payments dur
ing the year.
Still Lack $129,320,000.
The payments in excess of reve
nue receipts were met from the pro
ceeds of debt obligations. The
states, as a whole, after increasing
their revenue receipts for 1925 by
$115,176,000, of which $6,998,000 was
from the general property tax, still
lacked $129,320,000 of having suf
ficient revenues to cover all govern
mental costs, including capital out
lays.
The total per capita revenue re
ceipts were $13.19 in 1925, as com
pared with $12.32 in 1924 and $5.14
in 1917. Property and special taxes
represented 40 per cent of the total
revenue in 1925. The increase in
these was 98.8 per cent from 1917 to
1924 and 2.8 per cent from 1924 to
1925. Special taxes in 1925 includ
ed $85,894,069 inheritance taxes in
45 states, and $27,535,105 in income
taxes in 13 states.
Licenses constituted 34.3 per cent
of the total revenues for 1925. The
gasoline sales tax raised $87,353,194
in 1925 and motor vehicle licenses
amounted to $198,710,310.
Final Services
For Valentino in
Los Angeles Today
LOS ANGELES—The body of
Rudolph Valentino spent its last
night outside the tomb in the midst
of a silent guard in Guardian Angei
mortuary chapel. Outside a crowd
of thousands milled. They never
glimpsed the casket of bronze and
silver.
The body of the moving picture
actor, attended by his brother, Al
berto Guglielmo; his fiancee, Pola
Negri; his manager, S. George Ull
man; his producer, John Considine,
Jr.; actresses, actors, movie mag
nates, newspaper reporters and pho
tographers, formed the funeral
cortege at the little town of Alham
bra, 15 miles by railroad from Los
Angeles, late yesterday.
The funeral cavalcade was sent
by a roundabout route to the funeral
parlor.
Attendance at today’s final serv
ices has been limited to GOO persons.
Active pallbearers will be Norman
Kerry, Emmett Flynn, George Fitz
maurice, who directed his last pic
ture; Douglas Gerard, Mauel Reachi
and John W. Considine, Jr. The
body will be placed in a mausoleum
in Hollywood cemetery.
Parachute Strikes
‘Air Pocket; 9 Girl
Stunt Flier Hurt
ST. PAUL, Minn.—Gladys Roy,
airplane stunt performer, today was
reported recovering from injuries
sustained at the Minnesota state
fair late yesterday when the para
chute with which she leaped from
a speeding plane, failed to check
her fall sufficiently, throwing Miss
Roy violently to the ground.
A crowd of 25,000 persons
watched Miss Roy jump from the
plane at an altitude of 700 feet. The
parachute opened perfectly, but
when 100 feet from the ground it
apparently struck an “air pocket”
and dropped swiftly.
Hospital attendants announced
Miss Roy is suffering from a dis
located right hip. She will not be
able to continue her performances
at the fair which were scheduled
for the balance of the week.

CATHOLICS IN
MEXICOAPPEAL
TO CONGRESS
MEXICO CITY—In a petition
which the Catholic episcopate draft
ed yesterday for presentation in
congress this week they declare that
the provisions of the constitution
and laws affecting the church are
tyrannical, oppressive, and fatal to
the development and life of the
church.
Would Avoid Politics.
A statement accompanying copies
of the petition says the Catholics
are pledged to use all their influence
to force the federation and states
to reform or remove the laws affect
ing the activities of Catholic organ
izations.
After the preamble, explaining
that the Catholic church has no de
sire to mix in politics but will main
tain itself within its own proper
sphere, the petition declares that
while the government has the right
to dictate laws governing the church
in so far as its civil state is con
cerned, it has no right to invade the
territory belonging peculiarly to
the church.
Will Reopen Churches.
The petition promises that the
Catholics will reopen the churches
and schools and supply all the funds
necessary to their maintenance, not
seeking aid from the government,
and will help solve the problem of
illiteracy.
The petitioners assert that they
have no intention of interfering with
what the government calls its na
tional aspirations and the redemp
tion of workingmen, but rather is
in full sympathy with the uplift
movement.
The bill closes with the demand
that all church buildings be re
turned to the church.

PLAN TO KIDNAP
KING OF SPAIN
IS FRUSTRATED
BY RAFAEL MORAYTA.
StaA* Correspondent
The United Press
MADRID—The council of minis
ters will meet today to make final
decisions governing the liquidation
of the present crisis following the
announced suppression of the army
revolt directed by artillery officers.
Plans for the trial of the accused
artillery men will then be made.
Two high ranking officers have been
arrested for their part in the in
subordination, which was directed
against the rule of Primo de Rivera.
Gen. de Rivera has announced
that an artillery officer and one sol
dier were killed in putting down
the rebellion. Two other soldiers
are reported to have been wounded.
Under Cover of Revolt.
LONDON—The Daily Mail’s spe
cial Hendaye...correspondent reports
that a plot to Seize King Alfonso
of Spain and force him to sign his
abdication was only frustrated by
prompt suppression of the military
revolt in Spain and by the king's
departure from San Sebastian for
Madrid. According to the dispatch,
the plotters, who were described as
Spanish republicans, now living at
St. Jean de Luz and other frontier
towns, planned to cross the border
i'4 speedy automobiles and raid San
Sebastian as soon as fighting start
ed in the revolt.
They apparently hoped to find the
police and loyal troops so busily
occupied that they would be able to
reach the palace and seize the king.
The situation in Spain at the pres
ent critical moment, possibly in
volving, as is believed here, the fate
of Dictator Primo de Rivera him
self, is arousing increased interest.
It is thought not impossible that
the rebuff which Spain experienced
at Geneva in her failure to obtain
a permanent seat in the council of
the league of nations may affect ad
versely Primo de Rivera’s prestige.
Strong curiosity is also felt as to
how far the Spanish premier and
the Italian premier, Benito Mus
solini, may be working in conjunc
tion to obtain ascendency in the
Mediterranean.

Methodist Preacher
Weds Abie and Rose
BALTIMORE—It is a far, far
better thing to wash the dishes for
her Abie than to cavort in any old
musical revue, his “Irish Rose” has
decided.
So little Vera O’Connor eloped
with Nathan Abraham, and now she
will educate her hands instead of
her feet.
This particular Abie is a musician
in a popular Washington orchestra.
He met his Rose here a year ago
and they plighted their troth.
Then the Rose got a chance to
sign up with a New York revue.
“No, no,” said Abie. “Let’s get
married instead.”
So they hunted up a Methodist
preacher, so as to be absolutely neu
tral, and got the knot tied.

PUNISHMENT IS

TEKAMAH, Neb. While 12
healthy rats were being sentenced
to a bread and water diet for 20
days at Creighton university lab
oratory in Omaha, this method of
enforcing the Volstead law was suf
fering a temporary setback in Tak
amah, home town of the crusade.
Instead of bringing in Roy Car
son and Tom Nelson, two more vic
tims of Judge Orville Chait’s eccen
tric sentences, Sheriff “Dad” Smith
calmly announced that he c >uld not
find the mandate papers from the
supreme court. There was lalk
about Nelson’s plight in failing to
1 get someone to feed his hogs and
sheep during his 60 days’ sentence.
An Elderly Man.
As Nelson is one of the cham
pion hog callers of the county and
had intended to enter the national
contest at Omaha next week, it is
possible that this also will be looked
on as an excuse for him.
Nelson is an elderly man, and
may escape by getting a physician
to say that the diet would be harm
ful. His sentence, at any rate, may
be delayed several days. Carson is
a young man, without farm or fam
ily troubles or hog calling genius,
and there is less sympathy for him.
In the continued absence of Judge
Chatt, the youthful county dicta
tor who has decreed this punishment
for all liquor law violators, there is
no one in jail now on the starvation
diet. Joe Olinger, who drinks lem
on extract or anything else he can
get, is under a bread and water
sentence, but his physician, Dr. L.
E. Sauer, has advised against its im
position.
Gets Good Food.
It would weaken him physically,
the doctor told the authorities, and
would not do him a bit of good mor
ally. So they are feeding old Joe on
watermelon, grapes, corn, beef and
tomatoes, and yesterday one well
wisher sent in a good cigar.

ciated with Prof. .John 11. Commons,
internationally known labor author
ity and economist, will conduct a
course in Labor Problems, begin
ning Sept. 27, at the Milwaukee pub
lic library, under the auspices of
the Milwaukee extension division of
the university.
This course should be of especial
interest to workers and other stu
dents of labor problems.
To Outline History.
The subject will be approached
from the historical point of view,
taking up first the characteristic
American industrial setting, early
industrial practices, the pioneer
philosophy of personal liberty, the
lack of any closed-class element in
the population, the political back
ground which differentiates the
American labor movement from the
European movement, American so
cial history with its basic emphasis
on the American standard of liv
ing and the later developments of
American social life.
“This course is not primarily for
the training of either employment
managers or trade union leaders,
but is a presentation of the issues
which arise between capital and la
bor and an examination of the his
tory of those issues and the meth
ods employed by both sides of the
controversy,’’ Dr. Perlman explains
In his outline of the course.
For Writers, Too.
“The course is primarily designed
to be of service to the community
and group leaders, leaders in busi
ness and labor, journalists and
newspaper writers, personnel direc
tors, teachers, factory and store su
perintendents and other labor prob
lem students to whom such a course
would have practical as well as cul
tural -value.”
The class meets on Monday, 7:15
p. m., to 9 p. m., and will continue
for 18 weeks, except during the
Christmas holidays. Registration
days are Sept. 17, 18, 20 and 21.
The fee for the course is $lO, which
covers all expenses, save the price
of text books.

TIP TO EDITORIAL WRITER.
To the Editor of The Leader:-
Early this week a Milwaukee
newspaper came out in its custom
ary front page editorial, captioned
“Milwaukee,” and went on to some
length about the exhibitors at the
State Fair. It cautioned “smart
young men from the city” that it
would be w’ell for them to go out
and watch their country cousins
curry cows, and continued to in
sinuate that a few years from now
those serious-minded duffers who
are now smelling of cows will be
hiring the smart young men from
the city at S3O a week, while they
will have all the advantages of life
—through loyalty to the cow, I be
lieve.
All of which is very nice for a
bedtime story.
Taking a subjective example: I
was once one of those serious-minded
young men. I once curried sleek
Guernsey cows on a Wisconsin farm,
slopped Poland China hogs and
drove a team of 2,800-pound Perch
erons. In fact, I recall distinctly
raising a certain fine crop of pota
toes, also milking 14 of those sleek
cattle and slopping two broods of
hogs after working in the field all
day. I recall my pride when those
potatoes turned out 250 bushels to
the acre—but I also recall sacking
them, hauling them five miles over
country roads (with the team of
Percherons) and selling them for 35
cents per 100 pounds.
As I recall, it was always so with
farm produce. It seemed that the
game acted that way—when we had
something to sell the price auto
matically went down.
I have seen cases in Wyoming and
Nebraska where the stockmen would
find themselves understocked, buy
expensive cattle, overstock a sparse
range, and dig out the bones of 50 or
100 head of cattle from the fence
corner in the spring.
I have been \in Vermont in the
sap-running season and have seen
frugal New England Yankees sell
ing th6ir syrup for the cost of the
containers it was shipped in.
I have worked all day in a Wis
consin woods, then started at dusk
with a load of logs on a 10-mile haul
through ice, slush and sleet—and I
have been forced to sell those logs
for less than the cost of hauling, in
order to empty my sled, stack my
chains and get home.
So I did like many other serious
minded Wisconsin farm boys. I
went to the university, studied agri
culture —and came to the city.
Which is something for other seri
ous-minded young men to consider.
But why doesn’t the editorial

workers. Many of our department

jobs.

still be weeks of fine weather, these
same and many other employes
must begin again to work Saturday
afternoons.
The greed of these big business
men is a crying shame. They care
nothing for any holiday nor for any
working man or woman. To them,
the making of a dollar, regardless
of how, stands above everything.

SLEEP IS LIKELY
PHILADELPHIA—Irene du Pont
of the E. I. du Pont de Nemours
Co., Wilmington, Del., yesterday
told the convention of the Ameri
can Chemical society that sleep as
a necessity for humans may be done
away with through the development
of chemistry.
Pointing out that some adults
sleep a greater number of hours
than others, Mr. du Pont said it
seemed likely this was due to some
human systems requiring a longer
time to work out poisons that ac
cumulate.
“Would it not seem likely,” he
said, “that the reactions may be
hastened by some catalytic agent or
even that the antidote itself may be
prepared and administered, there
by either decreasing the amount of
sleep required or even doing away
with the necessity of sleep entire
ly?”
Would Boost Output.
Such a discovery, he said, would
add to both hours of production and
of pleasure and would greatly de
crease the cost of housing and of
factory production.
That chemistry might become the
means of creating a race of super
men and even change the nature of
human beings, were prospects held
before the 4,000 delegates by Mr.
du Pont.
Certain drugs, he asserted, tend
to stupify and prevent humans from
thinking clearly, while other drugs
to some extent stimulate the mind.
“Is it not possible,” he said, “to
suppose that there exist other com
pounds which might stimulate to a
greater extent so that mentally all
the users would become supermen,
or geniuses?”
Functions of Liver.
“It is proverbial that if one’s
liver is out of order, it definitely
does affect one’s outlook on life for
the worse and there can be no ques
tion that the liver’s function is es
sentially a chemical one.
“Other organs and glands pre
sumably have analogous effects, so
much so that it does not seem to
be unreasonable to suppose, that
one’s character itself is the result
of the sum total of certain chemical
reactions taking place hr the body.
“When the nature of this is un
derstood, we may expect that by
injecting proper-compounds into an
individual we can make his charac
ter to order.”

J-DAY LAYOFF
FOR DEMPSEY
IN TRAINING
ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—Jack
Dempsey awoke as a gentleman of
leisure today, with no prospect of
again using his fists until Friday.
The three days’ rest from train
ing is to be a real respite, accord
ing to present plans. Today there
was no definite program until eve
ning when the champion will be
host at a dinner in the Ambassador
hotel to visiting newspapermen.
Tomorrow and Thursday, plans
are for Dempsey to go where the
spirit wills —within a few limita
tions. Probably a long automobile
ride if the weather is fair will be
indulged in.
Yesterday’s workout showed the
fighter at his best —as far as speed
was concerned. His blows lacked
the force of the day before, but
they were evidently tempered pur
posely.
Frankie Carpenter felt the brunt
of the champion’s attack, the other
four sparring partners who engaged
with Dempsey having easier times.
Carpenter received a left to the; jaw
which ended his appearance after
suffering a continuous tattoo of
body blows.

SCOTLAND LACKS
FIELDS TO PLAY I
CRICKET fl
Cricket does not flourish in Scot
land for two good reasons, in tha
opinion of a writer in The London
Post.
“In the first place, good ground®
are few and far between, and
patches frequent—though to
miss with indigation the story
southern visitor who got out to
all-along-the-ground lob, which pu
up an old and obstreperous cock
grouse and so caught him in two
minds,” he comments.
“Secondly, there is so much ‘soft
ness’ in the weather that matches
are often abandoned, over 50 per
cent in the case of a notable club
last season.
“Yet the enthusiasm of A. K. Bell
of the Orange club—a sort of M. C.
C. —is likely to be the beginning of
better things. His gift of a ground
and pavilion for the benefit of
Perthshire cricket may lead to the
establishment of a nursery for prom
ising Scottish players, both amateur
and professional.”

MADUSHAW IS
NEW COUNTY
GOLF CHAMP
George Madushaw defeated Len
Fons, 4 up and 3 to play, in the 36-
hole finals of the Milwaukee county
golf championship yesterday. The
match was played at Grant park.
Madushaw, who came to the fore
this year in the state golf meet at
the Ozaukee Country club, losing to
Irving Peterson of Racine, in the
semi-finals, took an early lead in
the match, this being due primarily
to poor putting on the part of Fons.
Fons was three down when the
pair started the final 18 holes, and
Madushaw then ran it up to four,
after which Fons cut it down. On
the last nine he had Madushaw
down to a single hole advantage,
but missed an easy putt on the 12th
which would have squared the
match.

The Leader Page of Sports
NINE
I t ‘UNEASY UES THE HEAD-’
Each year a number of the
crowned heads of the sports world
are dethroned, and 1926 has been no
exception. I’m wondering if Jack
Dempsey, so-called heavyweight box
ing champion of the world, isn’t go
ing to get “crowned” in a fashion
that he hasn’t experienced since
“Fireman Jim” Flynn knocked him
out in one round in 1917.
Of all the champions who are left,
only Babe Ruth seems to have a
sure grip on his throne. The Home
Run King is too far ahead of any
of his competitors in his specialty
to w’orry about that title, and he
may also be the 1926 batting cham
pion of the American league. Bill
Tilden and Bobby Jones defend their
crowns next week, Walter Hagen
tries to keep his professional golf
championship a week later, and
Glenna Collett will meet the stern
est kind of opposition at Philadel
phia, still later.
Rogers Hornsby, for six seasons
the champion batsman of the Na
tional league, seems sure to loose
his crown, while the champion
Washington Senators are definitely
out of the 1926 flag race. Even the
Pirates may yet be absent from the
next world series.
And look at the list of those who
have lost! Truly, 1926, has sowed
many a razzberry in the field of
sport. Paul Berlenbach, Harry
Greb, Mickey Walker, and Rocky
Kansas, all beaten, and Kid Kaplan
has voluntarily given up his title.
Five fistic monarchs gone—get that,
Air. Dempsey? Then there are
others. Helen Wills was unable to
defend her tennis crown. Willie
MacFarlane and Jim Barnes lost
their United States and British open
titles in 1926. Gene Sarazen and
numerous others have lost minor
links championships.
A bad year for champions, this
year! Even so-called champions.

GRANGE’S MOVIE
BIG SUCCESS ON
BROADWAY
NEW YORK Some time back
propagandists were announcing that
Red Grange, the “galloping ghost”
of the University of Illinois foot
ball team, was “a bust” in the
movies, heading back to Wheaton
and ice trade, and done with the
show world for all time.
Grange’s first motion picture,
“One Minute to Play,” opened at
the Colony theater on Broadway
Sunday night, with the football star
making a personal appearance at
each showing, and from present in
dications—it is turning thousands
away and selling six weeks ahead—
may enjoy a run comparable with
those of the bigger film productions
of the past.
New York reviewers are agreed
that Grange’s film play ranks with
the best of all time and some even
go as far as to predict Red will
prove the natural successor of Ru
dolph Valentino.

SOUTH BEND, Ind. —(United Press) —A marked development
in the return of a kickoff—a. play highly specialized by Red Grange—
probably will be one of the S outsanding improvements of football this
year in the opinion of Knute Rockne, 'head coach at Notre Dame uni-
versity and one of the nation’s fore
most football authorities.
The soteky, hald-headed coach of
the famous wonder teams of Notre
Dame, said the return of a kickoff
had been neglected too many years.
“There has been little or no ef
fort heretofore to improve the
method of returning the kickoff.
This year I. believe this phase of
the game will be improved,” he said.
Sees Passing Game.
Rockne also expects to see for
ward passes as the principle means
of attack by many schools this
year.
“The success of Dartmouth and
several other schools in using the
forward pass last year has brought
this play into prominence and I
believe that many schools will fol
low their lead,” Rockne said. He
pointed out there were new techni
calities in forward passing, includ
ing a five-yard penalty for the team
attempting and failing to complete
two passes in the same sequence
of four downs.
Rockne has a habit of knitting
hit brows when he talks football,
especially Notre Dame. His brows
were knitted as he gave his version
of what the 1926 game would be.
Will Miss Enright.
He was asked whether Notre
Dame would flash on the field this
year with long returns from kick
off and a dazzling overhead game.
His only answer was the knitted
brows as Rockne does not care to j
talk of the plans for his team nor
will he talk much of the prospect
for the aggregation.
“I’ll have practically the same
bunch of boys I had last year and
of course I’m hoping they have im
proved,” he said. “We can’t forget
however, that Enright, the greatest
plunging fullback we ever had, is
gone and will be hard to replace.”
Predicts Mere Interest.
The veteran Notre Dame coach
this year expects even greater in
terest in football.
“People are learning more about
football all the time. They are be
ginning to understand the game and
interest comes with understanding
in any game. People have under
stood baseball and basketball, but
football was mere complicated.
Now they are coming to understand
it better and enjoy it more,” he ex
plained.

Net Officials Worried.
Officials of the tennis association
still refuse today to put their opin
ion on record about the startling
announcement that Miss Browne
has decided to turn professional.
But it was easy to gather that their
opinion had been changed about the
possibilities of open or professional
tennis.
“When it was first suggested that
Mlle. Lenglen might make a tour
of the United States as a profes
sional, we ridiculed the idea,” a
prominent member of the tennis as
sociation said today. “But for one,
I am now ready to believe that it
can be made a success. Mlle. Len
glen, of course, had to have some
good opponent to draw other than
curiosity seekers and in Miss
Browne she will have one of the
best and most popular players in
the game.”
The association, it was learned,
was considering a new rule that
would definitely forbid an amateur
player to appear in any kind of a
match against a professional, but
no hasty action will be taken.

BY CLAIRE POMEROYE
Jay Vannah walked into the
office of Frost, Bigelow and
Shute, early the next morning.
He spoke quietly to Gloria, and
she answered him with a faint
smile.
“Mr. Bigelow is already here,”
she said a little shyly. “Will you
go right into his office?”
She had steeled herself to meet
what she knew to be the crisis of
her life like this, calmly and
proudly. She had reconciled her
self to his going and tried her best
not to let herself hope that he
would find the loneliness and
isolation of faraway Argentina
too much for him—that he would
come back.
Vannah emerged from Bige
low’s office in a surprisingly short
time. He had completed all his
necessary arrangements, had re
ceived the drafts and had said
goodby to the old lawyer.
Gloria’s eyes were clear and
steady as she glanced up at him
as he came to a pause beside her
dcslk.
“My train is leaving at 2 o’clock
today,” he said with a curious
hesitation in his voice. I’ll arrive
in New York at midnight and go
right on board. She sails at day
break tomorrow.”
“What a wonderful voyage,”
murmured Gloria.
He did not answer at once and
she glanced at him again to find
his eyes boring into her and a
strange excited expression on his
face. She was startled by this
abrupt and unaccountable change
In him.
“Why—why, what’s the mat
ter?” she asked nervously.
And then there poured out of
his lips a storm of words, oh,
such beautiful words, which the
girl’s ears drank in thirstily. She
swayed before the torrent, and
with blissful disregard of the why
or wherefore of it all, found her
self clasped in his strong arms.
“I can’t go away like this,” he
whispered with that well-remem
bered plaintiveness. “I can’t do it,
Gloria, I can’t get away from my
love for you even at the other
end of the earth. I know that
now. Why won’t yon try to love
me just a little?”
She closed her eyes and drank
In the sweetness of his words.
“I’ll change all my plans,” he
promised hurriedly. “I’ll not go
to South America. I’ll stay right
here and make you see that I can
bring you all the happiness that
you’ve dreamed of Tell me
that you love me a little.”
She opened her eyes and looked
at him, compassionate for his
failure to understand.
“A little,” she repeated. He saw
the smile come into her eyes and
he dared kiss her on the lips.
“A little? Why, Jay, I’ve loved

“You just try and go without

And at this auspicious moment
the outer door of the office burst
open to permit the entrance of
two rollicking individuals who
seemed to be Mr. Carson Brooks
and Miss Evelyn Waye.
The four persons in this scene
stood as if thunderstruck.
Carson stared at the extra
ordianry spectacle of Gloria in
the embrace of Jay Vannah, her
arms about his neck and her face
snuggled against his shoulder.
And Gloria’s quick eyes grasped
the detail of an enormous corsage
bouquet of orchids which nestled
in the bosom of Evelyn’s trim
little tailored jacket—the orchids
and spang new white kid gloves
on her hands.
As if on a signal, the two girls
flew into each other’s arms and,
amid mingled tears and sobbing
laughter, said into each other’s
ears such things as women, the
emotional creatures, say to each
other under such circumstances.
The men, Jay and Carson,
frowned savagely at nothing in
particular, cleared their respec
tive throats of imaginative ob
stacles and tugged nervously at
their collars, which had suddenly

“HoW long does it take to get a

nah to Carson, out of the corner

an hour.

explosions of happy laughter, of
exclamations, half shouted in the
excitement.
“My cir is downstairs,” cried

house in 5 minutes and then out
to the Highlands to keep our ap

They were about to pour out of
the room when a sudden sharp
command halted them.
Mr. Bigelow, hat in hand, stood
upon the threshold of his office
door. He had heard it all.
“You’re a fine lot^you are,” he
cried in assumed anger. “Going to
have a wedding and leave the old
man out, hey? Not if I know it.
Wait for me—l have to give the
bride away.”
They greeted him with a jolly
laugh and finally were for leav
ing.
But still another joined the
party.
“Wait for me. wait for me!”
squealed a shrill, excited voice,
and from out behind the partition
formed by the tall steel filing
cabinet, emerged a fantastic fig
ure, ribbons flying, a flowery hat
perched at a rakish angle on its
head, a tightly rolled umbrella
clasped in one hand and an enor
mous handbag in the other.
“Wait for me—l’m the brides
maid!” cried Miss Ella Finch.

A correspondent coaching a
basketball team says that in his
athletic experience he has always
been told by trainers to “lay off
the sweet stuff.” But he has felt
for some time that the old train
ers were in error about that, and
he has, of late, given his boys
cube sugar between halves. Last
winter his boys lost but one out
of 11 games. Do the boys win in
spite of the sugar or because of it?
I should think a little sugar
between halves would rather help
the boys to win; unless the boys
on the opposing team also take a
little sugar between halves. In
that case it would make the game
a little faster.

at the Alhambra introduces him in
a role he has long threatened to as
sume—that of a jazz band leader a
la Wh*teman and Paul Ash.
Yes sir, they have a couple of
bawling trombones, of whining saxa
phones and they have as good a
pianist as ever played for Mr.
•Vhiteman —Heinz Roemheld him
self. At certain moments of the per
formance he abandons the baton for
the ivories and also engages in con
versation with Hazel Romaine,
billed as “Chicago’s hottest blue
singer.”
Babe Morries, dancer, is quite a
card in the vaudeville entertain
ment which is augmented by the
“pleated music box of Bud Sheik.”
The film version of The Old Soak
which fills the balance of the pro
gram, seems rather slow against the
jazz step of the Roemheld Alham
brans. Jean Hersholt appears in the
title role, but somehow the subtitles
fail to transmit the geniality of the
humor that lies in the central char
acter. After all there is no substi
tute for the human voice in a film
that by the very nature of its theme
needs the human voice to strike
home.

BIG PARADE MORE POWERFUL
THAN SERMON AGAINST WAR
There has been no war that has
not been an argument against war.
In that sense The Big Parade at
the Davidson is an anti-war argu
ment, almost as powerful as war it
self. That picture needs no preface.
Like a work of art it speaks for it
self.

There is war with all its initial
hysteria, its manifestations of so
called patriotism, its glamor of the
uniform. You see the hero of the
story, James Apperson, like so many
others marched into the butchery to
a gay time as on a holiday and for
a picnic. They are still on a joy
ride when they land in France, and
while the days immediately follow
ing have their strenuous moments
its May time and there is Melisande,
the French peasant girl, and the
war is somewhere at a far away
front. Then comes the crash
orders are to the front, the front,
FRONT! That scene, with its rush
of motor vehicles thundering past,
with its suggestion of the heart
breaks, the ntter helplessness of the
individual that would attempt to
cry above its din and raise his
hand against this ever forward
pressing monster that roars “To the
front, the front, FRONT!” that
scene is a masterpiece of direction
that holds the spectator in its grip
long after eye and ear have been
at attention. And after “the big
parade” has swept by, there lies in
the dust of the road that lone white
figure that had attempted to stem
the onslaught of that monster that
had roared to the front, the front,
FRONT Melisande a woman’s
heart quivering, bleeding in the
agony of a farewell, perhaps for
ever.
There you have your prelude to
the grim work that lies ahead of the
gay youths who marched into this
thing as on a holiday and for a lark.
They get their first taste of real bul
lets with an airplane raid and from
then on the hell of war rages in all
its fury, finding its climax in that
dugout scene with James Apperson’s
pal, Slim, bleeding to death out in
no man’s land and Jim, brushing
aside all orders to the contrary
storms over the top to save him.
“Are mm fighting this war or
orders? What in hell are we getting
out of this war anyway!”

it is as natural and direct as “the
big parade” of ambulances winding

Thomas Meighan Has
Good Picture at
The Wisconsin
A regular melodrama, with its
twists laid in South America, is the
vehicle in which Thomas Meighan is
making new friends and cementing
old ties at the Wisconsin theater
this week. Tin Gods is the title
of what many say is the best pic
ture that friend Tom has made
since The Miracle Man.
But Meighan, if he did naught
but walk around and smile, would
satisfy, so what is a role more or
less. However, in Tin Gods the
handsome Thomas does exceedingly
well and is helped throughout the
picture by charming Renee Adore
one of whose last acts is to jump
off a bridge in South America.
Briefly the plot: Meighan, a
young engineer, leaves his senate
campaigning wife and hikes to
South America to build a bridge.
His worries he tries to drown in
the flowing bowl and is off to a
good start when a fascinating per
son, who answers to the name of
Carita, comes along and takes Tom’s
Ynind off drink. She gives him
health again and the two fall in
love.
Along comes friend wife and Cari
ta, misunderstanding a speech she
hears between them, takes to the
bridge.
Aileen Pringle plays the suffra
gette wife. There is plenty of ac
tion and some good photography.
The usual elaborate stage presenta
tion tops the good picture.

Yesterday being Labor day, the
usual toilers took time out and
packed the Palace theater from
early afternoon till late at night, to
watch those behind the footlights
put in their best licks. And a real
holiday it was, too, with Taylor
Holmes, Wally Sharples, Ledova
and Rose and Thorn drawing rounds
of applause for their fine work.
And the union musicians were on
the job, lifter being out slightly less
than a half hour Sunday.

Taylor Holmes, the star of Silk
Mullane, The Rear Car and other
comic mystery successes, wasn’t the
least bit mysterious last night. With
a few choice dialect yarns and some
equally interesting poems, Mr.
Holmes appeared betwixt and be
tween all acts, introducing each of
fering with many laughable, if not
complimentary, embellishments. And
he has an act in his own right, too,
in which he reads his own poem on
the death of Rudolph Valentino.
A seemingly never ending bean
famine is responsible for the two
deaths irn the first scene sponsored
by Wally Sharples and company,
but the corpses come to life in time
to participate in the deathless nut
house scene. Then, too, the gang
climb into habilaments of the opera
and proceed to seek out Sally in va
rious sharps and flats. It’s good
comedy and the house roared.
More comedy was furnished by
Rose and Thorne, who are new to
this reviewer, but whom he firmly
hopes will come again soon. Miss
Thorne’s Swedish accent was well
nigh devastating and she had an ex
cellent partner in Mr. Rose. They
weren’t out half long enough.
There is little that can be added
to the laudatory things that have
been said of Ledova and her com
pany. This little lady captured our
fancy when she was here in The
Music Box Revue of some three
years ago and her appearance is al
ways an event. A genuine artist on
her toes, Ledova has cornered a
stringed orchestra which seems to
inspire her to real achievements.
Athlone who hails from Hartford,
Wls., seems to have grown some
since last w r e saw her, but she is
still singing the jazzy and pathetic
songs to good advantage, even
though an apparent cold hampered
her efforts yesterday. The Del
Ortos opened the bill with some
Spanish offerings.
The picture, starring Norman
Kerry, makes one remember Prin
cess Beverly, alias Guggenslocher, of
McCutcheon’s Graustark. J. P. C.
Breaded Pork Tenderloin With
Apricots.
Cut one pork tenderloin or fillet
in crosswise sections about one inch
thick. Flatten well with cleaver or
large knife. Then dip in well-beat
en egg, then in fine bread or cracker
crumbs and salt in drippings or but
ter to a delicate brown. Take care
that the pork is well-cooked through
out. Remove to a hot platter.
Drain one can of apricots well and
dip each piece of fruit in a little
flour. Saute in fat from the tender
loin, turning carefully with a spat
ula. Arrange the apricot halves
about the pork filets and garnish
with the chopped parsley or green
pepper. Make gravy from the fat
in the pan adding one-half cup of ap
ricot syrup.

DESSERT FOR EVERY DAY.
On the busiest day when time is
very precious, you might make
15-Minute Pudding.
Take one teaspoonful of baking
powder, a pinch of salt, and enough
good milk or fresh buttermilk to
make a drop batter. Butter custard
cups, drop a tablespoonful of batter
then a tablespoonful of canned cher
ries and another spoonful of batter,
and put to cook in a pan of boiling
water well covered for 15 minutes.
Serve with sugar and cream.
Edinburgh Pudding.
Take one-half pound of oatmeal,
one cupful of thick custard flavored
with vanilla, one and one-half pints
of water, one-fourth of a cupful of
milk, one-half teaspoonful of salf,
and two ounces of cocoanut. Cook
the oatmeal in the water with the
salt and milk, cool and turn into
the custard, pour into molds ana
serve, when molded, with cocoanut,
sugar and cream.
Lemon Meringue.
Take one pint of milk, three
ounces of sugar, one cupful of fine
bread crumbs, two eggs r the juice
and rind of a lemon. Mix all in
gredients and cook slowly until well
set, baking in a deep pie plate. Set
away to cool, cover with a meringue
and brown. Serve cold.
Snow Jelly.
Prepare any desired flavor of
gelatine, and when it is thickening
whip on top of any molded gelatin
of other flavor, using pineapple for
one and raspberry for the other.
Serve with whipped cream.
Spiced Tea Cakes.
Mix and sift one and one-half cup
fuls of flour with two teaspoonfuls
of baking powder, one-eighth tea
spoonful of nutmeg and one-fourth
teaspoonful of mace. Cream one
fourth of a cupful of shortening,
add one cupful of sugar, two well
beaten eggs, one-half cupful of milk
added alternately with the flour.
Add a few raisins and bake in
greased muffin tins. Cover with
maple frosting and sprinkle with
chopped filberts.—Nellie Maxwell.
FISH PISHES.
As canned fish is available in any
climate or market, one may have
fish at any season or in any locality.
The fresh fish are so much more
appetizing that we enjoy them when
ever available.
A firm-fleshed fish, not too fat,
like lake trout or pike, is good when
boiled. Clean and wrap in a cheese
cloth, drop in salted acidulated
water and cook until the fish leaves
the bones. Drain and serve with
parsley butter, lemon butter, maitre
d’hotel butter or hollandaise sauce.
A stuffed and baked fish is an
other good way of serving them.
Make the stuffing as usual, adding
onion and parsley for seasoning.
Molded Fish Salad.
Flake one-half pound of tuna fish
or salmon. Mix with one cupful cf
diced celery, one tablespoonful of
chopped green pepper, two table
spoonfuls of chopped olives and
three-fourths of a cupful of salaa
dressing. Add two tablespoonfuls
of vinegar and season with salt and
ter, add one-half tablespoonful of
gelatin in one-fourth of a cupful of
cold water for five minutes, dis
solve by placing over hot water,
then stir into the fish mixture.
Turn into small molds rinsed with
cold water, and set away to chill.
Serve on lettuce or water cress and
garnish with celery and strips of
green paper.
Fish Cutlets.
Melt three tablespoonfuls of but
ter, add one-half toblespoonful of
finely chopped onion and two table
spoonfuls of finely chopped pine
apple. Cook slowly for five min
utes, stirring constantly. Add one
third of a cupful of flour, and when
well-mixed stir in one-half cupful
each of milk and cream. Cook un
til smooth and thick; add two cup
fuls of flaked fish, salt and paprika
to taste. Shape into cutlets, dip
into egg and crumbs and fry in deep
fat. Drain on soft paper and serve
with a good sauce.—Nellie Maxwell.
Fudge Cookies.
One-half cup melted butter, one
half cup cocoa, one teaspoon vanilla,
two eggs, one cup sugar, one-half
cup flour, one-half teaspoon salt,
one cup chopped nuts. Put in pan
so that dough will be three-fourths
inch thick, bake in moderate oven
for 30 minutes. Leave in pan until
cool, then cut in squares.

side the castle. They’ve seen it right
on the edge of the woods and are
afraid to go outside the gate, so I’m
looking for it. I want to. chase it
away.”
Lafayette didn’t find the hyena,
but he showed, even at 8, the bravery
and desire to protect others that led
him to join the American colonies

Queen Elizabeth Liked
to Have Big Parades.
Boom! Boom! The drums were
beating loudly. Then the trumpets
sounded shrilly.
The people of London stuck their
heads out of their windows to see
what was happening. Marching
down the street came rows of drum
mers and trumpeters, plumes wav
ing, banners flying.
After them came rows and rows
and rows of men in gleaming steel
armor—lo,ooo of them, a regular
army, in fact. Rumbling over the
cobblestones came 10 big cannons.
It looked as though a war might
be starting. But the people of Lon
don knew better. It was only Queen
Elizabeth going to church!
Queen Elizabeth, born Sept. 7,
1533, loved parades and always had
one wherever she went. She loved
fine parties and balls, too, but she
was a very thrifty queen, so instead
of giving parties herself, she would
go on visits to the nobles of the
kingdom and order them to give
parties for her. Then they had to
pay for them themselves.

CHICAGO —All grain exchanges
in North America were closed yes
terday, Winnipeg as well as do
mestic markets, in observation of
Labor day.
Recent declines in wheat prices
to lowest points for the season sim
ply reflected the fact that United
States wheat is coming into com
petition with that in Canada. This
competition promises to become
quite keen during the next couple
of months, as,both countries have
large surpluses of wheat to dis
pose of. In the ordinary run of
events the United States gets the
bulk of the export trade during July
and August, after which Canada
holds the stage until around the
first of the year, when crops in Ar
gentina and Australia are ready lor
market.
Canadian Crop Same.
Late estimates indicate that the
United States raised nearly 200,-
000,000 bushels wheat more than
last year. This should offset the
loss in the European production, as
compared with last year. The Ca
nadian crop promises to be about
the same as in 1925. What Argen
tina and Australia will raise re
mains to be seen, as the crops in
the southern hemisphere arc three
to four months away from harvest.
It is understood that the Cana
dian pool controls a big half of
rhe crop tip there this year. Cana
dian markets are now substantially
ours, and while this relationship ex
ists it will be difficult for the Unit
ed States to sell more than scatter
ing lots of wheat.
Com Is Backward.
Statistical Information Indicates
that Europe will have to buy heav
ily of North American wheat. To
date, however, they have confined
their purchases to current require
ments. Economy in the use .of
wheat and substitution are being
practiced on the other side as never
before, as it is impossible to esti
mate how much of a saving this will
be during the season.
Corn is backward, and it needs
to be forced to maturity. Conse
quently, it is necessary that there
be plenty of warmth and sunshine
during the balance of this month.
Rain does the crop no good now,
and means just that much more de
lay in getting the crop ripe before
killing frost appears.

Farm Conference
At Salt Lake City
WASHINGTON —A conference to
discuss the agricultural and business
interests of eight western states has
been called to meet at Salt Lake
Oct. 1 and 2, it was announced yes
terday.
The gathering will be under the
auspices of the Chamber of Com
merce of the United States and the
local chamber of commerce. It will
be the first of five to be held this
year for the purpose of causing at
tention on agricultural problems.
States interested in the Salt Lake
meeting are Arizona, Idaho, Mon
tana, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah,
Wyoming and Colorado. It is ex
pected that 300 delegates will at
tend.

MADISON Following is the
weekly report of market conditions
issued by the state department of
markets:
“Butter The butter markets
were uneven during the past week.
During the latter part of the week
free offerings and a light demand
weakened the market. Prices de
clined, supplies being more than ade
quate for the light demand. But
ter prices are about 2 cents lower
than a year ago at this time.
“Cheese —Trading was generally
quiet during the past week. Buy
ers showed little interest. Prices
are about three-quarters of a cent
lower than a year ago at this Lime.
“Eggs Reecipts of eggs were
somewhat heavier than last week,
but lighter than last year at this
time. Spot market remal is un
changed with trading rather quiet.
“Hogs Hog markets underwent
sharp and frequent fluctuations dur
ing the past week. Prices at the
close were 50 cents higher than dur
ing the previous week. Best light
hogs at midweek reached $14.60, the
highest price paid in approximately
two months. Hog prices are about
80 cents lower than last year at
this time.
“Cattle Notwithstanding in
creased receipts, values on heavy
fed steers advanced as high as 50
cents, and in some instances more,
over the previous week. This in
crease in prices was due mainly
•to improvement in the dressed trade
and a broader shipping demand.
Prices are somewhat lower than
last year at this time.
“Sheep—A marked increase in re
ceipts was the outstanding feature
of the sheep market during the past
week. Closing values were 50
cents to $1 lower than the previous
week. Sheep prices are about 90
cents lower than a year ago at this
time.”

MILWAUKEE, TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 7, 1926
Farmers Should
Run Own Marketing
Jardine Contends
OSAWATOMIE, Kan.—The best
plan for the solution of the farm
problem, in the opinion of Secretary
of Agriculture William M. Jardine,
is development of marketing ma
chinery controlled by the farmers
themselves. The secretary made the
statement yesterday in ap address
at the Kansas Farmers’ union picnic.
Mr. Jardine warned his hearers
that no master what plans were put
into effect for the relief of the
farmer, they would fall short of
perfection.
“I believe,” he said, “that it will
be essential to devise some 'system
whereby producers will be enabled
to collectively sell a large portion
of their output.”

and steel products from the United
States for the first seven months of
this year amounted to 1,233,300
gross tons, an increase of 241,144
tons over the total shipped abroad
-during the corresponding period a
year ago, according to department
of commerce reports.
Exports from the United States
during July amounted to 194,717
gross tons, the highest monthly ex
port figure recorded during the cur
rent year, an increase of 35,211 tons
over the June figure.
Imports into this country of iron
and steel products amounted to 82,-
411 gross tons in July, a decrease
of 41804 tons from the total re
ceived in June of this year.
The total Imports during the
seven months’ period amounted to
695,380 gross tons, an increase of
139,027 tons over the imports dur
ing the corresponding period of 1925.
Canada remained first among the
nations to which thp United States
exports iron and steel products, tak
ing 79,651 tons, or approx’mately
50 per cent of the total exports.

CLIMB HIGHER

CHICAGO—AII grain prices were
a fraction higher than last Satur
day- in the opening of the Chicago
Board of Trade, although a water
logged grain belt seems to be drying
out today.
Wheat opened cent to cent
above the previous close, with Sep
tember at $1.29%. Reports from all
sections of the belt, especially the
Canadian northwest, indicate that
the fields are rapidly draining.
Normal temperatures and bright
sunshine prevail. This means a
heavy movement of the spring
wheat in the very near future.
Corn received too much rain dur
ing the last week, and reports of
damage are still pouring in from
Illinois and lowa. The fact that
three weeks of clear, warm weather
are needed to mature the crop
caused this cent to cent higher.
Oats ranged unchanged to cent
higher, but is a dull affair. Some
of the fields have been damaged by
the rain, but there is no demand
for the grain.

Inthe longrun
At the time when Valentino died we commented with
some disgust upon the fact that the newspapers gave him
columns and columns of space, while they gave but little
space to Charles W. Eliot who died the same day. Not that
we did not recognize talent in Valentino, but because his
merits were slight compared with Eliot’s—and we were by
no means always in agreement with Eliot either. For in
stance, he was obtuse in not realizing that monotonous
labor should have short hours.
Anyhow, the incident almost made us ashamed of our
occupation, since it showed up journalism in such a bad
light.
But The Christian Century comes along and bids us
be of good cheer. It admits that the papers gave Valen
tino at least 17 times as much space as Eliot, and most of
them more than that—but it reminds all cavilers that Val
entino will have ceased to be even a name in 10 years,
while that of Eliot will be remembered.
The correction is valid. It is the saving fact which
makes for optimism in all such distressing situations. It
applies to others whom we admire more than we did Eliot.
It applies to many who were very unpopular in their own
times.
One can run back over history and find numbers of
examples. Any popular entertainer could have taken the
public attention away from Jesus Christ when he was
crucified, but his name and work last longer. The same
may be said for Socrates, Bruno, Galileo, Servetus, New
ton, Darwin, and many others. It applies to William
Lloyd Garrison who was dragged through the streets by
a highly “respectable” mob. Garrison’s name and deeds
are remembered, to his credit. The names of the mobbers
are forgotten, and their deed is remembered to their dis
credit.
While Gene Debs is loved by large numbers of people,
he is hated by more. He has espoused the cause of the
oppressed, he has defended the persecuted, he has opposed
legal thievery, he has refused to support collective murder
—-in these pre-civilization days that is sufficient to explain
why he is hated. A movie star or a prize fighter could take
the front page away from him any day. But he will be
remembered when they are forgotten.
And so it goes. A certain measure of justice is done
in the long run.
THE STATE FAIR CAN GET ALONG
WITHOUT MILITARY EXHIBITS
Under the presidency of Glenn Frank we expect better
things of the state university than to have it make war
propaganda at the State Fair.
Why* should it plant machine guns at the fair, to turn
the thoughts of visitors from peace to war?
Why should it circulate a vicious pamphlet attacking
and misrepresenting most of the good organizations and
sincere peace lovers in this country?
Why should it try, by means of posters, to make vis
itors believe that the main object of an army is to kill
Insects, erect buildings and engage in other peaceful
pursuits?
An army could not escape doing a few useful things,
but its main object is to train men to kill other men—and
the state university and its president know this as well
as we do.
In many, many ways nowadays the war propaganda
is spread before the eyes and dinned into the ears of the
people.
Modern capitalism is in its imperialistic stage. It
has investments the world over and it seeks to maintain
or secure markets the world over. It also seeks to keep
labor in subjection at home. In pursuit of these pur
poses it wants a big navy and a regular army, supplement
ed by state guards and the military training of students
and others. It wants to be ready for any commercial war
that may come on account of its commercial exploits. It
also wants to have men and gases ready for service against
labor if needed.
It is mere hypocrisy, in the light of these facts, to
pretend that an army exists for purposes of peace.
We believe President Glenn Frank knows all this full
well. Perhaps he did not know about the exhibit. If such
is the case, we would suggest that he post himself and see
that this imposition upon the people of the state is not re
