Don’t Be Fooled
There are almost 1,200,000 Brit
ish miners on strike —have been
on strike for the last four months.
A British trade union delegation
of leading officials is in this coun
try soliciting funds for the great
army of striking miners. Already
in a previous edition of St. Louis
Labor we called attention to the
attempt of the Baldwin govern
ment to interfere with this collec
tion of strike funds for the Brit
ish miners. During the last 10
days additional efforts have been
made to deceive and humbug the
American trade union movement.
Twice the leading newspapers of
this country published very prom
inently news items that the Brit
ish miners’ strike was about
ended, that the ranks of the strik
ers were broken and the men fast
returning to work.
What were the alleged facts in
the case, as reported in those
press dispatches? The first dis
patch said that 6,000 men of one
district would return to. work un
der the Baldwin eight-hour and
wage-reduction conditions. An
other dispatch told us that 13,000
men in another district had re
fused to stand by the miners’
federation in its great defensive
war and would return to work.
Whether the men in both in
stances really did return to work
is yet an open question. How
ever, suppose these 19,000 men in
two districts did return to work,
what does this number of strike
breakers mean when compared
with the total army of 1,200,000
strikers? A drop in the bucket!
The main and sole object of this
strikebreaker news from London
is to counteract the work of col
lecting funds for the British strik
ers. Don’t be deceived! The
British miners’ strike is on and
will continue until Baldwin and
his mine owners’ combine come to
terms. —St. Louis Labor.

Color Filters for
Headlight Glare
The dangers of glaring guto
headlights, which are only partly
removed by dimmers and special
lenses, can be eliminated entirely
by the simple use of orange and
blue colored filters, according to
Karl D. Chambers, automotive
engineer, Asheville, N. C.
As described in Popular Science
Monthly, the filters would be ad
justable so that on cars traveling
in one direction on a highway the
headlights would give blue light
and the drivers would look
through blue filters attached to
the windshield. On cars going in
the opposite direction the colors
of the headlights and filters
would be orange. Since a col
ored glass filter passes light of
its own color, but stops that of
a complementary color, and since
blue and orange are complemen
tary colors, the result would be,
Chambers declares, that drivers
going in either direction would
have perfect visibility.

THE BASIS OF PROSPERITY
The old selfish axiom of capitalism says that pros
perity for all depends upon the profitable enterprises of
the rich. The new social axiom declares that the masses
are the basis of prosperity and that no industry is safely
grounded until it guarantees the prosperity of the masses.
The old dog-eat-dog and master-in his-own-house busi
ness man is becoming a backnumber. He had his heyday
in the early days of capitalism when small business was
the rule. Modern big business opens the way for a more
social spirit.
Big business has one great advantage over small busi
ness It can distribute prosperity and yet make big prof
its for its own insiders.
A concern that produces its own raw materials, trans
portation and power, uses up-to-date methods of produc
tion and salesmanship, and cuts waste to a minimum, can
increase production and lower costs to such a degree that
it pays better to raise wages and lower prices than to
fight the demands of organized labor for higher living
standards.
The only escape from overproduction and stagnation
is increased consumption. This requires higher wages anc
an increase of small incomes. The only concerns whicl
can afford to do this and really benefit from doing it an
the big corporations.
There are still too many corporation heads who fai
to live up to this modern enlightened business sense. Al
over the world, too many corporations still resent the de
mands of organized labor as an intrusion into their ow?
authority. But they will learn by their own experienc
that if it ever was good policy to fight modern labor stand
ards, it has ceased to be so.
On the other hand, many labor leaders still cling t
the old habit of making demands on the individual em
ployer which can be granted without injury only by th
industry as a whole. To the extent that this heritag
from an outgrown stage of capitalism still manifests it
self in lockouts and strikes, all members of a nation suffe
from it.
Individual selfishness without social understanding
will probably continue for a long time to block the wa;
to a more reasonable and mutually profitable arrange
ment. But we are emerging into an era in which gooc
sense on all sides will argue more and more insistently h
favor of working agreements which tend to raise wage;
and lower prices as a matter of good all around tactics
This tendency will enforce itself not only in industry
commerce and agriculture, so far as social condition?
have paved the way for it, but also in finance. Enlight
ened public opinion will not tolerate a perpetuation of
financial policies which enable a few big insiders to disor
ganize the whole world’s economy for their own private
profit and pleasure.
The modern up-to-date capitalist and labor leader will
agree that distributed prosperity is the best guarantee
of continued and permanent prosperity. It will therefore
become more and more a matter of public opinion to de
cide to what extent the mass of the people shall have a
voice and vote in the management of the big industries
which are at present socialized only for the benefit of a
few insiders.

October. It aims to pave the way for the United States
of Europe. The difficulties in its way t are indicated by

list Loebe in Germany, the Radical Bourgeois Herriot in

cialist Destree in Belgium, the Liberal Schuster in Czecho
slovakia. To carry out its program of disarmament, tariff
union, national independence through interdependence and
peace, Europe must have Socialist governments or at least
the leadership of Socialists in the advanced industrial
nations.

spirit which distinguishes the Pan-European from the im
perialist programs of the Pan-American and Pan-Asiatic
unions.

ed at Expense of

iast obstacle which had prevented

agreements for peace, security and

It appears today that the league
had gained Germany at the ex
pense of Spain and Brazil, both
of which countries demanded per
manent council seats last March
when it was proposed that Ger
many should be so honored.

BY HENRY WOOD.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
GENEVA—Germany was admitted
to the league of nations today and
immediately was elevated to perma
nent membership on the league coun
cil. The diplomatic equilibrium of
Europe and the league thereby was
vastly altered.
At frequent intervals during the
eight years since the close of the
war, Germany has been summoned
before the bar of allied or other
justice to explain, promise or to
deny.
Given Permanent Seat.
Henceforth, Germany may be ex
pected to occupy a comfortable chair
at international council tables and
her representatives will speak and
argue on a parity with the repre
sentatives not only of the nations
that were neutral but those which
opposed her during the war.
Simultaneously with its action
in creating a permanent council seat
for Germany, the league assembly
created three new non-permanent
council seats, thereby increasing the
membership of the upper house of
the league from 10 to 14. There
now are five permanent council
seats possessed by the British em
pire, France, Italy, Japan and Ger
many. One other permanent seat
is being held for the United States.

assembly’s rejection of Spain’s ciaim

BLIND PAINTER
SUCCESSFUL AS
SONG WRITER
A painter, and a good one, pos
sessed of as keen a pair of eyes as
ever a man of 60 boasted, Adrian
Blain Omerod was in on day bereft
of his sight and his right arm by a
blast of dynamite. By some strange
compensatory flash, the ability to
write verse superceded the ability
to paint houses and has carried him
through all the large cities of the
south, east and middle west, making
him enough to scrape out a living.
At no time has he been other than
the cheery, confident, lion-headed
old gentleman who presented the
city editor with complimentary
copies of 4 of the 24 pieces of mu
sic by which he is now becoming
known.
Lost His Evesight.
One morning in February, 1924,
he tried to pilot his motorboat, To
kolone, up the channel of Biscayne
bay, shading his eagle-bright eyes
against the brilliant Florida sun.
Two huge boulders barred the way
to a painting job he meant to tackle
about 25 miles from Miami.
He saw some workmen nearby
blowing out stumps. They lent him
two sticks of dynamite, the first of
which removed half the obstacle to
his progress. The second went off
in his hand and he is no longer able
to tell day from night.
It was while he lay in a hospital
recovering from the operations
which had failed to renew his sight,
that verses began to form in his
consciousness. They always Invade
his thoughts, thus uninvited, he
says.
His early verses appear in a little
booklet called Haphazard. Some of
the later ones seemed to him like
words for a song. While in Cleve
land he sought out Herman Hum
mel, a professional song writer, who
set them to music.
Was a Rover.
He now has 24 in print and 13
more ready to set to music. The
profits of these two forms of ex
pression are not only making him
at present self-supporting, but pay
ing his expenses from place to place
so that he can increase his output.
His headquarters are with friends
in Milwaukee, —705 Barlett Ave.
In his time, Omerod was a rover.
An unusually keen memory has
fixed the lay of practically every
city in the United States in his
mind, which now helps him to get
around with a minimum of diffi
culty.
three weeks he came and went and

have long ago lost all track of them.

builders of the nation, silent build
ers who drift from place to place,
turning up where labor is needed,
disappearing again when work be
comes scarce. Their inarticulate na
tures fill the government’s records
of missing men.

Catholics Have Little

MEXICO CITY—The bill pre
pared by the Catholic episcopate
asking for reforms in the laws gov
erning the church, which was for
mally presented to congress yester
day, will be studied immediately by
a special committee and by scores
of members of the senate and depu
ties who want to get the religious
question out of the way, according
to a statement at the house of dep
uties.
At the same time the bill will be
presented to all the state governors
and legislatures for study, since a
majority of the states must assent
to the changes in the constitution
required by the bill.
Some Hope Seen.
Notwithstanding some promises
of the political parties and encour
agement of the bishops, Catholic
Mexico today has little hope that
the bill will meet even with mod
erate success. The bill itself seems
to have come near making a split
in the Catholic ranks and there are
stories in the street that Msgr. Pas
cual Diaz, secretary of the episco
pate, has gone over to the side
seeking peace and was the chief
active agent in the presentation of
the bill to congress.
Catholic deputies from the state
of Pueblo have undertaken to fa
ther the bill in congress. A lively
fight between the Catholics and the
radicals in congress is expected.
Third Pastoral Letter.
Today the episcopate issued the
third pastoral letter, quoting the
pope as sorrowing for the Catholics
in Mexico and asking them to stand
by their guns and remember that
the present religious trouble in
Mexico is the most serious in four
centuries, since never before in that
time have “wounded pastors been
separated from their sorrowing, suf
fering sheep.”
“The concession of religion was
the signal for tho most formidable
national struggle throughout Mex
ico,” continues the letter. “Months
have passed and the public mourn
ing for the church continues and
the Catholic organization is becom
ing stronger and more intense.”

ROME—The special correspondent
of The Koelnische Zeitung, the or
gan of big business in the German
Rhine province, writes from this
city that the negotiations for the
formation of a French-Belgian-Ger
man iron trust have made a great
stir in the Italian Fascist camp.
“A well known Italian journalist
could not write a single article on
this subject without repeating over
and over that the formation of such
a steel and coal trust would mean
death to Italian industry,” the cor
respondent declares.
The paper II Messagero, which is
controlled by the Perrone brothers,
who used to head* the Ansaldo firm,
have been following for a long time
a policy of trying to prevent the
formation of a French-German iron
and coal trust.
Wails About Inevitable.
Il Messagero now greets the press
reports of the definite formation of
such a trust with the following
wail: “Not a single word of this
impending stupendous event in the
economy of Europe reached the
Italian consumer, so that he could
have informed himself how the
Italian iron industry might perform
the duties anjJ functions which it
has undertaken to perform in the
great frame of the national life.”
The editor predicts that the part
ly manufactured iron goods which
Italian industry has to buy from
abroad will be dearer from now on
and suggests that Italian industry
will have to adopt better methods
in order to save itself.
The only hope which II Messagero
can see is that British and Ameri
can industry will compete against
this Franco-German trust
Fears Political Results.
Another Fascist paper, La Stam
pa, fears the political consequences
which must follow in the wake of
this economic agreement between
Belgian, French and German basic
industries.
“Hardly eight years after the end
of the World war, we witness the
first stages of a German-French en
tente,” La Stamps writes. “It seems
destined to have a decisive influ
ence on the economic and political
future of this continent.” La Stampa
not^s that some Paris papers hail
this development as the first step
towards the great ideal of Europe’s
economic unity.
Most of the Italian papers seem
to dread the political after effects
of this economic agreement. If this
forecast is correct, they see in it
the end of Italian diplomacy’s
chance to exploit French and Ger
man differences.
Expect Press Campaign.
Some Italian papers say that the
big press of France and Germany
is strongly influenced by the iron
industries, and if the leaders of
these industries want to change the
former hostile sentiments of France
and Germany into a solid friend

Leader Special Service.
LONDON The British trade
unions will retain the general strike
as a weapon in the class war. This
decision has been affirmed by the
trade union congress, after an ex
haustive discussion in the labor
press.
The general sentiment of the
trade union leaders seems to agree
with statements recently made by
Arthur Pugh, chairman of the gen
eral council of the trade union con
gress, and C. T. Cramp, industrial
secretary of the National Union of
Railwaymen.
Their attitude is summed up in a
lecture given by Cramp before the
Easton Lodge summer school of the
Independent Labor party.
Strike Becomes Political.
The chief lesson of the recent gen
eral strike is that in order to be
successful, it must force the gov
ernment to resign, Mr. Cramp ex
plained. No government could af
ford to force an issue to the point
of such a national crisis as a general
strike without resigning in case of
a surrender.
Despite denials made during the
strike, the issue was not merely one
of economic adjustment, but of a
new national constitution.
No strike involving vital services
of the nation can be won, if it lasts
longer than two or three days,
Cramp thinks. The greater the num
ber of industries involved, the less
effective will the strike become, if
extended beyond this period.
Government Was Strong.
Some thought that the British
government was on the point of sur
render when the general strike was
called off, Cramp continued. But
he saw no evidence of such weak
ness.
On the other hand, the general
strike showed that practically the
whole working class supported the
miners. The solidarity and heroism
displayed by the workers were of
the highest order. It greatly in
creased the voting strength of the
Labor party.
Nevertheless, the general strike
did not force the mine owners or
the government to surrender. Car
ried to its logical conclusion, the
general strike deprived the workers
of food and of the means of com
munication necessary to carry the
struggle to .success.
Need Political Power.
As a means of defense, a short
general strike can be useful and
will undoubtedly be employed again,
Cramp thinks. But as a means of
political pressure, it needs the help
of the Labor party, in order to have
control of the machinery of govern
ment and shift the suffering from
the workers to the ruling classes.
Also, labor must have political
power for the purpose of dealing
with the efficient organization of

WHERE GLADIATORS FOUGHT
IN ENGLAND.
While at Newport, in the west of
England, recently, I took occasion
to run out the three miles to the site
of ancient Caerlon’, one of the most
interesting Roman sites in Great
Britain. Here is the largest amphi
theater in the kingdom, where in
Caesar’s days gladiators fought and,
according to tradition, Christian
martyrs were put to death. I re
membered that Tennyson once wan
dered here before he wrote The Mar
riage of Geraint and gave the place
fresh fame as the seat of the court
of King Arthur.
“For Arthur on the Whitsuntide
before
Held court at old Caerlon upon
Usk.”
Modern England has almost begun
to encroach on the old site, but ar
rangements are now made to further
excavate and preserve the place for
all time and it looks as though Eng
land will have in Caerlon a Roman
citadel to look at and not imagine
as at York and Chester, where the
past is almost all buried beneath
houses and street car lines. Ex*rpt
for the sight of a few ancient butt
resses, Caerlon is but a hilly mea
dow, but I hope to live to walk with
in or seat myself in its amphithe
ater, when tourists will seek it out
as they do Stonehenge today.

any alcoholic drinks to children in
the homes.”

junkpile yesterday by an American.

valides court yard. It will be re

HOLLYWOOD —The male fashion
plates of the movies are out-doing
the girl-stars in trick-style fads for
all.
And that, according to the connois
eeurs, is the “ne plus ultra” of
fashion, because Hollywood women
are noted everywhere for their
audacity in dress.
The necktie belt, knitted bow tie,
two-piece underwear, black shirt,
and red satin vest are a few of the
latest style foibles of the film
heroes.
Harry Langdon for example, has
brought out a distinctly Langdonian
paradox—a hand-knitted black bow
tie. The comedian, off screen, is
noted as one of the few sane dress
ers in the film city, where hair
grease was first popularized.
New Use for Old Ties.
But hundreds are copying the fad,
and the little old lady on a Holly
wood side-street who knits Harry’s
neckties is now being stormed with
Langdon admirers in search of
hand-knitted black bow ties.
■Walter Pidgeon, leading man for
Norma Talmadge, is wearing his
trousers without belts or suspend
ers, instead, he uses silk neckties,
new or old, wound around his wasp
ish waist, run through the pant
loops.
Black shirts, with an Italian
flavor, are widely worn by the
actors and their imitators. Joseph
von Sternberg is said to have started
thi;; fad. His shirts, with collar at
tached, are of shiny black satin.
Many extras, with an eye to econ
omy have adopted the fashion—it
aaves laundry bills.
Striped silk and linen underwear
In two pieces, the trunks in the
back with tasseled cords, hgve been
adopted by many of the screen
Idols, including Jack Gilbert, Con
rad Nagel, Norman Kerry and
others.
One for Barthelmess.
Another trick creation is the “rab
bit-eared shirt,” by" Richard Bar
thelmess. It is an ordinary soft
white affair, with the longest
pointed collars ever seen in these
much photographed parts. Those
who have glimpsed the collars at
close range declare the points are
more than six inches long.
Jack Mulhall is popularizing silk
golf sox—a comfortable idea for
Sunny California, at least. Ken
Maynard, th? new cowboy star, gave
boulevard admirers a thrill the
other day by appearing in a red
satin vest, covered with beaded de
signs.
Other foibles rumored by advance
agents, but not yet caught napping,
are bathing caps covered with
colored cartoons, snakeskin riding
boots, and three-colored shoe-strings.

DON’T NEED PREPAREDNESS.
To the Editor of The Leader:
I noticed that in the issue of
Unity of May 24, there appeared
items concerning several moves to
ward peace in this and other coun
tries. The following tells more of
a move in that direction, which was
mentioned in an earlier issue of
Unity:
On April 23 Senator Lynn J. Fra
zier, North Dakota, introduced a
concurrent resolution providing for
an amendment to the constitution
making war illegal and prohibiting
congress from appropriating money
for war purposes. The proposed
amendment reads, in part, as fol
lows
“War for any purpose shall be il
legal, and neither the United States
nor any state, territory, association
nor person subject to its jurisdic
tion shall prepare for, declare, en
gage in or carry on war or other
armed conflict, expedition, invasion
or undertaking within or without
the United States, nor shall any
funds be raised, appropriated or ex
pended for such purpose.”
For two years the Women’s Peace
Union, a national organization, with
headquarters at 180 Lexington Ave.,
New York city, has advocated the
advancement of a similar measure;
and it points out that the constitu
tion sanctions war, provides for an
army, navy and state militia and au
thorizes congress to prepare for war,
declare war and appropriate money
for war; that after 137 years of
trial many people in this country be
lieve that events have proved that
war is neither right, nor necessa-y,
nor expedient; that these people
wish to amend the constitution by
removing the sanction for war.
They wish war to be declared illegal
and to deprive congress of the power
to prepare for war, declare war or
wage war; and that similar groups
of men and women, organized in 20
different countries of Europe and
Asia as the War Resisters’ Interna
tional have cither adopted the same
program for their respective coun
tries or are working toward it.
Since 1789 the policy of increasing
our armaments has been continued
by successive administrations with
out consulting the people, and will
undoubtedly be so continued unless
a direct mandate to the contrary is
given by the people.
The above amendment provides a
means of consulting the people for
the first time since the adoption of
the constitution about the policy of
disarmament which may be success
fully achieved, through a constitu
tional amendment like the one pro
posed. This amendment should re
ceive the active support of all those
who think war is out of date; of all
who realize that war creates more
disputes than it settles; of all who.
are convinced that war never lessens
greed or hate, never eradicates any
antagonism or causes of disagree
ment of all who have decided that
war more often destroys than pro
tects life, liberty and justice; of all
who take literally the command
ment, “Thou shalt not kill,” and
hold that human life should be held
sacred under all circumstances; of
all who believe in the unity of man
kind and feel that they cannot de
stroy others without destroying part

Perfume to Dispel
Hospital Odors
CHICAGO —White walls do not a
hospital make—any longer. White
pain., once generally used in hos
pitals. according to the American
Hospital Assn., is being replaced
by soft grays, greens and pinks, be
cause of the therapeutic value of
color.
And nurses may wear a mild
perfume while on duty, to banish
th< odor of carbolic acid, chloro
form or ether. In fact, it is rec
ommended in the older hospitals
which cannot afford to install ex
pensive ventilating systems.
‘‘Why,” asks the association,
•‘cannot the ordinary ventilation
system that cleans and cools air
waft through the hospital a pleas
ing fragrance?”*

Fiancee of Youth
Slain By Mother
To Wed Saturday
Leona Timper, 18, fiancee of Oli
ver Sullivan, who was accidentally
shot and killed last January by a
revolver in the hands of his moth
er, will be married Saturday to
Joseph Gravelie, it was announced
today.
At the time Oliver was shot,
plans were being made for his mar
riage to Leona, which was to have
taken place the same month.
He was shot in a tussle over the
possession of a revolver between
himself and his mother.
A municipal court jury acquitted
Mrs. Sullivan when she was tried
on a charge of murder as a result
of the boy’s death.
Following the marriage Satur
day the event will be celebrated by
a few friends of the couple at the
bride’s home, 564 19th St.
THE PILGRIM MOTHER
A statue to the Pilgrim Mother
was recently unveiled at Plymouth
Rock, Mass. Through her we honor
every pioneer woman who endured
privation and hardships that a na
tion might live. Shoulder to shoulder
with her husband she built a home
in the wilderness and reared her
sturdy sons and daughters. She
cooked and sewed. She spun and
wove for her growing family. When
they were ill, she brewed potent
remedies from roots and herbs
such roots and herbs as are now
used in Lydia E. Pinkham’s Vege
table Compound.—Adv.

SEVEN
SPANISH KING
TO AIO CAUSE
OF ARMY MEN
ST. JEAN DE LUZ, France—
With an eye to the future of his
dynasty, King Alfonso yesterday
brought his influence to bear on
Premier Primo de Rivera to deter
the dictator from venting his feel
ings on 1,800 artillery officers in
volved in the alleged insubordina
tion which resulted in Sunday’s dec
laration of martial law.
Hold Stormy Scenes.
The council of ministers at mid
day was marked by stormy scenes,
during which Premier de Rivera
was balked in his desire to use the
nrniled fist against the dissenting
officers and again offered his resig
nation, which the king again re
fused, in order to avoid more com
plications at this dangerous mo
ment.
Premier de Rivera issued a state
ment saying the revolt was crushed
and preparations for the trial of
ti e leaders were being made.
Trouble Is Averted.
A competent authority says seri
ous trouble Sunday was averted
when the powerful army juntas who
are the object of Premier de Rivera’s
ire received assurances from the
king that the supposed offenses
of the artillery officers for which
the corps was disbanded would
be charitably considered. The be
leaguered garrisons were advised to
bow to the government’s will.

HARBIN, Manchuria—A practical
union of churches is reported from
Kuangchendze, a station on the
Chinese Eastern Railway near
Changehjun, where an exceptional
drought impelled the Chinese popu
lation to urge the local Russian
Orthodox Church to join them in a
community prayer for rain.
For' a^month the neighboring
region haa not felt a single drop
of rain and farmers were anxiously
searching the Sky for the sight of a
cloud which' would bring relief to
the parched fields. In despair the
population trityl to mollify the “God
of Rains” by prayers and offerings
—but the angehed Rain God re
mained deaf.
Finally the local Merchants’ guild
organized a mass prayer meeting of
farmers and merchants in front of
the Buddhist temple. At every shop
Incense and prayer-candles were
burning.
-Three days later the first rain of
the Season started the periodical
rainy season of Manchuria two
weeks ahead of its usual date.

sponded in the same silent vtay.

ing to Mr. Baker, and each one
wards off loneliness by knowing
every other one. They are organ
ized as the Milwaukee Silent club

MADRID—The government prom
ises early annulment of the state of
war decree issued last Sunday be
cause of the artillery revolt in an
official communique issued late yes
terday.
The government emphasizes that
the rebellion has been crushed and

ly the men who took part in the

Canopy Saves Life
Of Boy, 14, When He
Falls Six Stories
CHICAGO—William Shrader, 14,
son of Mrs. Mercia Shrader, fell
six stories from the roof of the
Hotel Hayes, where he was
playing with the children of the
owners of the hotel. The boy was
badly bruised and shaken up, but
not seriously injured, in his fall to
the pavement.
William was checked in his drop
by landing on a canopy extending
out from the second floor. His
bounce off the canopy into the street
saved his life.
Young Shrader had met the
Hayes children in the Hayes sum
mer home in Grand Beach, Mich.
John Hayes just returned from
Grand Beach yesterday and Shrader
went over to visit him.

No Names Left for
Smith W. Brookhart
DES MOINES —Smith W. Brook
hart, Republican senatorial nominee,
told a Labor day audience here yes
terday that Wall Street has run
out of names to call him.
“If a man disagrees once with
Wall Street,” the colonel said, “they
call him a radical.
“If he disagrees twice they call
him a Socialist.
“If he disagrees three times they
call him a Bolshevik.
“Wall Street has long ago run
out of name to call me, and most
of us out here, for that matter.”

SHEBOYGAN, Wis. Funeral

board of directors of the Pittsburgh
Coal Co., the Northern Furniture
Co. and the Security National bank
of Sheboygan. He was chairman of
the board of directors of the Reiss
Steamship Co. and a trustee of the
Northwestern Mutual Life Insur

GANGER GROUP
OF DISEASES,
EXPERT HOLDS
NEW YORK The theory that
cancer, contrary to general belief,
is a group of diseases which must
be separated before a cure can be
effected, was advanced yesterday by
William S. Bainbridge, cancer and
skin disease specialist.
Is New Theory.
Speaking before the annual con
vention of the American Academy
of Physio-Therapy, he expressed the
belief that multiple ailments, each
sustained by the other, were the ba
sis of all cancer, and that attempts
to eradicate it as one disease were
useless.
Dr. Bainbridge, who was chief
surgeon at the Brooklyn Naval hos
pital during the war and who is an
international authority on cancer
and skin diseases, declared that sci
ence, working on the multiplicity of
ailments theory, will soon have con
trol of the disease. a
Step to Everlasting Life.
Everlasting physical life, he said,
would be but a step as soon as sci
entists could discover the secret of
combating poisons thrown off in
ternally by body cells.
He pointed out that a portion of
a chicken’s heart had Deen kept
alive for 15 years by scientists at
the Rockefeller institute after they
had learned how to combat the poi
sons given off by the cells of the
flesh.

learned, unofficially, from an of
ficial of the United States Golf
Assn, that:
“Miss Mary K. Browne is still an
amateur golf player.”
Miss Browne, former national ten
nis champion, in announcing that
she had decided to turn professional
and join Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen in
a tour of the United States, starting
in October, expressed the regret
that:
“Turning professional in tennis
bars me from golf as an amateur,
and I love golf as much as I love
tennis.”

BADGER GAGERS
SEEK BIG
GAME HERE
MADISON, Wis.—Wisconsin uni
versity’s basketball team will en
gage another eastern live this win
ter in addition to Syracuse univer
sity if the present plans of Coach
Walter Meanwell and Business
Manager Levis materialize.- An ef
fort is being made to bring a strong
quintet west to meet the Badgers
in Milwaukee during the Christmas
holidays.
Letters have been dispatched to
Princeton, Cornell, Yale, Columbia,
Pennsylvania and Dartmouth, and
it is practically a certainty that
one of these will accept the terms
offered. The contest will be staged
in the Milwaukee Auditorium, a
definite date to be announced later.
Should the Badger schedule carry
two eastern games, an engagement
with Notre Dame, 12 conference
tilts and one with a strong minor
college, it will be the most attrac
tive slate ever played by a Wiscon
sin five. The proposed Milwaukee
intersection battle would also af
ford the alumni and public of the
state an opportunity to see Mean
well’s team in action against a
headline outfit, where in the past
basketball has been almost a close
proposition due to the limited seat
ing capacity in the university gym
at Madison.

up in thb 1925 chase.

Title for Hampton
Speaking of missed short putts,
as many golfers have been doing
since the Bob Cruickshank incident
in the Texas open, there is the fail
ure of Harry Hampton in the Cana
dian open at Toronto three years
ago.
Playing the ninth hole of the
Lambton club, a hole of some 200
yards or more, Hampton was going
well when he suddenly' ran into
trouble. His tee shot caught a trap,
He finally made the' green with
his third shot and then took three
putts. The third putt hung right
on the lip of the cup. A single
half turn and It would have been
down.

to the ball, jabbed at it with hii
putter and completely missed the
ball.

Two and a half games from first
place, our faltering Brewers will
make a double effort this afternoon
to make up lost ground at the
expense of the Saints, but they’ll
have to play a different brand of
baseball than they did yesterday
when the Saints with a'busher, Ed
die Mead, on the mound won, 4
to 2.
The dash and timely hitting that
characterized the work of the team
during its last home series was
notable by its absence. Charley
Robertson hurled a fine brand of
baseball and if he had only gotten
the. necessary support from his
mates he could have won.
Runners Die on Bases.
The Brewers had runners on the
sacks in every chapter except the
final and scored in but two innings,
the third and the sixth. In the
seventh the bags were loaded with
one down, but the runners died
waiting for a base hit. Richbourg
was caught stealing in the third
end it so happened that the next
two batsmen got on, again robbing
us of a chance to score more than
the one run in that round.
In the second with two down and
Flippin on first, McMenemy chased
Bruno Haas right up against a
fence in left center to pull down his
fly. This was just the reverse in
the seventh when Strohm hit a weak
fly ball to center, just short enough
to prevent Shulte coming IX from
third. These are hut two of the
breaks our pennant hopes didn’t get.
The Saints, on the other hand, had
thib Goddess of Luck with them and
the box score figures show what
happened.
Saints Score First.
The visitors were the first to
score, rushing one across in the
second. Wade led off with a single,
advanced to third on Haas’ single
and scored when Foss hit into a
double play. We got the run back
In the third after two were gone.
Shulte walked, reached third on the
second of Griffin’s four hits and
scored easily on a double steal with
the firstsacker. In the next chap
ter Strohm singled, but went out
stealing. Lamotte flied out. Flippin
then singled and McMenemy drew a
pass. Robertson, however, popped
out.
With two gone in the fifth, Griffin
punched out a double. Brief hit a
hard one to Mead which the latter
knocked down and tossed out the
runner.
The Saints grubbed the lead in
the fourth. Cullop got a life when
Flippin mussed up Jils grounder.
Stuvengen followed with a single
and Wade hit into a double play,
putting Cullop on third from where
^e scored on a wild heave by Rob
son. Haas lifted the ball over
Wit field fence for a home run
yooss flied out to end the inning.

The final St. Paul tally came in
the seventh after one was gone.
Foss singled to center and Hoffman
rolled to Robertson. The latter
waited for someone to cover second
to cut off Foss, but both Lamotte
and Flippin were slow getting to
the bag and when Flip finally raced
over to take the throw, Robby
tossed too low. Mead struck out, but
Wanninger singled to center and
Foss came across.

TUNNEY RESTS;
TO CONCENTRATE
ONRIGHT
STROUDSBURG, Pa.—Out in the
woods, in a quiet cottage far from
the stares of the fight fans, Gene
Tunney slept late today with noth
ing to look forward to but a good
long day of rest.
Tomorrow he will be back in the
ring again and perhaps his pore lip,
which has troubled the challenger
considerably, will be healed enough
to withstand his sparring partner’s
blows.
Tunney is now giving much time
to developing his right. He was
criticized yesterday for telegraphing
his blows —that is, acquainting his
opponent beforehand of the coming
of a lusty crash. Tunney's aides
know of that tendency, and are
ceaselessly working to overcome it.

If Diane had not answered her

old story to her, although Diane
was only 18. It was an old story be
cause ever since Diane had been

about marriage as if it were im
minent, a sort of adventure or en
terprise to be taken care of and
considered well in advance.
“I can think of half a uozen
girls, Dee,” went on her mother
comfortably, “who were In high
school with you, who have gone
off, and gotten married and every
one of them to some fellow with
out any money.”
Diane smiled pleasantly, but she
wgsn’t half interested.

Mrs. Colfax allowed her face to
become firm and when her face
went set that way, she had a cu

worth talking about.” Mrs. Col
fax looked thoughtfully at her
daughter, then added: “And Abby
was such a pretty girl.”
Diane’s smooth brow wrinkled
the least bit into a frown.
“What has that to do with it,
mother?” she asked seriously. “It
would be just as hard for Abby
If she was ugly as a mud fence.”
Her mother sniffed.
“But, she didn’t have to marry

sisted Mrs. Colfax impatiently.

and of family and breeding is a

can’t give her everything. She
has a right to have it.”
Yes, it was an old story to

TONSILS AND ADENOIDS.
Certain common causes of nasal
obstruction (mouth breathing) in
children, often overlooked when
children are operated upon for
“enlarged tonsils and adenoids,”
are nasal polyps, enlarged or
thickened turbinate or spongy
bodies in the nose (laymen speak
of excision of portions of these
turbinate bodies as having “bones”
removed), sinus infection, and
sometimes foreign body lodged in
the nasal passage.
In certain busy “clinics” and in
the offices of certain born nose
and throat specialists the opera
tion is done first; the proper ex
amination of the patient is left to
be done later if the patient fails
to derive the anticipated benefit
from the hasty surgery. People
who simply must have a “special
ist” for everything little reck the
sins of omission which are com
mitted by these same pet special
ists. People who imagine a phy
sician is a better trained or better
educated or more skilled physician
because he purports to be a spe
cialist, need a guardian to watch
over them.
It is no figure of speech, no
exaggeration, to say that in cer
tain communities where so-called,
school medical inspection is in
practice, children are sometimes
rushed to the operating room on
the mere suspicion of a nurse, or
worse, the whim of a teacher, and
without any proper examination
or diagnosis by a physician. It is
a shocking fact, at least I find it
so, that the wholesale operator in
his clinic sometimes has his first
sight of the patient after the pa
tient is anesthetized for the op
eration. This might be perfectly
proper and right, if the diagnosis
of the enlarged tonsils or the en
larged adenoids had been made by
a qualified physician. It is not all
right when the diagnosis has been
made by a nurse or a teacher.
It is not quite so shocking, per
haps, though deplorable enough,
that nurses employed in communi
ties where so-called school medical
inspection is in vogue, are encour
aged to attempt the diagnosis of
“adenoids,” and in some instances
nurses actually send parents no
tices that children have “adenoids”
and should be operated upon,
i'his is a disgrace, not so much
to the health authorities, who are
generally politically handicapped,
or to the school authorities who
are not competent to comprehend'
the malpractice involved, but par
ticularly to the medical profession
of the community where this
shameful practice is permitted.
Even the trained physician Is
not warranted in making a diag
nosis of adenoid enlargement or
of obstruction to breathing from
thickening or hypertrophy of the
adenoid body until he has either
felt the adenoid enlargement with
his finger or seen it with his eye.
It is the veriest guesswork, and
most frequently a mistake, to de
duce from a blank or dull expres
sion or from obvious mouth
breathing that a child has “ade
noids.” It is malpractice to sub
ject a child to an anesthetic and
operation for “adenoids” if the
physician has not seen or felt the
enlarged adenoid mass. It is un
fair to a child to jump to any con
clusion as to the nature of an ap
parent nasal obstruction or the
cause of mouth breathing without
a proper and careful examination
of the throat cavity and the nasal
cavities having been made. This
is strictly a physician’s work and
by no stretch of the truth can the
politician or the grafter on public

Bananas for Bimbos.
Are bananas a healthy food for
every one? Some doctors dispute it.
but I have read that they are almost
a perfect food for every one from the
age of 1 year. (I. V. G.)
Answer —Yes, they are excellent food
for child or adult when they are well
ripened. A banana well ripened is
flecked with brown spots, not black
spots, and the pulp is soft and sweet,
not mushy. Even green or yellow ba
nanas are wholesome and nutritious
rather more nutritious than potato—
when cooked. I told all about ba
nanas in an article printed here Fri
day the thirteenth of August. The
banana men have no bananas today,
I suppose. At least I never got a
hand. A baby may eat bananas as
soon as he may eat potatoes. That’s
at the age of 8 months, as a rule,
provided the potato or banana is well
cooked.

CHAPTER I.
Black Bear and Black Fly.
Rain kept on falling. Jack, Ja
net and Cousin Clyde began to
wonder if the storm were going
to continue all summer. It was
holding them up on their auto
camping trip with Jolly Jerry.
But the children did not mind
the delay in the least. They
were having a very pleasant time
at the sheep ranch of the Silent
Twins. During the day they
kept busy helping the Silent
Twins tend the sheep or playing
in the big barn. And in the eve
ning the Silent Twins told stories.
The children were not afraid of
wearing out their welcome, be
cause the Silent Twins were very
grateful to them for aiding in
saving the barn from burning up
when it was struck by lightning.
As they gathered around the
cheerful fireplace on their third
evening on the ranch, Jack
slapped suddenly at a buzzing fly
which had been annoying him.
He smashed the fly flat.
“There! That fly will not
bother anyone any more,” he said.
“I wish I had one big swatter and
could kill all the flies in the world
with one big swat.”
Ronald Twin nodded his head.
“Flies are bad,” he agreed. They
spread disease in addition to caus
ing annoyance. They should be
swatted.”
Roland Twin grinned. “It was
a good thing for big Black Bear
that he did not feel that way.
If he had swatted little Black
Fly there would not have been
any big Black Bear and there
would not have been any story to
tell you about Black Bear and
Black Fly.”
The children opened their ears
eagerly. They were keen to hear
the story of Black Bear and Black
Fly.
“Black Bear lived in the depths
of the forest. He found plenty of
food to eat and there were no
hunters to fear. So Black Bear
was contented and happy.
“Little Black Fly also lived in
the depths of the forest. And like
most flies, he was a bothersome
little chap. He was always buzz
ing around making a nuisance of
himself.
“He was a boastful fellow, too.
‘l’ll eat you up,’ he threatened as
he buzzed around Black Bear’s
head.
“That was a silly boast, be
cause he was so small and Black
Bear was so large. But Black
Bear just grinned at it. He was
a good-natured chap, and even
little Black Fly could not annoy
him. Perhaps one reason was
that he had such a thick coat he
knew Black Fly could not bite
him through it.

AUTHOR OF BIG PARADE LIVED WAR
SCENES HE SHOWS IN FILM
The career of Laurence Stallings
in literature and the drama has
been meteoric. In four years he
has co-authored a war play (What
Price Glory), written a best-seller
novel and supplied the original
story for The Big Parade, which is
held by many critics to be the best
motion .picture ever produced.
Laurence Stallings is a native of
Macon, Ga., where he received his
early education. He was graduated
from Wake Forest college, N. C.,
and is therefore a fellow alumnus
of the late President Woodrow
Wilson. Shortly after graduation
from Wake Forest, Stallings became
a newspaper reporter and got a job
from Maj. John Cohen, editor of
The Atlanta Journal. On this
paper he ran the routine of repor
torial jobs and also served on the
copy desk.
When America entered the war,
Stallings enlisted in the marine
corps as a private. After the pre
liminary training at Paris island
he was selected for the officers’
training school, from which he re
ceived his commission as second
lieutenant of marines. Stallings
went to France with the fifth regi
ment of marines in 1917 and fought
through most of the major engage
ments with the second division.
Before the armistice was signed he
had won a captaincy and he had
been severely wounded in the ter
rific Belleau Wood offensive.
Then followed long weeks in base
hospitals in France. On Christmas
eve, 1918, Capt. Stallings landed in
New York and caught his first sight
of the metropolis from a stretcher
as he was carried off a hospital
ship.
For many months he was a pa
tient in rehabilitation hospitals.
As soon Jis he was able to hobble
about, S fallings visited the Wash
ington newspaper offices intent upon
getting a job, as it was necessary to
continue treatments for his shat
tered leg at the Walter Reed hospi
tal there. He finally landed a place
as a copy reader on The Washing
ton Times. It was while he was
trying to establish himself in news
paper work again that the wounds
he received in France became so
serious he had to return to the
Walter Reed hospital where he suf
fered the loss of his leg.
In March, 1919, and after a long
period at the hospital, Laurence
Stallings was married to Miss Helen
Poteat, daughter of Dr. W. L.
Poteat, president, Wake Forest col
lege. He had met his wife in college
and became engaged before entering
the marine corps.
Herbert Bayard Swope gave Stal
lings a desk job on The New York
World about 1921. Shortly after
the publication of his novel Plumes,
Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer signed him
to a contract to go to Hollywood
and write the screen story of
America’s part in the war. On the
way to California, Irving Thalberg
of the Metro studios in Culver City

Peaches With Rice Cakes.
Cook one cup rice in three cups
of milk with one-quarter teaspoon
salt in a double boiler until liquid is
absolutely absorbed and rice is ten
der. Add one-quarter cup butter,
grated rind and juice of one-quarter
medium sized lemon and one-quarter
cup sugar. Mix thoroughly. Cool
and form into flat cakes, adding a
little flour if necessary to make it
of consistency that can be handled
well. Dip in flour and fry on hot
griddle. Serve with a peach half
for each cake. Add lemon juice
to taste to the syrup from peaches

VELVET LEADS
IN FABRIC'
FOR HATS
BY HEDDA HOYT.
Written for The United Press.
NEW YORK—New styles, fads
and accessories confront one each
day as fall approaches, and while
it is still too early to indulge in
bonnets and frocks of wintery fab
rics we can be forming an idea of
what is what in smartdom.
Velvet seems to be the outstanding
fabric for hats. Both dull and bright
colors are used. Shapes vary from
tarns, crushed turbans and small
brimmed sports models to wide
brimmed affairs. Often two colors
of velvet are combined in sort of a
patchwork manner to form tarn
shapes. Many of the velvet tarns
in the shops must be draped and
tacked to suit the wearer. Felt and
grosgrain ribbon combine to form
some of the smartest of tam or
sports shapes, and though felt will
be popular it will undoubtedly be a
season of velvet millinery.
Linings used in fur coats this sea
son are extremely lovely since many
of them are embroidered or ap
pliqued with velvet flowers down
the side-fronts or around the hem.
Many furriers are showing unlined
fur coats and permitting one to se
lect one’s own lining and floral de
sign. This is far more sensible than
showing a ready-lined coat since no
two women have the same idea as to
linings. One can have one of these
exquisite embroidered linings placed
in a coat for .$25 at several shops.
An udsual lining shown by an up
town furrier has a nile green back
ground with embroidered orchids
worked on the fronts. Huge velvet
roses adorn a black lined seal coat.
Zipper bathing shoes of bright
colored suede are among the mid
summer novelties. Red, green, yel
low, white and black are the colors
found among these zippered models.
The zipper fastening extends up the
center front of the shoe.
Plaid and checked velveteens are
on display in several department
stores. They can be made up into
straight-lined coats and into sports
frocks most effectively.
Little bunches of glass flowers or
grapes are new millinery trimmings
which may replace rhinestone orna
ments. White and bright colored
transparent glass is used, and these
little ornaments glisten like dew
drops.
English Currant Pie.
Mix together one cup of fresh
currants, two tablespoons flour, two
tablespoons water, one cup of sugar,
yolks of two eggs, place in unbaked
lower crust and bake until done.
Remove from oven and frost with
the beaten whites of eggs to which
two tablespoons of sugar have been
added and brown in oven.
Parsnips Southern Style.
Peel and boil parsnips. Split them
and lay closely in a shallow buttered
baking dish flat side down. Sprinkle
with salt and brown sugar and dot
with butter. Bake until a rich
brown, basting occasionally with the
syrup.

Cook one cupful of finely-cut car

Shrimp Sauce (For Fish).
Measure one-third of a cupful of
butter and melt half of it; add three
tablespponfuls of flour and cook* un

cook until slightly thickened; when

Add one cupful of shrimps, two tea

^.Orange; Whip.
Soak two tablespoonfuls of gela
tin in one-half cupful of boiling wa
ter, one-half cupful of sugar, and
stir until all is dissolved. Add one
and three-fourths cupfuls of orange
juice, one-fourth cupful of lemon

Peach Fritters.
Mix and sift one cupful of flour,
two teaspoonfuls of baking powder,
three tablespoonfuls of sugar, and
one-fourth teaspoonful of salt. Add
gradually one-third of a cupful of
milk, one well-beaten egg and three
peaches sliced in small pieces. Drop
by spoonfuls into hot fat and drain
on brown paper. Roll in sugar and
serve.—Nellie Maxwell.

slice or cut into quarters, cover
with one-half cup vinegar, one tea
spoon salt, one-eighth teaspoon pep
per and one tablespoon parsley.
Boil six eggs hard and pickle with
beets.

Rhubarb Puffs.
One-third cup butter, one-third
cup of sugar, one egg, two-thirds
cup milk, one and one-half cups
flour, one and one-half teaspoons
baking powder, one-third teaspoon
salt and some stewed rhubarb. Beat
butter and sugar together until
light and add egg well beaten, then
the milk and lastly the dry ingre
dients sifted together. Oil individ
ual custard cups and put two ta
blespoons' of stewed rhubarb into
the bottom of each. Then cover
with the puff batter about half full
to give room to rise. Bake in mod
erate oven about 25 minutes and
serve with stewed rhubard.
Sometime ago, I published a let
ter from one of our readers telling
ways to use old newspapers. An
other reader has sent additional
hints for using paper we might
otherwise waste. Oiled paper from
groceries—wadded, it becomes an
excellent stove cleaner which does
not need to be cleaned.
Save all clean pieces of oiled pa
per for wrapping lettuce, etc., in the
ice box.
The glazed paper may be saved
to wrap luncheon sandwiches or to
keep cookies and bread fresh.
Tied snugly down, this paper
makes a dustproof cover for open
pickle jars, or glasses of jelly.
Magazines may be sold for pa
per. All other wrapping paper may
be packed in neat tight bundles and
stored in an old tub or other fire
proof container and saved for fall
furnace lighting. If the bundles
are soaked and dried, they will
make excellent early fall fuel.

Freight Car Loadings Smash Previous All-Time Record
1.05 PER CENT
INCREASE OVER
AUG. 28,1925
Loadings Pass Mil
lion Mark in 14
Weeks This Year.
WASHINGTON—More cars were
loaded with revenue freight for the
week ended Aug. 28 than ever be
fore for any one week on record, ac
cording to reports filed today by the
carriers with the car service division
of the American Railway Assn.
The total for week was 1,136,-33
cars.
This exceeded by 11,795 cars, or
1.05 per cent the previous high rec
ord for all time, established during
the corresponding week of Aug. 28,
1925, at which time 1,124,438 cars
were loaded. The total for the week
of Aug. 28 this year was also an in
crease of 115,424 cars above the
same week in 1924 and was an in
crease of 47,442 cars above the pre
ceding week this year.
Surplus Freight Cars.
Loadings, have exceeded the mil
lion mark in 14 weeks this year, but
this heavy freight traffic is being
carried without a car shortage. In
stead there are nearly 120,000 sur
plus freight cars in good repair and
immediately available for service.
At the same time the railroads have
more than 5,500 servicable locomo
tives in gooC repair which they have
not found it necessary to put in
service.
Coal loading for the week amount
ed to 201,159 cars, an increase of
15,349 cars over the preceding week
this year but 10,609 cars below the
same week in 1925.
Miscellaneous freight loadings to
taled 414,478 cars, an increase of 16,-
004 cars above the week before and
410 cars over the same week in 1925.
Grain Products Up.
Loadings of grain and grain prod
ucts amounted to 57,219 cars, an
increase of 4,904 cars above the pre
ceding week and 240 cars above the
corresponding week in 1925. In the
western districts alone, grain and
grain products loading totaled 37,-
125 cars, a decrease of 3,671 cars un
der the corresponding week last
year.
Loading of merchandise and less
than carload lot freight amounted
to 268,982 cars, an increase of 3,-
405 cars above the week before and
4,190 cars above the same week in
1925.
Forest products loading totaled
70,902 cars, 835 cars above the week
before but 1,248 cars below the same
week in 1925.
Livestock Varies.
Livestock loading for the week
amounted to 31,235 cars, an increase
of 1,300 cars above the week before
but 506 cars below the same week in
1925. In the western district alone,
23,721 cars were loaded with live
stock during the week, 225 cars more
than the same week last year.
Ore loadings totaled 80,425 cars,
an increase of 5,368 cars above the
preceding week and 17,792 cars
above the corresponding week in
1925.
Coke loading totaled 11,833 cars,
an increase of 277 cars above the

MILWAUKEE RD.
HIT BY DAKOTA
CROP FAILURE
The Milwaukee road will fail to
earn its fixed charges by between
$1,000,000 and $1,500,000 this year.
This opinion was advanced by an of
ficial of the road yesterday, who
stated that the crop failure in
South Dakota will undoubtedly pre
vent the company from showing an
increase in earnings during the re
mainder of the year, as compared
with the same months of 1925.
Net Income Up.
Such a showing, however, would
indicate a marked improvement over
last year, when there was a net def
icit of $3,934,611.
He called attention to the fact
that the net railways operating in
come of the road in the first seven
months of the year was more than
$4,000,000 larger than in the same
period last year, adding that the Au
gust net railway operating income
would probably be the same as last
rear, when it amounted to $2,633,-
727.
Crops Are Fair.
Commenting on the outlook in the
road’s territory, H. E. Pierpont,
chief traffic officer, said:
“With the exception of the poor
crop conditions in South Dakota
and southern North Dakota, the
general outlook is good. General
business conditions in the Pacific
northwest are very satisfactory, as
are conditions on the west coast.”
Barring any adverse developments
which might occur between new and
the end of the year, it is expected
that the St. Louis-San Francisco
road will show the largest earnings
in its history this year. With the
exception of 1922, its earniugs have
shown a steady increase since 1920.
The surplus of $3,320,774 in the
first seven months was equal, after
allowing for the full year’s dividend
on the 6 per cent preferred stock, to
$5.76 a share on the $50,278,600
common stock. In other words, the
Frisco has to earn a surplus, after
charges, equal to only $1.24 a
share in the remaining five months
of the year to cover its $7 annual
common dividend requirement.
The 15th regular meeting of the
Trans-Mississippi Shippers’ Advis
ory board will be held at St. Joseph,
Mo., Sept. 15.
Vegetable Matter
Seen as Producer
Of Petroleum
PHILADELPHIA That chemi
cal discoveries will abolish the gold
standard and cause petroleum to be
produced from vegetable matter,
were two startling statements made
by Dr. James F. Norris, president
of the American Chemical society,
in his address before the convention
of that organization here yesterday.
With the abolition of the stand
ard value of gold, Dr. Norris pre
dicted, the economic system would
be based on the value of more fun
damental units, such as essential
commodities and labor.
On the topic of synthetically pro
ducing petroleum, the president said
researches were already being made
to counterfeit the long-drawn-out
processes of nature, whereby
“through the action of bacteria or
other agencies, formation of hydro
carbons from vegetable matter will
be quickly achieved, leading to dis
coveries of immense importance to
the industry.”

MILWAUKEE, WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 8, 1926
50,000,000 Tons
Of Freight Pass
Through Straits
SAULT STE MARIE—More than
50,000,000 tons of freight passed
through the St. Mary’s Falls canal
to Sept. 1 this year, compared with
49,000,000 a year ago. The traffic
for August, 1926, not only breaks all
previous records for August or any
other month, but makes up the de
ficiency caused by late opening of
the season. For the first eight
months of the year 50,443,706 tons
of freight passed through, compared
with 49,086,821 for the period 1925.
STEEL OUTPUT
85 PER GENT
CHICAGO—SteeI mills in the Chi
cago district resumed operations im
mediately after the holiday on
about the same schedule as was in
effect last week. Operations this
week are again expected to average
between 80 and 85 per cent of
capacity. f
Valley mills have resumed opera
tions at around 85 per cent of
capacity. Some finishing mills in
that district resumed Monday night
due to pressure for shipments. Sheet
and pipe mills are operating at 90
per cent while 40 of 53 independent
open hearth furnaces will melt in
Youngstown territory this week.
Buying in many lines of the iron,
steel and metal industries has been
small over the week-end. Prices are
somewhat uncertain because of the
lack of trading and it will probably
be near the end of the week before
any definite line on quotations can
be secured.
August steel ingot output is esti
mated at around 3,840.000 tons or
a daily average of 147,000 tons. The
industry as a whole, according to
these figures, employed about 82 per
cent of capacity.
During August a year ago the
steel industry produced 3.420,998
tons, a daily average of 131,577 tons.

HARVEST 78,000
TONS OF GRAPES
CHICAGO Michigan’s 26,000
acres of vineyards are loaded with
enough fruit to supply each one of
Chicago’s 3,000,000 people with 52
pounds -of purple grapes, writes
Frank Ridgway in The Tribune
from Michigan.
The stage is all set for the har
vesting of one of the biggest crops
of grapes ever known in the state.
Pickers will start their work in the
Champion vineyards this week.
The lowest unofficial estimators
put the grape crop at 78,000 tons,
or an average of three tons to the
acre. Most fruit experts say the
crop will average from three to four
tons to the acre and many vineyards
will reach from five to six tons.
Ninety per cent of the grapes in
the state are grown in the two
southwestern lake counties, Berrien
and Van Buren. About 90 to 95
per cent of them are Concords.
Grapes are expected to sell at a
reasonable price, so that every pan
try and cellar in the middle west
can be filled with a liberal quota of
jelly and juice. Growers say they
will be satisfied with SSO a ton.

INQUIRY FREES
ARMOUR FIRM
CHlCAGO—Directors of the Chi
cago Board of Trade, by a vote of
15 to 1, today exonerated the Ar
mour Grain Co. of charges that it
had run 5,300 bushels of rye screen
ings into a bin containing 20,000
bushels of No. 2 rye, in its 10,000,-
000 bushel Northwestern elevator in
South Chicago late last April.
Twenty witnesses were heard.
The session lasted all last night.
There wns no statement concerning
the identity of the one member of
the board who dissented in the vote.
While the government was cog
nizant of the whole matter—the
charges being that the screenings
were transferred without the super
vision of an inspector—the govern
ment took no hand in the matter,
deciding that it was a matter for
the Chicago board itself to decide.
It is understood that the exoner
ating decision did not mean that the
screenings had not been transferred
from a private to a public eleiator
but that the grain had never been
sold and that therefore there was no
transaction and no money was lost
to any one by the action.

RAIL COMBINE

vania road opens its fight before the
interstate commerce commission to
day to prevent the Philadelphia
Reading from acquiring control of
the Lehigh New England, a 200-
mile line running from Tamaqua,
Pa., to Campbell Hall, N. Y.

tance of the Lehigh New England,
the Pennsylvania is expected to
make a determined fight, aided by
other big systems, to prevent it from
passing into the hands of the Read
ing, it was said.

delphia and the anthracite region to

BULLETIN.
By The United Press.
HONG KONG—Seven British
Bailors were killed and 15 were
wounded, it was announced today,
in Sunday’s battle near Hankow
on the Yangtsee river when Brit
ish naval vessels engaged the
troops of Marshal Wu Pel Fu.
Commander Darley of the British
cruiser Despatch and two lieu
tenants were among the killed.
The two other officers were
wounded. The remainder of the
casualties were enlisted men.
CHlCAGO—Coincident with the
collapse of the northern armies at
Hankow following the Cantonese
capture of Hanyang arsenals comes
news of the serious naval defeat of
the British forces at Wanhsien,
Szechwan province, which likely
will result in foreign intervention,
according to a copyrighted Peking
Story in The Tribune.
Telegrams to the British legation
Indicate the gunboats Cockchafer
and Widgeon were put out of action,
owing to casualties of their person
nel. The converted merchantman
Kaiwo was also crippled. These
were the only boats engaged.
It is feared that white officers
and passengers of two British mer
chantmen and British Consul Estes,
who went to their assistance from
Chungking, have been slain. There
has been no word received from
them since the naval engagement,
which followed.
Owing to the shallowness of the
Yangtze river the British are un
able to send larger vessels above
Ichang. Wanhsien is about 400
miles above Ichang and Chungking
farther up the river.
The encounter at Wanhsien fol
lowed a Yangtze river accident. A
British merchant ship swamped two
junks filled with soldiers of Gen.
Yan-sen, who is allied with Marshal
Wu Pei-fu. Gen. Yang-sen then con
fiscated two Butterfield Swire
steamers, imprisoning the white offi
cers and passengers. Consul Estes
went to their rescue, but has not
been heard from since. Meantime
the British armed the merchant
ship Kaiwo and put aboard all
available marines, under command
of officers detached from the Cock
chafer and Widgeon.
As the two gunboats and the Kai
wo approached Wanhsien the shore
batteries opened fire and the war
ships replied. Having no cover, the
warships suffered heavy casualties
and soon -were reduced to an in
sufficient personnel. However, pre
vious to their retreat the gunboats
laid Wanhsien, a city of 150,000,
virtually in ruins.
The British legation is reporting
fully on the engagement to London.
The sentiment among Britons in
China is strong for a punitive ex
pedition.

CHlCAGO—Fathers of illegiti
mate children have no legal claim to
them nor any standing in a law
court on questions concerning them,

and mothers of the children were

custody, but did not wish to marry
each other.

Holmes, was the other mother. She
was given custody of her daughter,
Marguerite, 12.
NEGRO GIRL IS
DOCTOR; GIVES
TIP TO OTHERS
NEW YORK —When five ambu
lances dashed from the Harlem hos
pital the other day to the West
135th St. station of the Lenox Ave.
division of the I. R. T. subway,
where four persons were injured
and a score cut from broken glass
in a rear-end collision, observers
noted a colored girl of about 28 giv
ing first aid to the sufferers. Her
name is Dr. May E. Chinn, and it
was learned she is the third colored
doctor connected with a hospital in
this state.
Dr. Chinn is a New York girl. She
was born in Massachusetts, but left
that state at the age of 3, and has
received her education and rearing
in this city. Her mother is Lulu
Chinn, a caterer, and her father,
William Chinn, is a watchman.
Music or Medicine?
“I’m an only child,” Dr. Chinn
said in speaking of herself, “and my
parents did everything they could to
educate and help me. I’m mighty
fond of music, too, but when I
passed the medical exams I decided
that would be my career. But I still
play and sing. However, I’m glad
to be a doctor, and, while I dislike
talking about myself, I’ll gladly do
it if there is any colored girl who
may be interested and wish to fol
low in my line.
“If a girl ran stand the sight of
blood and Is not afraid of instru
ments I think being a doctor is an
ideal profession for her. Women are
naturally sympathetic and good
nurses and all those qualities go to
make up a good doctor.
Time Belongs to Others.
“Another thing a girl who wishes
to be a doctor must bear in mind is
that her time belongs to others. She
never knows when she will be free.
The very moment she has a few
hours off an accident may occur or
some one of her patients need her
immediate attention.
“And, greatest of all, a girl must
like people. A cold, unappreciative
doctor or a doctor who frightens
patients will never get the best re
sults. I believe colored girls are
naturally warm-hearted and tender
in their ways, and therefore I think
they would make very good doctors
in this respect.
Sewing Up a Tongue.
“What was my most thrilling ex
perience? Oh, horrors! Sewing up
a tongue! I was just starting out
on my first day’s work when a child
was brought to me who had fallen
and bitten its tongue so that it was
almost hanging out of Its head. I
felt a bit faint, but went to It
sewed the thing up as you might a
dress, and after that—it was easy.
I could do anything I”
Dr. Chinn began her education in
this city by attending a downtown
kindergarten; then she went to pub
lic school 93, then Morris. High
school, and finally to Columbia uni
versity, where she took a four years’
course and specialized in science and
bacteria. Later she attended New
York university for special courses
in medicine and studied at Bellevue.
She held a position as bacteriologist
at Flower hospital for two years
and has been with the Harlem hos
pital since June.
HOODS BANNED
BY NEW LAW
NORFOLK, Va.—Passage by the
city council of an ordinance prohib
iting persons from wearing masks
or hoods in public in Norfolk and
the appearance of New York detec
tives in Princess Anne county were
the day’s developments in the case
growing, out of the kidnaping of the
Rev. Father Warren, pastor of St.
Joseph’s Catholic church in Princess
Anne county last Wednesday night.
Father Warren, who is director
of a colored school for boys and
girls, was seat'ed in an automobile
listening to a boys’ band from his
school play at a concert when 30
armed and hooded men drove up in
seven cars. They dragged the priest
from his car, took him away, and,
after subjecting him to questions,
let him go.
Kidnaping of the priest caused in
dignation among Catholics and
Protestants alike. Father Warren
received telegrams from throughout
the nation. Many persons offered
financial assistance to employ de
tectives to run down the mob, since
Princess Anne authorities showed
little Inclination to investigate.
Editorial protest by newspapers
caused Judge B. D. White to sum
mon a grand jury to investigate the
case. The investigation will begin
Monday.

of three persons at Folsom yester
dy was caused by a snake at a
railroad crossing. William Aitken
of Camden, N. J., tried to dodge
running over the snake and suc
ceeded, but he failed to see the
Cape May flyer which hit the auto
squarely. Rose McGannon and
Anna Skinner, each 25, of Toronto,
and William Williams, 5, of Cam
den, N. J., were killed.

highway, 40 feet wide will be con
structed along Lake Michigan from

Mich., it was announced yesterday.

Saugatuck, is expected to be con

gun. The new highway will be a
1 relocation of state road 11, which is
replete with sharp turns.

an A. F. of L. body, and the strike is now under A. F. of L.
auspices.
This removed the only objection the bosses said they
had to the recognition of the workers. They vociferously
claimed they could not confer with the workers so long as
there were any Bolsheviks at the head of the strike. Affili
ation with the A. F. of L. has eliminated the few Bolshe
viks—and the bosses still refuse to parley I How is that
for a sample of boss ethics?
The Textile Strike Bulletin does not exaggerate very
much when it says that—now that the bosses are hugging
a company union and refusing to confer with the A. F.
of L.—“the issue is one of life and death to all organized
labor in America.” No doubt it is an exaggeration, but it
is excusable, for the issue is surely a very grave one for all
organized labor in America.
The Bulletin does not exaggerate in the least when it
adds, “The whole power of the American Federation of
Labor and of the entire American labor movement must
be mobilized to meet this challenge of the Passaic mill
owners.”
It must. We hope the leaders of the A. F. of L., the
leaders of the international unions, and the leaders and
rank and file of all local unions in the country realize it.
Should the bosses win the Passaic strike, company union
ism would be given a great boost.
Company unionism is already about a million and a
half strong—about half as strong as the A. F. of L. This
evil has crept upon the labor movement within a very few
years, and is growing. Along with its twin devil, the “open
shop,” it constitutes the greatest menace to labor that
exists at the present time—excepting, of course, the profit
system, which is the father of devils.
Beware, union men. Mobilize your forces to fight this
company union menace. Back up the Passaic strike until
it ends in a glorious victory.
THE SACRED COW MUST BE
PROTECTED AT ALL HAZARDS
The secretary of labor, James J. Davis, warns the
workers against the Bolsheviks. Now let the Bolsheviks
warn the workers against Davis, and all will be well.
It is hard to tell which is the more injurious to labor,
the bolshevistic extremists or the complacent believers in
letting “well enough” alone. Probably the latter, since
there are more of them. In this country the Bolshevists
are scarce and becoming scarcer.
The labor secretary, with all his complacency, does
sometimes betray that he knows not all is “well enough.”
He states, for instance, that some industries have become
so badly overdeveloped that they cah produce as much
in a few months as they can sell in a year—and he admits
that he does not know of any remedy for this condition.
It would not be orthodox for a Republican to know
a remedy for it, unless a fake remedy, for Republicans
must always worship the sacred cow of private profit,
whereas the remedy involves the abandonment of this
idolatry.
If the gr^at industries were collectively owned, it
would be a fine thing if they could produce a year’s supply
in a few months, would it not? That would give the
people more leisure in which to improve and enjoy them
selves. If they did not want to take so long a vacation
from work, they could shorten the daily working time
and have more leisure every day.
But it would not do for a Republican secretary of
labor to announce so reasonable a solution of the problem
—for the sacred cow must be revered, and if the industries
were collective there would be no profits for parasites but
only for the useful people.
ANOTHER MIRACLE IS IN ORDER
If oil is going to be exhausted in half a dozen years
the old saying that necessity is the mother of invention
will have to be trotted out and turned from theory into
practice.
It will be up to Edison, Ford and others to provide
a substitute, and it may be up to each owner of a car to
pay a pocketful of bucks for a new device. What will the
new motor power be? Electricity? Alcohol? If electric
ity, where is it to come from? Water? Air? If alcohol,
the farmers will be in clover, at least in the corn belt.
Maybe the scientists will at last tap the marvelous atomic
energy which they are always raving about. If no sub
stitute at all is found, there will be one compensation:
the streets and roads will become safe once more and the
human race will again learn what legs are for. But that
is only a remote possibility. Our inventors and scientists
have already worked many miracles and they can work
another.

SOVIET RUSSIA, STRIKE BREAKER
European labor circles are shocked and deeply
aroused by the revelation that the Moscow government
joined the Tory government of Great Britain in efforts
to break down the locked-out and striking miners.
German Socialist papers were the first to call atten
tion to this fact, after a Communist t leader in Hamburg
had charged the Amsterdam trade union international
and the German labor unions with failure to support the
British trade unions.
Taking up this lie, the leader of the German seamen
in Hamburg declared that the shoe was on the Communist
foot and that the Moscow government had concluded big
contracts with British firms for the delivery of oil and
gasoline for the purpose of replacing coal with them.
It is further reported that Cook, secretary of the
British miners’ federation, had asked the Moscow govern
ment to stop its deliveries of oil and gasoline to England,
and that the Russian trade delegation refused the request.
Cook complained that Russian Soviet agents were travel
ing all over England and trying to induce British capital
ists to burn oil instead of coal.
The Moscow offer was so tempting that some British
concerns accepted it. The Socialist press of Germany
also claim that the Moscow government, in order to con
ceal direct shipments of oil and gasoline from Russian
to British ports, ordered reshipments from European
ports to England.
While the Russian trade unions were bragging about
the big amounts of money which they sent to the British
miners, the Moscow government was making deals with
British capitalists to break the British miners. Quite a
drop from the “world revolution.”
The German Communist press tried to prove partly
that deliveries of oil and gasoline from Russia to Eng
land were stopped during the trouble, partly that no more
was delivered than before the mine war. Some communist
papers claim that only old contracts were filled, others
say that no new contracts were made. But the executive
committee of the German federation of labor in Hamburg
sticks to its charges.
The Leipziger Volkszeitung writes: “It has been as
certained beyond a doubt that precisely during the British
coal crisis the Russian Soviet government made great ef
forts to install a large scale gasoline sales organization
in England. It is known as The Independent Oil Dis
tribution Company. The All-Russian naphtha syndicate
helped to found it. Several Conservative members of the
British parliament sit in its board of directors.
“So the Soviet government fraternized with the worst
enemies of the British miners, in order to share profits
with them from strike breaking and supply them with
weapons to fight Labor. Yet at the same time the Soviet
government fraternized with the miners and strengthened
their resistance by grants of money, merely because it has
an interest in making the strike last long enough to enable
it to replace coal with oil on a fairly profitable scale in
the industries Just because it requires time to effect
the change, the Soviet government is interested in keeping
the strike alive until the change has been achieved.”
L’Humanite, the Communist organ in Paris, admits
the truth of the charge, but says the British miners don’
appreciate the economic needs of Soviet Russia and
demands to stop oil deliveries in spite of the fact th
financial help from Russia has more than offset any injury
that the Russian oil deal with the British Tories could in
flict on Labor.
THEY SEE THE POINT
In the flood of rebuttals which Newton D. Baker’s
demand for the cancellation of the remaining allied war
debts has evoked, there is one statement which shows that
the Wall Street leaders see the main point of this issue
very plainly.
The Washington bureau of the New York Commercial
says: If Mr. Baker’s proposal were followed to its logical
conclusion, it would lead also to the cancellation of
Europe’s commercial debts to the United States.
It is further stated that the commercial debts press
more heavily on European life than the war debts, and
that a movement to cancel also the commercial debts
would have a disastrous effect on the world market.
But the cat was let out of the bag long ago when Sen
ator Smoot told his colleagues that even private loans to
Europe would never be repaid. What Wall Street fears
is not so much the cancellation, as the effect on public
opinion of a frank admission that loans to Europe are
not safe.
STEPS TOWARDS SOCIALISM
The Belgian Socialist party follows the lead of the
Austrian and proposes a new program, in which practical
steps for the transition to Socialism appear as present
day tasks to be achieved by the public representatives of
the party.
Among the new sections of this proposed program is
also one dealing with a practical application of Socialist
ideas to land tenure and farming. The old program de
mainly with farm labor, not with farmers.
The British Labor party has already presented
farm program in parliament, and the educational sections
of the party are seriously considering the best methods
of controlling the big banks and Industrial corporations
with a view to giving the increasing members of the party
in parliament a firm foundation for their practical ac
tivities.
The German trade union and Socialist leaders are
making efforts to train their best talent for the task of
making effective that part of the German constitution
which gives to the workers a voice and vote in the manage
ment of the industries.
