VOTE STUDY
THROWS LIGHT
ON OUTCOME
Primary and Election
of 1922 Seen
Repeating.
A comparative study of figures of
the primary of 1922, the primary of
last Tuesday and the election of
1922 forms an interesting prediction
of what will be the probable out
come of the fight in the sth congres
sional district next November.
In the primary of 1922—which
was Stafford’s last previous effort
for congress Victor L. Berger’s
complete September vote as given
in the offcial record was 8,216.
Against that W. H. Stafford in that
primary polled a vote of 20,066 —a
margin of 11,850 —far more than
double the vote Mr. Berger drew.
Change in November.
In the main election of that year,
however, the entire vote Mr. Staf
ford drew was 26,274, while Mr.
Berger was elected with a vote of
30,045. In other words, Mr. Staf
ford merely increased his vote 6,028
—while Mr. Berger Increased his
vote by 21,029.
Mr., Berger’s total vote in the
election was three and one-half
times his vote in the primary, while
Mr. Stafford’s election vote was less
than one-third more than his pri
mary vote.
In percentages it would read some
thing like this:
Mr. Berger’s increase, 350 per
cent.
Mr. Stafford’s increase, just about
30 per cent
Wards Are Striking.
This is an excellent indication of
the customary increase in Mr.
Berger’s vote of the election over
the primary in his district.
The vote becomes more striking
when individual wards are ex
amined. For instance, as the accom
panying table shows, in the first
ward, a non-Socialist ward in the
primary of 1922, Berger drew 134
votes, but in the election of 1922 he
drew 856 votes, seven times as
many. In that same ward, Mr. Staf
ford drew 1,510 in the primary, but
only drew 2,418 in the election.
The second ward, also a non-So
cialist ward, also showed an inter
esting comparison. In that ward in
the primary of 1922, Mr. Berger
drew 348 votes. He raised that
total in the election of 1922 to 1,253,
nearly four times as many. Stafford
in that primary in the same ward
drew 792, and the best he could get
there in the election was 1,146.
Also in Fifteenth.
One more ward will suffice to
give the illustration. The 15th ward,
which is also classed as a non-So
cialist ward, in the primary of 1922
gave Mr. Berger a vote of 247. In
the election that followed that pri
mary, Berger increased that vote to
1.248, nearly six times as many. In
that same primary Stafford drew
1,457 votes and could only add 600
more votes in the election.
All this explains how the primary
vote of Mr. Berger of 8,216 in that
election grew to an election total of
30,045 —which sent him to congress
—against the primary vote of Staf
ford which was two and one-half
times as large, but which failed by
4,000 in the election to reach the
total Mr. Berger piled up.
This is taken as an indication of
what is most likely to be the result
of the election in that district next
November. We must not forget that
the Socialists do not need a big
primary vote because their candi
dates are nominated by a referen
dum. A few hundred votes are suf
ficient to nominate their ticket.

REFUSES BREAD
AND WATER DIET
TEKEMAH, Neb.—Ray Carson,
young farmer who is serving a 60-
day sentence for prohibition viola
tion —the first and last 20 days on
a bread and water diet- <.oday con
tinued to refuse the bread offered
him.

cell.
He has been, in the jail since
Tuesday night and has steadfastly
refused to eat the limited fare. He
spends most of his time reading and
thus far has shown no ill effects
of his fast.
Dr. 8. Luken, jail physician and
formes^ mayor of Tekemah, today
expressed fear that Carson would
be unable to stand the strain of the
sentence. He examined Carson be
fore he was brought to the jail here
and said his physical condition
would not permit the limited diet
much less the fast that Carson is
undergoing.
Thomas Nelson, who was sen
tenced with Carson, probably will
be brought to jail today. He was
to have started his sentence at the
same time as Carson but impassable
roads made it impossible for Sheriff
Smith to drive to the Nelson farm.
The sheriff this morning again at
tempted to drive to the farm.

The quest in its voice?
Shall We, my brother, this morn,
When heaven and earth are
reborn
Weep or rejoice?
The strains of Bosh Hashana, the
New Year’s hymn, rise from a thou
sand temples today and the sound
of voices is heard calling, “Lesha
nah Tova!”—a happy new year.
The three weeks holy season of
the Jewish temple began last night,
today being the new year’s day—
the year 5687.
Rabbi Joseph L. Baron welcomed
the new year at Temple Emanu-El,
501 Kenwood Blvd., today, 10 a. m.,
with a service of rejoicing. Several
hundred attended the candle service
and heard Rabbi Samuel Hirshberg
give the final sermon of the year at
the temple last night.
At Temple Beth El. 49th and Elm
Sts., Rabbi Philip Kleinman deliv
ered the sermon last night on A New
Year, a New Life. Today’s sermon
will be For Us or Against Us, and
tomorrow's, Life’s Greatest Test.
Services will continue at Temples
Emanu-El and B’ne Jeshurun, 10th
and Cedar Sts., tomorrow, Friday
and Saturday.
Yom Hakippurim, the day of
atonement, will climax the holy sea
son, Friday, a week from tomorrow.
Special observances will last from
Friday sundown until Saturday at
sundown.
The Festival of the Tabernacles
or Sukkoth will follow from
Wednesday, Sept. 22. until noon the
next day. Wednesday and Thurs
day, the last two days of the month,
the Festival of Conclusion or
Sh’Mini Atzereth, will bring the sea
son to a close.
Jewish School
Teachers Off
Without Pay
Milwaukee Jewish teachers who
are excused today and tomorrow
from their duties to attend the Jew
ish New Year services will take that
absence as a private excuse and will
not receive salary for the lost time,
according to information received to
day from the payroll department,
school administration.
The Jewish holiday, Resh Ha
shanah, accounted for the absence
of 14 teachers from Milwaukee pub
lic schools today, and it is antici
pated that as many will be absent
tomorrow.

Mining Officials
From Superior
Guest of City
One hundred fifty mining officials
from the Lake Superior district are
guests of Milwaukee engineers to
day.
The one-day visit to this city is
part of the program *of the Lake
Superior Mining institute, which is
holding its annual convention in
Ironwood, Mich.

over the North Western road.

Earl Stockwell, former sailor at

original thought was good, Mr. Can
bee said.

MUSEUM WILL
LOAN EXHIBITS
T 0 SCHOOLS
With recent enlargements of the
school service exhibits provided by
the Milwaukee public museum, prac
tically any subject a Milwaukee
school teacher wishes to teach can
be illustrated with museum speci
mens, according to Dr. S. A.
Barrett, director.
Can Be Borrowed.
More than 50,000 lantern slides,
which, Dr. Barrett points out, can
be borrowed by any accredited local
organization as well as schools;
hundreds of feet of film, groups of
birds, mammals, metals, svoods,
floral specimens, or industrial prod
ucts are stored in a huge basement
portion of the museum, awaiting to
do service in Milwaukee public
schools.
If it is the geography of the
South seas which is being studied,
there are scenic slides; if it is early
Wisconsin history which needs
illustrating, there is a series of dis
plays on early fur trading in this
state, on Indian pottery or the lum
bering industry.
Cost Is Small.
Since there is no endowment for
this purpose, or fund provided by
the educational system of Milwau
kee, as is the case in most cities,
a small service charge which
scarcely covers the cost of delivery,
Is made for these exhibits by the
museum.
With the opening of school and
anticipation of many calls for these
various exhibits, the clerical force
of the museum extension division
is busily getting all exhibits ready.

CLOTILDA AGAIN
WINS PRIZE AND
BEARS DAUGHTER
Clotilda Phoebe Longfield has a
daughter.
Clotilda, who is owned by the Mil
waukee county institutions, Wau
watosa, won first place in the aged
cow class at the State Fair last
week, giving birth to a daughter,
Tuesday night, six days after she
had been in the show ring.
Clotilda, blue-blooded dame of
Holstein society, blames it all to
habit. Last year she also w’on first
place in the aged cow class, against
the strongest competition in the
country. Last year she gave birth
to a calf seven days after she had
been in the fair competition.
Both this year and last, Gov. J. J.
Blaine was in the ring at the time
the aged cow class was being judged,
and for two years now Clotilda has
had her picture taken and has ap
peared in moving pictures with the
governor.
But primarily Clotilda is a proud
mother who believes that her place
is in the home, the show ring be
ing only incidental.

THREE
Teachers in France Have Big Union
,100 PER CENT
MEMBERSHIP
NOWREPORTED
Confederation Urges
Fight on Morgan
Policies.
Leader Special Service.
PARIS The post-war recon
struction of the French trade unions
brought a large number of public
school teachers over to the side of
the organized workers. As a result,
the National Teachers’ union affili
ated in 1921 with the Confederation
Generalc Du Travail.
The teachers resolved through
their national convention of 1925 to
start a vigorous membership cam
paign with the aim of getting a
100 per cent organization.
They gave out the slogan: Before
the national convention of 192 G
meets, every member of the teach
ers’ union shall have a card from
the Confederation Generale.
Record Great Success.
The national committee of the
teachers did everything possible to
arouse the teacjiers to class-con
sciousness and to the value of their
organization on the\ side of the
working class.
A recent report shows that out of
a total of 90 departmental sections,
including seven In the colonies, only
one single section reports less than
a 100 per cent membership.
In addition to these, 436 cards
of the Confederation Generale were
bought by sections in Morocco, 300
by branches on Martinique island,
and 20 in Indo-China.
The total number of cards sold
was 64,050.
Gain More Members.
Although representation in this
year’s national convention was
made dependent upon membership
in the Confederation Generale, only
19 sections reported a slight de
crease in membership, whereas 31
recorded Increases and 36 reported
their memberships intact.
The French teachers’ union now
Includes the vast majority of the
elementary teachers and is in a posi
tion to take care of their Interests
in negotiations with the educational
authorities.
In a large number of depart
ments, the teachers also co-operate
with the local trade councils. They
exert a great influence in the social
life through their affiliation with
the national body of labor.
Oppose Morgan Policy.
The Confederation Generate states
In a recent manifesto that it is op
posed to the Morgan policies and
asks its member to fight especially
a recent plan to turn over the
French telephone system to the
Western Electric Co. and to Mor
gan’s banks.
It calls attention to the wide
ipread propaganda of the Western
Electric in France and pointy out
the danger of such a policy for the
French working class and the na
tional independence.
French labor protests against any
scheme of the French government
that would give to American bank
rs more power over the lives of the
Verity of Frenchmen.
W. T. Fisher Heads
Bank of Workers
CHICAGO Walter T. Fisher,
Chicago attorney and widely known
as a civic leader, yesterday was
elected president of the Amalga
mated Trust Savings bank, op
erated by 35,000 clothing workers.
He will assume his new post at
once, continuing, however, his prac
tice as a member of the new firm of
Fisher, Boyden, Kales Bell. The
Amalgamated bank was founded in
1922 by the Amalgamated Clothing
Workers’ Union and was the first
labor bank to be established in Chi
cago and one of the first in the
United States.
Its deposits are in excess of $3,-
000,000. It has a large and grow
ing foreign business. Trades unions
are strongly represented on its di
rectorate.

Europe Prosperous,
A. W. Mellon Thinks
LONDON—Andrew W. Mellon,
American secretary of the treasury,
said that he failed to see any lack
of prosperity, in referring to his
European tour in a talk yesterday
with a representative of The Eve
ning Standard, which, that newspa
per carefully notes, was not an in
terview, but “a private conversa
tion.”
Mr. Mellon, who is sailing home
Saturday on the Berengaria, has
steadfastly declined to be inter
viewed in London, as he had in
other cities where he had stopped
in his swing around rhe continent.
Ht has mads courtesy calls only
on British treasury officials.
REVOLT CHIEFS
IN SPAIN MAY
GET CLEMENCY
CHICAGO—The state of war,
decreed in Spain Sunday, when Dic
tator Primo de Rivera put his heel
on the incipient revolt among the
artillery officers, was ended yester
day, says a copyrighted disjiatch
from Madrid to The Tribune. King
Alfonso signed the new decree and
is preparing to return to San Se
bastian to continue his summer
outing.
The official communique, disclos
ing that clemency may be shown
leaders of the artillery junta’s
plot, was hailed as proof that the
crisis had ended.
Meanwhile Premier de Rivera
went ahead with plans for the pleb
iscite Sept. 11 to 13, in which the
nation will express its sentiments
with regard to the dictatorship,
which then will be three years old.
That the government is not blind to
the political capital it can make of
the bloodless suppression of the plot
is made clear when it points out:
“The government always has cor
dially received cdmplaints from the
artillery officers and has offered
generous solutions of the problems
which have not been prejudicial to
any one.”
The artillery officers obeyed a
summons of the government to quit
the barracks and return to their
homes, where they are not confined,
after a talk with the king.
Court Martial for 150.
BAYONNE, France—Out of the
2,400 Spanish artillery officers, in
cluding six generals, incriminated
in Sunday’s insubordination, 150
will be court martialed, it is re
ported here.
The professors in the artillery
school at Segovia are destined to
suffer the most severe penalties.
AGED COUPLE
DEFIES RULE OF
HOME, ELOPES
CHICAGO—Dove leaps in where
a board of directors fears to tread.
Until yesterday there was a rule
at the Altenheim (German Home
for. the Aged) prohibiting the inter
marriage of its inmates.
That rule was a creature of the
board and it was all right, but the
question whether a couple that
broke the prohibition would be al
lowed to re-enter never came up at
th j home until yesterday when Her
man Horn, 82, and Maria Leps, 77,
both Inmates, eloped and were mar
ried. So the rule becomes an issue
and must be considered.
Mr. Horn and Marla, shortly after
9 a. m. quietly packed a few belong
ings and slipped away from the
home. An hour later they appeared
at the county building and took out
a license. About the same time, the
superintendent of the home found a
letter Horn had left, stating their
intentions.
Now it was assumed last night
from the license that the aged couple
had been married during the day.
Neither had any income or savings,
it wa^ stated, and they were ex
pected back at the home.

HINT POLICE
IN ON MELLETT
MURDER PLOT
CANTON, O. —Before the Canton
civil service commission which yes
terday began hearing the appeal of
S. A. Lengel, deposed police chief,
for reinstatement, 15 witnesses were
put on the stand by counsel for
Mayor S'. M. Swarts in an effort to
show that Lengel blundered in con
ducting the inquiry into the murder
of the publisher, Don It. Mellett and
that he had intimate contact with
known law violators.
Stories Are Damaging.
All of the testimony, counsel for
the mayor insisted to the commis
sion, shows either how the deposed
chief “bungled the inquiry” or how
he had contact with the underworld
and permitted members of his de
partment to have similar contact.
John A. McDonald, motorcycle of
ficer, testified that Lengel and Ben
Rudner, one of the trio indicted for
the murder of Mellett, had a con
ference in an alley three hours be
fore the murder.
Laura Hardy, city police signal
operator, testified that although she
sounded sirens and flashed lights on
police signal boxes for 22 minutes,
beginning 35 minutes after the mur
der, only one officer answered the
signals; also, that she was unable
to locate Sergt. Vongunten, left in
charge of the department.
Tells of Auto Visit.
H. R. Fowler, neighbor to Lengel,
testified a mysterious curtained
automobile with dimmed lights and
three occupants visited Lengel’s
home an hour before the murder.
Charles Graham, a tinner, testi
fied that in his presence Carl Studer
and another man he believes was
Louis Mazer, also indicted for the
Mellett murder, talked to Max
Levin, Studer saying that Mellett
was to be “bumped off” if he didn’t
“shut up.”
Unions Vote Curb
On General Strike
BOURNEMOUTH, England—The
British trades union congress, after
wrangling for hours yesterday v cted
overwhelmingly against granting the
general council direction and con
trol of any labor struggle without
limitations.
The motion was strongly opposed
by C. T. Cramp, president of the
railway men, who said his unions
opposed giving any furthei powers
to the council.
“The moldy tradition that we can
solve our troubles with general
strikes has got whiskers which all
the razors in Bournemouth couldn’t
remove,” said Mr. Cramp.
He added that “the strike was a
success, but it was an inconspicuous
success and it had better not be
tried again.”
President Bevins of the transport
workers also opposed the motion,
which was defeated by 3202,000
votes against 848,000.

INFLUENCE IN
ECUADDR SEEN
Leader Special Service.
GUAYAQUIL The Socialist
weekly. El Faro, here, recently pub
lished a manifesto of the labor fed
eration of the Guayas district de
scribing the evil influence exerted
by the foreign bankers on the eco
nomic and political life of the state
of Ecuador.
The manifesto declares that the
bank capital of Ecuador is com
pletely in the hands of Wall Street
financiers, who by a policy of sys
tematic inflation have forced every
old party government to accept
larger and larger credits in ex
change for the most valuable con
cessions in the country.
Make Public Crisis.
The present government, however,
shows some resistance to foreign
extortions. Thereupon the banks,
under Wali Street orders, stopped
payment and brought about the
failure of many Ecuadorian busi
ness concerns.
The crisis still continues. The
industrial and commercial life of
Ecuador is in disorder. New fail
ures are of daily occurrence.
The Socialist representatives of
the Guayaquil city council have de
manded the appointment of a com
mittee to regulate price fluctua
tions. The labor unions appeal to
their members to face coming
events with firmness and confi
dence.
Colombia Also Suffers.
The labor unions in the United
States of Colombia have also taken
steps to protect their members
against the practice of foreign
money lenders who disturb the do
mestic conditions in the service of
American imperialism.
Encouraged by the example of or
ganized labor in Mexico and South
American states, the labor unions
of Colombia are demanding better
working conditions, decent quarters
for ships’ crews, and social insur
ance.

SHIPPING BOARD
STANDS PAT FOR
AMERICAN FLAG
WASHINGTON —The government
has no intention of changing its
policy to do its utmost to encourage
a privately owned American mer
chant marine and it will not sell its
ships to any but American citizens.
The United States shipping board
gave this reaffirmation of policy
yesterday in answer to the sugges
tion recently made to President
Coolidge at White Pine camp by
Matthew T. Brush, president of the
American International corporation,
that the shipping board fleet should
be sold without regard to nationality
of buyers or guarantees that the
shipping would be under the Ameri
can flag.
Commissioner Philip S. Teller,
chairman of the ship sales commit
tee of the board, issued a statement
vigorously attacking the suggestion
attributed to Brush and condemning
it as probably “a last and frantic
attempt on the part of certain in
sidious foreign interests masquer
ading under the title of American
ownership to withstand and over
come the competitive element of
ocean transportation which the
slowly but persistently growing
American flag merchant marine has
unquestionably created to the bene
fit of shippers and travelers alike.”

PHILADELPHIA, Pa. The
American Chemical society was told
yesterday that the iron age is about
to pass before the advance of the
age of alloys.
Dr. Irving Langmuir, assistant di
rector of the General Electric Co.
research laboratory, in telling of the
dawn of the new era, declared plain
metals no longer are sufficient for
the world’s work.
Have New Method.
He envisioned the day when sky
scrapers would be constructed of al
loyed steel welded together instead
of riveted.
This transformation from riveting
to 'welding, he said, will be hastened
by the recent discovery of a method
of atomic hydrogen welding, which,
he said, produces a heat capable of
welding all knbwn metals.
lodine From Seaweeds.
lodine from seaweeds as a pre
ventive of high blood pressure and
hardening of the arteries was out
lined before the Chemical society
convention.
Dr. J. W. Turrentine of the bu
reau of soils, United States depart
ment of agriculture, said studies in
government laboratories show that
excess weight of advancing years
may frequently be attributed to an
inactive thyroid gland, indicating
an Inadequate supply of iodine in
the system.
Is More Active.

seaweed was shown to be some 200

crease or restore the normal func

est that you are giving prominent
place in your newspaper to the re
production of posters submitted in
a national safety contest und also
to semi-weekly articles on safety.

important public service. The pre
vention of accidents is necessary
and entirely practicable.

the field of preventive medicine and
surgery, and untold benefits have
accrued to the people of the civilized
world because of the educational
work conducted by the medical pro
fession and the others engaged in
constructive health work. The
same results can be achieved for
safety.
It is a pleasure to commend this
support of your newspaper to the
effort to diminish the number of
preventable accidents in our city.

fered as a result of the World war.

IF 1 IS, RULE
MOBILE, Ala. A decision, re
garded as of far reaching import
ance in the matter of prohibition
law enforcement, was handed down
yesterday by the Alabama court of
appeals.
The court, in an opinion written
by Judge W. H. Samford, held that
where a party of moonshiners go
about their business armed and with
intention of resisting arrest if in
terfered with, and one of their num
ber shoots and kills an officer who
makes a raid upon them, all mem
bers of the moonshining party are
guilty of murder.
The decision was handed down in
the case of Harold T. I awrence.
Lawrence was charged with the
murder of R. W. Buckner, an officer,
the evidence showing that Lawrence
was a member of a party of moon
shiners and that Buckner was shot
in a raid upon the party.
When Lawrence was tried in cir
cuit court on the murder charge,
the case resulted in a mistrial, there
being some doubt as to whether the
fatal shot was fired by him. Law
rence was held without bail in cir
cuit court and the case went to the
court of appeals on his petition for
a write of habeas corpus, which was
today denied. He will remain in
jail until tried.

INDIAN GUIDE
SUES STILLMAN
FOR $500,000
NEW YORK—Frederick K. Beau
vais, the Canadian Indian guide
who was named as co-respondent in
Janies A. Stillman's suit for divorce,
came to New York yesterday and
announced that he was suing Mr.
Stillman for .$500,000 for libel, slan
der and defamation of character.
Offered Pay to Aid?
It was said a copy of the Sum
mons and complaint has already
been served on Mr. Stillman, through
his attorneys, who accepted service
for him.
The principal allegation in Beau
vais’ complaint. Atty. A. S. Rosen
thal said, describes an alleged offer
to the guide of .$250,000 if he would
consent to aid Mr. Stillman in his
efforts to get a divorce from Anne
U. Stillman, which the guide re
fused.
How, He Figures It.
Beauvais contends that the un
favorable publicity he received from
the divorce suit, in which Mr. Still
man sought to prove that the guide
was the father of Mrs. Stillman’s
son, Guy, has caused him to lose
money, since people no longer will
employ him and shun him as a
“home breaker.”
$4,000,000 Left to
New York Charities
By J. L Kane Widow
NEW YORK—Bequests to charit
able institutions aggregating nearly
.$4,000,000 were made in the will of
Mrs. Annie C. Kane, widow of John
I. Kane, which was filed for probate
yesterday. The residue of the es
tate, the value of which is not
stated, is left to the executors for
distribution to charities as they
may determine. The total estate is
estimated at $10,000,000. The only
bequests to relatives, except persoh
al effects and real estate at Bar
Harbor, are SIOO,OOO each to two
cousins, Fannie Marie Cottenet and
Rawlins Lowndes Cottonet. Real
estate at Bar Harbor, with house
furnishings and objects of art, goes
to Peter Augustus Jay, nephew of
John I. Kane.
Two bequests to Columbia univer
sity of $500,000 each are provided
for, the first being a permanent
fund in memory of Mrs. Kane’s
father, William C. Schermerhorn, to
be used for religious instruction,
and the second an outright gift
without limitation as to its use.
The Home for Incurables likewise
gets $1,000,000, on condition that a
part be devoted to the erection of a
building for the treatment of incur
able cases of cancer.

ideal breakfast for school children,

ered undernourished letters to the
parents asking that the pupils be
given more nourishing food.

FATE OF OHIO GANG TOLD IN
SPECIAL ARTICLE IN THE NATION
NEW YORK —What has become
of all of the members of what was
known as the Ohio Gang during the
Harding administration, is told by
Edgar Mels in a recent issue of The
Nation under the title Fate of The
Ohio Gang. The article follows:
“Fate and the Ohio Gang.”
By Edgar Mels.
Flanked by cohorts of press
agents and captained by their
leader, Harry Daugherty, the Ohio
Gang swooped down upon Washing
ton in the spring of 192 b. The
Best Minds took office and estab
lished a record of inefficiency, graft,
and political thieving that will prob
ably never be fully exposed Much
of it is lost beyond recall; more is
buried deep in mountainous re
ports of senate committee hearings.
The law has been slow to move
against the political adventurers
who pillaged the public till during
the Harding regime, although a few
are behind bars. And, as was
pointed out in The Nation for July
28, the oil scandal is forgotten while
the men involved still evade justice-
Dead, 111 or in Jail.
But if the mills of men have been
slow in their grinding, the mills of
the gods have ground both fast and
fine. Death, who knows no party
and is susceptible to no influence,
has gathered an amazing crop
among the members of the Ohio
Gang. With very few exceptions
every notable member of Harding’s
retinue of personal friends in office
is ill, dead, in jail or under indict
ment.
Let us begin at the top. Warren
Harding, riding along Pennsylvania
Ave. to take the oath of office, lit
tle dreamed that within three short
years he would die. Amiable, lik
able, a weak man for so great an
office, a good country editor and
a negative senator, Harding was
the tool of the Ohio Gang. Person
ally honest, he permitted the gang
to do as it pleased. Only when
Howard Mannington grew reckless
did Harding assert himself. He or
dered Mannington to leave Wash
ington.
Son Is Accused.
Daugherty, the real commander of
the Harding administration, is in
failing health. His case is being
tried now. His son, Draper, who is
accused of having shared in the en
terprises and profits of the gang,
has been in a sanitarium, from
which he was recently released.
Jesse Smith, Daugherty’s best friend
and collector (so termed by Daugh
erty himself), died in a mysterious
manner In Daugherty’s apartment in
the Wardman Park hotel in Wash
ington. That he did not commit
suicide is my belief. He knew too
much about the inner workings of
the gang. His doom was sealed and
he paid the price.

EUROPE NEVER
WILL DISARM,
OBSERVER SAYS
CHICAGO—Every nation at the
preliminary disarmament conference
at Geneva is seeking to disarm every
other nation, but has no intention of
disarming itself, says W. B. Shearer,
expert on naval affairs, in a copy
righted dispatch reprinted by The
Tribune from The New York Times.
Shearer has been watching the
Geneva conference and now is on his
way home. “Tell America just what
bunk this disarmament is,” he said.
“Only the United States is really
pleading for disarmament,” Mr.
Shearer said. “We gave the spec
tacle to the world in 1922 of the vol
untary surrender of our naval su
premacy, and we now are trying to
give more away, even though every
one knows there have been virtual
repudiations by all the other powers
of the 5-5-3 agreement.
Taking No Chances.
“There is not any European power
or nation willing to make any sacri
fice which would jeopardize its se
curity. Every one of them knows
that if it is to survive it must lie
prepared to defend itself and none
knows that better than England.
As frankly as can be done the Brit
ish have let everyone know they will
never disarm at sea, and no one who
considers for a moment not only the
character of the British empire bur
the chaos which would follow aban
donment of her sea supremacy ever
thinks of blaming her. England
without a fleet -would have the alter
native of starvation or surrender.
Germany “Playing Possum.”
“On the continent it is just as much
the duty of France to hold her posi
tion of authority as it is for Eng
land to do it on the sea. There al
ready is an armed ring being drawn
about France, challenging her au
thority and seeking to curb her
power by cutting her off from food
and man supplies from her African
empire.
“Germany is playing possum, but
no one doubts her ambitions and her
intentions.”

meeting since the summer vacation.

clared no decision has been given by

reau, favored the type of safety

paving, and opposed the erection of

mended that the district attorney’s
office be authorized to prepare a bill
through which Milwaukee can get
legislative authority for such traf

OLD ARSENAL;
CITE HISTORY
PITTSBURGH Allegheny Ar
senal. center of Pittsburgh’s war
activities since 1814, today was
placed on the auction block.
The historic landmark, viewed by
all important personages who have
visited Pittsburgh since the days of
Lafayette, will go to the highest bid
der, its usefulness having disap
peared.
The Old Pile of Masonry was
never’ the scene of battle action, but
was the site of one of the disasters
of the civil war. Seventyfour chil
dren, 70 of them girls, were killed
there when engaged in making cart
ridges for use by the union army.
Several buildings in the arsenal
were demolished by the terrific ex
plosion, but were soon rebuilt.
When the United States entered
the World war in 1917 and Pitts
burgh became one of the centers of
munition manufacturing, the arsen
al was utilized as a warehouse. The
war ended, the arsenal was leased
for commercial purposes, and it will

After passing through Tromso
Sound, I reached Tromso, which is
beautifully situated on an island of
the same name. Considering how
far in the north of Norway, the
little place is, it is wonderfully
prosperous with good buildings and
suburbs. Some of the most graphic
descriptions of Nordland and Nord
land life, are those given by Jonas
Lie, the famous Norwegian novel
ist. He spent the most impression
able years of his life in and around
Tromso, where his father was sher
iff. “If there is a home for a won
derfully beautiful idyll,” he writes,
‘‘it must be in the fjord villages of
Nordland in the summer time. It
is as though the sun kisses Nature
all the more lovingly because he
knows how short a time they have
to be together. ‘Even the great
Nansen, when his good ship Fram
on her way to the Polar Seas,
passed by the coast, he said, “It
is unique—a fairyland—a land of
dreams. We felt afraid to go on too
fast for fear of missing something.”

praise. So when the University of

is good, it is certain that the praise
is well deserved.
The approaching meeting of

kle” was a player who never got

nois team of 1914.

CHICAGO—Who is entitled to h<
called the dean of baseball? In
vestigation shows that no one now
prominently connected with the na
tional pastime has a better claim
to the title than has Toe Cantillon,
who today reaches the Goth mile
stone on his journey through life.
But Pongo doesn't boast of .he
honor. In fact, he is a trifle touchy
on age, or the use of the word,
“veteran.”
Nevertheless, the records show
that this is Cantillon’s 47th year in
baseball. Either as a player, um
pire or manager, Joe has been con
tinuously before the fans for nearly
half a century. He was playing be
fore any of the present-day stars
saw the light of day. His services
antedates that of the veteran John
J. McGraw, New York, or any other
major league pilot and about equals
that of Owner Comiskey of the Chi
cago White Sox, a man who forsook
the diamond to become a vested
magnate many years ago. In fact,
long after Commy had his private
office and had hung up his gilt
sign, Cantillon dug up pennant after
pennant with his spiked shoes on
the first base coaching line.
Best Known in A. A.
Cantillon’s fame, however, has
been confined almost entirely to the
minors. Before going south to be
come manager of the Little Rock
Southern league club his chief field
of operations had been the middle
west and it was in this territory
that he achieved his greatest dia
mond victories.
The American association knew
him best of all. For many years he
piloted the club in Minneapolis, re
turning to that city from 'he man
agership of the Washington Ameri
cans, when he and his brother Mike
bought the franchise. His stay in
Washington was comparatively
brief and his success about parallel
to that of other managers who tried
to land a winner for the national
capital in the early days.
Quits As Umpire.
When time had decreased his
usefulness as a player Cantillon
never left the park, so to apeak. He
tried managing, then umpiring, but
the latter job twisted his viewpoint
until he found his mind working
against his heart. So he dropped
the arbiter’s role and resumed as a
pilot—the job in which he has ever
found the most satisfaction.

NEW YORK—With only 16 games
to go, the St. Louis Cardinals held a
three-game lead over the Cincinnati
Reds in the National league pennant
fight today tnd were odds to win
the pennant.,

double-header from the Reds,
moved to within three and one-half
games of the Cardinals and were
in third phee only half a game be
hind Cincinnati. The Pirates, vir
tually counted out of contention
after their recent slump, attacked
the Reds savagely and put renewed
hope in their supporters that they
might yet snatch the victory.
Play Two Today.
Both the Cardinals and Reds are
idle today, and Pittsburgh, by beat
ing the Chicago Cubs in the scheduled
double-header, can move Into second
place and gain a full game on the
Cardinals.

to play, against 16 for the Cardinals
and 18 for the Reds. Only one of
the odd breaks of baseball, by which
the Cardinals might slump and the
Pirates play perfect baseball, could
give Pittsburgh the penuant. If
both teams win every remaining
game, St. Louis still would have the
pennant by a full game.

FOURTH HORSE
IN RACE IS
WINNER
NEW YORK —A weird ruling in
the steeplechase at Belmont park
yesterday overshadowed the run
ning of the historic Matron stakes
in which H. P. Whitney’s Pantelia
galloped to easy victory and added
$18,275 to her earnings.
Four horses started in the steeple
chase and it turned out to be a trav
esty. Amstello, the odds-on favorite,
unseated his jockey at a jump on
the back stretch when far out of it.
Lady Jacquenetta, running in the
colors of Al Davis, popped over the
various jumps in an unschooled way
and was beaten 50 or 60 lengths by
Oyster Bed and Bonnacourt, which
ran in the interest of the Winburn
stable.
Bonnacourt made all the running
by a wide margin, but at the home
turn ran outside a beacon so that
his stable companion came along to
win easily. Then to the consterna
tion of hundreds in the stand Bon
nacourt was disqualified for running
out of the course and Oyster Bed
was disqualified with him. This
gave the purse to Lady Jacquen
netta.

[FAMOUS CATCHES
An athletic event is like almost
everything else in life —there’s a
catch in it somewhere. There are
catchers in baseball who are looked
upon with great favor by their man-
Bagers, and there
are “catchers” in
boxing whose
managers would
be glad to get rid
o f at a dime
a dozen. Then
again there are
certain catches
that stand out
above others,
either because of
some unusual or
important incident
connected with
_ them.
Fe K Murray. gueh catch
was Harry Hooper’s, in the last
game of the 1912 world series be
tween the Giants and the Red Sox.
Hooper’s great feat came in the
sixth inning when he made a back
ward leap against the outfield fence
to grab Doyle’s apparent home run.
And it was in the tenth inning that
Snodgrass made his famous muff of
Engle’s fly. The catch that Fred
missed was as famous as the one
that Harry made.

has the happy faculty of keeping
his name in the public prints, went
out to Mitchel field on Long Island
and caught a baseball dropped by
Capt. H. F. McClelland at an alti
tude of about 250 feet. The Babe
failed on his first six attempts at
higher altitudes, and it isn’t to be
wondered at, as the plane was
traveling 100 miles an hour.
“Brick” Muller, famous All-
American end of the University of
California, caught many footballs
in his gridiron career, but none that
went so far as the one dropped to
him from the top of a tall building
in San Francisco last year.

made a record catch this summer,
when he hauled in a 582-pound
broadbill swordfish after a five
and a half hours’ struggle at Cata
lina island. That broke the record

and regulation 24-thread line were

SAYSJONES
By The United Press.
LOS ANGELES—Howard Jones,
veteran gridiron mentor and now
head coach of football at the Uni
versity of Southern California, ex
pects to see more kicking in the
games this fall than in those of past
seasons.
“The new forward passing rule,
prescribing a five-yard penalty for
two unsuccessful passes in the same
sequence of downs, will not mate
rially effect passing,” the former
lowa mentor said, “but it will bring
about more and better kicking.
Other Changes Slight.
“Quarterbacks generally dislike
to call for a kick on the third down
and usually with eight yards or less
to go they won’t. It’s a different
proposition, however, when the
scoreboard shows third down and
13 or more to go, as it frequently
will with the new pass penalty.”
With the exception of the addi
tional kicking and the continued de
velopment of the forward pass at
tack, Jones believes there will be
very little change.
The Pacific coast will continue to
play a brand of football that will
compare favorably, if not actually
excel, that played in the east and
mid-west, the coach said.
“Four Pacific coast teams must
be included in any rating of the 12
best elevens in the country,” said
the man who guided lowa to two
Big Ten conference championships.
Coach Jones expects Dartmouth
and Notre Dame to have the strong
est teams in their respective sec
tions, of the country. Washington,
California, Stanford and Southern
California will be the leading elev
ens in the Pacific conference, he
predicted.
Has Strong Team.
The Trojan coach regards Stan
ford, California and Notre Dame as
the toughest encounters on the U.
S. C. schedule.
Jones was traditionally reticent
about discussing the prospects of
his own team.
“We should have a better team
than last year,” he said, “with 21
letter men, of w’hom 19 were with
me last season, on the squad this
year. But we have a tough sched
ule.”

PHILADELPHIA—With the
greatest chance a foreign team has

cup away from the United States,
France, with a fine team of young
sters was to play a veteran Ameri
can team in the opening matches of
the greatest classic of tennis at the
Germantown Cricket club this aft
ernoon.
The concern of the United States
Lawn Tennis Assn, over the real
danger of the French threat and
the disposition to take no chances,
was indicated when Billy Johnston,
the star little Californian, was nom
inated to open the challenge round
against Rene La Coste, one of th®
three aces on the invading team.
Johnston’s Game Better.
When Vinnie Richards, the young
New York star, was ranked as No.
2 player under Bill Tilden in the
seeding of the draw for the na
tional championships which start at
Forest Hills, Monday, it was sur
mised that he wpuld be selected to
play in the singles instead of John
ston.
But the wise minds of the tennis
association figured that Jobnston’a
game was best suited to beat either
Borotra or La Coste and that Rich
ards and Williams would.be Amer
ica’s best bet in the doubles. The
French team (doubles) has not
been announced and will not hav«
to be named until late this after
noon.
Johnstone and La Coste will ba
followed by the second singles bat
tel between Bill Tilden, national
champion, and Jean Borotra, the
w T ell known “bounding basque.”
Deny Pro Jump.

would join Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen
and Miss Mary K. Browne on C.
C. Pyle’s professional troupe were
laughed off by the French players.
La Coste wouldn’t talk about it,
but his teammates pointed out that
he was in tennis for the sport of it,
that his father is a millionaire au
tomobile manufacturer and that
money is no inducement to him.
Tilden, who also has been men
tioned as a possibility, refused to
comment. “I said several weeks age
that there were possibilities in open
or professional tennis,” he said,
“under proper supervision and man
agement and if the right kind ol
players were engaged in it. That’s
all I have to say now.”

SYNOPSIS.
Diane Colfax is the only daughter,
IS, of Miriam Colfax, whose philosophy
of marriage Is that ‘‘a girl who car
ries a man without money Is just
throwing her life away." Mrs. Colfax
harps upon this subject to the tolerant
amusement of her daughter whose
beauty and amiability draws many ad
mirers. Freddie Tyler is Diane’s latest
conquest. He has Invited her to go
riding with him, but her mother for
bids because he is poor and unimpor
tant.
The Beauty That Was Diane’s.
The only reason that Diane Col
fax was not vain and wilful was
that her Inherited common sense
had shielded her from the temp
tation to take too literally her
mother’s valuation of her femi
nine charms. Ever since Diane
had entered high school five years
before, she had been to almost
everybody, “the prettiest girl in
town,” and she hated it. She had
hated it when she was a
youngster and just as persistently
as the name stuck to her, just so
persistently did she resent it.
And she resented more than n y _
thing else the painfully obvious
fact that her mother gloried in
her fame.
Diane possessed elusive beauty,
hard to definitely set down on pa
per. It was a friendly sort of
character which drew people to
her and the longer one knew her
the more one was confused by her
myriad charms. She had devel
oped beyond the very slender,
boyish stage and there was a hint
of maturity in her suave figure.
Her complexion was perfect and
her abundant good health gave
her an air of wholesomeness. She
wore her chestnut curly hair in
the modish French bob fashion,
and although many of the other
girls in her set attempted to imi
tate her they succeeded only in be
coming not disagreeable carica
tures.
Diane, as somebody once said,
“was tremendously effective with
out being the least bit affected.’’
There were four of the Colfax
clan and the only time in each 24
hours when it was certain they
might be found together, was at
the dinner table at a little before
7 o’clock, and even then the fourth
and ■wholly irresponsible member
of the family, Master Bichard
Gaillard Blodgett Colfax, could
not be counted upon. He was
pretty sure to turn up ar some
time during the course of the
meal with elaborate explanations
accounting for his tardiness, such
as only a 12-year-old boy can
muster.
Judson Colfax was a very
youthful husband and father so
far as the externals went. He
was a tall, slender and rather so
ber looking man with hair gone
prematurely gray and with a cu
rious habit of speaking of the
most commonplace things as if
they were tremendously exciting.
One could never tell just how to
take Jud Colfax. He was one of
these men of whom you always
think as being brilliant and quite
wonderful. He had a personality
that won a great many friends,
not always friends of the right
sort. This trait was but one of
a number of conspicuous charac
acteristics to which his daughter
had fallen heir.
Jud Colfax had walked out of
college in his senior year to elope
to a nearby Gretna Green with
beautiful and vivacious Miriam
Blodgett, nearly 20 years ago. He
had been 21 and the starry-eyed
Miriam only 17.
Many were the predictions of
dire things to come to the newly
wedded couple. Jud had no mon
ey and apparently no resources.
“We’ll get along somehow,” he
told his bride, his blue eyes snap
ping with self-confidence. “I
know one thing—l’m never going
to worry.” And Jud Colfax never
had. He had obtained a job in

quisitively.

Diane’s father clucked sympa

She pretended to be scornful.

anda.
Diane kept her rendezvous with

store.

higher, making the chair alto

A young woman who has
charge of the physical education
of a group of girls, but apparent
ly has not had the proper training
for her position, writes that
smallpox has been prevalent in
the vicinity and there has been
some talk of having the girls vac
cinated. Is vaccination worth
while, she asks, or is it, as she
believes, a humbug? She says of
course she has no medical reasons
for her belief but she “under
stands” that quite a number of
doctors share her views.
A serious fault with the pio
neer physical education program
at present being established here
and there about the country is
that the school authorities ar
ranging the program do not com
prehend the value or importance
of this part of a common educa
tion, and so they are prone to em
ploy Instructors who have not
been properly trained. The school
boards are inclined to look upon
physical education very much as
they generally look upon “physi
ology and hygiene” in the com
mon school—it is a matter of no
importance, rather a farce to be
carried along to please a few nuts
in the community. That is the
view the average politician educa
tor takes of these subjects. That
is the explanation for the com
mon practice of designating any
old teacher who has some spare
time as the “physiology” teacher
—no matter’ at all if the teacher
hasn’t the lirst notion of what
physiology or hygiene means. It
is all the bunk anyway. If the
taxpayers want to pay for it, ’let
’em have a good imitation
they’ll never know the difference.
From the context of this young
woman’s query it seems that she
is going to have something to say
about the question of vaccinating
the girls who are unfortunate
enough to be under her incompe
tent charge. Certainly she did
not learn in any reputable or rec
ognized school, normal school or
college that vaccination is a hum
bug. She derived that notion
from bad reading—reading fake
physical culture publications and
other shady or disreputable mag
azines—magazines which are cir
culated to carry all the rotten ad
vertising to the gullible reader.
I am an opponent of compulso
ry vaccination. I believe this
country is now sufficiently liter
ate, or rather the population is,
to understand plain words. Let
the state advise vaccination for
everybody and provide the vac
cine for the purpose and give the
best assurance it is possible to
give that the vaccine is suitable
for the purpose. Then let the
people be vaccinated or not, as
they prefer. Personally. I like to
keep well vaccinated and to keep
my loved ones well vaccinated.
I advise every parent to see to it

Leukoderma.
You have several times referred to
a skin condition known as leukoderma,
which I understand is a loss of the
pigment from spots in the skin. Would
such a condition be likely to be in
herited from a mother who has had
it in several patches for five years?
(Mrs. F. L. C.)
Answer—No. The cause of the loss
of pigment from the white patches is
unknown, but there is no evidence that
the condition is heritable.

find of any value. The wiser course
would be to leave such difficult tech
nical matters to the judgment of your
physician.

It is at the country club dance,
at the hotel ball or informal danc
ing hours at the seashore or moun
tains that youth really comes into
its own. Consequently it is the
summer dance frock which should
receive the utmost attention from
the girl planning a summer time
wardrobe.
The debutante frocks of greatest
charm are usually fashioned of
chiffons and are most alluring in
pastel tones.
With many evening gowns show
ing a princess tendency in line, it
is important to recall that a flare
generally lies at the end of the
fitted gown. The summer evening
gown must flare and flutter in its
silhouette.
Many frocks of chiffon, designed
along slightly bouffant lines, to suc
ceed the popularity of winter time
taffeta robe de style, are gracefully
flaring in chiffon and feature trans
parent hems of tulle and are worn
over a brilliant slip of silver lame.
Other gowns which possess a
graceful flare use flounces to
achieve their results, while others
employ shirrings which begin at
the hem and end above the knee,
leaving a full and often irregular
hem line at the bottom.
Dorothy Mackaill, whose clothes
are remarkable in their simplicity
and modishness, has selected for
the summer months a dancing
frock of youthful charm and ap
peal. It is of pale rose chiffon,
snug as to waist and full as to
sides, featuring tiers of flounces
down the side and a princess effect
in the front. Rhinestones rupply
the note of brilliance in dainty
floral patterns. A scarf is formed
in bertha effect in front and trails
gracefully down the back. Miss
Mackaill is seen in many stunning
and interesting outfits in the First
National film, “Subway Sadie.”

SEX APPEAL OF
DANCE FOE OF
SERIOUS DRAMA
A most human individual is head
lining the Palace Orpheum bill this
week; a man whose preciseness in
speech would lead one to believe
him almost curt, were it not for an
almost eveready smile and a laugh
that is as hearty as it is infectious.
And, perhaps, what is even more
attractive, is his natural sense of
humor and his fund of information,
impressions, stories and what not;
things wl)ich he lives and acts and
enjoys again for your pleasure.
Seated across the dinner table
from Taylor Holmes last night, the
writer and his host, Robert A.
Burns, author of the Jury Woman,
found the “going” easy, listening to
oen of the best known stage stars of
the day.
With the talk naturally turning to
“shop,” Mr. Holmes found time to
lament the present day influences
which are having a hampering ef
fect on the drama.
“Dancing is by far the most dan
gerous foe of the legitimate,” de
clared Mr. Holmes as we lit cigar
ets and prepared to enjoy the lake
breeze.
David Belasco Knew.
“The youth of today can take his
girl out to a public dance hall and
for less than a dollar bill he can
dance, talk and make love to his
heart’s content. Why should he pry
himself loose from a $lO note to
see a show in which there is little
or no sex appeal, which is the dom
inating factor in modern life?
“And a play must have sex ap
peal if it wishes to get anywhere.
Such has always been the conten
tion of David Belasco and his suc
cesses prove the truth of his asser
tion that ‘to take the element of
sex out of a production, is to re
move all interest in that offering.’
“Not only the dance, but the ‘mu
sical leg shows’ have been a thorn
in the side of the really worth while.
The good plays on Broadway right
now' are hard pushed to exist while
mediocre musical shows are turning
’em away at every performance.”
Refreshments here interrupted
the chat, but the conversation
veered back again to the discussion
of plays.
“There Is hardly any money in
farce these days,” went on Mr.
Holmes, whosf principal successes
were comic mystery plays and
comedy.
Nervous Wreck Recalled.
“The trouble with a farce is that
it fails to hang together throughout
the entire show. A play must re
volve around an idea. Take The
Nervous Wreck, for instance. It
had an idea. There was a chap
who wanted pills; who had to have
them and who was genuinely angry
when he did not get them. There
are thousands like him; men and
women to whom their fancied ills
are real worries.”
And Taylor Holmes should know,
for The Nervous Wreck was one of
his best achievements to take rank
along side of Seven Chances, The
Rear Car, Smooth as Silk, The
Hotel Mouse with Frances Starr,
Tomorrow’s Price and, last but not
least, No! No! Nanette, in which he
has just finished a 76-week run on
the coast.
It was Mr. Holmes' rendition of
Kipling’s Boots that made A. H.
Woods give him the chance in To
morrow’s Price, which established
him as a serious actor of parts, just
as His Majesty Bunker Bean put
him on top in the comedy world
some eight or nine years ago.
Mr. Holmes recites Boots and
and tells many stories over at the
Palace this week, although not as
many as we heard last night. And
even a stalled auto didn’t faze
him, though it temporarily halted
the journey back to the Palace
later. —J. P. C.

an orange. Bake in layers and ice

remaining whites until stiff, add
powdered sugar, the juice and grat

is thick enough to spread.

cherries and seedless raisins with
preserved orange and lemon peel
mixed and cut into shreds. Fold
in gradually one pound (four cup
fuls) of flour. Bake in a well
greased paper-lined tin for three
hours. If carefully packed in tin
this cake will keep for months.
Alhambra Bonbons.
Chop very fine in a meat chopper
one-half cupful of blanched al
monds and one-fourth cupful of
seeded raisins. Mix with one to
one and one-half teaspoonfuls of
honey or maple sirup to make a
paste that will roll into balls. Roll
in granulated sugar and cinnamon
or in chopped almonds. This may
be used as a bonbon with halves of
walnuts.
Fudge.
Take two cupfuls of sugar, one
third of a cupful of corn sirup, one
half cupful of milk, one tablespoon
ful of butter, two squares of choc
olate or the same amount of cocoa
—less if not liked so strong. Boil
to. a soft stage, cool before stirring
then beat until creamy. Adding
other flavors, nuts or dried fruit,
will make a different fudge.—Nellie
Maxwell.
Tomatoes and Eggs.
Grease muffin tins. Put one thick
slice of unpeeled tomatoes into each
tin. Season with salt and pepper.
Break one egg on top of each slice.
Again season with salt and pepper
and put a small piece of butter on
top of each egg. Bake in oven un
til egg is set, but not hard. Serve
on rounds of toast and garnish with
parsley.
Corn Pudding.
Put one quart of fresh corn cut
from cob, one teaspoon salt and one
quarter teaspoon pepper, three eggs,
slightly beaten, two cups milk, three
tablespoons melted butter into
greased baking dish and bake in
moderate oven until firm.
Green peppers stuffed with rice
and hamburger: Cut tops off of
green pep)pers, scrape seeds out.
Make mixture of hamburger, one
chopped onion, salt and pepper to
taste and a little rice that has been
parboiled. Fill peppers with this
mixture and put in baking dish,
cover with tomatoes (canned) or
tomato sauce and bake one hour or
until done or cook on top of stove
in a large stew pan very slowly.
Keep covered until done. Serve
hot.
A new salad which is being served
on the summer roofs in New York
is of alligator pear, pineapple and
tomatoes. It sounds queer, but is
really delicious.
Swiss Chicken.
Prepare chicken as for frying,
and roll each piece in flour which
has been seasoned with salt and
pepper in heavy frying pan. Heat
two tablespoons lard and one of
butter. Brown the pieces of chick
en in the hot fat. When all have
been removed from the pan, put
two tablespoons flour in the fat and
stir until slightly brown, then add
one and one-half pints of sweet milk
and stir until mixture thickens.
Pour this over the chicken and add
more seasoning If necessary. Bake
slowly in covered dish until tender.
Red Pepper Preserves.
Cut real fine. Soak in weak salt
water over night. Have pan of boil
ing water ready and lift peppers out
of salt slowly into the boiling wa-
ter. Let boil until tender. Have
ready the thick syrup. After the
peppers have drained well lift them
into the boiling syrup and let boil
up well and can. For thick syrup
use one part water and one part
sugar.

HOW TONSILS CAUSE DISEASE.
BY ELMER HESS, M.D.,
Erle, Pa. Member Gor gas Memorial
Institpte.
Focal infection means a spot in
the human body which is infected
with disease germs.
When this infection and its by
products can escape easily from the
tissues of the body, there is little
chance for damage to other parts
of the body.
If these poisons can be thrown off
at their source, the patient is usual
ly not in danger. But if the foci
of Infection cannot be thrown off,
the body tries to handle them to
the best of its ability.
The blood picks up these poisons
and the white blood cells try to de
stroy 1 the germs. As a result of
this battle between the germs and
white blood cells, the kidneys are
overtaxed.
If the kidneys cannot eliminate
these poisons satisfactorily, and the
blood becomes overwhelmed, then
something happens in the other
organs. The tissues of the body
most susceptible to damaging influ
ence from these poisons are the
joints, the kidneys, the heart and
blood vessel walls.
Besides the tonsils, the most com
mon location for these foci of infec
tion are located in the teeth, sinuses
of the head, gall bladder, appendix,
prostate gland in the male and Fal
lopian tubes in the female.
Today let’s consider the tonsils.
When healthy they are of no danger
to the system. In childhood they
catch and destroy much infection
that otherwise would get into the
system. But they are dangerous or
gans after they, themselves, become
infected; because from them, often
as a starting point, these serious gen
eral conditions arise.
Therefore, every diseased tonsil is
a dangerous tonsil. It has been
said, and rightfully so, seldom does
one reach adult life with healthy
tonsils. Does this mean that every
tonsil in an adult should be re
moved? Not at all.

Fruit Salad With Cheese Straws.
Six slices pineapple, two large red
apples, two-thirds cup sliced
peaches, one cup white grapes and
12 maraschino cherries Use one
slice of pineapple for each serving.
Core apples but do not peel. Cut in
thin slices leaving some red peel
on each. Skin and seed the grapes.

crisp lettuce leaf. Combine the oth
er ingredients in order given, then

ing made of equal quantities of
mayonnaise dressing and whipped

straws with this salad: Cheese

butter, two cups flour, one teaspoon
baking powder. Put flour,* baking
pow’der, cheese and butter together
in a bowl and mix thoroughly with
hands to a smooth paste. Cool on
ice. Roll very thin, cut into long
narrow strips and bake in hot
oven. To get uniform straws, the
dough can be forced through a pas
try tube before chilling. This
makes about four dozen straws.
These straws are also nice to give

against Deere Co. by the Moline
Implement Co. of Moline, successor
to the Moline Plow Co. Slander and
violation of the Clayton anti-trust
law are charged. One suit filed in
the United States district court asks
$300,000 damages on the grounds
that Deere Co. entered into con
tracts with its dealers by which, they
were required to agree not to handle
Moline products. The other siiit, filed
in the state court of Missouri, al
leges circulation of false statements
reflecting upon the financial condi
tion of the Moline Implement Co.

sumers of steel see the continuance
this fall of their activities through
this month and next at the rate of

its weekly review of the industry.

would turn out to be nt the expense
of fall business,” the review de
clares. “Counting theoretical ca
pacity at 56,000,000 tons a year,
June was an 80 per cent month,
while in July there was a decrease
to 78 per cent. Present estimates
of August run from 81 to 84 per
cent with indications of a close ap
proach to the 84 per cent of May in
finished steel products.

that rail inquiries in considerable
volume will come out this month.

ducers of steel In the Chicago dis
trict show that in the first fight
months of this year sales of rolling
mill products were 13 pc J cent more
than in the like period of 1925 while
shipments were 12 per cent more
this year. Due to the slow develop
ment of railroad programs, west
ern freight car works are on the
verge of a shutdown.

ite is unchanged, standing at. $19.46

ORGANIZATION
SALE HOPE FOR
FARMERS, VIEW
PHILADELPHIA—OnIy through
organization can agriculture be ade
quately synchonized with the eco
nomic fluctuations of the nation, ac
cording to Oscar G. Mayer of Chi
cago, president of the Institute of
American Meat Packers, who presid
ed today at the session of the Amer
ican Congress of Industry.
“The agricultural problems of the
individual farmer are inseparable
from the current problems of agri
culture in general,” Mr. Mayer said.
Sympathy Not Altruistic.
“A corresponding situation in in
dustry has led to the trade associa
tion movement. If industries are or
ganized, there is even more reason
why agriculture should be. It is a
fact, however, that the greater need
is accompanied, is even accounted
for, by greater difficulties.
“My sympathy with farm organ
ization is not altruistic; it is prac
tical and is based on business rea
sons. Organization means system;
lack of it means lack of system. If
the agriculture which underlies pur
industry is disorderly, the industry
itself will have elements of disor
der. If it is organized, the industry
may find its situation and its trends
becoming increasingly orderly.
“From the farmer’s viewpoint and
from the viewpoint of the disinter
ested observer, there are other rea
sons why the farmers should be or
ganized. In that way they can help
themselves, and they should help
themselves. We should help them
also, just as they should help indus
try with its problems.”
“I can understand the attitude of
the industrialist who says that he is
opposed to the McNary-Haugen bill
or any other specific legislation
looking toward farm relief, but I
cannot understand the industrialist
whose attitude is solely one of op
position.”
“If agriculure is asked to interest
itself in the economic problems of
industry, then industry should feel
an equal obligation to interest itself
in the economic problems of agri
culture. I hope all industrialists
will take this view.”
Co-Op Bill Presented
To Aid Farmers
PAUL SMITH’S, N. Y.—Officials
of the American Farm congress, it
is learned, have presented to Presi
dent Coolidge and 50 or more con
gressmen, the draft of a bill de
signed to aid farmers by co-opera
tion. The measure, it is stated, is
along similar lines to the Fess bill,
defeated at the last session of con
gress.
The bill was presented at the
summer white house today by W.
I. Drummond, Kansas City, Mo.,
chairman of the farm congress.
He gave the principle contained
in the proposed measure as “keep
ing the initiative with the farmers
by permitting them to retain con
trol of selling surplus farm com
modities through co-operatives
which the government would
finance but not run.”

TRUST GUARDS
SELFRIDGE’S
NEW YORK —“I regard my busi
ness as a great public trust. I want
to leave all my affairs in order
when I die, so that the business can
go straight on. That’s why I’m
forming a £2,000,000 ($10,000,000)
trust to take over a share of the
capital of the firm of Selfridge’s.”
This statement was made by H.
Gordon Selfridge, formerly of Chi
cago and founder of the great Amer
ican department store in London,
says a copyrighted dispatch from
London to The Times today. The
shares in the new trust are avail
able for subscription today. They
are 1,000,000 6 per cent cumulative
preference shares of a pound sterling
each and 100,000 one pound sterling
ordinary shares. Purchasers of pref
erence shares will be able to take
one ordinary share for each 10 pref
erence shares. Offers for ordinary
shares alone will not be accepted.
“I have been feeling for some
time the necessity of making some
such disposition,” said Mr. Selfridge.
“I want to know that, whatever
happens, the business which I
founded and into which I have put
so much of myself will go on. I
should like Selfridge’s, naturally, to
remain in the family, but I do not
want to feel that, if one of my de
scendants is weak and incapable of
administration of this great firm it
will go down with him. The trust
provides against that.”

western Michigan hit a lucky streak
this year in their fields, orchards,

tures. Lack of gracing in Muskegon

NEW YORK Another railroad
consolidation battle was begun yes
terday before the interstate com
merce commission. The contestants
are the three great eastern trunk
lines, the New York Central, the
Pennsylvania and the Baltimore
Ohio, and the prize is control of the
Lehigh New England, which is
the trunk line gateway to New Eng
land.
Officials of the Reading railroad
are seeking permission to lease the
Lehigh New England for 99 years
at $1,069,000 a year. But the Read
ing is owned by the New York Cen
tral and Baltimore Ohio, and so
the Pennsylvania is putting up a
fight against its chief competitors
getting control of the New England
gateway.
The Reading officials argued that
their plan will afford a new and
more direct route into New England,
especially for the movement of coal.
The Pennsylvania officials coun
tered with the argument New Eng
land traffic would be facilitated
equally well by a joint traffic^ ar
rangement over the Lehigh New
England by all the roads and that
the Reading plan of consolidation is
unnecessary.

terday for a five weeks’ tour of its

NOW FOR NOVEMBER
A New England nurse examined a boy who was so
absurdly healthy that he had to answer No to all of her
questions as to whether he had had chicken pox, measles,
scarlet fever, whooping cough, et cetera. He thought he
was placing himself at a disadvantage in making negative
replies to her questions, so he eagerly volunteered the in
formation, “I have had chiggers I”
The men and women who voted the straight Socialist
ticket on Tuesday are the only ones in Wisconsin who are
in the pink of political condition. They haven’t even had
chiggers.
The primary crippled the Madison machine badly. It
will not be working well from now on. Those who sup
ported it at the primary should now be able to see that
they have been deluded.
The reasonable thing for good citizens to do now is to
work for the success of the entire Socialist ticket—for the
Socialist candidates for United States senator, congress,
the state offices, the legislature, the county offices.
We must send Socialists to congress from both the
fourth and fifth districts. We must increase the number
of Socialists in the state legislature. We must elect a So
cialist sheriff. The Socialist candidate is neither a fanatic
nor in league with the underworld.
Nearly two months remain before the election. The
old party candidates for the various offices will sow the
state knee deep with propaganda. Don’t let them fool you.
Remember that they are only after the offices and that
they have no principles back of them. Talk it over with
your associates and help us to restore sight to the blind.
PUBLIC OPINION ON CRIME
IS VERY BACKWARD
A Chicago paper collected a number of interviews
from its readers regarding the desirability of paroling
Leopold and Loeb from the penitentiary some time in the
distant future. Most of the replies did not indicate any
conception of the real nature and purpose of “punish
ment.”
The boys should be kept there until such time as they
would be good citizens if they were released. And it might
take a bevy of disinterested psychologists and psychia
trists to discover when that time comes.
There is always a cause of crime. Perhaps some men
have such bad inherited and acquired qualities that they
might have to be isolated from the main body of society
permanently. But most of them could be cured of the
criminal tendency by the proper treatment.
Hitherto and at present the idea of society has been
asd is to punish the criminals.
This idea of punishment is all wrong. It certainly
has failed to get results. Most criminals are repeaters.
Arbitrary punishment merely made them still more sore
at society and converted them into confirmed criminals,
when they could just as well have been reclaimed and
made over into good citizens. To say nothing of the fact
that this would be the humanitarian thing to do, it would
also be the economical thing to do.
The present attitude of society toward violators of
the law is savage. True, it is slowly changing—and that
is encouraging. But punishment is still uppermost in the
treatment of prisoners, and it is getting the most rotten
results.

Tony Sender in U. S.
Comrade Miss Tony Sender will
lecture throughout the United
States under the auspices of the
national office, v Socialist party,
during the fall months. Any or
ganization that wishes a date
should get in touch with national
headquarters at once so that
their dates may be placed in line.
Miss Tony Sender, youngest
member of the German reichstag
and considered the most beautiful
woman member of any legislative
body in the world, who is one of
the most striking figures in Euro
pean political life, is now in the
United States on a speaking tour
for the Socialist party.
Miss Sender represents Frank
fort in the German national par
liament. although at the last elec
tions she was elected from two
districts at the same time, the
other being her native Dresden in
Saxony. She was elected to the
first parliament after the German
revolution when she was barely
21 years old and she has served
continuously since 1919. Before
that, at an age when most girls
have no more serious thoughts
than clothes and parties and good
times, she had played a highly
significant part in the drama of
the German revolution, having
been the leader of the revolution
ary committee of the soldiers,
sailors and workers in Frankfort
am-Main.

A native of Saxony, Miss Sen
der was living in France in 1914,
where she was an active worker
in the Socialist party despite her
extreme youth. Her principal ac
tivities were in the direction of
peace and understanding between
France and Germany. Upon the
outbreak of war, however, she
was expelled from France, and
she threw’ herself with all the
energy she possessed into the So
cialist movement in Germany,
working feverishly for the end of
the war and the overthrow of the
monarchy. She aligned herself
with the Independent Socialists,
the larger faction of the Socialist
movement in Germany and the

For the last two centuries, historians have said that
the British ruling class always knows when it is time to
deflect a violent revolution by making concessions to the
middle and working classes.
We shall now be able to watch this axiom put to the
test. When the Labor government was permitted to seize
the reins of governmont, it looked as if the old axiom was
right. But recent developments in the coal crisis make it
doubtful.
The British Tories have never before been challenged
to a fight that means complete abdication, if they lose it*

revolution of the capitalist class. Its concessions then
meant a longer lease of power for it.

ers leaves no hope to the Tories for a longer lease of power

interests, regardless of -whether this means falling below

foreign countries will be negligible. American promises
have lost a good deal of weight since the Dawes plan am
the allied w r ar debt settlements.

pledges. All of them claim to be arming only so far as
the national defense demands it. The question as to what
size the armies, navies and air forces must be, in order to
guarantee effective defense, always ends in the assertion
that the best defense is the attack.
I It is much easier to conceal the number and quality
of submarines, airplanes and war chemicals than that cf
the big army, navy and air units. And so long as Amer
ica sends out armed forces on imperialist errands to for
eign countries, it is well to realize that a defense of
American interests does not .nean merely a defense of the
United States main land.

Establishment of excess fare
zones at the city limits on all
street car lines was suggested to
the state rail commission today as
being the only means of relieving
Milwaukeeans of bearing the bulk
of the burden of the cost of furnish
ing street car service to outlying
communities which are opposing an
nexation.
The suggestion was made by Atty.
Henry Disch, who with Aid. Paul
Gauer, Socialist, 17th ward, ap
peared as representatives of the
Bay View Advancement Assn, at a
public hearing held by the commis
sion in city hall to determine senti
ment relative to the establishment
of one-man car service on the Oak
land-Delaware car line.
No Protest at Hearing.
Mr. Disch’s suggestion came when
Atty. Charles R. Hammersley, repre
senting the village of Shorewood,
requested that the single fare zone
on the Oakland-Delaware line be ex
tended from Atwater road to the
north village limits.
The Electric Co.’s request for a
permit to operate one-man cars on
the Oakland-Delaware line prob
ably will be granted, as no protesta
tion was made to it at the hearing.
R. H. Pinkley, assistant general
manager of the company, was the
only person to testify relative to the
proposed order for the one-man cars.
He pointed out that the Oakland-
Delaware line has the lightest traf
fic, of any lipe in the city and that
the introduction of the one-man cars
■will permit a reduction of the inter
val between cars during non-rush
hours of from 7% to (J minutes.
An Unfair Burden.
Mr. Disch’s suggestion that the
city limits be established as the one
fare limit in all cases, he declared,
is based on the economic unfairness
of Milwaukeeans bearing the bur
den of suburban street car service.
“Suburban lines, available sta
tistics show, seldom pay operating
expenses, and are kept up by the
lines that feed them from the city,”
declared Mr. Disch.
“It is plainly unfair for the street
car riding public of Milwaukee to
bear the burden of furnishing one
fare service to these outlying com
munities which are constantly fight
ing annexation. The equitable
method of adjusting this would be
to establish the city limits as the
limit of one fare transportation on
all lines.”
The hearing was conducted by C.
M. Larsen, chief engineer of the
commission.

BY WILLIAM WELLARD.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
ST. MARGARET’S BAY, England
—Georges Michel, veteran French
swimmer, broke the English channel
swim record here early today when
he completed the crossing in II
hours and fix minutes.
Having left Cape Gris Nez,
France, at 8:32 last night, Michel
splashed ashore here at 7:38 a. m.,
conquering the channel within eight
minutes of the goal he set for him
self.
Michel lowered the record set
Aug. 30 by Ernest Vierkotter, a Ger
man, who swam the channel in 12
hours and 42 minutes.
It was Michel’s 11th attempt to
make the crossing.
Tells His Story.
En route to Folkestone, Michel
told his own story of the swim, de
claring that champagne helped him.
“My official time was 11 hours,
and 5 minutes,” he said. “I was
ill twice. About 1 a. m. I became
very seasick. Then at 3a. m. I got
cramps and felt terribly cold. The
sea was calm except the last two
hours.
“Champagne helped me. I took
two drinks.
“I also ate two lumps of sugar
soaked in cognac and coffee. I ate
nothing else. I feel fine now. I’m
glad I took the record for France.
“I was in the artillery during
the war, perhaps opposite Vierkot
ter. lam going to the consulate be
cause I have no passport. I’m like
a prisoner of war,” he added
laughingly.
Is Former Champion.
Michel is about 45. He is the
former French distance swimmer.
Most of his swimming has been
done in the Seine, though he often
has attacked the channel. He
trained ■with Bill Burgess before
Burgess swam the channel in 1911.
Michel is unmarried. He is a huge,
broad-shouldered powerful man.
