j MINE STRIKER VIEWS REFUTEDj
(The following is another letter
from Mrs. Doris Berger Welles to
her parents, Congressman and
Mrs. Victor L. Berger. Other
letters from Mrs. Welles on the
British coal strike and the Labor
party in England and Scotland
will follow.—Editor.)
LOSSIEMOUTH, ON THE NORTH
SEA, SCOTLAND, Aug. 16.
Somewhere I have an orderly list
of all the things I must tell you.
Perhaps it would be better to get it,
but, as a matter of fact, it’s too com
fortable here in the garden over
locking the sea to bother. I’ll tell
you in the order I remember.
First there was Cambridge.
I stopped at that point before, I
think. It was enormous fua, though
it rained considerably. The most
beautiful lacy Gothic buildings,
crumbling and vine-covered, with
ancient courtyards and impressive
old towery gates. It was utterly
beautiful. The church at Kings col
lege was the best, I think, of any
thing we’ve seen—delicate, slender
arches—tall and exquisitely inter
laced, and at the end gorgeous radi
ant windows. We were stricken with
the beauty of it.
Tea at H. G. Wells’.
After we returned to the Labor
school at Easton Lodge there was a
fancy dress party. Cynthia Mosley
wore helter skelter things, and sang
Negro spirituals exceedingly well.
The next day I can remember only
one thing of—tea and tennis at the
H. G. Wells’—the famous writer—
and an excursion through their
house, which Is very, very lovely.
But first—-H. G. Wells himself. He
looks like his pictures, only much
less certain. His wife, who Is slight,
and self-possessed by dint of sheer
determination and practice, took a
seat at the head of a table in a dear
little summer house in their burst
ing garden.
The conversation dealt chiefly
with certain boys’ schools, and
wasn’t very profitable for me from
the point of view of an interview.
But I was altogether tongue-tied
and much too scared to venture
more than a syllable now and then.
After that they played tennis. He
proved to be surprisingly active for
one of his years.
Mr. Keynes Comes.
The next day came John Meynard
Keynes, the famous economist, who
resigned as the British expert in
Versailles because he considered the
Versailles treaty impossible. He has
a pale statistician’s face, with nice
surprising blue eyes.
He spoke that night at the Labor
school. There was quite a rumpus.
He’s a liberal whose economics are
quite in accord with those of the
Labor party, but whose attitude is
hopelessly at variance because he
refused to apply these economics as
they do.
For instance, he agreed that,
economically speaking, the mines
were being subsidized —whether the
government gave a certain sum of
money outright, or whether the
miners’ wages were cut or their
hours lengthened. But the thing
that aroused the summer school
group was that he said the wages
were quite high enough, and it was
better to subsidize the industry
(since it is obviously in need of
some subsidy) by cutting wages
than by a government fund.
Mosley Refutes Keynes.
Mr. Mosley spoke first—a most
stunning sort of talk, in which he
ironically pointed out that Keynes
talked like a Marxian but his propo
sition was that of Adam Smith. He
was definitely not on the side of the
worker.
Then Pat Dolan spoke—just
diving into Keynes and recommend
ing a fortnight’s work in the coal
mines. And others talked too—all
much in the same vein. Finally H.
G. Wells rose and suggested, with
more persuasion than I had seen be
fore, that the summer school was
being fanatic and boorish, and that
as for himself he’d enjoyed Mr.
Keynes’ speech and was quite in
agreement with it. Wells was aca
demic, but somewhat well taken for
all of that.
The evening ended with a fine
speech of Pat Dolan’s bidding us
farewell and sending warm and
friendly messages to papa in
America—about whom he said some
very nice things.
The next day we drove to London,
had lunch at the Cheshire Cheese
(the famous old coffee shop where
Samuel Johnson regaled the think
ers of his day), then went off to
see the London Tower and West
minster Abbey.
American Socialist Stand Praised.
Aug. 17.
I forgot to tell you about the
league of nations argument we had
at Easton, at the end of which Pat
Dolan made a tremendously good
speech for the attitude of the Ameri
can Socialist party which has re
fused its Indorsement fit the last
national convention. Pat is a great
fellow—and always I wanted most
heartily to indorse what he said.
I made a speech of a few words on
it —I was scared as a rabbit.
Just as we left Easton Lodge the
Countess of Warwick showed me
her rooms—made from the stables
of past glorious days, since the War
wicks have lost much of their
money.
In fact, all of England seems to
me infinitely theatrical, which ob
servation is probably as penetrating
as that of the old lady who found
Shakespeare so full of quotations.
But every now and then I’m shocked
into incredulity by hearing some
one say to a butler or footman.
“Bring her ladyship’s cloak, Dodds.”
It’s enormously comical to me.
Meeting of Miners.
At the meeting of miners, which
was held in an open field and at
tended by about 1,000 persons, the
Mosleys were hailed with the most
heartening enthusiasm.
And their speeches were corking.
Mr. Mosley used every possible
phrase—every known appeal, to stir
them and to hold them —and in the
end they were wildly enthusiastic.
Then Cynthia Mosley spoke more
quietly, but with most convincing
and sound sense, and for whom
there were spontaneous words of ap
proval and admiration from the
crowd. Mosley appealed to them to
stick it out—since they were the
leaders of a glorious battle for all
workers in every country—and the
forerunners of a new era which
promised much for the present and
everything for the future —all in the
hypnotic manner of a born exhorter.
Cynthia Mosley told them that
they had two weapons—the eco
nomic and the political—and urged
their use of both.
Live on Bread, Potatoes.
Most of the men wore scarfs about
their necks and were pale. But
their shoes were blacked and
around the group was a fringe of
women jiggling perambulators.
After the meeting we went to the
home of the organizer who told us
that for the most part the men were
living entirely on bread and pota
toes, and that slowly they were
going back—which made it more
fiercely difficult still, for those who
stuck. The organizer said that in
their spare time they paint and
write poetry and do similar aston
ishing things. Around the walls of
his dining room were some surpris
ingly good pictures—done by one of
them.
In Birmingham Mr. Mosley is a
hero. They adore him—and they
are quite wild about Cynthia. I’ve
never seen a much better reception.
The sort of enthusiasm papa was
received with just after the trial.
But mind you, this wasn’t even
an election.
MacDonald in Difficult Position.
Last night we all went out, and
when we returned, there was a
packet of Milwaukee Leaders left
by MacDonald for me, and lo—on
the front page, the story about the
investigation of some cribbing at
the Wisconsin bar examination,
which interested me greatly, of
course.
He’s quite striking looking—
MacDonald is. Gray mustache and
clear eyes and sinuous build. And
he’s quite devoid of any affectation,
though he’s obviously very proud—
proud of the days of his power,
and his position as leader.
At present he’s in a difficult posi
tion. There is a group of younger
men—Mosley, Strachey, Plummer,
Wheatly and others, who are forc
ing the movement always “more to
the left” —not the kind of wild and
uproarious left we have in America,
but to a less compromising attitude
than that of MacDonald. They have
the rank and file with them. All
of. them are spirited and able talk
ers, and running the radical press.
It leaves MacDonald pretty much
between the devil and the deep blue
sea.
MacDonald Reads Milwaukee Lead-
er Regularly.
At the picnic he told us he read
The Milwaukee Leader every day—
not the whole of it, but the Find
ings and the editorials. He asked,
laughingly, what The Leader would
say of him if he visited Guggenheim
when he went again to the United
States, and I responded that we’d
razz him tremendously.
He reminisced about one thing or
another. He is serious, not witty
like Dolan.
To our amazement Cynthia Mos
ley told us he really meant it when
he spoke of being a Presbyterian—
and that as a matter of fact, he
does go to the severe gray “little
kirk” in Lossiemouth every Sun
day.

LAURA KNIGHT
CHOOSES STAGE
FOR HER ART
In an exhibit by Laura Knight,
celebrated English artist, hung this
week at the Milwaukee Art insti
tute, 456 Jefferson St., a woman’s
keen Interest in how the other half
of the world lives, seems to center
around the dramatic.
Fully one-third of the 82 etchings,
aquatints, lithographs and drawings
of Miss Knight being shown have
for their subjects those behind the
footlights or under the big circus
top, and into these she pours the
wealth of her flare for character,
and her knowledge of line and anat
omy—a knowledge and skill in han
dling of w’hich she is surpassed by
few.
Studies Are Intimate.
Her studies are intimate ones,
even when she draws the crowd, of
which she also is fond. By means
of very few lines, and incomplete de
tails, she yet achieves an astonish
ing feeling of movement.
Every figure she suggests becomes
a character under her skillful brush
or pen. A dressing room, intricate
by reason of its very sketchiness,
becomes alive and vibrant from
wardrobe mistress to the dancer in
the background.
Nomore scrupulous care to anat
omy could be found than in Sleep
ing Dancer, every muscle of whose
lithe little body is relaxed.
Colors Less Interesting.
In Youth and Age, Miss Knight
again show's her thorough knowl
edge of anatomy, contrasting as she
does in every line and feature, the
inroads which time makes upon the
visage of age.
Miss Knight Is a good draughts
man, filling her spaces admirably.
She inclines to the modern and at
all times seems very sure of the ef
fect which she wishes to achieve.
Aug. 18.
Least interesting, perhaps, are
those few sketches in which color Is
employed, her use of which seems
almost photographic rather than
imaginative.

the tribune. Whereas the German
stuck close to the written text of his
speech, Briand spoke extemporane
ously. The applause for the French
man exceeded that for Stresemann.
As he moved forward to ascend the
rostrum, Briand paused by the Ger
man seats and cordially greeted
Stresemann.
“No more war and no more suffer
ing hereafter with our international
differences,” the French statesman
said. “We will go before the courts
like private individuals. France has
no more further need of heroic dem
onstrations than has Germany, and
in the future we will work together
like brothers. I don’t mean to say
that all differences and difficulties
have been settled, but that hereafter
we will settle them peacefully.”
Following this, Sir Austen Cham
berlain, British foreign secretary,
led the principal delegations in a
handshaking procession past the
German seats.

SOCIETY QUEEN
WRITES EXPOSE
OF 'SMART SET'
•NEW YORK—Mrs. Philip Lydig,
urst wife of the late W. E. D.
fitokes and mother of W. E. D.
Stokes, Jr., to whom bis father left
the bulk of his vast fortune, piib
liely declares that the greatest social
menace of the day is the example of
immorality set by the rich and fash
ionable comprising the so-called
“smart set’’ of New York.
Boni to Purple.
By birth Mrs. Lydig, who. as a girl,
was the beautiful Rita D’Acosta, in
herited her own high social position
which she has maintained through
the years in New York city. A wom
an of the widest culture, an art ex
pert, extensively traveled, with an
acquaintanceship compreheding the
great of Europe and America for
the past 20 years, what she now de
clares is indeed startling. This first
expression of Mrs. Lydig’s opinion
of the smart society of which she is
a part appears in the form of an
article in the October issue of The
Red Book magazine, entitled Mar
riage Without Love.
In the course of her article, which
will inevitably be the chief topic of
discussion over eastern teacups for
days to come, Mrs. Lydig does not
hesitate to open dark closets in the
houses of smart society ami drag
forth into the glare of daylight the
skeletons that have been hidden
there.
Among other stories that she re
lates is one of a recent young and
fashionable bride, who was told by
her husband’s physician that if she
did not cause him to lessen his
drinking he would be dead in a year.
“Leave it to me,” replied the bride;
whereupon she made it her business
to see that on the table beside her
husband’s bed there was placed each
night a bottle of whisky. The man
died of alcoholism in less than the
time prophesied, and his bride in
herited his great wealth. “Clearly
a case of murder,” declares Mrs.
Lydig.
Another of the skeletons she re
veals is of the domestic life of a
man and woman of the highest N6w
York society, which was believed
generally to be the happiest in all
the smart set. Yet when the wife
was told by her physician that she
had cancer, and doubtless would not
live six months, she gave a luncheon
party in celebration at Sherry’s and,
bidding her guests goodby, withdrew
to the top floor of her sth Ave.
house and never emerged therefrom,
dying in a few months, “and glad to
go,” says Mrs. Lydig.
Has Caused Sensation.
Altogether, nothing more sensa
tional relative to New York’s rich
and fashionable has ever been told
by one in a position really to know.
In justification of her action in pub
lishing her article Mrs. Lydig says:
“All over America people are watch
ing the conduct and ideals of the
fashionable rich —the so-called
‘smart set’—of the east. I believe
that those ideals are false ideals,
tragic ideals, which it is disastrous
for America to imitate. The convic
tion is my justification for pre
paring and publishing this reveal
ing series of articles on the futility
of fashionable life.”

A MOUNTAIN UNDER THE
EARTH.
In the course of my wanderings I
have often found myself in the
bowels of the earth, not only in coal
and salt mines, but in the famous
caves of Kentucky and the Crystal
caves of Bermuda, which latter
might also be said to be under the
sea, but I still reserve a praise I
give to no other, for the wonderful
Grottoes of Han in Belgium. Not
only are they the most remarkable
caverns in Belgium, but some of
their chambers adorned with count
less stalactites and stagalmites, are
among the lovelist under the earth.
In the chamber known as the Salle
du Dome, 500 feet long by as many
broad and 430 feet high, is probably
the most wonderful known to man,
with a lake at one end and a lofty
hill or underworld mountain at the
other, at least it looked that way
to me in the mysterious artificial
light of the cavern. When in Bel
gium seek out Rochefort for its 20
minutes’ car ride to the Grottoes of
Han, with as much enthusiasm as
you seek for the battlefield of M a
terloo. It is a trip that will pay
you quite as well.

CHIEF TO LEAD

PEKING —War has been declared
by Marshal Sun Chuan Fang, ruler
of the five eastern provinces of
China, on the Canton government,
whose troops have been invading his
territory, it is announced in dis
patches from Ranking, capital of
Marshal Sun, in Kiangsu province.
His Territory Invaded.
Marshal Sun reached his decision
to enter the conflict for control of
central China in which Marshal Wu
Pei Fu, central China leader, is bat
tling the Bolshevik Cantonese, after
his Kiangs! province had been in
vaded by the southern armies. He
is said to be preparing to take the
field personally in command of his
troops.
It is estimated that two weeks
will be required to place the desired
50,000 men in the field.
Decision of Sun to take part in
the struggle on the side of Wu Pei
Fu has relieved the anxiety of the
latter’s allies here.

King Strips Rank
From 8 Artillery
Generals in Spain
MADRlD—Reduction of the num
ber of artillery generals from 18 to
10 was ordered yesterday in a royal
decree issued as the result of the
revolt of artillery officers. This
order is understood to be a compro
mise measure, Gen. De Rivera hav
ing desired the dissolution of the
artillery corps entirely, while the
king was opposed to such a drastic
•tep.
Eight artillery generals will lose
their rank and the artillery will be
taken from the direct command of
artillery officers.
Beginning of End?
HENDAYE, France—“The recent
.uprising in Spain marks the begln
ning of the end of Primo de Rivera’s
power,” Prof. Miguel de Unamuno,
leader of Spanish intellectuals, said
yesterday.
“The artillery unrest, although
without political foundation, showed
that the king is nothing but a pup
pet in the hands of Primo de Rivera
and his clique,” Unamono said.
“The artillery officers had the
king’s promise. That is why they
rebelled, but Anido made the king
withdraw his promise and that is
why the movement failed.”
Even Insect Bite
On Prince’s Arm
Is News for U. S.
LONDON—A Daily Mail dispatch
from Biarritz says the Prince of
Wales’ right arm is considerably
swollen and quite painful as a re
sult of bites inflicted upon his
hands and arms by insects, possibly
mosquitoes or the more poisonous
sand gnats.
The prince consequently was un
able to play golf yesterday.
A physician is said to have dress
ed the arm, but the doctors attend
ing the prince do not believe the
poisoning is serious.

to an ultra-democratic country like
Uruguay.

Leader Special Service.
OSLO Negotiations are under
way for the amalgamation of the
Norwegian Labor party with the
Socialist party. The principal dif
ference between them is the fact
that the Norwegian Socialist party
is a member of the Socialist inter
national, whereas the Labor party is
not affiliated with any interna
tional.
This difference is no longer a
question of principle, however, but
mainly a question of one man’s im
portance. The present leader of the
Labor party, Tranmael, who was
formerly the secretary of the united
Socialists, joined the Communists
after the war and has always at
tacked the Socialist international.
It is thought that Tranmael will
have to be dropped before a union
of the two parties can„be achieved.
Communists Lose Out.
The efforts to reunite the two
wings of the Socialists reach back
several years. They began in 1922,
soon after the Norwegian Labor
party had refused to join the Mos
cow international.
Since 1922 the Labor party, whose
members comprise the majority of
the Norwegian trade unions, has
been compelled to fight the Commu
nists with the help of the Socialist
party.
The Moscow propagandists were
gradually defeated, and as the Com
munists continued to split among
themselves, Communism in Norway
has been reduced to a negligible fac
tor.
The Labor party is today the
strongest political party in parlia
ment and in the labor unions. The
Socialist party holds second place.
The Communists lost their hold in
the last municipal elections.
The recent municipal elections
forced the Labor party to co operate
with the Socialists, and their rep
resentatives in parliament have long
been compelled to stand together
against the old parties.
The main issues which still sep
arate the two parties are interna
tional. Aside from their difference
concerning affiliation with the So
cialist international, the principal
obstacle to collaboration is the re
fusal of the Labor party to indorse
the league of nations and to vote
funds for delegates to It.
This implies, of course, also a re
fusal of the Labor party to work
with the international labor bureau
of the league in Geneva.
In domestic politics, their only
real difference is over the military
question. The Labor party demands
a transition from a standing army
to a militia, whereas the Socialist
party demands complete demilitar
ization.
Union Must Come.
However, these issues do not
play any important role in present
Norwegian politics compared to eco
nomic questions. Norway does not
play an important role in the league
of nations, and the payments to the
league’s labor bureau are small.
The military differences between
them are mainly theoretical, because
the leaders of both parties under
stand that neither the organization
of a militia nor demilitarization are
possible w’ith the present composi
tion of parliament.
So far as the Socialist Interna
tional goes, the Norwegian Socialist
party thinks that the Labor party
■an express its owns views! nside it
as well as outside.
Conditions push strongly toward
a reunion c-f the two parties. It
is hoped by the majorities on both
sides that unity can be achieved
soon.

THE MILWAUKEE LEADER, FRIDAY, SEPTEMBER 10,
RICH TREASURES
FOUND IN GREEK
BEEHIVE TOMB
CHICAGO Further light has
been thrown on the origin of “the
glory that was Greece” by rich
treasures found in a beehive tomb
near Dendra this summer by a
Swedish archaeological expedition,
according to a copyrighted story in
The Tribune.
Hellenists agree that the discov
eries of this expedition, which for
several years has been engaged in
pushing back the hands of the ciock
of Greek history, are the most im
portant In Mycenaean archaeology
since the gold cups of Vaphio were
found in 1889. The expedition’s re
port on its work this summer has
just arrived in London.
The village of Dendra is at the
foot of an acropolis crowned by the
ruins of the Homeric fortress of Mi
dea, which, with the citadels of My
cenae and Tiryns, composed the fa
mous trinity of Mycenaean castles
in Argolis.
The beehive tomb contains four
chambers.
In one of the chambers lay two
skeletons, one of a man and the
other of a woman, who are called by
the excavators “king and queen.”
The skeletons were surrounded by
objects placed there by relatives
3,000 years ago. Both lay out
stretched on beds of clay.

DIVORCE FROM
FRENCH FLIER
CHICAGO —The Parisian divorce
court yesterday cleared away the
wreckage of one of the most bril
liant post-war romances when it
granted the former Consuelo Mat
maker’s petition for divorce from
Capt. Charles Nungesser, famous
French flying ace, who emerged
from the war with a ton of medals
and almost no limbs, according to a
copyrighted Paris story in The Trib
une.
Mme. Nungesser, who is a
daughter of the late J. R. Hatmaker,
confidential secretary to Cornelius
Vanderbilt, asked for a separation
oil the grounds of “incompatabil
ity.” The petion was filed last Oc
tober, although »the pair had not
been living together for months be
fore that. There are no children.
The girl, who figured in New
York ahd Paris society; married the
French hirdman in the English
church at the Brittany resort of Di
nard, in 1923.
Capt. Nungesser had worse luck
than all the French aces who sur
vived. Often he had to be lifted
into his plane during the war. One
leg and one arm were shot off, as
well as his chin, all of which were
replaced artificially, with the result
that the heroic get-up—uniform and
dozens of medals—in which Capt.
Nungesser appeared at his wedding,
masked the tragic wreck that was
more a mechanical doll than a hu
man being.
Mme. Nungesser is living with her
mother, Mrs. William Waters, at
Biarritz.

INDEPENDENCE
reader Special Service.
TOKIO The Pan-Asiatic con
gress which met in this city during
August was attended by delegates
from most Asiatic nations. Prom
inent among them where duly ac
credited leaders of Nationalists so
cieties in Turkey, Persia, India,
Siam, China and the Philippine
islands.
The Japanese government did not
permit the congress to hold public
sessions all the time, but it did not
stop the delegates from entering
the country and holding meetings
closed to the public for the discus
sion of delicate subjects.
Many Japanese delegates at
tended, mostly men of democratic
leanings. Some European and Amer
ican visitors were admitted to the
meetings, and European press cor
respondents treated the affair
seriously.
Demand Their Independence.
The dominant note of the Pan-
Asiatic congress was the demand
for national Independence. This
was voiced most emphatically by the
East India and Chinese delegates,
who stressed the need of close
solidarity between all Asiatic na
tions in defense against the foreign
imperialists.
The Chinese delegates pointed oiit
that East India was the strategic
base of foreign imperialism in Asia
and that all Asiatic nations would
benefit if the British could be driven
out of India.
Nearly all the proposals made at
the congress were adopted unani
mously. It was decided to establish
a Pan-Asiatic news bureau with a
view to sending out reliable in
formation about events in Asia and
counteracting the propaganda sent
out by European and American
agencies.

CRAVE DANGER
-IN PROPAGANDA
SEEN DY SOLON
We Expect Honest
Debts Paid, He
Says.
WASHINGTON —Current clamor
here and abroad for cancellation of
Europe’s debts to the United States
may be traced in large measure to
the “subtle, strong and well financed
propaganda” of American banking
and manufacturing interests, accord
ing to Senator Pat Harrison, Demo
crat, Mississippi.
So grave is the danger of the
propaganda, the senator, just home
from a tour of the continent, be
lieves, that he would have every can
didate, Republican or Democratic,
who favors cancellation, repudiated
by the voters.
Hits Baker Move,
“It’s hard to wake up the people
to the danger of cancellation,” de
clared Senator Harrison. “They as
sume the loans were made in good
faith and they assume that their
representatives in congress will pro
tect their interests.
“But when such fellows as New
ton Baker, who is well known in
Europe as a former secertary of war,
advocates cancellation, and Mr. Ed
munds, editor of The Manufacturers’
Record, accepted as the mouthpiece
of American manufacturers, advo
cates cancellation, and Frederick
Peabody of Boston asserts openly he
is going to organize to bring about
cancellation, it encourages Europe
to believe its just obligations may
be avoided.
Must Act Soon.
“The time has come for us to
stand up and tell the world that we
expect honest debts to be paid. If
this goes on much longer, and if
France falls to agree to the debt set
tlement terms which she herself pro
posed, I would have the president
immediately prohibit the visaing of
nny passports to France until such
time as France does agree.
.“And I don’t believe the American
legion should even consider holding
its convention in Paris next year as
long as the existing feeling in favor
of cancellation and against the
United States continues in France.”
Big Yearly Loss.
The senator asserted that it is not
generally understood that cancel
lation of the debts would mean the
loss to the treasury of approxi
mately $200,000,000 annually which
are now being received from those
countries whose debts have; been
funded.
And he took advantage of the op
portunity to point out that those
who are urging cancellation most
Rigorously are outstanding advo
cates of a high protection tariff, who
realize, he said, that the failure to
cancel will provide a strong argu
ment for a downward revision of
the tariff.
Tariff reductions will be neces
fcary, he declared, If debtor nations
having no gold are to be permitted
to pay their obligations by sale of
their products in the United States.

U. S. BEHIND IN PEACE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
Will Europe forge ahead of the
United States in basic, constructive
work for the abolition of war?
Word has come within the past few
days that 70 persons of prominence
in public life, representing 14 of
the most important countries in the
world, have signed a manifesto urg
ing the league of nations to pro
pose the abolition of. military con
scription to the nations that belong
to it.
Among the signers of this anti
conscription manifesto are Bertrand
Russell, H. G. Wells, Georges Du
hamel, George Lansbury, M. P.; Al
bert Einstein, Romain Rolland, M.
K. Gandhi, Arthur Ponsonby, M.
P.; Norman Angell, Henri Bar
busse, Margaret Bondfield, Edward
Carpenter, Miguel de Unamuno,
Count Harry Kessler, Rabindranath
Tagore, Annie Besant, Paul Lobe,
president of the German reichs’tag;
Ellen Key, Lady Marion Parmoor,
England; Lord Parmoor, L. Ragez,
Switzerland, and Helena M. Swan
wick, England. Names of citizens
of the United States do not appear
because our country is not a mem
ber of the league.
The manifesto was published on
Aug. 29 in the principal countries
of the world, and was given to the
public of the United States through
the Women’s Peace Union, 180 Lex
ington Ave., New York city. It
criticises conscription as making
wars more likely because it pre
pares the minds of people for war’s
possibility and makes them regard it
as occasionally inevitable. Also it
attacks conscription sharply on
moral and ethical grounds. It says
in part:
“By the universal abolition of con
scription, war will be made less
easy. The government of a country
which maintains conscription has
little difficulty in declaring war,
for it can silence a whole popula
tion by a mobilization order. When
governments have to depend for
support on the voluntary consent of
their peoples they must necessarily
exercise caution in their foreign
policies. By the universal abolition
of conscription we can take a de
cisive step toward peace and liberty.
“Conscription involves the deg
radation of human personality and
the destruction of liberty. Barrack
life, military drill, blind obedience

SMASH ALIBI
OF VESTRYMAN
IN HALL CASE
SOMERVILLE, N. J.—The most
startling development since the
Hall-Mills murder inquiry was re
opened came late last night when
Ralph V. Gorsline, a vestryman of
St. John the Evangelist church in
New Brunswick, broke down after
11 hours of police questioning and
confessed being in De Kusey’s lane
with a woman the night of the mur
ders.
Girl Is Quizzed.
Late yesterday afternoon, un
known to Gorsline, Katherine Ras
tall, whom Gorsline claimed he es
corted to her home in New Bruns
wick on the night of the crime, was
also brought in and questioned. At
midnight both Gorsline and the girl
were being held incommunicado, al
though no formal charge had been
preferred against either.
The break in Gorsline’s alibi
came when at the end of more than
10 hours’ quizzing he stubbornly
persisted in his original statement
of how he spent the evening and
night of the tragedy in which the
Rev. Edward Wheeler Hall and his
choristor sweetheart, Mrs. Eleanor
Mills, were slain.
Suddenly Inspector Underwood
snapped a paper across the table.
He ordered Gorsline to read it. The
document purported to be a state
ment signed by Miss Rastall in
which she admitted having been
near the scene of the murders with
Gorsline.
Admits Hearing Shots.
The tall, gaunt vestryman stif
fened in his chair. He stared at
the signature which the police in
sisted was that of Miss Rastall.
With an air of dejection Gorsline
threw the paper down and cupped
his chin in his right hand and
gasped out:
“Well, that’s right. We were
there. We did hear the shots. But
aside from that neither of us knows
anything. We did not see who fired
the shots. We don’t know who
killed Dr. Hall and Mrs. Mills.”
Following the vestryman’s break
down, the state police officials set
tled down to an all night siege. It
was evident they regarded the two
witnesses as of vital import to the
inquiry.

ALDERMEN TO
TAKE PAY FI6HT
TO HIGHER COURT
The state supreme court will be
asked to immediately rule upon the
legality of the self-voted salary in
crease of the members of the Mil
waukee common council, which was
declared illegal, in an opinion
handed down by Circuit Judge
Walter Schinz, late yesterday, it
was announced today by Clifton
Williams, special assistant city at
torney, who is representing the
aidermen.
Mr. ’Williams and Atty. George
Burns, who is representing City
Treasurer John I. Drew, have
agreed to take the case to the higher
court at once, it was learned today.
Pay Is Held Up.
The council, several months ago,
voted to increase the salary of its
members from $1,860 to $3,000 a
year.
Mr. Drew refused to honor salary
vouchers issued under the new
ordinance, despite an opinion by Mr.
Williams that the aidermen, under
the home rule law, were within
their rights in increasing their
own salaries.
Voids Old Law.
Mr. Drew contended that in vot
ing to adopt the ordinance declared
void by the court, the council also
voided the old salary law so that
the council now is practically “serv
ing without pay.”
Drew will refuse, he says, to pay
the aidermen their old salaries of
$1,860 a year until an entirely new
salary ordinance has been enacted
by the council.
He adds, however, that he will be
guided in this matter by the ad
vice of his personal attorney,
George Burns, and the city attor
ney.
Cites Home Rule Law.
Mr. Williams, in arguments be
fore Judge Schinz several weeks
ago, contended that the council, un
der the home rule amendment, was
within its rights in voting itself a
salary increase.
Answering his arguments, Atty.
George Burns, appointed to fight
the increase, maintained that if
the council were allowed to increase
the pay of its own members during
their term of office, that body
would be empowered to dominate
every public office and department
of city government. Judge Schinz,
in handing down his decision, said,
in part:
“The city at no time elected that
the section of the charter which pro
hibits aidermen from voting on a
question of direct interest shall not
apply to it, nor did it at any time
amend or repeal it.
Part of Ruling.
“No reference is made to this sec
tion in any of the proceedings had
in connection with the passage of
the city ordinance which provides
for the increased pay of the coun
cil members. The city at no time
expressed its unwillingness to be
governed by that section.”
“Certainly the state is free to
take appropriate and necessary ac
tion in case of abuse or excess of
the power granted cities under the
home rule amendment. The power
granted to cities is limited by the
act itself.”

\ASKS DIGNITY
FOR INDUSTRIAL
TRADES OF U. S.
NEW HAVEN, Conn.—Harold S.
Falk, Milwaukee, told members of
the American Society of Mechanical
Engineers here yesterday that in
dustrial trades must be given new
dignity and made more attractive
if boys of the right character are
to be developed. He spoke at the
technical session in connection with
i machine tool exhibition at Yale
university.
“The machinist is as good a man
as the bookkeeper and he gets as
much pay. It remains to make him
as highly respected a member of the
community as the bookkeeper is,”
declared Mr. Falk.
“Boys will not go into the trades
until they and their parents feel
that the work is just as desirable
as is clerical work —until the molder
and patternmaker are just as im
portant in civic organizations and
clubs —and in the eyes of young
ladies, too—as the bank clerk and
the insurance office man.”
MUSIC AGAIN
FOR CHICAGO
THEATERGOERS
CHICAGO Saxophones sobbed,
pianos clanged and drums rumbled
again today in 400 Chicago moving
picture and vaudeville theaters
when 3,000 musicians who had been
on strike since Sunday returned to
work.
Officials of the Musicians’ union
called off the strike early today
when the musicians were granted a
wage increase of $4.50 a week for a
two-year period.
The question which held up peace
negotiations now goes before an
arbitartion board.
That is, whether 29 of the smaller
theaters should be allowed to cut
their orchestras from four pieces
to an organist or pianist if they de
sire.
Both exhibitors and the union
will appoint two members of the
board and Dr. Karl A. Meyer, chief
of staff of the Cook County hospital,
was agreed upon as chairman.

ROSH HASHONAH
OBSERVED BY
JEWS IN CITY
Milwaukee’s orthodox Jews cele
brated Rosh Hashonah today with
services in the several temples.
At temple Beth El, 49th and Elm
Sts., Rabbi Philip Kleinman will
speak tonight on Life’s Greatest
Test.
Month Is Holy Season.
Observance of the Jewish New
Year was started yesterday by the
weird call of the Shofar, the sacred
emblem of the old religious ritual.
The holy season will continue
throughout the month.
Rosh Hashonah is interpreted as
intending a day of remembrance
when not only God calls to mind
everything His children have done
during the past year, to pass judg
ment on them according to their
works, but when the children of God
should remember their deeds and
properly evaluate them.
Rabbi Blames Parent.
Rabbi Joseph L. Baron blamed
parents for the passion for pleasure
which possesses the youth of today,
in his sermon yesterday at Temple
Emanu-El, 501 Kenwood Blvd.
The Sabbath of Repentance will
be observed tonight in both liberal
and orthodox temples. The holy
day season will continue for three
weeks, climaxing with the Day of
Atonement, Yom Kippur, next Fri
day.
Following Yom Kippur comes the
Festival of the Tabernacles or Suk
koth, Wednesday, Sept. 22, until the
following noon. As part of the
ceremonial of the day, the law or
dains that the Israelite shall take
on the first day of the festival, the
fruit of the goodly tree, the branch
es of the palm tree, the boughs of
the thick-leaved trees and willows
of the brook and to rejoice before
the Lord.
Fruit to‘Temples.
This is observed by bringing
citron fruit, palm branch, myrtle
and willow into the temple.
The festival is intent and cere
monial a thanksgiving festivals, the
earliest form of harvest feast.
The festival has of late been used
to encourage charity. The fruits of
the fields are brought to the temple
as a sign of thankfulness and after
the services are sent to the hospi
tals or the poor.

both the physician and the rescue
squad with its pulmotor arrived a
few minutes before the child died
their aid was unavailing.

JUDGE LINDSEY
SAYS MARRIAGE
TIES WEAKENING
DENVER, Colo.—“It «s my be
lief,” says Judge Benjamin B. Lind
sey, judge of the juvenile and fam
ily court of Denver, “that marital
infidelity, so-called, is not only in
creasing, but that it has become in
a larger number of instances than
is commonly suspected, rationalized
and deliberate on the part of the
parties involved.”
Judge Lindsey’s conclusion as
stated, he publicly utters in the
course of one of the most sensational
social articles that has ever ap
peared. Moreover, the judge, whose
fame as a counselor of hundreds,
when in Denver seek him out in his
court rather than are brought to
him, cites numerous concrete cases
from among the hundreds that have
been presented to him, to support
his conclusion.
The Moral Revolt.
His article, which he calls The
Moral Revolt, appears in the current
October issue of The Red Book. In
the course of it Judge Lindsey does
not hesitate to come out into the
open and discuss with startling can
dor the conclusions that his court
cases of middle-age social derelic
tions have warranted in his own
mind. Among others he cites at
length that of a prominent Denver
man and his wife, whom he calls
Mr. and Mrs. Blank, both people of
education, wealth and cultuie, who
mutually agreed upon courses of
what can only be called “infidel
ity.”
In his comment upon this case
Judge Lindsey thus expressed his
own point of view.
“That the old customs are resist
lessly changing is self-evident; but
we have many little King Canutes,
who seem to think they can stop
this tide of growth, and of economic
and social readjustment to a ma
chine age. It would be much bet
ter, I think, to guide the change
Instead of attempting the impossible
and sinful feat of stopping or hin
dering it.
“But their idea of ‘guidance’ is
compulsion by law and social pres
sure. That is not guidance. Edu
cation, and efforts at clear thinking,
and clear expression of such think
ing are guidance. Such guidance
exerts the only sort of compulsion
that human beings will consistently
.and permanently obey.
Clergy Is Alarmed.
“That there has come about a
loosening of the marriage bonds, as
are agreed, particularly those of the
clergy who are so alarmed about it.
“Generally speaking, I think that
a reasonable freedom for the indi
vidual in thought, conduct and daily
life is the only bondage that can
really bind. I think we are very
far indeed from having that kind of
freedom —and that the story of the
Blanks is one instance of a violent
reaction away from marriage as so
ciety and the church insist on hav
ing it. What makes the conduct of
Mr. and Mrs. Blank startling is
that its violence seems to have
about it a kind of rationality, a cool
reasonableness, which makes it
doubly effective and perilous.
“Personally, I am satisfied that
society should leave to individuals
who compose it a very large liberty,
if it does not patently infringe on
the social rights of others—partic
ularly children.”
U. S. Has Largest
Jewish Population

than that of any other country in
the world, says David Trietsch, a

ity on Jewish statistics, in The Jew
ish Tribune yesterday.
Estimating the Jewish population
of the world at 18,000,000 —an in
crease of 150 per cent since 1881—
Mr. Trietsch says the number of
Jews in this country is 4,000,000.
Poland has a Jewish population of
4,000,000 and Russia is next with
3,000,000.
New York leads the cities of the
world with a Jewish population of
2,000,000.'

CAL WORRIED
OVER DEFEAT
OFLENROOT
CHICAGO President Coolidge
stoically surveyed yesterday the re
sults of the primaries last Tuesday,
which yielded evidence of the un
popularity of sortie of his policies,
writes Arthur Sears Henning in The
Tribune.
When he reached the executive of
fice yesterday his secretary laid be
fore him a dispatch from Wisconsin,
whic hremoved all doubt that Gov.
Blaine had defeated Senator Leu
root. leader of the fight for the
world court in the senate and a
loyal administration supporter.
Praised By Cal.
The president was deeply inter
ested in the Wisconsin contest and
not until yesterday did he give up
hope that Lenroot had pulled
through. Lenroot was the only Re
publican primary candidate whom
the president publicly lauded. He
praised Lenroot in his speech at the
unveiling of the Ericson monu
ment.
The president made no comment
on the primary results which in
cluded not only Lenroot, but the vic
tory of Senator Moses, Republican,
New Hampshire, leading opponent
of the world court and frequently
at cross purposes with the admini
stration, over Robert P. Bass. Bass
made his bid for the nomination
with the pledge that he would sup
port the president on all questions.
In addition, there was the intelli
gence that Senator Cameron, Repub
lican, Arizona, who was renomi
nated Tuesday, had recanted his
support of the world court.
A Serious Blow.
The only bit of complete satisfac
tion the president was able to get
out of the primary results was the
renomination of Senator Oddie, Re
publican, Nevada, who voted for the
world court and generally supports
the administration.
Coming on top of the replacement
of Cummins by Brookhart, the loss
of Lenroot is a serious blow to the
administration, for he will be re
placed by another La Follette sen
ator, increasing the Insurgent Re
publican bloc which frequently joins
the Democrats to put the admini
stration in a hole.
With the re-election of Senator
Wadsworth, Republican, New York,
and several other Republican sen
ators in doubt, the administration
faces rough sledding in the next
congress, even if the Republicans
are sufficiently numerous to effect
a nominal organization of the sen
ate.

VOTING WOMEN
WORLD'S HOPE
--LADY ASTOR
NEW YORK—Asserting that she
was proud to belong to “both her
countries,” Lady Nancy Astor,
American born member of the Brit
ish parliament, last night discussed
prohibition, flappers and the differ
ence between English and Ameri
can women and asserted that in the
voting women of the two English
speaking countries lay the best hope
of democracy and world peace. She
expressed her views in a speech at
a meeting of the League of Women
Voters in her honor. More than
1,500 persons were present.
Lady Astor began her speech by
answering some questions asked by
reporters on her arrival in this
country.
Prohibition Big Problem.
“Now as to prohibition,” she said,
“I could not answer that question
intelligently unless I traveled from
the. Atlantic to the Pacific and from
Mexico to Canada. But I can say
this, that It impresses me and de
presses me that the people who are
saying that prohibition is a failure
are the ones who have failed to try
it, and that the people who deplore
the lawlessness of rum runners are
the ones who are breaking the law
themselves. Rum runners would
starve if citizens obeyed the law.
“I can’t tell you what I think of
prohibition, but nobody has asked
what I think of drink. I can tell
you what I think of drink. It has
caused more misery than any other
one thing in the world. It has
caused political, moral and social
corruption and never has it helped
man In his struggle from the ma
terial to the spiritual.”
Takes Off Hat to Flapper.
Lady Astor took a most tolerant
view of flappers.
“I don’t quite know what a flap
per is,” she said, “but I suppose
they mean a modern young woman.
I may be amazed at the sight of
short hair and short skirts, Tut
surely these are far healthier than
long skirts and tight waists and
curl papers and all thO other para
phernalia that we women have had
to put up with for years. I have
not had intelligence enough to bob
my hair, but I take off my hat to
those who have.
“I believe this Is a transition time
for women. They have been abnor
mally guarded and protected up to
now. They may be sowing wild oats,
but I don’t believe the modern girl
is any less virtuous than her grand
mother, although she may be more
venturesome.

FRANCE'S ILLS
NEW YORK —In an article en
titled “France Victorious but De
feated” in the current issue of Mc-
Call’s magazine, Col. Edward M.
House declares that failure of the
United States to keep obligations
made by President Wilson at Paris
is the cause of present troubles in
France.
The isolation policy of the United
States threw post-war burdens on
France, says the article, which made
it impossible for her to practice
economies and balance her budget.
“That is why there is so much bit
terness against the United States,”
writes Col. House. “It is believed
that nearly all of the troubles that
have come to France, and to Eu
rope for tliat matter, have come be
cause the United States failed to
keep the obligations made by the
piesident of the United States at
Paris in 1919.”
Col. House defends the war presi
dent against charges of negotiating
an early peace.
“The armistice terms were agreed
to by all the allies and their naval
and mililary advisers,” he says. “I
asked Marshal Foch during the dis
cussion whether from a purely mili
tary viewpoint he approved an im
mediate armistice. He replied that
since the terms we were making
were the same we would make were
the allied armies in Berlin, he did
not believe another life should be
sacrificed.”

GIRLS GAINING
HEALTH AS THEY
DOFF CLOTHING
CHICAGO—She may be short on
clothes, but she’s long on health;
her frequent marcelles cover a
permanent wave of thought, and her
knees may be bare, but they’re
never weak.
Who? Why the modern American
girl, fall model, 192G —rouge, lip
stick, powder puff, abbreviated cos
tume and all.
Authority for the statement? Dr.
Herman N. Bundesen, health com
missioner of Chicago.
She’s been getting better and bet
ter every day in every way since
she rolled away the hoopskirt and
began rolling her hose, he says,
seems like every time she takes
something off in the way of attire
she puts something on in the way
of charm and health.
“One of the most important rea
sons for ill health was improper
posture,” Dr. Bundesen explained.
“The girls began to get rid of that
when the wasp waist went out of
style. A watch would not run right
if there was a great dent in it,
would it?
“I am not advocating any fewer
clothes for the modern girl, but sun
light is one of the best things for
all ills of humans. So is air. The
modern girl is getting more of both
because she wears fewer clothes.
“She eats more sensibly than the
old-fashioned girl and she’s going
in for athletics, too. That helps.
She has more in her head because
she’s taking part with men in the
business of the world.”

idly throughout China.

ernments are believed powerless to
take effective action to facilitate the
pacification of China. The admin
istration here has definitely deter

intstvention.

jarry their campaign northward to
ward Peking.

ward with 294 cars of troops, loot
ing as they retreated.
Though Wu has announced he
will attempt to recapture Hankow,
the department advices said “there
seems to be doubt of his ability to
return.”

DAVENTRY, England—The Mar
quis of Northampton holds that
many rich people in England are
dirty and have been badly brought
up. He so expressed himself in a
recent speech at the grammar
school here.

have never been clean all their lives
because they have never been taught
otherwise,” he said.

slap at the cooking in English
homes, which, he declared, was
worse than in any other country he
had visited.

be increased. The. general tax rate
is $2.C9 per SIOO of valuation.

NEW YORK (United Press)—St.
Louis is cemented in first place in
the National league pennant race
just a little more solidly today.
The inability of the Pittsburgh
Pirates to get more than an even
break with the Chicago Cubs in yes
terday’s double header added an
other to their “lost” column and
made it just that much harder for
them to catch up with the leaders in
the 19 games they still have to play.
Cards Meet Braves.
St. Louis, after a two days’ rest,
meets the league end Boston Braves
today. In the meantime Cincinnati
and Pittsburgh, fighting it out for
second place, will be at each other’s
throats in a double-decker at Pitts
burgh. If St. Louis beats Boston
and Cincinnati and Pittsburgh break
even, the Cardinals will make an
other gain. On the other hand, if
the Cardinals lose and one of the
second place teams scores a double
victory the three-game lead of St.
Louis will be hard hit.
Yanks Eight Ahead.
It’s about all over but the shout
ing in the American league. The
Yankees increased their lead to
eight games over the Cleveland In
dians by beating the Boston Red Sox
while the Redskins were losing to
the Tigers. Anyone interested in
mathematics might figure that If
the Indians perform the remarkable
trick of winning their 17 remaining
games and the Yankees lose nine, or
more than half of their remaining
17, that Cleveland could win.

gerate the talent of the Montana

Frank Luce, subbing for Bunny

ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—Among
the happenings of Jack Dempsey’s
three-day vacation was choice of
two new sparring partners who in
the ordinary course of matters
should find themselves in the same
ring with Dempsey today.
They are Tommy Loughran, Phil
adelphia light heavyweight, and
Jimmy Slattery, Buffalo. Both are
ready to show their wares and it
will be to an invigorated opponent,
for the champion all day yesterday
was fidgeting to be back in the ring
again.

nity was also expectant. It is likely
Jack will box eight or nine rounds
at least and against six opponents.

beneficial will be determined by bis
ring conduct today, the wise ones
believe.

tomorrow and Jean Borotra would
have to defeat Johnston to take the

pointment in yesterday’s matches.

spired determination that enabled
them to put up such a gallant fight
last year. Perhaps they have be
come discouraged by their narrow
escape against the Japanese team
and by their defeats in the national
doubles championship.

to win his match from La Coste at

little California star coasted through

ster in the fourth.

ENLARGED ADENOIDS AND
INCONTINENCE.
Among the conditions which
physician^ frequently presume
responsible for bed wetting and
the correction or removal of which
so often fails to correct the habit,
are congenital phimosis in male
children and enlargement of ade
noids and tonsils in boys and girls.
Of course congenital phimosis re
quires circumcision in any case.
If this is neglected or postponed
in infancy it may be done later
in childhood. But in the majority
of cases in which circumcision is
done with the hope that it will
correct the bed wetting habit and
without an actual need of it—-
that is to say, where the phimosis
does not interfere with urination
or with cleanliness —the result is
disappointing.
In a considerable number of
cases in which enlarged adenoid
bodies or enlarged tonsils or both
are removed with the hope of cor
recting a habit of bed wetting in
children over 3 years of age (bed
wetting up to the age of 3 years
is not necessarily abnormal, the
result is a happy one, not only in
the general improvement of the
child’s physical and mental vigor
but in the correction of the noc
turnal incontinuence).
When these surgical remedies
are applied in any case for the
correction of bed wetting, no posi
tive results should be expected un
til several weeks after the opera
tion. Even in the most favorable
circumstances a child does not
cease wetting the bed until two
or three weeks after the removal
of the adenoid obstruction or the
circumcision.
Enlargement of the adenoid
body (I am trying to avoid the
term “adenoids” because that con
veys the suggestion of a “growth”
and parents should know that the
adenoid body is a normal struc
ture in the roof of the throat
cavity, a structure of the same
character as the tonsils, having
identical functions and subject to
the same disease conditions as
are the tonsils), is one of the most
common causes of obstruction of
breathing through the nose. But
there are several other causes of
such obstruction which are nearly
as common among children. In
many instances in which removal
of large adenoid masses proves
disappointing in results, the ex
planation is that there are present
other causes of nasal obstruction
which require treatment. Among
these other causes of mouth
breathing in children are polyps
in the nasal passages, enlarged
or thickened turbinatv bodies (the
“bones” or spongy bodies of the
nasal chambers), overlooked sinus
infection, and sometimes over
looked foreign body lodged in the
nasal passage.
The. presence of any such ob
struction of the nose causes de
ficient oxidation of the blood,
produces anemia, often headache,
and in most cases nightmare or
other disturbance of sleep. It is
during the nightmare that the
urine is passed. The normal or
voluntary control of the sphincter
or purse string muscle of the uri
nary bladder is in abeyance dur
ing sleep.
Children over 3 years of age
who wet the bed should have any
nasal obstruction properly treat
ed, whether by surgical or by
medical or other means, but the
P'Aoper treatment of any such con
dition is by no means the only
treatment the bed wetting habit
calls for. Children under 3 years
of age who wet the bed require no
particular treatment, other than
ordinary training.

To Pickle Green Beans.
Wash, string and break fresh
green beans into small pieces. Then
place them in a large granite pan or
a crock and sprinkle two handfuls
of salt over them and let stand over
night. Lift out of the brine in a
stone jar, allowing a tablespoon of
brine to each quart of beans and
weight down. If the brine does not
cover the beans in a day or so, make
more brine by boiling a heaping
tablespoon of salt in a quart of wa
ter. Then pour enough of this over
the beans to cover them as soon as
it is cool. In cooking the beans for
table use, soak out the salt in cold
water and then epok as usual.
Fried Corn.
Prepare by cutting grains down
each row of tender young ears of
corn. Then pulp and juice are
pressed from the cob with a blunt
knife or fork. Season well with
salt and pepper and a dash of cay
enne. Chop one onion fine and mix
with the pulp of six ears of corn,
then turn into a frying pan in which
one. tablespoon of butter has been
melted. Stir continuously until well
cooked and lightly browned and
serve hot.

cessories. And who can blame

Pocketbooks have never been so

be considered smart. Shapes of
handbags vary from large or me
dium-sized envelopes to Hat pouch
effects. Bags with long strap han
dles are not as new or smart as

pearing ones. On many of the
pouch bags we find the" short strap

into the bag when one wishes the
handle-less model.

sorts, calf leather, suede, velvet,

ing how many black bags are being

ors which come in both suede and

square envelope of suede with the

velope shapes are made exactly

vet models. A handsome dressy

modernistic designs on dull back
grounds.

LAMB AND MUTTON.
Mutton is so well liked in England
and used so freely that it seems
strange that we in America cannot
serve it oftener and more freely.
When mutton is properly killed
and cared for there is no objection
able wooly flavor. The meat should
never be touched with the hands
after handling the wool, as the wool
grows on the skin and the oil from
it flavors the meat. Remove the
skin carefully before cooking.
Roast Leg of Lamb.
Rub salt, pepper and onion with
any sweet fat all over the meat.
Place in a roasting pan and sear
it well in a hot oven. Now add one
half cupful each of water and sliced
onion, one cupful of sliced toma
toes, eight peeled potatoes around
the leg of lamb. Roast in a hot oven
and serve very hot with a gravy
made from the liquor in the pan.
Mint sauce may be served with the
lamb. To prepare it, mince a half
cupful and pour over it a table
spoonful of boiling water, cover and
let stand, adding a tablespoonful of
vinegar and a little sugar to serve.
Mutton Stew.
Put a neck piece of mutton on to
stew in boiling water with a small
onion. Simmer until tender, then
add a can of peas, thicken the gravy
and serve with the peas poured
around the meat. Add seasonings
of salt and pepper after the meat
is partly cooked.
Mutton en Casserole.
Brown a pound* or less of mutton
cut from the shoulder and in serv
ing-sized pieces. When well
browned season well and dredge
with flour. Add one cupful or more
of carrots, a cupful of peas, one
onion to the meat, cover and bake
in a casserole for two to three
hours. Serve from the casserole.
Barbecued Lamb.
Cut cold roast lamb into slices
and reheat them in the following
sauce: Two tablespoonfuls of but
ter, one-half tablespoonful of vine
gar, one-third cupful of currant
jelly and one-fourth teaspoonful of
mustard. Cook until the lamb is
weU-heated and flavored. Nellie
Maxwell.

crumbs to make a stiff batter, then
drop from a spoon on a hot greased
griddle. Brown on both sides and

Aristotle and Plinius erroneously
ascribed it to luminous rays pro
duced in the eye, believing that all
night prowling animals possessed
such eyes which enabled them to see
in the dark.
It was not until the early part of
the 19th century that the true rea
son was discovered and it is now
well known that the light is merely
reflected from the inner coat of the
eyeball from some external source
of illumination.
It then occured to some of the
bright minds of the day that if one
could look into an illuminated eye,
without getting in the path of the
rays of light entering the eye, the
deep structures of the eye could be
seen.
In 1851 Helmholtz devised an in
strument which to this day is known
as the ophthalmoscope and by the
means of which the whole interior
of the eye may be viewed as under a
microscope.
The first ophthalmoscope was
crude, consisting merely of a glass
plate about an inch in diameter
which could be tilted from sidq to
side and thus reflect light into the
eye. A lighted candle was placed
behind and to the side of the eye
under examination. The light from
the candle, reflected into the pupil
by the plate, illuminated the interior
of the eye, revealing it to the ob
server looking through the small
aperture.
Such an important aid to science
could not remain crude long. Today
it has been developed into a com
pact, self-lighted instrument, so de
vised that a large number of lenses
are made to revolve in front of the
aperture.
Here, then, is an instrument
which enables the physician, trained
in its use, to see and recognize dis
eases of the blood vessels, of the
brain and spinal cord, of the kid
neys and other organs, often long
before pronounced symptoms of
these diseases have manifested
themselves. It is a means by which
diseased changes in blood vessels
and nerves in a living being can be
daily observed and studied. t

ILLNESS PUTS

CHICAGO —Forced by illness to
lighten his burden of responsibili
ties, Charles H. Markham, presi
dent of the Illinois Central system,
will retire from the presidency
Sept. 15 to become chairman of the
railroad’s board of directors, it was
announced yesterday.
He will be succeeded by Law
rence A. Downs, president of the
Central of Georgia railway, a sub
sidiary of the Illinois Central.
Forced to Quit.
The change was effected at a
meeting of the board of directors in
New York Wednesday, when the of
fice of chairman of the board was
created and Mr. Markham elected.
“A severe illness in the early
summer served as a signal to me
that I should relinquish the detail
and much of the burden of respon
sibility I have been carrying, for
many years,” Mr. Markham said.
This has bee naccomplished by
the change approved by the board
yesterday.
Is 65 Years Old.
Mr. Markham is 65 years old. H e
was born at Clarkesville, Tenn., and
after having been educated in the
public schools of Addisou, N. Y., be
gan his career as a section hand for
the Atchison, Topeka Sante Fe
railroad.
Working his way up through the
various branches of the business, he
became president of the Illinois
Central in 1910.
Downs Is Purdue Grad.
His successor entered the service
un 1896 as a rodman in the engi
neering department. In 1898 he be
came roadmaster and in 1907 was
named assistant chief engineer of
maintenance of way.
From 1910 to 1915, he was divi
sion superintendent and from 1915
to 1919 general superintendent of
the Illinois Central. In 1924 Mr.
Downs became president of the Cen
tral of Georgia railway and the
Ocean Steamship Co. of Savannah.
He is 54 and a graduate of Pur
due university.

NEW YORK—Sales of machin
ery tools are running quite up to
expectations in most sections of the
country, American Machinist re
ports. The volume of Inquiries
reaching the market point to good
business throughout the fall sea
son.

land district have experienced a
slight upward movement in buying.

the south business is less active
than earlier in the year.

plants are planning extensive pro
duction schedules.

ture, who now are in Chicago, will

fore forming any future policy in

cago Board of Trade, it was stated

for alleged mixing of rye screenings

to the board of trade may await his
examination of the report of the
board of trade’s action.

CORN BORER RELENTLESSLY
ADVANCES ON BADGER STATE
MADISON The European corn
borer is coming closer and closer to
Wisconsin.
This dreaded insect pest, which
has infested three corn-growing sec
tions of America since its introduc
tion from central Europe about 10
years ago, is slowly traveling west
ward, despite the ceaseless efforts
of state and government specialists.
Take 10 Years.
“At the rate it is now spread
ing, it will take 10 years before the
borer reaches this state,” declares
C. L. Fluke, entomologist at the
Wisconsin college of agriculture,
who has examined the dangerous
pest at close range.
“But on. the other hand,” he
emphatically says, “it may at any
(ime be accidentally carried here in
corn or other products. Probably,
it is already in the state.”

Borer Most Deadly.
“The corn borer is the most dead
ly pest that has ever invaded north
ern farms,” remarks Fluke. “It
feeds and grows on the inside of
corn and thus can not be fought
with sprays and poisons.”
The borers cause the tassels to
break down, the leaves to die and
they riddle the ears and stalks with
holes.
When full grown, the borer is a
worm, about an inch long, grayish
white and sometimes slightly pink
ish in color. On each segment of
its back, there are two dark spots,
making in all about 10 pair of
conspicuous marks. It spends the
winter in corn stalks and some
times in other thick-stemmed plants,
such as burdock. After resting in
the spring, it changes to a yellowish
brown moth, which lays the eggs
for another generation of borers.

In Michigan Totals

of 1925, Charles J. Deland, secre
tary of state, announced today. The

GERMANY PLANS
TO FLOAT LOAN
BERLIN—Dr. Reinholt, German
minister of finance, intends soon to
raise a big loan—according to one
estimate given in financial circles
200,000,000 marks—in money mar
kets abroad, it was announced here
today.
Dr. Reinholt said the loan would
be made at a time to be selected by
Germany and would not be based on
the gold mark for foreign currency,
but on the German reichsmark.
The loan, following Germany’s ad
mission to the league of nations as
an equal with the’ great powers, is
intended as demonstration to the
world of the growing strength of the
German republic.
“We have passed the time,” the
foreign minister said, “when a Ger
man loan must be based on the gold
mark or foreign currency. The Ger
man reichsmark now must be the
only foundation where all German
financial dealings here and abroad
shall be based. When the German
loan is placed it must be issued in
German marks. That will happen
as soon as- the time is propitious
both politically and financially.”
Rumors current here lately that
the gold currency again would be
put into circulation in Germany
was denied in official circles.
Synthetic Rubber
Failure Is Seen;
Shortage Feared
PHILADELPHIA—Synthetic rub
ber is not a success and a shortage
in the supply of natural rubber
seems imminent. Such was the con
sensus of opinion at the raw rub
ber symposium of the American
Chemical society here yesterday.
Experts from Canada, England, Hol
land, Germany and Brazil as well
as from the leading American rub
ber companies were in attendance
and none of them was able to point
out defintely any way of increasing
the rubber output of the world until
the trees now being planted come
into bearing,- which will require
about seven years.

THE BIGGEST BUSINESS CONCERN
IN THE WORLD
There are over 355,000 persons employed by the
United States postoffice, according to figures just made
public by the department.
Of this number 48,716 are city carriers, 67,671 are
clerks, 45,181 are rural carriers, 50,601 are postmasters,
and 20,411 are railway postal clerks. The rbst come under
miscellaneous groupings.
Think of the injustice involved in depriving these men
and women of their full political liberties!
The postoffide is the biggest business in the world.
Despite its drawbacks, due to old party politics and
methods, it is one of the most efficient businesses in the
world. It is far more efficient than most privately-owned
industries.
If the postoffice were a privately-owned trust, how
much do you suppose you would have to pay to have a
letter taken to another city and delivered? Probably some
where from 10 cents to a quarter. Uncle Sam does it for
2 cents, no matter how far the letter goes, just so its des
tination is within the United States.
That’s because there are no stocks and bonds attached
to the institution, and no private owners. If it were a
private trust, it would have many millions of stocks out
standing—and they would increase in amount from time
to time—and the stockholders would insist upon having
at least seven or eight per cent unearned dividends on the
stock. There would also be many millions of bonds out
standing—and they would constantly increase in amount
—and the bondholders would have to be paid at least
six or seven per cent unearned interest.
For proof, see the privately-owned street railways,
electric plants, gas plants, telephone companies, etc. You
pay high rates to them because they are privately owned.
And you will keep on paying high rates to them until they
are publicly owned, like the postoffice.
BLUNDERING EXECUTIVES
Why will big business executives spend money like
water to maintain spy systems, and “welfare” systems
when they could avoid all that, and be on good terms with
their workmen by recognizing a bona fide labor union?
The New Republic has been editorially puzzling over
this problem, and it concludes that the executives are so
unpractical that they don’t know any better. It believes
that many of the “open-shop” executives are actually sin
cere in believing that they are upholding a.great American
tradition when they oppose union labor.
This seems incredible. One could almost as easily be
lieve that a bank robber thinks he is serving God when
he robs a bank.
Maybe some bank robbers do believe that, however—
and maybe some employers believe they are serving true
Americanism when they oppose the unions.
If so, it must be because they are so simple-minded
as to believe all the lies they hear and read about the
unions—about the alleged despotism of walking delegates,
the soldiering on the job, etc.
Of course, there have been some places where the
unions made the mistake of electing dishonest skunks as
officials, and these have given unionism a black eye—but
any posted man knows they are exceptional.
Anyhow, there is great need of unionism making its
principles and methods more widely understood, and cut
ting the ground out from under objectors who are against
it merely because they have believed lies about it.
ALL ABOARD FOR BRAZIL
A new law in Brazil makes it incumbent upon em
ployers to give vacations of 15 days a year, with pay, to
employes. An American vice-consul makes this report,
hnd he says it applies to all employes on a salary basis.
Perhaps he made it clear just who all this means, but the
abbreviated account which comes to us does not say as to
that.
Employers are allowed to grant the vacation when
ever they wish, either 15 days at one time or in install
ments of five days or more, provided the entire number
of days is given during the year, and they are required
to pay the employe for the vacation time before he leaves.
On the other hand, the employe is compelled to take
the vacation, and he is forbidden to work for anybody
else while on leave. This, of course, is to make him get
the benefit of the vacation and return refreshed, so that
it will have done the employer good as well as himself.
Brazilians do not believe in overdoing this thing of
working. In addition to the compulsory vacation law
they have about 70 holidays per year. These, added to the
Sundays, make about 120 non-working days per annum,
besides the vacations. Come on, boys, let’s go to Brazil.

THEY MUST PROVIDE JOBS
About 4,000,000 men are unemployed in Germa^.
With their families they represent about one-fifth of the
total population. In a thickly settled country not as large
as the state of Texas, so many unemployed are very notice
able. Their poverty is felt by the storekeepers, transpor
tation companies, landlords and bankers.
The Socialist party, which already polls over one
fourth of the total vote, always gains by such conditions.
Winter is not far away. The taxpayers have to keep the
unemployed alive. The old party government is, there
fore, deeply worried about this problem.
So the state and national governments reluctantly
do something that old party statesmen hate to do: They
set aside public funds to provide jobs for the unemployed
and tide them over the winter. The trade unions, whose
members vote the Socialist ticket and who have now the
constitutional right to vote on matters affecting even pri«
vate industry, keep up the pressure on the old parties.
The national government of Germany has set aside
13,500,000 marks for the building of canals. It has in
duced the railroad managers, in spite of their indignant
excuse that the Dawes plan already eats into vheir profits
to use 20,000,000 marks from railroad funds and to tak<
up a loan of 100,000,000 marks for new stations, bridges
shops, dwellings of employes and electrification.
The railroad managers protest that the present con
dition of the railroads does not warrant such a huge pro
gram, but the government does not want to increase th<
Socialist vote any more than is inevitable. It insists anc
the capitalists see the point and yield.
The national government will also spend 30,000,00 i
marks to build homes for farm workers. The state gov
ernments must chip in enough to finish 25,000 new farn
homes during the next two years.
The Prussian government will borrow 60,000,00(
marks to build homes for city workers with the help oi
the municipal governments. This will mean an additior.
of 12,000 homes to the regular building program. Othei
public funds will be raised for other unemployment work.
Of course, 250,000,000 marks will not go far to keep
4,000,000 men employed. But at least the government
considers the situation as serious enough to do something
about it. The reichstag will devise other methods of
tackling this problem.
The German labor unions refuse to let the govern
ment turn the unemployed over to charity. Under their
pressure, the government has agreed to pay unemploy
ment benefits for at least 52 weeks, and to begin negotia
tions for plans to take care of the unemployed beyond
the 52-week period.
The Prussian government is planning to raise a loan
of $200,000,000 (about 1,000,000,000 gold marks) in the
United States. American money will help to tackle the
unemployed problem in Germany, but the unemployed in
the United States can stand in the breadline and sleep
under newspapers in parks, if the police will let them.
Labor Omnia Vincit!—in Europe. And when it does,
organized labor in the United States will wonder why it is
so far behind the procession. Being a tail to the old p
ties is not a good way to defend the interests o^
workers.
THE CHINESE GAIN GROUND
After months of lying about the progress of the
Chinese national armies against the forces of foreign im
perialism, the big news bureaus now have to admit that
Chinese leaders have advanced so far against the northern
armies that even the British patrol boats on the big rivers
are no longer safe.
With the capture of Hanyang and the impending sur
render of Hankow, the Cantonese forces control the great
industrial heart of northern China and make it impossible
for the Peking government to offer any effective resistance
short of foreign intervention on a large scale.
So the weight of Russian Soviet support for the Can
tonese and the control of the vast hinterland of China by
the Canton-Moscow combination now begin to press di
rectly on the foreign imperialists.
The Chinese generals who have so far been allied
with the foreign powers can no longer find the men and
materials in China to defeat the Cantonese. Only foreign
money and armies can supply the deficiencies of the north
ern armies. An international war against the Cantonese
is now the issue which the big powers must face. They,
will think twice before they undertake it.
We do not believe that the British and American gov
ernments, the two most involved next to the Japanese, will
attempt on a large scale what they undertook in the Boxer
rebellion. A world war in Asia in the wake of a world
war in Europe would knock the last props from under the
capitalist system. The powers will have to pull back their
claws and dicker with the Cantonese. Why not now?
THE REVOLUTIONARY ATOM
Prof. James F. Norris, of the Massachusetts Instil
of Technology, declared that enough energy can be u.
locked from the atom to revolutionize the capitalist sj s
tem and do away with the present arrangement between
capitalists and wage workers.
Science has done a lot for the social revolution, but
so far it has been more destructive than constructive. If
the unlocking of the atom should prove to have a more
constructive effect, it would be a great improvement over
past services of science to capitalism.
We would hail Prof. Norris’ promise with more en
thusiasm, if science were a little closer to the secret of un
locking the atom.

Germs Make Milk Sour
MILK sours because of the "affection” for it
of tiny germs, called lactic acid bacteria.
Lactose, which is milk sugar, is con
verted by these bacteria into lactic acid. When
development of this acid has gone far enough,
the milk sours.
Lactic acid bacteria are everywhere and their
numbers multiply fast in ordinary market milk if
the milk be warm, while at a cooler temperature
their multiplication is slower. In evaporated
milk, which is simply pure cow’s milk sterilized
in cans and with 60 per cent of the water re
moved, lactic acid gems have no opportunity to
get to the milk, which explains the reason why
the evaporated product in hermetically sealed
cans will keep indefinitely on the pantry shelf.
Lactic acid forms on the milk proteins, causing
them to precipitate in the form of a curd. When
small quantities of acid are present, the precipi
tate is floceulent. When large quantities are
present, the precipitate is heavy and forms a
compact curd.

there are certain species of fish that do
sing, or at least make a noise. There is a variety

though it is a sort of mussel and cannot com
pete with the nightingale, sings. It produces a
long, low, fluty sound which hias a musical
quality, according to the Pathfinder. Since these
fish do not have a throat and vocal cords, it is
remarkable how they produce this singing sound,
apparently by some manipulation of their double
shell. One authority points out that dryness does
the trick. This theory is based on the fact that
the sounds only occur after tho tide has been out
for a considerable time, leaving the fish high and
dry on the rocks.
There are other singing fish, too. What ti e
Scotsman calls the butterfish makes a noise from
the back of its throat when caaght by a line or-*
net. If you have ever angled an eel you know
that they make a singing noise when the hook
is being removed from their gills. The familiar
gurnard grunts loudly when caught with a line.
It makes a strange, croaking noise, more like tho
cry of a crow than that of a fish.

Present Fashions May Be Traditional —With Imnortant

By MARY MARSHALL
THE street costume is cast for a most important role in the
autumn wardrobe. Now if ever the American woman likes
to go on foot. After a summer spent out of town she finds
almost childish pleasure in strolling about the shopping section,
buying leisurely, looking in the shop windows, stopping hare for
luncheon and there for tea. She is even persuaded to take walks
in the city parks—though she wouldn t dream of doing so in
summer or winter.
The more formal sort of afternoon parties are usually fore
stalled until later in the autumn. The season has not yet begun
for the bridge luncheon and half-past-two bridge party that
provide recreation and an opportunity to display afternoon finery
to innumerable American women later in the year. If you do
play bridge at this time of the season it is a casual, more informa,
occasion when smart street wear is most appropriate.
The selection of an autumn ward
robe is always more satisfactory m
this country—or at least in mos
sections here—than the choosing of
spirng clothes. So frequently our
spring is a spring in name only.

able only in clothes

sweltered in such “L,

There is another pleasing pros
pect in buying clothes *or aut
Many of them are wearable under
a winter coat even after autumn
days have past. Spring clothes, on
the other hand, have no such ad
vantage. You cannot do anything
to make them cool enough for
summer. If you must be eco
nomical, it is a good plan to buy
Jour autumn clothes with this idea
in View. The street frock or coat
frock, which you buy now with
the idea of wearing with a fur col
lar and no wrap, can be worn be
neath a fur or cloth coat right
through the winter. The
weight autumn suit may be worn
under a wool sport coat in winter
or it may be made quite warm b>
wearing it with a velvet blouse or
