France Favors the Suit
There was a time when the two
piece suit and separate blouse was
xpore widely worn in America than
in France. French women had
more readily adopted the mode o£
the separate one-piece frock. They
wore it with fur scarf on warmer
days and with cape or coat as the
days became cooler. Miss America
clung to her two-piece suit. The
girl who worked in an office con
sidered the washable blouse and
suit skirt as an indispensible sort
of work-a -days uniform. It was
the invariable sport costume here;
and there were hosts of well
dressed American women who felt
tfrnt they were never so well and
smartly dressed for the street, in
warm weather or cold, as when
wearing the two-piece suit. It
seemed then to be practically suited
to the American tempezament and
conditions. We clung tenaciously
to the idea of having something
washable next to our arms and
necks. A cloth or silk frock that
was sent to the cleaners only occa
sionally seemed all very well for
the French women. Our warmer
summer climate and extreme fas
tidiousness explained to us then our
prolonged devotion to the washable
blouse.
Now it is the French woman who
favors the two-piece suit and sepa
rate blouse. Having finally adopted
the mode for one-piece frocks we
are unwilling to wear anything else.
Girls who work in offices consider
the simple little one-piece frock of
silk or cloth as the only smart,
convenient type of costume for
working hours. Every American
who has recently been in Paris
realizes how much more generally
worn suits are in France than here.
Don’t imagine that the suits worn
by French women are all of the
ensemble type, with a blouse made
to go with the skirt and jacket
The separate washable silk blouse
is much in evidence. Separate
knitted ct crochetted jumper
blouses are also frequently seen as
the accompaniment of the two-piece
suit
On With the Dolman
It is always interesting to see
which one of the French fashions
brought out in late summer will
make the strongest appeal in this
country. Those that survive here
are not always—in fact not often
those that survive in France. It is
thus that there is always a mani
fest difference between fashions
here and in France—even though

same source.
It is obvious already that the
frock with dolman type of sleeve
bas made strong appeal tp Ameri

It is especially appropriate in line
for the street frock or coat frock.
It is cut in such a way that, in
spite of its bagging lines beneath
the arm it does not prevent per
fectly free arm motion.
The bolero is another autumn
mode associated with the name of
Vionnet that is much talked about.
This bolero is longer than the one
we have been having and it sis
flatter also. It adapts itself well tc
the autumn frock to be worn with
out a coat.
Many of the autumn frocks are
made with collars that are high

uncomfortable. Older women as a
usual thing look better in the lower

silk, velvet or fur, while only the
women with slender necks should
attempt the really high collars that
are seen on a few of the au
tumn frocks. It takes more than
youth and a slender neck for a high
collar. The proof of such few
fashions is in the wearing.

Many Languages
Contain the Tale
Of Puss In Boots
Puss In Boots, a tale which no
doubt you all have read and en
joyed, was written by a Frenchman
named Charles Perrault about
1679, but,~like many other stories
of its kind, is found among the
folk-stories of other countries with
other names and characters.
The story of Perrault waa prob
ably taken from one called “Piace
voli Notti,” by Straparola. Then,
there is a Norse version in a story
called “Lord Peter.” and in the
Swedish “Palace With Pillars of
Gold.’l Sicily has a similar story
also.
Jhere is, moreover, a Hindu ver
sion, discovered in Bengal about
1884. The most complete moral is
found in Zanzibar, in the tale called
“Sultan Darai.” Here the charac
ter that corresponds to Puss in
Boots is a gazelle. The ingrati
tude of man is punished by the
loss of all he has gained; the ga
zelle, which dies of neglect, is hon
ored with a public funeral.
There are interesting facts to be
learrfed out almost all of the
stories you have read or will read
as time goes on. Learn something
about the authors and the history
of the stories as you read them;
they will be just that much more
interesting.

Author of “Prince Erik of Glaagsbaden”, “The City of the Deep”, “The Head Hunters of San Bias”, etc

AT Lakeview Academy, there
-were two annual events which
had stood out in the traditions of
the old prep school for a good many
years. As a matter of fact, these
two events meant more to the
majority of the student body than
did the educational advantages of
the school. From the opening of
the fall term until Thanksgiving,
they were the main topics of con
versation, and from then on, they
were still talked about as prospects
for the following year.
The first of thesfe events was the
annual class rush, which consisted
only of a mighty battle between
Freshmen and Sophomores, Juniors
and Seniors, for the rather ques
tionable honor of planting a flag
atop the flagpole in the center of
the Quadrangle. The second event
was Lakeview’s annual gridiron
battle against Blenton, a rival
school in the neighboring town of
the same name.
Both these events came to the
minds of Rickey Dale, Lakeview’s
football coach, and “Uncle Joe”
Thomas, the trainer, as they stood
on the sidelines of the sun-burnt
football field, watching the monot
onous scrimmage work of squads
in practice but more particularly
watching the activities of one of
the backfield men on the scrub
eleven. The object of their atten
tion, a lad not more than fifteen
but big for his age and looking
even bigger in his football harness,
seemed to be really the guiding
spirit of the other ten aspirants
for a regular position on Lake
view’s team. Raw material as they
were, he had whipped them into
a smoothly-running machine that
was giving serious opposition to
the veterans of the regular team.
When he carried the ball, he some
how managed to find holes through
tbe line of the regulars; he seemed
to be all over the field at once,
tireless in his energy, undaunted
in his enthusiasm.
The reason that the coach and
trainer thought of the last class
rush as they watched him was that
it was this same young man who,
the year before, had performed the
unheard-as feat of planting the
Freshmen’s flag with its proud
numerals, ’29, on the pole. Against
the newly released spirits of the
Sophomores and the brawn of the
upperclassmen, he and the other
Freshmen had battled for two long
hours, until h 6, finding a hole in
tjie human ring that surrounded the
pole., as he was nhw finding holes
in the scrimmage line, had scamp
ered up the staff and tied the flag
to the very tip, where tradition
ruled it must remain for the- entire
school year. For that feat, he had
been unanimously elected class
president and captain of the Fresh
man football team. And the dis
play of the same type of athletic
prowess was now causing the coach
and the trainer to comment on him.
“What do you think of him,
Joe?” the coach asked.
“A likely stripling, coach—a
lively ’un. And a bom football
man, .if I do say it.”
Coach Dale nodded. Then, in a
voice that carried across the grid
iron like the thunderous boom of
a September storm, he cried, “Hey,
Manley, come here.”
The boy heard him, and came
trotting across the field, motioning
for another scrub on the sidelines
to take fiis place. “The only thing
I’m afraid of,” the coach said to
“Uncle Joe” as Manley approached,
“is that after being lucky in the
class rush, and making the regular
team, he might get the big-head.
There’s nothing that ruins an ath
lete easier than that.”
“Ye needn’t be fearing that with
him,” the trainer “Not
if I’m a-knowin’ 1 lads. He’s a
square ’un, all wool and a yard
wide, or I’ll jump in the creek.”
Young Bob Manley trotted up
and saluted the two men. He was
breathing rather heavily from his
exertions,; it was a hot day, the
beginning of the football practice,
and the work Coach Dale had put
his men through had been stren
uous. His cheeks were flushed with
the glow of perfect health, even
through the dirt of scrimmage
work, and he moved with the
supple energy that bespeaks the
born athlete.

ley?” Coach Dale

“What’s the matter, sir?” stam
mered Bob. “Am I—have I done
something wrong?”
His discomfiture was so evident
that Dale could not restrain him
self from breaking into a laugh.
“Joe and I have decided to put
you on the regular team,” he ex
plained, “and it’s cUst'. nary among
the veterans to beat up every new

Bob’s mouth fell open, and then
a huge grin spread over his face.
“You mean I’ve made the team?”
he questioned incredulously, “the
regular team?” And as the coach
lodded, he exclaimed a lone “gosh!”
And then, glancing over his shoul
der at the squad on the field, he
laughed aloud. “Thank you, Mr.
Dale. And you, too, Uncle Joe.
Thank you a lot. But I’d better
be hurrying off. Those fellows are
going to have to step some if they
want to catch me. He wheeled
and was off, while the two men
stood and smiled as he made with
lightning speed toward the club
house.
His retreat, however, was signi
ficant to the veterans on the field.
They knew Coach Dale of old, and
they knew his practice of giving
all new members on the team a
chance of escaping initiation. As a
matter of fact, there was not much
of a chance for the newcomer. It
was inconceivable that he could get
off his football togs, take his show
er, dress and escape from the build
ing, all in the five minutes’ head
start allowed by the coach. If he
did, however, he escaped initiation.
Seeing Bob racing off the field,
the older players knew exactly
what had happened. Although the
coach had not told them they could,
they stopped scrimmage at once,
and came running in a body toward
Dale, while the scrubs looked after
them in amazement and wondered
what kind of tfootball this could be.
“Has Manley made the team?”
demanded Steve Waters, this year’s

Dale nodded.
“Whoopee,” cried Waters, “get
ready, boys! Get ready for some
pummelling. We’ll see what kind
of stuff this Manley is made of.”

after their new member, Coach
pale stood with watch in hand, pre
tending not to hear accusations
that he was spreading the time,
that he was allowing Manley more
than five minutes—for it seemed
so to these finely-built, clear-faced
fellows who wanted to be after him.
“Get ready, now,” said Dale, his
arm raised, as he watched the sec
ond hand of his watch circle
around. “Go!”
And they were gone—the eleven
of them, while others who had bean
on the sidelines on the opposite side
of the field went trailing after.
It began to look bad for young
Bob Manley. Yet a good many
boys would have taken the beating
in store for him, and a lot more
punishment, to get his reward.
On the heels of each other, the
squad pushed through the door of
the dressing room, shouting with
glee for Bob Manley to show
himself. But'inside they stopped,
blank expressions on their faces.
“He’s gone,” murmured someone.
It seemed so, for the dressing
room, its walls flanked with lock
ers, was bare, but for the long, low
benches on which the athletes sat
to dress.
“Maybe he’s in the shower room,”
suggested another, and they troop
ed In there, but that room, too,
was deserted. Nor was Bob Man
ley found anywhere else in the little
building, although the squad
searched thoroughly. Disconsolate
that their bird had escaped, they
returned to the locker room, where
they began throwing off their uni
forms for the cooling, bracing effect
of the showers. Suddenly Steve
Waters spoke.
“It’s a funny thing, fellows, but
I’ve just seen a sight that I would
n’t believe possible.”
“What’s that?” asked “Runt”
Davis, the heavy center of the
team.
“Why, I never thought, these
benches of ours would be able to
move. Look there,” and he pointed
to one of the long benches that
surely had moved from its ’position
in front of the lockers to a point
near the door.
All of them looked, and as they
did, the bench took impetus, and
slid hurriedly to the door. “Runt”
Davis lunged toward it, and stopped
it. Lifting it up, he disclosed be
neath it, lying on the floor, the
figure of Bob Manley.
“So that’s how our eel tries to
slip away, eh?” demanded Steve
Waters. “What do we do to him,
fellows?”
“Murder him,” came the cry.
“Wait a minute,” said Bob, “I
was half way out when you caught
me. Therefore, I ought to get only
half as much punishment.”
“There’s logic in that,” said
Steve. “Fall to, team —give him
half as much as you could.”
And fall to they did, with slaps,
kicks and pushes, until Bob’s head
was in a whirl. “If this is half
as much,” he panted as he was
shoved about the room, “what
would it be if I got full measure
“About as much as you’ll meet
in that game with Blenton this
Thanksgiving,” Steve answered.
“But that’s enough, fellows. I think
he's showed his metal. Now three
cheers for Bob Manley, the baby
of the team. And then three moro
for the team. Ready?” s
From a score of lusty throafs
the cheers went up, until an old
physics professor in a nearby build
ing rushed to his window in wonder
whether some enemy was invading
Lakeview. Meanwhile, in the lock
er room, Bob Manley, grinning
broadly, was having his arm pump
ed with congratulations. He was a
member now—a regular—one of
the team!

Mark Twain said about the
weather “Everybody complains
about it but nobody ever does
anything about it.”
Last spring there were many
complaints about the slow com
ing of warm weather.
The Department of Agricul
ture now reports that due to
this weather the berry crops
now harvested were enormous
and broke all records; that the
apple crop was almost 37 mil
lion bushels larger than last
year; the peach crop 15 million
bushels larger and the produc
tion of pears almost 5 million
bushels larger than last year.
So the cool spring was not
without its compensation. It
held back the blossoms until
the danger of frost had passed.
There is no more hard boiled
comment on American life than
that written bjr E. S. Martin,
editorial writer for the comic
weekly, “Life,” He is a real
hard-shelled conservative. It is
interesting, therefore, to read
the following paragraph in
which he makes an observa
tion that is true of all growing
large cities—even of Milwau
kee:
“But the main disease New
York is now suffering from is
over-production of tall towers
and buildings which are rapidly
producing unmanageable con
gestion in the business centers
and imparting an intolerable
nervous tension to life.
Some universities have for
bidden their students to use au
tomobiles during their college
course in the interest of more
democratic student life.
The question has been raise#
recently in the University of
Wisconsin at Madison in par
ticular.
However, the latest prohibi
tion of the use of autbrpo^les
comes from an entirely diner
ent quarter. John J. O’Connor,
Bishop of the Roman Catholic
Diocese of Newark, N. J., has
ordered that the priests in the
city parishes of that diocese
give up their automobiles. He
explained that priests in the city
did not need them in his opin
ion.

MADISON—A sensation in Wis
consin politics occurred late yester
day when The Madison Capital
Times, official state paper, and of
ficial La Follette progressive organ,
called upon the followers of Sen
ator Robert M. La Follette to de
feat Congressman Schafer, 4th dis
trict, Milwaukee, and to dlect Ed
mund T. Melms, Socialist candidate,
to congress in place of Schafer.
The editorial, written by W. T.
Evjue, follows:
Text of Editorial.
“Of course, there is only one
break in the Wisconsin delega
tion, and that is not the result of
the election. Congressman Schafer
quite discreetly waited until it
was too late for an opponent to
file nomination papers before
making his attack on the progres
sives. Mr. Schafer ever.since has
been the special pet of The Mil
waukee Sentinel, which has been
using Schafer as a megaphone to
launch its attack on the progres
sive ticket.
“Mr. Schafer, however, has an
other hurdle to cross. Edmund
T. Melms, the Socialist candidate,
has always been a formidable con
tender from the 4th district.
Schafer has ditched the progres
sives and there is only one thing
left for the progressives of the
4th district— to vote for Melms.
The Capital Times hopes that
Melms will be sent to congress
in place of Schafer.’’
See Complete Alignment.
K With the indorsement of Melms
to succeed Schafer by the progres
sive forces here there evidently will
be a complete alignment in Milwau
kee county between the La Follette
forces and the Socialists to elect
Melms and Berger to congress, since
Stafford, Berger’s opponent,, is an
old-time reactionary and a sup
porter of President Coolidge.
Labor, the official organ of the
16 railroad labor unions, including
the brotherhoods, has already in
dorsed Berger for election against
Stafford. It is expected that Labor
will follow with an indorsement of
Melms against Schafer since The
Madison Capital Times has lead off
the move to defeat Schafer.
During the primary campaign
President Robertson of the Brother
hood of Locomotive Engineers and
Firemen, sent a telegram into Wis
consin withdrawing the brotherhood
support from Schafer because of, his
desertion of his progressive stand.

Water Rate Cut Sought
By Big Factory Users
FOUR CONCERNS
FILE PETITION
WITH R. R. BODY
Sliding Scale Favor
able to Corpora
tions Is Asked.
The sliding scale of water rates
for Milwaukee, which would give to
the big consumer a more favorable
rate than that enjoyed by the house
holder and small consumer, is being
sought through a petition filed to
day with the state rail commission
by four of the largest corporations
in the city.
The signers of the petition are
the Pabst Corporation, The Pfister
Vogel Co., The Palmolive Co. and
Albert Trostel Sons. The petition
asks a revision of the Milwaukee
water rate and the establishment
of a sliding scale.
Schedule Was Filed.
Several months ago the state su
preme court ruled that Milwaukee
can not legally establish its water
rates except with the approval of
the rail commission.
Following this decision the city
attorney’s office filed with the com
mission, July 20, a schedule of the
Milwaukee rate.
No action was taken, and under
the state law, which provides that
unless action is taken within 10 days
rate filed is automatically ap
proved, the city’s present flat fate
of 7 cents per 100 cubic feet be
came legally effective.
Cun Reopen Question.
The law provides further, how
ever, that the commission can at
any time reopen the matter and
must do so upon the petition of any
consumer.
The fight which the four com
panies, who presented the petition
today, have waged against the Mil
waukee water rate has been a long
one.
At the time the common council
increased the rate to 7 cents in 1920
these companies began paying the
increased rate under protest and
brought suit to recover the amount
of the difference between the old
and new rate, claiming that the new
rate was illegal.
The supreme court recently held
that the contention of the companies
is legally correct and that they are
entitled to a rebate of the excess
payment plus damages.
No Action Taken.
No action to recover this money
money from the city has been be
gun, however, but the corporations
now are seeking to establish a slid
ing scale rate which would mean a
saving of thousands of dollars each
year to them.
It is expected that the rail com
mission will hold a public hearing
at an early date on the question of
revising the rate.
Mayor Daniel W. Hoan, the coun
cil and officials of the water de
partment have long been bitterly op
posed to the establishment of a
sliding scale rate, holding that the
small consumer is entitled to an
equal benefit from the municipally
owned water works to that of the
large corporations.

SET FOR HUGE
KLAN TURNOUT

Staff Correspondent
The United Press
WASHINGTON—The white hosts
of the K. K. K. will sweep down
Pennsylvania Ave. Monday 250,000
strong, according to pronouncements
of Klan headquarters, in their an
nual Klonklave and Klonvention.
Will Be Prepared.
Police, however, claim a few
thousand more than were here a
year ago will attend—and “clock
ing” of the march last year showed
40,000 to 50,000 attending.
The police are taking no chances
though, and all leaves and vacations
falling on the three days of the Klan
visit have been revoked, and re
serves have been ordered to be ready
for call.
Same Line of March.
Whether marines should be or
dered to guard the treasury as they
did last year is now being consid
ered.
The line of march will be the
same as last year. The convention
will be held in the auditorium. The
legation has not been announced for
the usual fiery ceremony.
One of the principal items of busi
ness to be transacted is the selection
of an imperial wizard as world
leader of the order. Hiram Wesley
Evans, who has held this position
several years, has been recommend
ed for re-election by a recent Chi
cago meeting of imperial officers,
grand dragons and other Klan of
ficers, and he probably will bo
named for the position without much
opposition.
Must Show Faces.
It was first planned to hold this
meeting at Philadelphia, in the
course of a Klan demonstration as
a part of the Independence Sesqui
centennial celebration, but Philadel
phia authorities were inhospitable
to the plans for a huge national
meeting in connection with the
“klonvocation.”
The parade permit allows the
Klansmen to parade in uniforms, ex
cept that all of the visors must be
I’fted to show the Klansmen's faces.

FIVE INJURED

Dictator Unmoved
By Attack,
Report.
ROME, Italy A bomb was
thrown here today against Premier
Mussolini.
He was not injured.
This was the second recent as
sault on the Italian premier. A
few months ago he was shot
through the nose by a British wom
an fanatic but was only slightly
injured.
Unmoved by Attack.
The bomb was thrown in front
of the public works department.
Mussolini was unmoved by the
attack and calmly directed his
chaffeur to drive him to the for
eign office.
Two more bombs were found In
the pockets of the premier’s as
sailant.
The bomb thrower was promptly
arrested.
The attack was made shortly aft
er Mussolini had left Villa Tor
lonia, his summer residence.
i Four passersby were slightly in
jured by the explosion. The at
tacker was identified as Ermete
Giovannini.
Is Fifth Attempt.
The entire cabinet and diplomatic
corps called to congratulate Musso
lini on his deliverance from another
attempt on his life.
It was the fifth instance of actual
violence against the premier since
he became dictator of Italy.
Giovannini was said to be a youth
who had come here from France
for the purpose of attempting to
take Mussolini’s life.
When Mussolini reached the for
eign office an Immense, crowd be
gan to gather there and soon was
Cheering “11 Duce” wildly.
Had Gun, Too.
Flowers began pouring in from
Mussolini’s friends and soon the en
tire interior of his private office
was practically filled with blossoms.
Later reports indicate^ that the
four persons injured by the bomb
might have been more seriously
hurt than at first believed. Police
also announced that a thorough
search revealed the assailant of the
premier was carrying a revolver as
well as two bombs in addition to the
one he threw.
Five Are Hurt.
BERLIN—A telegraphic union
dispatch from Geneva said that five
persons were injured by the bomb
which was' thrown today against
Premier Mussolini of Italy in Rome.
The dispatch specified that Musso
lini escaped unhurt.

With two murders In less than
a week, and the life of a third
shooting victim hanging by a
thread, Kenosha, some of its deni

Chicago for the title of “crime
center of America.”
KENOSHA —After having shot
and perhaps fatally wounded his
wife, Joseph Magnin, 41, owner of
a padlocked roadhouse near here,
shot and killed himself today as
deputies entered his room to ar
rest him.
Mrs. Magnino has three revolver
wounds in her legs and attending
physicians say her condition is se
rious. She was shot after a quar
rel with her husband, which is said
to have lasted through most of the
night.
“Raided” Gaming Table.
According to officers the couple
had quarreled frequently since a
year ago when Mrs. Magnino “raid
ed” a gambling table at which her
husband was playing and confiscat
ed all the money.

more bitter and W. W. Wolf, hear
ing shots at the roadhouse, called
the sheriff.
Deputies Tom Jester and Ray
Willem were sent to the roadhouse
and found it locked. They broke
down the door and entered. Mrs.
Magnino hobbled out and handed
them the revolver, which she had
wrested from her husband. She
then told them where her husband
was hiding.
As the officers entered the room
they heard a loud report and Mag
nino fell upon the bed mortally
wounded, the charge of a shotgun
having torn away part of his head.
He died within a short time.
Mrs. Magnino is being attended at
a local hospital. The couple has
two children, Rena, 15, and Joseph,
Jr., 8.

than the wedding ring?

dear?
The questions are asked when one
learns that Milwaukeeans spend
more than twice as much annually
for dog licenses as they do for mar
riage licenses, and four times as
much for hunting licenses as for the
bridal writs.

mately $21,310 was spent for hunt

fire house.

from the discarding of the fiery
steeds, hand pumps and steamers,
to bungalow fire stations with lace
curtains.

took up golf, they showed no out
ward signs of contempt.

John F. Howard, Haverhill,

The sons, Albert and John, made

vorce from their mother, the first

marriage to Mrs. Eleanore Philipp,
Milwaukee widow, who died recent
ly in Mexico City.
Howard was arrested when his
sons followed him to Mexico in an
attempt to secure a financial settle
ment for their mother. Howard
caused their arrest on charges of
assault and forcibly entering his
apartment.
They were never tried, and it is
believed, have now left Mexico.
They contended that their father
secured the divorce by means of a
false witness.
A suit for $125,000 for alienation
of affections, brought by the first
Mrs. Howard against her successor,
is still pending in circuit court here,
and attorneys have indicated it will
be continued against Mrs. Philipp-
Howard’s estate.

WASHINGTON Shooting of
American sailors by Chinese sol
diers in the fighting about Hankow

by this government at the present
time, Washington officials indicated

gunboat on the Yangtze river.

Bailors aboard the destroyers, Pope
and Stewart, had been injured while
steaming to Hankow, state depart
ment officials said that even if the
men had been wounded, there is no
responsible government with which
to lodge a protest at present.

ships are at Hankow, with others
above and below the city on the
Yangtze river. America i^ in the
lead with five, the Pope, Stewart,
Palos, El Cano and Pigeon. The
British Gnat and Bee, four Japanese
ships and two French also are on
the scene. The other warships,
above and below Hankow, all are
awaiting orders.

der severe rifle fire near Yanglo,
east of Hankow, ,today, during
which two United /States sailors
were wounded, while the British
Bee suffered damage from field ar
tillery.
Fighting has been resumed at
Wuchang, but Hanyang is dominat
ed by the Cantonese.

munity is threatened. The present

inen Daly, secretary of the St.

HUNGARIAN LAW
LIKE NIGHTMARE
TO JOURNALIST
Leader Special Service.
MANCHESTER A special cor
respondent of The Manchester
Guardian, who studied conditions in
Hungary under Dictator Horthy’s
regime, reports that under para
graph 7 of the new emergency laws,
“any one circulating untrue state
ments tending to diminish the
prestige of the Hungarian state or
nation or to damage its repute, is
liable to imprisonment up to five
years.”
This paragraph is stretched arbi
trarily to persecute Liberals and
Socialists, even if they have not
done anything, the correspondent
declares.
“It hangs like a nightmare over
every Hungarian, especially if he is
a journalist, who is openly critical
of the government or of the present
system.”
Suppress Democratic Freedom.
“It has made freedom of speech
impossible and has destroyed liberal
journalism in Hungary,” the cor
respondent continues. “Even to say
that there ever was such a thing as
a white terror in Hungary is an
offense under this paragraph,
although the white terror is as
much a historical fact as was the
red terror in the French or Rus
sian revolutions.
“An example of the petty injus
tice possible under this paragraph
is the following:—The wife of a
magistrate at Miskolcz was talking
to her husband one evening before
an open window. She said that
Hungary was an impossible country.
She was overheard by some passer
by, reported to the police and sen
tenced to one month’s imprison
ment.
“A Liberal is worse off in Hun
gary than a Socialist. The Socialist
at least has a party and a press be
hind him. If he is prominent and
his case is one of particularly fla
grant injustice a big stir is made
on his behalf, and the trade unions
may even take action. Rut Hun
garians who belong to no big party
or have no international connec
tions are at the mercy of the system
the moment they dare to oppose or
criticise it openly.
Persecute Public Benefactors.
“An example is that of Ladislas
Fenyes. He is an aristocrat and a
humanitarian. He is not a party
man, although he writes for The
Nepszava. He is highly sensitive to
injustice and suffering.
“His work is mainly amongst the
poor. He is the most popular man
in Budapest, and whenever he visits
the slums of the city the children
run to meet him. He has the cour
age which makes it impossible for
him to keep silence over the ter
rible things he hears and sees—
things anyone may hear or see in
Hungary if he will only take the
trouble. He has no international
connections, so that if anything hap
pens to him there is no stir in
Vienna, Berlin, Paris, London or
Moscow.
“He was released from prison a
short while ago. The time he spent
in a dingy cell with barred windows
overlooking a stone courtyard was
two years—without a charge, with
out a trial, without even an explan
ation. By a cunning use of the
laws relating to libel and sedition
(including the emergency law al
ready described) he has again been
enmeshed.
Courts Are Jokes.
“He has been sentenced to three
years’ imprisonment without hav
ing done the slightest wrong. He
has appealed against the sentence.
There is little hope that it will be
reduced by more than six months or
a year, if at all, although if it is
allowed to stand it will be yet an
other dark stain on the record of
Hungarian justice.
“The lives of men like Ladislas
Fenyes and many whose names will
never be known are one long mar
tyrdom. Arrest and imprisonment
without a trial are still frequent.
“Nor are they a small matter,
even if release is not long in com
ing, for if there is no immediate
confession of guilt, then a confes
sion is extorted by blows or by tor
ture—not, of course, when the pris
oner is at all influential and likely
to take action afterwards, but in
the many cases, most, in fact,'when
the prisoner is an obscure individual
and unable to seek redress.”

of conditions in Italy under Mus
solini, written by a correspondent
from Liguria:
“We are still living in an atmos
phere of battle. The economic
battle, this time, for there have
been several. There ■was the battle
of the lira, for instance, which was
to have stabilized the lira at half
its face value; a great many de
crees were issued and withdrawn,
while the lira went on falling. The
battle continues, but the metaphors
have become those of defence.
“Stabilization is denounced as a
surrender to the offensive of Anglo-
American finance, and Mussolini
has promised to defend the lira to
the last drop of blood.
Bread Gets Dearer.
“Then there was the corn battle.
Last year the government declared
that Italy must produce all her own
corn; a heavy duty was imposed on
imported corn and huge premiums
given to growers. The price of
bread has risen continuously and
disconcertingly, the average con
sumption per head has fallen —a
serious matter when the standard
of living is as low as it is in Italy,
and where bread and macaroni are
main articles of food.
“Beginning /in September all
bread will be made with an admix
ture of bran. Nevertheless, we are
told the corn battle is proving a
success; indeed, the government
was crying victory even before the
corn was cut. Against whom the
battle is directed is not very clear.
“I have been told by competent
authority that the whole campaign
was a bluff, inspired by the big
landowners, and that Italy can
never grow sufficient corn for her
needs, but would do better to con
centrate on the more suitable areas.
Want No Imports.
“The Fascist! have even found in
the sickness of Italian industry a
new war cry. Italy must be self
supporting! The press includes in
a common reprobation the importer
of comestibles and live stock and
the dressmaker who goes to Paris
for her models. All imports must
cease!
“The numerous decrees which the
government has issued by way of
remedy do not bear serious ex
amination. The paper saved by the
reduction of the newspapers to six
pages can only be negligible. It
would be excellent if building oper
ations were to be restricted to
workers* dwellings, for while lux
urious villas are going up on all
sides, the housing question among
the poorer classes is lamentable.
‘‘But no decree will induce build
ing speculators to turn from a
profitable to an unprofitable specu
lation, and I fear the poor can hope
for no zealous defence from a gov
ernment of which the finance min
ister, Count Volpi, has openly de
clared his satisfaction at southern
unemployment as making for low
wages.
Corruption Spreads Far.
“Again, economy in the civil serv
ice was a Fascist slogan in 1922;
but the number of state employes
has increased enormously under the
Mussolini regime—there were too
many friends clamoring for soft
jobs for services rendered.
“At the same time, one wonders
how much the present crisis is due
to the prevalence of what a well
known writer amiably calls dexter
ous accountancy in Fascist finance.
“For while the Fascist! boast of
regenerated Italy, never has finan
cial jobbery and dishonesty been so
prevalent, nor bankruptcies and
bank failures, brought about by
flagrant dishonesty, so numerous.
“The Banca Garibaldi, the col
lapse of which has brought ruin to
a large section of the countryside,
had even sold the securities left
with it in deposit.
“And yet, I do not think there is
any immediate hope of widespread
and active protest. For the oppo
nents of Fascism have grown
weary, and the majority, in order
to live, have joined the Fascist!.
The number has nearly doubled,
and the Freemason of yesterday is
the Fascist of today.

crowds who do not approve of this
form of culture.

BRITISH TORIES
LOSE LAST HOLD
ON BIRMINGHAM
LONDON English Labor has
won over the Tories again!
Birmingham, which for genera
tions has been under the control of
the Chamberlains and considered
one of the chief conservative strong
holds, is now completely labor.
Saw It Coming.
In the municipal elections of Aug.
29, the second half of the Lady
wood constituency in which Birm
ingham is, followed the first half,
which returned Labor candidates
several months ago, by giving La
bor a substantial majority, with the
result that Birmingham is now en
tirely lost to the Tories.
The handwriting on the wall was
seen as long ago as that election
when Capt. Tom Mosley, significant
figure of the younger Laborites, lost
to Neville Chamberlain by only 70
votes.
Defeat Is Convincing.
Mosley and the present financial
minister stood against each other
again and Mosley was returned
with such a convincing majority
that Chamberlain left the constit
uency and has since stood from
a neighboring one.
Considering the number of times
which Chamberlain has represented
Birmignham in parliament, the fact
that the Chamberlain family is the
richest one in the city, Birming
ham’s recent revolt is considered by
Labor as presaging a significant
rout of Toryism.

Monkey Led Police
To Grave of Slain
Master, to Slayers
MADRAS Police records here
have just revealed how a trained
monkey brought about the discovery
of a brutal murder.
Manikham, a noted criminal, has
been released from prison after
serving 20 years as an accomplice in
the killing of a Hindu showman
named Shanharini. The latter had
amassed a big fortune while travel
ing about India with his trained
animals. Manikham learned of the
showman’s wealth and, with two
aids, waylaid him in a Hindu village
one night, killing him with a
hatchet.
The monkey, which was much at
tached to his master, climbed up a
tree and witnessed the whole affair,
later going to the Madras police Svu*
tion, where he jumped into a win
dow, catching the police inspector
by the coattails and annoying him
until the officer followed him to
the scene of the murder.
The animal dug open the grave
where the bandits had buried the
Showman. The police then led the
monkey through neighboring vil
lages until the animal saw Manik
ham and attacked him, revealing
the murderer, who later confessed.

Break Between
British and Russ
Unions Complete
LONDON Quarrels at the
Trades Union congress at Bourne
mouth yesterday almost led to
blows, the most serious starting
when the pro-Russian delegates
tried to start a debate on Thurs
day’s telegram from M. Tomsky,
Russian labor leader, who was
barred from England. They were
held down amid shouts and jeers.
John Bromley, member of parlia
ment, around whom a big row was
waged Thursday, speaking for the
general council, charged that the
Red Internationale tried to ride
roughshod over the workers of Eu
rope, saying they had caused splits
in France, Germany and elsewhere
which “were much more serious
than our disagreements here.”
The congress finally voted over
whelmingly to indorse the council’s
stinging reply to M. Tomsky’s note,
telling the Russian to mind his own
business. The break between Brit
ish and Russian trade unionists is
now held to be complete.

Episcopal church conference here
reveals that there has been a de
crease in church members, Sunday
school enrollment, church societies

in Wisconsin.

members were taken in. This is a
decrease of slightly more than 2
per cent.

and six churches less.

world’s greatest light airplane com
petition for cash prizes totaling $25,-

competitions in that the winner- of
the first cash prize of $15,000 will
be required to maintain a sustained
performance of daily flying—rain or
shine—between now and next Fri
day, every other day over a differ
ent course ranging from 212 to 373
miles in length* for a total distance
of approximately 2,000 miles.
The same airplane and engine
must be used throughout the com
petition, but certain minor repairs
will be permitted the contestants
without disqualification.
Seek Light Plane.
The first prize will go to the
light plane that during the six
days of the competition carries the
greatest useful load per unit of fuel
consumed. All machines, however,
will be required to maintain an
average speed of at least 50 miles
an hour, and each* will be required
to carry a load including pilot and
passenger of not less than 340
pounds.
In addition prior to actual parti
cipation in flights the owner of each
machine was required to give a dem
onstration of the practicability of
the machine from the point of view
of private ownership. This involved
the dismantling of the machine,
housing it in a shed not more than
10 feet wide and 10 feet high, its
removal from the shed and reas
sembly In a time for the whole
process not to exceed an hour.
The competition marks a new de
parture in defining the limits of
light airplane construction in terms
of engine weight instead of engine
horsepower. Heretofore it has been
customary to define a light airnhine
as an airplane with an engin not
more than 1,000 cubic eeni -;ers
cylinder capacity, which d.^ ioped
approximately 20 horsepower. In
the present competition the only
limit on the engines is their weight,
which it is specified shall ex
ceed 170 pounds.
Great Strides Made.
strides have been made in
the i,; year in the construction of
light engines and the promoters of
competition expect that before its
close several new world records for
light airplane performance will have
been established.
The money for the prizes is be
ing put up by The Daily Mail of
London, with a view to the ultimate
development of a light airplane that
is safe, economical, that can be
housed In a small space and that

TWO ‘DRAGONS’
CAUGHT ALIVE,
BROUGHT TO U. S.
NEW YORK—Two giant lizards
arrived yesterday on the Aquitania.
Each is 8 feet long, weighs 200
pounds, has a body as thick as a
man’s, covered with armor, and can
rjm faster than a man.
The “dragons” were captured by
Douglas Burden of the American
Museum of Natural History on the
island of Komodo in the Malay
archipelago. f
The likeness of the "dragons”
has been blazoned on the flag of
China for 4,000 years. The b’g liz
ards have red forked tongues and
sometimes hiss like escaping stepm.
Their legs -are short and stubby
and’ each foot has four claws. The
tails are spiked.
The “dragons” are carnivorous.
They are the only ones in captiv
ity.
The Aquitania butcher pushed
two chickens into the cage for the
lizards’ morning meal, and they
roosted almost contemptuously on
the spiked tail of one of the mon
sters, both of which moved list
lessly.
Prof. E. R, Dunn, of Smith col
lege said one “dragon,” in the wilds,
jumped on a horse and injured it so
severely it had to be shot. Another
ate at one meal the hind quarters
of a deer, “and it was back for more
two days later.”
It is believed the “dragons” are
descendants of a species that once
lived in China and Australia.

mained until her resignation, June
5, 1923.

WASHINGTON—Reports of re
ceipts and expenditures during the
last three months were filed with
the clerk of the house of represen
tatives yesterday by the Anti-Saloon
League of America and its sub
sidiary organizations in Illinois,
Pennsylvania and Indiana, in ac
cordance with the federal corrupt
practices act.
The meager reports list only
trifling amounts as compared with
the hundreds of thousands of dol
lars which admittedly pass through
the league’s hands annually. The
reports adheres to the league’s pol
icy of reporting only those amounts
specifically given, solicited or spent
for political purposes, a policy de
nounced as a subterfuge by the
members of the senate slush fund
committee.
Balance of $8,178.
For the political action committee
of the parent organization, Andrew
Wilson of Washington, its treasurer,
reports that with a balance of
$8,178.48 on hand June 10, contribu
tions of $1,600 brought the funds
available during the quarter to
$9,778.48.
During the three months, the only
Important disbursements beyond of
fice expenses, according to the re
port, were allowances of SSOO each
to the state organizations in New
York, Pennsylvania, Ohio and 1111-
nois.
E. E. Olcott of New York was the
largest contributor to the rational
fund, the report continues, with four
gifts at various times, totaling $950.
George B. Safford, superintendent
of the Illinois Anti-Saloon league
and secretary of its political com
mittee, reported that since April 14
the Illinois league has collected only
$424 “to be used in the senatorial
campaign” and that “SBO has been
spent to date in preparing and mail
ing 2,000 letters to voters of the
state.” Mr. Safford’s report fails
to list the contributors of the $424
and does not mention the receipt
of SSOO from the national organiza
tion.
In Indiana, according to O. H.
Palmer, treasurer of the state’s po
litical action committee, no con
tributions have been received, nor
have any expenditures for political
purposes been made in a year. The
Pennsylvania league, through Allan
Sutherland, treasurer of its political
action committee, reports receipts
©f $947 and expenditures of $339.25.
The Democratic national commit
tee, in its quarterly report filed by
James W. Gerard, the treasurer, in
dicates contributions of $23,356.86
received at the Washington and
New York headquarters since June
1, 1926; disbursements of $19,287.31
during the same period and a bal
ance on hand on Aug. 31 of $lO,-

OLD FACES ON
U. S. CHILDREN
-NANCY ASTOR
NEW YORK—According to Vis
countess Astor, American born
members of the British parliament,
bringing up children and playing a
part in politics do mix, and each
adds zest to the other.
Lady Astor, who sailed for Eng
land today, received reporters and
aired her views on men, manners,
morals and politics yesterday.
Women Good Politicians.
“Women are good politicians be
cause they are good mothers,” she
said, “and are always tackling
things from the point of view they
would like for their children.”
She has six children, four of
whom joined her during the inter
view.
Her only serious criticism of this
country was leveled at American
parents’ method of rearing children.
“Children here have such old
looks on their faces —they are far
too old for their ages. Maybe they
have too much liberty. Perhaps
they have too many cinemas, and
have too much sentimentalizing at
tention paid to them in public.
Excess of Cosmetics.
“Too much spending money? I
don’t know. Each of my children
had a dollar yesterday for their
thrilling spending in the five-and
ten-cent store.”
Lady Astor spoke of England:
“It’s the most democratic coun
try in the world. I can ask the
prime minister a question any time
I want.”
The English, not the Irish, are
the most humorous people, she con
tended.
Excessvie use of cosmetics, she
said, makes the American girl look
“like the last days of Pompeii.”
Scott Again Will
Test Train’s Speed
CHICAGO “Death Valley”
Scotty, the old miner who made rail
road history 21 years ago when he
rode the Death Valley Coyote, the
fastest train that had ever traveled
between Chicago and the west coast,
arrived in Chicago yesterday.
He is en route to New York,
where he will parallel his feat of
two decades ago by chartering a spe
cial train from New York to Los
Angeles to find out just how fast
steel and steam can take him back
to California.
The entire country watched that
record-breaking run of 1905, when,
at the behest of Walter Scott, for a
consideration of $5,500, Engineer
John Findlay piloted the locomotive,
baggage car, dining car and Pull
man, the entire train weighing ex
actly 170 tons, from the La Grande
station at Los Angeles into the Dear
born station at Chicago in 44 hours
and 54 minutes. The last 239 miles
were made in 239 minutes, the spe
cial whirling past massed crowds
who gave cheer after cheer as the
Coyote hurtled past.
‘Joker’ Exempts
Cider With Kick
CHICAGO—ReaI cider with a
pre-Volstead “kick,” no matter how
alcoholic, may be sold legally if it
contains a preservative.
This “joker” in the prohibition
law was revealed yesterday when
United States Commissioner Henry
C. Beitler dismissed Adolph Gill,
proprietor, and Arthur Kurs of the
Tunnel restaurant.
Gill and Kurs were arrested in a
raid two months ago when dry
agents seized 800 gallons of cidei
containing more than 6 per cent
alcohol.
Capt. William F. Waugh, defense
attorney, proved the cider contained
benzoate of soda, and for that reason
was legal, because the law spe
cifically exempts all ciders contain
ing a preservative.

WASHINGTON—Whether actual
progress has been made In the bat
tle, begun slightly more than a year
ago by Gen. Lincoln C. Andrews to
make the nation dry, will be deter
mined when the 24 prohibition en
forcement administrators meet with
government officials in Washington,
•week after next, treasury officials
said yesterday.
Refuses to Boast.
Pending the receipt of first hand
reports from the men he selected
to carry out his policies, Gen. An
drews refused either to boast or to
admit that liquor flows more freely
today than it did a year ago.
The general, however, is inclined
to think that the reported higher
costs of alcohol destined for the
bootleg trade and of liquors indi
cate that some progress has been
made.
“Some of my friends in various
parts of the country are grumbling
over the price of good whisky,” he
said. “Some say it is almost im
possible to get. I have also been
informed that the cost of alcohol
has gone up to $6 a gallon. That is
quite an increase over a year ago.”
Give Up Idea.
Two formulas prescribed by the
prohibition unit to completely de
nature alcohol so as to make it un
fit for a beverage have been aban
doned because of the discovery that
the concoctions produced may be
easily renatured by bootleggers into
booze for the illicit trade.

LABOR COLLEGE
DEAN TALKS AT
HOSIERY MEET
PHILADELPHIA, Pa. “Organ
izations are like automobiles, some
have splendid engines and motive
power, but no brakes, and others
have all brakes and no engines,”
said A. J. Muste, dean of Brook
wood Labor college, in an address
before the 15th annual convention
of the American Federation of Full
Fashioned Hosiery Workers, being
held here. He went on further to
tell of the conditions in the textile
industry. “The textile industry is
highly overdeveloped because of the
wartime expansion, changes in
style, speed up of machinery, long
hours and continued reinvestment
in new machinery. This condition
of the industry makes it hard to
organize, although the present time
is more favorable then ever,” he
said.
Two Sides of Coin.
Education was also touched on by
the speaker, who stated that this
phase of trade unionism is develop
ing rapidly. Mr. Muste stated:
“Education and organization are the
two sides of one coin.”
Josh Lieberman, secretary of the
Pioneer Youth of America, also
addressed the convention on the ne
cessity of creating social-minded
ness in children, so that they grow
up normally and happy and develop
into good citizens. He said: “The
influence of the military is very
noticeable in some children’s move
ment, which makes them less use
full in teaching children social
mindedness.”
Organization Is Theme.
Organization work is the principal
thing facing this convention, with
its 60 delegates from 20 cities. New
methods of organizing are being
evolved. A study will be made of
old age pensions for the members of
the organization. A scholarship for
a two-year course had been re
established at Brookwood Labor
college, Katonah, N. Y.

CANADA'S OWN
RAILROADS ARE
PROSPEROUS
TORONTO —An amazing thing
has happened with the Canadian
National Railway system. Five
years ago it was regarded as a
“white elephant” which would land
Canada in the poor house; as a
millstone that would drag the coun
try down to destruction. The new
ly organized system was a vast
mass of railway mileage, including
the old Canadian Northern, the
Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand
Trunk, the Intercolonial, and the
Canadian government railways.
The first three, privately owned,
were faced with bankruptcy; the
public owned systems were noto
riously unprofitable.
To save the country’s credit the
government of the day decided to
take them all over and operate them
as a single public utility. During
the dark days of depression follow
ing the war money had to be poured
into the system like water to keep
it going. All the croakers and anti
government ownership authorities
said the country was committing
suicide.
Urged Quick Sale.
As recently as a year ago it was
urged that the country should wash
Its hands of the system and sell it
to the first cash buyer for anything
it would bring.
In the present election campaign
the National Railway system has
almost disappeared as an issue.
Premier Meighen has taken occa
sion to prove by an exchange of tel
egrams with Sir Henry Thornton
that he is doing nothing to interfere
with the railway president’s ad
ministration of the road. The in
cident is a tribute to the public’s
satisfaction with Thornton’s work.
The Montreal Star, leading jour
nalistic opponent of the government
system, whose quondam “whisper
of death” campaign was based
largely on the railway bogey, admit
ted the other day that Thornton is
“doing amazingly well,” and while
adhering to its private ownership
principles, declared: “Private own
ership of these railways is today
not a practicable proposition.”
This revolution of opinion is
based on a remarkable improve
ment in the system’s finances.
Briefly the situation is this: It
takes $70,000,000 a year to cover
all interest charges on the Cana
dian National investment. Of this
$40,000,000,is due annually to out
siders holding bonds or stock in the
/various companies that make up the
system. The other $30,000,000 is
interest on money advanced at va
rious times from the public treas
ury, some of it going back almost
to confederation and quite properly
in the view of many an item to be
charged against Canadian National
earnings.
Deficit of $3,000,900.
When the Canadian National sys
tem was first formed the earnings
were not sufficient to pay the cost
of operation, let alone leave any
thing for interest on investment. In
the first six months of 1922 there
was an operating deficit of nearly
$3,000,000.
What has been happening? Last
year the C. N. R. earned a little bet
ter than $30,000,000 over its oper
ating expenses. In other words, it
was able to pay its own expenses
and to turn in $30,000,000 to help
pay interest. That was for the cal
endar year ending Dec. 31, 1925.
By the end of the fiscal year,
March 31, 1926, the net earnings
had reached the point where they
were able to take care of all the
Interest due the public with the ex
ception of $5,735,502. Mr. Robb, iri
his budget speech last April, placed
the increase in the net earnings of
the road in less than four years at
$43,000,000.
Air Trespass Is
Novel Charge in
SIO,OOO Lawsuit
LINCOLN, Neb.—The fall term
of district court here will be called
upon to decide what constitutes tres
passing in the air in a damage suit
set for trial shortly after Sept. 20.
Charging that the roar of air
planes from an aviation field ad
joining his farm frightened his
chickens, causing a 20 per cent de
crease in egg production, and im
paired his own personal health,
Emil Glatt, farmer near here, asks
.SIO,OOO damages from the Lincoln
Standard Aircraft corporation.
Glatt also seeks a permanent in
junction against the aircraft cor
poration to prevent its airplanes
from flying over his farm. Glatt’s
request for a temporary restraining
order was denied. The unique suit
is being watched with interest by
aviation companies throughout the
country.

Accused Danced
After Committing
Murder Is Charge
GARY, Ind.—William Donaldson
danced for his fellow steel mill em
ployes after he came to work the
night on which the state charges
he had murdered Joseph Mullins, it
was testified at Crown Point yes
terday, at the trial of Donaldson
for murder.
Stephen Yaros, a mill worker of
Gary, told the story of the dance
in court late yesterday. Donaldson,
according to the testimony given
Wednesday by Mullins’ widow, was
in love with her and he and she
agreed to kill Mullins. Donaldson
did the shooting, she said, as she
and her husband walked one eve
ning last April in a park at Gary.
Charges of third degree methods
were made before adjournment for
the day. The defense, charging that
John Smith, Gary police captain;
Sheriff Ben Strong and Jailer Don
ald Metz had used force to get a
confession from Donaldson, will
strive to prevent the introduction
of that confession today.

THE MILWAUKEE LEADER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 11, 1926
NO COP EVER
RAN LIKE THAT;
FAKE REVEALED
CHICAGO—A slim high school
sprinter masqueraded as a police
man in police games at Ogden park
yesterday and caused considerable
excitement by running rings around
a few dozen hefty coppers. The ex
citement almost amounted to dis
order when the youth’s identity was
discovered.
Herman Horowitz, 20, graduate of
Marshall High school, grinned last
night as he told of his feat. The
grin was visible through bars at the
detective bureau. Horowitz today
must answer charges of impersonat
ing an officer and disorderly con
duct.
Tells How Come.
Horowitz said he was entered in
the races at the suggestion of
Samuel Melnick, director of the
Chase park playground, where he
trains, and with the co-operation of
Sergt. Fred W. Salter of the Sum
merdale station. He took the name
of Edward Le Fevre, a regular mem
ber of the Summerdale team.
Horowitz entered the 220-yard
race and finished 10 yards ahead of
his nearest competitor. There was
considerable praise for him and no
suspicion.
Then came the one mile relay in
which the traffic division, Wood
lawn, Summerdale, and New City
stations had teams entered. The
Summerdale team was trailing until
it was Horowitz’s turn to run. Then
he picked up his feet and ran in a
way which made the judges stare.
Captain Gets Busy.
“No copper ever ran like that be
fore,” commented Capt. Patrick
Hogan, head of the traffic division.
This sentiment was echoed by others
and the captain led a delegation to
ward the dressing room where the
Summerdale team was celebrating
loudly.
Capt. Hogan won the ensuing
arguments by marching Horowitz
away under arrest. He may prefer
charges against Sergt. Salter today,
he said later.

My European
Excursions
By Edwte Robert Petre
THE LAKE OF GARDA.
The Lake of Garda, a little off
the direct route to the famous cities
of Italy, has not been visited by the
tourist as much as have Lakes Mag
giore and Como, although it is eas
ily seen on the Milan-Venice line at
Desenzano, at its southwestern ex
tremity. It was here that I alight
ed and took the lake steamer to
Riva, which before the war was in
Austria. Calling as we did at the
little snore resorts en route, I had
a fine opportunity to see the amaz
ing beauty of this lake country.
There is never monotony of scene
on the Italian lakes, but on Garda
the contrasts are striking. In the
north, about Riva, the surroundings
are rugged and wild and precip
itous cliffs tumble into the dark
depths. Limone, noted for its
lemon cultivation, and other little
villages on that shore nestle in the
shadow of the cliffs, the lemon trees
terraced on the hillsides. On the
western shore, Tremosine is the
most remarkable village, perched
high and almost dangerously on the
rock. From ancient to modern days,
poets of all climes have praised this
lake —Catullus, Virgil, Dante, Goe
the, Heine, Cardueei and Tennyson.

BOUND TO HAPPEN.
Ways of Escape. By Noel Forrest.
Little, Brown Co., Boston. $2.
“What is wrong with this pic
ture?” might be written at the con
clusion of the prologue to Ways of
Escape, which in swift resume pic
tures Stephen Heath as entirely
self-satisfied and bent on moulding
the world to his liking. And the
answer, which would inevitably fol
low —that Heath’s luck was due for
a cropper—would fit exactly the
novel which follows.
As one reviewer has said, the
theme of Ways of Escape does not
need proving. When a boy of 14
says calmly, “I shall barry a very
beautiful girl and we shall have
four children,” and then proceeds
to grow up and bring exactly this
about, one might easily surmise
that a vast tyranny over that wife
and those children would be part
of the sacrifice. And when one
reads, a few pages further along,
his contention that “There is no
such thing as luck. I look ahead
and leave nothing to chance,” then
one is sure that his kind of man is
going to have haixl sledding.
He does. Each of his children as
well as his wife plans through suf
fering a way out from under his
heavy thumb, and the interest of
the book lies in watching the suc
cess of their enterprises and conse
quent disintegration of Heath's the
ories and life.
It is a carefully written and well
built up piece of work. Its chief
fault lies in the somewhat too near
ly perfect construction of Heath
himself. His very consistency
makes him a little unreal and the
various events which break him,
a little too sure to happen in just
the way they do.
The background against which
Forrest depicts the gradual growth
of the spirit of revolt against
Heath’s autocracy, in the town as
well as in his own family is proof
of the author’s capability. He has
drawn English family and town
life, lacking neither humor, pathos
nor restraint.

ANOTHER HISTORICAL
ROMANCE.
The Black Hunter. By James Oliver
Curwood. Published by Cosmo
politan Book Corp., New York.
$2.00.
The Black Hunter is a story of
the 1750’s in Quebec, and, as its
jacket says, if one has the spark
of romance in his soul, this novel
of the days of the flashing rapier
and stealthy tomahawk will fan it
to a blaze.
Though most of the dramatic
events marking the end of French
dominion in Canada nearly two cen
turies ago are lost, Curwood, who
in his foreword claims ancestry
with these days, endeavors to re
construct them as nearly as the
tenets of romance permit. In only
two instances, and these entering
the story but casually, have his
torical happenings been slightly
changed, he says.
So for the most part, actual de
parted shades of the French Domin
ion “rise from their graves in
strange romantic guise. Again their
ghostly campfires seem to burn and
the fitful light cast around on lord
and vassal and black-robed priest
men steeped in antique learn
ing, savage hords those who
with dauntless hardihood put to
shame the boldest sons of toil.”
The character for which the tale
is named is based on a mysterious
hunter of that time, around whom
all sorts of gruesome tales and
superstitions had arisen, but who,
as history itself is called upon to
verify, did nothing dishonorable or
traitorous
Anne St. Denis, daughter of a
fighting seigneur, is the center
around which swirl the intrigues of
France’s most powerful officers in
the New World. The wicked Fran
cois Bigot, last Intendant of New
France, Deschenaux, the serpent in
man’s form who paves the roads for
Bigot’s amours, and Hugues de
Per.n, Bigot’s chief ally, and hus
band of the beautiful Angelique
whom he gave to Bigot for a mis
tress in exchange for favor and for
tune, all representatives of the Old
World, stand out iff marked deca
dence against Anne; her lover. Da
vid, a son of the forests, and the
wierd weaver of romance, Peter
Joel.
The Black Hunter successfully
throws the spotlight on this pic
turesque period of American his
tory.

Pander $100,000,000
Power Corporation
NEW YORK Financial circles
were much mystified about the pur
pose and the men behind the new
Mississippi Central Power corpora
tion in Maryland. The potential
capitalization of the company, as re
vealed by the articles of incorpora
tion, is $100,000,000.
In utility circles here, it is quite
generally believed that the company
represents a holding company or
ganized by Electric Bond Share
interests for the purpose of consoli
dating certain properties of its sub
sidiary concern, the Electric Power
Light corporation.
Under the Maryland charter
granted the Mississippi Central
Power corporation, the company
may beengaged in various lines of
business, including manufacturing,
storage refrigeration, telephone,
telegraph, radio, street railways and
bus lines.

CHALMERS CO.
BUSINESS HITS
NEW HIGH PEAK
Business of the Allis-Chalmers
Co., West Allis, has reached the
highest level in the past six years,
it was announced yesterday at the
annual September directors’ meet
ing, which was attended by Otto
Falk, president; Fred Vogel, Jr.,
Oliver C. Fuller, Charles Pfister,
Dr. C. E. Albright, all of Milwau
kee; Charles W. Cox, Oscar L. Gu
belman and James Mortimer, New
York, and James Winchester, Wil
mington, Del.
Unfilled orders Sept. 1 stood at
$13,456,000, an increase of $56,000
over the Aug. 1 total and nearly
$3,500,000 over Jan. 1 bookings.
The previous peak was $14,000,000
in February, 1921.
Approximately 6,900 employes are
now on the company’s payroll,
bringing the working force up to
the number during the 1923 indus
trial boom.
Sees Good Outlook.
President Falk expects brisk bus
iness to continue for the rest of
this year at least.
“The outlook is excellent,” he
said yesterday. “It now appears
certain that crops will be satisfac
tory in most parts of the country,
assuring a good farm demand for
manufactured products. With the
agricultural situation favorable and
labor fully employed, there doesn’t
seem to be any reason to look for
a letup in business.
“There has been a lot of com
plaining about agricultural condi
tions, but judging from our contact
with the situation the farmers are
in good shape. They are buying
large quantities of tractors and
tractor parts and in a majority of
instances are meeting payments
promptly.
“Underlying conditions generally
are healthy. Although business has
been good, overbuying has been ab
sent. Merchants are moderately
stocked up, which is a good sign.”
Mr. Falk declared that improved
efficiency in railroad transportation
has been a big factor in promoting
stability in industry.,
Competition from abroad has had
no noticeable effect on Allis-Chalm
ers’ domestic business, according to
Mr. Falk, although it is very severe
in South America, Africa and other
lands where European manufactur
ers are making a strong bid for
orders.

THRESHING IN
CANADA HALTED
BY HEAVY RAIN
MONTREAL —Because of recent
heavy rains in the prairie provinces
a delay of a few days in threshing
operations over a large portion of
that area is expected. General
trade conditions are reported as
rather unsatisfactory in Noya
Scotia. Business is improving in
Quebec. Seasonal slump is being ex
perienced in Ontario.
ket quotations.
Great Britain.
August with splendid holiday
weather prevailing was unusually
quiet. Only about 50,000 coal miners
are working. Coal is being im
ported at the rate of about 1,000,000
tons a week. Gradual improvement
in the employment situation is ap
parent.
Germany.
The fall fair in Leipzig has been
disappointing. It is reported that
there were 8,500 exhibitors and ap
proximately 50,000 visitors. Sales
were chiefly confined to German re
tailers replenishing stocks and plac
ing Christmas orders. Textiles are
depressed, with the exception of
novelty goods.
Italy.
The stock exchange is quiet after
midsummer recess. The cotton in
dustry is tied up on account of the
prices for raw materials which were
considerably above the present mar
ket suotations.
Norway.
A strong attempt is now being
made to effect a settlement of the
labor dispute in the paper industry,
one of Norway’s most important ex
port branches. The labor situation
remains quite threatening in several
minor industries, however. Busi-
ness in general continues dull and
inactive, but prices have been very
stable during the 4 last two months.
Sweden.
Sweden is steadily but slowly pro
gressing economically. Activity in
trade and manufacture has in
creased during the last few months.
Building activity has declined, how
ever, and the iron industry is still
in a very unfavorable position. The
saw mills have extended their work
ing time, as is usual during this sea
son, but they nevertheless continue
to report a materially reduced out
put.
Denmark.
The decline in the cost of living
index, which amounted to only about
5 per cent, instead of the expected
8 or 9 per cent reduction, was ex
pected, will nevertheless benefit
Danish affairs through a reduction
of public expenditures.
Argentina.
Favorable weather conditions in
Argentina during the week ended
Sept. 4 have produced a more opti
mistic outlook for agriculture. Rail
way freight rates to the seaboard
on shipments of corn and oats have
been reduced as an aid in the move
ment of large export surpluses of
these crops. The cattle market is
quiet but prices are good.

CHICAGO— Notwithstanding that
the earnings of the Atchison, To
peka Santa Fe railway in Octo
ber and November last year were
exceptionally large, W. B. Storey,
president of the road, is of the opin
ion that business will continue good
and enable the road to show total
operating earnings in the remaining
months as large as in the corre
sponding period last year.
Mr. Storey said that the increase
of more than $7,000,000 net railway
operating income for the first seven
months should hold until the end of
the year, “Our August and Sep
tember earnings should be larger
than last year when the net rail
way operating income amounted to
$5,055,066 and $6,047,775, but I
doubt whether we will be able to
top the large earnings of October
and November last year,” he said.
Commenting on the wheat crop
which has helped materially in larg
er earnings this year, Mr. Storey
said: “I would judge that about
50 per cent Of the crop has been
moved. Whether the balance of the
crop will be moved between now
and the end of the year depends
largely on the price situation.
“It is impossible to say at this
time what action the directors will
take on dividends at their next
meeting.
The order for 124 cars placed by
the New York Central railroad was
distributed as follows: Ten coaches,
five passenger and baggage, 20 bag
gage and 5 baggage and mail cars
to the Amerian Car Foundry Co.;
30 coaches to the Pullman Car
Manufacturing corporation; 34 sub
urban cars to the Standard Steel
Car Co., and 20 milk cars to the
Merchants Dispatch Transportation
Co. The Erie railroad has ordered
26 steel passenger car frames from
the Pressed Steel Car Co.
The annual convention of the In
ternational Railway General Fore
men’s Assn., which has been in ses
sion at the Hotel Sherman for the
last four days, was concluded yes
terday. C. A. Barnes of Chicago
was named president.

Chicory Yield Big
Around Michigan
OWOSSO, Mich—Brazilian cof
fee growers will lose out on the
sale of many tons of beans this
winter if coffee makers in restau
rants and hotels over the country
use up the enormous tonnage of
chicory roots being raised in Mich
igan this season. Isabella county
farmers alone have more than 700
acres and expect an average of at
least six tons to the acre, and many
fields will probably yield 10 tons.
Little is known about chicory in
other parts of the country, but it is
one of the main crops with farmers
in some sections of Michigan where
practically all of the Un;ted States
crop is grown.
UNFILLED STEEL
ORDERS DECLINE
NEW YORK—Unfilled orders on
the books of the United States
Steel corporation as of Aug. 31, last,
totaled 3,542,335 tons, a decrease
of 60,187 tons as compared with the
3,602,522 tons reported for July 31.
The total compares with 3,478,642,
June 30, and 3,512,803 as of Aug.
31, 1925.
The corporation’s shipments to
customers in August are estimated
at more than 1,100,000 tons and in
coming business in excess of 1,050,-
000 tons.
The decrease of 60,187 tons in
forward orders in August reflects
largely, heavier shipments of steel,
deliveries exceeding, those of July
by several thousand tons a day.
Steel operations are on the up
grade. The country’s production in
creased from 78.20 per cent in July'
to 85.78 per cent in August. United
States Steel’s operations gained
from 84 per cent early in August
to nearly 90 per cent at the start
of this month.
Steel Prices Firm
As Pooks Open
YOUNGSTOWN Books are be
ing opened for the fourth quarter
business in merchant steel bars and
plates. Makers are accepting plate
tonnages at $1.90 a 100 pounds, but
are holding firm to 2 cents a pound
for bars. For the final quarter sheet
bars are firm at $36 a ton and slabs
and billets at $35. Cold strip steel
is readily obtainable at 3.50 cents a
pound, the recent level of 3.60 hav
ing disappeared. Steel scrap is up
50 cents a ton, prices now ranging
from $lB to $18.50 with the former
price as an absolute minimum for
heavy melting.

GRAIN PRICES
SLUMP WITH
OPENING TRADE
CHlCAGO—Yesterday’s govern
ment reports caused grain prices to
sag on the opening of the Chicago
Board of Trade this morning.
Wheat was 1 to cents under
the previous close. The United
States crop report was somewhat
bullish on this grain, but the Cana
dian figures was bearish. It was
in line with most private estimates,
placing the dominion crop at 375,-
000,000 bushels.
An increase of 121,000,000 bush
els in the corn supply was indi
cated by yesterday’s report, which
was generally bearish. These fig
ures did not come as a complete
surprise, yet the opening was
%@%c lower.
The crop reports were bullish on
oats. That grain ranged from
%c lower to %c higher.
Provisions opened unchanged.
European Bonds
Make Excellent
Showing in Week
NEW YORK—Strength displayed
by foreign issues was a feature of
the bond market during the last
week. Buying was especially marked
in the French issues, extending over
the government municipal and cor
porate securities.
Italian bonds were strong and
gains were made In other portions of
the foreign list. This undoubtedly
was a reflection of the marked im
provement that has taken place in
international financial and economic
conditions, with strong governments
in France, Belgium and Italy, com
mittee to programs of stabilization.
German Industrial bonds, which
have been bid up through the profits
made available by their stock tend
ency to react, but were still In de
mand. United States treasury se
curities were somewhat unsettled by
the uncertainty over the form of
government’s September financing.
A Grand Rapids man who was
afraid he might become the father
of twins, for the second time, and
feared the extra expense that
would be entailed, took out a $5,000
insurance policy to be paid if his
fears were realized. As it hap
pened, he wasted his money.

PHILADELPHIA—FoIIowers of
college football this season will see
the most scientific forward passing
in the history of the game, according
to Louis A. Young, head coach,
University of Pennsylvania football
team.
Young, always an exponent of the
passing game, believes that the
short swift pass, thrown with the
same accuracy as a baseball pitcher
hurls the ball toward the plate, will
be used extensively during the com
ing season.
Short Passes Plentiful.
“Forward passing this year will
be scientific,” said Young. “From
conversations I have had with other
coaches it looks as though the new
rule concerning the five-yard penal
ty on incomplete passes after the
first down will cause more passes
rather than limit the number of
passes.
“One thing is certain. Coaches all
over the country will have to per
fect their defense against short
passes and will also have to have
men ready for long passes, particu
larly if the defensive backs are
drawn up close to the line of scrim
mage.
“I believe, however, that the dar
ing features of the forward pass will
be virtually eliminated because there
will be less chance taking. Coaches
are going to instruct their quarter
backs to protect small leads by play
ing straight football, especially in
important contests.
“The loss of five or 10 yards when
a team is in a tight place late in the
game, with the score against them,
will be nothing compared with the
possibility of a 35 or 40-yard gain
if the pass is successful.” That is
why I believe that the spectators
will see considerable forward pass
ing in the second half.”
More Work For Q. B.
Young is convinced that the quar
terback of the coming season cam
paign will shoulder added burdens
with the new rule and that the
quarterback will make or break his
team according to his judgment on
passes. The .Pennsylvania coach
plans to put his forward passing
backs through a long course of in
struction in accuracy. He expects to
erect targets at the preliminary
training quarters at Sea Girt at
which the passers will shoot the
pigskin.

NEW YORK—For the first time
since before the war, Germany is
represented among the world’s i ec

of 1:52 1-5, is one of nine new

federation.
Five U. S. Marks.

ranft’s discus throw of 157 feet 1%
inches, made at San Francisco in

broad jump mark of 25 feet 10%
inches, made at Chicago in June,
1925; and Charles R. Brookins’ 220-
yard hurdle performance, 23 sec
onds flat, registered at Ames. la., in
May, 1924.
Two relay records, 41.9 for the
quarter mile by the University of
Southern California, made in 1925,
and 7:42 for the two-mile, made by
Georgetown in 1925 at the Pennsyl
vania relays, also were accepted.

MINNEAPOLIS Dr. Clarence
W. Spears, Minnesota football coach,
did not look forward to the open

33 Send in Cards.
Some time ago, Dr. Spears sent
out 150 letters to candidates of all
descriptions that he figured would
be back in school this year. En
closed in that letter was a post
card which the athlete was to re
turn, answering questions as to the

know where he stands. He has
heard some reports that Neil Hyde,
giant tackle, might not return to
school this year because of the death
of his father. He has received no
word from the promising young
man and early reports may be true.

Rule Not Important.
“The rule was designed to stop
the practice of a losing team in re
sorting wildly to the overhead game
in the last few minutes of play.
But in such a case, what difference
will five yards make Or 10 or 15
for that matter?”
“If a team is depending on luck to
win a game at the last moment, it
is willing to risk the loss of a few
yards.
“Where the rule may be impor
tant is in such a situation as this:
“A team has the ball on the oppo
nents’ four-yard line. A pass is
tried on the first down and fails.
Then, with an incompleted pass
drawing a five-yard penalty, it
would seem at first glance to be
poor strategy to try another over
head play.
“The opposing team will recog
nize this and the backs, more or
less unconsciously, will draw in to
face a rush attack.
All Guess Work.
“But just as soon as the opposing
backs are drawn in, the chances of
a successful pass are improved and
it might be the best possible foot
ball strategy to order a pass.
“Its all guess work, you see, and
that’s what makes football so pop
ular.”
Coach Crowley insists that foot
ball’s popularity is still on the up
grade.
“Professional football will not af
fect public enthusiasm for college
football,” he said. “The only danger
of professional football, as I see it,
is that college players are likely to
try for individual stardom in the
hope of receiving an attractive offer
to play professionally.
“That would be a bad situation,
because here in the colleges we train
teams, not individuals.”

tirely by Austrian and German

“But the army of tourists Tvho
swept down upon Salzburg during
August were mainly Americans, and
the success of this seventh Festival
has been so overwhelming that next
year many British and American
artists of prominence will wish to

“The all-star character of these
August programs has been amazing.
Imagine an operatic performance
with Jeritza, the American favorite,
Max Pallenberg, greatest European
comedian, Fritzi Massary, world
star of operetta, and Bruno Walter
as conductor. Imagine an orches
tral concert directed by Richard
Strauss. Imagine productions of
Everyman, the Miracle, or Turan
dot, with Max Reinhardt directing,
and a list of actors including Lady
Diana Manners, Lily Darvos, Alex
ander Moissi and others. Imagine
an audience, perhaps assembled in
formally in the square and then
driven by the rain into the new
Playhouse, composed of celebrities
of every nationality—Franz Molnar,

Hofmansthal, author of Everyman,

“The Festival is given annually
by Yhe Vienna State Opera, the
Vienna Philharmonic society, the
Rose String Quartet, and other or
ganizations, in honor of the memory
of Mozart, who was born in the
‘Salt City.’ The artistic directors
include Clemehs Krauss, Franz
Schalk, Richard Strauss and Bruno
Walter. The programs cover the
whole field of music and drama.
“There is nothing like it any
where else in the world today. The
Wagner festivals at Bayreuth in
pre-war days were somewhat simi
lar, but this year the 50th anni
versary of the first Bayreuth Fes

political boundaries. No visas are

nationalism of art than by the

statesmen.”
