HYBRID NOTHINGNESS OF JAZZ POOR
FOUNDATION FOR AMERICAN OPERA
BY PHRYGIAN.
NEW YORK—The popularity of
syncopated music has not yet run
its course. Indications are that
another year or so will put it back
where it belongs among the milder
items of amusement. In the mean
time, the wilfully serious-minded
composer, always late to grasp
things not in his own medium, still
thinks it has possibilities as a reg
ular art form.
There will be, from all appear
ances at present, several attempts
at the jazz opera spoken of last
year. Among others reported is
George Gershwin, who is said —not
authentically—to be working on a
version of Lulu Belle. W. Frank
Harling, composer of A Light From
St. Agnes, which went rather well
at the Chicago opera last year, will
1 be represented by Deep River, to be
produced by Arthur Hopkins. And
then there is Beems Taylor at work
for the Metropolitan opera on ma
terial that will probably not be de
void of the current rhythmic un
rest.
Deep River Blues.
Mr. Harling is furthest along in
his work. It will appear early next
month. The press pronouncements
sent out in the meantime are amus
ing for the fact that they repeat
everything that has been said for
two years. If Mr. Harling thinks
that he reveals something when he
says: “Jazz is not a thing to be
deformed and travestied in cheap
dance halls, but to be taken seri
ously as a new rhythm, a new con
tribution to music, the most impor
tant in the last 100 years,” he does
not deserve much success with his
new opera. The dance halls—we
will be polite and omit the word
cheap—were the cradle of jazz and
are today its chief inspiration. If
they ever go out of business, jazz
may go along with them because it
is their evanescent needs that It
caters to. Where would it be today
if certain dance steps, old dances,
like the Hesitation, Tango, Maxine,
Fox Trot and One Step and more
recent ones like the Collegiate,
Toddle, Charleston and what-not
had not their vogue?
His further statement about the
most important thing in the last
hundred years is plain silly. Jazz
is a repetition of a rhythm and that
is neither new nor important. To
place it above the countless benefits
to music of the past century is to
exhibit poor judgment or lack of
perspective or both.
There may be something in this
talk about jass operas, but it will
likely not get anywhere. There have
been similar fruitless fads in the
past. If a performance should really
be devised that met all requirements
of the real song and dance show, it
would merely be another musical
comedy. The trouble with these ex
periments that high-brow musicians
persist in making in forms for which
they have not the slightest fitness is
that they result in a hybrid nothing
ness.
Misplaced Imitation.
The only legitimate attempt we
have seen so far was Carpenter’s
Sky Scrapers ballet, produced by
the Metropolitan last season. But
it must be remembered that was a
ballet, not an opera, and it was in
tended as an interpretation of the
modern age. Carpenter did not try
to show how jazz should be writ
ten; he was a sight-seer, not a
guide. All this is said without prej
udice to Harling’s new opera. It
may be good or bad, but even if it
is good the composer’s ideas about
it are all wrong.
Just as the American composer
used to think he had to write an
opera about Indians, if he wrote
one at all, now he thinks it must
be jazz. The Indian theme has
failed to produce anything signifi
cant, and the other is well on the
same way. Perhaps the American
composer is trying too hard to be
something instead of himself. We
have spoken to several recently and
they are all rather sniffed at being
influenced in any way by the mod
ern European composers. Henry
Hadley refers to Stravinsky’s as a
“bastard art,” another thinks them
all passing fancies. Yet it cannot
be denied they exhibit better musi
cal instinct and just as much inno
vation. It might also be noted that
they are not always harking back
to ancestry for inspiration, admit
ting that American precedent was
Indian or Negro or any other race,
why must musical material be based
on it? The great American com
poser will not be found among these
conscious strivers for individualism.

Whether the devil finds work
for idle hands to do was not
strictly within Diane’s personal
knowledge, but certainly she was
made conscious that her own life
of idleness was a frightful bore.
Mother would not allow her to
strike out like some of the girls
she knew and get a job. Nor, to
tell the truth, was Diane espe
cially keen on going to work. In
the first place, she had no special
skill or knowledge to fit her for
any kind of genteel employment.
Diane and her mother had dis
cussed the subject only once.
“If you are going to be just a
working girl,” her mother had
said, discouragingly, “you might
as well ask your father to get you
into the bank.”
“I would love that,” Diane had
said bithely.
But when Mr. Colfax had heard
of it he had smiled whimsically.
“I don’t really think we could
place a piano player down at, the
bank,” he had remarked dryly,
and that had become a little pri
vate family joke.
Diane played the piano in a su
perficially pretty way. But she
lacked true musicianship and was
perfectly aware of it. She hadn t
the training and it was only when
she was pretending to herself
that she felt the slightest ambi
tion in music.
So it must be confessed that
Diane led a sort of listless life
of leisure. There didn’t seem to
be anything else for her to do.
She had volunteered her services
to the day nursery, for instance,
but she found the duties there
were by no means playful ges
tures. She found the somewhat
messy children a severe trial to
her stiff ideas of cleanliness and
mental poise. She satisfied her
self, when she failed, with the
philosophic reflection that at
least she had tried.
Diane had volunteered to serve
«m lots of committees for parish
irk, but somehow she never
get to a meeting on time
she forgot the assignment
,hich fell to her lot, and after a
time dear old Doctor David, the
rector of St. Giles church, left
Diane Colfax out of his calcula
tions.
On ordinary week days Diane
found the shaded verandas of
the the country clubhouse as good
a loafing spot as any. It afford
ed one means of escape from the
too constant society of her moth
er. Diane was genuinely fond of
her mother and took a great deal
of pride that her mother was
young enough in years and in
spirit to be a trusted companion.
But lately Diane had noticed
mother was dropping into a bad
habit of being extra-maternal.
She had begun to tincture her de
sires with authority. Diane
found this Insufferably tiresome.
Sometimes her conscience trou
bled her. This idleness was sap
ping her spiritual vitality, and
the more she became aware of it,
the more she wept, figuratively,
at the futility of bringing about
a radical change in her life.

gloomily munched a sandwich,

BY CLAIRE POMEROYE
sipping from a tall glass of iced
tea between bites. She found the
sandwiches and other refresh
ments provided by the middle-aged
Swiss couple who held the kitchen
franchise of the country club, an
easy excuse to loiter. She had
wound up at the clubhouse today
with no better motive than that
she had no better place to go.
Her profitless meditations were
interrupted by a cool, superior
voice. “What in the world are
you doing out here at this time
of day—and all alone, too?”
t)iane turned to smile an em
barrassed welcome to a tall,
rather sensational looking girl
who stood in the doorway of the
grill room.
“Hello,” she said cheerfully,
swallowing the last morsel of her
sandwich. “I was just bored at
home and Tom Atkinson drove by
^the house and I bailed him and
made him fetch me out here. It’s
rather restful out here, you know,
Cora.”
The blonde girl—Cora Savage
—joined Diane on the veranda.
She threw herself into an easy
posture and, without speaking,
produced a rather ornate ciga
rette case. She selected a ciga
rette, lighted it with careful de
liberation and then threw Diane
a rather purposely baffling smile.
‘‘You don’t smoke, do you,
dear?” she murmured, as if in
condescension.
“No,” admitted Diane. “I never
have learned right, I guess. The
darn smoke gets in my nose and
makes me sneeze and every time
I try I’ve always felt so silly to
make such a fuss about it.
“It’s rather a nuisance after
one has the habit,” conceded
Cora, with a little grimace. ‘‘l
run out of cigs sometimes and
then I feel I must have one and
go almost frantic till I get one.”
“How dreadful,” smiled Diane
banteringly, not believing a word
of it.
Cora laughed lazily.
“Next to an empty flask,” she
said, her bright blue eyes fixed
absently upon the distant land
scape, “the aching void of an
empty cigarette case is the most
depressing thing I know of.”
Diane rewarded this obvious
braggadocio with the giggle of
encouragement which Cora Sav
age expected.
Cora Savage was the rebel of
the country club set. She was
about 20 and the only child of
Jefferson Savage, who was re
puted to be one of the three
wealthiest men in town. There
were whispers about Cora Sav
age. She had lived abroad a year,
unattached and unchaperoned
when she was 18 or so. When
she had come home there had
been rumors that she had had a
tremendous love affaii* with an
Italian nobleman or maybe it
was a French marquis. There
were hints, even, that she was se
cretly married.
In any event, Cora had always
been calmly contemptuous of the
settled conventions. She indulged
in the most extraordinary be
havior and wore the most con
spicuous frocks and carried on
the most daring flirtations. But
because it was Cora Savage, cen
sure was slow to crystallize. Even
the tabby-cats, the matrons grow
ing stout and dowdy, who consti
tuted a reluctant fringe of the
country club crowd, did not dare
to breathe of scandal. To tell the
truth,, they were afraid of Cora's
agile imagination and they feared
her tongue. She handled sar
casm and had a knack of subtlety
in purring conversation, more
deft and expert than a man’s.
Sometimes Diane admired her,
and in other moods she was the
least bit afraid of her. Cora pre
tended to believe in ideas which,
when Diane reflected upon them,
seemed almost shameful—brazen
ly immoral. But when Cora
talked about her notions, which
she was free to do sometimes to
the embarrassment of present
company, she seemed logical and
natural enough.
“"Woof! This place is a
morgue,” exclaimed Cora sudden
ly. “Come on, I’ll drive you back
to town. If one could only get a
little toddy here as you could if
this were a civilized country—”
Cora dropped Diane at the Col
fax place, waving a greeting to
Mrs. Colfax, who sat idly rock
ing on the veranda. Then she
disappeared with increasing speed
down the street toward the cen
ter of town.
“Diane," asked Mrs. Colfax,
casually, “is that Savage girl
a—er —a good girl?”

acterize them; and Robert was so
perfectly well aware of his many

been the last person in the world
to condemn any young lady from
sharing in his own opinion of him
self. But. it was with no thought
of treason to Flora that he
watched the maiden as she paused
for an instant at the door of a

stepped into his car he said to his

ward the restaurant. I am sure
she was looking at me; but I
didn’t dare to look in her direction

nize any of my friends on the

plain.”
And that night he saw her and

“Oh, that’s all right,” said Kit
tie “you told me your boss didn’t

he! he I”—and Kittle giggled very

catch him making eyes at you I’ll
punch his head and throw up my
job. And as soon as I get a raise

restaurant and we’ll set up house
keeping in that little flat we
looked at last week—or one just
like it.”
The next morning Robert

apartments in doleful dumps. He
and Flora Bedlow had had a fall
ing out. Flora had intimated

ert had taken offense—-and there

you goosie. Who cares If you do
think well of yourself—l think
well of you too.”
“Horrah cried Robert. “Peter,
jour salary is doubled from to
day.”

Chemists Finish
2-Day Symposium
On Crude Rubber
PHILADELPHIA, Pa. —On the
whole present methods of rubber
cultivation are satisfactory, said
Henry P. Stevens, consultant of the
British Rubber Growers’ Assn, of
London, in a paper read yesterday
at the concluding session of the two
day symposium on crude rubber held
in connection with the American
Chemical society convention here.
Mr. Stevens was unable to attend
the sessions and the paper was read
by W. H. Cape, New York.
“No radical alterations are to be
looked for in the production of plan
tation rubber in the future,” he said.
“As a whole, the present methods
are satisfactory.”
Two important facts brought out
at the symposium, in the opinion, of
chemists, were the cultivation of
the guayule shrub as a source of
America’s future rubber supply and
the inability of science up to the
present to produce a synthetic rub
ber suitable for commercial pur
poses.

Liberty Too Much
For Myrtle; Big
Elephant Is Dead
CRANBROOK, B. C. Myrtle is
dead.
Cranbrook is mourning, and a cir
cus man who knelt by the still
form of the big elephant, who had
given him so much worry and
trouble and grief, wept real tears of
sorrow.
The harsh mountain country of
the northwest, and two bullets from
an Indian’s rifle brought an end to
Myrtle’s high adventure. She will
be buried in the bush where she
was found, about 9 miles from the
city, near St. Joseph Creek.
Myrtle, be it remembered, with
four companions, escaped from the
Sells-Floto circus, while it was play
ing in Cranbrook, Aug. 6.
Wednesday she was captured, but
she refused to walk and collapsed
completely on the ground.
Veterinaries found Myrtle had
lost nearly all her toes, her knees
were brazed, she was thin and
drawn, there were two bullet holes
in her hip, and she was developing
pneumonia.
Straw bedding was brought from
Cranbrook. Food was donated by
the citizens, and even blankets. The
circus men stayed at the side of
their big patient night and day, but
last night she died.
Glenn Frank Back
After European Trip
MADlSON—Returning this week
from a summer’s tour of Europe,
President Glenn Frank of the Uni
versity of Wisconsin, stated today
that while abroad he had had con
ferences with several leading Brit
ish and French scholars and that
important appointments may result
from these meetings.
“My trip was intended principally
as a rest.” President Frank said,
“and I did nothing official on the
trip. But I visited with many educa
tors in England and France, and it
is entirely possible that some new
appointments may be made.”
Plans for a new office at the uni
versity. which will include the pres
ent registrar’s office, are under con
sideration now, Frank stated. He
said an announcement of the change
would be made soon.

Defends Volstead
Act and Predicts
Dry U. S. Congress
APPLETON, Wis.—Stating that
the time is coming when the United
States will have a dry congress to
aid in the enforcement of the pro
hibition act, Dr. Clarence True Wil
son of Washington, defended the
18th amendment in a short address
before the annual state conference
of Methodist ministers now in ses
sion here.
Dr. Wilson, a staunch believer in
prohibition was applauded by the
gathering as he left the platform.
Dr. H. C. Logan, Milwaukee,
charged a lack of leadership on the
part of the clergy resulting, in a
noticeable indifference on the part
of laymen to their respective
churches. He urged a better sup
port of foreign missions, and added
that a great percentage of Metho
dist churches depend on missionary
aid.

MANY FOLKS BESIDES SHAW
You will remember that when George Bernard Shaw
was banqueted, on his seventieth birthday, he said among
other things, “Socialism made a man of me.”
Our good friend, The Nation —which, we are persuad
ed, is not much if any opposed to Socialism thinks Shaw
was talking nonsense when he made that assertion. He im
plied, says The Nation, “that whatever value his plays
possess derives from the faith which through all of them
he has so valiantly kept.” But, it adds, “think of the faith
ful Socialists—faithful to the end—who have not been
brilliant, or convincing, or moving, or valiant, or glorious
ly wrong. And think of the writers in this day they are
few, it must be confessed —who have been some of these
things without the aid of Socialism.”
In short, it thinks Shaw has genius, and his genius
would have made him write brilliantly even if he had never
been a Socialist.
Allow us to say in reply that Shaw ought to know.
We seldom use the word “infinite,” but we think the oc
casion warrants us in saying that Shaw is in an infinitely
better position to know whether or not Socialism gave
him his inspiration than any writer on The Nation.
But, first, let us say that most of those scrub Socialists
which The Nation lists among the futilities were not futile
at all. They led noble lives. They arranged Socialist
meetings, they took subscriptions to Socialist papers—
they circulated Socialist literature. Socialism gave them
their inspiration to make their lives worth living just
as it did Shaw.
Certainly Shaw would have made a mark in the world
if he had not been a Socialist —but would it have been a
good mark? Perhaps he would have been an international
banker, or an imperialist “statesman,” or a conquering
general-—or some other brilliant scum of the earth. He
would have made a hit—but he was what he was because
Socialism, exactly as he says, made a man of him.
The three greatest literary men of the period—Shaw,
Wells and Anatole France—are or were Socialists. Let
us see The Nation try to laugh that off.
After it finishes the job of laughing it off, it might
try laughing off the facts that the greatest poet in America
is a Socialist and the greatest novelist in America is a
Socialist.
One may be born with genius—but there has to be
something to inspire it, and there has to be something to
keep it from wandering into vicious channels. It is no
accident that the greatest literary geniuses of the period
are Socialists. This happens simply because Socialism
is the great timely inspiring social movement of the age.
IF AN INDUSTRY IS A PUBLIC
TRUST, THE PUBLIC SHOULD OWN IT
An American, formerly connected with a Chicago
department store, Harry Gordon Selfridge, went to Eng
land a score of years ago and started a department store
showing the British how such things are done in America.
He has just made the front pages by creating a $10,000,-
000 trust to take over the control of the business so that
it will continue when he dies.
In announcing this move he says, “I regard my busi
ness as a great public trust.”
Very true. A necessary big business is a public trust
sure enough.
But, that being admitted, why not treat it as one?
If it is a public trust—as he admits—why create a
private trust to take it over?
If it is a public trust, why does he not turn it over to
the public?
That would seem to be the logical—in fact, the neces
sary—thing to do, once it is admitted that a great busi
ness is a public trust.
Then why is it not done? The only reason we can
discover or imagine is that, while lip service is given to
the fact of its being a public trust, the devotion to private
profit is so strong that it overcomes the will to carry out
the conviction. We hope, however, that one of these times
a big business man who admits that his business is a public
trust will have the courage of his convictions and act ac
cordingly by giving the business to the public.

GERMANY IN THE LEAGUE
Germany is at last in the league after years of plots
and bargains against her that read like dime novels. Ger
many goes in, Spain goes out, Brazil has been out for some
time. Russia, Turkey and Mexico are still outlawed. The
plots continue with increasing speed.
Germany can be a power for peace in the league.
Peace between Germany and France can also promote
world peace. But we hear the war drums in the Mediter
ranean and in the Far East throbbing louder and louder,
no matter how silent they may have become along the
Rhine.
Nor is peace between France and Germany as secure
as some recent economic and political pacts between them
may seem to indicate. A tendency in this direction is cer
tainly gaining momentum. But with men like Poincare
and Clemenceau still playing a leading role in France,
and the militarist princes in Germany still plotting re
venge, only a slight misstep may explode the highly
charged European arsenal.
The Eupen-Malmedy incident showed that the silly
nationalist egotism still dwells in Poincare. Negotiations
between unofficial agents of Belgium and Germany for a
return to Germany Of Eupen and Malmedy in exchange
for a cash consideration were well under way, when Poin
care vetoed the deal on the foolish ground that it was a
revision of the Versailles treaty. But so were the Dawes
plan, the Locarno pact, the Ruhr and Lorraine iron and
coal pacts. A little more of the Locarno spirit would
have gotten around the difficulty.
Every day brings new evidence to show that Germany
is invited into the league, not so much to make peace more
secure, but to gain her as an ally in a new balance of
power plot.
The situation in the Mediterranean and in China
has become so tense that peace along the Rhine is indis
pensable to the imperialist powers. To put the little Latin
dictators in their place and to fight the supremacy of
Soviet Russia and of the Cantonese in China, there must
be no sparks left along the Rhine.
Soviet Russia holds the big trumps in China with the
Canton leaders. The European borders of Soviet Russia
have been fairly well spiked with bayonets in the pay of
England or France. But the Asiatic borders of Russia
are not so well secured. In Asia, the British empire has
a weaker front than Soviet Russia.
China is theoretically a member of the league, but
the Cantonese in league with Russia hold the biggest part
of China. The puppet government in Peking represents
only a few war lords and foreign imperialists. They are
now in the defensive and hard pressed.
Germany in the league can act as a champion of So
viet Russia and China, if her government is ruled by far
sighted leaders, who cannot be bribed by New York, Lon
don and Paris bankers. But nobody can doubt that the
gods of imperialism are getting very thirsty for blood.
They understand too well that a lasting predominance of
Soviet Russia in. China is a far greater threat to the im
perialist empire than the utopian world revolution of the
third international.
Huge bribes will be offered to Germany and Soviet
Russia to sell out to imperialism. The economic need of
both nations is great. Socialization is still far away. The
temptations to leave China to her fate and buy alleged
curity at home will be great in certain German and Ku
sian circles. We may hope that Germany will protect th&
peace in spite of all temptations, but^with old Darty lead
ers one can never be sure, and with certain Communist
leaders even less.
KOLLONTAYS NEW POST
Alexandra Kollontay has been sent from her- post in
Sweden to the Mexican capital in place of the Russian
ambassador there. Sweden and Norway are lost to Soviet
diplomacy. They have fallen into the net of the New York
and London bankers. Their labor movement is swearing
off Moscow.
The Mexican labor movement has no more use for the
Communists than the Mexican government. But the in
ternational situation has made it necessary for the big
bankers to make up their minds whether to settle accounts
first with China or with Mexico. The Mexican post is
therefore a real outpost of Moscow, from which flank
attacks can be directed against Wall Street. This may be
useful to Mexico, also, while China needs American at
tention more.
Maybe the Moscow government figures that the clever
and able Alexandra will be better able to impress Presi
dent Calles than a man. Maybe her influence with Amer
ican Communists counts for an additional point in her
favor. She is also a mediator of rare ability and might be
transferred to Washington, if things should turn out that
way.
The American Ambassador Sheffield will find Alex
andra a charming rose with more than one thorn. Cal
Coolidge would do well to send brains plus beauty chap
eroned by some masculine lady down there in the place
of Sheffield.
A PREMATURE LAUGH
The Pan-Asiatic conference which met during August
in Tokio was closely watched by the European pres
Naturally the Russian, German and Austrian press d»
cussed it at length. It was also recorded fully in the
British and French press. But the Italian Fascist press
treated it as a joke.
Avanti, the organ of the left-wing Socialists in Italy,
tells the Fascist editors that they laughed tod soon. The
Pan-Asiatic conference was attended by delegates from
most of the Asiatic nations, notably from India, Persia,
Turkey, Siam, China, Philippines and Japan.
These delegates were all sympathizers of Asiatic in
dependence movements. They had to hold secret meet
ings, because the Japanese government did not want them
to disturb its relations with England and America. But
the Japanese government did not prevent the meeting. If
England and America can use Japan, they won’t need
Mussolini. That Fascist laugh may turn into a snarl.

MADISON, Wis.—Arguments for
and against the submission of a
beer referendum to the voters of
Wisconsin at the November election
will be heard by the state supreme
court during its September session
beginning here tomorrow. This
hearing Is scheduled for Sept. 18.
Atty. Gen. Herman L. Ekern will
appear for the state in opposition
to tbe petition of the Anti-Saloon
league, represented by S. A. Fulton,
seeking from the court an injunc
tion against the referendum on
amending the Volstead act.
Started by Socialist.
Although the injunction would
restrain the secretary of state and
state printing board from placing
the proposed referendum on the
ballot, the secretary of state’s office
according to law today is proceed
ing with instructions to county
clerks to publish notices of the
general election including the ref
erendum.
The referendum was authorized
by the last Wisconsin legislature
in two joint resolutions introduced
by Senator Walter Polakowski, So
cialist, one authorizing the submis
sion of the question to the voters
and the other directing the secre
tary of state to place it on the bal
lot. The double action was contrary
to the established custom, which
provided for placing such a matter
on the ballot by a bill, passed by
both houses and signed by the gov
ernor.
Question for Court.
Legality of the action based upon
the two resolutions will be deter
mined by the high court.
The first five days of this week’s
session will be devoted to hearing
of oral arguments. The total of 272
cases are on the court calendar fol-
lowing its summer recess. First de
cisions on the cases pending are ex
pected some time in October.

DEDHAM, Mass. —A five-year
battle to defeat the electric chair
was renewed In superior court here
today when defense counsel filed 61
affidavits in quest of a new trial
for Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo
Vanzetti, whose conviction has
aroused world-wide interest.
Asst. Dist. Atty. Dudley P. Ran
ney, directing the state’s case, sub
mitted 27 affidavits to refute the so
called “new evidence” that the de
fense claims to have unearthed.
Sacco and Vanzetti did not appear
in court. Clestino Madeiros, con
demned New Bedford slayer, upon
whose alleged confession the defense
basis its claim for a trial, also was
absent.
Sacco and Vanzetti were convicted
in connection with the death of
Frederick Parmenter and Alexander
Berardelli, at South Braintree, April
15, 1920. They have never been sen
tenced, the fight to save their lives
proving one of the most extraordi
nary court battles in history.
The first of the 61 affidavits filed
by William G. Thompson, chief de
fense counsel, was that of Sacco,
who said he had no part in the rob
bery and murder at South Baintree,
April 15, 1920, was not present
when it occurred.
Prior to Nov. 15, 1925, Sacco went
on, Madeiros, who was confined in
Dedham jail, where the affidavit
was held, said to him:
“Nick, I know who did the South
Braintree job.” Sacco said he
thought Madeiros was kidding, so
he said nothing.
Note Is Received.
About Nov. 18, a runner in the
jail named Miller handed Sacco a
magazine from Madeiros. Sacco
found in the magazine a slip of pa
per which read:
“I hereby confess to being in the
South Braintree Shoe Co. crime and
Sacco and Vanzetti was not in said
crime. (Signed) Celestino Madei
ros.”

PFISTER-VOGEL
WATER CLAIM
Demands Additional
$73,750 From
Company.
A claim of $262,267.41 by the
Pfister Vogel Leather Co. for ex
cess water rates paid, plus triple
damages, came before Judge Charles
Aarons in circuit court, today, and
was met by a counter claim of the
city for $73,750.
The Pfister Vogel Co.’s
claim, which is one of several based
on a recent supreme court decision,
holding that the city had no right to
increase, its water rates of 1921 from
4V& to 7 cents per 100 cubic feet,
without consent of the railroad com
mission, is based on tbe full amount
of taxes paid from 1921 to 1924, plus
an amount three times the total
taxes.
Hit at Claim.
The city, in opposing the claim,
contends that the Pfister Vogel
Co. did not make its payments under
protest and that all the company is
entitled to recover is the difference
between 4^ and 7 cents, without an
additional penalty.
From 1924 to 1926, the city also
claims, the company paid no water
taxes whatever, as a result of an in
junction restraining the city from
enforcing the new rate, pending the
supreme court decision.
The city also attacks the com
pany’s claim that it suffered dam
ages amounting to the taxes paid
into the city treasury. The city con
tends that all the damage the com
pany suffered was the interest from
1921 to 1924. Arguments in the mat
ter are expected to consume the en
tire day.
Urge Holding to
7 Per Cent Rate
Retention of the flat 7 cent per
100 cubic feet of water rate for
Milwaukee is urged of the' state
rail commission through a resolu
tion which will be considered by
common council late today.
Four large Milwaukee corpora
tions, The Pfister Vogel corpor
ation, The Palmolive Co., Albert
Trostel Sons Co., and the Pabst
Corporation petitioned the com
mission Saturday to introduce a
sliding scale of rates which would
give a lesser rate to the larger con
sumers and a higher one to the
householder and small consumer.
Hit Small Consumer.
The council through a resolution
introduced by Aid. Joseph P. Car
ney, nonpartisan, points out that
the sliding scale system of rates,
if put into practice, would greatly
decrease the rate or the large con
sumer, It declares that the so-called
flat rate system has proved satis
factory during all the years that
the water works has been in exist
ence and will, in the opinion of the
council, continue to prove the most
satisfactory rate.

WHIPPET LEAD
BEING FOLLOWED
Following the announcement of
the European type light car, the
Whippet, made several weeks ago
by Willys-Overland, Inc., another
large manufacturer has presented a
remodeled type of four-cylinder car
in the light car field and other an
nouncements are expected to fol
low.
It is stated in the automobile
trad i circles that the Whippet type
of light motor car is the forerunner
of a general trend in this direction
by a number of manufacturers but
it is expected that the Whippet will
remain the only truly European type
light car built in this country for
some time to come.
That a tendency on the part of
other manufacturers to lighten the
weight of their cars will be evi
denced in the new production seems
inevitable to the better Informed in
the industry, but it is generally con
ceded that it will be some time be
fore other engineering departments
will be in a position to thoroughly
Europeanize their products.
In the meantime the usual discus
sions regarding a product as revolu
tionary as the Whippet in its field,
may be expected.
Reports from Willys-Overland
show that better than 18,000 of the
Whippet models are already in use
and that these cars are exceeding
all expectations of the manufactur
ing company in the performance
records they are establishing for
owners throughout the country.

Cessetea, in which the fine penman

observed characteristic.

telling of the last supper and the
betrayal of Jesus Christ. It came
into the possession of the univer
sity two years ago through the ac
tivities of its near-east research or

WILDEST WARDS
OF U. S. FOUND
IN LUZON, P. I.
„NEW YORK—-The wildest race
under the American flag is one of
the 78 tribes in the Philippine
islands, each of which speaks a
separate language or dialect and has
certain cultural distinctions setting
it apart from the others, although
all are embraced in three general
cultural groups, the Christian Fili
pinos, Mohammedan Moros and pa
gans. This assertion was made re
cently by Kilmer O. Moe, former
superintendent of the Luzon Agri
cultural school, speaking before the
Pan-Pacific Research institution at
Honolulu. Describing one of these
races with Scotch traits, Mr. Moe
said:
“We hear on the plantations a
preference expressed for Ilocanos.
They are regarded as more indus
trious and thrifty. There may be
something in the theory that they
have a larger infusion of Chinese
blood, for the Ilocano coast borders
the China sea, but I think it is rath
er a matter of environment. Like
the Scotch, they occupy an inhos
pitable land where the most stren
uous labor is necessary to maintain
life. This has forced them to form
habits of industry and thrift not
acquired by peoples in easier cir
cumstances. This hardy lot Is char
acterized by its pioneers and set
tlers, and its ability to undergo
great hardships. The members of
this group stand out in stfong con
trast with the easygoing Tagalogs
and Visayans.”
Mr. Moe said that living in the
Cordilleras of northern Luzon are
the Ifugaos, the terrace builders.
Telling of their enginering ability,
he said:
An Unforgettable Sight.
“No one who has ever seen their
magnificent terraces will ever for
get the sight. They extend up sides
of the mountains until they lose
themselves among the mists of Ihe
mountain tops. Like an enormous
stairway of a race of giants they
follow the contours of the hills and
valleys. Here the Ifugaos have
built their villages. This sturdy
mountaineer race has established
here a gee-string civilization as old
as the hills. Their quaint houses
are rich with evidences of culture
which has been developed by an
isolated people over periods of tens
of centuries.
“It has been estimated that nt
the present rate of construction It
must have taken at least 2,000
years to complete their terraces.
When the fact is taken into consid
eration that the terrace builders had
to carry on their work with their
weapons of warfare near at hand,
and that the numerical "strength
of the tribe was weakened through
head hunting raids and constant
warfare, it is very evident that
this estimate is too conservative.
“At any rate these matchless ter
races are indelible records written
on the rocks of the untiring efforts
of this early Malay stock to wring
a sustenance from the inhospitable
mountain sidd. Like the pyramids,
they stand as one of the outstand
ing features of past human endeav
or. They are by all odds the big
gest single engineering accomplish
ments of the Malay race in the
Philippines or elsewhere either for
that matter. The lowlanders, who
strut about in borrowed feathers
and who are ashamed of their
brothers in the uplands, should pon
der this important fact.*’
Idongots the Wildest.
The “wildest individual under the
American flag” is the Ilongot, living
in the Sierra Madre and the coast
ranges of Luzon, separated from the
habitat of the Ifugaos only by the
Magat valley. Concerning the Ilon
got, Mr. Moe said:
“He is a thousand years behind
the Ifugao in social and political
progress. The theory has been ad
vanced that the Ilongot tribe is com
posed of renegades and outlaws
from several other communities,
whose hand is against every man.
From their homes in the thick
jungles they steal out of their forest
retreats to fall upon the wayfarer or
resident of the valley and leave him
a beheaded and dismembered corpse.
Each little locality is usually occu
pied by families having blood or
social ties. Several such localities
within a few hours’ travel of each
other form a friendly group. Out
side this group all other Ilongots, as
well as other people, are blood ene
mies, to be hunted, murdered and
decapitated as occasion permits.
“The ways of the wild man are
devious and strange. It is pathetic
to see these peoples grope their way
forward and upward toward a high
er plane. With this tribe it is the
male who falls victim to vanity and
bedecks himself in gay colors and
useless trinkets. I was once enter
tained by members of the tribe along
the upper reaches of the Cagayan
river. Among the hosts was a
gaudily arrayed warrior who evi
dently set the fashion for the com
munity. Besides his richly colored
beads and feathers he had some
how been able to secure a sleigh bell
of the ordinary type.

NEW TYPE OF
PLANE INVENTED
DAYTON, O.—An airplane that
will be harder to “crack up” than
most of those now flying has been
designed by D. E. Dunlap, aero
nautical engineer, and soon will be
ready for test flights.
Two of the fruitful causes of
trouble when an airplane goes into
a nose-dive are the propeller and
heavy power plant, which often are
forced back upon the pilot, injuring
or killing him.
Dunlap’s ship will have two mo
tors placed between the wings and
at the sides and back of the pilot
and his companion. They are
“pushers” with the propellers in the
rear. This eliminates dirt from the
engine and the terrific noise and
gives passengers a clear view direct
ly ahead.
Of more importance, it permits
the ship to be built with a blunt
metal nose. When it comes down
on its nose, it will simply “nose

Strassburg Paper Leads Move For Alsace-Lorraine Freedom
FEAR OF RIOT
x BLOCKS FRENCH
OPPOSITION
Provinces Germanic
in Race, Writer
Says.
CHICAGO—A movement for free
dom in Alsace-Lorraine, fostered by
Dr. Eugene Ricklin’s newspaper, Die
Zukunft, which cries its hatred of
French rule has been launched, ac
cording to a Strassburg story copy
righted by The Tribune.
Paul Schall, 30, art student and
transient writer in an interview yes
terday answered the attacks upon
the autonomist organ.
Can’t Curb Paper.
“In spite of all the attacks upon
Die Zukunft,” IMr. Schall said, “this
autonomist organ in two years has
reached a relatively large circula
tion, which since has been its sole
source of income. Strassburg and
Alsatian business houses, and even
the directors of the autonomist
movement, do not dare risk French
censure by advertising with us.
“Our readers, numbering 30,000,
range from the intelligentsia to the
workers, including a small but grow
ing slice of the bourgeois.
“Periodic efforts to stamp us out
are useless. Die Zukunft merely
changes its offices and publishes
elsewhere. They cannot stamp out
expression of public opinion and
convictions. A quarter of a million
persons, approximately 75 per cent
of the population of Haut Rhin, Bas
Rhin, and Moselle—and that’s only
a conservative estimate—would vote
unhesitatingly for an autonomous
government in a plebiscite.”
Riot Is Feared.
French officials, although their
executive powers in the district are
extremely elastic, have taken no
drastic measures against the news
paper other than to look the other
way when nationalists and royalists
demonstrate against it. It is feared
any overt act might lead to serious
rioting, particularly In Strassburg.
The political director of Die Zu
kunft is Dr. Ricklin, who, French
editors and anti-autonomlsts charge,
Is suspected of sedition, because for
14 years he was president of the
Landtag or provincial diet. If that
be treason, Dr. Ricklin and his sup
porters say, “make the most of it.”
The reiterated assertion by Gen.
Taufflieb, senator from the depart
ment of Bas Rhin and Strassburg,
that Alsace-Lorraine is racially
French, was answered by M. Schall.
Germany In Race.
“If Alsace-Lorraine is French be
cause the tricolor flies over its post
offices then you may as well say
that Hindus are Londoners and
Senegalese are Parisians. For all
France’s efforts in the last eight
years to make us French and its
legislative efforts to make German
a secondary language, the apparent
fact is that the provinces are Ger
manic in race and Germanic lingual
ly and culturally. The language
used by the newspapers of Strass
burg alone is one indication of the
lingual predilections of these peo
ple.”
Officials Are Imported.
Another important factor in the
^Aeral situation is mainly political.
/Since the “liberation” of the dis
tricts, Moselle, Haut Rhin, and Bas
Rhin have been governed in most
matters by a series of Paris ap
pointed commissions, ranging from
the superior council of Alsace and
Lorraine to the consultative com
mittee of Alsace and Lorraine, and
from the hated chief of the Herriot
ministry to the consultative commit
tee of today.
The personnel of these various
legislating bodies has changed vir
tually with every new cabinet, and
a fresh set of Paris politicians has
come each time, seeking to intro
duce new French ideas into a com
munity which, first, is particularist
and individualistic, and which, sec
ond, in Germanic in spirit and race.
Therefore, it is only natural that
the Alsatians, who had their own
landtag or diet before the war, have
come to regard the present ever
changing provincial regime with
hostility.
Railroad Passenger
Business Shows Ist
Gain in 5 Years
WASHINGTON—After five years
of almost constant decrease in rail
way passenger business and earn
ing. figures made public by the in
terstate commerce commission show
that for the first six months of 1926
railway passenger revenues exceed
ed those for the corresponding
period of 1925.
Passenger revenue of class one
railroads for the six months ended
with June aggregated $504,254,107,
compared with $498,526,206 for the
corresponding period of 1925, While
the increase was only $5,727,841, it
is regarded as indicative of a gen
eral trend, because in recent months
there has been a gradual increase
in passnger revenues.
The 1925 passenger business was
23 per cent under 1920. The de
crease was attributed mainly to in
creased use of automobiles and bus
compitition.

tions.

KING’S SISTER
FORCED TO SELL
PRICELESS ART
LONDON—Financial losses, it has
been disclosed, have forced King
George’s sister, the Duchess of Fife,
to sell her almost priceless collec
tion of Romney paintings and the
antique furniture of her palatial
London home.
Further sales may be necessitated
by chaotic conditions in the affairs
of the late Lord Farquhar, trustee
of the estate of the Duke of Fife,
who died in 1912.
Lord Farquhar was a leading
banker, an associate of members of
the royal family, and close friend of
King Edward VII. He died in 1922
at the age of 79, and a sensation
was caused when it was announced
that his will provided legacies, some
as high as $750,000, to various mem
bers of the royal family, including
King George, Queen Mary and
Prince George.
The largest legacies were left to
Princess Arthur of Connaught and
the boy earl of Mac Duff, respective
ly daughter and grandson of the
Duchess of Fife.
It was soon hinted that the estate
might not be large enough to meet
all the legacies, but the first real
insight into Farquhar’s financial
affairs came when the Conservative
party took over a large portion of
the estate, claiming it represented
party funds of which Farquhar for
many years had been the treasurer.
The Farquhar legacies are not
likely to be paid, it is said.

MEXICO SEEKS
IMMIGRANTS;
BANS PAUPERS
MEXICO ClTY—Abandoning the
cry “Mexico for Mexicans,” Mexico
is going into the field for immi
grants.
The new immigration bill just
drafted in the department of agri
culture, which will be introduced
with President Calles’ approval this
week, has features which distinguish
it from immigration bills of Mexico
or other countries. Mexico bids
only for farmers, who must come
with certificates of character and
sufficient funds to make a deposit
guaranteeing payment on home
steads on irrigated land.
Hang Out Sign.
The sign, “No Paupers Need Ap
ply” is hung out. Mexico will have
immigration agents in all countries
in which it seeks immigrants, who
will work jointly with the Mexican
consuls, the latter issuing the cer
tificates of health, character and
financial standing demanded by the
government.
Mexico wants no laborers who
may enter in competition with Mex
ican laborers. It wants only immi
grants who will become independent
farmers and add to the stability of
the country. The failure of agra
rianism has taught the government
that small farmers cannot be
brought into existence at the ex
pense of the lalger farms, for the
killing of their credit kills thj credit
of others and injures all other na
tional credits, according to officials.
Plan Good Roads.
No more lands will be seized to
make homes for immigrant farm
ers. The millions of acres of na
tional lands will be subdivided into
townships, with good roads connect
ing the farm regions with the near
est large market towns. All lands
must be paid for.
The government already has irri
gation works in the north and south
of the republic and will start new
irrigation projects to give good land
to the immigrants. Concessions will
be given to private irrigation and
colonization companies who comply
with the new immigration law.

MADISON —With many diseases
of a communicable nature at a low
ebb this summer, it is probable that
some will record the lowest preval

knowledge. This is deduced from
tabulations made by the state board
of health.
Find Little Smallpox.
The state is at present practical
ly free from smallpox. The records
show less smallpox in the first six
months than for many years-, past.
Health officials credit this to the
heavy vaccination during the last
year’s outbreak. Tn the first half of
1925, the state reported 1,265 cases
and 118 deaths from smallpox,
while in the corresponding period
of 1926 the cases were 206 and there
was only one death-.
T. B. Bate Up.
Tuberculosis in the first six
months showed an increase in
deaths, the total being 1,009, as
compared with 912 for the similar
period last year. Measles was more
prevalent than for the last six-year
period. Typhoid fever deaths for
the half-year were 18, an increase
of two over the 1925 half-year
period.

NON-PERMANENT
LEAGUE SEATS
FOR 9 NATIONS
BY HENBY WOOD.
Staff Correspondent
The United I’ress
GENEVA —The league of nations
today puts in operation its machin
ery for the election of nine non
permanent members of the league of
nations council, thereby solving the
last league problem held over from
the chaotic March session. The elec
tion is expected to take place
Wednesday.
Plan of Allotment.
Foreign Ministers Briand of
France, Chamberlain of England
and Streseniann of Germany are ex
pected to return to their respective
capitals immediately after the elec
tion, leaving subordinates to repre
sent them at remaining assembly
sessions.
The plan of allotment of the non
permanent seats calls for three coun
cil members of nonpermanent status
to surrender- their membership an
nually. The assembly, will? reserve
the right to declare certain nations
eligible fbr re-election.
One Contest Seen.
Wednesday’s assembly is expected
to elect three fbr one year, three for
two years, and three for a full three
year term, thereby permitting the
plan of rotation to become effective
next year.
Belgium, and Uruguay are believed
assured of re-election. The other
seven nonpermanent members, all
newcomers; to Hie council, probably
will be Poland; Holland, Rumania,
China, Portugal,. Salvador and either
Chile or Colombia. The principle
contest of the election ia expected
between the two Latin-American
countries.
Turks Want Seat
Pourparlers are going on for the
immediate admission of Turkey to
the league, with a nonpermanent
seat in the council for the- Angora
government. The negotiations are
being handled through the French
senator Henry de Jouvenel, former
high commissioner for Syria, who
recently visited Constantinople and
Angora and conferred with high
Ottoman officials.
A provision in the Lausanne
treaty specifies, that Turkey is to
join the league. Since the- solution
of the Mosul problem Angora has
indicated its, readings to join the
Geneva organization if it is given a
council seat as recognition of its
prestige as chief of the Moslem
people.
It is feared, however* that it is
too late to give Turkey council
seat at this session*,

MONTPELIER, Vt.—Another Re
ublican primary reverse for the
^jlidge administration will be re
corded on Tuesday when Senator
Porter Dale, Republican, Vermont,
will be renominated without opposi
tion.
Though representing the native
state of the president and of Atty.
Gen. Sargent, Senator Dale does
not bask in the favor of the ad
ministration. In fact, disfavor has
been his portion for some time, at
least since he voted for the soldier
bonus, voted to override the presi
dent’s veto of the bonus, voted for
the postal pay raise before provision
was made for increased postal
revenue, and made some unkind re
marks about the attorney general.
Hits Sargent’s Ability.
As a manifestation of magnani
mity befitting the occasion, Senator
Dale voted to confirm the appoint
ment of Mr. Sargent to the cabinet,
but not without indicating the meas
ure of the concession to official
amenities by expressing his low
opinion of Mr. Sargent’s legal abil
ity. It then became known that
there was a political, if not per
sonal, enmity of long standing ex
isting between the senator and the
president’s choice for attorney gen
eral.
As the primary campaign came on
it was bruited about that the ad
ministration was going to get Dale’s
scalp, even if it should be necessary
for the attorney general to retire
from the cabinet and attend person
ally to the scalping by becoming a
candidate against Dale for the sen
atorship.
Pick ex-Governor.
This proved erroneous. It was not
the attorney general but Mr. Sar
gent’s senior law partner, former
Gov. Stickney in the Ludlow, Vt.,
firm of Stickney, Sargent Skeeles,
who was selected to oppose Dale in
the primary.

CHICAGO Headed by Miss
Belle Sherwin of Cleveland, presi
dent, members of the board of di
rectors of the National League of
Women Voters will gather today at
the home of Mrs. William Gold Hib
bard, Winnetka, for a mid-Septem
ber conference on affairs of the
organization. which will continue
all week. Mrs. Hibbard, who is
fourth regional director of the
league, will be an absent hostess,
as she is in Europe.

meet with the directors until
Wednesday, all the sessions being
closed. Mrs. James W. Morrisson,
first vice-president of the league,
will have charge of the social and
business meetings, assisted by a
committee.

International Suffrage Alliance in
Paris in June, is expected to speak
on that topic, and to discuss the ex
clusion of the Woman’s National
party from the alliance.

DAMAGE AND LIABILITY CASES
To the Editor of The Leader:
The present half-satisfying
awards granted by Wisconsin courts
in cases of damage and liability,
prove that one so-called progressive
state judiciary is acutely near
sighted.
At the present time, for instance,
judge-made rules will allow only
specific damage awards.
When a human being submits to
an operation upon tonsils, what re
putable surgeon would remove only
one of the diseased members?
There have been similar damage
and liability claims in Wisconsin
courts in recent times, the results
of which are only half-satisfying in
comparison with those of other
states.
The electorate of the future will
put an intelligent stamp of approval
on Socialism, instead of the thread
worn progressivism, in Wisconsin
ballots.

SCARE JUVENILE OFFENDERS.
To the Editor of The Leader:
As a follow up of what I read in
Saturday’s Leader regarding how
juvenile court is conducted, I would
like to say that I think such circum
stances are poor ones in which to ex
ercise either a ready wit or biting
sarcasm. And I believe both have
been frequently aired while helpless
children stood by, tongue-tied.
Orating to a boy under 16 also
seems to me gross misuse of judicial
position, tying, as it inevitably does,
the lad’s tongue and thus ruining
the purpose for which it is uttered.
No judge who utters a brisk, dra
matic “Come, come, my boy, we like
boys here who tell us the truth,”
gets the truth from a scared juvenile
court defendant.
Nor does it seem to me to further
the understanding between county
and culprit, to point out a bit of
rouge or lip stick, and ask the own
er, in sarcastic tones, if she doesn’t
think it would be better to put her
thoughts on helping her mother
rather than upon personal adorn
ments. The latter idea may be a
worthy one, but such a presentation
is bound to alienate any responsive
ness with which a child might other
wise meet the court, after which
understanding is impossible.
The laws of character analysis
are more recent than those of the
third degree. And few adults who
have not studied psychology realize
how quickly superior sounding
words become third degrees, but the
laws of understanding and sym
pathy are surely older still.
There is an old saying—you can
catch more flies with sugar than
with vinegar. And nowhere, it
seems to me, does this apply more
aptly than to the procedure in ju
venile court. J. T. C.
Milwaukee.

G. 0. P. RECORD
WASHINGTON Turning back
control of the government at Wash
ington to the American people is
the fundamental issue of the na
tional campaign, according to a
“book of facts” issued jointly yes
terday by the Democratic senatorial
and congressional committees.
Prepared by Senator Gerry, Rhode
Island, chairman of the senatorial
committee, and Representative Old
field, Arkansas, chairman of the
congressional committee, it is de
signed to supply verbal ammunition
for Democratic orators. A foreword
announces “facts that expose the
fallacies on which the Republican
party depends for the winning of
votes in this year’s national cam
paign.”
For Big Business.
“This record reveals,” it says,
“the administration of government
by that party during the last six
years is one which has been con
sistently subservient to big business,
even to the point of paying semi
judicial bodies, like the trajdc com
mission, in its interest; which has
continuously increased expenditures
on normal government activities;
which has failed utterly to deal
with such a problem of vital na
tional import as that of farm re
lief which has depressed agricul
ture, the textile industry, the small
banker and the small merchant,
and which has robbed the United
States of that worldwide respect
we enjoyed during the last Demo
cratic administration.
“The facts show that alike in its
domestic and in its foreign policies
the Republican administration
more especially, if that is possible,
since President Coolidge went to
the white house —has been morally
and intelectually bankrupt.
Ashamed of Record.
“Republicans themselves are
ashamed of the record during the
Harding regime when the Daugh
ertys, the Falls, the Forbeses, the
Jesse Smiths, the Howard Manring
tons polluted the channels of justice.
President Coolidge, who lagged so
far behind public opinion in punish
ing Harry Daugherty, shows a sim
ilar lack of moral indignation in his
attitude toward corruption in pub
lic life. The essential spirit of Re
publicanism in government is one
of cynicism, of contempt for the
intelligence and tidalism of the
common people of the United
States.”
It is asserted that the Democratic
party is ready to provide “real farm
relief” if given control of congress.
Creation of an export marketing
corporation and adjustment of the
tariff to a competitive basis are in
cluded in the Democratic farm pro
gram.
My European
Excursions
By Edwin Robert Petre
18,000 SQUARE MILES OF
MEADOWS.
The densely populated countries
of Europe may vie with each other
in telling of how many persons live
to the square miles, but Sweden,
if it could do so, might tell of how
many grassy glades and how many
million wild flowers it supported to
the square miles, for as much as
12 per cent of that country is oc
cupied by its beautiful dales and
meadows, while over half the coun
try is given up to woodlands. There
are countries in Europe with over
600 persons to the square mile; in
Sweden there are only a sparse 32.
What this means to the tourist who
wants to get away from the crowds
can be easily imagined. I have
traveled for hours on the plains of
Skane, and through the well-wooded
province of Smaland, by lonely
lakes and meandering streams, and
in the immense expanses north of
Svealand, so majestically criss
crossed by mountains, and enjoyed
the silences of nature through hun
dreds of square miles that could
not boast even 32 fellow human be
ings.

EDDY ASSERTS
GOVERNMENT OF
SOVIET STABLE
Commission Returns
After Study of
Conditions.
NEW YORK—After a month’s in
tensive study of conditions in Soviet
Russia, members of the Sherwood
Eddy commission returned to the
United States, expressing the con
viction that this country should
recognize the Russian soviet gov
ernment. The commission and un
official delegation made the recom
mendation without passing in any
way on the merits of the soviet
system from a political viewpoint.
The delegation was the first
group of Americans to enter Russia
to study the political, economic, so
cial and religious conditions to de
termine the advisability of recog
nizing the Russian government.
Problems Are Studied.
Lawyers, writers, eduactors and
prominent churchmen composed the
delegation. Two women members
made a study of the woman problem
under the soviet regime.
Members of the delegation said
the Russian authorities placed at
their disposal government docu
ments as well as allowing them un
hampered access to all government
Institutions and industrial plants.
The Americans interviewed promi
nent soviet leaders.
Admitting there were phases of
the soviet system which seemed oo
jetcionable to outsiders, the com
mission members declared the soviet
government had greatly benefited
the masses of the people and was
one the most stable governments
in Europe.
Head of Delegation.
Mr. Eddy, secretary for Asia of
the national council of the Young
Men’s Christian Assn., headed the
delegation. Other members were Dr.
Charles C. Morrison, editor </f The
Christian Century; Dr. Mathew
Splnka, Chicago, and William Dan
forth, manufacturer, of St. Louis.

The issue of the strike has come

make any concessions and insist on
abject surrender. They obviously
mean to starve the million miners
and their families into it. Mean

having committed itself some
months ago to “a general reduction
of wages throughout the country”

steel themselves to renewed resist

whither he has gone for his vaca

Daily More Desperate.
And so the situation grows daily
more desperate. Whereas at first
workers all over England gave
everything they could spare—even
their tawdry jewelry often—in
spirited sympathy with the heroic
struggle of the men, voluntary con
tributions become inevitably scanter.
During the first few weeks of the
strike many families had more to
eat than they had had since 1921,
the time of the last strike. Since
1921 their meager wages have been
cut because of the deduction which
is made every week to pay back to
the “Guardians” for relief given
them then. And every penny doled
to them during these 17 weeks is
a mortgage on their future wages.
They know the meaning of that.
They’ve paid since 1921, for the last
strike.
And so it is not charity that is
given them weekly by the Guardi
ans. It is a burden which they
must bear for years to come.
Dole Very Limited.
The amount they get is very lim
ited —as little as $2 a week for the
mother, and 50 cents additional for
each child. Unmarried men get
nothing. And it is only food—not
cotton to mend their clothing, nor
a penny for cobbling their shoes.
For 17 weeks, nothing of these.
In some districts the “Guardians”
have refused all succor. In others,
school authorities have denied to
strikers’ children the usual school
feeding. For lack of nourishment
for themselves, mothers cannot
nurse their babies. Everywhere
parents go starkly “without” that
the children may eat. In one dis
trict a school authority weighed a
half-starved child, and pitilessly de
declared that only those children
who were even punier would be
fed.
The most remarkable feature of
the strike is that after months of
the most horrible privation there
should be still the solidarity of pur
pose which these 4,000,000 people
show through the widely scattered
area. From Scotland to the south
of England, Cook is greeted with
most idolatrous ovations and liter
ally carried on the shoulders of the
men from place to place.

To observers the spirit is almost
increditable. To outsiders the un
flinching, almost dogged opposition
to longer hours is not quite under
standable. They do not know that
the seven-hour day in the mines
means seven hours of actual dig
ging that the miles which the men
walk (or crawl) under the surface
of the earth to get to the coal face
itself are not counted in the work
day. There are men who are obliged
to walk as many as four miles from
the entrance of the pit to the place
of digging—and back again to their
hovels, but these weary hours go un
paid.
The men who go back—and it is
undeniable that more are weaken
ing as one hopeless day follows an
other—are impelled by hunger and
fear, not lack of faith in their lead
ers.

Contrast in Rural Lands.
But in reckoning the endurance of
the strikers, Cook and the other
leaders must deal with the insidi
ously unnerving factor of idleness.
The enforced leisure is at once
strange and disturbing to men who
are unaccustomed to it. And more
even than the shortage of bread and
potatoes, this imponderable factor
contributes increasingly to a dubious
outcome.
A curious impression one gets,
driving through rural England and
Scotland. On the one hand are
glimpses of acres and acres of feu
dal parks and gardens—the vast es
tates owned by the aristocracy.
Sometimes the fences w r hich protect
these luxurious grounds from the
vulgar view, stretch for miles along
the road. On the other hand are
the smoke stacks of the mines, nu
merously scattered through most of
the country. And close by, the dis
mal rows of little gray hovels where
the miners live, six and eight in a
single room.
In the great estates are sunken
gardens and exquisite fountains
brought from Italy. In the min
ers’ homes is neither light nor wa
ter. The beds are used in shifts.
The overcrowded rooms are foul
with the intimate living of too many
human beings.
Admit Subsidy Needed.
The fact that the coal mines as
they are now organized dp not pay,
and cannot, is admitted by both
sides. The question, according to
such economists as John Maynard
Keynes, is who is to pay the sub
sidy necessary for their maintenance
until some reorganization is effect
ed, and what is to be the nature of
the reorganization.
The owners, and apparently the
Baldwin government, insist that
the workers pay the subsidy in long
er hours and reduced wages. The
miners declare that the government
must pay the subsidy until the in
dustry is nationalized and managed
as a unit instead of in unprofitable
and competing veins: as at present,
i Battle of All Workers.
And because they feel that theirs
is but the beginning of the strug
gle which confronts labor in all
British industry—a conviction en
gendered by Baldw himself —the
miners are stirred to an almost
epic heroism. It has become not
their battle alone, but that of all
workers in England. They fight not
only for their own standard of liv
ing but in a more glorious and
mightier cause, for a more abundant
life for their children’s children.
Whether they win or lose, this
spirit lends strength to their deter
mination and grim fortitude to their
sacrifices.

KANSAS FLOOD
LOSS PLACED
AT $2,000,000
BURLINGTON, Kan.—Flood wa
ters of the Neosho river which
swept this section had caused prop
erty damage amounting to more
than $2,000,000 and the loss of three
lives, it was estimated today.
The flood followed a downpour
of rain totalling 11 inches.
Six Feet Deep.
Ohe hundred and fifty families
in Burlington were homeless and
other towns in the river valley re
ported extensive damage from the
flood. Scores of farmers living in
the lowlands were forced to flee
with their families ahead of the
rushing torrent.
Railroads and highways were in
undated. Water stood six feet
deep in the business section of Bur
lington, Sunday, but receded here
late last night.
The area affected by the flood
approximates 150 square miles and
reports indicate scores of farm
homes have been damaged by the
water.
Had Ample Warning.
Persons in the flooded area had
ample warning of the danger and
made their escape in boats.
Charles Rodgers, 60, a farmer,
died of heart disease when warned
by a neighbor to flee for his life;
Billy Brandon, 4, was drowned
when a boat in which he was being
rowed to high ground capsized.
Jack Grieg was struck and killed
by lightning.
A similar flood swept Burlington
four years ago.

GIVES EXCUSE
FOR BIC FEE IN
METALS CASE
BY E. W. LEWIS.
Staff Correspondent
NEW YORK—Documents setting
forth opinions of a Swiss jurist on
the legality of the American Metal
Co., were read into the record of
the Harry M. Daugherty-Thomas W.
Miller trial today.
Daugherty, former attorney gen
eral, and Miller, former alien prop
erty custodian, are on trial charged
with conspiracy to defraud the
government in connection with the
return of the property.
Led to Conspiracy.
Col. William Rand, of defense
counsel, offered the documents as
a foundation for parts of his cross
examination of Richard Merton of
Frankfort, Germany, whose nego
tiations were with the late Jesse
Smith, the late John T. King,
Daugherty and Miller are alleged
to have actuated the conspiracy and
brought about the restoration of the
$7,000,000 in assets involved.
Richard Merton, the wealthy
German financier, again took the
stand today and told how he came
to this country in 1921 in an at
tempt to obtain a return of the as
sets of the American Metal Co.
He said bankruptcy of the Metal
bank of Frankfort, the Swiss Metal
Co. of Basle and the Frankfort
Metal Trust Co. probably would
have resulted had he failed.
Haste Was Necessary.
He said haste was necessary to
prevent the financial collapse of the
Merton fortunes, therefore he was
willing to pay the late John T. King
$441,000 “commission” to handle
the case.

Government to Lose $17,460,000 by Sale of Five Ships
CITE COSTS TO
RECONDITION
BIC U.S. LINERS
Vessels Could Be
Purchased for
$14,938,000.
WASHINGTON—On the basis of
appraised values the five passenger
vessels of the United States lines
offered for sale by the shipping
board will mean an actual out-of
pocket loss to the government of
$17,460,000, not including such
amounts as may be paid later to the
Germans to compensate for the
seizure of the ships during the war.
The shipping board has spent
$11,342„030 on the Leviathan, of
which $8,000,000 represents the
original cost or reconditioning. On
the George Washington, $4,209,049
has been spent, $3,000,000 of which
was for reconditioning. On the Re
public, $4,847,502 has been spent, of
which $3,500,000 represents the cost
of original reconditioning.
Vessels Are Appraised.
The shipping board has placed
appraised values on the vessels of
the United States lines as follows:
Leviathan, $6,867,900; George
Washington, $2,146,300; Republic,
$3,348,200; President Roosevelt, sl,-
287,000, and President Harding, sl,-
287,000. The last two ships were
built by the board at a cost of
about $6,000,000 each.
On the basis of the appraised val
ues, the five going ships of the
United States lines, with a guar
antee of continued operation for 10
years, could be bought for $14,938,-
000, or $17,640,000 less than they
have cost the government. Whether
the board will seriously consider
such an offer is not known at this
time.
Will Oppose Sale.
Some members of the board will
oppose the sale of the line at such
a figure, it is understood. The
“minority” in the board believes
that an attempt is being made to
get rid of the United States lines
before congress meets and it is ex
pected that it will oppose the sale
unless assurance is obtained that
the line will be better off under
private operation than under gov
ernment operation.

REMOVAL OF 2
0. S. JUDGES IN
ALASKA ASKED
WASHINGTON—Prompt removal
of two federal judges and a federal
district attorney, accused of “scan
dalous misconduct” in their admin
istration of Alaskan territorial af
fairs, is demanded in a long tele
gram sent to President Coolidge by
Basil Manly, director of the People’s
Legislative Service, an organization
founded by the late Senator Rob
ert M. La Follette.
On Cal’s Shoulders.
Responsibility for widespread
bootlegging, drug peddling, vice,
corruption, and other crime is
placed squarely on the president in
the telegram, which says that, al
thziugh the senate judiciary com
mittee disapproved the reappoint
ment of Federal Judges Reed and
Ritchie and Dist. Atty. Shoup, “you
have allowed them to remain in of
fice —a disgrace to the federal bench
and a menace to law enforcement.”
Reed, Ritchie and Shoup were
originally appointed at the sugges
tion of former Atty. Gen. Harry M.
Daugherty. Before their terms ex
pired a number of department of
justice investigations seemed to sub
stantiate charges against the trio,
and the then attorney general, .Har
lan F. Stone, and Asst. Atty. Gen.
Mabel Walker Willebrandr both
recommended that the men be
dropped.
Too Corrupt, Claim.
President Coolidge, however,
named them for reappointment, and
the nominations were referred to
the senate judiciary committee,
which, after hearings, unanimously
urged their withdrawal, “to prevent
exposure in the senate,” according
to Manly, who quotes one senator
as asserting that “conditions were
too corrupt, too indecent and too
scandalous to be publicly discussed.”
Judge Ritchie, according to the
charges reviewed in Manly’s tele
gram, is a fugitive from justice in
Utah and has “surrounded hiinself
with questionable characters.”

Radio receiving sets of the best reproductive
quality should be made available for all, and
we hope to make them cheap enough so that
all may buy.
The day has gone by when the radio receiv
ing set is a plaything. It must now be an
instrument of service.

America has purchased for one million
dollars station WEAF from the American
Telephone and Telegraph Company, that
company having decided to retire from the
broadcasting business.
The Radio Corporation of America will
assume active control of that station on
November 15.
National Broadcasting
Company Organized
The Radio Corporation of America has de
cided to incorporate that station, which has
achieved such a deservedly high reputation
for the quality and character of its programs,
under*the name of the National Broadcast
ing Company, Inc.
The Purpose of the
New Company
The purpose of that company will be to pro
vide the best program available for broad
casting in the United States.
The National Broadcasting Company will
not only broadcast these programs through
station WEAF, but it will make them avail
able to other broadcasting stations through
out the country so far as it may be practic
able to do so, and they may desire to take
them.
It is hoped that arrangements may be made so
that every event of national importance may
be broadcast widely throughout the United
States.
No Monopoly of the Air
The Radio Corporation of America is not in
any sense seeking a monopoly of the air.
That would be a liability rather than an
asset. It is seeking, however, to provide
machinery which will insure a national dis
tribution of national programs, and a wider
distribution of programs of 'the highest
quality.
If others will engage in this business the
Radio Corporation of America will welcome
their action, whether it be cooperative or com
petitive.
If other radio manufacturing companies,
competitors of the Radio Corporation of
America, wish to use the facilities of the
National Broadcasting Company for the
purpose of making known to the public
their receiving sets, they may do so on the
same terms as accorded to other clients.

A Public Advisory Council
In order that the National Broadcasting
Company may be advised as to the best
type of program, that discrimination may
be avoided, that the public may be assured
that the broadcasting is being done in the
fairest and best way, always allowing for
human frailties and human performance, it
has created an Advisory Council, composed
of twelve members, to be chosen as repre
sentative of various shades of public opin
ion, which will from time to time give it the
benefit of their judgment and suggestion.
The members of this Council will be an
nounced as soon as their acceptance shall
have been obtained.
The President of the new National Broad
casting Company will be M. H. Ayles
worth, for many years Managing Director
of the National Electric Light Association.
He will perform the executive and adminis
trative duties of the corporation.
Mr. Aylesworth, while not hitherto identi
fied with the radio industry or broadcast
ing, has had public experience as Chairman
of the Colorado Public Utilities Commis
sion, and, through his work with the asso
ciation which represents the electrical in
dustry, has a broad understanding of the
technical problems which measure the pace
of broadcasting.
One of his major responsibilities will be to
see that the operations of the National
Broadcasting Company reflect enlightened
public opinion, which expresses itself so
promptly the morning after any error of
taste or judgment or departure from fair
play.
We have no hesitation in recommending the
National Broadcasting Company to the
people of the United States.
It will need the help of all listeners. It will
make mistakes. If the public will make known
its views to the officials of the company from
time to time, we are confident that the new
broadcasting company will be an instrument
of great public service.

NO ONE MAN TO
CARRY BALL
FOR ILLINI
URBANA, Ill.—There’s no use
denying the fact that there is a
spirit of optimism in the University
of Illinois football camp as the Illini
gird themselves for the opening of
practice Wednesday.
When work begins Wednesday
morning, Coach Zuppke will direct
60 players. The outlook is for a
veteran line and a green backfield.
‘•Red” Grange is gone and the Illini
must look to three untried players
to carry the ball.
Ineligibilities, always a fly in the
ointment, are not many among the
players favored, but two of Zuppke’s
veteran linemen have scholastic
tangles to unsnarl before they are
eligible. If these two men come
through, “Zup” will have from end
to end practically the same line
which he used last year. Add, a like
ly sophomore, such as Nowack, the
big tackle from Pana, and the Illini
should have a pretty up-and-coming
line.
The backfield combination at the
outset is likely to be Timm, Lanum,
Peters and Daugherity. All of these
men are eligible. The first three as
freshmen won their spurs last year
and Daugherity was the regular
fullback. None of them is a Grange
but each can do his bit in carrying
the ball and Illinois may have a
well-rounded backfield with the
ground-gaining power distributed in
stead of concentrated in one star.

FOREST HILLS, N. Y.—The an

toms of falling off lately and has
been beaten by Vincent Richards,

by the latter in the Davis cup
matches last week, the first time
Tilden ever had been defeated in
Davis cup play.
Bill Johnston, who beat both La
Coste and Jean Borotra In the Da
vis cup play, is considered Tilden’s
chief menace. Borotra is one of the
few stars not competing in the tour
nament starting today.

Richards, William Johnston,

Williams, Takeichi Harada of Ja
pan, Manuel Alonzo of Spain and a
few others are certain to make the
play lively and interesting.

DEMPSEY’S WORKOUTS
SECRET AFTER TODAY
STROUDSBURG, Pa.—Gene Tun
ney was to do his usual training
round today. A little road work, a
short while with the punching bag
and few not too strenuous rounds in
the ring, was the accepted program.
Tomorrow he will leave the ring
entirely alone, and the same prob
ably Wednesday, all because he be
lieves he is in too fine a condition.
Tunney’s fine physical condition
so long before a fight prevents him
from doing gruelling work in the
ring or out, his trainers say. The
challenger is laying low, but by Fri
day may swing into hard training
again.

M. U. GRIDDERS
START WORK
TODAY
LAKE BEULAH, Wis—The tig
drive is on again, with Coach Frank
J. Murray and almost 50 candidates
for the 1926 Marquette university
football team in training for the
fall campaign in Marquette’s island
camp here.
Headed by Coach Murray and
Capt. Don Craine, the Hilltop ath
letes invaded the island late yes
terday. The first bit of actual grid
practice is set for tomorrow.
Sophomores Look Good.
Although most of the youngsters
in camp here now are newcomers to
the varsity squad and despite the
fact that the task which faces the
Hilltop coaches is a gigantic one, the
case is not hopeless. There are few
lettermen to count on, but many of
the incoming sophomores are big
husky fellows, with good records
both in high school and on the 1925
freshman team.
Marquette will build its eleven
from the center out and back this
fall. With Capt. Craine, Ed O’Neill
and Tom O’Malley all ready to
play stellar ball at center, and the
Kampine brothers both back for the
guard positions, the coaches have
little to worry them at those posi
tions. Among other linemen who
came to camp yesterday were Red
Johnson, Rhinelander; Clarence
Muhlick, Kenosha; Denver Shimek,
Manitowoc; Lloyd Lund, Green
Bay; Sam Randall, Bay City, Mich.;
Bill Clancy, Nowotny, Gibout,
Smith, Possler and others.
Bader Among Missing.
Dick Bader, veteran fullback from
Green Bay, is among the missing,
but is expected at any time, while
Joe Leary, Janesville fullback and
punter, was among the first to re
port. Quarterbacks on hand are
Jay Quasney, East Chicago, Ind.,
and Alex Hurley, Milwaukee, with
Frank Murnane, St. Paul, Minn.,
and Rupert O’Keefe, Cavalier, N.
D., overdue. Halfbacks here are
Joe Carson, El Paso, Tex.; Johnny
Kub and Joe Vallier, Milwaukee;
Walter Gebert, Merrill, Wis.; Har
ry Reichert, Milwaukee; Tim Moran,
La Crosse; Jack Geraghty, Home
dale, Idaho; Harry Clancy, Eau
Claire, and some others.
AMATEUR GOLF
TITLE PLAY
OPENS TODAY
SHORT HILLS, N. J.—America’s
amateur golfers met today in the
30th annual championship tourney.
A somewhat cloudy sky, but other
wise good golf weather, greeted the
players as they started out In the
first of the two 18-hole qualifying
rounds.
Headed by Bobby Jones, Atlanta,
title holder for the last two years,
every leading amateur was present
with the exception of Jess Sweet
ser. England and Canada also had
representatives present.
The qualifying medal rounds to
day and tomorrow will decide who
will tee off Wednesday when match
play starts and the players begin to
eliminate each other down to the
two who will meet in the finals.
