RINGWORM OF HANDS AND
FEET.
A new form of ringworm, af
fecting chiefly the hands and feet
of persons who patronize public
gymnasiums and swimimng pools,
has been recognized in the last
few years. This condition was
formerly called “eczema.”
In a technical article on the
prevalence of the trouble, Dr.
Joseph Brumberg, Buffalo skin
specialist, remarks that doubtless
there have always been a certain
number of cases of this form of
ringworm, but it seemed to come
to a crisis when three or four mil
lion young men were thrown into
such close contact in the army.
A few years after the army was
demobilized the trouble became
quite prevalent among the general
population.
Dr. Brumberg finds that the in
fection occurs wherever people
walk about barefoot, as in gym
nasiums, baths, athletic clubs,
swimming pools, summer resort
beaches, or in the home. One af
fected person leaves a bit of loose
skin which carries some of the
ringworm fungi; the next bare
foot person comes along and picks
up the flake of skin on his toes
and so acquires the disease.
Touching or scratching his toes
witß his fingers, the victim
spreads the trouble to his hands
and forearms, and sometimes to
other parts of the body.
Characteristic features of this
ringworm dermatitis are:
1. White, moist, lardlike de
posits between the toes.

On the hands the ringworm le
sions are well defined patches,
readily mistaken for simple ec
zema, situated on the sides of the
fingers and between the fingers.
On the hands or feet the trouble
may be mistaken for ivy poison
ing at first.
The ringworm spores are found
by microscopic examination of a
bit of skin shaved off the top of
a blister.
In order to eradicate the ring
worm spores from the skin it is
necessary to (1) remove all dead
skin and scales; (2) scrub to the
limit of endurance with soap and
water; (3) persistently apply
such parasiticides as salicylic
acid, potassium permanganate, or
chrysarobin. In some cases mild
X-ray treatment helps, but X-ray
alone will not cure.
Some reader reported a year
ago that he had found an effec
tive remedy for an obstinate itch
ing lesion between the toes. He
said a single daily application of
a rather strong solution of sali
cylic acid in alcohol put an end
to the trouble. I should suggest
that 30 grains of salicylic acid
in an ounce of water if alcohol
Is not obtainable, is strong
enough, and one painting or
swabbing of the affected oortion
of skin each day is sufficient.
Even this should not be used for
more than a week, unless under
medical observation.
It would be mighty bad treat
ment to apply any such parasiti
cides to a simple eczema or sim
ple dermatitis from contact with
irritating chemicals, for instance.
So before you undertake to an
nihilate the ringworm fungi be
sure you have ringworm.

People with very high blood pres

they have inherited a good arterial
system, eat the proper diet, and do
not undertake too strenuous physi
cal exercise. A great many prema
ture deaths are prevented by the
physician who discovers high blood
pressure and advises the patient
how to live with it.
Another important cause of in
creased bk»od pressure is kidney
disease. This often follows acute
infectious diseases, such as scarlet
fever, tonsilitis, rheumatism and ab
scess formations around the teeth.
Careful treatment is necessary
when these diseases are present, to
prevent development of kidney dis
ease and, with it, later development
of high blood pressure.
Another cause of increase in
blood pressure is arterial disease.
This may be caused by the infec
tious diseases previously mentioned
and requires the same preventive
measures. I* is especially impor
tant in all these cases to keep the
blood in circulation, in as bland and
unirritating form as possible. For
this reason, all irritating sub
stances, such as the various season
ing agents, mustard, horseradish,
pepper and vinegar, also alcohol,
should bo sparingly used.

In the years of drab obscurity be
fore wealth and fame arrived,
Charles Chaplin wrote a vaudeville
sketch, Twelve Just Men, and sold
it for $25 to Ernie Lotinga, an Eng
lish comedian. With Chaplin’s per

High blood pressure and harden
ing of the arteries do not neces
sarily accompany each other. A
pipe-stem artery may be accompan
ied by low blood pressure, and ar-

The chief danger in high blood
pressure is rupture of the blood ves

take place on some sudden increase
in physical exercise, such as climb

tension is one of the contributory
causes of high blood pressure. It is

which usually accompanies business

A COMPLETE PICTURE STORY
IN A WEEK
Son of the Sheik, at
Wisconsin, Much
Like Father.
The power of photobraphic pro
duction makes it possible for those
who admire the acting of the late
Rudolph Valentino to again see him
act, this week in The Son of the
Sheik at the Wisconsin theater.
As if to appease the crowd of
palpitating flappers who followed
so closely the details of his death,
Valentino in this, his last picture,
takes two roles, that of the sheik
and of his father.
The picture is much like the
Sheik. The photography of desert
sands, moonlight effects, Arab
camps, Is artistic in its beauty.
The acting of Vaientino is excell
ent, made more definitely noticable
because the rest of the cast plays
up to Valentino instead of to the
camera audience. Valentino is the
oustanding actor in the piece,
simply because Valentino is the only
actor who is allowed in the center
of the lens.
Action in the piece is rapid
enough to satisfy the most impetu
ous. Arab camp scenes, dancing
scenes, knife fights, horse back es
capades, all pass in swift succes
sion on the screen.
Plot is lacking, as it usually is in
this type of picture where the hero
escapes from his captors barely in
time to leap to his horse, outwit
his pursuers, and overtake the girl
and sweep her saddle to his own.
But of course that was not Mr. Val
entino’s fault.
Aside from the feature picture,
the most interesting numbers on
the variegated program was the
selections from the Song of the
Flower, played by the Wisconsin
theater orchestra, Glenn Welty con
ducting, and Joe Termini’s Somno
lent Melodies in which the enter
tainer amuses the audience with
clever and unique string music.

Here is a nice dish of meat to
serve sliced cold as a luncheon or
supper dish or for sandwich filling
to carry on a picnic:
Sliced Pressed Beef.
Take a shin of beef and two
pounds of the round. Crack the bone
of the shin, put the meat into a
kettle, cover with cold water and
bring slowly to a boil. Add salt and
pepper, two tablespoonfuls of vine
gar, a large onion sliced and cook
all together until the meat falls
from the bones. Skim out the meat
and bone and reduce the liquor by
boiling; when half the quantity,
strain through a cheesecloth. Pick
the meat from the bones in small
bits. To the meat liquor add a
pinch of powdered mace, cloves, all
spice and cayenne and one-half tea
spoonful each of celery salt and
mustard. Boil the liquor and re
turn the meat to it, mixing thor
oughly. When well heated through
turn into an earthen bowl or njold
rinsed in cold water; cover with a
weight and set away to cool.
Simple Dessert.
Butter slices of bread and place
in a deep baking dish, coyer with
canned blueberries or fresh hot
stewed ones. Cover and let stand
an hour or two and serve unmolded,
or heat and serve hot with sugar
and cream. Any juicy berries may
be used in place of blueberries.
Eggs Scrambled With Ham.
Break three or four eggs into a
saucepan, add a little milk, season
ing of salt and pepper and butter,
then add one-half cupful of chopped
cooked ham; stir until well mixed
and serve with buttered toast and
fried potatoes.
Macaroni With Kidneys.
If possible, get young lamb kid
neys, if not, beef kidneys will do.
Scale, cut in small pieces and brown
in a large frying pan with part lard
and part butter. Add one medium
sized onion and enough water to
keep from burning. Cook 15 or 20
minutes, then add one can of to
matoes, cook down and season to
taste. Boil until tender, imported
macaroni, drain and place on a
large platter. Pour over the kid
ney mixture.
Molded Fruit Salad.
Beat the yolks of four eggs, add
four tablespoons vinegar, one-quar
ter teaspoon mustard, four table
spoons sugar and one-quarter cup
butter. Season with salt and pep
per. Cook until it thickens and let
cool. Dissolve two tablespoons gela
tine in one-half cup fruit juice and
add one-half cup boiling water.
When this cools, add to the dress
ing. Whip one cup cream, and add
to dressing and gelatine. Into this
mixture stir one cup bananas, one
cup pineapple and one cup peaches,
Mold in three small baking powder
cans and serve sliced with whipped

Kidney Omelet.
Four kidneys, six tablespons but
ter, one tablespoon chopped parsley,
two tablespoons cream, salt and
pepper to taste. Melt three table
spoons butter in frying pan. Skin
kidneys, cut out into small pieces
and toss in hot butter about three
minutes. Whip whites of eggs to a
stiff froth, then add yolks, season
ing, parsley and cream, last the
kidney. Make the remaining but
ter hot in frying pan, pour in ome
let pan and fry over fire about six
minutes. When the edges are set,
fold edges over so the omelet as
sumes an oval shape, be careful that
it is not done too much. To brown
top, hold pan before fire or put in
oven, neves* turn an omelet over in
pan. Slip carefully on a hot dish
and serve immediately. This can
be halved for a small family.

rots and boil them until tender, cool
them and pack into quart jars. Fil!
the jars to overflowing with a hot
liquid made by boiling together for
five minutes a pint of vinegar, a cup
of sugar and two tablespoons of
mixed spices. Seal the jars at once.
Corn Sauce.
Cut fine, one large head of cab
bage, let it stand over night and in
the morning drain off the water.
Boil one dozen large ears of corn,
chop fine three green and three red
peppers. Dissolve two tablespoon#
of mustard in vinegar. Mix all in
gredients together and cover the
mixture with vinegar. Add two
tablespoons of salt and a pint of
vinegar. Boil the whole for half an
hour. Seal the sauce in pint jars
which are still hot.
Chicken Chartreuse.
One cup cold cooked chicken, salt
and pepper and a little grated lemon
rind, One egg, one cup chicken stock
or half cream and half stock, two
level tablespoons granulated gela
tine. Mince the chicken fine, pass
through a sieve, season to taste.
Soak the gelatine for 10 minutes in
the cold, stock. Then heat to boil
ing point and when the gelatine la
dissolved strain it over the chicken.
Add the yolk of the egg lightly and
the white beaten to a froth. When
partly cooled, turn into a mold and
put aside until very cold. When it
has set, unmold and cut in very thin
slices.
Sponge Pound Cake.
Beat one-half cupful of butter to
a cream, add the grated rind of a
lemon and gradually beat in one
half cupful of sugar and beaten
yolks of four eggs, one cupful of
flour sifted with a tablespoonful of
cornstarch and a teaspoonful of
baking powder; lastly, fold in the
stiffly beaten whites of the eggs
and bake in a loaf 30 to 40 minutes.
For a fine-grained cake use one-half
teaspoonful of baking powder; the
texture of this cake is like sponge
cake. —Nellie Maxwell.

American Imports Top Exports, Newest Survey Reveals
COUNTRY LESS
SELF EXISTING
IN 25 YEARS
Export Up 70 Pct. Im
ports Jump 300
Per Cent.
NEW YORK—American food im
ports now exceed exports, according
to a survey published today by
Dominick Dominick. The growing
industrialization of the United
States has rendered it less self-suffi
cient so far as food supply is con
cerned.
Twentyfive years ago American
exports of foodstuffs were very
much greater than imports, it is
pointed out, but since that time
these exports have increased about
70 per cent, while food imports have
increased almost 300 per cent.
Europe Best Customer.
Last year the imports of food
stuffs into this country were val
ued at $928,000,000 or 21.9 per cent
of the total import trade, and ex
ports at $892,000,000 or 18.5 per
cent of the total exports.
Europe is of course by far the
best customer for American foods
and the decline in American exports
is generally attributed to the post
war poverty of that continent. As
far as foodstuffs are concerned, how
ever, a proportionately declining
European demand was in evidence
long before the war.
See Unfavorable Balance.
In the years 1905-1909 Europe
consumed 80 per cent of the food ex
ports from this country and during
the next five years 70 per cent. The
war period was abnormal, but in the
four years beginning with 1921 the
percentage declined to G 8 per cent.
It is about 64.5 per cent today.
An unfavorable balance of trade
In foodstuffs is therefore a condition
likely to continue. Due to the char
acter of the commodities, this does
not make America seriously de
pendent upon foreign food supplies.
It will be offset by the. export of
manufactures, for which a new and
more evenly distributed demand is
being developed.

meat has not declined,” the letter

weight and that beef has reflected
such declines as have taken place.

under that of a year ago and it re
flects the increased supply of heavy
cattle and quality yearlings. Prices

ago.

choice cattle which constitute,
roughly, about a quarter of the re
ceipts, and selling below last year’s
figures, it is equally true that the
beef obtained from them is well be
low last year’s prices.”
“Considering beef cattle in toto, the
commons and mediums as well as

higher than they were at the begin
ning of the year and beef prices are
not out of line.”

ROADS' RUNNING
EXPENSES UP
CHICAGO —That the railroads of
the United States are in a position
to handle a much greater volume of
traffic without greatly increasing
their operating costs is indicated by
the operating figures covering the
operations of the class 1 railroads
in the first seven months of 1926.
During that period when freight
traffic rose to the highest levels in
American railroad history, a larger
percentage of the gross operating
revenues was saved for fixed
charges and dividends than in the
corresponding period last year.
The operating revenues of the
class 1 railroads in the first seven
months of the year, according to
the bureau of railway economics,
totaled $3,584,739.17 as compared
with $3,418,506,499 in the same
period last year, an increase of 4.9
per cent. The operating expenses
totaled $3,584,739,917 as compared
with $2,622,298,154 last year, an in
crease of 2.8 per cent.
Excepting persons killed at high
way crossings there was a reduc
tion in the first month of 1926 in
fatal railway accidents to all
classes of persons, it is pointed out
in The Railway Age in its current
issue. The number of passengers
killed declined from 52 to 41. The
number of employes killed on duty
declined from 628 to 619. The num
ber of all persons killed who did
not meet their deaths at highway
crossings, including trespassers, de
clined from 1,788 to 1,678. On the
other hand, the number killed at
highway crossings increased from
771 to 859, or about 11% per cent.
The Atchison, Topeka Santa Fe
railway continues to report an in
crease in car loadings over a year
ago. In the week ended Sept. 10,
the road loaded and received from
connecting lines 40,204 revenue
freight cars as compared with 35,-
993 in the same period last year, an
increase of 11.69 per cent.

HOLO PRIMARIES
OCRING WEEK
X BY PAUL R. MALLON.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
WASHINGTON—The last of the
states’ 42 primary elections and six
conventions choosing nominees for
congress will be held this week.
Tomorrow candidates will be des
ignated in eight states —Massachu-
setts, Maryland, Colorado, Louisi
ana, Michigan, Vermont, Washing
ton and New York. Wednesday and
Thursday Connecticut conventions
will perform the same function.
This will clear away the pri
maries for opening of the interparty
fight of the Democrats and Repub
licans for control of the next con
gress.
Three Prominent Issues.
The issues, aside from local ques
tions, involved in the primary finale
are the same that have character
ized the previous 34 races —prohi-
bition, the world court and, in some
localities, the Ku Klux Klan.
All but two of the eight states,
Michigan and New York, are staging
senatorial races. The most important
contest is in Colorado, where Sen
ator Rice W. Means, Republican, is
faced with opposition of three can
didates. In the Democratic race
there William H. Adams, former
leader of the state senate, and Sam
uel Johnson, district judge, are con
testing for the right of opposing the
Republican candidate. Prohibition
and the Ku Klux Klan are the is
sues involved.
Situation in New York.
In New York the primary will in
volve only congressional nomina
tions because the senatorship has
been placed in the hands of state
conventions whose delegates are
chosen in the primary. The conven
tions of both Democrats and Repub
licans will be held Sept. 29.
A prospective Democratic presi
dential candidate is involved in
Maryland, where Gov. Albert C.
Ritchie is seeking renomination.
Representative John Phillip Hill,
nationally known beer advocate, is
seeking the Republican senatorial
nomination against Senator Weller,
incumbent.
Word brought to Republican and
Democratic headquarters here indi
cates that Senator Butler, chairman
of the Republican national commit
tee of Massachusetts; Senator Wes
ley Jones, Republican, Washington;
Senator Broussard, Democrat, Lou
isiana, and Senator Porter H. Dale,
Vermont, will succeed in their at
tempts for renomination. Dale has
no opposition.
DOLL CUSTOMS
ARE OBSERVED
IN MANY LANDS
NEW YORK —Because of the an
tiquity of the doll it is expected
that various customs and traditions
would become woven about it in va
rious parts of the world.
In the Orange Free State in
Africa every Fingo maiden re
ceives upon maturity a doll which
she retains until she becomes a
mother. Then her motho" gives her
a new doll which she carefully con
serves until she has a second child,
and so forth. These doHs are held
sacred and the owner neyer volun

In ancient Rome the girls fre

The River Ganges occupies a
prominent position in the religions

the stream. Fortunately, this cus

sense it still survives, for at certain
times of the year the ^udren give
expression of their thanksgiving by
casting their dolls into the sacred
stream.
When a girl is born in Japan she
fs given a small collection of dolls
known as the Hina —that are ef
figies of the emperor and empress
and five court magicians. The
child is never allowed to play with
these dolls except on holidays, the
chief of which is the Hina Matsuri,
the feast of the dolls, which falls
on March 3.
When a Japanese girl marries
she takes her Hina with her, keep
ing the collection of dolls until
her eldest son marries, at which
time they are presented him. In
this way some families possess a
number of Hinas, some which are
hundreds of years old.

MRS. HELENA MIZER.
Funeral arrangements for Mrs.
Helena Mizer, 88, pioneer resident
of Milwaukee, who died Saturday,
were conducted today at Gesu
Catholic church, Grand Ave. and
12th St., with burial in Calvary
cemetery.
Mrs. Mizer came with her family
from Germany when she was nine,
the family crossing in a sail boat
and being on the ocean two months.
After landing at Quebec the family
came to Milwaukee where the
father, Werner Trimborn, estab
lished a home in 1847.
Mrs. Mizer is survived by two
daughters, Mrs. George R. Best and
Mrs. Anna Dietz.
MRS. MARGARET EGAN.
Funeral services for Mrs. Mar
garet Egan, 86, one of the oldest
residents at the Milwaukee Catholic
Home for the Aged, 544 Astor St.,
who died yesterday, will be held at
the home chapel tomorrow, 9 a. m.,
with burial in Calvary cemetery.
Mrs. Egan was a widow 50 years
and lived with relatives in Milwau
kee until taking up her residence
in the home, 11 years ago.
JOHN C. POTTER.
Funeral services for John C. Pot
ter, 47, Wauwatosa, who died Aug.
15, at Hendaye, France, will be held
at Wauwatosa tomorrow, 2 p. m.,
with burial in Wauwatosa cemetery.
Mr. Potter, a son of Milton B. Pot
ter, Wauwatosa, died as the result
of heart trouble suffered while
working as one of 15 American Bell
Telephone engineering experts sent
to modernize telephone systems of
France and Spain.
His wife, Winifred Durham Pot
ter, and three children, John,
Eleanor and Jean, were with him
when he died and accompanied the
body to America. Besides his widow
and children Mr. Potter is survived
by his father and mother, a brother,
Charles, and a sister, Alice, all of
Wauwatosa.
GUSSIE BRYSON.
Gussie Bryson, 30, a veteran of
the World war, died at the National
Soldiers’ Horse hospital, late Sat
urday, 5 :20 p. m.
He is survived by the widow,
Mrs. Pearle Bryson, and one child,
who live at 430 sth St. Mr. Bryson
has been in the home since Sept.
28, 1925.
The body will be sent to Ataka,
Tenn., for burial.
JAMES F. WILSON.
James F. Wilson, 81, who served
in the Civil war with Co. E, 104th
Ohio infantry, died at the National
Soldiers’ Home hospital, yesterday.
He is survived by the widow, who
lives in Chicago. Funeral arrange
ments have not been completed. Mr.
Wilson entered the home March 17,
1920.
The child welfare law adopted
April 14, 1926, provides for the ap
pointment of child welfare commis
sions in cities and towns in Greece.
Every city or town is required to
provide funds for the maintenance
of infants deprived of mother’s care
and for the women nursing them.
Physicians or midwives attending
births must report them within 24
hours. All births must be registered
by the police and lists sent weekly
to the local child welfare commis
sion, which must investigate and aid
needy cases.

“THINK OF THESE THINGS"
A thinking man is the worst enemy the Prince of
Darkness can have—said Thomas Carlyle.
He is also the worst enemy of other devils —such as
capitalism.
The great trouble is that people do not think enough.
This is painfully true of the majority of the workers.
For many years, they have permitted a few capitalists to
skin them out of most of their earnings. Accordingly,
they and their families have been deprived of nearly every
thing except the bare necessities of life—and often even of
those. Their children as a rule have left school just when
their education was really beginning, and have been swal
lowed up by the industrial dragon. They have also died
by the millions because of undernourishment. The lives
of most of the workers have been stunted—some more
some less—it is only a question of degree.
As St. Paul said, “Think of these things.”
It was the evolution of industry that produced these
conditions —but it is the ignorance of the workers that
has prolonged them.
The industries became ripe for the change to collec
tivism long ago. Had the workers been thinkers, the
change would have been made long ago—and poverty and
the other social evils would have been left behind.
But most of the workers were not thinkers. They did
not know what caused their troubles. They spurned the
few Socialists who tried to tell them—and went on in their
ignorance and its consequences.
More of them are thinking now than ever before —but
all too many of them are still steeped in ignorance.
If you are one of those who have not yet begun to use
the brains that nature endowed them with, make a start
immediately. Read, study, think. Enlighten yourself—
and thus prepare yourself to enlighten others. It is only
by the general enlightenment of the workers that the
working class can muster the power to emancipate itself.
ANOTHER SUGGESTION
An Englishman visiting in America writes:
“In the part of a candid friend I should like to ask
why Americans leave so much litter in the trains and op
the streets. And why do not the railways make it easier
for a stranger to know what is the name of the station
which he is approaching? It is true the official shouts
something, but what it is he says no one can tell except
those who do not need to hear it.”
An American can only stand mute before these
charges, for they are in the main true. We are a careless
people in throwing things around and letting them lie,
and even spitting on the sidewalk. The health department
in this city says it is making progress in stopping the
latter, but the progress is not noticeable, as anyone can
see by observing men on the street. Not all railway men
call stations inaudibly, but all too many do.
And the charge of non-understandable calling is as
applicable to the street cars as it is of the railroad trains.
When a conductor urges the passengers to move up the
aisle so as to make room for more sardines—suckers,
rather—he usually speaks -with the utmost distinctness
and can be heard with perfection right up to the other
end of the car, despite the noise. But when he calls the
name of a street, too often nobody can tell what it is, not
even those close to him, for it is only an inarticulate
mumble. Of course there are exceptions.
We don’t blame the conductors for this or any other
shortcomings of the system. They obey instructions, ana
it simply shows where the emphasis was placed when the
instructions were given to them.
11,000 MILLIONAIRES
There are 11,000 millionaires in the United States,
according to an article in a banker’s journal, which would
not be likely to exaggerate the number, but would be more
likely to minimize it in order to allay discontent.
Add to these the near-millionaires and the rest of the
very rich, and you have a comparatively small body of
men who rule America. This is the real “ruling class.”
Some of these men do useful work, managerial work, in
industry, but in ttieir capacity as capitalists they do no use
ful work, but are mere parasites living off the remainder
of the people..
Is it any wonder there is discontent?
While many of the people could not explain the eco
nomics of the situation they nevertheless have the feeling
that these men do not earn their incomes. Their feeling
is accurate. The Socialists explain it logically. They also
explain how the condition may be changed.
For there is no use grouching about the millionaires
and the near-millionaires. They get rich according to the
rules of the game, most of them. It is the game—the
capitalist system—that is wrong. It is based upon the
idea that the few shall have much, and not earn it. and
that the many shall have little, and earn it. The system
must be changed.

HORTHY HUNGARY'S NEW SCANDAL
The scandal of the huge franc and crown forgeries
by the pillars of Hungarian society is still agitating the
European press. Now the explosion of the Hungarian
arsenal on Csepel island shows a flash that forgery is
not the only pastime of the Horthy-Bethlen circle.
Under the Trianon treaty, Hungary was obliged to
give up all military arms and supplies to the allies. But
the military experts of the allies found very little war
material worth confiscating in Hungary. In the confu
sion following the collapse of Austria-Hungary, the Bol
shevist revolution and the Rumanian invasion, the ruling
class of Hungary cleaned out some of the largest Austrian
arsenals and concealed the loot in subterranean caves of
castles and government buildings.
The unsettled state of the Balkans and the effect of
Soviet Russia on European conditions induced the allied
governments for a while to wink at these Hungarian vio
lations of the Trianon treaty. Especially the influence of
some American millionaires, whose daughters had married
Hungarian noblemen, had much to do with this lenient
carelessness of allied inspectors.
The matter did not rest there. The Hungarian dic
tator bought at cut-rate prices large consignments of arms
and ammunition from the Austrian government during
the inflation period. And then the Hungarian Krupp,
Manfred Weiss, began to set up war factories along the
bank of the Danube under various industrial disguises,
A silk factory, a chemical fertilizer plant, shoe and leath
er goods factories, secretly produced war supplies for the
Horthy government.
The Csepel explosion suddenly called the attention
of the European press to these secret war preparations.
With the forgery cases hardly settled, a new wave of
bitter denunciation is launched against the Horthy gov
ernment.
That the European Socialist press makes the most of
this incident and compares it with the speeches at the con
ference to usher in disarmament, which is now at work
in Geneva, is natural. But this explosion serves as a text
against Horthy, Bethlen and the big bankers who finance
them, even in the old party press of Europe.
One of the most scathing editorials against Horthy
Hungary appeared in The Manchester Guardian. It calls
the Hungarian government a scandalous regime, basing
its judgment upon a personal investigation of Hungarian
conditions by one of its special correspondents.
Taking up the hypocritical plea of the Hungarian
ruling class to the effect that the disorganization of their
industries is due to unjust peace treaties, The Guardian
declares:
“When we remind ourselves how unfair the peace
settlement has been, we incline to look upon the recal
citrant and militant spirit of the Hungarian ruling class
with indulgence and even with sympathy.
“But when the conduct of the Hungarian governing
class is revealed to us at close quarters, we cannot help
feeling that, however unjust the present frontiers may b
this injustice is not the main cause of Hungary’s pr^l
unhappy condition.
“For the main cause we must look, not to the new suc
cessor states beyond these ill-drawn frontiers, but to the
old Hungarian governing class inside them.
“The picture of these gentry which our correspondent
paints is as black as pitch. But if our readers compare
it with other authoritative and impartial portrayals, we
believe they will agree with us that its hue is not exag
gerated.
“In passing judgment upon the Hungarian oligarchy,
as opposed to the down-trodden mass of the Hungarian
common people, the extreme of reprobation much more
nearly hits the mark than the extreme of praise.”
HELP FOR BRITISH MINERS
The British miners are still in the trenches and need
help urgently. The European labor unions have scraped
the bottom of their money boxes. They are badly off
themselves, having to support millions of unemployed who
get little support from the old party governments.
Through the Amsterdam trade union international,
the European trade unions have given a loan of about
$500,000 to the general council of the British trade union
congress. But with about 1,250,000 miners out, this
amount does not go far.
The American trade unions are better off than the
European. If the starved and underpaid Austrian work
ers can subscribe $50,000 for their British friends, surely
the rich American trade unions can afford to support
generously the workers over there who are protecting the
American living standard with their bodies.
THE NEXT LEAGUE MEMBER
Who will be the next to join the league of nation
after Germany? Not the United States, if the recent
vote against the world court senators is a reliable indi
cation. Perhaps Turkey or Soviet Russia?
The Soviet diplomats still act very coyly, and maybe
some of them really mean it. But when we note the many
concessions to foreign corporations in Russia, and the ef
forts of Soviet agents in the leading countries of Europe
and America to get in touch with big business, we cannot
take the Russian fulminations against the league very se
riously.
We do not believe that Spain and Brazil will stay out
very long, either. Another turn of the wheel, and there
will be a different tale to tell, although hardly a better one.
Russia in the league would be one plotter more.

METALS CASE
DEFENSE HAS
OPEN CONFLICT
BY E. W. LEWIS.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
NEW YORK—Efforts to intro
duce into the Daugherty-Miller con
spiracy trial today certain corre
spondence of the Swiss Metal Securi
ties Co. and John Foster Dulles,
New York attorney, brought out
sharp conflict between attorneys for
the two defendants.
After yesterday’s indications that
Thomas W. Miller, former alien
property custodian, and Harry M.
Daugherty, former attorney general,
would act independently in defense
of the joint charge against them—
each fighting his own battle —to-
days’ developments were considered
significant.
Objects to Letters.
Max D. Steuer, attorney for
Daugherty, objected strenuously to
introduction by United States Attor
ney Emory R. Buckner of the cor
respondence. It was pointed out that
the way for the evidence had been
opened by the cross-examination of
Richard Merton by Col. William
Rand, attorney for Miller.
“Col. Rand,” exclaimed Steuer,
represents a different and separate
client than I and he is conducting
the defense of his client in the light
of the best advice he had.
“What purpose he had in view,
however, I don’t divine.”
Judge Julian R. Mack, presiding,
commented that he thought Steuer
had acquiesced to the evidence by
his silence.
The letter finally was admitted,
against Steuer’s exceptions.
Merton, the German financier
who is alleged to have paid $441,000
in commissions to the late John T.
King for securing return to his
group of $7,000,000 of seized assets
of the American Metal Co., was un
der examination by Buckner.
Quizzed on Owners.
He was closely questioned on the
internal organisation of the Swiss
concern. He said its activities were
controlled largely by an executive
committee which was composed of
himself, his brother, Alfred: Fritz
Zahn, Basle, Switzerland, and Leo
pold Dubois, Basle, Switzerland,
who is also a financial adviser to
the league of nations.
He told of the meetings of the
committee and how finally the letter
to Dulles in New York was sent
asking advice on the possibility of
securing return of the seized prop
erty.
Decide on Course.
Steuer objected vigorously to
Buckner’s questions and finally
moved for a mistrial, alleging Buck
ner had shown a letter not admitted
in evidence to the jury, and that he
was asking improper questions. The
motion was overruled.
It was brought out that Merton
had considered two methods of pro
cedure. One, which he said Dulles
favored, was for the Swiss company
to go into bankruptcy and permit
the creditors to claim the American
Metals assets. The other was to
seek return of the property on the
grounds of non-German ownership.
The latter course finally was fol
lowed.

Amendment to Zoning Act Is Enacted by Common Council
STREHLOW ASKS
REDUCTION OF
15-FT. SETBACK
Amendment Also Re
duces Yard Space
to 3 Feet.
Amendment of the zoning ordi
nance to rectify what property own
ers have declared to be virtually a
“confiscation of property,” was en
acted by the common council, late
yesterday.
Aid. August W. Strehlow, Social
ist, 20th ward, is the author of the
amendment, which was passed by a
unanimous vote.
Circuit Judge Oscar M. Fritz re
cently ruled that under the exist
ing zoning law, a 15-foot setback
was required along the entire long
side of a corner lot and a yard
space, or the distance between build
ings on inside lots must be at least
6 feet. This meant that on a 40-
foot corner lot but 25 feet could be
utilized for building purposes.
The Strehlow amendment provides
that the setback shall be 10 per
cent of the frontage of the lot. Thus
on a 40-foot lot the set back will
be only 4 feet and on a 30-foot lot
3 feet. The amendment also reduces
the yard space to three feet.

PROFESSOR HITS
DICTATORSHIP
OF MUSSOLINI
The dictatorship of Premier Mus
solini of Italy, Fascism and the fail
ure of democracy in America were
assailed by Alexander A. Bruce, for
mer North Dakota supreme court
justice, and at present professor of
constitutional law in Northwestern
university, Evanston, 111., speaking
before the Optimist club at the Mil
waukee Athletic club yesterday.
“When Mussolini dies Italy will
be worse off for having had nim,
the speaker said.
“When he goes, what will remain?
There is no government in Italy to
survive him; the parliamentary sys
tem is completely in rout.
“Fascism is a social disease, a
gospel of violence, a jingo, ex
pansionist, imperialistic movement,”
Mr. Bruce said.
“It is sophisticated word-spinning
around the incidents of an energetic
and unscrupulous man’s march to
power. It is government by force
and intimidation. It has no place in
America.”
Pointing out the lack of pure
democracy in America, and the room
for progress, Mr. Bruce said: “As
long as a sensuous movie kisser at
tracts more attention than the late
President Charles Eliot of Harvard,
so long is the theory of a pure de
mocracy an idle dream.”
Mr. Bruce characterized America
as “the most lawless civilized na
tion on the earth individually, but
the most law-abiding collectively.”
The speaker berated the late Ru
dolph Valentino, film star, as the
arch-kisser of America, while the
whole principle of front page news
paper publiicty for motion picture
lovers was assailed.
Mr. Bruce asserted that a judge
never should be retired unless for
dishonesty or corruption.

DIVORCE A N 0
ALL PROPERTY
A marriage that started with an
elopement and which was referred
to by the court as “a bad ship
wreck,” ended today when Judge
Charles Aarons in circuit court
granted a divorce to Mrs. Treva
Frank, nee Jones, from Raymond
Frank, young Milwaukee attorney.
The decree was awarded on the
grounds of cruel and inhuman treat
ment. Mrs. Frank was awarded the
custody of two children and given
all the real estate holdings, includ
ing a home in Fox Point and an
apartment building at Oakland and
Cambridge Aves.
Claims He Beat Her.
Mrs. Frank testified that her hus
band was possessed of an ungovern
able temper and that he beat and
struck her on various occasions.
From her testimony it developed
that they had been married twice,
the first time April 1, 1923, and the
second time in November, 1924. The
second marriage was entered into,
according to Mrs. Frank, after she
had discovered that the first mar
riage had been performed within a
year after Mr. Frank had obtained
a divorce from his first wife.
Homes Are Encumbered,
According to Mrs. Frank’s story,
married life was an uphill fight
against odds. She stated that
when they moved into their Green
Tree Road home it was incomplete,
without water, without furnace, and
she had to crawl up an eight-inch
plank to reach the front door.
The property, the value of which
is said to be about $30,000, has an
incumbrance of about SII,OOO, and
the Cambridge Ave. home, valued at
$17,500, has a mortgage of $4,200. It
will require about ssjooo, she said,
to put the Cambridge Ave. property
into shape for rental.
Frequently, Mrs. Frank testified,
when she asked her husband for
money, he would give her sl, with
the admonition not to spend it all.
Worse Than Dog?
“I lived worse than a dog,” she
declared.
Frank informed the court that as
a result of the divorce proceedings,
his cdreer had been ruined, that he
was “up against it,” and that he
planned to make a new start in an
other city.
He agreed that the property be
given to his wife and that he pay
$lO a week for the maintenance of
his two children. Frank, under a
court order made last week, will
have to pay $25 alimony arrears by
noon tomorrow or face a jail sen
tence for contempt of court. He is
SSO in default, _
FULLER RITES
WILL BE HELD
AT LA CROSSE
Advices received early today state
that the automobile accident in
which Miss Evelyn Fuller, 20, Mil
waukee State Teachers’ college stu
dent, was killed early yesterday, oc
curred at Chetek, Barron county,
Wis., 15 miles south of Rice Lake.
Miss Fuller was thrown through
the windshield of the car in which
she and Miss Helen Wheeler were
returning to Milwaukee from an
outing in Douglas county, when
their car, driven by Miss Wheeler,
collided with another coming onto
the highway from a drive.
Suffered Skull Fracture.
The driver of the second car, re
ported to be a school teacher at Che
tek, is said to have lost control of
her car when she saw that a colli
sion was imminent.
In the crash that followed the
car occupied by the Milwaukee girls
was hurled against a post and Miss
Fuller, crashing through the wind
shield, struck the concrete road on
her head, suffering a fractured
skull.
She never recovered conscious
ness.
The members of the party, includ
ing Mr. and Mrs. J. Russell Wheeler
of this city, and their daughter,
Helen, who is recovering from the
shock and is said not to have been
seriously injured in the crash, re
mained at Chetek awaiting the ar
rival of I. B. Knutesen, father of
the victim.
The Wheelers live at 572 Mar
shall St., Milwaukee.
Burial In La Crosse.
A telegram received from Chetek
today, 11:30 a. m., stated the body
of Miss Fuller is being taken to La
Crosse, where the funeral will be
held Wednesday, 2 p. m., from the
residence of H. L. Colman, with
burial in the Knutesen family lot at
La Crosse.

Chinese Troops
Massed to Repel
Ships of Britain
SHANGHAI—That Great Britain
and China rapidly are drifting into
a war situation, which is almost cer
tain to involve the United States, is
the general belief here, owing to
the renewed Chinese outbursts
against the British.
Reports last night stated the Chi
nese militarists in the upper Yangtze
region are massing troops and artil
lery on the river banks, awaiting
the threatened British expedition
back to Wanhsien to release the
cargo boats held by the Chinese
militarists.
When the British steamer Kiang
wo, bearing the dead and wounded,
dropped down river the ship again
was fired on by the southern troops
at Hankow, forcing the boat to re
turn up river. Finally, an Ameri
can destroyer stationed in the Han
kow district went to the rescue, re
moved the wounded, and brought
them to a Hankow hospital.

JUSTICE, NOT CONVICTIONS!
To the Editor of The Leader:
I have noticed that whenever dis
trict attorneys run for office they
all brag about the number of con
victions that have occurred during
their terms of office. Police judges
also brag about the number of cases
they can dispose of in a short period
of time.
Yet it is neither the number of
convictions nor the number of
cases disposed of which should
count in an official’s record, but the
justice which has been done and the
equity involved.
Rushing such vital matters does
no good, and causes an untold
amount of sorrow.

GENEVA— French recommenda
tion, voiced by Paul Boncoui, that a
general conference on disarmament
should be convoked at the earliest
possible date was the outstanding
event here yesterday. M. Boneour’s
action furnished evidence to many
of the delegates that France sincere
ly desires to reach a disarmament
agreement.
Following France’s* decision,
whereby her army would be reduced
by 2,700 officers and steps would be
taken to establish a 12-month in
stead of an 18-month military serv
ice for youths.
Delegates Are Puzzled.
Many of the delegates, however,
find it difficult to reconcile this gen
eral political attitude of France
with the technical difficulties which
have arisen repeatedly in the mili
tary, naval and air problems in
preparation for a general disarma
ment conference.
A modified resolution was adopted
by the league assembly’s disarma
ment commission today, emphasiz
ing the necessity of concluding as
soon as possible a convention on the
private manufacture of arms.
Part of Conference.
It approves making this problem
an integral part of the general dis
armament conference, provided this
conference can convene before next
September, but insists that, should
the general conference not material
ize within the period of one year,
private manufacture of arms should
be treated by special conferences.
Three Involved
In Kidnaping of
Priest Identified
NORFOLK, Ya. —Seven witnesses
testifying before a special grand
Jury investigating the kidnaping of
the Rev. Father Vincent B. Warren
by a hooded mob in Princess Anne
county yesterday told how the priest
was taken from his automobile
while listening to a concert given
by a college boy band from St. Jo
seph’s academy and spirited away
In the darkness.
Because the investigation was not
concluded, the evidence in detail
was not make public. Five other
witnesses are to be examined. The
Jury adjourned until Sept. 30. As
a result of the testimony three
members of the mob have been
identified and their arrests are ex
pected before the grand jury re
convenes.
As a precaution against interfer
ence with witnesses by sympathizers
of the hooded fraternity, extra of
ficers were placed on duty around
the court house, but they were not
needed.

ALLIED DEBT
TO U. S. PAID
BY GERMANY
NEW YORK—Add $63,000,000
which England receives in 192
-27 in reparation payments to $lO,-
000,000 collected from Italy under
the Volpi-Churchill agreement to
$20,000,000 more from France under
the Caillaux-Churchill agreement,
and deduct the total from the SIBO,-
000,000 which Great Britain annual
ly pays into the United States
treasury. The result is $07,000,000
which Englishmen must actually
take from their pockets to meet the
obligations Baldwin accepted in
Washington, writes Louis Fisher,
from Berlin, in an article in The Na
tion, under the headline: How
America Fools Herself. The Mighty
British lion groans under this bur
den, and London experts tell you
that it furnishes one of the explana
tions of Great Britain’s economic
straits.
It will require the application of
tons of pressure before the chamber
of deputies approves the French
debt-funding treaty with the United
States; a Paris daily calls the Ber
enger pact “onereux, dangereux,
immoral” because it involves $30,-
000,000 in 1926-1927. This sum plus
the $20,000,000 paid to England
makes $50,000,000, as against $150,-
000,000 which France will obtain
during that year in reparation pay
ments.
She Pays Penalty.
In other words, Britain sighs
when she pays $67,000,000, France
complains though debt payments
yield her a surplus of $100,000,000,
but the Dawes plan taps Germany
to the tune of $285,000,000 in 1926-
1927 and more than double that
figure each year after 1928. This
is Germany’s penalty not for start
ing the war but for losing it.
Assuming the ratification of the
Berenger-Mellon accord, the allies
will, in 1927-1928, be paying the
United States about $230,000,000.
And in the same year Germany will
pay the allies about $417,000,000. In
reality, then, Germany is funding
tho allied debts to America.
Germany pays. After notes, con
ferences, bayonets, and Ruhr inva
sions failed to collect marks, the
Dawes scheme is accomplishing that
worthy purpose with a thorough
ness which is as cruel as it is
futile.
The account is a simple one. Un
less it wreck its currency and un
balance its budget, a nation can in
the long run transfer money abroad
oirly on the basis of a foreign trade
surplus. Now, the recent report of
Mr. S. Parker Gilbert, agent general
for reparation payments, covering
the nine months from Sept. 1, 1925,
to May 31, 1926, shows that during
that period Germany had an active
trade balance of 17,800,000 marks.
But in the same nine months Gil
bert transferred abroad some 600,-
000,000 marks, which leaves a de
ficit of approximately 582,200,000
marks. Germany’s “invisible ex
ports” are greater than her “in
visible imports,” so that this de
ficit is even more serious, but it is
bad enough at 582,000,000.
Make the Rounds.
How did Germany make up the
loss? By borrowing 850,000,000
marks in foreign countries, most of
it in the United States. America is
thus financing reparation payments,
while Germany piles up a huge debt
on which interest at 8 per cent is
charged her. The money borrowed
in Wall Street goes to London,
Paris, Rome, etc., in the form of
Dawes annuities, is there heavily
discounted, and then wanders back
to Wall Street and Washington ear
marked “allied debt payments.” The
sooner Americans realize that this
silly circle is self-reception the
sooner they will be prepared to
listen to common sense on the ques
tion of cancelation.
These loans gradually enslave an
increasingly large part of German
industry to American capital and
burden the country with a debt the
interest on which alone Is stupend
ous. Moreover, they are demoral
izing the entire German economy.
During the last 30 months the
United States lent Germany close
to $500,000,000, says Secretary Mel
lon. Much of this gigantic total is
now changing hands on the bourse.
The stock market blossoms, and
credit is cheap and easy to find be
cause the crisis of the last eight
months does not diminish.
Factories are idle, production
fails, and industry cannot absprb
much money. So the money is used
for bourse speculation which is
often misread as prosperity. Nor
is the increase in savings-bank ac
counts a trustworthy index of con
ditions. The minister of finance
hints, and a brilliant expert in the
ministry of finance tells me plainly,
that a large, if not the larger, part
of these deposits represents sums
borrowed in America by states and
municipalities for power stations,
gas works, etc., and placed by these
on savings account until the funds
will be required for operations.
End Is Seen.
The presence of much foreign
gold in Germany thus prevents the
reparation situation from growing
critical and creates an impression
of smooth progress which is illusory.
But when Churchill’s statement in
the house of commons immediately
after the signing of the Franco-Brit
ish debt settlement explicity envis
ages a reduction of reparation pay
ments it is clear that such a con
summation might not be objection
able even to the two countries in
volved. Indeed, there is reason to
suspect that England is pressing for
a revision of the Dawes plan, since
it would inevitably lead to a re-ex
amination of the entire debt prob
lem.
Preliminary pourparlers have per
haps commenced already. One may
never know just why, about a fort
night ago, Gov. Norman of the Bank
of England, Gov. Strong of the New
York Federal Reserve bank, and Mr.
Gilbert suddenly decided, quite in-

mate of Antibes on the French

their health, and by accident re

Paints Dark Picture.
The foreign Dawes instalment col
lectors in Mr. Gilbert’s office are
optimistic, or at least they say they
are, and serve to their visitors large
portions of hopefulness based pre
sumably on the conviction that with
in five or 10 years and with the aid
of foreign loans Germany will be
sufficiently restored to meet from
her own means the obligations im
posed on her by the Dawes experts.
The German ministry of finance,
however, paints a dark picture.
The prevailing opinion is that Ger
many will not be in a position to
pay the 2,000,000,000 marks which
will be required of her in 1927-1928.
Next January the question will be
answered definitely. All depends on
the unemployment curve.
Germany today counts 1,742,000
who receive a dole plus about 200,-
000 who obtain aid under the poor
law, and then there are 700,000-odd
on part time despite the fact that
many hands find work during the
summer on the fields and in con
struction enterprises.
If the number of the jobless rises
next winter, or even if it remains
stationary—and this will be clear by
January—Germany will be unable
to pay the full amount of repara
tions.
May Raise Billion.
At best she will raise 1,000,000,000
marks, and for the rest her creditors
would have to declare a partial
moratorium or give the government
a loan or revise the plan. Now, in
a debt-developed world moratoria
are dangerous precedents, while the
country is already bent too low un
der the tasks of raising interest and
amortization on previous loans to
make a new 1,000,000,000-mark loan
a profitable or rational undertak
ing. Remains the modification of
the Dawes plan.
The Dawes plan is predicated on
the rehabilitation of the German
economy. The speed of this rehabil
itation, however, has not kept pace
with the steep rise in the annuities
schedule. This is a German as well
as a world problem, and the diffi
culties are:
1. Unemployment is here to stay
as it is in England, and unemploy
ment is merely the most evident re
flection of .a sub-normal industry:
2. Germany has already paid
more than she could afford and she
has reduced the standard of living
of the masses below a decent limit
to do so. Wages and the economic
level of the workers are so low, and
the amount of work required of
them so high, that to tighten the
vise in order to raise more funds
for reparations would be, as J. M.
Keynes has said, to court serious
political disturbances.
Tariff Walls Hurt.
3. Germany’s industrial revival
depends, in the final analysis, on
the extension of her foreign trade.
But such development is hampered
by protective tariff w&lls and im
poverished markets everywhere. In
dustry could probably absorb some
of the free money and labor in the
country if it could find buyers
abroad. Increased domestic con
sumption would also make matters
better. But neither of these condi
tions exists.
The benefits of the Dawes scheme
must not be denied. It took the
reparations problem out of the
hands of generals and put it v/here
general staffs and French politicians
could not touch it. With the effi
cient Gilbert at the helm, default
on the part of Germany can only be
due to her incapacity to pay rather
than to lack of good will. The
Dawes plan confirmed the currency
stabilization, paved the way to a bal
anced budget, and made possible the
influx of huge sums of money in
the form of foreign loans.
In a word, it provided a breath
ing space. It is largely for this
reason that, so many Germans are
reconciled to outside control of their
customs, finances, railroads, and, in
part, of their industries. It Is large
ly for this reason, and because trib
ulations have dulled their pride,
that Germans swallow insuKs such
as the classification by Sir Andrew
McFadyean, commissioner of con
trolled revenues, of coffee, tea, co
coa and tobacco as “luxury ar
ticles.”
This is the tone which Sir An
drew’s countrymen assume iu Egypt
and India, yet the Germans do not
protest.
To this moral disadvantage must
be added far greater economic dis
advantages. Despite the foreign
loans which they have received, the
federal and state governments In
creased their taxes in order to meet
their share of the Dawes annuities;
despite foreign loans to trusts and
corporations, wages have not risen
nor has production. The cost of
living is 140 per cent of pre-war.

charges higher freight and passen
ger rates, thus damaging business,

BRITISH UNIONS
GIVE FACTS ON
GENERAL STRIKE
Leader Special Service.
LONDON The British trade
union congress has given the right
reply to the attacks of the Mos
cowers, reports The Daily Herald.
It has told the simple truth about
the reasons for which the general
strike was called off.
There is no mystery about it. The
Communist cry of “treason” is rub
bish. The general council of the
British trade union congress called
the general strike off, because they
believed that the report of the Sam
uel committee offered the best
chance of settling the coal dispute
which the miners could get.
Leaders Were Right.
“Events are now proving that the
council was right,” The Herald de
clares. “If the miners representa
tives had agreed to accept that
memorandum as a basis for negotia
tion, work would have been resumed
three and a half months ago.
“The only men who would have
had to sacrifice anything were the
most highly paid ones, The Herald
asserts. None would have received
less than 50 shillings ($12.50) per
week.
This seemed a reasonable settle
ment to the majority of the general
council. When the leaders of the
miners rejected it, the council felt
that it would be futile to ask the
other trade unions to sacrifice their
own jobs any longer.
The council was satisfied that no
matter how long the general strike
would continue, the situation would
be the same in tne end.
Minority Are Wrong.
This is the true reason for calling
the general strike off at the time,
The Herald repeats emphatically.
There is no other. It ought to satis
fy all who want the facts.
The attacks directed by the Com
munists in the minority movement
against the leaders of the trade
unions are not honest. They are
dictated by the object to spread
hatred and to disrupt the British
trade union congress for the benefit
of Moscow.
The British trade unions, how
ever, have no reason to destroy their
own movement in order to open the
way for Communist experiments.

THE MEANING OF PLAY
Today, when the need of
Jthe playground is recog
nized, we cannot appreciate
the intensity of feeling that
pervaded the propaganda
for playgrounds.
A poem, What Do You
Care, by William Edward
Ross, of which we quote the
second and the last stanzas,
was used extensively in this
propaganda.

Over the bridges, the hills,
and the fen,
Streams the procession of
undersized men
Climbing the stairs to the
waiting machines;
Lowered in cages to death
marked ravines.
Look at their faces; sad,
pinched and worn!
Look at their garments;
threadbare and torn!
Look at their swagger;
their precocious air,
Some mother’s babies, but—
What do you care?
What do you care the ar
raignment doth read
What is your plea to the
true bill of greed?
What can you offer by way
of defense?
You who judge lives by
their value in cents.
Sponsor of slavery’s misery
filled pen!
They are your chattels,
these undersized men!
What will you say when the
judge, truly fair,
Cries, “These are my chil
dren, but —what did
you care?”
To widely different people, play and the playground
has a different meaning.
With those who grudgingly argue: ‘‘Why spend
money for playgrounds? Nobody gave us play
grounds—” we cannot stop to reason. Their number is
gradually decreasing through force of circumstances.
From my file on Playgrounds, I take the following
complaint, omitting names: “Mr. W., who resides on the
northeast corner of and streets, complains
that a ‘gang* of boys and girls, roller skating during the
day and part of the night, make life miserable for himself
and for his wife, who is an invalid. They skate so much
an# so often that they are wearing out the pavement and
the sidewalk there and will cause expense.”
To such as these play of children is worse than use
less, it is a costly nuisance.
ti*
•Then there are those who look upon play as a harm
less spending of leisure time. Benignly they hold:
“Jugend will austoben” (Youth must blow off force) and
the most harmless place is the playground.
To them the playground is a convenience, for it per
mits the child to have what it needs at the same time
keeping it out of mischief and danger.

There is a third group which has done much of the
pioneer work necessary to even the road for playgrounds.
These see in play an agency that reduces delinquency
and crime, stimulates health, physical growth, industrial
efficiency, and makes for better morals, good citizenship
and community spirit.
The Playground Association of America proclaims
its purpose to be to promote normal wholesome play.
It announces a constructive creed of 12 articles, of which
all of the above are a part.

Finally there are those who see in the play of the
child a meaning, deeper and greater than just the play
ful waste of leisure time.
They hold that we have not yet gotten very far in
our understanding of the child and its world, the work
ing of its mind, the meaning of its endeavors and its re
lations to its jworld. We not only lack in understanding
the child—we misunderstand him.

They point out that we have no proper word to
designate or express the activities of the child. When
the child builds a house of pebbles and sand it tries to
create something that it has seen, or imitate what it has
seen done. And it is so with baking mudpies, building
dams in the gutter, or putting dolly to sleep.
We add to our difficulties in understanding of the
child by applying different terms to the identical activ
ities and interests when they appear in man. What we
call working and acting when done by man is only play
and making believe when done by the child.
And we multiply our difficulty when the identical
traits are virtuous in man and vicious in child, as when
persisting in a pursuit is disobedience and obstinancy in
child, but perseverance and willpower in man.

This group of people points out that the child in
its play is serious and intent. In fact, its play is the
most serious thing in its life. Hence the play of a child
is a very important factor in the making of its life.
Viewed from this position, play and the playground
is destined to rank as a most important branch in the edu
cational plan of our schools.
Who has not met the man of 80 or 90 years old that
prides himself on having made a living since the age of
eight, when his parents left him an orphan?
To us this seems preposterous. How can a child of
eight go out and make a living? Perhaps, if we can pic
ture to ourselves a society in which the family did its
own growing of food, packing, canning, preserving, card
ing, spinning, weaving and making of garments, we can
also conceive of things for the 8-year-old to do, and the
“old man’s” claim does not sound so very preposterous
after all.

far removed from reality and real life.

of young men and women, all of them over 23 years of

Government Plans Anti-Smuggling Agreement With Canada
PACT WILL BE
2-WAY AFFAIR
TO PLUG LEAKS
Kellogg Now Is Ar
ranging for Con
ference.
BY JOSEPH S. WASNEY.
Staff Correspondent
The United I’ress
WASHINGTON A new anti
smuggling agreement with Canada,
similar to the one recently arranged
with England, will be negotiated
late this month by Canadian and
United States officials, Assistant
Secretary of the Treasury Andrews
announced today.
The pact will be a “business
agreement” for the exchange of in
formation to prevent liquor smug
gling, and not a treaty, Andrews
said. The arrangement will be a
“two-way” affair to stop the flow
of rum into the United States and
also to end smuggling of bootleg
liquor into the dry provinces of
Canada from America.
Now Arranging Meet.
Secretary of State Kellogg now
is arranging the date for the con
ference, it is understood. Whether
the meeting will be held in Ottawa
or Washington has not been deter
mined.
Andrews, a representative of the
state department and an official of
the department of justice, will rep
resent the United States at the
meeting. Canada will name its rep
resentatives after the conference
has been officially called.
While the Unrfed States now has
an anti-smuggling treaty with Can
ada, means of putting it into effect
have not been perfected.
Plan Double Patrol.
Canada, it is understood, will be
asked to allow American patrol
boats to chase rum runners in Ca
nadian waters. A double border pa
trol may also be arranged, the Unit
ed States using prohibition patrol
forces and Canada her Northwest
Mounted police.
Information of smuggling activi
ties would be exchanged by every
agency of the two governments. Ca
nadian customs officials would
“tip off” American authorities
when a liquor ship left port for an
American destination and if nec
essary dominion officials could ap
pear in American courts to testify
against rum runners.

JOIN IN WRITING
‘BOOK OF LIFE’
CHICAGO —In an effort to orient
the collegiate mind, lead the public
consciousness into an enlightened
concept and control of evolutionary
processes, and to outline the great
story of modern science, 1G of the
ranking scientists of the University
of Chicago have collaborated in the
writing of a GOO-page book called
The Nature of the World and of
Man. The volume is soon to be pub
lished by The University Press and
will be supplemented this winter in
a program od downtown lectures.
Each of the scientists was limited
to 10,000 words in giving the funda
mentals and the latest conclusions
in his field, but the remarkable
thing is that the book has taken on
the unity, the coherence, the march
of one great epic poem. The secret
of this may be found in the state
ment stressed in the book that ’the
basis on which science rests is the
orderliness of the universe.
Opens With Heavens.
The world as looked upon by the
chemist, the invisible and micro
scopic, and the infinite galaxies of
suns found by the astronomer, are
ruled by the same laws and have
the same basic content. One of the
writers finds in this a source of
profound spiritual inspiration, but
the philosophical view of it all is
not presented, except as it has
crept in.
The book opens with a view of
the heavens. This chapter by Prof.
Forest Ray Moulton shows bow sci
ence has placed the earth as a speck
in the solar systems, how the laws
of the solar systems have been dis
covered, the earth weighed and
measured, the chemical constitution
of sun and stars determined.
The orgin and early stages of the
earth are discussed by Prof. Rollin
T. Chamberlin. The growth of the
earth and the beginnings of life
come in this section, which is fol
lowed by the story of geological
processes by Prof. J. Harlen Bretz.
Forms of Energy.
From this the story passes, to a
consideration of energy, radiation
and atomic structure by Harvey
Brace Lemon.
The nature of chemical processes
is given by Julius Stieglitz. The
whole universe, stars, and animals
and industry, consists of two kinds
of matter—elements and compounds.
In the transformation of matter lie
the health, safety, comfort, the story
of medicine, and of the great in
dustries/ Y
Prof. Newman goes Into the nature
and origin of life, emphasizing the
basic oneness of all science.
Henry Chandler Cowles writes a
chapter of interactions between
plants and their environment. W. C.
Allee contributes on the evolution
of the invertebrates. Then comes
the evoltuion of the vertebrates by
Alfred S. Romer, the roots of the
tree of life, it is shown, going down
from birds, whales, elephants and
man to the lower chordates.
More Paddies Than
Lassies in Ireland
DUBLIN One reason Irish girls
smile is that they are in great de
mand, for the current census shows
that there are 41,000 more men
than women in the Irish Free State.
This proportion of girls to men is
the lowest of any European country.
In northern Ireland there five 40,-
000 more men than girls. In Great
Britain there are 1,0000,000 more
girls and women than there are

CO-EDS CALLED
LICENTIOUS BY
UNIVERSITY MAN
CHICAGO —American co-eds have
been indicted as “gin drinking, li
centious animals” in the current is
sue of The Witness, magazine semi
officially sponsored by the Episco
pal church of Omaha, just issued.
The charge against the co-eds was
written by W. O. Cross, who gradu
ated from the University of Illinois
in June.
“The invasion by women of the
university has made drinking a
part of dating, which also included
dancing and petting,” he charges.
“Women now participate in drink
ing bouts to an extent which to the
unitiated is astounding.”
Cross then described an orgy
he said he witnessed on a sleeping
coach en route to a football gome
last fall. “Collegians of both sexes,
most of whom were quite drunk,
staged a pajama dance in the aisles
between sleeper berths.
“The inebriated woman is a bun
dle of animality,” he continued.
“Mixed drinking begins with a lit
tle party after the dance, the pet
ting session, and after inhibitions
have been lulled and passions
stirred by sensual music.”
Drinking in student days has
been a tradition, Cross’ article as
serts, but since the participation of
the college woman it has become
bacchanalia, he concluded.
“As one man puts it, ‘women have
descended to the bestiality of men.’
Ancient Gate to Be
Restored to Oxford
OXFORD, Eng.—An ancient gate
of oak, which was set up nearly 800
years ago and swung for 500 years
at the entrance to Balliol college
before It changed its location, has
been found and returned to its old
place.
The gate was made and hung in
1288 and it was already a venerable
antique when, in 1555 Ridley and
Latimer were burned at the stake
only a few yards in front of It, after
they had been convicted as Protest
ant heretics.
Towards the end of the 18th cen
tury, when the front quadrangle of
the college was demolished and re
built, the gate was taken down. Dr.
Harding Newman, a fellow of Mag
dalene college, Oxford, acquired it
and hung it at the entrance of his
private garden at Nelmes, In Essex.
Ivy grew over it and after Dr.
Newman’s death the gate was for
gotten.
But 18 months ago J. Rochelle
Thomas of the Georgian Gallery, St.
James, London, discovered the an
cient gate and purchased it. More
than 100 coats of paint were scraped
away and the old oak planks and
struts found still in a perfect state
cf preservation.

EDITOR MAGEE
IN APPEAL FOR
A FREE PRESS
CHICAGO —“Give me liberty to
know, to utter and to argue freely ac
cording to my conscience, above all
other liberties.”
With this quotation as a text,
Carl Magee, doughty editor of The
Albuquerque, N. M., State-Tribune,
speaking yesterday at the Sherman
house before a joint meeting of the
Advertising Men’s post of the Amer
ican Legion and the advertising
council of the Chicago Association
of Commerce, launched into an im
passioned plea for the freedom of
the press.
Page From Own Book.
When Editor Magee said, “If our
editors are not to be at liberty to
tell of the official conduct of those
in public life and if public senti
ment will not support us, then how
can people ever learn enough to cor
rect the abuses of government,” he
was tearing a leaf out of his per
sonal notebook.
For, following some of his stories
about former Secretary of the In
terior Albert B. Fall’s activities, he
was tried for libel, 11 times cited
for contempt of court, and finally
obliged to serve two days of a peni
tentiary sentence until pardoned by
the governor. A year ago last
August, shooting in self-defense, he
claimed, to protect himself against
the attack of former Judge David
Leahy, who had sentenced him, he
killed a bystander. Last June, at
his trial, the judge took the case
away from the jury and instructed
a not guilty verdict.
Recalls Mellett Death.
Departing from his own experi
ences, Mr. Magee found cause for
alarm in the death recently of Edi
tor Don Mellett of Canton, 0., and
the contempt proceedings against
Editor George R. Dale of Muncie,
Ind.
Of the Ohio editor the editor from
New Mexico said:
“Don Mellett was right In his
charges of corruption. But he had
to die in order that the people of
the United States might know the
corrupt alliances that are being
made.
“Can we profit by Canton and bj
Indiana? We can if we support the
liberty of the press in matters of
public concern. I have no interest
in private scandal.”
165 Enrolled in
School for Deaf
DELAVAN, Wis.—Sessions at
the Wisconsin School for the Deaf
are in full swing with an enroll
ment of 165. It is expected that the
enrollment will reach the 200 mark
within a week or two.
Pupils at the school are well di
vided among the different grades.
There are a number of beginners,
children of from 3 to 10 years of
age, and these are being taught the
rudiments of lip reading.
The present system of teaching
the deaf calls for lip reading as
much as possible in place of using
the sign language. Many of the
students still communicate among
themselves and others by the sign
language.
SUSTAIN HOAN’S
CARNIVAL VETD
Mayor Daniel W. Hoan’s veto of
the amendment to the city’s carnival
ordinance, was sustained, late yes
terday, by a unanimous vote of the
common council.
The vetoed amendment would
have provided that three “rides,”
such as merry-go-rounds, ferris
wheels, whips, and so forth, would
be permitted operation under a city
license. The unamended ordinance
provides that not more than two
can be operated.
“I am vetoing this amendment for
the reason that the present ordi
nance seems entirely satisfactory
and I do not believe the change ad
visable,” the mayor declared in a
communication, accompanying the
the veto.

AUTO OWNERS
SHOULD CARRY
INSURANCE. VIEW
“Automobile owners should carry
liability insurance or have some
other form of protection for the bene
fit of such members of the public
as they injure, or whose property
they may damage,” said Civil Judge
Joseph Cordes, late yesterday, in
rendering judgment for the latter in
the case of Charles M. Fowler,
against Andrew Szopinski, 683
Mitchell St.
Szopinski had damaged an auto
mobile parked at the curb on Okla
homa Ave. for tire repair, at the
same time injuring three persons.
He promised to pay damages, but
when the bill of SB3 was presented
he said that the injured ones might
as well take his car.
The judge stated that a person
who cannot afford a small amount
of liability insurance should not
drive an automobile and endanger
the lives of other people.
“Dealers maintain that liability
insurance makes drivers careless,
but I carry such insurance myself
and do not believe this,” said the
judge.
“You cannot be careless if you
carry liability insurance, for if you
are you endanger yourself and dam
age your own automobile, and these
risks are not covered by your public
liability insurance.”

RIXEY HURLS
SHUTOUT AS
ALEX LOSES
Eppa Rixey, Cincinnati pitcher,
shut out the Brooklyn Robins, 4 to
0. Ills victory jarred the St. Louis
Cardinals out of a one game lead in
the National league race, and the
Cincinnati Reds are now tied with
the Cardinals, each having won 82
games and lost 60.
The Cardinals found themselves
in a tie by dropning a game to the
Boston Braves, 5 to 4. It was the
second consecutive lost game for the
veteran pitcher, Grover C. Alex
ander, whose first St. Louis’ ap
pearance put the Cardinals into the
National league lead.
The Pirates lost a leg in the race
by dropping a game to the Giants,
9 to 5. Home runs by Kelly and
Lindstrom featured for the Giants.
The Chicago Cubs hit when hits
meant runs and beat the Phillies, 3
to 1.
Pitcher Shaute won his game
from Washington by knocking out
a double for Cleveland in the
seventh, with the bases filled. The
score was 0 to 3.
The Detroit Tigers took both
sides of a double-header from the
league leading Yankees, 4 to 3 and
4 to 1. The result reduced the
Yankees’ lead over the Indians to
five and one-half games.
The Philadelphia Athletics split
with the White Sox, taking the first
game, 5 to 2, in 13 innings, and
losing the second, 3 to 2.
BOTANIST GROWS
SPUDS ABOVE,
BELOW GROUND
ITHACA, N. Y.—Forcing a crop
of tubers to grow above ground in
addition to the one below, and caus
ing the Jerusalem artichoke to car
ry this hitherto unknown behavior
on into the fourth generation, were
the feats in plant grafting related
today by Prof. L. Daniel of the
University of Rennes before the
meeting here of the International
Congress of Plant Sciences.
The French botanist told how he
had succeeded in grafting the top of
the Jerusalem artichoke, which is a
perennial reproducing by means of
underground tubers, on the root of
the common sunflower, which is an
annual reproducing by seeds. The
Jerusalem artichoke produced seeds,
a departure from its usual custom,
and the offspring resulting from the
planting of these seeds bore tubers
above ground as well as below, and
kept this up for four generations.
The strain thus produced seems to
be a departure from the artichoke
parent in other ways as well, so
that Prof. Daniel has named it as
a new variety. Inasmuch as it has
carried its acquired peculiarities
through several generations, he
claims that here is a genuine case
of the much-disputed inheritance of
acquired characters. He states that
he has succeeded in getting compar
able results in other plants by simi
lar peculiar grafts.
MANY CHANGE
DISCOVERIES
AID SCIENCE
NEW YORK—Romance still per
vades science in this age of pains
taking research, recent events in the
laboratories of two great industrial
concerns show.
During experiments at the Wil
mington plant of the E. I. DuPont
de Nemours Co. research on a new
quick-drying finish for automobiles
and furniture was at a stand-still
because the liquid persisted in "set
ting” into a jelly. As an experi
ment, some caustic soda had been
added to the mixture preparatory
to placing it in a mixer.
Is Covered Over.
Upon starting the mixer the ma
chinery broke down, and, as sev
eral days were required for repairs,
the material was covered overhand
set aside. When the cover was re
moved a few day later the chem
ists were astonished to find that the
pasty material, presumably through
a rearrangement of its molecular
structure, had become almost as thin
as water. Here, practically in its
finished form, was the product for
which they had long been seeking.
At another plant, in the research
laboratories of General Motors,
tests were being conducted to de
termine the cause of "knocking” in
gasoline motors. One of the chem
ists conceived a brilliant idea. Pos
sibly, he thought, knocking in mo
tors was due in some way to the
colors present inside the cylinder
during combustion. Going *o the
chemical storeroom he asked for
some colored chemical soluble in
gasoline.
A Great Help.
Out of some 10.00 J at hand, the
storekeeper gave him lodin, the only
chemical in the lot which had the
property of eliminating knocking.
The color guess was wrong, but, due
ro the happy circumstance of pick
ing up lodin, it was possible to solve
the riddle of knocking in gasoline
motors and to work out the theory
of nntidetonants which, it is be
lieved. will bring about revolution
ary changes in the design of inter
nal combustion engines.
Schaeffer May Not
Defend Cue Title
NEW YORK—Word was received
today from Jake Schaefer, 18-1 balk
line billiard champion, which indi
cates he apparently is not in any
hurry to defend his crown. He
wrote from San Francisco that he
did not expect to come east until
about December, and had not yet
decided whether he would make any
road tours. He spoke of participat
ing in an 18-2 tournament which
he expects to be held some time in
February.

Dogs Kill Kitten,
Attend Funeral
MONTEREY, Calif.—lf dogs have
souls, or even intellects adaptable to
psychologically suggestion, kittens of
this city may in the future enjoy
unrivaled freedom from canine
molestation.
Jack and Norman Steward, young
sons of the Monterey postmaster, re
cently were presented with a few
days’ old kitten. The pet became not
only the center of attraction to the
neighborhood children but the
neighborhood dogs, the latter be
coming so boisterous that the kitten
died in the resultant commotion.
Jack and Norman rounded up the
dogs, an approximate 30, and lash
ing them together, led them unwill
ingly to the kitten’s funeral. Re
luctant participants in the cortege,
the dogs were still more reluctant
spectators while the fluffy body of
their victim was lowered into its
grave.
They were released only after the
last handful of dirt had been
sprinkled. They had been given a
lesson, but it remains to be seen
whether they benefited thereby.
Discover Book Not
Of First Edition;
Dreams Fade Away
CHICAGO—The dreams of a hum
ble bank official named Warner,
who for a fortnight believed him
self rich after obtaining an ex
traordinary high price for a copy
of the first edition of Pilgrim’s
Progress, have faded away, ac
cording to a copyrighted London
story in The Daily News. The deal
ers in antique books who purchased
Warner’s treasure have returned it
to the auctioneers, declaring that it
was only a second edition.
Experts who carefully compared
the volume with the first edition in
possession of the British museum
found everything all right until they
reached the last page. There, they
observed, Warner’s copy had five
lines of errata which did not ap
pear in the museum’s edition.
Warner inherited the book, to
gether with many others, from his
mother. Believeing that they might
bring in a few dollars, he sent them
to the auction rooms where the
Pilgrim’s Progress fetched the high
est price paid for a single volume in
the last three years.
