The “Big Parade” goes into ac
tion this week, and when Bobby
Janes teed off at 11:30 yester
day, with D.Clarke Corkran, who
shot a 67 in the 1924 tournament
at Merion, as his partner, he will be
the first of the Big Four—Jones,
Til den, Dempsey, Ha ken —who seek
to retain their crowns within the
space of two weeks.
This tournament, which began
with each contestant playing a
round of medal play yesterday and
today, and then the leading 32 play
ers being paired for two 18-
hole rounds tomorrow, with the
remainder of the matches at 36
holes, again has all the earmarks
of a Bobby Jones championship. No
golfer since Jerry Travers’ victories
in 1912 and 1913 had won two ama
teur tournaments in a row, until
Bobby equaled the record last year.
No player has ever won three in
succession, so Bobby has a new
mark to shoot at.
But who is there to stop him?
Eight former champions are en
tered, but only Ouimet, Evans or
Guilford appear to have a slight
chance of affording any opposition.
Will it be one of the “younger set,”
such as Frank Dolp, the western
amateur champion, or Bobby’s little
playmate of last year, Watts Gunn?
Then there is always George von
Elm to be considered. Too bad that
Jess Sweetser is out of it.
I wonder how It feels to be sit
ting on top of the golfing world, as
Bobby is at present. King of 5,000,-
000 golfers! Imagine it! Bobby has
it all over Jack Dempsey, except
when it comes to making money,
because there aren’t nearly 5,000,000
heavyweight boxers. Or even 50,000.
This amazing young man, in the
space of 17 days, with an Atlantic
voyage between, won both the Brit
ish and American open titles, and
what a pity it Is that he didn’t also
win the British amateur, so that he
might now be shooting for the un
heard-of honor of winning all four
of golf’s biggest prizes in one year!
BOBBY JONES
TOPS GOLFERS
WITH 70
SHORT HILLS, N. J.—The 140
golfers competing for the national
amateur title, started on the second
18-hole qualifying round today with
the most brilliant golf ever played
by Bobby Jones, titleholder, as their
inspiration to greater efforts.
Of the 144 who started yester
day only 14 could break 80 on the
difficult Baltusrol course, which
held grief for nearly all except
Jones.
His 70, two under par, was four
strokes better than the next player,
George Dawson, Chicago. Next were
Laurence Upson and Paul Haviland,
Connecticut, with 76 each.
The field was cut by four when
Frank Dolp, western amateur title
holder, was disqualified.
Jones Two Under
Par to Qualify
In Golf Tourney
BALTUSROL COUNTRY CLUB,
SHORT HILLS, N. J.—The cham
pionship golf of Bobby Jones came
to the surface again today when the
young Atlanta wizard negotiated the
tricky Baltusrol course in 70 strokes
to take the lead in the first day’s
qualifying play of the National ama
teur championship. With other stars
of the links, such as Max Marston,
George von Elm and Francis
Ouimet floundering around the 80
mark, Jones went out in 36 and
came back in 34, besting par by two
strokes.

INDIANA JUDGE GRANTS
INJUNCTION TO HALT
DEMPSEY FIGHT
INDIANAPo£IS, Ind.—James A.
Farrabaugh, attorney, was to leave
here today for Philadelphia to begin
a second round of legal action to
prevent Jack Dempsey, heavyweight
champion, from fighting Gene Tun
ney, challenger, a week from Thurs
day at Philadelphia.
Farrabaugh last night won an
injunction here restraining Dempsey
from meeting Tunney for the cham
pionship until he first meets Harry
Wills, Negro challenger.
The injunction was issued by Su
perior Judge Clinton Givan, who ex
pressed doubt whether it would be
effective in Pennsylvania. Farra
baugh immediately decided to insti
tute similar proceedings in Phila
delphia, using the same evidence in
troduced here.
The attorney represents the Coli
seum club in Chicago, which holds
a contract with Dempsey for a fight
with Wills.
Attorneys who represented Demp
sey in the suit in superior court
here expressed the opinion that the
injunction would have no effect in
Pennsylvania.
New Injunction Sought.
Attorneys for the Coliseum club
declared that while the local in
junction was not binding on tbe
Pennsylvania courts, there was lit
tle possibility of an injunction be
ing denied in Pennsylvania.
The petition for the injunction
was filed in Superior court here
while Dempsey was on his way east
to start training for the fight with
Tunney.
Dempsey stopped off ir. Indian
apolis and attorneys for the Coli
seum club who had trailed him
from Los Angeles seized the oppor
tunity to file the suit.
Holds Contract Valid.
Judge Givan declared that “if
the Pennsylvania courts follow the
constitution they cannot help but
issue a similar, or at least a tem
porary injunction.”
In his opinion Judge Givan held
that Dempsey “did have a valid
contract with the Chicago Coliseum
club which would have been en
forceable under the Illinois laws.”
The court found that Dempsey
had violated the contract first by re
fusing to fight Harry Wills and then
by refusing to be examined for life
insurance as a preliminary to the
bout.
Evidence is conclusive and undis
puted that the Chicago Coliseum
flub has suffered thousands of dol
lars damage. Judge Givan declared.
The Coliseum club brought suit
on the ground that Dempsey had
violated terms of a contract said to
have been signed in Los Angeles last
March between the club and the
champion for him to fight Harry
Wills, Negro challenger.
The club disclosed in its evidence
that Dempsey admitted destroying
the original contract after he had
signed it.

BY WILLIAM BRADY, M. D.
IT STANDS TO REASON.
In the course of a letter about
the advisability of wearing rubber
tennis shoes all day and every
day at her work in charge of a
public playground—and I think
such shoes all right for that pur
pose—a young woman remarked
that she has had ample opportun
ity this last season to observe the
truth of a rather irritating asser
tion I have made from time to
time. She said that she had found
that youths who smoke have bad
principles or none. I have re
peatedly asserted that I should
not trust a youth who smokes.
By a youth I mean any person
under the age of 21 years.
It stands tov reason, I submit,
and I challenge argument of this,
it stands to reason that the youth
who can’t do without the narcotic
or stimulant effect of tobacco is
subnormal or abnormal. A normal
healthy young person finds plenty
of stimulation in youth itself and
needs no such fillip, no such
bracer for that tired feeling, as
the tobacco user gets from a
smoke.
The normally active youth
doesn’t crave tobacco, because
athletic and other wholesome ac
tivities answer so much better the
impulse of restlessness, the desire
for a thrill, the demand for ex
citement.
So I repeat, the youth who
smokes is subnormal or abnormal.
His or her education is sadly in
adequate or incomplete.
Very often, it seems to me, the
fault of education lies in the neg
lect of physical training. The
average youthful smoker has no
physical training; physical train
ing was unknown, unrecognized
or just a farce in the school
where such a youth has wasted
his or her earlier years.
I am not an anti-tobaccoist, I
like tobacco myself. I have never
seen any evidence that temperate
Use of tobacco harms an adult.
But I believe the use of tobacco
in youth is exceedingly detrimen
tal, both physically and morally,
and. I hail and support any move
ment to suppress such an evil.
But it seems to me that the
remedy is in the hands of par
ents, teachers and employers.
True, employers have found the
smoking youth a worthless sort
and discriminated against him.
Physical directors or athletic
trainers have found him no good
and excluded him from consider
ation. But parents and teachers
have been rather too lenient and
negligent in dealing with the be
ginning of the tobacco habit in
youth. A real school man should
expel from school any youth who
may be caught smoking, in school
or out of school. A good parent
should exact from the boy or girl
a solemn pledge against the use
of tobacco before the age of 21,
or if the child is not amenable to
moral suasion, then beat it out of
the youngster’s hide. If the young
ster is mentally deficient, then he
or she should be placed under
suitable restraint. To let a boy
or girl have his head and go his
or her pace in this one of the
gravest sins of omission which
parents these days commit.
Bpy or girl, the smoking youth
is no good.
Such a youngster is abnormal
and requires watching.

SEASONABLE SUGGESTIONS.
To give variety and elegance to
informal meals there is no better
aid than a well-stocked fruit closet.
This is the time of the year to fill
the shelves with jams, jellies, pre
serves and conserves. The follow
ing suggestions may be worth while
in regard to their use:
A cornstarch pudding topped with
a spoonful of strawberry preserves
or any other small fruit, makes a
plain dish quite out of the ordinary.
Any pudding like rice, bread, left
over cake with plain custard is
richer and more tasty with a spoon
ful of jelly or jam dotted over it.
Milk toast is delicious served with
blueberry jelly, blackberry jam or
loganberry preserve.
A firm jelly may be cut into cubes
to use in fruit salads, to garnish
cocktails, cake frosting, as well as
ice cream.
Jelly rolls, jelly tarts, jelly dough
nuts and jelly omelet are all easy
to make if one has plenty of jelly.
Jams or jellies are good to serve
with waffles and griddle cakes;
piled in layers with plenty of butter
and jelly on each layer, they may
be cut as pie and are served as
dessert.
Very small baking powder bis
cuits, opened and spread with but
ter, then with jam or jelly are fine;
cover and serve hot as a tasty sand
wich.
Apple sauce with a few spoonfuls
of strawberry jam addded makes
an entirely different sause.
Crush strawberries until well
mashed, then take equal measures
of sugar, stir and let stand in a
cool place until all the sugar has
been well dissolved and absorbed by
the berries. Have cans well steri
lized and cool, fill and seal without
cooking. Keep in a very cool cellar
and they will be good to the last
can. Raspberries and other small
fruits may be canned fresh in the
same way. This is the time to pre
serve watermelon pickles for the
winter. Soaked over night in salted
water, then cooked in clear water
until tender and then dropped into
a spicy vinegar and sugar and
scalded, then canned, they will be
a welcome dish in the winter.—
Nellie Maxwell.

the Jameson group, over s9,ooo,uuu,

Pennsy Railroad
To Spend 8 Million
For Safety Control
NEW YORK —The Pennsylvania
railroad has announced an $8,000,000
program by which automatic train
control and other additional safety
devices will be installed on 1,150
locomotives and along 1,530 of its
14,355 miles of main track. These
devices virtually are to eliminate
human mistakes, and make certain
the avoidance of accidents, if as ef
fective as hoped, the use of the de
vice probably will be extended.
The locomotive cabs will contain
duplicates of the usual signal lights
by which the train operation is con
trolled when they are read by the
engineer. But when these signals
change along the right of way the
color of the duplicate lights in the
cab will change accordingly, and a
whistle inside of the cab will call
the attention of the engineer to the
fact of change.
Should the engineer and fireman
fail to heed danger or caution sig
nals, the automatic device will stop
the train. That device is known as
the stop and “forestaller” and will
set the airbrakes. This device can
only be released from within the
cab, thus showing whether the engi
neer has acknowledged the fact that
the track ahead was not clear.

Perfect Chemical

Application for a public service
patent, to cover the use of a chem
ical, ethylene chlorhydrin, to hasten
growth of potatoes and other plants
has just been made on behalf of the
Boyce Thompson Institute for Plant
Research by Dr. F. E. Denny, a
member of the staff.
Quicker growth is promoted by
breaking up the rest period occur
ring aijter harvesting, and so hast
ening the sprouting of the dormant
buds.

whole in a solution of ethylene
chlorhydrin of the proper strength,
stored in closed containers and
planted in 24 hours; or they may be
treated with vapors from the ethy
lene chlorhydrin, spread by electric
fans, or the tubers may be cut and
soaked In a water solution of the
chemical.

NEW FARM BILL
IDEA BY FESS
WASHINGTON Senator Fess,
Ohio, just back from campaigning
in Maine, and recently in confer
ence with President Coolidge, talked
here yesterday about the farm re
lief question.
He will offer a revised form of
his farm relief measure at the com
ing session of congress and is hope
ful it will pass. He is seeking to
get the measure in shape to insure
it “nonpartisan” support. He has
little expectation, however, of get
ting the backing of the progressive
Republicans.
“The difficulty with farm legis
lation,” Senator Fess said, “has been
that the Democrats and the Repub
licans have been unable to agree
on the tariff. The measure that we
will offer at the next session will be
designed with the idea of compro
mising these dofferences, so that a
farm bill can be enacted.
“The agriculturists of the west
have the erroneous idea that the
tariff works against them. Our
plan will permit the farmers to or
ganize just as labor has (lone, and
turn the farm produce market from
a buyers’ market to a sellers’ mar
ket. If the farmers can control
their market through co-operation
their troubles will be over.”

FRANCE FINDS
SUPPLY OF OIL
PARIS—OiI in small quantities,
but still oil, has been struck in the
south of France, near Beziers on
the Gulf of Lyons.
Water “contaminated” with oil
has been known near the little vil
lage of Gablan outside of Beziers
since the 17th century, but quite re
cently two geologists were moved to
investigate its industrial possibil
ities. Their efforts were rewarded,
for three pockets were located at
depths around 500 feet, which be
tween November, 1924, and March,
1926, yielded 1,500,000 gallons of
crude oil.
Unfortunately this product was
characterized by the di’awback of a
10 per cent parraffin content, but
even after the process of refining the
total output reached a figure well
over 1,000,000 gallons.
The future value of these wells is
impossible to predict, says Dr. R.
Brunshweig, engineer of the French
bureau of mines, but the quantity
thus far produced is a respectable
contribution to the ever-increasing
demand of the French nation for
more gasoline for automobiles.

Describes Death
Of Plants After
Attack of Fungus
ITHACA, N. Y. —The death throes
of a single plant cell, a microscopic
tragedy that is repeated by the bil
lions in every grain field or truck
patch attacked by smut, rust, blight
or any of the hundred other destruc
tive plant diseases, was. described
here today before £U session of the
International Congress of Plant Sci
ences by Prof. J. Beauverie of the
University of Lyon.
AVhen the feeler-like thread of the
fatal fungus reaches the cell some
poison which ic emanates throws the
cell’s living substance, the proto
plasm, into a state described as
“hypertonic” —roughly analogous to
fever. Death soon ensues and the
breakup of the cell content follows.
First, the protoplasm becomes finely
granular; then, when water enters,
certain special denser bits of it
swell up into tiny bubbles and burst.
The minute green bodies that give
the plant its color become granu
lated and run together, giving off
droplets of oil. In the end the
fungal thread is left in full posses
sion.
In addition to certain technical
considerations, Prof. Beauverie
pointed out that the solution of this
microscopic problem is the basis for
attack upon the great economic prob
lems presented by plant diseases,
which cost the world millions yearly.

IS PROMISING, 1
VIEW OF GRACE
CHICAGO Eugene G. Grace*
president, Bethlehem Steel corpora
tion, yesterday expressed confidence
in the outlook for the steel industry
and general business of the current
year and beyond, and an entire ab
sence of fear over the possibility of
keener industrial competition from
Europe.
Steel Buying Up.
“Buying of steel for the fourth
quarter is gathering momentum,”
said Mr. Grace. “There is no ques
tioning of prices, as in fact con
sumers appear glad to place their
business at prevailing prices. Actual
fourth quarter business is in hand
and our advices as to the situation
with leading consumers indicate
that for the balance of the year op
erations will improve to the extent
of the increased fall demand.
“Construction is continuing at a
heavy rate and the carriers are in
need of much steel, especially for
track maintenance work.
Exports on Climb.
“We are exporting more steel than
is being imported. We met foreign
steel competition before the war,
and can do it again. Stabilization
of foreign currencies is taking from
European producers the advantages
they enjoyed in the way of rela
tively lower prices.”

OPPOSE MOVE
IN G. A, R, FOR
DISBANDMENT
Milwaukee’s delegation to the
GOth national encampment of the
Grand Army of the Republic in Des
Moines, la., Sept. 19 to 24, will op
pose any efforts that may be made
to disband the organization, Frank
A. Walsh, former national vice
commander, who will head the lqcal
representatives, declared today.
Says It’s Premature.
“We have not received official
word of any movement afoot to dis
band the G. A. R., but we would
certainly oppose any attempt along
that line,” Mr. Walsh said.
“I do not feel that the time is
ripe to speak of disbanding an or
ganization which still is as active
and has as large a membership as
the G. A. R.”
Dispatches emanating from Des
Moines to the effect that a commit
tee consisting of three former na
tional commanders had been ap
pointed to report on plans for dis
bandment of the body and disposi
tion of its funds and records,
brought forth Mr. Walsh’s reply.
25 Leave Sunday.
The Milwaukee delegation, repre
senting the E. B. Wolcott post, will
.consist of 25 members and will leave
Sunday for Des Moines.

CONFUSED HEADS CANNOT TEACH
Some old party editors who are more remarkable for
the vigor of their partisanship than for the balance of their
minds, take a fall out of Viscount Robert Cecil of Great
Britain for saying that ‘there is no incongruity between
belonging to the league of nations and patriotism of a most
burning quality.”
It is pointed out by these editors that American league
enthusiasts often talk as if loyalty to the league should
take precedence over loyalty to the United btates. And
from this alleged fact they jump to the conclusion that
one cannot be at tjie same time an internationalist and a
nationalist.
We beg to differ. The propaganda for the league and
world court in the United States is financed by some of the
same people who dragged the United States into the Woild
war. In other words, it paid them then to be hundred per
cent nationalists and pitch into the international
Now it pays them to have the American government in
the league, or at least in the world court. They are doing
it for American interests, namely their own. They don t
find any difficulty about being nationalists and interna
tionalists at the same time.
Of course, there are a lot of addle-pated champions
of pacifism and internationalism who are just as illogical
as the dull old party editors. But criticizing them with
the same sapheaded superficiality that is typical of them
does not teach clear thinking. It only creates more con
fusion and partisan animosity.
Just as big bankers, industrial captains and mer
chants find it possible to be national paytriots and yet to
champion an international body like the league, so the
workers of every country can be intensely patriotic, that
is intent upon their'own national interests, yet at the same
time benefit by the aid, advice and co-operation of their
International organization.
The difficulties that arise over such matters are not
due in the main to internationalism, but to the class an
tagonisms at home. Internationalism today is a new
lineup in the class war. It is just as impossible under the
conditions of, private capitalism to defend the interests
of all classes by nationalism as by internationalism.
So long as the league and world court are ruled by
old party governments, they will be used by capitalist
cliques for the same purposes as the national government:
To exploit the majority of the citizens. Big business finds
internationalism quite compatible with loyalty to its own
pocketbook, but hates to see the workers gain strength
by international co-operation with the comrades of their
own class.

The Milwaukee Sentinel blames the Socialists for
the defeat of Senator Lenroot in the Republican pri
maries. It reflects sadly that Socialists are such individ
ualists that they won’t listen to the hints of their own
leaders. In spite of all warnings to stay out of the old
party quarrels, says The Sentinel, many Socialists voted
for Blaine against Lenroot.
The Sentinel congratulates Lenroot on his fine cam
paign and pours balm on his feelings by lambasting the
Socialist's who didn’t listen to the advice of their own
party and who failed to fall for the Lenroot literature.
Well, whining about declining party responsibility
and kicking Socialist sympathizers for acting like old party
voters may be some relief for disappointed Tories, but if
these sympathizers had voted for Lenroot against Blaine,
The Sentinel’s conscience would have been very easy about
such lack of party responsibility.

THEY WISH FOR PEACE
The speeches .of Foreign Ministers Briand and Strest
mann at the Geneva meeting of the league of nations cele
brate Germany’s entry with formal wishes for peace.
We believe that both men are honest in their desire
for peace. Perhaps they are also honest in their belief
that peace is possible without changing from private cap
italism to Socialism. But that is as far as they go. It
is not enough to make even sincere peace wishes come true.
While these two leaders of France and Germany were
shaking hands, French and Rumanian military experts
met with Polish in Warsaw to talk matters over that boded
no good to peace. The Warsaw meeting was at least as
significant as that in Geneva. Perhaps more so, because
Briand is Poincare’s minister.
While Briand took office under Poincare with the
understanding that the Locarno policy should dominate
French foreign affairs, Poincare does not believe in the
Locarno spirit. The meeting of the military experts in
Warsaw immediately after the formal conclusion of the
French-Rumanian treaty shows that Poincare still pursues
the object of surrounding Soviet Russia with a steel wall
and shutting her off from Germany.
Germany’s economic interests are being tied up more
and more with those of France and Russia on the one hand,
with those of the United States on the other. They ought
to make for peace and would if the statesmen of the old
school did not persist in keeping up their armaments and
their secret military pacts.
Unfortunately economic pools between bankers and
industrial leaders of different nations do not mean co
operation without friction. Such pacts, like most business
bargains, are generally made under pressure, either fi
nancial or political. One or the other of the parties to a
pool feels that he got the worst of it. At the first oppor
tunity, he will try to exert pressure to do better.
While some private interests can be amalgamated by
international pools, it is the nature of private capitalism
to keep the economy of one nation opposed to that of
others and to emphasize the resulting antagonisms rather
than to extend the natural interdependence into an all
around co-operation.
Even when large industrial sections of one nation co
operate on a fifty-fifty basis with those of another, the
capitalists always try to prevent the workers from sharing
in the benefits. When organized labor is not equally
strong on both sides on the frontier, and when labor
standards differ appreciably in two countries, friction is
inevitable and will always implicate the governments in
the long run.
There are some powerful American business interests
that try to bring about economic co-operation between
France, Germany and Russia. Other American leaders try
to prevent it. The same is true of French, German and
Russian leaders. So the clash of private interests within
each nation keeps alive international frictions.
Briand and Stresemann may express sentimental
peace wishes, yet will be unable to do anything effectiva
for the elimination of economic and political differences
which led to war in the past and will do so again.
Modern statesmen schooled in old party ideas, even
when talking peace, still persist in maintaining the funda
mental causes that produce wars. Maybe it is some prog
ress to have them realize the need for peace. But we don't
expect any practical results from them, so long as they
fight those far-seeing demands of labor leaders schooled
in the economics of Socialism, which aim to

INHERITANCE A GOOD THING OR
EVIL?
Sir Josiah Stamp’s address on Inheritance is a remin
der that things are not always what they seem, and that
what passes for economic science at the British Associa
tion is too often only a cloak for antiquated and rather
shabby prejudices. It is really time for economists to
make up their minds either to bSse their statements upon
ascertained facts as in other fields of research, or to aban
don the claim that their assumptions should be classed
as science.
Take the assumption upon which Sir Josiah Stamp’s
address was based. Shortly it is as follows:
“The power of handing on accumulated wealth is an
immense stimulus to an able man.
“As a result the able man exerts his ingenuity to the
highest degree, creates new capital forms, and builds up
more efficient organization—from all of which the com
munity benefits.
“It is no doubt true that individuals in the next gener
ation are not so well off as they would have been if the
accumulated result had been inherited socially—but then
the wealth might never have come if it had not been in
tended for the heir.”
Upon what known facts is this assumption made? Is
it true in the light of our knowledge of human nature?
In our view the most fallacious of all theories is that
which regards personal gain and the right to bequeath
riches as the most potent of human incentives.
Can Sir Josiah imagine that great inventors, or even
great business men, are always saying to themselves s
“What shall I get? How much shall Ibe able to leave?”
Surely everyone knows that in human beings of any worth
the desire to do things is far greater than the desire to
do other people.
Next, Sir Josiah assumes that accumulation of capital
and that savings for renewals and improvements in in
dustry are safer under the present system of ownership
and distribution than they could be under any other.
For evidence against this it is only necessary to ex
amine the return of municipal enterprise from one e r
of the country to the other. If under private ownership
wealth is put aside for further wealth production, it ca«
be done better under public ownership. Sir Josiah gives
his case away by admitting that today the real saving
“goes on silently through company reserves, etc., and
never becomes anyone’s spendable resources at all.”
Under this system the community has no voice in the
use to which accumulated reserves are put. It may be
that they are spent for useful ends—but more generally it
is for useless ends.
The more, therefore, that accumulated wealth ceases
to pass into the hands of individuals and the more intends
to come under the control of the nation the better it will
be for all concerned. For that reason Labor will support
extended restrictions of the right to inherit—a right which
is against the public weal.—London Herald.

again go out of their banks unless
the rain ceases.

ings.

roads were hours behind schedule

EXPECT 2,000
AT MEETING OF
AFRICAN CHURCH
More than 2,000 persons from four
states-will assemble in the Milwau
kee Auditorium, Sept. 22, for the
annual Chicago district conference
of the African Methodist Episcopal
church. The convention will last
five days.
The program was announced to
day by the Rev. Eugene Thompson,
general chairman of arrangements.
Three sessions will be held daily,
with a special meeting each night.
The opening day program will be
climaxed by a banquet at which the
visitors will be welcomed by Mayor
Daniel W. Hoan, the Rev. Harry S.
Wise, secretary, Milwaukee Council
of Churches and other prominent
Milwaukeeans.
Music will be furnished by St.
Mark’s chorus of St. Mark’s A. M.
E. church. This church, founded
in 1860, is the oldest colored church
in the state. Its congregation will
be official hosts to the visitors.
The night session, Sept. 23, will be
devoted to educational problems,
with addresses by Ernest Dyett,
Joliet, Ill.; President Gilbert H.
Jones, Wilberforce university, and
Dean George F. Woodson,' Paine
Theological seminary, Wilberforce,
0.
Noted missionaries from Africa
and the West Indies will relate their
experiences at the Sept. 24 meeting.
The Rev. R. H. Mayhew, Trinidad,
and Bishop Sampson Brooks, Li
beria, as well as the Rev. Carl Tan
ner, Chicago, will be among the
speakers. There will be a concert
Sept. 25 and Sept. 26, a special ex
cursion train will bring 1,000 dele
gates from Chicago for the Young
People’s service. A large chorus and
orchestra has been trained for
weeks in preparation for this event
Plankinton and Engelmann halls
of the Auditorium will be used for
the convention.

By a campfire in the forest sat a

They had built the fire with the
help of flint, in wilderness style,

hunting with you nearly a whole
week,” he said. “It will be hard
to go back. I have to go to school.”
“You will come with me again,”
said the red man.
“Not for a while,” replied the boy,
and fell silent. His father had
built a settlement on the shores of
Lake Otsego and there the boy lived.
He had made friends with the In
dians and the white hunters and
trappers. There was nothing he
loved better than going with them
on trips into the forest. Now he
would have to give it up for a
while.
“Whenever you come,” said the
Indian gravely, “you will always be
welcome among my people.”

Cooper, born Sept. 15, who wrote

Ape Is Descended
From Man, Is Claim
BERLIN Prof. Max Westen
hofer, custodian of the Pathological
museum of the Berlin university,
said yesterday that the ape is de
scended from man and not man from
the ape. He points out that chim
panzee cubs resemble human beings
much more than do their parents.
He says that certain inner organs
give evidence that man’s ancestors
lived for a time in water. These
peculiar characteristics are missing
in apes, which, he declares, “shows
that the ape represents the subse
quent development and proves that
man is the older form of mammal.”
Prof. Westenhofer elucidated this
theory before the anthropological
congress now in session at Salzburg.

FORTY MILLION
EUROPEANS
SEEKING RIGHTS
Leader Special Service.
COLOGNE—The Koelnische Zeit
ung gives in a recent issue a survey
of the constructive policies outlined
by the congress of the national mi
norities which closed its sessions in
Geneva, Aug. 27.
There are about 40,000,000 people
forced to live under European gov
ernments of other nationalities than
their own. The leaders of these mi
norities 1 have wisely avoided the
pitfalls of so-called irredentism,
that is, of preaching national libera
tion by force.
Most of the big governments
would probably welcome irredentist
movements as an excuse for the
bloody suppression of domestic oppo
sition leaders. The minority leaders
do not intend to offer such openings.
Make Sane Demands.
Instead of preaching revolt, the
leaders of the minority movement iu
Europe insist that the minorities
must work for their rights within
the frames of the present states.
The general plan laid out by the
congress is to work for laws which
shall guarantee freedom to the mi
norities for the expression of their
own culture.
In order to give legal basis to
the freedom of nationality within
each state, it is proposed to separate
the governments from the control of
matters of culture. Every national
ity should be free to speak its own
language, read its own literature,
teach its children its own culture
in addition to the general educa
tion given by public schools.
So far only one small European
state, Esthonia, has realized this
ideal. It is called autonomy of
culture, and it has worked well for
the Esthonian government and for
the national minorities under its
rule.
Demand R?al Equality.
Aside from freedom of national
culture, the leaders of the Euro
pean minority movements also de
mand economic and legal equali
ty for the minorities with the ma
jorities.
At present the national minori
ties suffer a great deal from eco
nomic and legal discrimination cf
the majority governments against
them. Under the pretext of land
reform, their real estate has been
confiscated, often without any
compensation. Labor laws put
them at a disadvantage. Taxation,
trade licenses, election laws ham
per the minorities in many ways.
For this reason, the Geneva con
gress of the national minorities set
up the rule that the laws of any
nation should not make any distinc
tion between the native majorities
and the national minorities.

the Geneva labor office of the
league of nations, declaring that
the Washington eight-hour pact is
in danger.
Mr. Thomas describes the efforts
made in the spring of 1926 to over
come the obstacle which had pre
vented the ratification of the eight
hour pact by the leading industrial
nations.
A conference was held in London
during March. The labor ministers
of Belgium, France, Germany, Great
Britain and Italy attended it and
tried to reach an agreement on the
interpretation of the provisions of
the pact.
Conference Made Progress.
The conference was a success,
The Guardian continues. The min
isters agreed on a text. It looked
as if the pact would soon be ratified
by at least five governments. But
a few weeks after the return Of the
miinsters to their own countries two
events changed the situation for the
worse.
First, the British government re
pealed the seven-hour law for the
miners. Mr. Thomas admits that
this does not formally endanger the
eight-hour pact, but the moral ef
fect is bad on all the other govern
ments.
If the British miner has to work
eight hours he will work as long as
the miner in Upper Silesia, half an
hour longer than the miner in the
Ruhr, and 50 minutes more than
the French miner.
The world is told dramatically
that in Great Britain, the home of
the shorter working day, the lead
ing men consider it necessary in the
interest of national welfare to ex
tend tho working time.
Blames British Example.
Mr. Thomas hints that the bad
British example had a lot to do
with the second event which
changed the conditions for the early
ratification of the eight-hour pact
for the worse.
In June the Fascist government
abolished the eight-hour day and
decreed the nine-hour day for all
Italy. Under the Washington pact,
overtime beyond eight hours was
to be paid for at the rate of 25
per cent plus. The Italian laws
of March, 1923, provided for the
same overpay- But the legal nine
hour day abolished this extra pay.
It was serious enough that the
governments should delay the rati
fication of the eight-hour pact.
But now the bad example of Eng
land and Italy has started a drift
away from the pact. Mr. Thomas
fears that the governments will en
gage in a competition for the long
est working day. It would ba more
disastrous than competition for the
biggest military establishment.

By Edwta Bobart Petra
THE HOME OF THE SILVER
BIBLE.
My Swedish excursion this week
brought me to Uppsala, the Swed
ish Oxford, for its great university
was founded in 1477. The Uppsala
Cathedral took up some of my time,
for it is the largest in Sweden and
was commenced in the year 1280
and took 155 years to complete. Here
is buried Gustavus Vasa and his
consorts and also many others with
renowned names. Here also is the
tomb of Carl von Linde, or Lin
naeus, as the great bontanist Is bet
ter known. Emanuel Swedenborg,
the founder of the Swedenborgians,
also lies interred in this beautiful
cathedral. Uppsala Castle, which
dominates the town, also deserves a
visit to honor its nearly 400 years.
At the university I came across
that famous treasure of the north,
the Codex Argenteus, the Silver
Bible, a translation into the
the Gothic language of parts of the
Gospels, made by Bishop Ulphilas.
It is the only Gothis manuscript in
existence and is supposed to have
been written about A. D. 500. It
formed part of the spoils of war
taken from the Swedes from Prague
in 1648.

president of the National Federa

don and whose dictates decide what

will be longer, the materials will be
of bright hues, and a slim effect will
characterize the cuts.

CHlCAGO—Superhighways for
Cook county came a 'step nearer
reality last evening when a $15,-
000,000 bond issue for widening ex
isting pavements and building new
ones in a spider web system cover
ing Chicago, was recommended
unanimously by the emergency high
way advisory committee appointed
by President A. J. Cermak of the
county board.
A $23,000,000 three-year program
was adopted after an afternoon of
discussion between state and county
engineers, county commissioners and
other members of the committee of
which D. H. Burnham of the Chi
cago plan commission was the chair
man.
Widening Is First.
This program, which involves the
improvement or addition of 521
miles of roads in the county, is ex
pected to be accepted in general at
the next meeting of the county
board and the work started with
highway funds until the $15,000,000
is voted upon at the November elec
tion.
The bond resolution carried the
recommendation that the widening
of existing roads be undertaken first.
Within four months, it was stated
at the meeting, the engineers of the
plan commission will have a full
program of super-highways ready
for new action and a new bond issue.
The plans adopted yesterday will be
modified if necessary to meet the
new plan, which may call for 200-
foot boulevards.
State to Pay.
The question of apportioning the
costs of making the bond issue and
the tax funds legally sound in ap
portioning the work was not taken
up, as this is the job of the county
committee attorneys. The state has
accepted $3,885,500 already as its
allotment of the cost and will put
it under contract at an early date.
Funds are legally available for the
city’s portion, it is said. This is
estimated at $6,535,000.

PROFITS FROM
STATE'S DRY
ACT 52,000,000
MADISON, Wis. More than
$2,000,000 receipts over the expendi
tures of enforcing prohibition have
been diverted into the state treas
ury since 1920, L. C. Gunderson,
state prohibition commissioner, said
today.
Here’s the List.
Gunderson listed the following re
ceipts and expenditures for the en
forcement of the old Mulberger law
and the present Severson act for
the fiscal years 1920 to 1926:
Fines collected and paid into
state treasury to Jan. 1, 1926,
$2,048,563; permit fees, $184,150;
witness fees (non-appropriated),
$7,108.70; non-intoxicating license
fees, 10 per cent, $125,562.91; sale
of seized alcohol, $60.75; sale of
confiscated vehicles, $2,085.89; fees
appropriated, $16,041.11; total ap
propriations, $3(50,000; disburse
ments, $333,041.95; balance, $2,380,-
494.40.
Enforcement Cost Lower.
“The above figures,” stated Gun
derson, “show that the coffers of
the state treasury have been in
creased to the amount of over
$2,250,000 since the advent of pro
hibition in this state, from 1920 to
1926. None of the fines for viola
tion of the state prohibition act dur
ing 1926 have been included in this
report.
The appropriation to the state
prohibition commissioner for en
forcement of the first prohibition
law, known as the Mulberger law,
was $15,000 annually, plus the fees
appropriated.
The present state prohibition law,
known as the Severson act, went
into effect July 1, 1921. Under this
law the state prohibition commis
sion is given an annual appropri
ation of $60,000 for the enforcement
of prohibition in this state.”
Chicago Man Says
Labor Conditions
Poor in Holy Land
NEW YORK—Judge Harry M.
Fisher of Chicago returned yester
day on the Majestic from Palestine,
where he studied the ’economic con
ditions of the country.
He said he found an industrial
depression and 5,000 out of employ
ment, chiefly in the building trades,
because deflation of currency in Po
land had stopped money coming
into the country. He said the agri
cultural outlook was good and the
wine cellars at Richonel Zion, the
second largest in the world, next
to Bordeaux.
“Work is under way on the rail
road from Haifa to Beirut, a dis
tance of 60 miles, which will be ex
tended along the coast to Tripoli,
another 40 miles,” Judge Fisher
said. “When that is finished through
trains will run from Paris or Calais
to Cairo, via El Kantara on the
Suez canal.”

NEW CREATION

DEMONSTRATED
CHICAGO—Thomas A. Edison’s
latest bit of wizardry was Intro
duced to Chicago last night by his
son, Charles Edison, president of his
father’s industries at Orange, N. J.
It is a new process phonograph
record which plays for 20 minutes.
And it may be turned over to play
another 20 minutes. Whole operas
may be presented on a single record,
each side playing as many as eight
selections.
At a banquet given by young Edi
son last night to phonograph deal
ers at the Palmer house, the new
record was demonstrated, and the
reason for its creation by the fa
mous inventor was given.
“The radio permits music lovers
to sit at ease while whole programs
are heard without moving from
their chairs,” Mr. Edison said.
“People have wearied of changing
their phonograph records after each
three or four minute offering.
“So we are bringing our records
which will play a goodly number of
selections, and for 40 minute periods
with only one change—a turnover
of the record. During the 40 min
utes the reproducing point travels
more than a mile.”

LUDENDORFF
WEDS WIDELY
KNOWN WRITER
MUNICH—Ten years ago Ger
many was thundering with the name
of Gen. Erich von Ludendorff,
quartermaster general of the Ger
man army. Yesterday the almost
friendless little dictator of Ger
many’s handful of Fascists married
Dr. Mathilda von Kemnitz, the co
respondent in the July divorce ac
tion brought by his wife.
A Quiet Affair.
The ceremony was attended only
by a dozen officers who had partici
pated in the general’s attempted
Munich revolution three years ago,
and a few relatives.
Gen. von Ludendorff wore the full
military evening dress of the Bavar
ian order, and the bride wore a
traveling suit. Her two sons, each
of whom was presented with a mo
torcycle by their new stepfather,
acted as witnesses.
The wedding party arrived by
automobile at the office of the city
magistrate of Tutzing, near Munich,
where the burgomaster performed a
civil ceremony.
No Signs of Glee.
Fifteen minutes later the pair ap
peared on the steps, received flow
ers, shook hands, and departed for
Berlin on their honeymoon. There
were no speeches, hurrahs, or signs
of jubilation.
Gen. von Ludendorff’s second wife
is one of Germany’s first feminists.
She achieved considerable literary
success and then took up politics.

WASHINGTON—A plea to re
turn the American dead from
French war cemeteries was made
today by Senator Thaddeus H.
Caraway, Arkansas, who just re
turned from France. He visited
Flanders field, where 30,000 Amer
ican soldiers are buried.

the United States has been carried
to the extreme of writing “To hell
with the Americans” and other
vicious epithets on crosses marking
the graves of America’s war dead.
“Congress should pass legislation
to bring back every one of the 30,000
American boys who sleep in
France,” declared Caraway, bitter
from the sights he has witnessed
in the cemeteries.

TEKEMAH, Neb.—An attempt

rary injunction against the sen

TEKAMAH, Neb.—The bread and
water sentence of Roy Carson, 35,
former liquor law violator,
was reduced 10 days when it was
found on physical examination that
Carson, who is on his seventh day’s
diet in the Burt county jail, was
undernourished and that continu
ance of the diet was inadvisable.
The original sentence imposed on
Carson by County Judge Orville
Chatt was 60 days in the jail with
the first and last 20 days to be
served on bread and water, By his
order today Dr. 11. W. Benson,
county physician, ruled Hbit (.‘arson
must serve three more days on
bread and water, making 10 for his
first stretch on the diet, 23 days
on full rations, 10 on bread and
water and 10 more -days on the
same diet if his condition under
supervision at that time is found
to stand it.
Under complaint of another bread
and water prisoner, Thomas Nel
son, Craig farmer, that he was ill,
a physical examination was given
him. Nelson, who is 50, is on his
fourth day of diet and is held in the
same cell as Carson.

STATE GUARD
OFFICER DIES
CAMP DOUGLAS—Lieut. Col.
Charles R. Williams, chief quarter
master of the Wisconsin National
guard, died at his home on the mili
tary reservation here today.
His death followed several
months’ illness. Col. Williams suf
fered a stroke of paralysis last
spring and for several months was
confined at the Madison general
hospital. Later he recovered and
returned to his home here.
A second stroke, however, dis
abled him and he was forced to give
up his active duties during June of
this year. A third stroke proved
fatal.
For more than 35 years Col. Wil
liams had been one of Wisconsin’s
outstanding soldiers.

WASHINGTON Controls of
state political organizations slipped
from two leaders In yesterday’s

dicted. Nine states held primaries.

wrested from the Senator Phipps-
Senator Means group, returns in
dicated. Charles W. Waterman,
who is opposed to the Klan, de
feated Rice W. Means, incumbent,
who was head of the influential
claims committee and one of the
most active “drys” in the senate.
Name Dry Speaker.

who has been chief executive for
three terms, lost a fourth nomina
tlbn to Mayor Fred Green of lonia.

gressman, who received fees for dry
speeches, defeated his “wet” oppo
nent.
The anti-world court group made
its gain and the “wets” obtained a
more militant anti-prohibitionist in
the indicated victory of Representa
tive John P. Hill, Republican, over
Senator Weller, world court advo
cate, described in the campaign as
“dry-damp” in the Maryland sena
torial primary.
The renomination of Gov. Albert
Ritchie, Maryland, prominently men
tioned as a Democratic presidential
possibility, assured Ritchie of fur
ther consideration for 1928.

indicated the candidates were run
ning as had been expected without
upsets on account of any national
issues.

isiana, an avowed “wet,” defeated
his opponent, according to returns.

court.

South Carolina, a dry and a world
court advocate, apparently was nom
inated for re-election. Senator
Wesley Jones, veteran Republican
senator from Washington, was re
nominated. Returns in Massachu
setts, Vermont and New York had
no national significance.

chusetts, chairman of the Repub
lican national committee, was re
nominated.

mortem examination, to be conduct
ed today, shows death was due to
electrocution, an inquest will be or
dered.

gan the reading of 27 affidavits and

Saves Boy’s Life;
Gets Gift of New
Suit for Heroism
CHICAGO Melville Colver re
turned to work yesterday with a
new suit—the prize of heroism.
Last night he was riding on an
“L” train when the brakes brought
the train to a sudden stop on a
bridge over the Chicago river.
“We’ve hit a boy,” the motorman
shouted. Young Colver peered out
the window and saw a tattered red
sweater floating in the murky river
waters.
He leaped to the water and
dragged Ralph Grieg to the shore
where the boy was brought back to
consciousness. The little boy had
been badly lacerated on the head
and was nearly drowned.
After his heroic act Colver dis
appeared and at his home today his
father said:
“Oh, he’s back at work. Wo
bought him a new suit and he
wasn’t hurt by the splash.”

BRIBERY CASE
Investigation into the charges
that a former 3rd St. saloonkeeper
escaped indictment by a federal
grand jury after he had paid bribes
of more than $1,500 to a federal
prohibition agent, are being investi
gated by the United States district
attorney’s office, it was learned late
yesterday.
The saloonkeeper is said to have
admitted to federal officials that ho
paid the money to the agent. The
agent told him that he would keep
S3OO for himself and pay the bal
ance to “higher ups.” No arrests
have been made.
The saloon was raided by the
agent involved and two others. Only
real beer was found and samples
were taken. The grand jury did not
indict the proprietor.

ITALY TO SEND
FRANCE NOTE ON
BOMBING PLOT
ROME —The Italian foreign office
is busy preparing a note to the
French government on the subject
of the activities of Italian anti-Fas
cists in France. The note will be
civil in tone and will not impart in
any way the violent expressions in
dulged in by the Roman newspapers
or other mediums of Fascist opinion
directly after the attempt on Pre
mier Mussolini’s life Saturday.
Feeling Is Unfriendly.
The tension of the public feeling
against France appears to be relax
ing rapidly under the soothing treat
ment of official hands.
The speediest measures are being
taken to revive the death penalty
in Italian law. King Vidor Emman
uel has returned to Rome from the
war maneuvers in the province of
Umbria to sign the death penalty
decree, which will come up before
an extraordinary session of the
council of ministers.
Poincare Resents Attack.
PARlS—Premier Raymond Poin
care bad a long conversation with
the Italian ambassador, Baron Ro
mano Avessano, today, concerning
the bitter attacks against France in
the Fascist press In Italy. M. Poin
care politely, but firmly, informed
the ambassador that France deeply
resented the unjustifiable attitude
taken by Italy in connection with
the recent attempt on the life of
Premier Mussolini.

NEW YORK—Except fcr evening,
knees continue to be “in,” while
arms, unless they are intricately
draped, are decidedly “out,” advance
showing of autumn and winter fash
ions yesterday at the Kenneth Saw
yer Goodman Memorial theater by
the Fashion Art League of America,
decidedly indicated.

dress reveals the blouse-back and
the batwing or dolman sleeves that
distinguished wartime fashions, and,
except for the pegtop skirt, the

blousey from the waist up and slim
from the waist down.

tail in this year’s clothes, accord

are correspondingly more feminine
and intricate. Metal brocades,- vel
vets, chiffon and velvet brocades
are among the fashionable fabrics.

DOCTORS STRESS
CARE OF SMALL
HUNTING WOUNDS
MADISON—With the opening of
the hunting season in Wisconsin
this week, nimrods are warned in a
bulletin issued by the Wisconsin
State Medical society to beware of
so-called “trivial injuries.” So many
little accidents have caused such
serious results in the past that the
health committee of the State Medi
cal society has issued a special bul
letin of “Bewares” for hunters.
“As the hunting season ap
proaches it may be wise to remind
hunters that they should beware of
other things than the dog,” declares
the bulletin. “Every season brings
its appalling list of casualties and
fatalities which can be diminished,
mainly by following the age old
maxim, ‘an ounce of prevention is
worth a pound of cure.’ Prevention
of accidents calls for ‘horse-sense,’
a rare commodity, as may be seen
from the frequent changing of seats
in a boat or skiff, dragging a gun
muzzle foremost over a fence or
through the brush, or carrying load
ed guns in improper positions.
“After accidents have happened,
the serious ones will receive prompt
attention and need no further men
tion at this time. It is the slight
wounds, so-called trivial injuries,
that are often neglected, and there
fore call for consideration.
“Punctured or penetrating wounds
usually do not cause much immedi
ate pain or inconvenience and are
therefore prone to be neglected, but
owing to the airtight wound that
results, the germ of lockjaw finds
favorable conditions for growth and
may not manifest itself until after
10 or more days, when treatment
is a serious problem and the out
look grave. Prompt, competent at
tention at the time of the injury
will prevent serious developments.
Lacerated wounds: Scratches
from bushes, thorns, trees, wires,
notably barb wire fences, leave
open surfaces for the absorption of
infection with possible resultant
blood poisoning. Such abrasions
should be cleaned and then pro
tected from contamination by clean
dressings.
“Sprains of joints are often more
serious than they seem to be at
first, and such injuries call for
X-ray pictures to exclude bone in
jury and to be followed by rest—
by splint or plaster supports—in
this w r ay markedly reducing the pe
riod of disability.
“One other frequent source of in
disposition calls for. emphasis,
namely, care in the choice of drink
ing water. If there is any doubt
about the nature of the supply, be
on the safe side, and drink only
boiled water.”

Brunswick.

turned into a public bawdy house.

government also lost the two Otta

La Pointe with participating in a
wild party on a government launch.

Doucet also suffered defeat.

constitutional issue raised by the

parliament, forcing Mr. King to re
sign as premier.

BARRED FOR LIFE IN ILLINOIS

i By Boxing Com-

CHICAGO—-To halt an alleged
gambling coup, the Illinois boxing
'commission has called off the ban
tamweight championship fight be
tween Charlie Phil Rosenberg, New
York, and Bud Taylor, Terre Haute,
Ind., scheduled for tomorrow night,
has barred Champion Rosenberg
and his manager, Harry Segal, for
life in Illinois rings, and has award
ed the championship to Taylor.
Rosenberg had previously been
barred from rings in New York
and California following reports of
unethical conduct.
Commission Statement.
The Rosenberg-Taylor bout, sched
uled for tomorrow night, was called
off following reports that New
York gamblers had descended in
Chicago with heavy bets to place on
Rosenberg.
The boxing commission, in its
Statement, barring the bout and
conferring the title upon Taylor,
gives as the official reason for the
action:
“Segal and Rosenberg ignored our
rules pertaining to forfeits after
the commission had granted several
days grace, and further because of
the injection of political and other
influences pertaining to our ap
pointment of a referee. Segal and
Rosenberg, in our opinion, are not
the caliber of men who belong in
boxing.”
Forfeits Due July 24.
According to Chairman O. W.
Huncke of the Illinois commission,
forfeits should have been posted
July 24. The forfeit was to have
been $12,500.
The gamblers, it is said, wanted
to be sure that the decision would
not be too unfair to Rosenberg,
and were prepared to back their
bets with threats as to what would
happen if Taylor won. Detectives
had been ordered to appear at the
ringside to forestall any violence,
but the commission heard of the
action and called a halt.
Segal and Rosenberg were taken
completely by surprise when in
formed of the commission’s ruling.
Both were at Mullen’s gymnasium
when told of the news, Rosenberg
In the ring working out with a
sparring partner.
Segal declared that he had been
preparing to deposit the forfeit
money today and was furious be
cause of the decision.
May Box Graham.
Taylor is ordered to defend the
title that the commission has thrust
upon him in Chicago under the di
rection of Promoter Jim Mullen
against an opponent who must be
improved by the boxing board. Mul
len stands to lose in the neighbor
hood of $5,000, which he has al
ready paid out for advertising,

daily dozen and another dozen or
two besides. These exercises will be
continued daily throughout the stay
In camp.

men and the backs were separated
for practice on fundamentals. Line
Coach Freeman Fitzgerald handled
the candidates for the forward wall
and started them out with practice

that great stress was placed on the
work done by the tackles. Several
men were tried in those positions
and with two varsity vacancies ex
isting, it will be a critical post to
fill this fall. Jerry Kelly, Chicago;
Clarence Mublick. Kenosha, and Dan
Smith, Grand Forks, N. D., were
outstanding yesterday.
The backfield men were separated
lb** groups of four and with a
printing and labor in making prep
arations for the bout.
Mullen took the commission’s ac
tion stoically and was busy last
night trying to line up a match be
tween Taylor and Bushy Graham»
who Is regarded in New York as
Rosenberg’s most formidable chal
lenger. Mullen stated that in his
opinion the commission had acted
justly.

Mullen added that he had gone
before the commission personally on
three different occasions to ask that
Segal be given more time to post
the forfeit. He said that the com
mission had granted his request
each time, but when Segal fail to
appear at the commission’s office
yesterday with the money, as he
had promised to do, the action fol
lowed*

NEW HEARING
SOUGHT ON
INJUNCTION
INDIANAPOLIS—(United Press)
—Frank Symmes, attorney repre
senting Jack Dempsey, announced
today a new hearing will be sought
in the injunction proceedings by the
Coliseum club of Chicago in su
perior court here seeking to pre
vent the heavyweight champion
from meeting Gene Tunney in Phil
adelphia, Sept. 23.
An injunction was granted the
Coliseum club Monday night by
Judge Clinton Givan, who ruled
that the club had a contract with
Dempsey to fight Harry Wills, Ne
gro challenger.
The motion for a rehearing will
be based on a bill of exceptions by
attorneys for Dempsey on ques
tions put to witnesses at the first
hearing, Symmes said.
While the local court is without
jurisdiction over the Philadelphia
fight, attorneys for the Coliseum
club, using the Indiana decision as
a precedent, are expected to make
a move in the Philadelphia courts
for a similar injunction later in the
week.
Suzanne Is Barred
From Benefit Net
Tourney in France
PARIS —Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen
was given a slap in the face today
by the French Federation of Lawn
Tennis, of which she once was the
pride and joy.
Upon receiving information that
Suzanne is arranging a big benefit
tournament for the “busted mugs”
association of French wounded vet
erans, in which she plans to ask all
French net stars to participate, the
federation board was called together
hurriedly and it announced a for
mal ruling that “In no case will it
authorize exhibitions or tourna
ments in which the new class of pro
fesionals will take part.” “A dis
tinction must be made,” the decree
explains, “between professors of ten
nis and the class of players created
by C. C. Pyle, whose purpose is the
earning of money from tourna
ments.”

The Boy That Never Existed.
The diary of a healthy boy
which contained so many good
health suggestions that I printed
it here just as the boy’s mother
wrote it, appeared Friday, July
31, a Brooklyn reader, B. E.
wrote:
Dear Dr. Brady:
In your fake letter yester
day you describe a boy that
never existed. He is not human.
He is either a god or the devil
in disguise. Look out for him.
Sincerely,
B E
On receipt of Bill’s pretest I
turned up the article again. The
boy, I find is 13 years old. He
has always enjoyed getting his
feet wet, going without a cap,
leaving his coat open in the cold
est winter weather, hitting the
hay early at night, getting up
about 7o’clock mornings, doing
some radio exercises with his
dad and finishing of this matu
tinal sport with a shower. This
last does seem a little too good
to be true. It might have been
better had mother told how they
had to use moral suasion about
the bath. I’m inclined to doubt
the reality of the boy on this
score myself. Going in swimming
would have been different.
This healthy boy never ate
meat until a year ago and now
takes it once or twice a week. I
know a good many sturdy lads,
some of them athletes of excep

ular,” suggested a man dressmaker,

H. C. Delzell, impressario of negli

mean.”
Anyway, red’s going to be popular
this printer.

How is the ticker? How is the
pump? Slang, but expressive!
The heart pumps the blood
stream through the circulatory sys
tem,. working continuously 24 hours
a day, approximately 70 strokes per
minute, from months before birth,
until, like grandfather’s clock, it
stops 1
We might liken the heart to a
four-cylinder motor, for it has four
chambers and four sets of valves.
When the valves of our automobile
get sticky or leak they can be re
moved and ground so as to open
and close without loss of power.
Carbon is removed from the cylin
ders. But not so with the valves
FRINGE POPULAR
THIS FALL; TIER
SKIRT EFFECT
BY HEDDA HOYT.
By The United Press.
NEW YORK—Fringe again be
comes extremely popular for evening
occasions, forming tiered skirt ef
fects, cape-backs, hem finishes, etc.
Both silk and beaded fringes are
used and among the newer silk types
are fringes printed in contrasting
designs. One can purchase this
printed fringe by the yard and it
is most effective if combined with
a dress of georgette of the same
color as the background of the
fringe.
For instance, a Nile green geor
gette frock has a two-tiered skir:
formed of Nile green fringe printed
with huge pinkish roses with deep
er green stems and leaves. The
fringe in narrower width is repeated
on the rear bodice where it forms
a deep bertha effect. Hawaiian
straw fringe in gay colors is also
among the novelties. Metal fringe
adorns metal cloth wraps and
gowns.
Vivid-hued dresses of afternoon or
evening type invariably use the
large ragged chrysanthemum as a
shoulder corsage. The flower match
es exactly the shade of the frock,
often being made of the same ma
terial.
Transparent velvets are entering
into the mode for fall. Some plain
velvets are so sheer that they are
transparent when held to the light
and checks and plaids of velvet de
signed on chiffon backgrounds also
supply the demand for transparency.
Since fall will see much black in
frocks and wraps, the colored geor
gette handkerchief edged with wide
black silk lace or net becomes a
smart accessory. Little squares of
ecru georgette bordered deeply in
black lace make an adorable hand
kerchief for dress wear. One can
make these, kerchiefs at little cost
and with little effort.
Evening slippers need not match
the gown with which they are worn,
according to fashion. Recently we
have seen smart women adopting
such combinations as pink satin
slippers and pink hosiery with white
beaded frocks, green brocaded slip
pers and flesh hosiery with coral
hued frocks and Chanel red satin
slippers with fushia-toned frocks.
Chiffon is at present by all odds
the most important material for the
evening gown. Younger women pre
fer plain chiffon unadorned except
by skirt embellishments of self-ma
terial, whereas matrons prefer bead
ed chiffons with softly bloused
backs and gently flaring hemlines.
Often the little patent leather hat
box which we see girls carrying
holds nothing more than a neatly
folded rubberized raincoat and rub
berized rainhat. If caught in a rain
storm milady dons these rubberized
garments placing her street hat in
the hatbox until the storm is over.
From a postpourri of fashion
notes are these:
There is still the monthly predic
tion that skirts will be longer and
they are still short.
Lounging pajamas are wrought in
silk and satin and velvet and metal.
Sleeping pajamas are purchased
at the men’s counter and are quite
plain.
You don’t step in a step-In any
more. It fastens up the back.
Velvet is “very good.”
It’s the V-neck this year,,
The Heart
and cylinders of the heart. What
we do to the valves of the heart
has to be done when the heart Is
pumping, sometimes two or even
three or more times per second.
Organic heart disease, that is,
the disease that affects the valves,
particularly, is usually caused by a
rheumatic infection, originating in
some focus of infection such as ton
sils or a tooth. But the heart is
subject to other assaults^ Over
work, both physical and mental; the
emotional sprees of worry, envy
and anger; all contribute to caus
ing the various diseases of the
heart, such as dilatation, weakness
and degeneration of the heart mus
cle, the irritable heart and nervous
heart.
And to think that the poor heart,
on which are piled all kinds of in
dignities, must keep Working—“tick
tack! tick-tack!” without intermis
sion as the seconds, minutes, hours,
days and years roll by.
When you realize that more
people die from heart disease than
from any other one cause, you see
how important it is to care for the
heart and protect it.
The prevention of heart disease
consists, principally, in the preven
tion of rheumatic attacks, by pro
tection against vicious infections, by
removing the foci of infection, and
improving the natural resistance
against infection —in staying well
by right living.
How necessary, then, to watch
for the children! The school in
spection, now generally in opera
tion, is doing admirable work.
It has been well said: “The
healthy know not of their health;
but only the sick.” So, if your
heart is doing its work smoothly,
normally, you are unconscious of it.
Only when in trouble does the
heart thump, or give pain, or other
uncomfortable sensations in the
chest.
Finally, to keep the heart in con
dition
Improve your resistance by prop
er eating, exercise, fresh air and
sleep.
Sultivate cheerfulness, good will
toward man; avoid physical and
mental excesses.
If you have symptoms, go to
your pnysician, follow his advice
and mend your ways.

luncheonTother dishes.
Sometimes for luncheon trj’ this
tempting combination:
Tomato Rarebit.
Put two tablespoonfuls of butter
into a saucepan, and when melted
add two tablespoonfuls of flour.
Pour on gradually three-fourths of
a cupful of thin cream and as soon
as the mixture is thickened, add
three-fourths of a cupful of strained
tomatoes mixed with one-eighth of
a teaspoonful of soda; then add two
cupfuls of finely cut cheese, two
eggs slightly beaten, salt, mustard
and cayenne to taste. Serve as soon
as the cheese is melted on hot gra
ham crackers or toasted bread.
Ham and Noodles.
Butter an earthen baking dish,
put into the bottom a layer of boiled
noodles; add a layer of cold boiled
ham cut into bits, then another of
noodles, repeating until the dish is
full. Cover with buttered crumbs,
dot with butter and bake in a mod
erate oven until hot.
California Mince Pie.
Pour one cupful of boiling water
over one cupful each of apricots and
prunes. Let stand three hours, re
move the skins from the apricots
and then stones from the prunes.
Cook in the water in which they
were soaked until nearly all the
water is cooked away. Mix the
dried fruit with one cupful of rai
sins, one-half cupful of minced cit
ron, the juice of an orange, one-half
teaspoonful each of cinnamon,
cloves and nutmeg and one-fourth
cupful of walnut meats, one cupful
of sugar and one-half cupful of al
monds. Bake in two crusts.
Creen Onions on Toast.
Cook the tender green onions,
stems and all, and serve them but
tered on toast or in a cream sauce,
using three or four over each piece
of toast; they are also good served
with a drawn butter sauce as for
asparagus.—Nellie Maxwell.
Turnips a la Poulette.
Turnips cooked in this way are
a very delicious vegetable. The
small white turnip is best for this
dish. Pare and cut into Quarters
three cupfuls turnips. Soak in cold
water for almost one hour, adding a
squeeze of lemon juice to the water.
Then cook turnips in boiling salted
water until almost but not quite
tender enough to serve. Drain well,
put In frying pan with one and one
half teaspoons butter or margarine
and let cook slowly without brown
ing until quite tender, adding one
cupful of stock or boiling water;
also add a bit of lemon juice. When
turnips are tender, drain them and
cover with two cupfuls of highly sea
soned white sauce, using three table
spoons flour as thickening and add
ing the beaten yolk of one egg and
one tablespoon chopped parsley. Re
move from fire, stir in quickly one
teaspoon lemon juice and a dash
of cayenne pepper. Serve.
Brussels Sprouts With Brown
Butter.
Prepare one quart of Brussels
sprouts. Wash in two waters. Put
in pan with one quart of boiling
water, with teaspoon salt, boil 20
minutes, drain. Place in same pan
with small piece of butter, season
with one-half teaspoon salt and a
wee bit of pepper. Toss lightly and
put in a hot dish. Place in a fry
ing pan, one tablespoon butter, put
on fire until it becomes a brown
color. Pour over sprouts and serve.

NEW YORK —What is taken here
to indicate the entrance of Standard
Oil interests and the Rockefellers
into the South American oil fields
on a big scale was the announce
ment yesterday of the formation of
Trinidad Oil Fields, Inc.
It said that Trinidad Oil Fields,
Inc., had been formed by influential
American interests with British
associates and had taken over some
27,000 acres of valuable oil proper
ties in Trinidad. An aggressive
drilling campaign has been started.
It added that P. A. Rockefeller
would shortly go on the board of
directors.
GRAIN PRICES
HOLD STEADY
AS PIT OPENS
CHICAGO—There was but little
change in grain prices in today’s
opening on the Chicago Board of
Trade. Wheat was fractionally
lower, corn was unchanged, and
oats slightly higher.
Reports of snow at Edmonton
and Calgary, Alberta, of rains south
of the border, and of general tem
peratures of 35 to 40 degrees over
the northwestern wheat country
mean a delay in the movement there.
Liverpool was cent to 1 cent
higher. Yesterday’s export business
was 800,000 bushels.
These factors should mean higher
wheat values, yet that cereal opened
cent to cent under yesterday’s
levels. This was because our ad
vance was due mostly to short cover
ing, while Liverpool’s was caused
by higher freight rates because of
increased coal tonnage.
Corn showed no change from yes
terday’s final quotations. This cereal
was firm on the news of more rains
in Nebraska, Kansas, lowa and Illi
nois. The pit is now almost entirely
a weather affair, and these unfavor
able conditions should bring some
advance during the session.
Oats ranged from unchanged to
cent higher, and borrowed
strength from corn.
Lard opened two points lower.

cheap copper. Inquiry is good and

buying will increase in the next few
days, especially if the stock market
continues strong.

result of the decline good buying is
expected to come in for October
metal.

ume but with the outlook promising
for still higher prices later in Ine
week.

stock, and compare with sl.Bl a

stock, which was the best year since
1917.

o^l HOME.GARDEN
Fall-started lawns are thoroughly
practical and, as a matter of fact,
usually get a better start than
spring-started ones because of the
delay in waiting until the soil is
workable. It is in mellower and
more easily workable condition in
the fall than in the spring and fall
sown seed will get the earliest pos
sible start.
It may even be sown on the snow
during the winter to good advantage
if the soil is prepared and ready for
it. A lawn is a garden for grass and
should be so considered.
Needs Good Care.
Good lawn grass doesn’t take so
kindly to rough treatment. It re
quires a garden prepared as care
fully as it should be for vegetables.
UTILITY DUYING
HOLDS STEADY
NEW YORK —Active buying of
electrical equipment by central sta
tion companies, industrial plants
and transportation lines featured
trading in the past week, Electrical
World reports.
Industrial plants are steady buy
ers of general-purpose motors and
orders to date are ahead of last
year. Heavy buying of switching
equipment and control apparatus oc
curred in the past week. Negotia
tions under way in various sections
of the country indicate an active
sales volume throughout the remain
der of the year.
In New England an order for roll
ing mill equipment involved $200,-
000. Utility companies have be
come more active in the New York
district. Activity in textile mill
electrification is reported in the
southeast, with appliance and range
sales also good.
The middle west reports steady
business, interest centering in cable,
weatherproof wire and various
kinds of distribution equipment. On
the Pacific coast lumber and shingle
mills are good buyers of electrical
equipment.

Losses Decrease

FARMERS OWN
ST. LOUIS BANK
WASHINGTON —Farmers in the
sixth federal land bank district,
comprising Illinois, Missouri and
Arkansas, now own all the stock of
the Federal Land Bank of St. Louis.
They have acquired the last of the
stock of that institution held by
the treasury, A. C. Williams, federal
farm loan commissioner, announced
today.
The acquisition of the bank is in
accordance with the act of congress
creating the 12 federal land banks
comprising the system.
“The treasury department,” said
Commissioner Williams, “made
practically all of the initial invest
ment to get these banks started, but
the law provided that as borrowers
joined the local National Farm
Loan Assn., they were to take stock
in the association in an amount
equal to 5 per cent of their loan,
this to be in turn used to purchase
stock in the federal land bank.”
Farmers in this way, have al
ready acquired all of the stock held
by the treasury in eight of the 12
banks. The total stock held by the
government in the remaining four
banks amounts to a little over
$1,000,000. Farmers now have cap
ital exceeding $56/000,000 in the 12
banks.

Watermelon Crop
One of Biggest
In Indiana History
SEYMOUR, Ind.—Up the James
Whitcomb Riley highway through
Jackson county’s watermelon and
cantaloupe patches, where the
sweetest melons man every stuck a
tooth in are grown, 40 pounders are
smilin’ on the vines on every side
of the road, writes Frank Ridgway
in The Chicago Tribune.
More than 2,000 acres of water
melons and cantaloupes have been
grown in the county this year, and
the quality and yields have been ex
ceptionally high. Jackson county
growers have marketed at least GOO,-
000 watermelons, weighing an aver
age of 30 pounds each. They have
pulled from 500 to 700 melons to
the acre. Cantaloupes have yielded
an average of 4,000 to the acre,
weighing about four pounds each.
The growers’ return on an acre of
melons is roughly from SIOO to $l5O.
The return on cantaloupes is usual
ly somewhat more than it is on
watermelons, growers say.

SUGAR BEETS
INVADE AREA
OF PEA CROPS
Sugar beets are trying for a place
in the crop rotations of many farm
ers who,are located in Wisconsin’s
leading pea growing districts.
Beets were introduced as a cash
crop into some of the pea sections
this year. They are expected to
prove satisfactory, explains A. H.
Wright, of the field crops staff of
the Wisconsin College of Agricul
ture, because when properly culti
vated beets leave the field well
cleaned of weeds and in excellent
condition for succeeding crops.
“Throughout the state the beet
crop appears to be above the aver
age of recent years,” Wright re
ports. “The stand is even and the
recent hot weather caused the beets
to mature at a fast rate.
“In most cases this year’s crop
was planted on suitable soil and a
rather general use of fertilizer was
made by the growers.”
Beet growing in Wisconsin has
become a million dollar industry.

Autumn trade has been opened
with the greatest movement of com
modities ever handled by the Amen*
lean railroads.
Loadings of revenue freight dur
ing the week ended Sept. 4 totaled
1,151,346 cars. Not only was it the
biggest week in railroad history, but
it marked the 15th million car week
thus far this year and brought total
loadings up to 35,850,857 cars,
which is 1,153,064 cars, or a full
week’s business, above the first eight
months of 1925.
All Commodities Up.
But the full tide of autumn busi*
ness is still ahead, so the present
record probably will be exceeded.
However, the current total marks an
increase of 15,113 cars over the pre
ceding week, which established the
previous high record, and is also an
increase of 48,561 cars over a yean
ago.
The highest freight loading foi*
any one week in each year since
1922 follow: Oct. 24, 1922: 999,718
cars; Sept. 25, 1923: 1,097,493 cars;
Oct. 23, 1924: 1,113,053 cars; Aug.
29, 1925: 1,124,438 cars, and Sept.
4, 1926: 1,151,346 cars.
The current report shows in
creases over the preceding week in]
the loading of all commodities ex
cept coal and ore. It is noteworthy}
that loadings of miscellaneous
freight were 17,088 cars above the
preceding week and 8,378 above the
same w’eek last year. This is evi
dence of the expanding trend of gen
eral trade. Another notable feature!
is the fact that the present record
breaking flow of commodities is be
ing handled without car shortage or
other transportation difficulties.
This attests to operating efficiency}
on the part of the railroads;
“Good business now seems as
sured for the rest of 1926,” Leonard
P. Ayres, vice-president of the Cleve
land Trust Co., said yesterday.
“Prosperity prevails in mdst lines of
industry; trade is going well; agri
cultural conditions and prospect*
are much better than they prom
ised to be three months ago, and
employment is general with wage*
high.
The outlook for the autumn sea
son is splendid, with record-breaking
business in prospect, according to
James Simpson, president of Mar
shall Field Co., who returned from
Europe yesterday. He said nothing
but a catastrophe could upset U
nation’s prosperity during the^
year.
The rubber industry generally it
in a healthy state and faces a pros
perous year in 1927, in the opinion:
of President H. T. Dunn of Fisk?

Will Open War.

ner of Americanism from the ram

tle cry is no longer 4 Americans,
guard your own,’ but ‘Americans,
seize your destiny.

court of international justice and re
main there,” he continued, “will be
i backward step, taking us far back
co the foreign policies in vogue be
fore the founding of the republic.”

Erection of a monument to the
American eagle in the form of a wa
ter fountain and monument com
bined, on the lawn of the new
$1,000,000 clubhouse of Milwaukee
Aerie No. 137 of the Fraternal Order

will come to Milwaukee to make the
awards.
Deputies Look for
Bomb, Find Head,
Feet of Rooster
Aroused over the appearance of
a suspicious looking package in his
roadside mail box on 82nd Ave., led
Michael Wojcinski to telephone
West Allis police last night.
“It looks like a bomb,” Jojcinski
told police. He was told to open
the package, but disregarded the
advice.
A West Allis police sergeant con
sulted the city map and several min
utes later informed the recipient of
the package that he was unable to
do a thing as his home was outside
West Allis limits where he had no
jurisdiction.
Wojsinski then called the sher
iff’s office. Several sheriff’s dup
uties, newspaper reporters and pho
tographers made the trip to investi
gate. Deputies Henry Bender and
William Koenig, after obtaining
several long poles succeeded in get
ting the package from the box.
The cover of the box was torn
off, exposing the head and feet of
a rooster. A neighbor's boy is sus
pected.
Dr. Bowman O K’s
Advertising for
Modern Dentists
Newspaper advertising, guaran
teed work, a standard system of
prices, all matters formerly frowned
upon in the dental profession as out
side the bounds of'ethics, now are
considered ethical since modern
dentistry has outgrown the bounds
of professionalism, and is now a
business and a profession combined,
according to Dr. J. A. Bowman, 428
Grand Ave.
The Modern Ethical Society of
Dentists, a comparatively new or
ganization, of which Dr. Bowman is
a member, believes in following
business principles in the dental
profession and finds them success
ful.
This modern plan by which a den
tist standardizes his operations and
expenses and can advise a patient
in advance of the cost of proposed
work, is giving the patient new con
fidence in dentists.

Work has been started on the first
unit of the Lake St. highway.

precede the construction of a 20-
foot width, which is to be com
pleted Nov. 15. Other units of the
new concrete road between Milwau
kee and the Pewaukee lake district
will be built next year.
