tion, from Wauwatosa Ave. to 39th
St., let by the state highway com
mission, was given to the Nickel-
Grahl Construction Co., Medford,
Wis.

and west drive, each 30 feet wide,
and a 30-foot boulevard strip be
tween.

WHO WINS THE PROGRESSIVE FIGHT
IN WISCONSIN?
While The Milwaukee Sentinel is still bewailing the
alleged fact that Socialist votes helped to give the Re
publican nomination for United States senator to Gov.
Blaine, The Capital Times comes back at the standpatters
with the charge that 100,000 stalwarts voted for the pro
gressive candidate Zimmerman in the effort to give the
state to the Coolidge machine.
“In 1922 the stalwarts polled 147,379 votes for Wi
liam J. Morgan for governor,” writes The Capital Times.
“In 1924 the stalwarts polled 157,138 votes for Hirst for
governor. In this campaign, however, the stalwart candi
date for governor polled less than 40,000 votes. Where,
then, did those 100,000 stalwart votes go in this primary.
The Capital Times has no difficulty in tracing the
trail which led 100,000 stalwart voters from the Perry
camp to the Zimmerman tent. From the day of the elder
La Follette’s death, one stalwart leader after an o^ r
lined up with Zimmerman and helped him to smash the
La Follette machine.
In this campaign, The Capital Times continues even
Senator Lenroot masqueraded as a progressive. Unab e
to win by sailing under their own colors, they moved over
into the progressive tent and in this campaign t ey were
all progressives. They shed the regalia they have worn for
30 years and put on new disguises.
To this presentation of the facts by The Capital
Times we have but to add that Lenroot’s machine went so
far as to claim that some Socialist leaders had indorsed
him, thus giving the false impression that the Socialists
should vote for the Coolidge candidate in the Republican
primaries.
We leave it to the voters of Wisconsin to decide
whether journalistic morality can sink any lower than it
has in The Sentinel, which whines about the alleged So
cialist support for Blaine after its own candidate has
openly asked for Socialist votes in the Republican primary.
We cannot understand any more than The Capita
Times how any progressive can vote for Zimmerman when
100,000 stalwarts back him. We ask with The Capital

THE BIG PARADE
The Big Parade, by Laurence Stallings, now running
on the screen at the Davidson theater, is a war story very
different from the monstrous sentimentalities which lured
Americans into the shambles. It is different, because it
was conceived by one who went through the thick of the
slaughter. Unlike other war writers, he teaches a lesson
of peace, a hatred of war.
Stallings does not glorify the incredible stupidities of
militarism. He makes them ridiculous. He shows how
boys ignorant of life are made drunk with music and noise,
lured away to serve as cannon-fodder, not knowing what
it is all about. He shows war in all its nastiness, bestiality,
horror and futility. He is eminently fair, even to the
Germans, having been in close touch with them where
men are men.”
In all the screened war scenes of the world, there is
probably not one other so true and so gripping in its ap
peal to human reason as that of the German and American
boy, both wounded, cuddling together in a shell-hole and
staring at each other through the bloody mist, wondering
helplessly at the dreadful abomination which makes them
enemies. We hope that nobody will miss this film who
has an evening or an afternoon to spare.

There Are Sounds
Folks Never Hear
In church, while the organ is
playing, have you ever felt the
pew you are sitting in, and the
floor beneath your feet, begin to
tremble with a mysterious sort of
rumbling that seems to come from
nowhere? Perhaps, a bit startled,
you have looked around appre
hensively at the walls and ceil
ings. Then, in a moment, you.
have realized that the source of
the strange rumbling is within
the church itself somewhere
among the pipes of the playing
organ.
What you may not have known,
however, is that the vibrations
which shake the objects about you
are nothing more or less than
sounds. They are really part of
the church music; the deepest
notes of the organ. Yet so low
are they pitched that while your
body can feel them as vibrations,
your ears cannot hear them at all.
In fact, says Popular Science
Monthly, all about you, in the
noise and hubbub of modern, life,
the air is full of sounds that you
cannot hear. Just as there are
notes so low that your ears can
not catch them, others are so
shrill that you are hopelessly
deaf to them. Countless creatures
may be conversing in shrill lan
guages that you never have heard.
Many scientists believe that some
animals, like the bat, and many
insects, can hear tones so shrill
that they are forever inaudible to
human beings. Certainly there are
insects which have apparatus ap
parently adapted for producing
such tones. It is quite possible
that these creatures can talk to
each other continually in sounds
to which we are hopelessly deaf.
It is possible, too, that some
day we may find a way to repel
or attract insects by inaudible
waves. Thus, we might set up
silent noise machines to keep mos
quitoes or flies away from our
houses. On the other hand, if we
could find a noise that harmful
insects liked we might play this
siren song for them and draw them
into traps.

BY LEON ROWLAND.
MARS HIDES IN THE LEAGUE
The governments never tire of extolling the covenant
of the league of nations and the Locarno pacts as the
greatest guarantees of peace so far devised by man. The
official editors take their cue from the governments. So
every day, readers of the big press are assured that peace
is made more and more secure.
This practice is continually belied by the growing
armies, navies and air forces, but the editorials cover these
war preparations with a curtain of noise. So the deliber
ate deception lulls the people into false expectations.
Mars still hides in the league with the full approval of
the same minds that devised its peace covenant.
Immediately after the adoption of the league cove
nant, the league permitted the conclusion of special
“guarantee” pacts between members. Every one of these
pacts was made with the co-operation of military experts.
In this way the powers betrayed the carefully framed as
sertions of their peaceful intentions and showed that the
members of the league were returning to the old balance
of power diplomacy. They were not honestly co-operating
in the league for arbitration of all differences, but pre
paring to settle matters of imperialism by force and mil
itary alliances.
Nevertheless it became the practice to file copies of
these guarantee treaties with the league secretary—per
haps to make the deception more complete. Not that ths
statesmen fooled one another about their real intentions.
Even if the secret clauses of these guarantee pacts could
be hidden from the public, the spies of the government
can easily get them. But registering such guarantee pacts
gives the official editors something smooth and oily to
write about.
The ink was hardly dry on the Locarno pacts before
it became known that the British Foreign Minister Cham
berlain had made secret promises to the French, German
and Italian governments which he could not equally keep
to all of them. The effect of this revelation was of course,
to disclose once again the old British policy of keeping the
continental European powers guessing and divided.
The Locarno pacts did not cancel the existing guar
antee pacts between France, Poland and Czecho-Slovakia,
nor the little entente, nor the guarantees exchanged be
tween the British and American governments. Neither
did they prevent the conclusion of new guarantee pacts
with secret military clauses.
Recently new guarantee pacts have been concluded
between Spain and Italy, France and Rumania, Greece and
Jugo-Slavia, Rumania and Poland., The treaties are sure
to guarantee more trouble, but no peace. As usual, every
government claims that there are no secret military
clauses, but they don’t believe one another. Filing such
treaties with the league secretary proves nothing. Secret
clauses are not filed in public.
Meanwhile Mars is becoming bolder all the time.
Mussolini keeps up bad blood between France, Spain and
Italy. At the same time England and France each strive
to make an ally of Germany. Another attempt on the life
of Mussolini stirs Europe. Fascist leaders openly blame
the French government for sheltering Italian anti-
Fascists. The French give back tit for tat. Chamberlain
hovers satanically in the background and pulls his wires.
The American naval expert comes back from his ex
perience in the Geneva disarmament meeting with the
loudly voiced conviction that disarmament is the bunk.
So it is, but the American disarmament policy is as much
the bunk as the European.
Nobody but the Socialists have the good sense and
courage to say that all this bunk is due to the economic
powers that work even more secretly for conquest than
their political servants.
CANT AND COMMERCE
Greed dearly loves a halo. It loves to feel the shining
symbol of holiness round its head. It loves to wear an
expression of devout piety, and roll its eyes to Heaven
and mumble prayers.
Then Greed is truly happy. Then it can reach out
with an ardent sanctimoniousness and grab what doesn’t
belong to it.
In any case, under any circumstances, it will plunder.
But it very much prefers to do its thieving with a spiritual
zeal.
That explains why America, where Greed, in the guise
of Capitalism, has reached the height of its power on
earth, is such a wowsery country.
The vast majority of the American people are neither
greedy nor godly. In that respect they are pretty much
like the peoples of all other lands. They are not brigands,
and they’d rather be classed as sinners than as saints.
But American capitalism is always snuffling about
sacred things. “Things of the spirit come first,” says Mr.
Calvin Coolidge, who is president of the U. S. A. and the
spokesman of big business too. “Unless we cling to
that,” says he, “all our material prosperity,” says he,
“overwhelming though it may appear, will turn to a
barren sceptre in our grasp,” says he.
Reading that unctuous sentiment, what a spectacle is
conjured up I The fat and oily thieves of commerce, cling*
ing to the things of the spirit—and to other people’s prop
erty at the same time! The most efficient robbers that
the world has ever known, going through the pockets of a
continent with a hymn upon their lips!
“We must not sink into a pagan materialism,” says
Mr. Coolidge.
Certainly not. That would be very poor Christianity
—and dashed bad business.
Sharpen the claws that clutch the loot, but never for
get to praise God, from whom all blessings flow.
Such is American capitalism —the canting crook of
the ages!—Australian Worker.

brought flood conditions to many
sections of the middle west have
caused more than $12,000,000 dam
age and resulted in deaths of at
least 20 persons, it was disclosed in
a survey.
Kansas and Illinois suffered the
most serious damage from the
floods. Each of these states was
damaged about $5.(XK),000 and the
flooded conditions still remain. The
same states have reported five fatal
ities each as result of the storm.

the middle west by states was out
lined by the weather bureau river

lowa, $500,000.
Indiana, S2SO,(XX).

shows the following: Illinois, 5;

braska, 2. and one each in Indiana,

eight hours, railroad officials re
ported. Many washouts have been

ported in Illinois and Kansas, con
siderable property damage has been

lowa, Indiana and Wisconsin. Each

ington. 1). C., where Harry M.

erty-Miller conspiracy trial here to

butler, white-haired, and shaking
with nervousness, testified that for
a year, beginning on the day War
ren G. Harding was inaugurated
president, he and a cook were the
sole servants in that much talked
of house.
Smith Paid Salaries.
He and the cook, he said, had
come from the household staff of
Edward B. McLean, Washington
publisher and friend of President
Harding.
Jesse Smith, he testified, paid his
salary, the cook’s salary, and all
bills of the establishment.
McLean, he added, ownel the fur
niture.
Calling of the old butler marked
the opening of the government’s at
tempt, to establish a connection be
tween Daugherty and transactions
which followed Richard Merton’s
agreement to pay John T. King
$441,000 for obtaining return to
German and Swiss owners of $7,-
000,000 assets of the American
Metals Co. seized ns German prop
erty during the war.
Often at Breakfast.
Daugherty and Smith usually
•breakfasted together and frequently
had lunch there together, he said,
while they had many breakfast and
luncheon guests.
Asked to name some of the peo
ple who frequently called there he
named William J. Burns, detective;
Col. Forbes of the veterans’ bureau;
Guy D. Goff, former federal district
attorney in Milwaukee, now senator
from West Virginia and at that
time an assistant to Daugherty;
Howard Mangdon, Col. Miller, co
defendant with Daugherty, and the
late John T. King.
After Smith and Daugherty moved
from the house to a suite in the
Wardman Park hotel, Miller said he
continued as butler for a short time,
and then was given a position in the
file division of the department of
justice, remaining in that position

od of a month when he returned to
the hotel ns butler for Daugherty
and Smith.

Miller, on cross-examination said
he had been impressed with the close
friendship between Daugherty and
King.

and John Durkin, secretary to King,
who testified yesterday, was re
called.
lie testified under questioning by

Wells Makes an Appearance.

turned around and there was a
murmur of something more like ac
claim than greeting.
“Here, H. G., come hero and sit

as a mother might cajole her over
indulged child. “Right here. There's
plenty of room, and I’ll pour you
some tea.”
Wells hesitated for a portentous
moment. An ingratiating smile
played the while on airs. Wells’ lips,
but she waited. Then he decided.
He would sit beside her, and yes—
he would have tea. No, no, no—
only one drop of milk. T, t, t, t,
but that was three, fully three. He
protested it almost pettishly, and re
fused to have bread and butter—

YOM KIPPUR
SERVICES OPEN
FRIDAY NIGHT
Tom Kippur services will begin
tomorrow at sunset in Milwaukee’s
orthodox Jewish synagogues, con
tinuing until Saturday at sunset.
Tom Kippur, the day of atonement,
is considered the most important
day in the Jewish year.
At Temple B’ne Jeshurun, 240
10th St., services will be held, ac
cording to Rabbi Charles Levi.
Day of Prayer.
“Tom Kippur is a day of prayer,
of continuous services in the syna
gogue lasting the entire 24 hours,”
said Rabbi Levi.
“It signifies a reconciliation be
tween man and man, the offering
of prayers to God for pardon and
forgiveness of sins. The ideals of
the day are a returning to God, con
tinuous devotion and prayers and
devotion to one’s fellow man, shown
by gifts to charity.”
Hold Conclusion Services.
The sermon at Temple B’ne Jesh
urun tomorrow night will be on
Conscience, Conduct and Character.
Saturday noon Rabbi Levi will
preatch on, Wanted Generous
Hearts and Willing Souls, and at
3.30 p. xa. he will conduct memorial
services for those who died during
the year. At this time gifts are of
fered by the congregation in honor
of those who died.
From 4:45 p. m. to 5:45 p. m. Sat
urday the conclusion services will
he held, when the sermon will be on
The Endless Sabbath Day.
The thanksgiving festival, the
Feast of Sukkoth, begins Wednes
day, the services lasting, In ortho
dox Jewish temples, throughout the
entire week.

at an early date, according to infor
mation received by the city attorney
today.

was recently made by Charles Ham
mersley, attorney for the village of
Shorewood.
Plan Is Opposed.
At the time the request was made
Henry Disch, attorney for the Bay
View Advancement Assn., opposed
the proposal, finding out that it is
unfair, in his opinion, to force the
city lines to carry the financial bur
den of furnishing street car service
to suburbs which constantly fight
annexation.
Mr. Disch pointed out that subur
ban lines are seldom even self-sup
porting, and that to place them on a
one-fare basis merely Increases the
burden of the urban lines.
For City Limits Zone.
One-fare zone limits should in all
cases be placed at the city limits,
Mr. Disch opined. He pointed out
that the city of Milwaukee now is
furnishing urban car service to ap
proximately half of the immediate
surrounding suburban districts.
He declared that all these lines
are being operated at a loss, and
that the deficit must come from the
more frequently patronized city
lines.

city attorney’s opinion be in favor

the state necessary to come under
the jurisdiction of the pension fund.

capacity clause of the pension
rules.
The school board members of the
pension board took the position, in
voting, that Mrs. Pearse had ful
filled the requirements of the pen
sion fund and that no discretionary
powers were invested in the pen
sion board.
One Is Absent.

Meehan, Mrs. Meta Berger, Harry

man.

ber, was absent.

take-off.

gnthered at the field when the delay
was announced. (Japt. Fonck, Lieut.
Lawrence W. Curtin, U. S. N„ Jacob
Islamoff and Charles Clavier, the
r rew to undertake the epochal
flight, were ready for duty. Pro
visions for the 3,000-mile trip were
aboard.

stop the leak were unsuccessful and

The Reverend Sir. Parkman and
his wife and son were on their way
to church. The clergyman and his
wife walked in front, all dressed up
in their Sunday best and looking
very dignified. Behind them came
their son, Francis, just a wew steps
back of his stately parents, which
was the way children walked in
those days.
The Reverend Parkman bowed
politely to all the people he passed.
They bowed In return —but they
smiled in the strangest way- The
Reverend Parkman frowned. He
had seldom seen people with such
merry expressions on their faces
on Sunday morning. It did not
seem quite proper.
As he neared the church he began
to think something was wrong.
People did not smile as they passed
—they actually laughed.
Suddenly he turned around. To
his horror, he found that his son
was walking gravely along, in his
starched Sunday clothes, carrying a
dead rat by the tail! “Francis, drop
that!” shouted his father.

CHARMS CAUSE

SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. Psy
choanalysis, as practiced by a
feminine “love actor” who adver
tised ‘cures” for broken homes, was
blamed yesterday by Lynn G. Law
rence, graduate geologist of the Uni
versity of California, for the dis
ruption of his marital romance. His
wife, Mrs. Cela Lawrence, has
brought suit for divorce.
Was Lured Away.
In the deposition filed by Law
rence as a defense agairst the suit,
he charged he had been lured from
her side through the psychoanalyt
ical charms of Mrs. Grace Palmer
Craig, aged 55. He is 29.
Mrs. Craig, named as co-respond
ent in Mrs. Lawrence’s suit, is pro
prietor of an elaborate studio for
the teaching of menticulture. She
advertised her ability to produce “a
true love that makes no demands.”
Mr. and Mrs. Lawrence, not “en
tirely happy,” determined to visit
Mrs. Craig's studio.
The love doctor's first prescrip
tion, Lawrence contends, was a 30-
day trial separation. To this the
Lawrences agreed, with the under
standing that they were to report
to Mrs. Craig for further instruc
tions at the end of that period.
Wanted More Advice.
But Lawrence returned for fur
ther counsel sooner, his deposition
admits.
“Mrs. Craig analyzed the situa
tion so beautifully that 20 minutes
later I was making love to her,” he
declared. “I could not help myself.”
Clandestine meetings thereafter
were frequent, he asserts.
Mrs. Lawrence, despite her trial
separation, had kept tabs on her
husband and the night of Aug. 14,
with her attorney and two friends,
raided Mrs. Craig’s studio at 4 a.
m. They found the subservant Law
rence with Mrs. Craig.

BRITISH LABOR
RAPS BARRING
OF 2 RUSSIANS
Leader Special Service.
LONDON The British govern
ment’s order tc refuse permission
to Tomsky and Meluichansky, So
viet delegates to the British trade
union congress, to land in England
was vigorously denounced by the
British labor leaders.
The executive of the trade union
congress had been duly notified of
the exclusion of the Russian fra
ternal delegates by the British home
office.
However, J. R. Clynes, M. P., for
merly a member of Ramsay Mac-
Donald’s labor government, de
clared the action of the British gov
ernment petty and foolish.
Could Do No Harm.
"The borne office has announced
in the papers that Tomsky is not
to be allowed to land in Bourne
mouth or to deliver any message to
the trade union congress,” Clynes
said.
“That I regard as a petty and
provocative interference with the
right of labor to establish interna
tional relations. It will furnish
the Communists with another cry.
It will not strengthen the arm of
the Tories. It will not weaken the
Labor party.”
Tomsky could do no harm by
talking to the trade union congress,
Clynes said. Besides, the British
home office was not treating the
Russian delegates as fairly as the
Russian government had treated
British visitors to Russia.
"Several deputations lately have
gone from England to Russia, in
cluding one deputation of Tory
members and of Tory employers of
labor,” Clynes recalled. “If Tory
members have a right to go to Rus
sia, a Russian trade union leader
has a right to come to this coun
try.”
Protest Is Not Serious.
On the other hand, the labor cor
respondent of The Manchester
Guardian writes that the general
council of the British trade union
congress will not be seriously put
out by the exclusion of the Rus
sian delegates.
Tomsky may have said some sav
age things about the Tory govern
ment, but he has also said some
very vicious things about the Brit
ish labor leaders. ‘lf he were al
lowed to go to the trade union con
gress, there is no telling what dread
ful things he might tell the dele
gates to their faces, and how he
might instruct them in their duties
toward the miners.
“Relations between the British
and Russian trade unions are much
strained since the general strike.
Perhaps if the home secretary had
considered the advantage of the
Tory party a little more, he would
have risked the contamination that
these two Rusisan leaders might
spread and let the quarrel take its
course.”

SHOOT AT MOON,
SAYS PROFESSOR
LONDON Rumors that some
lH>dy in Moscow wants to shoot at
the moon has aroused the academic
criticism of Prof. A. W. Biekerton,
the astronomer, who says flatly in
The Daily Mail, that it cannot be
done.
“In order to escape the gravita
tion of the earth,” he points out,
“your projectile needs a velocity of
seven miles a second.
“The thermal energy necessary to
carry .1 gramme of matter at this
speed is 15,180 calories. The energy
of a gramme of a Krupp shell is
about 100 calories: that of Big
Bertha —the gigantic gun which
shelled Paris —was 400 calories.
“The energy of a gramme of our
most violent explosive—nitroglycer
ine—is less than 1,500 calories. Con
sequently, if the explosive had noth
ing to carry except its own weight,
it has less than 10 per cent of the
energy necessary to enable it to es
cape the earth. To reach a distance
of four miles in the air, the projec
tile would need a thermal energy
unit mass equal to 7,500 calories.”

SEEK TO AVERT
DEPLETION OF
HALIBUT SUPPLY
KETCHIKAN. Alaska—To almost
all people a halibut is only a fish,
but to the members of the interna
tional fisheries commission and to
thousands of persons in soutlieatern
Alaska it is a subject of intense
study, for it is their means of livli
hood. That the supply should be
depleted is a catastrophe which they
seek to avert.
Have Close Season.
It was with this view in mind that
the Canadians and the United States
recently established an international
closed season. 'William F. Thompson,
director of Investigations for the
commission, has already begun work
which will tend conclusively to es
tablish the life history of the hali
but. This investigation is being con
ducted by a scientific staff, gather
ing data at first hand—on the
“banks.”
Part of the work accomplished
during the last year and a half was
to tag 4,000 halibut. According to
Mr. Thompson many of these have
been caught later on the banks and
comparatively little movement or
migration has been noted.
Like Tree Rings.
,r We take from the head of the
fish examined a small bone called
an otolith,” he declared. “This bone,
and indeed all the bones in the body,
show annual rings just as a tree
does, and from it we can arrive at
a close estimate of age. The female
halibut from Hecate strait grows to
a length of 30 Inches, or a weight
of 20 pounds (cleaned and headed)
in 10 years; the male to a length
of 32*4 inches, or a weight of 15
pounds.”
Misinformation at
Postoffice Doesn't
Pay Agent Finds
Misinformation, nt least at the
postoffice, doesn’t pay.
A commercial representative of a
New York firm will learn that. He
went to the parcel post window at
the Milwaukee office and presented
a parcel for Insurance and mailing
to a high ecclesiastic in Chicago.
As specified in postal regulations,
the clerk, R. A. Miller, asked the
contents of the parcel and received
an answer “just merchandise.” A
further inquiry as to whether it was
of a breakable nature received an
indignant negative answer.
A subsequent inspection proved
that a fancy bottle of high-priced
toilet water had been packed in a
thin cardboard box, with a single
sheet of tissue paper for padding,
and enclosed was a personal note.
To comply with postal law, the
parcel was held, and the sender
notified to provide better packing
and first class postage, but mean
time the traveler had moved on and
the parcel is being held.

Stop That Noise.
To the Editor of The Leader:
I wish that the police of Milwau
kee would silence the unnecessary
noise made by motor truck drivers
and antomobilists who find them
selves momentarily slowed down or
stopped in a traffic congestion.
I believe that truck drivers are
the grossest offenders. I have heard
them rend the air in the vicinity of
hospitals, for instance, without the
slightest regard to the disturbance
created. And many automobilists
take out their impatience in pro
longed tooting which does no good
whatever and simply makes legiti
mate sounding of the horn impos
sible. Residents along otherwise
quiet streets in Milwaukee are be
ing roused by night by screeching
horns which all day long make of
fice buildings almost unbearable for
those trying to work within them.
Some truck drivers, according to
information received from those
wh< complain, have their horns on
their vehicles attached to the ex
haust pipes instead of to batteries.
Thus nre the piercing shrieks emit
ted that deafen the pedestrian
caught In the din of a traffic block.
Doctors tell me that nurses report
hospital patients starting up fre
quently from the noise of such
horns.
I understand that in Chicago and
other large cities where the ma
jority of drivers know their busi
ness much better than the majority
in this city, that blowing of the
horns on boulevards and nrterials
of heavy traffic, is not permitted.
That when a horn is heard on such
a thoroughfare, it is a signal of an
unusual haste —that of a doctor, a
fire official, or other emergency
factor—and way is made for the
owner of the horn. And for the
rest, simple and silent rules of the
road nre observed, for the consid
eration of everybody concerned.

Art in Milwaukee.
To the Editor of The Leader:
Since the Milwaukee Art institute
has attempted, during the past few
years, to co-operate with the art
instruction in the public schools of
the city, it seems to me extremely
fitting that the same personality
should be at the head of both.
Alfred G. Pelikan has proved ca
pable, energetic and resourceful ns
director of art in the public schools.
Since he came to Milwaukee, there
has been a noticeable increase of
interest in art and the way it is
now being put across in the schools.
The institute, under the acting di
rectorship of Walter Goepel, has en
deavored during the past year to
project that interest created in
school to all extra-curricular de
gree. Saturday classes to augment
the instruction in the public schools
grew last year to encouraging pro
portions. Talent developed under
the instruction of Mr. Pelikan and
others from the public school art
teaching corps, who devoted Satur
days to classes at the Art institute,
which speaks well for the manner
in which this alliance between in
stitute and schools was conducted.
Now that it is proving possible
further to co-relate the work of
these two, in the placing of Mr.
Pelikan at the head of both, I be
lieve that every Milwaukeean inter
ested in the world of the two
should be glad that this work prom
ises to go still further during the
coming year.

board, who rode to victory on the
wave of anti-Klan sentiment, while
the victors themselves were scratch
ing their heads and trying to re
member when, if ever, 'Waterman
had declared opposition to the Klan.

CHICAGO—The future of legalized boxing in Illinois was made un
certain today by the reported resignation of O. W. Iluncke, chairman of
the recently formed state boxing commission, 011 grounds which are under
stood to include evidence of crooked gambling.
Iluncke refused to confirm or deny reports of his resignation and the
office of Gen. Len Small at Springfield was likewise silent. From sources
close to the state administration, however, the report was given con-
siderable weight.
Proponents of legalized boxing in
Illinois fear that the game will be
thrown into confusion nnd turmoil
which may result in its complete
collapse if Iluncke is relieved of
his post.
Gun Play Hinted at Fight.
Report of Mr. Huncke's decision
to withdraw from the tangled af
fnirs of boxing came as a climax to
the sensational banning of the
Rosenberg Taylor bantamweight
title fight, scheduled at the Cubs’
park tonight.
The fight was called off Tuesday
on Chairman Hucke’s orders. Basis
for the action was said to be the
failure of Harry Segal, Charley
Rosenberg’s manager, to post $12,500
forfeit mcney. The real reason be
hind the banning of the fight is said
to be the uncovering of an t ttempt
by a clique of New York gamblers
to win the fight for the champion
by bribery or gun play.
Gunmen, it is said had obtained
ringside seats at Cubs’ park. Their
presence was to intimidate the ref
eree if the gamblers had failed to
reach him prior to the battle. Bud
Taylor was to be denied the de
rision at any cost. The fight officials
had taken cognizance of the gunmen
story to such an extent that de
tectives had been hired and given
seats behind the gunmen.
Had the fight been staged the
thousands at the SIOO,OOO battle
might have been witnesses to a gun
tight.
Commissioners’ Lives Threatened.
Mr. Iluncke admitted yesterday
that threats have been made against
the lives of the commissioners. lie
admitted that his home is bombard
ed by anonymous telephone calls and
that the crooks of the game hound
the boxing czars continually.
He admitted that rowdyism has
been evident at fights held here and
the commission had been forced to
call in the national guard. Soldiers
from the second infantry regiment
will attempt to preserve order at
future shows, he said.
Mr. Iluncke, in his refusal to dis
cuss reports' of his resignation,
bared the inside story of the com
mission's dealings with Segal, nnd
his failure to post the forfeit money
after several days grace had been
extended. In addition Mr. Huncke
told of the innumerable difficulties
which the boxiug commissioners,
John Righcimer, Paul Prehn and
liimself, have been forced to sur
mount to keep the revised boxing
game on a level of decency.
Title Bout Tactics Bared.
“I had the first misgivings on
Regal’s sincerity last Saturday,” Mr.
Iluncke said. “The commission, of
course, knew of Rosenberg’s record
in New York. We had heard the
story of the Ro»enberg-Shea fiasco
and we were on guard. Stories came
in last week of money pouring in
to bet on Rosenberg and the sub
sequent tumbling odds on Taylor.
But we had no definite proof that
was not O K until Segal
Tailed to turn in his signed contracts
and forfeit money on Saturday.
“I called Jim Mullen, the pro
moter of the fight, and told him
Segal mnst post the money imme
diately or the show’ would be called
off. A short time later Mr. Mullen
called and said Segnl swore he would
post the money before the close of
the day. But he didn’t.
“On Sunday I got in touch with
Rosenberg nnd told him the money
must be paid immediately. It wasn’t.
We had no other course to follow
save to call the fight off.”

NEW YORK —The world series
should start at the Yankee stadium
here Oct. 2, with either Cincinnati
or St. Louis facing the Yankees for
the world championship.
At this late date, with the season
10 days from its end, it is possible
to guess at the outcome with fair
chance of hitting the mark.
Half Game Apart.
Cincinnati and St. Louis were still
at the head of the National league
today, only half a game apart, and
with both teams showing every
sign of being able to fight its way
to the finish without weakening.
There is no groat choice between
them —both pitching staffs are
working in world series form and
the batting and fielding of the teams
leaves little to be desired.
Pirates Lose Ground.
The Cardinals showed their best
form in beating the Phillies, 9 to 2,
in the first of their six-game series
in Philadelphia yesterday. The Reds
had much less trouble disposing of
the demoralized Brooklyn Robins,
7 to 2, but will be called on for their
real form today against the bean
spilling Giants, while the Cardinals
again meet the Phillies in a double
header, giving them a good clianee
to regain the lead.
The Giants, while they have noth
ing to gain, are in a mood for up
setting apple carts, as evidenced by
their 0 to 5 defeat of the Pittsburgh
Pirates yesterday. It put the Pi
rates three and one-half games be
hind the Reds and three behind the
Cardinals. They still have a theo
retical chance, but it would be an
amazing upset.
Indians Drop Opener.
The situation of the Cleveland
Indians is more desperate than that
of the Pirates. They dropped to
six and one-half games behind the
Yankees when New York beat them
yesterday, G to 4, in the first game
of their six-game series.
The l’ankees can cinch the pen
nant by taking four of the remain
ing five.

STROUDSBURG, Pa.—There was
an air of apprehension in Strouds
burg today and those citizens who
were planning a trip out to chal
lenger Gene Tunney’s headquarters
to view his ring actions, were not
quite sure they would see him.
Tunney yesterday disappointed a
big crowd when he failed to appear
for his expected workout.
Billy Gibson, the heavyweight’s
manager, explained that Tunney is
now so near his expected Dempsey
bout weight that no chances can be
taken. A too strenuous road jaunt
yesterday brought Gene down to
near 180 pounds that a session with
his sparring partners was bound to
cut the weight too fine. Hence the
last minute change.

velopment.

Milwaukee, resulting in a broader
market for equipment, The Ameri

dle west has shown gradual im
provement in the demand for ma
chine tools.

witnessed an upward trend in busi
ness in machinery and machine
tools, nearly all sections of the
country experiencing a moderate
gain in activity. The volume and
quality of the inquiries received by
manufacturers and dealers indicate
that business this fall will be main
tained at satisfactory level.
Quite a number of good orders
have been closed in the Detroit dis
trict for single pieces. Manufactur
ers of automobile accessories and
electrical apparatus have been more
active in the Chicago district. Ex
port inquiry has revived in the Cin
cinnati market.
Conditions in New England terri
tory are better than in August, with
export business more of a factor. A
steady volume oi business has been
placed in the New York and Phila
delphia markets. Buffalo continues
with a fair number of new orders
from a variety of users of tools.

Fall Rains Pound
Indiana Tomato
Crops to Ground
INDIANAPOLIS Brandywine
Valley farmers have suffered heavy
losses from rains that flooded their
corn and small grain fields. Along
the Brandywine, Blue and Rock riv
ers and small tributary streams wa
ter lnu backed up in fields, leaving
the corn half submerged for nearly
a week.
Warm days that followed the rain
have practically cooked the ears
which are just past the roasting
stage. The corn has been left
soured and tangled in the mud.
Ripe red tomatoes have been
pounded, into a pulp by the heavy
rains and left half buried in the
mud. The loss here, as in many
other tomato growing sections, has
been heavy during the rainy sea
son.

fodil is the earliest large flower
suitable for cutting that blooms in
the garden. In favorable seasons
we sometimes get a chance to pick
a bouquet from the garden in March.
April is daffodil month.
The supply this year will not be
adequate to the demand, so early
orders should be sent in for daffodil
and narcissus bulbs or the gardener
is likely to face disappointment. A
well-drained soil with plenty of
moisture available, humus being
needed to hold it, is the requisite for
daffodils and if the soil is inclined
to be acid a dressing of lime should
be given in the form of hydrated
lime or ground limestone.
Daffodils Need Shade.
This should be raked into the soil
after the bulbs are planted. A dress
ing of hardwood ashes will be even
better, as the ashes not only fur
nish lime but potash as well, a fer
tilizer which is excellent for bulbous
plants.
Daffodils appreciate shade, not
that they grow any better, but the
flowers will be much more lasting.
A single hot day in early spring
plays havoc with daffodil bloom.
We can have some of the popular
trumpets this fall, such as Emperor,
Empress, Golden Spur and a few of
the choicer ones in limited supply.
The supply of the poet’s narcissus is

during the last month greatly ex

dication that factories are stocking

gains over both the previous month
and the same month a year ago.

riod amounted to 2,621.309.313
pounds, compared with 2,482.515,433
pounds in July, and 2,485,415,172
pounds in August, 1925.

entirely accounted for in larger re
ceipts. Freight coming into the city

parisons, amounting to 525,179,61 G

Simpson Praises
Europe's Lead in
Commercial Flying
CHICAGO —James Simpson, pres
ident cf Marshall Field Co., on
his return to Chicago yesterday
from a visit to France and England,
deplored the fact that Europe lends
America by long odds in commercial
aviation.
“I think Europe is far ahead of
America in commercial aviation,
and we should lose no time in clos
ing up the gap.” Mr. Simpson said.
“Chicago should take the lead in
providing plenty of landing fields.
With our lake front we have an
opportunity that does not present it
self to other cities.
“They have a regular air schedule
from England to the continent ns
well as all over the continent
“Landing fields are only 25 to 30
miles apart, making for a maximum
of safety. There are pilot training
schools and. in England particular
ly. groat attention is paid to the
physical as well ns the mental fit
ness of the aviator. I would rather
fly in an English machine with an
English pilot than with any other.”

STEEL ORDERS
ARE MAINTAINED
Steel orders during the first half
of September were maintained at
the brisk July-August rate, accord
ing to the weekly trade reviews just
issued. Producers, according to
Iron Age, will be satisfied if new
business can be maintained for the
rest of the month at the present
rate.
A slight falling off in the demand
for structural steel is noted.
Chicago mills have 05,000 tons of
rail inquiries before them, and there
are also pending 18,000 tons for the
Texas Pacific and 12,000 for the
gulf coast lines.
“Increasing use of the lakes for
the movement of rolled steel, par
ticularly into the Detroit district,
accounts for some recent deviations
from the usual reckonings of mill
prices,” Iron Age says. “With the
falling off in structural steel awards
since the first of the month the
week’s total was 29.000 tons. The
scrap market at Pittsburgh has
weakened, as both consumer and
dealer demand has subsided, and on
steel work grades the decline is 50
cents.”
The Iron Age composite price re
mains unchanged. Finished steel is
2.43 cents a pound, and pig iron
$19.40 a gross ton.

CHICAGO—Two articles in a
father obscure little publication
have brought forth numerous
“Knights” to defend the honor of
the midwest co-ed.
And the same articles have made
their author —Wilfred O. Cross
one of the most unpopular men in
the mlddlewest's younger set.
Wrote Two Articles.
Cross, a gray-eyed philosophical
young divinity student —who last
year was an under-graduate at the
University of Illinois —wrote two
articles concerning, the American
collegiate body for The Witness,
a national religious magazine.
The first piece called the co-eds
“licentious animals,” depicted a
mixed “pajaum party” aboard a
football train, told of gin being de
livered at a quarantined soroity
house, and generally upbraided the
women of the campus for lowering
the morals of the American colleges.
Change Is Seen.
The second article, which ap
peared today, charged that causes of
“morality or immorality are more
likely to be found in the masculine
mind”—because woman’s chief in
terest is to live for the selection of
a mate—that a new licentiousness
has been invoked in American life;
that the ‘“gospel of the college men
is the gospel of I’ooh Pooh”; and
that scholastic standards are being
lowered through presence of “hot
dates, daring dancers, artful petting
and hip flasks.”
And then the knight defenders
came to the rescue of the American
college students.
Dean Wants Proof.
A dean at the University of Illi
nois demanded that Cross prove all
of his assertions.
President Kinley of the Univer
sity of Illinois said it seemed hardly
worth while “to encourage the ego
tism of an irresponsible boy.”
Deans of women in other middle
western schools denied their charges
were petters and gin drinkers. Pas
tors upbraided the youth.
Only one defender did he have.
Joseph Beatty Burtt, alumnus of
the University of Michigan, offered
legal aid to young Cross and said
“colleges should investigate their
own cases rather than brand Cross
as a criminal.”
The young divinity student, he v
ever, paid little heed to the charges
and denials.
“I know these things to be true.
They are my observations of
campus life. I can prove them,” he
Mid.

phistication for culture and polish.

Drug Thieves Raid
Racine Dentists 9
Offices; Take Dope
RACINE, Wis. The long,
shadowy arm of Chicago’s dope traf
fic has oxtemied itself into the
small towns of Wisconsin.
Apparently restrained by a de
termined effort of the government
to curb the traffic in the larger
cities, the dope venders have turned
their eyes to a new and easier
means of getting their drugs—the
office of the small town dentist.
Twice within the last week den
tists in Itacine have reported that
their offices were broken into and
vials of cocaine and morphine taken
from their drug chests.
Each time the robberies were car
ried through with a smoothness and
finesse that betrays the system of
someone who knows the game. A
small steel instrument was used to
force the lock and open the door.
Nothing else was taken. Money
was ignored.

THINK A LITTLE FARTHER
One of our capitalist contemporaries, in a moment
of lucidity all too rare in that office, remarks with regard
to President Coolidge’s plan to help the farmer by reliev
ing the land speculator: “On that theory, any business
man who is reckless enough to gamble with extraordinary
risks could file a claim for reimbursement against the gov
ernment when he suffers the inevitable loss which he in
cited.”
Our contemporary should think a little farther along
this line, if it can stay lucid long enough. That very
theory was supported by it during the war with all the
heat of a sacred conviction.
Morgan Co. had speculated on the allies to win.
When they were losing, the big boss of Wall Street told the
Washington statesmen that he had scraped the bottom
of the box and that now the American government must
step in and pull his chestnuts out of the fire. Our con
temporary agreed with Morgan and wasted the forests of
several counties on the thesis that every patriotic Amer
ican mutt save the Morgan gamble.
It went even farther and continued to defend this
position for years after the armistice. It still wants Wis
consin voters to support a candidate for Jnited States
senator who backs Morgan’s attempts to sneak into the
back door of the league of nations and to permit the Re
publican standpatters to cancel in a dishonest roundabout
way what the Democrats tried to cancel openly under
sentimental disguises.
It does this now in the same two-faced way in which
it defended Morgan’s and Woodrow Wilson’s war policy.
It takes its cue from Coolidge and makes a great show of
denouncing the allies for demanding a cancellation of their
war debts, while it works in underhanded ways to send
back to the United States senate and house of representa
tives those candidates who are for dishonest and surrep
titious cancellation.
The government and the federal reserve board may
not be guilty of the plight of the land speculators, but
they are guilty of the plight of the real farmers, and they
set the bad example which the little speculators imitated.
Our contemporary is willing that the government
should grant relief wherever it is “for the best interests of
the country at large to do so.” That means in plain lan
guage “wherever it is for the good of the big thieves.”
But it would set up a loud cry of “paternalism, Socialism,
Bolshevism,” if the government should so far forget its
allegiance to Wall Street as to really do something for
its victims.
HAKENKREUZLER
We don’t want to be snobbish about it, but we cannot
let Arthur Brisbane mutilate a foreign language so per
petually as he does the German, French and Italian in his
celebrated column. If he wants to use foreign words to
show off his wide learning, he should at least copy them
right. Otherwise he will confuse his readers as much in
languages as he does in politics and ethics.
In one of his recent scraps, he talks about the Austrian
Jew baiters and calls them “Hankenkreutzlers.” That’s
awful. They are surely bad boys, but not as bad as that.
They are only “Hakenkreuzler.” And what is that?
“Haken” is German for “Hook,” not to be confounded
with “Hacke,” which means hoe or heel. “Kreuz” means
cross. A “Hakenkreuz” is a Swastika or Double Cross.
A “Hakenkreuzler” is one who wears a doublecross, a
doublecrosser. It is the right kind of a sign for that
bunch, also for editors who write bunk.
THE DEMOCRATIC CORPSE
The Democratic corpse in the state of Wisconsin still
jefks spasmodically in every election. Just what the
people think who pretend to revive it is hard to figure out,
unless it still seems to offer a chance to collect some money
£rom the national campaign managers and from local in
terests that seek to confuse the voters in the absence of a
real diSjcrsnce between Republicans and Democrats by a
multiplicity of candidates.
The big interests dread a clear issue and a clear divi
sion over it. But in spite of all their tricks, the issue that
really divides this nation, like all others, into two great
camps is harder and harder to dodge.
Names of parties will mean little as this issue pushes
itself to the front. Campaign programs will mean little.
The things that will mean much are the practical steps
which the statesmen actually take to meet the new con
ditions. Social evolution will not permit them to dodge
such steps.

nized as belonging to a house

Unknown Animal
Tracks Discovered
Ten to 15 different kinds of
animal tracks hitherto unknown
to science, have been discovered
by Dr. C. W. Gilmore of the
United States National museum in
slabs of stone taken from the
Grand canyon at three different
levels near the Hermit trail.
According to Dr. Gilmore, these
mysterious tracks range in size
from some no bigger than those of
a mouse to others which are as
large as the footprints by a lion.
Some of the footprints were
found in rocks 1,000 feet below
the present rim of the Grand
canyon, others were located in
rocks 1,400 feet down, while
others were in strata 1,800 below
the canyon rim. In no two of
these widely separated layers of
rock have tracks of the same kind
been discovered, Dr. Gilmore said.
The tracks are now being
named and classified for future
reference, and it is expected that
still other footprints new to
science will be found among the
many yet to be studied in the
slabs of rock from the same local
ity at present under investigation
at the museum.—U. S. Daily.

SETTING CHINA FREE
Nine world powers have decided to set China free ana
abandon the practice of keeping their police and judges
on Chinese soil, declares a Washington report. The humor
of this language is enhanced by the additional remark:
“This movement is entirely voluntary.”
In order to see the point of this humor, one must read
this report at the tail-end of a long article by Gen. H. J.
Reilly, who knows China. Reilly explains that the for
eign powers, especially the British, are up against it, un
less they can capture Canton.
Wan-hsien, where the Cantonese armies have cap
tured some British patrol boats, is some 1,200 miles up
the Yangtse river. The water is too shallow for large
warships and transports. A small army of 2P,000 for
eigners, such as handled the Boxer rebellion, would be
wiped out before it got half way.
The Cantonese have built forts along the river and
planted heavy artillery in them. They are so well con
cealed that the British patrol boats could not see where
the fire came from that damaged them.
Let us add that Hanyang and Hankow, the big indus
trial centers recently captured by the Cantonese, play
about the same role in the war activities of China as
Chicago does in the United States. Taking Canton away
from the Cantonese would have about as much effect on
their armies near Hankow as taking Savannah would
have on the armies around Chicago.
Reilly states the British fix mildly when he says that
even the transfer of the 75,000 white regulars from India
to the Chinese front, if possible, would not win China
back for the foreign powers. But it is out of the question,
because those white troops cannot be taken out of India
to fight Chinese. East Indian troops would take East
India from England.
The bulk of the military supplies for the Cantonese
does not come by way of salt water. Even if the foreign
powers could hold the big salt water cities of China, they
could not defeat the Cantonese by that method. The help
of Russia comes over land routes that cannot be cut off
without fighting Soviet Russia. Are the United States,
England and Japan going to start a world war against
Soviet Russia and China?
Hardly. It would be a greater folly with even more
disastrous results than the war against Germany. It
would not defeat Russia and China, even if a military de
cision over them could be secured. Russia and China
would win the peace as surely as Germany is winning it
after a lost war. And the industries of England, Japan
and the United States would bear the losses.
Besides, such a war would hasten the social revolu
tion in the big capitalist countries. It would be unpopular.
It would have to be carried through against the public
opinion of the majorities at home. It would overthrow
the old party governments along with the ruling classes.
The days of foreign bullying and strutting are over
in China. They will soon be over in India, too. The nine
powers will soon have graver problems to face than that
of trying to save their faces by “getting out voluntarily”
from a place from which the Cantonese have thrown them
out.
Instead of wasting any more billions and lives on
imperialist conquests that cannot be retained, the nine
pow r ers had better pull up the slack in their old capitalist
business at home. There are too many loose odds and 05
flying around and hitting the majority of the citizens 1.
the face.
The money and lives that would have to be "wasted on
a war in China would make England, Japan, the United
States and the other six powers fit for heroes to live in.
WHO OR WHAT STARTED THE WAR?
Prof. Barnes is ope of the chief exponents in
America of the “revisionist interpretation” regarding the
proximate causes of the World war. As we recall the
sound historical scholars in the field of international re
lations, and remember how they turned propagandists
for the government and for the war departments, and then
look at them today, we realize we must approach even so
emphatically phrased a book as this by Prof. Barnes (The
Genesis of the World War, by Harry Elmer Barnes) with
a great deal of seriousness. He states that “no trained
historian has yet given evidence of having examined the
new documents in a thorough fashion without having be
come distinctly converted to the revisionist point of view”
as w r as Prof. Barnes himself. The statement is a strong
one, and possibly not entirely true; but, saving the ex
ceptions, it is sound.
To educate the people to a new conception of the
real guilt for the World war has been the object of Prof.
Barnes. His thesis, briefly, is this: Nationalism, im
perialism, militarism, navalism, of which all nations were
guilty to a nervous degree, were the causes of the war.
Serbia deliberately plotted to murder the archduke and so
precipitated the crisis. Austria properly desired a strin
gent punishment of Serbia, even to temporary occupation
of Belgrade, but wished the troubles kept localized. Rus
sia, with an eye on Constantinople and the Balkans, was
set on interfering, even though she knew such interference
would bring about a general conflict. Her insistent mobil
ization precipitated war. France actually egged Russia
on because she herself wished a general European war
which would enable her to quell her radicals and secure
her revenge for the loss of Alsace and Lorraine 40-odd
years previously. England deliberately went into-the con
flict to dispose of a dangerous military, naval, and con
mercial rival, and bungled her pacific diplomacy so thv
war was inevitable. Germany gave Austria carte blanch®
with Serbia, expecting the troubles to be Balkan merely,
but really sought to avoid a general European war in
which she would have everything to lose and not much
prospective chance of eventual victory. America was
dragged in by allied and financial propaganda, and by the
pro-British sympathies of Mr. Page, who represented
Britain to Mr. Wilson more than he represented the United
States at the court of St. James.
Prof. Barnes sustains his thesis, although in perhaps a
trifle too vigorous language for sober history, with facts
gleaned from publications brought to light in Austria,
Germany and Russia by revolutionary governments. Na
tionalism and diplomacy were the causes of the war, na
tionalism and French desires for revenge for 1870-1871.—
Saturday Review of Literature.

WILL BEE
Only recently our well-to-do
ladies were collecting money to
purchase the home of Thomas
Jefferson. Donations were re
ceived from the most reaction
ary and conservative elements
of our population.
How interesting that no one
who made the donations had
ever been informed or had
ever possessed sufficient curi
osity to find out what Jefferson
really stood for.
He was more radical than any
one in American political life
today. Jefferson was a firm
believer in an occassional revo
lution. He wrote:
"1 hold that a little rebellion
now and then is a good thing
and as necessary in the political
world as storms in the physical.
Unsuccessful revolutions, in
deed, generally establish the en
croachments on the rights of
the people which have produced
them. Observation of this
truth should render honest re
publican governors so mild in
their punishment of revolutions
as riot to discourage them too
much. It is a medicine neces
sary for the sound health of
government.
"The spirit of resistance to
government is so valuable on
certain occasions that I wish it
to be always kept alive. It will
often be exercised when wrong,
but better so than not to be ex
ercised at all. I like a little
revolution now and then, it is
like a storm in the atmosphere.
God forbid we should ever be
20 years without such a revolu
tion. The people cannot be all
and always informed. The part
which is wrong will be discon
tented in proportion to the im
portance of the facts which they
misconceive. if they remain
quiet under such misconception
it is a lethargy, the forerunner
of death to the public liberty.
"What country can preserve
its liberties if its rulers are not
warned from time to time that
the people preserve the spirit of
resistance? Let them take arms.
The tree of liberty must be re
freshed from time to time with
the blood of tyrants. It is its
natural manure.”
If this last paragraph were
printed on the letterheads sent
out by the wealthy ladies gath
ering funds we have an idea
that Thomas Jefferson’s home
would never have been pre
served.
Thomas Jefferson also was a
firm believer in economic de
termination of political and so
cial institutions. He foresaw
the corruption and thievery of
the Coolidge administration as
a reflection on the economic in
terest of an industrial civiliza
tion. He wrote:
"I think our governments will
remain virtuous for many cen
turies as long as they are chief
ly agricultural and this will be
as long as tnere shall be vacant
land in any part of America.
When they get piled upon one
another in large cities as in
Europe they will become as cor
runt as in Europe.
“Corruption of morals in the
mass of cultivators is a phe
nomenon of which no age nor
nation has furnished an exam
ple. It is the mark set on those
who, not looking up to heaven,
or to their own soil and indus
try as does the husbandman, for
their subsistence, depend for it
on casualties and caprice of cus
tomers.
“Dependence begets subserv
iency and \enality, suffocates
the germ of virtue and prepares
fit tools for the designs of am
bition. While we have land to
labor then, let us never wish to
see our citizens occupied at a
work bench.”
Jefferson feared the owners
of industry would corrupt polit
ical life so as to grow richer by
control of government.
History has proved him cor
rect.

TOWN OF LAKE
‘CITY’ BATTLE
UP IN COURT
Claim No Written
Consent of Property
Owners Obtained.
When is a city not a city?
Around that question centered the
arguments in Judge Edward T. Fair
child’s branch of the circuit court
today in the injunctional proceed
ings instituted by residents of the
town of Lake against the town board
to prevent incorporation of the
township into a city and to hold up
an election tomorrow.
No Consent Obtained.
Counsel for Agnes Tomkiewisz,
who started the action in the name
of other town of Lake residents, con
tended that a town in order to be
incorporated as a city must have
the characteristics of a city, it must
not as the case in the town of Lake,
include large agricultural areas,
sparsely settled, and which have
little if any connection with the
residential nucleus from which the
incorporation movement issued.
Counsel contended further that no
written consent of the adjacent prop
erty owners was obtained as re
quired by law and that a result
the town board had no authority to
entertain proceedings for incorpora
tion and to call an election.
Court Can’t Interfere.
Counsel for the town board de
clared that the town of Lake is an
unincorporated village now and that
all the legal requirements authoriz
ing an election on the question of
Incorporating have been fully met.
The court, it was argued, had no
jurisdiction to interfere with an
election at this time, that an elec
tion was a political matter and that
an attempt to interfere with an elec
tion would amount to a suppression
of free speech and to an overthrow
of popular government.
Judge Fairchild was expected to
take the case under advisement late
today. The court indicated during
the early stages of the argument
that it had doubts, from the argu
ments presented so far, that the
town of Lake is an unincorporated
village now, as claimed.

WASHINGTON—On the basis of

Jacob Rosenthal, wealthy New

tary of State Kellogg, acting
through the American embassy in
Mexico City, today urged the Calles

MEXICO CITY—The murder of
Jacob Rosenthal, G 2, retired mer
chant of Woodmere, N. I’., by ban
dits, has aroused the American col
ony here. Rosenthal’s body was
found only three miles from where
he was kidnaped.
Three suspects have been iden

Rosenthal, as being members of the
bandit gang, and are being brought
to trial here. Two of the bandits
were shot and killed by the police
who recovered the* wealthy Amer
ican’s body.

Rosenthal was killed by bandits,
who kidnaiied him Sunday from a
party of relatives with whom he
was returning here from Cuerna
vaca, a resort city, when they
realized that police, pretending to
he paying SIO,OOO ransom, had
tricked them.
Two policemen, carrying a bag,
presumably holding the money, but
in reality loaded with iron bars,
met the bandits at a designated
spot in ihe hills near Cuernavaca.
Instead of handing over the bag.
the police opened fire. Two of the
bandits were killed. The others,
hiding nearby, plunged their kinves

Elimination of so-called “U-turns”
In Milwaukee’s congested downtown
district was recommended to the
common council last night by the
Milwaukee safety commission.
At the same time the commission
recommended the placing of small
reflex prisms on ali arterial high
way signs in such a manner as to
catch the rays of headlights and
call attention of motorists to the
presence of the sign.
Turns in Block.
Control of downtown corners, not
regulated by automatic stop and go
signs, by means of traffic whistles
was also recommended and the com
mission went on record as favoring
the progressive system of traffic
light control in preference to the
present synchronized system.
An extensive study by the com
mission is responsible for the recom
mendation to abolish the“ U-turns.”
Under the present traffic code, these
turns are prohibited at intersections
and are usually executed in the mid
dle of the block. This practice, the
commission declares, is hazardous
and obstructs traffic.
Agree to Amendment.
lu preparing the whistle recom
mendation, the safety commission
departed from the original sug
gestion of Police Chief Jacob G.
Laubenheimer for the elimination
of automatic traffic regulators and
the substitution of the whistle and
the officer for them.
The recommendation is that an
officer with a whistle he placed only
at such intersections as are not con
trolled by the regulators. Both the
chief and Capt. A. J. Murray of the
police department traffic bureau are
said to be agreeable to the amend
ment.

About 10,000 persons were present
at the ceremonies opening the ex
tension of The Electric Co. Center
St. car line from 51st St. to GOtb

City officials, officers of the trac

tended line.

Mayor Daniel W. Hoau, Aid. A. W.

extension; Aid Joseph P. Carney,
nopartlsan, 22nd ward, and William

Rita Reichert, 5, daughter of Al
bert C. Reichert, chairman of the
Center Street Business Men’s Assn,

stretched across Center St. nt 51st
St., permitting the car to pass over
the new line.
Following the ride to the end of
the new line and back, speeches were
given at 51st St.
The growth of Milwaukee within
the last 10 years was stressed by
Mayor Hoan. Ten years ago the
city had an area of 25 squarp miles,
and now has 33; building operations
then totaled $25,000,000, while last
year they were $45,000,000; five
miles of sewer laid in those years
was considered an accomplishment
now the yearly average is 45 miles,
according to the mayor.
There has been an increase of
125.000 in the population- during
that period.

Speaking of the growth of the
northwest side. Mayor Hoan stated
that when he lived at 30th St. and
North Ave., 12 years ago, all terri
tory west and north of there was
farm land.
Aid. Strehlow pointed out that the
territory served by the car line ex
tension was annexted to the city
only a year ago, and that it has
been two years since the trolley
service from 27th St. to 35th St. was
inaugurated. The street railway of
fers the only means of transporting
large numbers of people, he said.

spoke.

speeches. Music was furnished by

ployes’ Mutual Benefit Association

the town after the borough In Eng
land from which many of the lead

mally given its new name, which

Seen.
LONDON Rural police with
heavy special reinforcements
charged 2,000 strikers and their
wives at Doncaster yesterday in the
first serious disturbance of the Brit
ish coal strike for more than a
month.
Trouble has been brewing between
the rank and fde of the miners and
the safety men in several districts,
the latter going back to work in
defiance of the unions. When the
safety men were leaving the Don
caster pits, strikers assembled near
the entrances. Stones were hurled.
Police charged the strikers and
eventually dispersed them.
Prime Minister Baldwin last night
summoned the miners’ officials to a
conference in Downing St. today. He
will consult also with the president
of the mining association. It is un
derstood that the cabinet hopes to
get tlie men back to work while the
details of a solution are l>eing
worked out.
In political circles the opinion is
held that a scheme for district set
tlements. subject to national rati
fication, will be advanced. The idea
Is that the colleries should be made
a wide ring in which the local min
ers’ leaders would determine wages
and working lvours, in accordance
with local conditions.
The country expects Prime Min
ister Baldwin to take firm action,
end he is being called on by all par
ties except the Tory reactionaries,
who back the conservative mine
owners.

ZURICH—The executive of the
Socialist international has decided
to create a press fund which shall
form the financial basis for the in
ternational Socialist review, to be
published by the office of the So
cialist international.
The executive also adopted a reso
lution stating that one of the main
tasks of the next international So
cialist congress shall be to lay down
more fully the principles of action
which shall guide the Socialist
parties in their attitude towards the
league of nations.
It was decided to appoint a com
mittee with power to study ways
and means for the democratization
of the league.
Acknowledge Some Benefits.
The executive recognizes the serv
ices which Socialists as representa
tives of their countries in Geneva
may render to the principles of the
international by co-operation to
wards better relations between the
nations, the resolution further
states.
“But in order to make their ac
tivity for the cause of world peace
and international Socialism as fruit
ful as possible, it is necessary that
the. individual parties should define
the prelimiuar.y conditions on which
they empower one of their members
to accept or to retain a mandate in
the assembly or in the council of the
league.
“They should at all times investi
gate whether circumstances and the
directions given by governments
permit the execution of the mandate
under conditions reconcilable with
the general interests of the labor
movement and the decisions of the
Socialist international.
Should Continue Study.
“It is also necessary that an in
timate and continuous contact be
maintained between such delegates
and their parties. Finally, the So
cialist international shall consist
ently investigate the problems which
occupy the league of nations and
define its stand towards these prob
lems.
“In this way it should supply the
individual parties anu the delegates
themselves with the necessary liases
that will enable them to fulfill the
duties in the sense indicated above.”
Among other matters taken up by
the executive’of the Socialist inter
national was the attack on the eight
hour day by the capitalist govern
ments, especially of the British and
Italian.
The resolution cn this subject de
nounces the nine-hour decree of the
Fascist government as a violation
of the Washington eight-hour pact.
It also condemns the extension of
the working day for the British
miners, as decreed by the Tory gov
ernment of England.
Blame Capitalist Reaction.
“Responsibility for these crimes
of capitalist reaction rests with all
governments which still frustrate or
delay the ratification of the Wash
ington convention,” the resolution
continues. “Therefore all the greater
significance attaches to the success
of the Belgian Labor party which
lm3 carried through the ratification
of the Washington eight-hour pact
in spite of the severe financial crisis
in Belgium.”
The executive urges all Socialist
parties to make a combined effort
to secure a ratification of the eight
hour pact by the governments of
France, Germany and Great Britain.

BTREATOR—Chicago high school
teachers are opposed to schools of
more than 2,000 pupils. A resolu
tion introduced at the convention
of the Illinois Stale Federation of
Labor, in session here yesterday, and
which was adopted after being con
curred in by the committee on
schools, urges adoption of the slogan
“No high schools of more than 2,000
pupils.”
Miss Florence Curtis Hanson, del
egate from the Chicago Federation
of Women High School Teachers, in
troduced the resolution, supporting
it with answers to the questionnaire,
“What objection is there in the
large high school?” The majority
of teachers, she said, were opposed
to large high schools. Among the
answer the to questionnaire were:
Rap Big Schools.
“Creates lockstep methods of
education.”
“Gives instruction for the mass,
not the individual.”
“Destroys leadership.”
“Injures children in hall rushes
and transportation accidents.”
“Gives an opportunity for dis
honesty.”
“Widens the breach between
student, parent and teacher.”
“Costs parents more money.”
“Makes uniformity nil ideal.”
Miss Hanson read the report of
the committee, which was adopted*
unanimously, and which urges in
particular the organization and
unionization of every school teacher
in the state.
She said that parents of school
children should Insist they he
taught by teachers who “have the
union label.” Part of the report
was a program of notion for 1916-
17 which was adopted by the con
vention for Illinois schools. II
includes:
Normal 5-scour day in the publi<
schools.
Single salary schedule for those
having equal experience and prep
aration.

and pupils.
A cultural wage with annual
automatic Increments.
Payment for absence due to ill
ness, quarantine or family deaths.
Abolition of the rating system to
be replaced by intelligent co-op
erative supervision.
A pension after 30 years’ service.
A maximum of 1,500 pupils to n
building; 30 pupils to a class.
School buildings that are com
fortable. safe, sanitary and well
equipped.
Teachers’ participating
In the determination of educational
policies.
Democratic trial, appeal, salary
and educational hoards, including
representatives of the teaching
staff and organized labor.

ENGLISHMAN
WINS $5,000 IN
CHANNEL SWIM
LONDON —Norman Derham, an
Englishman, completed a swim
across the English channel today
and won $5,000 offered by Lord Rid
dell. owner of The News of the
World, for any citizen of Great Brit
ain who could better Gertrude
Ederle’s time for the crossing.
Derham came ashore at St. Mar
garet’s Bay, near Dover, at 10:57
a. m. today, 13 hours and 50 min
utes after entering the water at
Cape Gris Nez, France
Is Third Englishman.
Miss Ederle’s record time across
the channel on Aug. G was 14 hours
and 31 minutes.
Derham was the third English
man to ever swim the channel.
Ernest Vierkotter, a German,
swam across late in August, low
ering Miss Ederle’s record, and a
few days later Georges Michel, a
Frenchman, established another rec
ord by achieving the swim in 11
hours and G minutes.
His Third Attempt.
Today’s was Derham’s third at
tempt this season. He entered the
water nt 9:01 last night and his
effort was vouched for by The News
<<f the World when that paper an
nounced that he had won the prize
■ffered immediately after Miss
Ederle triumphed.
Twentyone swimmers have chal
lenged the channel this season.
Their attempts aggregate 34. Five
of the 21 wore successful, and of
he five, two were American women.
In all 10 persons have swam the
channel since 1875, an average of
one successful crossing every 5.1
years.
Order Sesqui Gates
Closed on Sunday;
Kendrick Refuses
PHILADELPHIA, Fu.—Although
the sesquicentennial exposition was
ordered yesterday to close on Sun
days. Mayor Kendrick announced it
would remain open pending an ap
peal of a decision by the Dauphin
county court.
The court held that the exposition
is “worldly employment,” that it is
not work of necessity or charity and
that the amusement and recreations
within the grounds are in violation
of the Sunday blue laws of 1794.
The action was brought by the
state, the atttorney general contend
ing that the centennial by operating
commercial features on Sunday ex
ceeded its charter rights. The state
also pointed out that the legislature
appropriated $750,000 for the state’s
participation in the sesquicentennial
on condition that It should be con
ducted “in strict conformity with
Sunday observance.”

Waupun; R. Beihl, city manager,
Two Rivers; D. B. Drowatzlcy,

mayor of Washburn.
“While municipal ownership
seems to he on the wane and the
cities and villages seem to be selling
out their municipal plants to large
utility interests, it appears to me
that it will he but a very short time
before the increase in rates for util
ity services will increase to such an
extent that there will be a wide
spread campaign for municipal own
ership,” said Mr. Hammersley.
“An investigation should be made
as to whether or not ic is advisable
for the municipalities to sell their
municipal plants to the utility in
terests and a study made of the
possibility of greatly increased
rates ns a result of the acquisition
by the utility interests of these mu
nicipal plants, and what recommen
dations can be made to protect the
public from increased rates for util
ity services.”

GERMAN BANK
DEPOSITS JUMP
NEW YORK—Figures received In
the financial district disclosing that
deposits of leading German banks
are now greater than they were
prior to the war caused wide com
ment today. The six lending insti
tutions increased deposits GO per
cent in one year, which is taken as
an indication of the great economic
improvement that has taken place
in central Europe.
On June 30 deposits of these
banks totaled 2,412.000,000 marks,
against 2.101,000,000 on the same
date in 1913.
It is pointed out, however, that
the increase is not general, but
rather reflects a tendency toward
concentration of banking business
in the six banks, which include the
four “D” hanks, Commerz bank and
the Mitteldeutsche.
Another angle of the situation is
the reduced purchasing power of the
mark, which, like the dollar, is be
low its pre-war level. It is estimated
that from 20 to 25 per cent of de
posits represent foreign money left
in German hanks on short term.
The government also pursues a
policy of keeping a large part of
current tax returns in lending
banks, so that the money does not
lie idle.

punish railroads for not complying
with its orders was begun yester
day when the department of justice
instructed the United States attor
neys of the eastern district of Vir
ginia and the district of Indiana to
institute penalty suits against the
Chesapeake Ohio and the Cincin
nati, Indianapolis Western rail
roads.
An attempt will be made to col
lect forfeitures from these carriers
for disobedience and failure to com
ply with an order issued by the
commission under Section 15 of the
interstate commerce commission net.
The railroads involved had filed
tariffs with the interstate commerce
commission proposing increase in
certain freight rates.
As the increased rates were op
posed by certain interested parties,
the commission held hearings and
decided that the proposed increased
rates were not justified and ordered
the carriers to cancel their tariffs
on or before a specified date. The
carriers failed to cancel the tariffs
at the specified time, the Chera
peake Ohio continuing the in
creased rates 24 days and the Cin
cinnati, Indianapolis Western 59
days after the commission ordered
the tariffs canceled.
That the August earnings of the
railroads were larger than last year
and that the carriers are assured
of a continuance of heavy traffic
the balance of the year was indicat
ed yesterday by officials of some of
the leading systems.
Hale Holden, president of the Chi
cago, Burlington Quincy railroad,
said: “Our August -gross and net
operating income was slightly above
the $15,063,899 and the $3,670,352 of
last year and we expect to hold the
gain of about $2,000,000 in net rail
way operating ineome in the first
eight months until the end of the
year.
“Our estimated gross revenue and
net operating income for August
showed an increase of about $500,-
000 over the $10,786,999 and $2,-
636,364 for August last year,” said
Ralph Budd, president of the Great
Northern railway.
The gross revenues of the Chi
cago Rock Island Pacific railway
in August are estimated at $12,537,-
000, an increase of 8.4 per cent over
last year, according to E. N. Brown,
chairman of the executive commit
tee.
The total number of freight cars
loaded and received from connect
ing lines by four of the leading
railway systems in the Chicago dis
trict showed a slight gain in the
first 14 days of September as com
pared with the same period last
year. The individual reports of the
carriers are as follows: Illinois
Central, 95,542 ears, against 92,-
147 last year; Milwaukee, 84,028,
against 54.125; Rock Island, 08,366,
against 68.603, and Burlington, 75,-

COPPER BUYING
IN FALL BOOM
NEW YORK—The expected Sep
tember buying movement in copper
has apparently set in, for the volume
of sales in the past week has been
the largest since the active weeks of
July, Engineering and Mining Jour
nal reports. Zinc also has been in
heavy demand. The price of tin
reached a new high for the post-war
period, while silver held its own in
a quiet market. Lead has been
somewhat weaker.
All producers of zinc reported ex
ceptional business, principally to
galvanizers, but there has been pro
nounced aversion to paying more
than 7.45 cents a pound. The fa
vorable statistics increased buying
interest.
London operators continue to
boost tin and the market here fol
low’s. Supplies are scarce and an
other high reeord price, 69% cents
a pound, was paid for prompt
Straits.
Swiss Export Trade
Dcreased By War
GENEVA—The external trade of
Switzerland, like that of the rest
of Europe, is not so great as it
was before the war. But the Swiss,
although they complain about the
falling off of their trade, have not
really suffered more than other
European countries.
For in 1924 their exports came
to 56.4 per cent and in 1925 to 90.4
per cent of its total in 1913.
At the same time Swiss Imports
have increased to a larger amount
than their exports in the last year.
There is, however, a good deal of
unemployment in Switzerland, es
pecially in the building trades and
in the watch and clock industry.
