GHEMIGAL TRADE
REPORTED UP
NEW YORK—Since the first of
the month there has been a change
for the better in the chemical in
dustry. Buying interest is more
apparent in both the spot and con
tract markets and a firmer price
tone Is in evidence, Chemical and
Metallurgical Engineering reports.
The weighted index number has ad
vanced slightly and now stands at
113.59, which compares with 113.33
a month ago, and 112.84 Septem
ber, 1925. Firmer prices prevailed
for denatured alcohol, tin silts, cal
cium arsenate, aniline oil and other
coal-tar chemicals.
Snrjplus stocks of industrial al
cohol have been reduced and the
position of the market is firmer in
all directions. Interest in sulphur
has been increased by the report
of the formation of a new company
to operate in Texas. The surplus
stocks of nitrate of soda and conse
quent curtailment in production has
brought about a serious situation
in the mining districts in Chile.
Vegetable oils have been easier
in the past month and the weighted
index number has settled at 154.2 G,
as against 15C-.50 last month, and
156.04 in September a year ago.

to $128,453.

M’FADDEN BANK
BILL IS ORBED
CHICAGO —Members of the Chi-
eago and Cook County Bankers'
Assn, and their guests were urged
last night by Representatives Mor
ton D. Hull, Illinois, and Otis Win
go, Arkansas, to work for passage of
the McFadden bill, with the Hull
amendments, as the solution of the
branch banking issue fairest to both
sides of the controversy.
The occ&sion was the monthly
dinner meeting of the association at
which there was a record attend
ance of members and middle west
bankers. More than 500 bankers
were present.
“The two essentials of a fair so
lution,” said Congressman Hull,
“are justice to the national banks
that are now suffering from state
branch bank competition and a safe
guard against the extension of
branch banking in states which do
not now permit the practice. The
proposal which came from the
joint conference committee of con
gress did not conform to either of
these essentials. If the McFadden
bill is passed without the so-called
Hull amendments, the next step
will be a bill giving to national
banks the right to do branch bank
ing wherever situated without re
gard to state laws.”
Congressman Wir.go urged the
bankers to awake to the danger to
independent unit banking that con
fronts them in the passage of the
McFadden bill without the Hull
provisions.

FLOODS RUIN
IOWA'S CROPS
CHICAGO —Thousands of acres
of rich lowa farm land and millions
of dollars’ worth of crops and farm
property are menaced by flood,
owing to the weakening of the
Skunk river levee and its penetra
tion in a dozen or more places by
the waters which are six feet above
the flood level stage.
In western Illinois and in eastern
lowa residents along the Illinois
River valley were said to be aban
doning their homes, moving their
families and goods to places of
safety and driving their flocks of
sheep, herds of cattle, pigs and
poultry to higher ground.
Farm land in the vicinity of the
city is flooded and losses to crops
are said to be heavy, though def
inite figures are not available.
Indiana rivers, which had receded
some from the recent heavy rains,
were again raging torrents last night
following torrential downpours the
night before. Farmers have aban
doned hope of saving the corn crop
in the White river bottoms in Pike
county. Broken ievees have per
mitted the flood waters to spread
over hundreds of acres of corn,
clover and alfalfa.
Farmers in central Illinois, ac
cording to the department of agri
culture, have given up hope of be
ing able to salvage unthrashed small
grains in the fields.
Kansas is more fortunate in re
gard to crop loss than the states fur
ther north and east, hut communi
cations, both by railroad and high
way, are seriously affected and it
may he some days before they are
normal again.

In a sense there is no country in
Europe that you can see in one sum
mer, but this is pre-eminently so
with Switzerland, some of the
grandest districts of which you
would only want to see in the
winter. But even if you confined
yourself to the summer lands, there
is many a delightful rail trip, lake
trip, highway excursion or jaunt
along some famous bridle path that
you would not have time to “take
in.” Lik* the old fashioned au
revoir formula of the New England
farmers, the Swiss parting always
has a “Come again” tone in it.

from France through Geneva, from
Germany through Zurich or from
the Italian Alps, it is best to have
a well outlined schedule of just
what you want to see and “go to it.”

travelers who have benefited by the
low exchange in France, Germany
and Italy, not to blame Switzerland
that it did not suffer in its cur
rency during the war. What you
get for your dollar in Switzerland
is worth more than a dollar, espe
cially if you plan your own trip and
avoid abject dependency on others.

Here is a story which might go
along with Mr. Stocker’s story en
titled “How I Won the Battle
With Tuberculosis in My Own
Home,” Mr. Stocker's story is or
was distributed in pamphlet form
by the Tuberculosis society, 310
Jefferson St., Detroit, free to
Wnyne county residents, 5 cents a
copy to others. The present story
might be entitled “How Tubercu
losis Tends Toward Recovery,”
for as far as the story shows the
lucky woman did little enough to
win the battle. I shall not give
the address. It is of no impor
tance.
My Dear Doctor Brady:
Your recent comment anent the
importance of what the tubercu
losis patient has in his head
prompts me to tell you my ex
perience.
About 20 years ago the doctors
found that I had TB. I followed
their treatment and consulted my
physicians frequently, but got no
better. The tendency of both was
to keep the thought of disease up
permost in my mind.
Knowing that the tendency of
nature is toward health, I decided
to go on my own and give old TB
a race. I knew that if I could
build up my body faster than TB
could tear it down I should win.
From thinking disease I begun
to think health. I knew notiiing
about suggestion in those days,
but 1 adopted the idea that I was
going to be well—that nothing
could prevent me from it.
I had no money, so must earn
my living as I went along. I saved
my strength all I possibly could
—denied myself all social pleas
ures that I might get plenty of
sleep, though I usually went to
the theater once a week, during
the season. Some diversion seemed
absolutely necessary.
I ate good, nourishing food, and
was at all times optimistic..
I ran an elevated temperature
for six months, but after thnt I
began to get better. It wns a
long uphill fight but I won. I
left TB behind in the race, and
now he is so far behind that I
know he will never catch up with
me again.
Although I was cured of TB I
still was below par. I took cold
easily, had a hacking cough, and
lacked my former energy. After
dragging along that way for sev
eral years I took the advice so
often given by doctors and had a
general examination. I told the
physician of my old trouble. He
congratulated me on having sound
lungs, with only one small scar.
The blood count showed that I
had anemia, and after a series of
about 40 treatments for that I wns
pronounced a well woman.
I now approach the decline of
life with absolutely nothing to
complain of.
I did not mention fresh air, ns
I had very little of it. My work
through all those years was in the
basement of a- big department
store.
I have found many useful sug
gestions in your daily articles and
hope they will continue.
If you think my story will bene
fit others you may pass it on.
Yours Truly,
Mrs

ative energy kept him at his bench

Galsworthy continued his study of

came occupied with the newer psy
chology of pretty ladies. Mr. Gals
worthy continued his survey of Eng
lish mortals, all in a superb novel
ist’s style.

ATTACKER OF
CO-EDS TUNES
STORY DOWN
CHICAGO —Wilfred O. Cross, ex-
I'niversity of Illinois student whose
articles on Morality of Undergradu
ates, published in The Witness,
Episcopal weekly, have quickened
students and educators throughout
the middle west to challenging de
nials of his indictment of co-ed
morality, came to Chicago from his
home in Potomac, 111., last night.
He will spend the next few days
with the Rev. William O. Spofford,
managing editor of The Witness,
who arrived from New York yester
day. And he will go east to enroll
Sept. 28 as a divinity student in
Berkley Theological seminary at
Middletown, Conn.
Story Tuned Down.
In a letter to The Daily mini, the
student publication at Urbana,
Cross had tuned down his first sen
sational and semi-specific charges
to a statement that in “a bit of
hack writing—l merely asserted
that times end manners have
changed since the co-ed came to the
university.’’
But last night, in the editorial
rooms of The Witness, Cross, who
is an Englishman, 25, in this coun
try since 1014, maintained that the
only error in his articles was one
of literary emphasis, rather than of
facts.
Made Slight Mistake.
“My mistake,” Cross said, “was
an artistic one. I placed too much
emphasis, I now realize, on the first
part of my statement. Yes, the
statement about the pajama party
in the sleeping coach, the gin drink
ing and the rest, that was true. But
I, perhaps, projected it too much
into the limelight, inasmuch as the
latter part of the article, the real
hub of it so far as I am concerned,
was not printed until a later issue.”
Still maintaining quietly that he
could substantiate every word of
every sentence which he had writ
ten, the student-author explained
that he would not do so because of
the embarrassment it would cause
people and institutions.
Hits Cross Theory.
Modern psychology, said by Cross
to be at the basis of the moral lax
ity among college students, does not
intend to set a standard of morals.
This is the view taken by Nathaniel
Butler, professor of education at
the University of Chicago, and one
of the best known educators in the
United States. His analysis of stu
dent morality follows:
If you should pick at random
1.000 young men and women who
are now in American colleges, and
another 3,000 of the same age who
are not and never have been, the
moral and intellectual level of the
former group would be found to be
higher,
The safeguards brought to bear on
American students are more thor
oughly organized and constantly in
operation, not only in their intellec
:unl but also in their social life in
college and outside. When young
people go wrong in college it will
usually be found that they began
to move In that direction before
they came to college.

CUBELA CHILD
CUSTODY GIVEN
AUNT, UNCLE
Holding that Mrs. Mildred Cubela,
divorced wife of the late Dr. Harold
Cubela, has not passed the period
of probation and that she is not
entirely ready to assume so
delicate and important a task, Cir
cuit Judge Charles Aarons, today
awarded the custody of Barbara,
Mrs. Cubela’s daughter, to Dr. and
Mrs. Lawrence Cubela, 035 Murray
Ave., uncle and aunt of the child.
Allowed to Visit Girl.
The mother was given the priv
ilege of visiting the child at the
Cubela home every Thursday from
2 to 4, and to take the child with
her on Saturdays and Sundays, nl
ternatingly, for the period of two
hours.
The grandmother, Airs. Sophia
Boehme, who has been taking a
great interest in both Mildred and
the baby, will be permitted to
visit little Barbara twice a month.
Must Learn Control.
In declining to allow the mother
to have the child at this time,
Judge Aarons pointed out that
under proper environment and in
fluence he expects to see Alildred
reaching the stage where she can
be allowed to have the control of
her child. “Before she can take
control of the child, however, she
must have control of herself,” the
court said.
Judge Aarons also indicated that
the present order is always subject
to change.

6,750 TAKE TO
MARSHES; DUCK
SEASON OPENS
Milwaukeeans, 0,750 strong, yes
terday were biding in ambush here
and there throughout Wisconsin,
shooting at the enemy. The enemy,
although unarmed, has the advant
age of air flight.
The duck season opened yester
day. The 0,750 hunting licenses is
sued so far tihs fall exceeds by 1.250
the number issued at this time last
year, according to County Clerk
William J. Cary.
Before daybreak yesterday alarm
clocks uttered insistantly. canvas
breeches and coats were pulled on,
shell boxes were filled, dogs were
called, and the long trek over
marshes and lakes’ edges began.
/1 daybreak shot guns sounded,
mixed with the honking of excited
mallards which circled high in ths
air, lighting in the safety of the
center of the lakes and amidst the
wild rice.
Game wardens, too, were on the
job early, prepared for a busy sea
son.
Valentine Raeth, state conserva
tion commissioner, reported that at
Big Muskego lake, southwest of the
city, more t'ian 000 hunters were
hidden in blinds when the day be
gan.
He estimated that more than 3,000
birds were bngged but that most of
the l were mud hens, or coots, very
few ducks being bagged.
Five hunters were shot, none of
them seriously.
INDIANS WOULD
BUILD OWN DAM
ON WOLF RIVER
Opposition to the plan of the Wis
consin Power Co. to build dams on
the tribal lands of the Alenominee
Indian reservation at a cost of $3,-
000,000, was given by a delegation
of representatives of the tribe, who
told Alaj. J. J. Kingman, United
States resident engineer, at a hear
ing in the federal building late yes
terday, that they wish to develop
their own water power.
The company petitioned for pri
ority rights for a three-year sur
vey, and for a license to construct
dams. Alaj. Kingman will forward
his findings together with the pe
tition and the arguments advanced
by both the company’s and the In
dians’ representative to federal au
thorities at Washington, D. C.
The power company proposes to
erect six dams, five of them on In
dian territory, and all on the Wolf
river.
Indian representatives stated that
a survey had already been made for
the tribe by a United States engi
neer. The Indian delegation, con
sisting of four members of the tribe
elected at a recent powwow and
headed by Alitchell Oshkenaniew.

CHICAGO’S FLOODED RESERVOIR
The Illinois river is so full of water that The Chicago
Tribune has to let up on its everlasting demand for 10,000
cubic second-feet from Lake Michigan and to admit that
“sometimes” Chicago sanitary district can get along with
out its “full” quota from the big lake.
The trouble with the Chicago sanitary district now is
not lack of water from Lake Michigan, but so much water
in the Illinois river that the Chicago sewage must be kept
from backing into the lake.
The Chicago Tribune’s remedy for this threat to the
health of all lake cities is not the building of a modern
sewage disposal plant by Chicago, but the conceited and
comfortable plea that Lake Michigan is Chicago’s “res
ervoir” which may be “tapped or shut off according
to the sweet or rotten will of the Chicago sanitary board.
But at the same time The Tribune sees well enough
that this sudden opulence of water is very embarrassing
for its claims and that the other lake cities will be rein
forced by loud protests from the Illinois valley cities,
which are being flooded by the careless handling of the
sanitary district. It warns the board to use less lake
water when the river is flooded by rain.
But if the sanitary board has to admit that it does
not need 10,000 cubic second-feet all the time, and that it
is turning the Illinois valley into a swamp and backing
the Chicago sewage into the lake as well as into the front
lawns of the down-river residence districts, it amounts
to an admission that Milwaukee and the other lake cities
were right and Chicago was wrong.
If the excessive withdrawal of lake water by Chicago
had not lowered the level of the lake so much, there
would be a better flow of water in the Illinois river, Now
even the flooding of the river by rains backs the water
into the lake with all the Chicago sewage and drowns the
valley cities of Illinois.
That’s what comes of disregarding the laws of com
mon decency and extending the inconsiderate practices of
private capitalism into the fields of interstate sanitation.
If the Chicago sewage now threatens to fertilize the mil
lionaires’ lawns on the lake front, Chicago is getting a
dose of its own smelly medicine. We only hope that
Chicago will not become a center of epidemics spreading
in all directions from this hearth of iniquity.
‘OUR WAR’ IS OURS NO LONGER
Do you remember how the whole Northcliffe press
and the bought American dailies used to scream about
eight or nine years ago that England and France were
fighting “our war” and that we must get in “to defend
civilization and democracy?”
Perhaps you have forgotten all that lying propaganda,
in spite of the allied efforts to keep it alive. For now
“our war” is ours no longer. The anti-cancellation forces
in the two old parties, who continually have to face the
revolt of the voters against the world court and against
higher indirect taxes, now don’t want to hear any more
about “our war.”

CAPACITY TO PUT IT OVER
The financial press of the United States almost unani
mously rejects Newton D. Bakers demand for a cancel
lation of the allied war debts and reduction of Germany’s
Dawes plan payments. The argument against this de
mand is always: There’s no hurry. Let’s wait and see
how things will work out. Let them pay according to
their capacity.
Boiled right down to dollars and cents, capacity to
pay means rather capacity to put it over the American
voters. So long as they will stand for paying out of their
own pockets what Europe will not or cannot pay, the
Wall Street leaders will leave enough debts hanging over
Europe to use as a pressure for new deals over there and
for misleading campaign slogans at home.

THE STRAIN ON THE DICTATORS
One of the most significant phases of the strugg 1
between the forces of Democracy and Fascism is the per
ceptible change in the attitude of the dictators towards
the trade unions and,the Socialist party.
Every dictator started with a violent attack on the
forces of Democracy under cover of a war on Bolshevism.
The trade unions and the Socialist parties found them
selves attacked from two fronts. They braved both the
Communist and Fascist attacks.
The Communist waves gradually ebbed away. Very
little is left of them outside Russia. The Fascist excuse
of Bolshevism no longer serves in attacks on the trade
unions and Socialists.
The dictators are now faced with the fact that they
did not crush the real force of Democracy. The breach
made in the labor front by Communist splits has been
repaired so well that Labor can pit its main forces against
Fascism. The dictators have felt the difference for some
time.
The Hungarian dictator, Horthy, early in his career
realized that he could not stamp out both Socialism and
Communism. He tried to weaken the Socialist opposition
by offering a compromise to some Socialist leaders and
persecuting the left wingers. This policy soon wore itself
out, as the right and left wing of the Hungarian Socialist
party began to draw together in defense of their common
interests.
The Spanish dictator, Primo De Rivera, made the
same discovery. He found that inevitably the opposition
in the Spanish army, so far as it did not identify itself
with the reactionary generals, got in touch with the Social
ist leaders. The Communists of Spain and the Catalonian
anarchists were unable to wreck the Spanish trade union
and Socialist movement. Rivera had to tolerate that much
Democracy.
Dictator Pangalos in Creece could not crush the trade
unions and Socialists in spite of all the help which th<
Communists lent to his efforts. In Greece, as in the other
Balkan countries, the trade unions gradually wore out
the Communist disrupters and disowned them. The
democratic forces of Labor kept enough opposition alive
against Pangalos to make his position untenable. The
new dictator who followed Pangalos will not last any
better, if he fails to respect the spirit of democracy.
Mussolini, the ideal of all other dictators, also finds
himself bending under the everlasting strain of problems
which he cannot master. The economic conditions of Italy
are going from bad to worse under the pressure of world
market slumps beyond the reach of the dictator. The lire
is not stabilized. Instead of improving conditions, the
dictator has to decree privations for the mass of the Ital
ian citizens.
After putting the regular trade unionists and Social
ists outside the law, Mussolini discovers that they continue
to be just what they were before his decrees and that their
influence, driven under ground, is even more remarkable
than it was in the open light of the day.
The official organ of Mussolini expresses the dic
tator’s embarrassment by attacking the Socialist leaders
one day and begging them half-heartedly next day to help
the government in the economic crisis which stubbornly
defies all dictatorial decrees.
The ax is already laid at the root of the dictatorships
In a little while, the people will get tired of the perpet'
foolish promises, flourishes and decrees which seek t<%
economic facts with bragging words. Nothing fails i
failure.
WHEN DOLLARS AREN’T DOLLARS
When the Americans compute how much of the war
debts, including principal and interest, we have already
forgiven, we forget one thing: the shifting value of the
dollar. True enough compared with the lira, the franc
or even the pound, the dollar has been a rock of steadiness.
But as Prof. Irving Fisher has recently reminded us the
dollars the allies borrowed from us during the war were
worth from 51 to 53 per cent of the 1913 dollar. Today
the dollars which they are to pay back are w r orth about 67
per cent of the 1913 dollar in purchasing power. This is
surely a factor which we should take into account wdth
regard to foreign indebtedness.
It is just as surely a factor of which we should take
account as regards domestic debts. It would be difficult
to imagine the woe that arises alike from inflation and de
flation of the instable dollar. (As£ the farmers; they
know!) Nominally the value of the dollar is based on
gold which itself fluctuates in value for all sorts of rea
sons. It is as if we tried to measure distance with a fluc
tuating yard stick.
All this is unnecessary. It is scientifically possible
to have a dollar constant in value which value is deter
mined by the index numbers of a group of standard com
modities instead of by the value of gold or the process of
expanding or contracting bank credits. Few reforms
within the present system would do as much good as a
genuinely stable currency. But neither bankers nor poli
ticians have the energy or perhaps the desire to propose
so elemental a reform. And as yet neither the farmers
nor industrial workers have vigorously demanded it.—

A Garage Without Doors
A. NOVEL idea for a garage owes its con
ception to Hugh S. Grigsby, of Rich-
mond, Va. One odd thing about it is that
it has no door. How, then, does one put a car
into it, or take the machine out? Very simply.
By lifting one end.
The structure is of sheet metal, and, looked at
endwise, it has the shape of an arch, or, more
descriptively, an inverted U. Seen from one side,
its outline is semicircular.
It is made in two sections, the ends of which
are angle-iron frames, and the sections telescope.
Call one section A and the other B. The end
frames of both rest on the ground. When A
is lifted it pasfees back and over B, like a hood.
If B be raised, it passes beneath A.
Thus an entire half can be swung up by lever
handles to open the building at either end, or
drawn downward to close the building after the
car has been run inside.
The TOP That Represents a DANCER
A “GYROSCOPIC TOY,” newly invented by
William C. Clausen, of New York City, is
in effect a top so contrived as to represent
a dancer pirouetting on one toe. Fixed beneath
the bust of the figure is a circular metal plate.
The toe upon which it twirls is set in the tip of
a shoe that holds a little ball which acts in the
manner of a castor. Between the shoe-tip and
the centre of the aforementioned plate extends
vertically a slender rod which, pivoted at both
ends, freely revolves.
Rigidly secured to this rod, one-third of the
distance from its upper end, is the hub of a
horizontally-set wheel, beneath which, and like
wise secured to the rod, is a spool wound with a
cord.
A skeleton frame of outwardly-extending
wires surrounds the wheel, affording means of
attachment for a ring that guards the rim of the
latter. The wires are connected above to the
aforementioned plate, and, at their lower ends, to
another plate beneath the spool.
Through the centre of this second plate is a
hole, so that the vertical rod can revolve freely.
The cord, wound on the spool, extends outwardly
through an opening, and, when it is quickly
pulled, it causes the wheel to revolve with great
rapidity. The revolution of the wheel, which has
a rim of lead, keeps the figure of the dancer
erect while it twirls on its toe, in obedience to
the principle of the gyroscope.
As it does so, the other leg, which is attached
by a pivot, swings outward in a realistic manner.
The skeleton frame of wires being covered and
concealed by a short skirt, the figure dances like
a veritable coryphee of the ballet.

This can be done in a moment, and the de
signer can then apply, in colors or otherwise,
the design he has in mind.' The pad is not neces
sary, for the celluloid card may be carried in a

From the dragons-and-frogs seismoscope of
the ancient Chinese inventor science leaps over
the centuries to the present to what is perhaps
the most sensitive instrument yet devised for
measuring infinitesimal distances, Prof. Whid
dington’s vacuum tube ultra-micrometer. This
instrument, with which a distance of five-bil
lionths of an inch actually has been measured,
according to J. E. Anderson, M. A., in Radio
News, consists of two very high frequency os
cillators which are loosely coupled to each other
and adjusted so that there is an audible beat
between the frequencies of the two. The oscil
lators are carefully shielded from all outside dis
turbances which might affect the frequencies;
and they are also shielded from each other ex
cept for the intentional coupling necessary to
produce the beats. Their construction and de
sign are such that the frequencies remain as con
stant as possible with changes in operating con
ditions.
The vacuum tube seismometer might prof
itably be employed in warfare for determining
the location of big guns. When heavy guns are
fired they start an earth wave similar to seismic
disturbance, and this wave may be detected and
measured by means of the vacuum tube seismo
meter at a considerable distance away. Two such
seismometers would be required definitely to lo
cate a gun. Each instrument would determine
the line connecting it with the gun, and the
intersection of these lines would be the location
of the gun.

after several successful seasons

produced by fashionable dressmak
ing houses and circulated among an

ALIVE—AFTER CENTURIES
Centuries ago, a man named Samuel Pepys held an
English government position in the admiralty. Around him
were kings and princes and titled members of nobility, proud
of themselves, and living lives of fashion. Samuel Pepys
saw them all, though it is probable that they did not see
him so often, and each night, year after year, went home
and wrote in his diary of all the things that had happened.
No matter how hard he had worked that day, no matter
how many pleasures were before him, he always wrote in
his diary before going to bed.
Today, most of the princes and noblemen of that time
are forgotten. And the Diary of Samuel Pepys remains
one of the foremost books of literature—a book that you
will comment on, probably, when you are an upperclassman
in college.
This is a good example of what modesty and determina
tion will do—an example of how it lives through the centuries.
Whether it is writing a diary or doing your work—stick
to it—follow the thing through to the end.

HEAR DEBATE
IN REFERENDUM
ON BEER TODAY
MADISON, Wis.—Whether or not
voters of this state may express
their longing for beer on the ballot
at the general election in November
is scheduled for argument in the
Wisconsin supreme court late today.
During the 1925 session of the
Wisconsin legislature and in its clos
ing days, a resolution introduced by
Senator Walter Polakowski, Mil
waukee, Socialist candidate for re
election, was passed as follows:
“Resolved by the senate, the as
sembly concurring, that there be
submitted to the voters of the state
of Wisconsin at the general election
to be held in this state in November,
1926, the following question, so as
to determine if a maority of the
people of the state of Wisconsin de
sire the Volstead act amended:
Question for Voters.
‘Shall the congress of the United
States amend the Volstead act so as
to authorize the manufacture and
sale of beer, for beverage purposes,
of an alcoholic percentage of 2.75
per cent by weight,under government
supervision but with the provision
that no beverage so purchased shall
be drunk on the premises where ob
tained?’
Later another joint resolution was
passed instructing the secretary of
state to place this question on the
official referendum ballot to be used
in the November general election.
Fulton Signs Complaint.
S. A. Fulton of West Allis, repre
senting the Anti-Sloon league,
brought action to restrain the sec
retary of state, the state treasurer
and members of the state printing
board from taking the necessary
steps to include this question on the
ballot. Walter H. Bender, Milwau
kee attorney, will appear for the op
ponents of the beer referendum,
while members of the attorney gen
eral’s office will present the de
fendants’ arguments.
The plaintiff, in his brief filed
with the court, alleges that the sub
mission of the question is illegal be
cause it is brought about by means
of two joint resolutions and not in
the customary form of a bill passed
by both houses and signed by the
governor. He further contended
that this submission involved an il
legal expenditure of state funds.
Claims Are Denied.
Answering in their brief, the de
fendants denied that the submission
of the question to the people or the
expenditure of state funds therefor
(which in any event, they said,
would not exceed sls) was unau
thorized.

water remained steady at the 22.1
foot mark today, after a rise of less
than two inches in 24 hours ending
Friday night.
While the levees protecting the
city and adjacent land are holding,
workmen are on guard against
breaks and tons of sand are being
heaped on the water walls to pre
vent their crumbling.

mains flooded. About 65 homes are

is not expected to reach other city
districts.

would do considerable damage, riv
er men say. At some points the
water has reached a point within
less than two inches of levee tops.

sure against, the levees, would create

storms come before the river re
cedes. however. Beardstown will not
experience a recurrence of the flood
of 1922. when the river went, to a
record high mark of 25.1 feet.

incorporation was instigated by pro
moters of the annexation program of

poena was withdrawn and the name

amended complaint.

built upholstery shop, now at 710
3rd Ave., the only shop in Wiscon
sin using the union label on its
product.

office in 1920 as a member of the
assembly, representing the eighth
assembly district.

stitutions.

tee. and is a member of the Mil
waukee Fourth of July commission,

WAR VETS THUNDER GREETING
TO ORPHEUM ENTERTAINERS
Almost a decade ago, the flower
of American manhood went over to
France to “face the music”—the
music of screeching shells, murmur
ing machine guns and the piteous
moans of the wounded.
Some of them came back two
years later to face more “music” of
broken lives, shattered bodies end
the monotonous song of despair.
And last night, in the theater of
the National Soldiers’ Home Tu
berculosis hospital, these victims of
war’s mockery faced the music
again—this time eagerly and with
smiles of anticipation.
And they took an augmented
barrage from five Palace Orpheum
theater acts with no more serious
casualties than, perhaps, sore palms
from excessive applause and aching
sides from unaccustomed laughter.
They began to file into the
theater around 5 p. m.—anxious for
their weekly vaudeville treat, made
possible through the courtesy of the
visiting players and James A. Hig
ler, manager of the Palace theater.
Bath Robes Prevail.
They entered in silent disorder,
as though they knew what was
coming and would conserve their
smiles and jokes.
And they came, too, in all stages
of comfortable disarray. Here and
there a bathrobe-swathed figure slid
into a seat along side of a precise
ly garbed pal; the swish, swish of
bedroom slippers on a bare floor
could be heard in the wake of some
hard-heeled shoes.
Eyes that had lost their sparkle
glowed again in happiness.
As-, to the show itself —who can
tell who enjoyed it the more, the
actors or the audience? The writer,
seated in a balcony which ran along
one side of the theater, seldom has
heard, in the Palace theater, the ter
rific applause that carried the
thanks of the audience to each retir
ing act.
Actors Work Hard.
Their numbers were not many,
but their hearts were full of thanks

filtered sludge under all conditions.

commission for a contract to put
them in working order at an approx
imate cost of $72,000.

U. S. Protests as French Force Yanks in Army
MILITARY FAILS
TO RECOGNIZE
CITIZEN RIGHTS
Confusing French
Laws Cause of
Trouble.
CHICAGO —The practice of the
French military officials in order
ing American citizens of French
birth or extraction into the army
as soon as they set foot in the coun
try of their ancestors is causing
considerable worry to the American
authorities, according to a copy
righted Paris story in The Tribune,
A dozen new cases recently have
been brought to the attention of
Washington and seven firm protests
have been filed with the French for
eign office.
Under the confusing provisions of
French law, no Frenchman is per
mitted to become a citizen of am
other country without the consent
of the French government. This
consent is never forthcoming, with
the result that France claims as her
own nationals bona fide citizens of
the United States and other nations
as far removed from their ancestral
country as the second generation.
When these Americans come to
France to visit relatives they are
stunned to find themselves under
arrest within a short time after ar
rival.
An extraordinary example of this
situation has just developed. Robert
de Bonneville of New Orleans, born
in the United States of an Ameri-i
can father. The latter’s father went]
to America as a young man and re
mained until his death. De Boune
ville recently decided to visit the
native country of his grandfather,
but upon his arrival at Havre was
arrested and placed in the Bth regi
ment of French zouaves, on the
theory that he still was a French
man and had not done his military
service.
Obtaining leave he hurried to
Havre and placed his case before
the American consulate. The pro
test now has been filed with the
French government.
Louis Levy, born in New York
city in March, 1882, of a French
father, served honorably in the
United States army, but was seized
for military service as soon as he
arrived in France to visit relatives.
Is Called Deserter.
Alfred Cornette, born in Italy, be
came a naturalized American citizen
In 1919. After seven years’ resi
dence he returned to France to visit
his mother and remained here to go
into business. He was seized and
is now serving in the 95th Infantry.
Emile Mionx of Illinois, a natur
alized American citizen, returned to j
France this* year to visit relatives.
After spending several weeks, he
returned to Havre to sail on the
Savoie, but was arrested as a de
serter from the French army.

of shoes was introduced into Massa
chusetts as far back as 1629, when
one Thomas Beard brought over

INDUSTRIAL
ORGANIZATION
PLAN REVISED
Leader Special Service.
MANCHESTER—The Manchester
Guardian reports that its managers
have undertaken a new experiment
in industrial organization, by which
they hope to secure more harmoni
ous relations between employers
and employes.
Proceeding from the conclusion
that industrial war does not pay the
victor any better than international
war, the managers of this Liberal,
daily have tried a new ways to
put the relations of capital and la
bor on a more equitable footing.
The basis of the new policy is the
transformation of all craft unions
in The Guardian plant into one in
dustrial union.
Make Joint Agreement.
The relations between this indus
trial union and the company are de
termined by a joint agreement,
which The Guardian prints in full.
Its most significant points are
compulsory arbitration of all differ
ences, and the complete elimination
of the strike as a means of settle
ment. Trade union standards are
guaranteed as a minimum. There
are also pensions and other benefits.
The scheme ns a whole is intended
to give employes an equal share
with the management in the con
trol over matters which directly af
fect them.
This aims to enable them to take
a far greater share than heretofore
in the efficient organization of the
whole concern. It Is hoped in this
way to enlist the active interest and
pride of the employes in the suc
cess of the venture.
Had Various Motives.
The managers avow a variety of
motives for this step. One is the
desire to keep the press active as an
essential part of democratic govern
ment in times of social crises.
Another reason is to keep the way
open for social progress. For the
time being the current trade union
standards are to be the basis of
arbitration. But the idea of the
plan is to be expanded in proportion
as experience proves that more ade
quate and far-reaching methods of
social progress are possible.
The present methods of industrial
bargaining have grown up during a
century and cannot be considered
the last word. They are not satis
factory. They are permeated with
the assumption of inevitable con
flict. They offer too little room for
co-operation.
The managers of The Guardian
expect that the trade union con
gress may not like the new plan,
but thinks that it suits its own em
ployes and will justify itself in its
working.
Estate of Half
Million Left to
Trusted Employe
OMAHA, Neb.—A. H. Warren, a
trusted employe of the McCord-
Brady wholesale grocery, yesterday
came a step nearer to a .$500,000 es
tate upon the death of Mrs. McCord,
widow of W. P. McCord, founder
of the firm, who died two months
ago.
When Mr. McCord, a financial and
political loader, died he left his en
tire estate to Warren, with orders
that during the lifetime of his wife
and only son, James, the interest
derived should go to them, but upon
their death Warren was to get the
principal and use it as he saw fit.
Warren had been a trusted em
ploye for 42 years, and the will
noted that a “son could not have
been more loyal—to him I owe most
of my success."
Warren has been made president
of the firm and has given young
McCord, the son, an official position
In the business.

SPAIN SWEPT
BY WAVE OF
LOVE CRIMES
MADRID A wave of “love
crimes” is passing over Spain.
For the last three or four months,
nearly every day, has added to the
list of victims the names of young
girls who were either killed or in
jured by their “novio,” or lover.
Made Shots Tell.
The latest of these “tragedias de
amor” which resulted in the death
of two lovers, took place in Ginzo,
Galicia. Rafael Boente was engaged
to pretty Consuelo Barciela, whose
father lived in Cuba. Consuelo’s
mother was not opposed to the mar
riage of the couple, but demanded
they wait until the father had re
turned from America. Rafael would
not listen.
The day he learned there was no
chance of getting married immedi
ately he shot his “novia” on the
doorstep of her mother’s home. Con
suelo was only wounded, but having
closed the door could not go back.
She ran to a neighbor’s house. Ra
fael pursued and shot her again, this
time fatally. Whereupon, he shot
himself and fell dead on the body of
his sweetheart.
Stabbed in Baek.
Grado, in Asturias, was the scene
of another typical crime. Amalia
Queipo refused to fox-trot with Joee
Molina and was stabbed In the back
in the midst of a dance.
A few days before, a similar
drama had taken place in Almeria,
where the ex-“novio” of a senorita
belonging to a prominent family as
sassinated her in the Casino Munic
ipal.
In most cases, it Is the man who
murders the woman, but in several
instances the woman acted first,
with the same fatal results. Span
ish love is still as dangerous as ever
and Carmen’s “Beware!” remains
unchanged.

FINDS DA VINCI

BERLIN —Discovering that Leon
ardo Da Vinci was the world’s
greatest southpaw painter, and
using this clew on all the canvases
attributed to him, Maurice 11. Gold-
blatt, the Chicago art expert, has ob
tained the evidence for his expose,
which, he says, will startle the art
world when he addresses experts In
Paris in October.
Mr. Goldblatt, whose findings al
ready have been accepted by the
Louvre and Berlin galleries, expects
to announce the forgotten name of
the great artist whose work was dis
covered in 37 paintings accredited to
Da Vinci and other masters.
Mr. Goldblatt made the discovery
of the lefthandedness of Da Vinci
in Chicago. Two years spent in Eu
ropean public and private galleries
have substantiated his belief. Prac
tically all of Da Vinci’s undoubted
drawings show lines from the right
to the left, whereas many with the
lines from the left to the right are
the works of other persons.

CITIZENSHIP
CLASSES WILL
BEGIN MONDAY
English and citizenship classes for
new Americans begin Monday, with
daytime classes, and Tuesday for
night classes.
These classes are all free. In
them the foreigner can not only
learn how to speak, read and write
English, but can prepare for second
citizenship papers. Application
blanks for citizenship papers can be
obtained in the class rooms.
30 Buildings in Use.
Night school classes in academic
and commercial subjects, craft
work, athletics and music begin
Tuesday. More than 30 school build
ings and social centers will be in
use this winter.
Information concerning night and
citizenship schools can be found on
telephone posts in almost every
block. Miss Dorothy Enderis. depart
ment of extention, Milwaukee pub
lic schools, stated today.
In addition to posters and pla
cards generously distributed
throughout districts of the city com
posed chiefly of foreigners, the alert
foreigner who wishes to attend night
school can find literature regarding
night school activities at the public
library and at all social centers,
Miss Enderis said.
Special Delivery
To Britain, North
Ireland Now O K
Letters and other mail matter,
with the exception of parcel post,
can hereafter be sent special deliv
ery to Great Britain and northern
Ireland, upon the prepayment in
stamps of 20 cents i» addition to
the regular postage, according to
advices received from Washington
today.
This follows closely an announce
ment that a similar arrangement
had been made with Germany and
the Irish Free State.
It is explained that either spe
cial delivery or ordinary postage
stamps may be used for this pur
pose, but in the space underneath
the stamps and above the address
the word “express” must be stamped
in red ink.

THE WEEKLY BOOK CORNER
A BOOK WORTH READING.
Matter, Man and Mind. By W. F.
F. Shearcroft. Published by The
Macmillan Co., New York.
We thoroughly enjoyed this clear
ly and simply written summary of
scientific progress. We recommend
it as a rare treat to all who want
a satisfying general statement of
the modern views on geology, phys
ics, the atom, radio research, psy
chology, aviation, evolution, relativ
ity and kindred subjects.
The author is a moster of popular
style. He makes complicated prob
lems easy. He has a gitt of getting
with a few words to the kernel of
a problem. He is eminently fair to
all, scientists as well as their op
ponents. He does not waste any
time on mystic nonsense.
If we may venture a criticism, it
is that we would have liked to see
a few paragraphs in the chapter on
The Mind of Man covering the posi
tive outcome of philosophical re
search. Philosophy has become a
natural science quite as reliable »s
psychology. A few words to this
effect would have completed and
rounded out what the author has to
say about behaviorism.
We realize, however, that official
philosopny has not much to tell a
man like Sbearcroft, and he prob
ably had no opportunity to become
aeqainted with such writings out
side our official circle as those of
Josef Dietzgen. which offer a reli
able method of logical research to
all sciences, by which they can test
the correctness of their results as
truly as a chemist can test his ex
periments.
The conscious will, the uncon
scious instinct, the logical move
ments of the human brain, in short,
the whole sensory and thinking ap
paratus of man, with its laws of
development, are all discussed in
this book with a simple mastery
which shows deep study and mature
judgment.

the others devoted each to a spe
cific character of the clique who
for a period consumed his atten
tion.
A flagrant Roman youth of 16,
a wayward and Impulsive Roman
princess, a fascinating cardinal and
other figures of Roman life make
these divisions interesting in the
extreme.

as any other part chosen at random,
is indicative of Mr. Wilder’s style.

A History of the United States
Since the Civil War. Vol. 111. By
Ellis Pazson Oberholtzer. Pub
lished by the Macmillan Co., New

Part 111 of this history by Mr.
Oberholtzer covers the years from
1872 to 1878. It begins with Hor
ace Greeley's futile campaign to win
the presidency and ends up with
the time of the Hayes administra
tion.
The author does not conceal the
corruption which had grown up un
der the Grant administration, but
he says little about the fundamen
tal problems which impelled Gree
ley and his Labor friends to take
up the fight for a capture of the
national government.
He devotes most of his work to a
discussion of the political phases of
life in the United States, especially
the influence of carpetbag govern
ment on the political fortunes of
the Republican party in the south
ern states.
Those who are interested in the
different angles of the four-cornered
fight for the presidency and the
political method which brought
about Greeley’s defeat will find
plenty of authentic data here.
The financial panic and “the
crime of ’73” are again treated
mainly from this political angle. To
get the popular viewpoint in addi
tion to the official one, one must
read the Populist literature of that
day, which Oberholtzer neglects,
w’lth the exception of a few Grange
statements.
Oberholtzer is right enough in
stating that the farmers of that
day “uttered a great amount of bal
derdash,” but he could have found
quite as much balderdash in the
literature of the bankers and old
party statesmen.
This bias often shows itself in
Oberholtzer's work. It crops up
every now and then in his discus
sion of the Indian wars. Although
he strives to be fair and states the
position of the Indian’s friends
fully enough, he cannot quite con
ceal his animosity against those
who take the red man’s part against
the whites.

er edition of the revised and en
larged edition. Edited by Harriet
Monroe and Alice Corbin Hender
son. Published by The Macmil
lan Co., New York. $2.50.
To anyone at all interested ir
the ownership of books of verse
this volume cannot but appeal. To
those whose library space or whose
pocketbook is limited, it has the ad
ditional allure of being both com
pact and inexpensive.
There is always a certain intan
gible but very real satisfaction
from a discriminating selection of
verse, whether it be of one author
or of one age, between the covers
of one book and here again the
newly published anthology of 20tb
century verse in English meets
every desire. Its purpose has been
fully accomplished and in addition
to what the original volume con
tained, its pages contain the best
both of English and American verse
of the last five years.
Harriet Monroe's editorship of
Poetry: A Magazine of Verse, the
most authoritative organ of the art,
has kept her in touch with the poets
both of this country and England.

of selection from books and i»eri
odicals by Alice Corbin Henderson,
co-editor of the volume.
The table of contents reveals two
ways in which this volume Improves
upon its predecessor. Prominent
poets are represented more gener
ously than in the former one, and
important new names have been
added.
In this addition, considerable
space has been given to Maxwell
Bodcnheim, Hilda Conkling, Ade
laide Crapsey, H. D„ Arthur Davi
son Ficke, John Gould Fletcher,
Agnes Lee, Wallace Stevens. Allen
Upward and William Carlos Wil
liams. There is at toe same time,

son Gibson, Vachel Lindsay, Amy

St. Vincent Millay, Ezra Found. Ed
win Arlington Robinson. Carl Sand
burg, Sara Teasdale, William Butler
Yeats.

ed in this very representative list,

ested in the fact that one poem by

of English at the University of Wis
consin and recognized scholar in
comparative philology, is included in
this collection. It is Indian Sum
mer, and although others might
wish that several additional things

and powerful.

a discriminating but very satisfao.
tory addition to any library of col
lected verse.

BY JOSEPH WASNEY.
WASHINGTON—The administra
tion has decided to draft further
civil power for its war against
liquor, it was learned authoritative
ly today.
A supreme effort is to be made
this fail and winter to make the
country bone dry. Assistant Sec
retary of the Treasury Andrews,
dry czar, will outline the new pol
icies to his administrators when
they meet here Monday. The dry
czar is now planning to stay in of
fice at least until Christmas to di
rect the new offensive against rum
trusts.
Prohibition Is Wanted.
Meantime reports from President
Coolidge's summer retreat indicate,
the government increasingly be
lieves, prohibtion is the choice of
the majority of the people.
The president is expected to call
on government departments to aid
the treasury in carrying out the
provisions of the Volstead act. The
commerce department will be re
quested to enlist the services of the
steamboat inspectors and lighthouse
keepers in giving information on
rum smugglers.
The postoffice department will be
asked to have letter carriers, rural
carriers and other employes report
location of stills and wildcat brew
eries. The labor department will
he urged to use its border immigra
tion inspectors to reinforce the pro
hibition patrols.
To Use Field Force.
The department of agriculture
probably will use its field force to
report moonshine plants. Atty. Gen.
Sargent will probably be requested
to have bis department co-operate
more closely with the treasury in
securing prosecutions.
President Coolidge may even re
quest cabinet officers to designate
special officials to co-operate with
Andrews In the dry drive.

FRANCO-GERMAN
PEACE MOVES
CHICAGO —The basis for an ac
tual entente between the Paris and
Berlin governments was agreed on
yesterday by Foreign Minister Aris
tide Briand of France and Foreign
Minister Stresemann of Germany,
who motored to Thoiry, just over
the French border, and lunched to
gether, says a copyrighted dispatch
from Geneva to The Tribune. They
then conferred for more than four
hours on all the problems outstand
ing between the two countries.
Reach Full Accord.
“We have reached a complete ac
cord to consider all outstanding
problems between the two countries
in ensemble instead of dealing with
them separately and in detail.” said
M. Briand. “I am very much con
tent. If our governments act favor
ably on the bases of agreement we
reached yesterday we will continue
our collaboration. From our meet
ing may come a consolidation of
peace even more grand than the
accords signed at Locarno.”
Herr Stresemann declared: “This
means a new European understand
ing. We went over everything and
discussed all our differences. If
slight differences come up. the spirit
shown yesterday proves they surely
will be overcome.”
A subcommittee of 14 members of
the league of nations council has
been summoned to meet late today
to receive the report from the
judicial committee on the reply to
the United States covering the sen
ate reservations for adhering to the
world court. It is believed the coun
cil will oppose the report, which
accepts the American conditions and
gives the United States the same
privileges enjoyed by members of
the league council.
BERLIN Reliable diplomatic
sources late last, night received a re
port that, the German delegation at
Geneva had achieved a great vic
tory, settling Germany’s problems in
the immediate future, as a result of
Foreign Minister Stresemann’s meet
ing with Foreign Minister Briand.
According to the report, the allies
have given Germany the following
concessions:
1. Complete evacuation of the
Rhineland, to begin immediately.
2. Return of the Saar valley to
Germany, without a plebiscite, with
in 15 years, as written in Woodrow
Wilson’s treaty.
3. Return of Eupen and Malmedy,
which Belgium holds.
4. End of the military control in
Germany.
5. Lifting of investigations and
control by the lea cue of nations of
Germany’s military forces.

FREE SPENDERS
CHICAGO —History is repeating
itself and in France today, as was
the case a few years ago in Ger
many, the people are on a spending
spree, brought on by the inflation
and a consequent lack of confidence
in their currency, according to
Claire Mendel of the staff of the
Paris edition of The Tribune, in a
special article published today. An
acute consciousness that their
safety, as individuals, depends upon
their ability to convert their money
into goods, chattels and real estate
is one of the underlying reasons for
this situation.
Are Free Spenders.
Another is a protective measure
taken by the government, which pro
hibits the exportation of more than
1,000 francs from the country in one
transaction.
Larger and more modern hotels,
innumerable co-operative apartment
buildings, elaborate suburban de
velopments and a congestion of
automobiles in the larger cities that
would rival that of New York, bear
witness to the tendency of present
day France to be a “free spender.”
Tight Only At Banks.
Automobile factories are going at
full blast, and so great has been the
demand that delivery on pleasure
cars of the more standard makes
cannot be had for six weeks or two
months. Large estates outside of the
more important centers of popula
tion have been subdivided and are
rapidly being disposed of to city
dwellers.
The oily place in France where
money seems to be at all tight is at
the banks, which demand 8 per cent
interest with collateral, and even
then appear not too anxious to make
loans.

HOMES, OFFICES
ARE PREDICTED
TOLEDO Folks in scores of
American cities of the future may
drive on underground roads, live in
underground homes and work in un
derground offices as a result of the
development of the science of venti
lation or electrical air control, ac
cording to W. S. Currier, head of
the United States weather bureau
in Toledo.
That will be one way of getting
away from the vagaries of bad
weather and solving the congestion
problem in big centers of popula
tion, Currier said. It would assure
a supply of clean air in these sub
terranean passages, which was more
than the cave-dwellers of several
thousand years ago had, he pointed
out.
Smacks of Impossible.
“Men juggle temperature and hu
midity around like so many balls
and create lake breezes by power
ful fan machinery,” Currier added,
“but I doubt that they can manu
facture weather for the great out
doors. Of course, wonders have
been accomplished within buildings,
but artifically created rain, man
produced sunshine or snow at com
mand is a challenge that is ridic
ulous.
“In Toledo and all over the mid
dle west, in spite of complaints
about the heat, the summer aver
age was slightly below normal. The
average temperature has been 71
and the normal is 71.1. June was
4 degrees below normal; July, .0-1
below and August 1.90 above.
An Ideal Heat.
“The moisture in the air or hu
midity drops as the day progresses
if the sun is shining. Of course,
the capacity of the aid to form
moisture goes up with the tempera
ture. And temperature takes up
more space in the air as it rises.
An ideal climate, other things being
equal, would be a temperature of
85 and moisture below 50. Air mo
tion plays a big part.
“Moisture is good for vegetation
but not so good for animal life. The
lake regions, naturally, have more
moisture in the air than other sec
tions of the country. Moisture
brings about the sticky feeling.

Currier had a good laugh over

changing or moving around.
Remains the Same.
“Not within the life of any man

NEW GALSWORTHY PLAY OF HUMAN
SYMPATHY IS LONDON SUCCESS
LONDON—John Galsworthy, has
scored a success with Escape, the
first production of the new season.
Escape commences when the hero
punches a policeman in Hyde park
on behalf of a wronged young lady.
The policeman’s head strikes an
iron railing, he dies, and the hero
gets seven years for manslaughter.
He breaks jail, and Galsworthy
shows eight episodes in which the
hunted fugitive appeals for help and
never in vain. A lady who iinds
him under her bed bundles him off
with her husband’s razor, overcoat
and fishing rod; a magistrate recog
nizes him while he pretends to fish,
and lets him go. There are two old
maids into whose house he breaks;
one would give him up, the other
conceal him. At the end a clergy
man is about to lie to a police of
ficer, who asks the man of God
whether he has seen the fugitive.
This is too much for our hero. Rath
er than see a clergyman lie he will
go back to Dartmoor and serve out
his term.
The dramatist succeeds in show
ing the natural human instinct that
leads every individual as an individ
ual to sympathize with the runaway,
when brought up against him per
sonally, even while the man hunt
Is at fever heat.
Nicholas Hannen, as the man who
escapes, gives a splendid perform
ance. The play has aroused contro-1
Owen Davis Beats
Lope De Vega
Owen Davig is the Lope de Vega
of the contemporary d’ama. Lepe

The Idiot Staged.
A dramatic version of Dostoev
sky’s The Idiot is being shown at
Barnes.
“To set The Idiot on the stage—
how impossible a task, and yet, in
spite of inevitable failures and
omissions, how fascinating to at
tempt I” writes A. B. Walkley in
his review of the production. “The
task is impossible for a dozen rea
sons, of which the plainest is that
a picture on a vast canvas cannot
lend its effect to a copy in minia
ture. Prince Mulshkin is shown by
Dostoevsky as a man without guile
moving through a crowded and tor
mented world, as one of extraordi
nary gentleness and strength cast
amid wrath and violence, weakness
and degradation. The examples of
worldly terror that have been
chosen are. in the novel, violent as
flashes of lightning, but, like light
ning, they take their proportion
from the storm. On the stage this i
same lightning, separated from its
gigantic background, flashes in
melodrama. So it must be, however
skilful the adaptation. The Impres
sion of the novel is of a formless
ness that is the formlessness of hu
manity; the impression that the con
ditions of the theater make in
evitable is of a vain struggle for an
alien form.”
The play was well acted by a
group of young people, including
lon Swinley, Beatrix Thompson,
Stella Arbenina and Lawrence An
derson.

JEANNE EAGELS HAD OWN WAY
WITH ‘RED LIGHT SADIE' IN RAIN
Why has Rain, the John Colton
play in which Jeane Eagels comes
to the Davidson Monday night, at
tained that intangible thing known
as success?
Mr. Coltan denies that he is capa
ble of answering the question, ex
cept that he feels Jeane Eagels is
largely responsible.
Several years ago, when Colton
was in Hollywood, Maughan showed
him proofs of some short stories,
including one called Miss Thomp
son. Struck by its play possibili
ties he obtained Maughan’s permis
sion to dramatize the story when
the author declared that he couldn’t
see a play there.
But New York producers were
afraid of Rain. It was a de
parture and the box office could not
be overlooked. One day Jeanne
Eagels, under contract to Harris,
unearthed the manuscript from a
pile on the producer’s desk.
She read the play and announced
that Rain was to be her next ve
hicle. When lady stars make up
their minds, especially lovely, de
termined ones like Miss Eagels, pro
ducers usualy succumb. So Rain
was put on, after the usual hectic
period, according to Colton when
author and star were pited against
those determined to change every
thing—even the title.
“They wanted to call It Red 1
Light Sadie,” declared Colton.
“When I heard that I went out and
got drunk for three days. Who
wouldn’t?”
“And they wanted to put in a
bedroom scene. But Miss Eagels
believed In the play as it was writ
ten, and wouldn’t permit any
changes.”
Though based on Miss Thomp
son. Rain’s leading character was
considerably rejuvenated for the
stage. Instead of a cross, almost
middle-aged woman, she became a
beautiful young girl—hard, but
with the inescapable appeal of'
youth.
“Berlin or Russia might have
stood for Sadie as Maughan wrote
of her —but not the United States,”
concluded Colton.

Modern Dress for Opera.
From London comes the report
that The Mikado is going to be done
there in modern dress. The idea, if
carried to an extremity, is liable to
damage seriously the voices of our
opera singers. Where would the
average singer be without the fancy
dress costumes?
The effect of costume on voice in
opera cannot be overlooked. It la
difficult to imagine the characters
of operas like Aida, Butterfly, Car
men or Tristan appearing in street
clothes. A singer is helped in the
illusion of the plot if the details are
complete, and dress is part of that
detail. Love, for example, can be

QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS,
Diabetes.
I am coming to you to settle an
argument concerning the sugar dia
betes. Is It caused by eating too much
sugar or starch or by the lack or
failure of some organ of the body?
Can it be cured if caught early
enough? (F. W. H.)
Answer —It Is caused by both fac
tors—eating too much, particularly
starches and sugars—and the failure
or breakdown of the little glands or
groups of specialized cells in the pan
creas (abdominal sweetbread), which
produce the internal secretion called
insulin. Insulin controls the utilization
of starches and sugars in the body.
Probably the popular custom of lunch
ing and dining and nibbling as a
social pastime tends to exhaust and
destroy the insulin secreting glands.
Let’s call it just diabetes. If recog
nized early diabetes rnay be controlled
In all cases and cured In many cases.
Every sedentary prosperous adult who
begins to grow stout should look upon
himself as a potential diabetic. Henry
Ford, I believe, is one of the chief
factors of diabetes. Two mile of
oxygen on the hoof, three times a day,
la one of the greatest preventives.
Going to St. Ives.
A man lived with his brother sev
eral years while the biother had tuber
culosis. This man has since had three
wives, each wife of a different family,
and the three wives have died with
tuberculosis within the last 20 years,
likewise a daughter by one wife. The
man himself is apparently well and
healthy. Is it possible that he may
be a carrier of the disease without
himself having it? (A. B.)
Answer —It is possible, though I
know of no case in which such a
“carrier” has been scientifically de
tected. It would seem more likely
that the wives have lived in close
contact with some one Hl of the dis
ease. The man himse.lf may have tu
berculosis in spite of a healthy ap
pearance.

Her Old Lover, the Butler
BY RUBY DOUGLAS
The telephone on the tiny table
beside Mrs. Van "Warner's chaise
longue tinkled. It was the only
telephone in the house that
merely tinkled and its possessor
had spent much effort in having
the bell subdued. Problems such
as these were the most weighty
matters that fell upon the pretty
shoulders of the mistress of the
Holme Hillside.
“Yes?” she said putting her lips
to the glass transmitter. "Oh, yes,
Why—”
There was a long pause while
Clarice Van Warner evidently
listened to an amusing conversa
tion.
"But—of course. I couldn't re
fuse to let you have him—if you
really think it would be all right,
yess, indeed, I’ll have him there
at nine sharp. Goodby, dear.”
Clairce’s neighbor, if on living
two miles distant on the next es
tate may be called a neighbor,
Helen Simpson, had made a most
unusual req u e s t—if Clairice
would lend Hawkins, the new
English butler at Holme Hillside,
to her for one evening.
“You see, my dear, 1 have a
guest for the week-end—a girl
from London, who is perfectly
mad about bridge, and Tom and
I are just ordinary players. The
k snow has cut us off so thorough
ly from communication with the
rest of our friends that I was
wondering if it couldn’t be done
with safety. Nellie is sailing
home next week. We have four
others in the house for another
table and the happy idea came
to me to ask you for Hawkins.
He’s really quite a gentleman. I
know he plaws the game because
I have seen him watch us over at
your house as we played when he
was getting a bite of supper ready
for us.”
Hawkins did not intimate by
the flutter of an eyelash whether
the idea would be distasteful or
agreeable to him. He merely
dressed himself with great care
and departed in time to be ready
for cards at nine o’clock.
At the Simpson's he was
greeted as a friend and acted
his part admirably. The tables
were ready and he was presented
to his partner, Miss Hutchinson.
No one noticed the several
shades of palor that chased
each other across the faced of the
little English guest. Neither did
they observe the effort with
which James Hawkins held him
self together when he beheld his
partner.
The game progressed and both
of the young persons had resumed
a calm that seemed almost na
tural. Both played a good game
of cards and the hostess thought
she had made a great success of
her daring venture.
When the game was over there
was to be the usual bite to eat,
served on the card tables by the
fireside.
Hawkins rose and spoke to his
hostess, “I am taking a train to
night. Mrs. Simpson—perhaps my
hostess told you?”
“Oh—l’m sorry—but if you
must go—trains are most uncer
tain in this weather and driving
is treacherous.” Helen was re
lieved and yet she was a little
sorry to have the fellow depart.
He had proved himself so good a
partner. What tommy-rot caste
lines were, she thought.
Nellie Hutchinson was torn be
tween a hopelessness at having
lost again the man whom she had
loved for years and who had gone
out to America from their home
in England to “make good” be
fore claiming her hand —and re
lief at the strain she had been
under to keep her knowledge of
him a secret from those who
were about.
Seven of them sat about the fire
and chatted about the game, dis
cussing. among other features, the
charm and excellence in skill of
their new acquaintance, Mr.
Hawkins.
“He is a guest—or was—at the
Thorne home just down the lane.”
fibbed Helen glibly. “Quite a lik
able chap I thought.”
The telephone bell rang in the
hall. Helen herself answered it.
“My dear, It is for you.” she
said, surprised, and speaking to
Nellie. “An unknown lover —at
this hour!”

Nellie sought the telephone and
closed the small closet that en
closed it.
"Jim—” she uttered.
“Nellie—”
And then the butler of Holme
Hillside explained to her what
was taking place. He was inves
tigating the domestic service sit
uation in America for a series of
labor articles for an English mag
azine and he bad been finding out
at first hand just what were the
vexing problems. He had writ
ten to her but no reply had ever
reached him and his faith alone
was holding him close to the be
lief that she was still waiting for
him.
A few days afterwards Clarice
Van Warner called up her young
friend Helen to tell her that the
splendid butler was leaving.
"Whatever did you do to him that
night?” she asked.
“Nothing, my dear,” Helen re
plied, “but I am dying to talk to
you about something that seems
all very mysterious to me. A
’phone call late that night—Nel
lie’s sudden engagement in town
the next day and—now—Haw
kins leaving. I’ll be over.”
But by the time the two friends
had been able to get together, the
story had slipped out and the
romance was being discussed In
every group.
Nellie Hutchinson had married
her old lover, Hawkins, the but
ler, pro tem, of Holme Hillside.

skin and chill. Take out the inside
carefully and cut two slits on one
side of the tomato and then two
slits directly opposite; insert thin
slices of cucumber in the slits. The
tomatoes should be filled with well

Tomato Catsup.
Take three gallons of ripe toma
toes. scald and strain through mus
lin bag. To 10 pints juice add two
tablespoons salt, five of sugar and
two pints of vinegar. Put one pint
of chopped onions, three heads of
garlic in a muslin bag, boil all to
gether for 20 minutes. Just before
taking off fire, stir in one-half tea
spoon each of ground mace, all
spice, cinnamon and black pepper,
also one-quarter teaspoon of cay
enne pepper and one teaspoon dry
mustard. Take the bag of onion?
out, mix one tablespoon cornstarch
in one teacup of vinegar and stir in
gradually, boil two minutes. Bottle
hot and seal.

why I

MUSIC IN THE BLACK FOREST.
Here I am again at Baden-Baden
amid the shade of its woods and
gardens and where at this time of
the year, music is the topic of every
one every day. The orchestra Is on
duty 11 months out of every 12.
resting only in November. Its con
cert hall always seems to my un
forgetting mind one of the most
notable. Here Paganini brought
his violin, here Liszt played his own
work, here Caruso sang. Here Ber
lioz, Thomas, Anton Rubenstein
and Brahms have wielded the baton.
And who has been hece to see them?
Among the names of famous visitors
in the past 1 see Bismarck, Renan,
Victor Unco, Rossini, Clara Schu
mann, Offenbach and Turgeniev.
There is always music in the Black
Forest—dances, concerts, lectures
and operas and all the mental re
laxation that the beautiful sur
roundings encourage. In normal
years as many ns 80.000 visitors
will flock to the place, as if it werjs
true what Eugene Gulnot wrote la
1547, “There are two capitals of
rope: Paris and Baden-Baden.” i
Among the pupils of a certain
school in England Queen Mary an
nually gives a prize to the one who
is selected by the masters as having
best lived up to the motto, "Be go J
und do good.” This motto was
chosen by the queen herself.

BALTUSROL COUNTRY CLUB,
SHORT HILLS, N. J.—George Von
Elm, the Pacific coast star, was one
up on Bobby Jones today at the
•nd of the 18th hole in the final
round for the national amateur golf
championship.
Voa Elm, and the thus far un
beatable Bobby won their way into
the final round of the amateur
chanpionships yesterday, Jones
after a hard match with Francis
Ouimet, veteran of many a tourna
ment and Von Elm in decisive fash
ion over George Dawson of Chicago;
Third Meeting of Two.
This is the third meeting of Von
Elm and Jones. The first time they
met was two years ago at Merion.
Von Elm then was not match for
Jones, and he lost, 9 to 8.
This week the Californian, how
ever, has been playing golf which
many believed the best of his
career. Most of his matches he
won with greater ease than Jones
although perhaps his opponents
have not been as strong.
But today he has his chance, and
golfing immortality awaits him if
he can win the crown.
Weather Is Ideal.
It was a beautiful day. The sun
was out in all its mid-Scptember
glory and the green, rolling course
stretching beneath the Baltusrol
mountain was never in better con
dition.

ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—(United
Press) —Five days from now, when
Jack Dempsey enters the ring in
Philadelphia to defend his heavy
weight title against Gene Tunney,
the fans are likely to see some
quick action.
From the character of his train
ing and comment he has let fall, it
is believed Dempsey will go after
Tunney hard at the bell and do his
best in that round, or the early
rounds, to land one of his crushing
blows that few men can withstand.
It is certain that Dempsey will
not risk his title by letting Tunney
stay in the ring a second longer
than he can help, with every second
increasing the chance that the chal
lenger might laud one that would
put the champion in shape for a
beating.
Dempsey had tapcred down in his
training today and was taking
things easily. He planned a light
workout this afternoon.
Dempsey is confident and has told
his friends he is sure he can knock
Tunney out, the quicker the better.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa.—The tax

segregate the $600,000 purse of the
Dempsey-Tunney fight, today was
held over for a further hearing next
Tuesday by Judge Andenreid in
common pleas court.
The question of leasing radio
broadcasting privileges at the
Dempsey-Tunney fight in the Ses
qui-Centennial stadium still was un
settled last night.
It is understood that no impor
tant contracts can be made by Pro
moter Tex Rickard without the ap
proval of the Sesqui-Centennial
Assn., which will receive a percent
age of all receipts. It is also under
stood the exposition authorities are
under certain obligations to local
stations in radio matters.

that a plan was being considered
whereby there would be no broad
casting of the bout, but instead the
light news would be carried by tele
phone to halls and other places and
announced through amplifiers to
those who pay admission to these
places. This plan, it was said,
would need co-operation of tele
phone companies, who would be

NEW YORK—(United Press)
Eight straight victories in their re
maining games will give the St.
Louis Cardinals the pennant in the
National league, regardless of what
Cincinnati does.
The Cardinals took the lead in
the epic baseball struggle by crush
ing the helpless Phillies yesterday,
10 to 1, and now are a game In
front. The Cincinnati Reds, fight
ing gamely, were beaten in the 10th
inning by Frank Frisch, allotted bj
the New York Giants. With ths
score tied and two out. Frisch hit
a home run. It was a tough break
for the Reds and for Luque, who
had held the Giants to only two hits
in seven innings.
Edge With Cards.
The 5 to 4 victory of the Giant<
broke the tie between the Reds and
Cardinals for first place and put the
Rods in a poor tactical position.
They must meet the Giants again
today, while the Cardinals have two
games with the helpless Phila
delphians.
St. Louis can have no possible ex
cuse for not taking both games
If they do, and the Reds lose, th€
Cardinals will have a two and a
half game lead, with only seven
more games to play for the Reds
and six for the Cardinals.
Yanks’ Lead Cut.
Cincinnati is not a team to give
up without a struggle, however, and
they mean to go Into that final
game at Cincinnati a week from
tomorrow still with a chance for
the flag.
In the American league, the
Yankees are beginning to admit that
the thing looks serious. The Cleve
land Indians took their third
straight game from the leagtw
leaders and cut their load to three
and one-half games.

WASHINGTON Summarization
of the business situation for the
week by the department of com
merce, as reported today, shows im
provement in a number of direc
tions. The dollar volume of trade
as seen from -check payments cov
ering the second week of Septem
ber, continued to record increased
business over a year ago.
Distribution of merchandise, as
featured by carloadings, the first
week of the month was the largest
on record. Building contracts
awarded the first 10 days of the
month continued to show sustained
activities.
The production of bituminous coal
and behive coke the first week was
larger than in the corresponding pe
riod a year earlier, while the out
put of petroleum the second week
of the month, although averaging
lower than in the previous week,
was also higher than a year ago.
Wholesale prices advanced the
second week and were higher than
at any time in almost two months.
Compared with a year ago, however,
wholesale prices were 6 per cent
lower. Business failures reported
the second week, although smaller
than in the preceding week, were
more numerous than a year ago.

reflect accurately the condition of

Moto-Meter Co.
Purchases La Crosse
National Garage Co.
Sales of a controlling interest in
the National Gauge Equipment
Co., La Crosse, to the Moto-Meter
Co., New York, was announced yes
terday.
The National Gauge Equipment
Co. manufactures oil gauges,
ameters and other dashboard indi
cators for automobiles. The Moto-
Meter Co. is the largest producer of
heat indicators for motor cars in
the United States.
Steps are to be taken at once to
enlarge the capacity of the La Crosse
plant. It is proposed to bring the
working force up to 2,000 men. The
present pay roll lists 1,200 employes.
Although the consideration was
not disclosed, it is understood to ex
ceed $1,000,000.

PACKERS’ CASE
WASHINGTON—VaIidity of the
“Big Five” meat packers consent
decree, which was suspended by
order of the District of Columbia su
preme court last year as a result of
attacks by the California Co-oper
ative Canneries, is defended in a
brief filed by the department of jus
tice with the court of appeals of the
District of Columbia. Arguments in
the case are to take place on Oct. 4.

ing the validity of the original de
cree the appeal from the decision of
the district supreme court was filed
by Swift Co., and Armour Co.,
whose motion for the granting of
an order vacating the decree be
cause it was in excess of the court’s
jurisdiction, was denied.
Neither the government nor the
packers were satisfied with the
ruling of the lower court which was
made on the motion of the Cali
fornia Co-operative Canneries,
whose products were distributed by
Armour Co. before the consent de
cree forced the “Big Five" packers
to discontinue the handling of
groceries and other unrelated lines.

FINANCIAL SHEET
FACES CUURT
NEW YORK—Alleging that the
profits of the newspaper have been
dissipated gradually since 1921,
stockholders of The Journal of Com
merce and Commercial Bulletin of
New York made application in the
supreme court of this state for a
mandamus order directing the cor
poration to submit all of its books,
accounts and minutes for inspection
and examination. The application
will be argued Monday.
The corporation was incorporated
June 1, 1883, with an authorized
capital stock of the par value of
$700,000. The affidavit supporting
the petition charges that prior to
March Ralph R. Gevin owned a
majority of the stock of the cor
poration and was its president.
Gevin died last March, and his son,
Ralph R. Gevin, succeeded him as
president.
“From 1907 up to and including
1921,” the petition alleges, “divi
dends increased regularly year by
year, until a dividend of 140 per
cent was paid in the fiscal year of
1921. ending June 30 that year.
“Thereafter and coincidental with
the assumption of management of
the defendant corporation by the
Gevin interests after the latter part
of 1921, at which time Ralph R.
Gevin, deceased, was elected pres
ident and assumed control of the
corporation there commenced a
steady falling off of the dividends
declared, to-wit, 44 per cent in 1922,
40 per cent in 1923 and 20 per cent
iu 1924. In 1925, a dividend on the
common stock of only 4 per cent
was paid.”
