STARS OF DESTINY
Mussolini, after another lucky escape from a bomb,
brags of his star of destiny. He cannot draw any common
sense conclusion from his escape. Even the frequent at
tempts on his life offer him a chance to strut and brag.
A Darwinian law of correlation seems to decree that
such adventurers shall be more or less crack-brained. This
malady is called Caesarian spleen. It has the effect of en
couraging these madmen to pursue their headlong course
against reason and morality. But their mistakes get them
just the same.
Caesar could tell a fisherman to fear no storm, be
cause Caesar and his star were aboard, but that did not
stop Casca and Brutus. Napoleon went to Elba and St.
Helena in spite of his star and succumbed to his appetite
for fried onions.
Alexander of Macedonia, Belshazzar, Nebuchadnezar,
all believed in their star of destiny. If they had only used
their brains a bit, they could have foreseen the disaster
that overtook them. They could have avoided their dismal
failures.
What is Mussolini’s star of destiny? Nothing but the
American dollar. If that star fails him, he will go down
to defeat, disgrace, and almost certain death. If some
hired murderer of some foreign government does not get
him, his own mad dogs will when he stumbles and falls.
Nobody can escape from the effects of his big mistakes.
Mussolini has made so many big mistakes since his
first false step, his march on Rome, that his decline and
end can be predicted with more certainty than he can
foresee what his star of destiny has in store for him.
SAVING AND SPENDING
Economics has been called the dismal science, be
cause it used to be handled by dry-as-dust professors who
didn’t know any more about the workings of capitalist
business than the luckless readers who had to bear the
infliction of the professor’s rantings.
A recent series of articles in the Hearst press shows
that economics can also be very entertaining and hilarious.
Some readers of the Hearst papers suggested that it would
be better, if people didn’t put any money into savings
banks, but spent their money as fast as they got it. One
reader said that a $50,000 dinner gave employment to
cooks, waiters, trades people, etc., whereas a $50,000 de
posit in a savings bank lay idle and reduced the opportun
ities for employment.
Thereupon the economic expert of the Hearst press
jumped to the rescue of the banks with the profound
thought that banks lend deposited money out at interest
to railroads and other enterprises, thus making it more
productive of employment than a spendthrift dinner could.
Lean back and let this profound Hearstian economics
percolate into your noodle, you sovereign American voting
kings. You put your savings into a bank, and the banker
has the privilege to lend your money to some other cap
italist at two or three times the interest that he pays you.
The borrowing capitalist, who may be your employer,
uses your savings to extend his own business and to give
a job to some other fellow, who may be a fellow’ trade
unionist or a company man paid to spy on you. But you
couldn’t borrow’ on your own savings without paying a
tribute to the same bank to which you entrust your money.
Instead of engaging in an aimless debate as to w’hether
it is better to save or to spend, you ought to ask yourself:
How’ is it that a banker or some other capitalist has priv
ileges to do something with my money that the law w’on't
let me do? The answer ought to interest you. It w’ould
tell you why some writers are so anxious to have you save
in order that somebody else may be able to spend. You
might find out why your labor makes other people’s money
grow faster than your own.
THE DOUGHNUT AND THE HOLE
A high-priced editor tells his gaping readers that you
can reduce everything to atoms, but you don’t know w’hat
the energy of the atom is. You can go all through the
human brain and find no trace of the “soul” that is un
doubtedly there. And so forth, with the idea of keeping
people’s mind in a fog.
This editor, like so many bright people, talks as if
he were more interested in the hole of the doughnut than
in its dough. But he really isn't. He always gets the
dough and his readers get the hole. Offer him the soul of
n HniUr instead of its atoms, and see what he will say.

ganization of workmen and peas
ants but as it expanded into a

was “contrary to Scripture; it is

trary to nature, for it is to live
without labor.” The money-lender
was considered an outlaw and if

Luckless the youth who has
been so city-bred that he has
never sought in the long brown
grass at the edges of a pasture
for the fall crop of juicy red
haws. These little cousins of the
apple have a flavor of their own,
which no cultivated fruit can
hope to equal. What matter if
almost every one of them con
tains a worm —though sometimes
one has the ill fortune to find
but half of him? The appetite
of boyhood is not to be dulled by
such trifles as these misadven
tures in the study of vulgar frac
tions.
The hawthorn genus seems to
be a group of plants at present
engaged in a course of very active
evolution. No two botanists agree

ers are not to be admitted to com

the days when a portion of the

tributed to the salary of a min

In the old days there was even
a competition between high church
officials for the honor of punish
ing merchants who sold fraudu

their tenants, those who pray on
the poverty of the masses. Who
of us can deny that the competi
tion today is too often a rivalry
to see which church can obtain
the largest contribution from our
upper classes?
In this early period the workers
of various crafts had their simple
association for mutual improve
ment and Tawney shows that ec
clesiastical courts even went so
far as to punish the workman who
scabbed! Tawney mentions the
smiths who organized to abolish
night work “and summoned black
legs before the eccleciastical
courts” and obtained a decision
which “forbade anyone to work
between sunset and sunrise and
haled an offending journeyman
before the archdeacon.” This jour
neyman had offended three times
and was excommunicated “until
he would swear to keep the ordi
nance.” What a contrast with
our modern injunction judges!
With the rise of feudalism
based upon great landed estates
tilled by serf labor the church it
self became a great vested inter
est. As Tawney puts it. the
church was “implicated to the hilt
in the economic fabric, especially
on the side of agriculture and
land tenure.” The feudal lords
represented the most powerful
economic interest and wealth ac
cumulated in their hands. Church
investments in the same form of
property drew it and the lords
together. The serf was crushed
under insufferable burdens but
was promised release into a life
about its division into species.
There are notable and obvious
differences between haws, both in
fruit and flower and leaf, but it
is hard to find the kind of sharp
dividing lines that exist between
some other species: the haws sim
ply run into each other in the
most bewildering fashion, and
sometimes one finds on different
branches of the same tree fruits
that he would unhesitatingly call
different species if they came
from separate sources. Small
comfort grows on the hawthorn
tree for the believer in the un
varying fixity of species!
It is hard to imagine why no
enterprising horticulturist has
yet seen fit to try his hand at
improving the hawthorn and in
ducing it to grow larger fruits, as
our remote ancestors encouraged
the nubbinly little wild apples of
Eurasia. The fruits are smaller
than those of most wild apple
species, but the flower is there al
ready, as it certainly was not in
at least some of the original ap
ples.

The Tricks of
Counterfeiters
The portraits anti other free
hand decorations on the govern
ment notes are the work of the
finest artists in the country. Few,
indeed, are the men who can turn
out equally fine engravings. Dif
ferent vignettes on the same bill
are the work of different men,
each a master in his line. The
counterfeiter thus finds on every
note several types of engraving
and he must be an exceptional
artist to be able to duplicate them
all. In general, it has been found
that landscape scenes are more
susceptible of imitation than some
of the other types of vignettes.
Accordingly, a note never bears a
landscape alone. With it will al
ways be found a portrait, his
torical scene, allegorical interpre
tation, or some other tvpe of en
graving.
There are artists outside those
in the government employ who
can perform the same class of
work with the same degree of ex
cellence. However, they are as
sured such a large financial re
turn through honest endeavor that
there is no motive for them to
turn criminal. Furthermore, their
ranks are so limited that when
a particularly well executed note
appears in circulation the re
sponsibility can be fixed within
narrow limits. By watching the
few men who might turn out work
of that grade the secret service
operatives are never long in lo
cating the guilty party or parties.
When the work is that of a for
eigner the task is harder. Some
skilled engravers have come into
this country and set up counter
feit plants which baffled detection
for a time. Such a one was Al
bert Leon, who eluded the govern
ment men for two years.
One year the Pacific northwest
began to show an alarming in
crease of counterfeit 10-dollar
notes. Operatives searched high
rind low for the source, but at first
they got no results. Whoever was
doing the counterfeiting was an
expert engraver and his plant was
very cleverly concealed. The bogus
notes were examined for some
clew. They were printed on a
hi^h-grade bond paper of which
two sheets were pasted carefully
together to obtain the desired
thickness.
There was nothing particularly
unusual in this, but the silk
threads, on examination, devel
oped a startling peculiarity. Un
der the microscope it could be
seen that they were not silk at all.
They were the short reddish hairs
of some wild animal, or perhaps a
dog! “Malemutes.” said the de
tectives, at a guess. “Let’s start
working north. The fellow may
have been snowed in for the win
ter and couldn’t get silk threads.”
The steps by which the counter
feiters were run down are too
long to detail, but the guess work
proved correct. They ran the gang
to earth on Nootka island, an iso

Deer as Jumper
Many years ago I was talking
with a famous old woodsman of
the Carolina swamps and our con
versation turned to the subject
of deer, and particularly to the
question of their ability as jump
ers. Each of us was able to give
some remarkable examples of the
wild deer’s power as a jumper,
but neither seemed certain as to
the limits of this power. Finally
my friend said, “Well, I believe
that a deer can jump just as far
and as high as he has to.” While
we can not admit this there’s an
element of truth in it. It is not
often that a deer exerts all his
powers as a jumper; and more
seldom still is he observed to do
so.
As a matter of fact, a deer’s
motions are singularly easy and
graceful. When he jumps, he
seems to float over obstructions,
without careful approach and
without apparent effort. More
over, the deer is singularly sure
footed. During 30 years of hunt
ing. I have seen in the woods up
wards. I think, of a thousand
deer. Most of these were in flight,
in wild country, where the footing
was most treacherous; yet I never
saw an uuwounded deer fall
down. I have seen one blunder,
but his recovery was so rapid that
his loss of equilibrium was hard
ly noticeable.
I once measured the jump of a
deer which sprang from its bed
that is, the first jump it made
from a position flat on the
ground. I had approached this
deer on foot, across the dry bed
of a pond, lined with soft moss,
and was within about eight feet
of the creature when it sprang up
and away. It had been lying at
the base of a huge pine, in a tiny
clump of huckleberry bushes, too
small, one would think, to hide a
deer. There was a space of black
damp sand surrounding the pine,
so that I was able to measure the
jump with certainty. It was 14
feet 1 inch. But remember that
this jump was made from a lying
down position. While running, the
average jump of the wbitetail is
from 15 to 20 feet; but by small
effort a mature deer can increase
this distance amazingly— Archi
bald Eutledge, in St. Nicholas,
THE LEAGUE’S LAST STRAW
The prohibition forces are trying to put on the back
of the league of nations the last straw that may break
that patient camel’s back. They want the league to be
come a champion of prohibition in addition to all its other
assumed and never fulfilled duties.
The league has done nothing so far in any crisis which
placed it before a serious issue. It has balked and dodged
every fundamental problem, and has merely acted as the
long arm of the big powers which pulls the ears of the
little ones.
It has forced loans under conditions of usury on a
helpless nation like Austria, but it was told to keep its
nose out of the big debt settlements, and it did.
It warned the little Balkan powers that they must
not start anything which woujd mar the plots of the big
fellows, but it always bowed before the big stick. It even
aided and abetted Mussolini in his attack on Corfu and
forced Greece to pay damages for a crime she had not
committed.
The league has done nothing about British, French
and Italian atrocities in their colonies and mandated
territories. It will not do anything about the division of
Abyssinia by England and Italy. It will ignore the Hun
nish French deeds in Damascus and other parts of Syria.
It will continue to be blind against the iron heel of the
big powers in China.
The laws that rule the world, the deeds that shake it,
are not discussed and planned in the open meetings of the
league. They are plotted behind the closed doors of the
chancelleries. Information about them will always be
denied by the governments even to their own parliaments,
so long as old party machines rule.
Secret diplomacy is still the rule even in the council
of the league itself. Only to the extent that the govern
ments or parties of capitalism expose one another for their
own partisan ends, will public opinion get occasional
glimpses of the plots that aim to waste more lives and
money.
Since the league has done nothing towards solving
the problems which divide the capitalist world against
itself, it is natural that it should have dodged every at
tempt to interest it in labor laws, humanitarian improve
ments, social progress at large.
It may be that the league will take the prohibition
cranks to its heart. Its principal function has become that
of a forum for the cranks of all nations. It is always
willing to open its doors to the discussion of problems that
cannot be solved within the frame, of capitalist business,
and that for this reason never have any practical effects on
the policies of the old party governments.
It permits the little nations to strut, brag, holler and
gesticulate, but never acts upon their ideas. It offers to
the national minorities under foreign rule a chance to air
their grievances, without giving force to their voice and
vote. It lets windy orators waste day after day on things
that are pure figments of the imagination.
If the league opens a sideshow for the prohibition
cranks, it will have another dime-attraction. But it al
ready has so many of these, that one more may be one too
many for it. At any rate, it cannot force prohibition on
national majorities that don’t want it. And it may find
very soon that the nations are throwing the prohibitionists
out faster than it can take them in.
These sideshows have served a useful purpose fcr th
big insiders by taking the attention of the public otrX
secret mainshow. But of late people have learned u
estimate this function of the sideshows for what it is
worth. We doubt that a prohibition sideshow will serve
the league as well as the others.
THE GLORY THAT PASSES
Here is a price list of glory. It’s furnished by a
pawnbroker:
French Croix de Guerre 2.00
American Distinguished Service Medal...., 10.00
Belgian Croix de Guerre 2.00
French Legion d’Honneur 12.00
German Iron Cross 1-00
Mons Star (1914) 1-00
Mons Star (1915) 50
Italian War Cross 3.00
Some of those who earned these decorations with their
blood are dead. Others bear scars they will carry all
their lives, in lieu of the medals they have pawned for a
few pennies. Others, maimed or blind or dying, are eking
out existence as best they can. A fanfare of glory ac
companied the presentation of each of the medals. Troops
were drawn up, bugles blown. A general read a citation
of honor and pinned a bit of metal and ribbon on a proud
breast. And before the presentation—each represented
some outstanding act of heroism, of gallantry, of sacrifice.
Perhaps a life saved or a life given.
But the fanfare and the glory are gone. The heroism
is forgotten. In dark little corners of pawnshops the
w’orld over these symbols of sacrifice are lying, haplessly
awaiting the day when they may be bought by a collector,
or by some charlatan eager to pose as a hero. One won
ders what grimacing, mocking fate caused their once
proud owners to dispose of them.
Some of the grimmest pictures of war are painted in
the peace that comes after! —Dearborn Independent.

Gale, Blowing 130-Miles an Hour Out of
West Indies, Destroys Many Cities; Dam
age to Property Will Pass $100,000,000
Mark, Authoritative Agencies say.
BUILDINGS IN BOOM DISTRICTS
ARE CRUSHED BY STORM’S FURY
Water, Banked Up in Harbor By Power of
Gale, Sweeps Onto Shore, Wrecking What
Was in Its Path—Boats Tossed, as If Toys
Are Left on High Grounds.
BY AL. RECK
Staff Correspondent, The United Press.
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla.—Cities which were built over
night in the greatest era of development an American community
has ever known have collapsed overnight in one of the greatest
disasters ever to visit the North American continent.
A great hurricane, blowing 130 miles an hour out of the
West Indies, has devastated the Florida east coast from Palm
Beach south to Homestead. Many cities have been destroyed
and many hundreds of lives lost.
Authoritatitve agencies estimated the number killed at 471
in the larger cities alone. The Red Cross has received reports
the dead will reach 700 and some estimates run as high as 1.000
50,000 ARE HOMELESS.
Fifty thousand persons are estimated homeless and suffer
ing severe privations.
Property damage will surpass $100,000,000. It has been
estimated that Miami alone will show losses equaling that figure.
Hollywood, Fort Lauderdale, Hialeah, Pompano, Dania.
Hallandale, Moorhaven, Clewiston, Key Largo, Homestead, Coral
Gables, Muckway, and Key West all have suffered in varying
degree—the first six named and Miami to a point where prob
ably they will have to be rebuilt.
BREAKS UPON MIAMI.
It was six days ago that the hurricane was first born out
in the West Indies. It rolled westward and at 2 a. m. Sunday
it broke upon Miami from the northwest.
For four hours the wind roared and whirled at a velocity
of 130 miles an hour.
The great tower of The Miami News, famed the world over
for its architectural beauty, leaned to a 20 degree angle, twisted
and wrenched.
The 10-story Meyer Keyser Bank Bldg, was ruined.
BUILDINGS ARE WRECKED.
Building after building was blown down or was shattered
and torn.
Boats were tossed, sunk or destroyed in the harbor as if
they were but things of flimsy tissue.
People were crushed, injured and killed.
Wires were twisted into entanglements such as on the battlefields of
France.
Lights went out. Communication was an impossibility.
Railroad lines were disrupted and tracks destroyed.
Rain fell in torrents.
Water, banked up in the harbor by the vast power of the hurricane,
swept onto the shore, wrecking what was in its path and leaving boats
high on the land.
BOOM CITIES ARE TORN.
And while this was going on in Miami, other of the magic cities of
the Florida east coast were almost equal sufferers.
Hollywood, perhaps the most famous of the Florida developments
was wrenched and torn. Estimates of the dead there were placed at 200.
Fort Landerdale was visited with only slightly less fury. Fifteen
bcdies have been recovered from its wreckage and the casualties there
may be greater, Hialeah’s famous race track was ruined and 17 were
reported killed.
The storm swept inland over Lake Okeechobee and an aviator who
yesterday flew in that vicinity came hack with an estimate that probably
140 persons had been killed in Moorehavcn and Clewiston.
40 PERSONS ARE KILLED.
Another mn who had been over the territory said he estimated tht
dead along the railway between Moorehaven and Muckway at 4U.
Key West also suffered and 18 were reported killed there.
Aside from the lives lost, the most appalling disaster of the store:
was the wreckage of stores and warehouses, which meant virtually al
food supplies were destroyed. With railroad service paralyzed, it wa?
feared incoming supplies would be greatly delayed. Some food supplier
may come by water.
Virtual military rule prevails in Miami and other cities, but there
is shortage of troops.
WATER IS RECEIVED.
The first relief train, bearing 15 physicians, a corpse of nurses, med
icine and supplies, and carrying two cars of drinking water, arrived in
Mia ma today.
With thousands of men. women and children in need, it was feared
a crowd might storm the train. State militiamen, therefore, met the train
and maintained constant vigil over the supplies.
Despite strict precautions. looting has occurred. and one man was
shot by guards last night after he was caught pillaging in a destroyed
office building.
A temporary field hospital and morgue base was established at
4 a. m.. at Sebring. Fia.. and SOO of the most seriously injured from the
wrecked districts were assembled there. Reports said forty were dead
in Sebring.

WHISTLE AGAIN
SHRILLS ORDERS
T 0 VEHICLES
Control of Milwaukee traffic by
means of whistles was Inaugurated
on three important downtown cor
ners today.
“There would be more, but we
have only three whistles,” said Capt.
A. J. Murray, head of the police de
partment traffic bureau.
“The experiment of using
whistles, however, will be extended
to all downtown intersections, where
there are no automatic signals.
Motorists are advised by Capt
Murray that the whistles are not
signals for traffic to move.
One Blast—Two Blasts.
“The officers will direct traffic
with their arms as usual,” said
Capt. Murray.
“The whistles are to warn mo
torists that traffic is going to
change. One blast is the signal that
north and south traffic will be di
rected to proceed; two blasts for
east and west bound vehicles.”
The use of the whistle, which was
discontinued in 1921, is upon the
recommendation of the Milwaukee
safety commission. The corners
whereat traffic is now controlled
by means of the whistles are Wells
and West Water Sts.; Wells and
3rd Sts.; and State and 3rd Sts.
“The use of the whistle is more or
less of an experiment,” said Capt.
Murray.
“If their use proves advantag
eous it will be inaugurated on all
of the down town corners not con
trolled by automatic signal lights.”
The use of the traffic whistle
was abolished by the late Chief of
Police John T. Janssen upon com
plaint of virtually every traffic of
ficer in the city, who asserted that
during cold weather the metal
whistles adhered to their lips and
that their mouths were constantly
sore.
Rubber Wliistles Now.
“We have purchased rubber whis
tles which are guaranteed to be
usable in the coldest weather with
out producing any ill effects,” said
Capt. Murray.
Several months ago the police de
partment requested the common
council to abandon all autoamtic
signal lights and to permit the con
trol of all down town corners by an
officer equipped with a whistle.
This the council refused to do,
whereupon the safety commission
and the traffic bureau recommend
ed the control of traffic with whis
tles on all corners not equipped
with he regulators.

WOULD CHANGE

Changing the entire method of
sewage disposal employed at the
new $15,000,000 Jones Island sew
age disposal plant, is recommended
by Robert Cramer, Milwaukee con
sulting engineer and member of the
sewerage commission in a communi
cation forwarded to the commission
today.
Mr. Cramer advocates the puri
fication of sewage by the activated
sludge method, which he declares
has been proved successful.
He maintains that the attempt to
convert the sludge into fertilizer is
what is balking the successful op
eration of the Milwaukee plant and
holds that even if that problem is
solved, the cost of equipping the
plant and producing it will be too
great to make the production of the
fertilizer an economy
That the cost of making the
changes in the plant which will
make the production of fertilizer
ultimately possible is altogether
prohibitive, is the contention of Mr.
Cramer.
He points out that a pressing and
incinerating plant to cost .$150,000 is
necessary, four new sludge dryers
must be installed, the filters must
be altered and a complete deodor
izing installation that will cost a
large sum, must be made.
Mr. Cramer's communication will
be considered at the regular meet
ing of the commission Friday.

WISH TO REMAIN
TOWNSHIP, AVER
LAKE RESIDENTS
By a majority of two to one vot
ers of the town of Lake expressed
themselves as being in favor of re
maining a town, when they cast
their ballots Saturday in a special
election called to decide the ques
tion of incorporating the town as a
city.
An unofficial canvass shows that
1,420 votes were cast by persons op
posed to the plan of incorporating
the town as a city, while 784 votes
favored it.
Had the plan carried It would
have blocked Milwaukee’s expansion
to the south. It would have blocked
any annexation to the city except
the annexation of the entire incor
porated city.
The unofficial canvass of the
votes by precincts shows: Ist, 262
for. 422 against; 2nd, 67 for, 383
against; 3rd, 60 for, 161 against;
4th, 27 for, 183 against; sth, 189
for, 100 against; 6th, 179 for, 171
against.
Hoan O K’s Defeat.
Mayor Daniel W. Hoan today de
clared that the town of Lake citi
zens, in his opinion, had exercised
good judgment in defeating the in
corporation plan.
“With its exceedingly large area
and sparse population, the town of
Lake would have encountered in
numerable difficulties in attempt
ing to finance the improvements
which a city must have,” declared
the mayor.
“Taxes would have soared skyhigh
and improvements would have
proved Inadequate.
Milwaukee to Annex.
“Milwaukee has solved its an
nexation problem and is now able to
take In large tracts of land, fur
nish them with city Improvements,
and the advantages are so great
that there is now an actual demand
for annexation on the part of the
residents of most of the outlying ter
ritory.
“To have formed a city of the en
tire town of Lake, and thus prac
tically shut themselves off from an
nexation to the city and become a
part of a weak and struggling city
at the best, would have been a seri
ous mistake for the residents of the
township.”

COP SOLVES
MYSTERY OF
DIRTY MILK
The town of Lake mystery of The
Dirty Bottles, or Who Put the Fer
tilizer in the Baby’s Milk? was
solved today, according to Patrol
man Stanley Haack, when he
marched a milg wagon driver into
the Bay View station and an
nounced that he had caught him in
the act.
For weeks residents of the town
of Lake and of sections of Milwau
kee bordering the township com
plained that their milk was dirty.
Pieces of wood, gravel, earth and
even manure were found in the bot
tles.
In One Area.
The two dairy companies against
whom complaints were made were
unable to account for it. Bottles
from the same batches of milk, de
livered in other sections of the
city were clean. AH the complaints
were from one territory and con
cerned only milk delivered by two
companies.
No complaint regarding milk de
livered by a third company operat
ing in the same neighborhood was
made.
All this Patrolman Haack learned.
Then he discovered that the milk
salesman for the third company was
getting 82 apiece for each new cus
tomer he obtained.
His bonuses for new customers
began to increase coincident with
the complaints against the other
milk companies, the officer learned.
Trailed by Cop.
Daily he trailed the milkman.
Today, he says, he caught him. Ac
cording to Haack, he saw the milk
man take a bottle of milk from the
box used by two families at 1576
6th Ave., put his own bottle inside
and then open the bottle he had
removed.
From his gestures, according to
the officer, the man stooped as
though to pick up something, re
capped the bottle and put it back.
Haack arrested him when he came
back to the street. Investigating, he
found one of the bottles of milk con
tained a quantity of dirt.
The milkman denies that he put
it there. Police are holding him
without charge.

Germany to Pay France in Cash to Bolster Franc
SALE OF RAIL
BONDS MAY BE
AUTHORIZED
Full Accord With
France Aim of
Officials.
BERLIN —What is the price Ger
many must pay for the proposed
rapprochement with France? In
answer to this question, upon
which the peace of Europe largely
depends, it was learned that in re
turn for political concessions, Ger
many must make material conces
sions with which France hopes to
stabilize its finances. These are
said to include 500,000,000 gold
marks (about $120,000,000) in Ger
man railroad bonds, held by the gov
enrment, and whatever sum up to
2.000.000,000 marks (about $500,-
000,000) which Seymour Parker Gil
bert, the American agent-general for
the Dawes reparations plan, is will
ing to place at the nation’s disposal.
Holds Gold Marks.
Mr. Gilbert holds 11,000,000,000
gold marks (about $1,750,000,000)
worth of obligations in the world’s
biggest company,” the German rail
road system. Until now the Amer
ican, who is directig Germany's
salvation, has refused to permit the
flotation of these bonds on the
world market. The German lead
ers believe that when the time
comes that they can say they have
cemented Franco-German relations
and have saved Europe from anoth
er disaster, the reparations commis
sion will feel that Wall Street and
other nations will take any amount
of bonds offered.
According to the viewpoint of
President Hjalmir Schacht of the
German Reichsbank, Germany can
absorb internally German railway
bonds amounting to 1,500,000,000
marks (about $375,000,000). Dr.
Schacht is going to Paris after his
return from Vienna for the pur
pose of consulting French authori
ties and bankers.
May Sell Bonds.
There is some doubt, however, as
to whether Mr. Gilbert will author
ize the sale of more than 500,000,000
marks worth of bonds, which, added
to the German government's bonds,
valued at 500.000,000 marks, would
net $250,000,000. It is believed Ger
many will be able to absorb a large
part of these bonds at a small in
terest rate, whereas, if sold in Wall
Street or London, 7 to 8 per cent
Interest would be demanded.
Foreign Minister Stresemann has
the support of President von Hin
denburg, Chancellor Marx and a
large part of the people in his plans
for a full accord with France. Pres
ident von Hindenburg cut short his
Inspection of the army maneuvers
and rushed to Berlin where he will
hold a conference late today.
The purpose of the conference is
to voice support of Dr. Stresemann
and enable Germany to inform its
ambassador at Paris that the whole
nation is behind the German foreign
minister if Premier Raymond Poin
care will only accept the pact which
Foreign Minister Briand will pre
sent. German leaders are confident
the French cabinet will approve the
rapprochement at its meeting Tues
day.

BRITISH TRADE
UNIONS RETAIN
STRIKE WEAPON
Leader Special Service.
MANCHESTER—The Manches
ter Guardian calls attention to the
decision of the British trade union
congress to retain the general strike
as a legitimate weapon of trade
unions and emphasizes the grave
importance of this fact.
Trade union congresses today
have an importance equalled only
by great meetings of statesmen,
The Guardian says. The trade
unions have become a power, and
their leaders are men who know
their responsibilities and their pol
icies.
It is therefore a matter of great
est importance to understand the
weighty significance of the present
trade union policy.
Retain General Strike.
Arthur Pugh, chairman of the Brit
ish trade union congress, announced
that “as a means of resisting such
settlements of industrial disputes
(as the one attempted by the mine
owners) the weapon used by the
unions last May will not be left
unused when it is sought to en
force upon any section of the work
ers terms which have not been made
the subject of negotiations and col
lective agreement.”
In other words, the sympathetic
strike will be used again, if the em
ployers attempt to force local con
tracts on small sections of the work
ing class without negotiation and
agreement with the trade union con
gress.
The Guardian thinks that a gen
eral strike will always be lost, if
the public feels that it is directed
against itself rather than against
the employers. Or it may be a
strike against the government, and
in that case it will always become
a political question.
Wants More Light.
The Guardian feels that it ought
to have more light from the trade
unions on these points. It wants
to know how the trade union lead
ers propose to convince the public
that a general strike which im
poses suffering on the majority is
aimed only at the employers.
It would also like to know a little
more about the ideas of the trade
union leaders concerning the rela
tion of a general strike to politics.
The Guardian had rather expect
ed that the trade union congress
would instruct its chairman to
make, if not a public confession of
error, at least a more exhaustive
statement revealing the special oc
casions on which a general strike
would again be Invoked by the labor
leaders.
LEAGUE HELP
FDR ATTACKED
STATE URGED
GENEVA —Guarantee of security
to countries menaced by hostile
neighbors will be secured through
•‘financial assistance,” if the memo
randum submitted by the Finnish
delegation is accepted by the sev
enth assembly of the league of na
tions.
The scheme, proposed by Foreign
Minister Holsti, which gained the
approval of many delegates to the
assembly, was regarded by the
council of the league to be of such
importance as to merit detailed
study before it is debated. It will
be brought before a council com
mittee Wednesday, after which it
may come before the assembly.
The proposal is unique in that it
approaches security problems from
a different door, but seeks the same
end as the unfortunate protocol,
proposed by Foreign Minister Benes
of Czecho-Slovakia, which Great
Britain scuttled a year and a half
ago. Where Dr. Bentes’ scheme em
phasized military assistance under
article 16 of the league covenant,
Mr. Holsti’s plan envisages immedi
ate, unlimited financial assistance
for an attacked country.
For instance, should Poland be at
tacked by Russia, the members of
the league would advance financial
credits which would enable Poland
to buy unlimited supplies of muni
tions, cannon and airplanes from
Germany, England, France, or any
other accessible markets.
At the same time the league
members would be pledged to with
hold financial assistance, supplies
and credits from the aggressor
state.
Under this plan, it is claimed, all
countries would be able to disarm
to the very limit, inasmuch as the
maintenance of huge supplies of
war material would be unnecessary.
According to the American dele
gation of the preparatory disarma
ment committee, the Finnish scheme
is the most plausible proposal thus
far advanced to provide the much
desired security which the majority
of nations insist on as a prelimi
nary to disarmament.
The countries which are unalter
ably opposed to pledging themselves
to carry out the military features
of article 16, which is regarded as
holding the teeth of the covenant,
will be unable legitimately to refuse
c-operation under the “financial aid
plan.” it is declared.

THE MILWAUKEE LEADER, MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 20, 1920
URGES IRISH
WORKERSTO
GAIN POWER
Leader Special Service.
DUBLIN—The Voice of Labor, of
ficial organ of the Irish Labor
party, sums up the political situa
tion in Ireland in a recent article
which predicts the failure of the De
Valera movement and advises the
workers to develop the power of
their own class as much against
the capitalists who rule the free
state as against those who would
like to rule it through De Valeraism.
The present rulers of the free
state have made money through
their allegiance to the financial
power of London, The Voice of La
bor explains. These capitalistshave
no use for the Irish Republicans,
who are suspected of narrow-mind
ed protectionism and nationalism.
The Irish capitalists have made
a good bargain with their British
friends, The Voice of Labor contin
ues. They have exchanged their
power of national independence for
the position of hucksters in a pau
perized province. They have clung
to their petty profits at the expense
of the dignity and honesty of the
free state government.
But the Irish workers would gain
nothing by exchanging De Valera
and his friends for the present old
party rulers of the free state. De
Valera is still fumbling in search of
a magic formula which shall open
the door to political power to him.
But he has not yet grasped the es
sential economic problem of Ire
land.
The present ruling class of Ire
land, being in league with the Brit
ish, cannot be dislodged with dyna
mite or other “revolutionary”
methods preferred by the Repub
licans.
What Ireland needs is not a po
litical revolution for the benefit of
De Valera’s class, but a social re
construction for the benefit of the
working majority of the Irish peo
ple, The Voice of Labor concludes.
The Irish workers have the same
practical problems to solve that con
front the modern workers every
where. The workers must train
themselves as administrators, tech
nicians, financial experts in the
trade union movement, and as
statesmen in the high political posi
tions of the nation.
A political fanatic like De Valera
can destroy things, but he has no
social program of constructive prog
ress that would help the majority
of the Irish people one step for
ward out of their present condi
tion.

AT THE FIELD HOSPITAL AND
MORGUE BASE, SEBRING, Fla.—
Tales of horror that followed the
complete ruin of the town of Moore
haven, leveled by the tropical hur
ricane, were brought here today by
Wade H. Marlow, one of the first of
a rescue party to reach the stricken
town.
“I arrived in Moorehaven not long
after the levee holding Lake Okeech
obee had broken in three places, re
leasing its gigantic wall of water
upon the town,” Marlow told the
United Press.
“The water poured through the
streets and countryside at a depth
of 12 feet. Thore were no warnings
and the people had no chance to
escape.
Swim for Life.*
“Those who live today to tell of
the disaster saved themselves by
swimming and clinging to the wreck
age of flimsy homes that collapsed
under the first impact.
“A few made their way to two
story buildings which had remained
standing, and there we found them.
“The.v were too frightened and too
near physical collapse to venture
forth from their temporary shelter
and it was only after considerable
persuasion that we got them away.
“Fiftyone bodies had been recov
ered last night. They will be brought
here later.
Bodies in Water.
“We saw bodies of men, women
and children floating about on the
high waters but made no attempt
to recover them, first seeking pos
sible injured who were still alive.
“Effie Sutton and Mrs. Louis
Fallow were found perched on
shelves in their house, which was
floating away from its site.
“Searching further, we came upon
another house that was floating
and there we rescued W. H. Ed
wards and R. E. Green. They, too,
were riding the shelves.
“Wild animals and snakes fell vic
tims to the onrushing waters.
Cries Were Maddening.
"We would pass floating bodies
near which were dead animals and
snakes. The cries of the frightened
women and children were madden
ing.
“Only one child of the Dequilla
family of seven was saved. Of an
other family, named Bowman, the
father was the only one of six who
is alive today
Pitiful scenes are being enacted
at the morgue here as refugees
walk slowly through the somber
aisles seeking to identify missing
relatives.”

There is little danger that a
tropical hurricane or an intense tor
nado will ever strike Milwaukee, W.
M. Labovich, acting meteorologist of
the Milwaukee weather bureau, de
clared today.
The tropical hurricanes always
start in the calm moist air along the
equator, and, aided by easterly
winds, move northwest to the gulf
coast, then slowly curve north and
northeastward and pass south of
Wisconsin, he said.
Likened to Top.
The action of the hurricane is like
that of a top receiving on a table.
It revolves rapidly but moves slowly
from one side to the other of the
table, he explained.
Hurricanes move at the rate of
about 12 miles an hour, but usually
contain winds which reach a ve
locity of between 100 and 150 miles
an hour.
More than 30 per cent of the hur
ricanes occur in September, accord
ing to Mr. Labovich.
Lake Saves State.
The presence of Lake Michigan
and the typography of the country
saves Milwaukee from tornados, he
explained.
A tornado in its actions is much
like a hurricane, but it is more
local. The tornado is caused by
warm stagnant air gathering in one
place until finally a vacuum in the
center causes the whirling action.
Lake Michigan tends to keep air
cool and in circulation, while the
Wisconsin hills prevent the sweep
ing action which a tornado would
reach on a plains state.

SAFETY ZONES DANGEROUS.
To the Editor of The Leader:
The safety zones at street car
stops are made for the protection of
the pedestrian and motor vehicles
which invade them are subject to
reprimand.
And yet I escaped severe injury
and possible death the other day
only by the space between a scrap
ing of my coat and the catching of
my body by a street car fender.
I was standing well inside the
safety zone and there was no rea
son why my back should not have
been to the street car track, as in
reality it was. My attention was
concentrated upon finding seven pen
nies in my purse. The car creeping
past me was not the one I wanted.
The first I knew of my danger
was a workman’s curse when I
didn’t at first understand his gesture
for me to move out of the way of
the approaching rear fender. He
then roughly grabbed my arm and
jerked me away, but not before I
had felt the fender scraping my coat
Where it would have hurled me if it
had caught my body, is merely con
jecture, but it would have been pos
sible for me to be killed if my head
had struck any one of several pos
sible hard surfaces. The car was
turning the corner.
This incident jvas not the street
car company's fault, unless the fault
lay in not advising the proper au
thorities that certain of its cars
invaded the safety zones were turn
ing. But whoever plans and marks
the safety zones has been criminally
negligent in not more carefully
checking up their possibilities of in
jury as well as safety.
There may be other corners where
a person standing in a safety zone
is also endangered. A thorough
check up of this situation should be
made at once.

NEW YORK—The Fellowship of
Youth for Peace, whose meetings at
Concord, Mass., last June were se
verely attacked by rowdies, has now
become a part of The Fellowship of
Reconciliation as its youth section.
This action was taken at the an
nual conference of the two Fellow
ships at Watch Hill, R. I.
Tills brings the Fellowship of
Youth for Peace back to the position
it occupied when it was organized
in 1924 and it strengthens rhe whole
movement by uniting old and young
in a repudiation of war, exploita
tion and racial discrimination and
in commitment to a manner of life
creative of fellowship and unity.
The Fellowship of Reconciliation
has members and groups in all parts
of the United States and is organ
ized in 75 countries. The youth sec
tion has its clientele largely in the
colleges.

tary of the Women’s International
League for Peace and Freedom,

Civil Liberties Union and Bishop
Paul Jones.

Judges in Sixth Circuit Act to Curb Hasty Divorces
PLAN TO KEEP
COMPLAINT ON
FILE 90 DAYS
Urge Attorneys to
Help Prevent
Breaks.
LA CROSSE—Judges of the sixth
judicial circuit have applied the
brakes to hasty divorces by agreeing
that no divorce actions will be heard
in their courts unless the complaint
has been on file for 90 days instead
of the 20-day period formerly re
quired.
In explaining their action these
judges stated that it is the duty of
attorneys to do everything possible
to prevent breaking up of homes and
to effect reconciliations.
In the past, they stated, many di
vorce actions have been commenced
hastily and without any real inten
tion of proceeding further in the
matter than to discipline the erring
gpouse.
They hold that if a substantial
time is permitted or required to
elapse between the commencement
of the action and the actual trial,
the better judgment of both parties
will be given an opportunity to as
sert itself and many reconciliations
thus be brought about
Movies of Passaic
Strike Ready; Will
Make Rounds of U. S.
PASSAIC, N. J.—Workers in all
parts of the country will oe able to
ace actual scenes of the stirring and
heroic struggle of the 10,000 strik
ing textile workers of Passaic and
vicinity.
A seven-reel motion picture, The
Passaic Textile Strike, is now ready
for routing throughout the country.
It represents the biggest thing done
by labor in years.
This Is the first time that the
struggles of the workers have been
filmed during a strike. It is the
first time, too, that a labor picture
has heen routed for showing in or
ganized end unorganized territory
with the object of bringing home
to the workers the lessons of a
vitally Important strike and teach
ing the unorganized the need of or
ganization and workers’ solidarity
with which to successfully defend
themselves against the wage cuts
of the bosses. This picture brings
home more forcefully than 1,000
speeches the sheer necessity of a
united front of the workers with
which to meet the united front of
the bosses

MOTORISTASSN.
FOR STANDARD
DUMPER HEIGHT
CHICAGO A declaration in
favor of a standard height for
bumpers for all makes of automo
biles has just been made by the
Motorists Association of Illinois,
Chicago.
Hugo Meyer, secretary-treasurer
of the club, believes that a great
deal of property damage, lacerated
feeling, and general ill nature would
be eliminated if all cars were
equipped with bumpers which are
a standard height from the ground.
“We think that a standard height
of bumper would give a great deal
more protection to the motorist and
his property than the present sys
tem of having the bumper placed
on the front or rear of the car at
an indiscriminate height,” asserts
Mr. Meyer.
“If the rear bumper on the car
in front of you is 20 inches from
the surface of the road, and the
bumper on the front of your car is
24 inches from the surface, neither
has the slightest bit of protection.
Temper Is Lost.
“Suppose the man ahead of you
has stopped suddenly while driving
through traffic. He has four
wheel hydraulic brakes, and has
stopped, as the expression is, on a
dime. You are watching him care
fully, we admit, but his brakes are
just a little more efficient than
yours. Result —a bump. It may be
a slight bump, but experience has
taught that even a slight bump will
dent a fender, or a tire carrier, or
rip the spare tire cover, or smash
a lamp or two.
“He gets out, looks at the rear of
his car, snarls at you for not being
more careful, takes your number,
adds a few more remarks and goes
on his way. You, at tbe same time,
inspect your machine, give the other
driver ns good as he has sent, take
his number and go on your way.
Both of you are irritated, and pos
sibly the drive, which started out as
a real pleasure jaunt, has been
spoiled.
No Harm Done.
"Suppose, now, the rear bumper
on his car and the front one on
yours are the same standard height
from the ground. A bump—but no
harm done. You know the bumper
has taken the shock of the collision
and he knows the same thing.
“Bumpers at a standard height
from the ground will take the shock
of every collision, will save property
damage, temper and possible life.
Instead of tangling bumpers: in
stead of smashing lamps, denting
fenders or running tire carriers,
bumpers will he simply bumps, and
not ruinous collisions

ISSUE DON'TS
TO ELIMINATE
FIRE HAZARDS
Fifteen “don’ts” as a means of
eliminating unnecessary fire haz
ards in Milwaukee, have been an
nounced by the fire prevention bu
reau, fire department. Copies are
being distributed to every industrial
plant and household in the city,
Fire Chief Peter J. Steinkellner.
The ’’don’ts” announced today:
Watch the Iron.
Don’t fail to turn off the electric
iron when you have finished using
it, or when answering the telephone,
or in a hurry to leave the premises
Electric irons should always be of
the safety type, and should be
placed on metal stands during inter
vals of non-use.
Don’t increase the size of your
electric fuses. The fuse in your
lighting circuit should not be larg
er than 15-A (amperes) capacity.
Don’t go into closets or attic with
lighted matches or candles. Use
only portable electric lights, hand
flash-light, or do your searching in
the daytime.
Don’t use the “strike anywhere”
match in your house. Use only the
safety “strike on the box” match.
Be sure to keep all matches out of
the reach of children.
Don’t burn trash in the open
near buildings or fences, or permit
children to do so. Use properly con
structed incinerators.
Destroy Ail Rubbish.
Don’t allow rubbish to accumulate
on your premises, especially in the
basement or attic. All rubbish and
useless, discarded articles should be
disposed of Immediately.
Don’t put ashes in wooden boxes
or barrels, or against wooden par
titions.. Keep ashes in metal con
tainers.
Don’t use gasoline, benzine, or
other volatiles for cleaning purposes^
Use only the safety, non-combustible
cleaning fluids.
Don’t permit oily polishing rags
or mops to be kept in your house ex
cept in air-tight metal containers.
Don’t attempt to thaw frozen wa
ter pipes by applying an open torch
or flame of any kind. Pipes should
be wrapped loosely with cloth and
hot water applied.
Don’t discard matches, cigars or
cigarets until certain that all fire is
extinguished.
Use Pipe Thimbles.
Don’t permit unprotected smoke
pipes to pass through or near ceil
ings, roofs or wooden partitions.
(Properly ventilated thimbles
should be used when necessary to
extend smoke-pipes through parti
tions.) Brick chimneys, lined with
flue tile, should be built from the
ground to above the peak of the
roof.
Don’t permit unprotected open
fire-places. Proper spark screens
should always be placed in front of
open fire-places.
Don’t use gasoline, kerosene or
other oils for starting fires. Use
only paper and kindling wood.
Don’t fail to thoroughly inspect
your furnace, smoke-pipes and flues
before starting fires for the winter.
Flues should be cleaned once each
year. Defective or worn-out smoke
pipe should be promptly replaced.
LEVIATHAN RUN
WITH PROFIT
NEW YORK—The Leviathan is
now being operated at a profit.
Instead of showing a loss of
$1,000,000 a year, as predicted by
enemies of the American merchant
marine, the great ship is making
money.
During the fiscal year, ending
July 1 last, a little more than $lO.-
000 was placed to the right side of
the Leviathan’s ledger account after
charging off $500,000 for repairs
and special upkeep.
Tbe figures may seem small to
the uninitiated, but to the shipping
world they will prove amazing. It
has always been maintained by
those opposed to the American mer
chant marine that such big ships as
the Leviathan, Majestic and Beren
garia could not be operated at a
profit.
Holds Up Man to Get
Funds to Feed His
Babes, Goes to Jail
CHICAGO —Lack of work for
himself and food for hts babies
drove Leroy Laßart, 26, to robbery
yesterday. Conscience drove him
to the detective bureau last night.
To Lieut. Timothy Rohan he ten
dered $12.75, with the remark that
he couldn’t stand possession of it
any longer.
"I never did a dishonest thing be
fore in my life,” he said. “But
the kids had to have something to
eat. So I got a monkey wrench and
held up a man. I told him I’d kill
him if he didn’t hand over his
dough. Here it is, all I got from
him. Lock me up.”
A checkup disclosed that John
Smith had been robbed by Laßart.
The funds were returned to him
and Laßart was sent to a cell for
the night.

CANTONESE AND
FENG HOPE TO
GOVERN CHINA
PEKlNG—Marshal Wu Pei-fu. it
is reported, has retired north of the
Yellow river, in Monan province,
owing to heavy desertions among his
troops. Troops are leaving Peking
to re-enforce those on the north
bank.
The Cantonese forces are men
acing the walls of Wuchang, pre
paratory to its capture.
Wuchang Holds Out.
Twentysix Americans, for most
part Episcopalian missionaries, are
among the 31 foreigners in the
besieged city. The reason for the
stubborn defense at Wuchang is due
to the belief that the Cantonese are
determined to proclaim it a capital,
and that after joining Marshal Feng
Yuhsiang’s armies, now rallying
northwest of Peking, by the move
ment in Shensi and Honan prov
inces, they will ask foreign recogni
tion as the government of the ma
jority of the provinces.
The Cantonese movement down
the Yangtze river continues, with
Kukiang as the probable scene of
the next conflict.
Witnessed Fierce Fight.
PEKING —The United Press cor
respondent has just returned from
the 30-mile Chinese front, where the
allied armies of Marshal Chang Tso
lin of Manchuria and Marshal Wu
Pei-fu, central China leader, defeat
ed the Kuominchun (national army)
of Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang, in one
of the great battles of modern China,
in which 200,000 soldiers took part.
Today beyond Kalgan, 125 miles
northwest of Poking, the national
ists are endeavoring to recuperate
from the defeat, and the expected
consolidation of the nationalists
with the Cantonese forces which
have defeated Marshal Wu Pei-fu in
the neighborhood of Hankow pre
sages an extensive nationalist-Can
tonese drive to the sea over a front
of 1,500 miles.
The Cantonese, who hope soon to
eliminate Wu as a factor in central
China, would turn down the Yang
tze river toward Shanghai, while
the nationalists would seek to drive
back Chang’s army, which is now
trying to relieve Wu, toward
Mukden.
40-Pound Trout Prize
Of Canuck Waltonian
PORT DOVER, Ont.—Lake Erie
fishermen are setting a record this
year by the size of their lake trout
captures. The largest of the year
is a 40-pound monster, apparently
a wily patriarch which had grown
to his present size by skilled evasion
of fishermen’s nets for years past.
He was captured by the tug lonia,
which also brought in another of
almost the same weight, while the
Jean S. has a 25-pound specimen to
its credit. The lake’s great varia
tion in depth, it is believed, offers
refuges where the fish may hide in
safety and thereby avoid capture
before they are full grown.

MELLON BACK;
HE TALKS,BUT
SAYS NOTHING
NEW YORK—Andrew W. Mellon,
secretary of the treasury, has re
turned from Europe, but he re
fused to discuss governmental af
fairs with reporters. He reiterated
that his visit was not official, was
not related to international prob
lems. and was wholly social in
nature.
Didn't Discuss Debts.
One of the first questions asked
Mr. Mellon was:
“Did you not discuss the French
debt situation with Premier Briand
or other Frenchmen.”
“No, I did not discuss or say any
thing on the French debt,” was the
reply. “I met a number of men in
political and governmental circles in
Paris and other cities, but in every
case my calls were purely social
ones.”
Efforts to obtain an Inkling of
subjects discussed met with the
reply:
“You will have to excuse me from
saying anything or giving any im
pression concerning the subjects we
discussed.”
Talked With Mussolini.
“From your journeying in France
and Italy and Switzerland, would
you say there is a return of pros
perity
“It would serve no useful purpose
to go into that. One does not see a
country completely when touring
only through portions of it.”
He gave some impressions of
Mussolini, whom he had visited in
Rome. “I had some very pleasant
talks with Mussolini. He is very
cordial and a very interesting man.
He seems to have everything well
in hand.”
“And did you not talk with
Briand in France?”
“I saw a number of representa
tive Frenchmen. We convedsed on
many topics. I found the French
most cordial.”
Conscience Bothers
War Chicken Thief
NEBRASKA ClTY—With his
conscience bothering him because he
had stolen chickens during the Civil
war and desiring to “square ac
counts before it is too late,” Tim
Crook, SO, a war veteran, who lives
in the hill country near Miners
ville, Neb., went before District
Judge Begley here and asked to be
allowed to “plead guilty.” Judge
Begley told him to forget about it.
“You see, when I was in company
A of the 10th Kansas infantry,” the
veteran said, “we didn’t get to eat
but every once in a while, and a
stray shoat or chicken was our meal.
“I guess I shot and stole from the
big plantations as much as the next
one. We were fighting lots and eat
ing little, and maybe it was all
right, but I ain’t felt right about it
ever since.”

KNOW MILWAUKEE —WONDERFUL CITY
Milwaukee Maker
of Many Things
TVT OST industrial cities are dominated by one or
only a few industries. Milwaukee, however, is
a city of many industries. And statistics conclusive
ly prove that Milwaukee is the most versatile city in
its industries of all America.
A city built on such an industrial platform with so
many sturdy, important, vital planks is a wonderful
city in which to live. It is a city which can’t know
what other cities in the country call “hard times.”
Because all times are good times for Milwaukee,
with its host of different industries.
In the metal trades, Milwaukee makes all kinds of
things from the heaviest sort of powerful machin
ery to the finest kind of accurately-constructed wire
goods. Milwaukee makes hundreds of different
kinds of foods, from candy to flour, from meat
packing to milk products.
In the chemical and allied industries, Milwaukee
makes hundreds of chemicals, everything from
drugs and dyes to glass.
In the textile industry, Milwaukee makes everything
from the most adroitly designed millinery to sturdy,
sun-fighting awnings—clothing, gloves, hosiery—
most everything worn by man, woman, or child.
In the leather industry Milwaukee makes every
thing from boots to gloves.
In making of wood products
Milwaukee makes everything
to automobile bodies.
Yes, Milwaukee makes most everything from cigars
to great powerful shovels.
In the building industry, Milwaukee makes every
thing from mirrors to paving material.
And in the wholesale and jobbing business, Mil
waukee handles everything from coal to groceries.
Wonderful city is Milwaukee!. And it is about time
the world knew of its wonder.

HILLTOPS PLAY
BALL; TOO HOT
FOR FOOTBALL
LAKE BEULAH, Wis—Coach
Frank J. Murray and his Marquette
university gridders today start out
on their second and most intensive
week of preliminary training in
their island camp here, and every
one dug in deep this morning to
make the last week a success. The
squad returns to Milwaukee Sat
urday.
Yesterday was visitors’ day in
camp and more than 100 came to
watch the Murraymen go through
their afternoon paces. In the base
ball game, Dick Bader’s nine de
feated Rupert O'Keefe’s outfit, 4 to
3, in 10 innings.
Visitors were disappointed that
Coach Murray cancelled his sched
uled scrimmage, but the weather
continued so warm that the mentors
thought it inadvisable. In fact, it is
now doubtful that there will be
many scrimmages before the team
gets its first game with Lawrence
at Appleton, Oct. 2, as Coach Mur
ray is fearful some of his best men
might be kayoed before that test
which is being taken quite seriously
here.
Yesterday afternoon’s drill opened
with the men going through a new
type of calisthenics directed by Kay
Iverson, the Hilltop trainer. It was
something altogether new to the
Marquette men, consisting mostly of
breathing exercises as adopted by
Swedish gymnasts, and made a tre
mendous hit with the candidates.
Hard Scrimmage
Features Workout
At South Division
Scrimmage with mid season pep
and form was the schedule at South
Saturday, Coach Ihlenfeld driving
his men through 45 minutes, using
three sets of backs with two lines.
Gains through the lines were
scarce as the lines were well split
up and had regulars and reserves
from last year on both sides.
The teams used only a few plays
with Steinmetz calling on one team
and McCarthy on the other. “Doc”
Malone repeatedly tore around the
ends for nice gains, while Rlef and
lloschild did some fine receiving of
passes.
Scrimmage is starting earlier this
year ns South has the three hardest
games in the first part of the sched
ule.
As a pre-season game South will
play Racine High school at Racine,
Oct. 2.

Bohler New Beloit Coach.
Beloit, a member of the Midwest
conference, will have a new coach in
Roy Bohler, when the first call for
candidates is Issued this week.
Bohler, who comes to Beloit with
a great record gained at Washing
ton State, must build his 1920 eleven
with practically all new material.
Beloit’s schedule is the toughest in
many seasons, calling for games
with Notre Dame, Lawrence, Cor
nell, Ripon, Coe and others.
In the Normal school conference.

order named. Ln Crosse, with 13
veterans returning from last year’s
strong squad has the inside track tn
the race for honors, but reports
from Platteville predict the best
team in five years.
Local Normals Promising.
Milwaukee, with Coach Percy
Clapp starting his second year as
mentor, has an exceptionally prom
ising team. Milton (Jack) Murray,
formerly of Marquette University,
High school, will assist Clapp.

kosh will l>e forced to start the
season with an almost entirely new
team, while Stevens Point, Stout,
Superior, River Falls and White
water are not overly optimistic
over their chances to finish at the
top of the conference.

LOUlSVlLLE—Milwaukee’s last
chance to win a pennant in the
American Assn, since 1914, was
buried in a 7 to 2 defeat sustained
at the hands of the Colonels in the
first game of a double-header yes
terday.
By winning that game, the Colo
nels wiped out all mathematical pos
sibility of being dethroned by the
Brewers as the champs of the Hic
key loop, and, now being safely “in”
the title holders are making prep
arations to meet the Toronto, Inter
national league club, for the world's
minor league title. The Maple
Leafs also cinrhed the flag yester
day, finishing eight games ahead of
Baltimore.
Brews Win Second.
The Brewers retained their hold
on second place by winning the sec
ond game from the Colonels, 6 to 4,
but the position is by no means
cinched. The two games were played
before the second largest crowd
that ever snw a ball game In Louis
ville—l4,lo3 being the official count.
Joe Pawson was on the mound
against Claude Jonnard in the first
game and tc the former goes credit
for putting the last spike in the A.
A. championship for the Colonels.
He let the Brewers down with six
hits and in only one inning—the
second —did he permit any runs.
Jonnard hurled nice ball for five
rounds, but blew up in the sixth in
which the champions dented the
plate four times. He retired in the
next round, in which two more
were scored and Joe Eddelman fin
ished up.
Lamotte Hits Homer.
The two Milwaukee runs were
stored when Strohm hit a double
and scampered in ahead of Lamotte
when the Milwaukee second base
man dropped a home run into cen
ter field. After that Dawson settled
down and only five men reached first
base.
Singles by Guyon, Anderson and
Ellis gave the Colonels the first of
four runs in the sixth. Devormer’s
out advanced the two runners and
both scored on Cotter’s single. Cot
ter stole second and scored on
Shanks’ single. The two in the
eighth were the result of an error
by Brief, a double steal and Young’s
wild throw to center. A double by
Shanks and Dawson's single which
bounded over Strohm's head, gave
the Colonels their final run in the
eighth.
Sanders Wins Second.
Roy Handers was nicked for 10
hits in the second game, but the
Brews made the^r same number of
bingles count to better advantage to
win the nightcap, 6 to 4. Otis
Wicker, a bush leaguer, was on the
mound for the Colonels when the
second started. He lasted less than
four innings in which the Brewers
nicked him for nine hits and five
tuns, Ed Holley finishing up.
Four of the six Brewer tallies
were shoved over in the third,
’hbourg singled to left and took
i^d when the ball got aw’ay from
is. He scored on Shulte’s base
it to left. Griffin beat out a bunt
and scored along with Shulte when
Brief hit a double into right. A
two-bagger by Lamotte put Bunny
over.
In the fourth, a double by San
ders, a safe bunt by Richbourg and
Shulte’s infield out gave the Brews
another. A triple by Richbourg
paved the way for the final run in
the sixth. The game was called in
this inning by agreement to allow
the Brewers to catch a train for
Columbus where they ojien a series
with the lowly Senators today.

Despite a three-point defeat, the
Milwaukee Badgers carried off most
of the honors in their initial game
in tho National Pro Football league
at Athletic park yesterday when
they were downed by the Chicago
Bears, 10 to 7.
When it came to team personnel,
the Badgers were outclassed by the
visitors, hut the fierceness of their
attack after they were trailing by
10 points almost turned defeat into
victory.
The Bears, with such players as
Paddy Driscoll, Walquist, Healy,
Lyman and Sternaman in the line
up, is a teeam that is perhaps the
equal of any professional eleven in
the country.
Badgers Fighting Team.
The Milwaukee lineup consisted of
men, most of them just out of
school, and new at the professional
stuff, hut its enthusiasm and fight
more than offset its lack of expe
rience. t Given more practice in
which to holster its weak spots, the
Badgers should give Milwaukee the
best pro team it has ever had.
The Badgers’ best defensive work
was shown around the ends, where
Dilweg and Neacy, former Colgate
star, were playing. The two John
nies, Bryan, team manager, and
Heimsch, carried the ball well. Ash
more at right tackle and Burke at
center were others who did out
standing work for the Badgers.
The Bears kicked off to the
Badgers, who were unable to make
downs, and Heimsch puntetd across
the goal line from the 50-yard mark.
From their ow.i 20-yard line the Chi
cagoans, with Driscoll. Walquist and
Knop carrying the ball, advanced to
the same position on the Milwau
kee side.
Driscoll Kicks for Score.
The Badgers held long enough to
get the oval and thei\ returned it to
midfield, where Knop intercepted a
pass. Another return trip was start
ed hy the Bears, which ended with
Paddy Driscoll booting a drop kick
from the five-yard line, giving his
team a 3 to 0 lend as the quarter
ended.
Milwaukee appeared at its weak
est in the second period. Its of
fensive was unable to gain, and its
defensive crumbled, with the result
that the Windy City team gained
steadily on straight plays and then
sent Knop over for a touchdown
from the two-yard line. Driscoll
kicked goal, a drop. Score, 10 to 0.
In the third quarter the Badgers
opened up against the Bears’ revised
lineup which consisted of Sterna
man, quarter Senn and Mullen,
halves; Hnnny and Lemon, ends,
and Fleckenstein, center.
Badgers Score Touchdown.
Two forward passes, Heimsch to
Dilweg and Bryan to Hollquist, aid
ed materially in bringing the ball
to within a yard of the Chicago goal,
but the visitors held as the quarter
ended.
Hanny, punting from behind his
own goal, sent the ball 35 yards.
Several off tackle plays, two more
forward passes, and the pigskin was
less than two feet from the visitors’
goal.
Heimsch scored and Curtain, who

extra point with n place kick. Score,

LAKE GENEVA
SEEKS U. S.
ICE MEET
LAKE GENEVA. Wis.—Confer
ence between local men and officials
of the Western Skaters’ Assn, is
scheduled in Chicago today with a
view towards obtaining the national
skating meet at Lake Geneva this
winter.
Chicago skaters are reported to
favor Lake Geneva, as they have
been unable to secure the meet in
their city because of the inferior
quality of the ice. Should they
therefore work to bring the meet
here, the Geneva invitation will be
presented to the national committee
when it meets in Pittsburgh next
month.
The national meet lasts six days
and usually includes about Go<s con
testants from all sections of the
country. Thousands of spectators
also are the rule. Paid admissions
at St. Cloud. Ontario, last year num
bered 15,000,
Plans for financing the meet here
already are under consideration, in
cluding the furnishing of a grand
stand seating 5,000 persons and ade
quate shelter houses for the contest
ants.

ney, aspiring for the heavyweight

spiring landscape, breath mountain

day.

ent from the commercial attitude of

ism by Jack Kearns, his former

lantic City, and although he barred

This style was born of a grate
ful admiration for all things
French and a no less hearty dis
like of England. French empire
designs, clumsily adapted, deter
mined the new fashion, but it was
later modified by a New York fur
niture maker, Dunean Phyfe, who
brought out its latent loveliness.
In the early period the furniture
was large, massive, rectangular,
often topped by heavy cornices. It
had, however, one merit: it was
substantial and solid.
The mirror in the lower left
corner is the ancestor of our mod
ern bureau. It was during the
empire period that center tables
made their first appearance. They
were generally of the pedestal
type, with claw feet, closely re
sembling the dining room table
shown here, but on a smaller
scale. The four-poster bed was
still made, but without canopy.
The posts were heavy and ex
travagantly carved, with pine
apple finials, signifying hospital
ity. This motif, together with the
cornucopia, is used constantly in
empire ornamentation.
The classic lines of the period
were good, the outward curve
with rolled-over sofa arms being
especially graceful; but much of
this fundamental elegance was
spoiled by heaviness, over-orna
mentation and somber coloring.

pered with and criminally stained
an iniquitous reddish color, while
tho upholstery was of a corre
spondingly dark and depressing

here that I had changed my mind
about (a) the cropping of the
hair of women, and (b) the par

had sort of implied that the muti

that the participation in the bas
ketball game tended to make a
girl too bold. Soon afterward a
correspondent who called himself
“Jim” suggested that I hadn’t
changed my mind at all; he
thought I had just lowered my
standard. “Jim” and his argu
ment remihd me of a barberry
thorn; it got under my skin, all
right. But I still maintain that I
have actually changed my mind
on these points, and I do not be
lieve I have lowered my standard.
We still have with us the “dou
ble standard” of morals, although
it may not be quite so barefaced
as it was a generation ago. A
young man may still break the
moral law without suffering the
loss of his reputation; a young
woman may not.
It does seem that we are mov
ing toward a single standard and
getting farther away from the
double standard in recent years.
But this single standard which we
seem to approach is a lowered
standard, not the old ideal single
standard at all. Where there is
so much smoke there is usually
some fire; all the talk about flap
perism, the wild ways of modern
youth and so on has some sound
foundation. Nevertheless the
same old double standard on
which our fathers and grandfa
thers based their oat sowing pre
vails today. The young man of
1926 still “settles down” after a
more or less lurid interval and

pects to find himself a wife as
pure as a man’s children’s mother
ought to be. Some of the sad
wrecks in our crowded divorce
courts indicate that —that the sin
gle standard ain’t what she used
to be.
However, in spite of everything,
there are still plenty of good
women in the world, and as a
matter of honor and chivalry the
man who would marry a good

sent evidence of his fitness to

double standard of morals under

the onus of handing a certificate

sent, to an engagement.

standing is known to the parent
or guardian, and it is reasonable
though not infallible evidence

It is true that the average length
of human life has increased nearly
15 years in the last 20, but this in
crease has been obtained by the pre
ventive measures applied to the
early years and the saving of life
from 5 to 40.
The death rate after 45 years of
life in the United States has in
creased and is steadily mounting.
The average death rate of all ages
in the United States 4a 1023 was
90 per 100,000. The death rate
above 45 was 156 per 100,000.
An analysis of the causes of death
shows that the largest number of
deaths after 45 are due to heart and
blood vessel diseases; kidney dis
ease and cancer. But the arresting
fact is that more than half the
deaths in this middle life period are
preventable and should not occur
until many years later.
This sacrifice of life and energy
at its most productive period is not
only a sociologic factor of tre
mendous import; it is an economic
loss of incalculable value to the na
tion, because we are thus losing men
and women at the period of their
lives when, by training and expeii
ence, they are prepared to do most
for the country. It is unnecessary;
sheer waste of life and efficiency.
What may be done to prevent the
unnecessary deaths from the heart
and blood vessel diseases?
These diseases begin insidiously
and usually very gradually. They

The average man or women eats
too much and lives on badly pre

a regime, if adopted, is the result of

should be a yearly health audit and
the determination to follow the in

What has been said regarding the
heart and blood vessel diseases ap
plies equally well to kidney diseases.
They begin just as insidiously and
frequently do terrific damage before

The death rate of cancer in the
United States is on the increase. It
is agreed that continued irritation,
unsanitary habits and bad hygiene,
especially in persons who have a
history of cancer in the family,
cause the disease to develop in
human beings.
In its early stages, cancer is gen
erally curable. All persistent sores,
unnatural discharges and growths,
lumps or tumors are danger indi
cations and demand immediate
skilled examination and advice.
Despite this, however, most per

the wrecking of their health and
bodily vigor through drinking wa
ter, as it pours from the faucets,
but contaminated as it is taken
from the glass. The common drink
ing glass, that is not carefully ster
ilized between users, contains the
germs left by all other users and
these are absorbed with the drink.
As the ordinary requirement for

each day and this quota is met in
from 10 to 30 drinks the danger

SAVING TIME IN
PREPARATION
OF DESSERT
“At least 20 minutes a day can
be saved by making ‘double des
serts,’” suggests Mildred Weigley
Wood, of the American Home Eco
nomics Assn.. In the October issue of
McCall’s. And she proves it with
some clever recipes for appetizing
dishes. The general idea of her
plan is explained as follows:
“Two desserts in one may be of
two types. First is the kind which
can be made in sufficient quantity
to serve twice and which is of such
a nature that it can be kept over
an intervening day and served a
first and third day.
“A date pudding, such as the one
given below, is a good illustration
of this kind, for it keeps well sev
eral days if it is put in a tightly
covered dish or in the Ice-box. An
other illustration of this kind would
be the making of a covered pie, such
as apple, and baking a pie fihell at
the same time which two days later
could be used for a cream, butter
scotch or chocolate piey The extra
pie-crust takes almost no extra time
to make when the first pie is being
prepared.
More Variety, Less Labor.
“The second type of double des
sert is the sort where a foundation
mixture is made the first day and
part of it used for that day’s des
sert. Then with a slight variation
the remaining portion is served the
next day.
“These double desserts have, I es
timate, saved me an average of 20
minutes every other day and some
times more, both because of the
shortened time for preparation on
the second day and the saving on
dishwashing.”
Here are two of the attractive
recipes carrying out these ideas:
Date and Bread Crumb Pudding.
This serves a family of four
twice. It can lie served the first
and second, or first and third days.
Two eggs, one cup sugar, one and
one-half cups bread crumbs (soft
broken bread), one-half cup chopped
nuts, one teaspoon baking powder,
one-eighth teaspoon salt and three
quarters cup chopped dates. Beat
eggs until light. Add sugar, then H
bread crumbs, nuts, baking-powder
and salt mixed. Add dates and
bake in shallow pan in slow oven
(325 degrees Fahrenheit) about 45
minutes. Cut in squares and serve
with cream.
Coconut Cake and Pineapple Cake.
These two desserts are prepared
with the idea that a piece of fresh,
appetizing-looking cake suffices for
a dessert.
Use either a foundation yellow or
white cake, doubling the recipe if
small. Divide the batter so that
there will be enough in one por
tion for as many large-sized cup
cakes as there are persons to be
served. Bake the rest of the batter
in any form desired, as a loaf or
layer cake for a coconut cake. Pre
pare a boiled frosting and divide it
into two parts. Add shredded coco
nut to one portion for the large
cake. Leave the other portion plain.
While waiting for the frosting to
cool to right consistency, hollow out
cup cakes and till centers with well
drained shredded pineapple. Re
place tops and cover cakes with
plain frosting. These cakes keep
moist and are like fresh cake for
second day’s dessert, although pre
pared entirely the day before. Put
coconut frosting between and on top
of layer cake and serve the day it
is made.
