RDAD ORDERS
EQUIPMENT
CHICAGO—One of the largest
orders for railroad equipment in
some time will soon be placed by the
North Western road. The directors
have authorized the purchase of
various types of passenger and
freight cars which it is estimated
will involve an expenditure of be
tween $12,000,000 and $13,000,000.
The inquries for the equipment, it
is understood, will be released to
the car builders within the next 30
days.
The purchase of the following
equipment is proposed: 100 steel
passenger cars, 23 baggage and
smoking cars. 10 steel baggage cars
and the rebuilding of 35 steel pas
senger units. The freight equip
ment includes 1,000 automobile cars,
500 steel hopper cars. 500 stock cars,
250 steel ore cars, 100 gondolas, 100
Oat cars, 25 steel cabooses and 2
special gun cars.
The demand for railroad equip
ment in the last week was the
largest in some time. The Railway
Age announces that the Canadian
Gypsum Co. has ordered three loco
motives from the Montreal works of
the American Locomotive Co., and
that the Sudoesta de Bahia Brazil
has ordered three Pacific type en
gines from the Baldwin Locomotive
W orks.
The minority stockholders of the
Cleveland, Cincinnati, Chicago St.
Louis railroad have filed suit in the
United States district court at Cin
cinnati to enjoin the leasing of that
road to the New York Central rail
road, which recently announced that
it proposes to take over by lease
five rail lines now controlled by it
or its subsidiary companies. The
lines to be operated under the pro
posed lease are the company’s prin
cipal subsidiaries, the Michigan Cen
tral, the Cleveland. Cincinnati, Chi
cago St. Louis, the Chicago St.
Louis, the Cincinnati Northern, the
Chicago, Kalamazoo Saginaw
and the Evansville Terre Haute.
Under the proposed plan the lease
of the Big Four provides for an
annual rental of preperred stock and
10 per cent on the preferred stock
and 10 per cent on the common stock
not owned by the New York Central.
The minority holders contend that
the proposed terms of the lease will
prevent the accumulation of any
further surplus, as all the profits
will go to the New York Central
railroad and this in effect will give
the holders of the majority stock a
larger dividend than the minority.

MINERAL INDUSTRIES SHOWN
IN 2,000,000 FOOT MOVIE
WASHINGTON —The largest col
lection of educational motion pic
ture films depicting the mining,
treatment, distribution and utiliza
tion of the numerous essential min
erals ever compiled is in the pos
session of the bureau of mines of
the department of commerce. The
bureau’s motion picture library com
prises more than 50 subjects relat
ed to the mineral industries of .he
nation.
The more than 2,000,000 feet of
motion picture film now possessed
by the bureau represent an expen
diture of almost $1,000,000.
A number of films depicting the
production, refining and distribu
tion of petroleum have been made
by the bureau. The World Struggle
for Oil, a seven-reel feature, visual
izes the story of petroleum in all
parts of the globe, from the earliest
use of the material, as pitch,
smeared on Noah’s ark. The Story
of Petroleum, in four reels, begins
with the location of a new well by
the geologist and carries the story
to the distribution of gasoline by
service stations. Mexico and Its Oil,
The Story of a Mexican Oil Gusher
and Through Oil Lands of Europe
and Africa are other films depict
ing graphically the story of the de
velopment, by American capital and
enterprise, of the oil fields of for
eign lands.
Safety in Oil.
The bureau of mines is undertak
ing an intensive campaign for the
promotion of safety in the oil Indus
try. Two films, When Wages Stop,
or Safety First in the Petroleum In
dustry. and Live and Let Live, show
the safe and unsafe ways of produc
ing oil.

wholesalers and dealers in various

months ended with July, 1926, to
taled 2,370,817,000 gallons, com
pared with 2,039,881,000 gallons in

increase of 330,936,000 gallons, or
16.2 per cent, according to the
American Petroleum Institute.

32 states in July, 1926, totaled 424,-
705,000 gallons, against 376,058,000
gallons in July, 1925, an increase
of 41,279,000 gallons, or 12.9 per
cent.

reported for Texas was the largest
for any state in the list. It showed
a gain of 6,669,000 gallons over
July, 1925, or 15.6 per cent, and
4,293,000 gallons over June this
year. Indiana was second with 31,-
600.000 gallons, gaining more than
5,000,000 over July last year and
nearly 3.000,00 gallons over June.

lons, consumption in July of 29,-

STEEL EXHIBIT
IS NOW OPEN
CHICAGO—For five days the In
ternational Steel and Machine Tool
Exposition is now open to the pub
lic on the Municipal Pier. More
than 100,000 visitors are expected
to visit the big industrial display
in the course of its stay.
Coincident with the exposition,
meetings of the American Society
for Steel Treating opened at the
Drake hotel with industrialists and
scientists interested in the manu
facture, uses and production and
sale of iron and steel in its many
forms, attending.
The machines and tools which
make up the exhibits are said to
form the most complete collection
illustrative of America’s supremacy
in mechanical skill and industry,
ever assembled in Chicago. More
than $1,000,000 of machines, cap
able of producing practically every
kind of steel product in use
throughout the world, are on show.

NEW YORK—A week nfter the
earthquake of September. 1023,
alien the smoke and fumes had
partly cleared away from the east
ern coasts, careful observers as
serted that Japan was crippled
for 25 years to come. Such
forecasts seemed well based when
the damage was surveyed. Tokio,
the capital, almost completely de
molished; Yokohama a mass >f
ruins; wealth totaling between one
and one and one-half billion dollars
destroyed; the economic organiza
tion and the finances of the country
disrupted and weakened.
It is apparent that the prophets
were wrong. Almost normal condi
tions have returned to Japan, ac
cording to travelers. Silk exports
last year were the largest in the
country’s history, quotation on Ja
jmnese bonds indicate a return of
confidence, exchange is only two
points off par, and the trade bal
ance is almost normal.
Entire City Rebuilt.
Within three months after the
earthquake, tramways and railway
services were again in operation in
Tokio. and the water mains and
electric connections had been re
stored.
Permanent rebuilding was for
some time held up, but this labor
Is now rapidly nearing completion
and a new Tokio, with broad
Straight streets, adequate parks, and
rectangular divisions, is appearing
on the horizon.
Economic Reorganization.
Japanese statesmen have seized
this opportunity to reconstruct the
economic organization of the coun
try so that is would harmonize
with the industrial changes that
have taken place since the turn of
the century. Mr. Hamaguchi, the
finance minister, has recently point
ed out that three of the knottiest
problems bearing upon the finan
cial and economic structure of the
country have already been solved
tax reform, tariff revision, and the
reorganization of the semi-govern
mental banks. There still remain
to be readjusted the problems of
the general credit situation and the
Improvement of the country's for
eign trade.
Of these two, foreign trade seems
nearer to approaching normal. The
foreign trade balance is one of the
most reliable barometers of Jap
nneso prosperity. Japan has nor
mally an unfavorable trade balance;
before the war it was from 50,000,-
000 yen to 100,000.000 yen. This
unfavorable balance is offset by
various invisible imports estimated
between 200,000.000 and 300,000,-
000 yen annually. Subsequent to
the earthquake, imports took a tre
mendous jump, due to receipts of
lumber and other materials needed
for reconstruction purposes; while
on the other hand exports almost
eased. The year 1924 witnessed an
unfavorable balance of 643,057,000
yen.
Announcement has just been made
by the minister of commerce that
for the first six months of 1926 the
Unfavorable balance amounts to
897.500,000 yen, which compares
with 518,000,000 yen adverse bal
ance for the first six months of 1925
and 004,304.000 yen for the corres
ponding period of 1924.
These figures are considered de-1
Veptive. The first six months of
the year is the season of heavy im
ports; in July the tide turns with
ihe commencement of the outward
ilk movement. Last year this tide
n so heavy that the year-end
Xed an unfavorable balance of
jy 267,008,056 yen, and if the silk
crop proves as profitable this year
as last, the close of the year will
witness a trade balance almost
formal.
American prosperity, which is
Characterized by the United States
'departmen of commerce as having
Reached in 1925 the highest mark in
history, is largely responsible for
the great rebound in Japanese ex
ports. Silk ranks second in value
nmong the commodities America
purchased abroad —being surpassed
only by rubber. Silk purchases in
5925 amounted to $396,286,000. Of
these imports $360,659,000 came
from Japan, or 95 per cent of the
Japanese crop. The United States
|»ought other things from Japan,
bringing its total export to this
country up to $412,563,000. Forty-
Jour per cent of Japanese exports
last year came to the United States.

INADEQUACY OF
GIRLS’ SCHOOL
The extension of women’s rights
has not helped delinquent girls, Civil
J. E. Cordis asserted today at the
Optimist club luncheon in the Mil
waukee Athletic club, in which he
severely criticized the inadequacy of
the Wisconsin Industrial School for
Girls, 465 Lake Drive.
“The buildings are overcrowded,
old and insufficient,” Judge Cordes
said.
“There is an Inadequacy of bath
rooms, toilet facilities and wash
basins, and this is intended to be a
correction institution or reform
school.
“I inquired about fire protection
and was informed that there is a
night watchman, or rather watch
woman that she is the wife of the
fireman, and gets S3O a month to
make the rounds at night.
Woman On Job.
“No one believes she does so to
any extent; she has no mechanical
device to operate to record her
rounds and n superintendent cannot
learn much from her because she
doesn’t speak English. This insti
tution is under the jurisdiction of
the state board of control. Isn’t it
too bad about the poor old state of
Wisocnsin?”
Judge Cordes also pointed out
that in one building of the school
there is a sink, and above it, a one
inch pipe in which five holes are
hored. A small stream of water
flows out of each hole and this is
the only facility the girls in that
building have for washing their
hands and faces.
“You would laugh if it were not
so tragic,” Judge Cordes com
mented.
Judgment Must Be Used.
In remarking on probation as the
best remedy in the great majority of
instances. Judge Cordes emphasized
that judgment, founded on expe
rience, must be used in the appli
cation of probation measures and it
must not be abused or made light of
so as to become a joke.
“The boy must not go home to his
neighborhood to pose as a hero in
the opinions of other boys and cause
them to emulate his example. I have
been told that there has been con
siderable of this.”
From June 1,1924, to June 1, 1925
Milwaukee’s Juvenile court, accord
ing to figures presented by Judge
Cordes, handled 3.221 cases, involv
ing over 6,000 children.
Complaints concerning 894, were
settled by probation officers with
out court action. Of 2.6G1 delin
quent children, 1,426 were placed
on probation.

BERLlN—lncreasing prevalence
of nervous disease and mental dis
orders is the direct result of not
enough houses to go around, say
medical authorities here. Not only
do tuberculosis and infectious dis
eases always make decided gains
where there is overcrowding, but
the psychoneurotic element of the
population has been seriously affect
ed by lack of adequate accommoda
tions.
Physicians have often had to co
operate with the housing authorities
where tenants have become unbal
anced and nervously unstable as a
result of two or three families liv
ing in the same flat. In some in
stances tenants have killed other
tenants in a fit of mania and many
have become undu’y depressed and
insane, according to a report to the
Berlin Forensic society.
All the cases that have brought
about serious disturbances have oc
curred, it is said, among people that
before the war occupied their own
flats or houses and were not accus
tomed to sharing their dwelling
with others, who, under the present
circumstances, frequently come
from quite a different class of so
ciety.
Fifty families, with the aid of
mothers’ pension, lived on a aver
age of $924.68 a year during the
five-year period, 1920-1924, in Buf
falo, N. Y., according to records of
the Erie county board of child wel
fare. The per capital expenditure
was $194.26. Those 50 families
comprised 238 individuals, includ
ing ISB children of whom only 13
were over 1G years of age.

ARGUING AROUND SOCIALISM
J. Studdert Kennedy, chaplain of King George of
England, admits in The Dearborn Independent that the
unequal distribution of wealth is the cause of classes and
class wars, but does not believe that voting for Socialism
can bring the wisest and most honest men into power to
administer the properties of the nation.
“The mere transference of property power from the
self-seeking few, even if so they really are, to the self
seeking many, would not lead to the Kingdom of God, but
to chaos and confusion,” he asserts.
To that we readily agree. The king’s chaplain is
mistaken only in assuming that this statement refutes a
Socialist position. We know and teach all the time that
it is necessary to breed a social spirit in place of the short
sighted and selfish individualism taught in the schools of
private capitalism.
But what does the chaplain intend to do about it, aside
from declining to vote for Socialism? Nothing practical,
you may be sure. He says that strong and able men will
always get property and power, but they should be taught
that they are strong, able and property owners, because
God gave them these things in trust.
Well, there’s no profit in arguing that point with a
king’s chaplain. He would naturally claim that the king
and his lords stand in with God. We won’t even ask him
to explain why God has done nothing to help the people,
although he admits that God’s trustees have done badly.
We will only say that some day, not so very far away, the
people will take matters into their own hands.
The Dearborn Independent says that the chaplain’s
viewpoint on Socialism is new. Its editor ought to know
better. The king’s chaplain peddles the same old chest
nut which has served the ruling classes of all ages to
justify their brutalities and ask devout Christians to wait
for God to act.
We know very well that the trade unions and Socialist
parties badly need men and women with the experience
and ability to manage large enterprises. But we also be
lieve that they will develop such experience and ability
more rapidly by voting and working for them than by
waiting for the divinity of the king’s chaplain to hand
them out as a free gift.
Anyway, it is a libel on an All-wise and All-good
Being to say that he picked the ruling classes as trustees
for their strength and ability. According to the best
authorities of Christianity, Christ himself never thought
much of the rich and powerful. They haven’t improved
since his day.
OUR CANADIAN NEIGHBORS
The Liberal party has put Mackenzie King back in
power and dealt an effective rebuke to Gov. Gen. Byng.
Which shows that names don’t scare our own hundred
percenters.
American capitalists have invested about twice the
money in Canada that the British have. A Tory governor
working to make American money in Canada pay the
war debts of the capitalist government* in Great Britain
finds little love on this side of the Canadian border.
Great Britain is the largest single debtor of Uncle
Sam in Europe, and Canada the largest single debtor of
Uncle Sam on the American continent. Divine providence
just had to appoint a Liberal premier trustee of Canadian
wealth.
Byng is a sort of British Pershing. Wall Street
thought very highly of him, until he became governor
general of Canada and gave Wall Street a taste of its own
protective tariff. Then Providence had to decide whether
to be pro-British or pro-American, and, as usual, the side
with the strongest cashbox won. Now we are going to live
in sweet harmony with our Canadian neighbors on a reci
procity basis. But that does not go for Europe.
HORRORS! SOVIET MONEY!
Please note the following two items. They were not
meant to be read together, but somebody always spoils
a good plan. One item says that an American company
will do $60,000,000 worth of electrical work fo'r the Mos
cow government along the Dniester river. Another says
that the Arkansas American legion had an attack of shell
shock, because the Mena Commonwealth college was said
to have received SIOO,OOO from the I. W. W. and $50,000
from Soviet Russia.
The Mena story turned out to be a yellow bird hatched
in some badly battered legion brain, but the other story
is true. We haven’t heard any American legion local
raising hell about the soviet money that goes into Wall
Street pockets. Wonder why?

KIPLING’S POOR SHOWING
Without British imperialism, there would be no Rud
yard Kipling. This axiom is irrefutable. It puts Kipling t.
personal and literary case into a nutshell. If any one
wants to make a pun on that, he can go as far as he likes.
We mean to say that it was not Kipling's literary
quality, but the imperialist note in all his stuff that made
him one of the leading British writers. Within the narrow
and on the whole stupid circle of that imperialism, Kip
ling’s whole literary activity is confined
In all the bulky mass of Kipling’s writings, there is
hardly one whole page that sounds a social note. The
workers whom he glorifies at rare intervals are those who
sweat and swear faithfully in the service of British cap
italism and imperialism.
The only social line of his that we remember is that
which admits the claim of the workers to the wealth pro
duced by them, because they have paid for it in full with
their blood. But even this line does not make a plea for
Socialism. It is only a plea to the rich to treat their faith
full slaves better, lest they forget themselves and break
their chains.
Over against this lone instance in -which the working
people are considered as human there are sneers after
sneers at the workers who think for themselves and who
refuse to bear their class fate without protests.
Kipling’s Indian tales gave him the right sendoff.
Here he paints the soldiers and officials of British im
perialism as heroes carrying the white man’s burden. Any,
Indian who dares to think for himself is as much of at
villain as a British worker who hates capitalism and im
perialism. But an Indian who fights other Indians in the
service of London is a real man to pattern after.
The same narrow-minded nationalist view is ex
pressed in Kipling’s stories and poems dealing with other
governments. If they are the allies of British imperial
ism, they are great and noble creatures. If enemies, they
are wild animals, fiends in human shape, monsters that
must be exterminated for the good of human progress.
For human progress, morality, nobility and virtue mean
British progress.
When czarist Russia threatened India, it was Adam-
Zat, The Bear That Walks Like a Man. When the czar
became a British ally against the kaiser, Kipling cele
brated him as a great and noble man. He had not one
word of sympathy for the victims of czarism, except so
far as any sympathy of that kind could be exploited for
British imperialism.
Only when a millionaire’s son is soft and mushy and
unfit to ride on the neck of the lower classes, has Kip
ling scorn for him and praise for the “Captains
Courageous” that make a man of him. On the other hand,
“Soldiers Three” can be smutty and dirty roughnecks, so
long as they serve British rule they are fine characters.
They may even strip their clothes and run stark naked
through Lung-Tung-Pen to the glee of Indian women,
provided that the episode ends in a crushing defeat of re
bellious Indian men.
So we need not feel bad about it when this narrow
minded and vicious old man, having lost his son in the
World war that he hailed with joy, though millions of
other people’s sons had to die, turns sour against Uncle
Sam over a matter of pounds and shillings. He is still
the same old fogy that he always was. He never followed
in the steps of any Christ that could not be worshipped as
a Christ of British imperialism. The American imperial
ists, who are just as fogy on their own side, will come back
at him in his own -way.
ORGANIZED LABOR MUST REPRESENT
GENERAL WELFARE
The critics and enemies of organized labor frequently
declare that only a minority of the workers are within
the ranks of the movement, and therefore deny the claim
of leadership made by the latter. Facts sustain the charge
that only a minority of the workers are organized; but
facts also show that this minority give direction and S'
the pace for the mass.
There is no intelligence in a mob; it wastes its energy
in struggling at cross-purposes, and accomplishes nothing
but its own defeat. It is only when men confer and agree
upon an objective and a method of attaining it that ad
vancement is made. Organization is the sign of enlight
enment and the passport to progress.
But this is not a theory; experience speaks in support
of the claim. It has been the organized minority which
has formulated the demands of labor and has led in the
struggle for their realization. Yes, it has been the organ
ized workers who have put up the money and made the
sacrifice for the emancipation of the sodden mass of ig
norant and deceived workers who too often help to fasten
on themselves chains of slavery.
Wage increases and reduction in the length of the
working day have not come voluntarily from the employ
ers of labor but have been wrung from them by the or
ganized workers, often in spite of the resistance of the
unorganized workers. This fact the employers would like
to conceal if not deny. They would like to give the im
pression that they are the custodians of their workers*
welfare and that the activity of the unions is interference
with the liberty of the unorganized.
But these pretenses are not taken very seriously by
any one. The mass of the unorganized is now ready to
admit that all labor benefits from the efforts of the or
ganized; that the latter sets the wage scale and forces
reasonable working hours and proper working conditions.
Who ever heard of ‘'Chamber of Commerce” advocat
ing a wage increase or a shortening of the workday? Or
going before the legislature for social and industrial leg
islation?
On the contrary, millions of dollars are spent by the
employing class and its auxiliary organizations to block
industrial and social measures. In fact these are the
forces that must be met by every force making for humane
working conditions in industry. Child labor, minimum
wage and workmen’s compensation laws as well as factory
regulations have come in spite of the opposition of anti
union forces.
In spite of the propaganda in favor of the “American
Plan,” so-called, in the guise of “freedom for the worker
and the employer,” unorganized workers admit that thei r
real friends are the labor unions, and that the latter alor
stand for the interests of the toiler.
It is because of this responsibility and confidence that
organized labor must discharge its obligation with scrupu
lous care. It cannot afford to betray faith reposed in its
integrity, for it means a fatal weakening of its influence.
In other words, while it is not possible to get all the work
ers into the unions for various reasons it is possible to
enlist their sympathy and moral support in every salutary
undertaking of the organized workers—and no other sort
of object should be undertaken.
Organized labor must always put itself in the position
of leader of movements which have the general welfare in
view. Just in proportion to its adherence io this principle
will it extend in influence and increase in strength, and
enlist the loyal support of the mass of the people.—Minne
sota Union Advocate.

COLUMBUS. Wis.— There was an
epedemic of flat tires here today
following an attempt late yesterday
to pursue five bandits who raided
the First National bank here and
escaped with $5,500 in currency and
several hundred thousand dollars
in non-negotiable securities.
When news of the bank raid was
spread through the town every
available automobile was com
mandeered to carry a posse in pur
suit of the bandits.
But the bandits had not only
carefully planned the robbery, but
their escape as well.
All along the road over which
they traveled out of the city, they
scattered large headed roof nails.
Automobiles of the posse were put
out of commission as the result of
flat tires and the bandits easily got
away.
None of the five men were masked
and not a shot was fired during the
robbery. A few words of profanity
was the extent of the violence used
during the raid.
One at Wheel.
Four of the men entered the bank.
One stayed at the door as a guard,
while three gathered together all
cash and securities in sight. A fifth
man sat at the wheel of a waiting
automobile.
When his companion stepped into
the automobile with two sacks of
money and securities, he calmly
lighted a cigaret and drove away.
The bandits, according to the
cashier, Clarence Miller, were in the
bank just eight minutes. They all
wore overalls.
Eight persons were in the bank
at the time of the robbery and all
were forced to lie on the floor and
later crawl into the vault.
According to Miller the bandits
missed about $2,500 in a drawer at
the teller’s window and more than
$50,000 in Liberty bonds, which
were stored in the vault and which
they knocked to the floor while fill
ing their bags.
Chief Draws Gun.
Miller was talking to a Chicago
bond salesman when the bandits en
tered. The leader of the gang
walked directly to a counter where
Miller stood and pushing aside the
bond salesman, drew a revolver.
The other bandits also drew their
revolvers.
Then the bandits started gather
ing together all of the cash and se
curities in sight and placed their
loot in two bags. Before leaving
th building the bandits ordered all
those in the bank to crawl into the
vault. Miller pleaded with them
not to lock the vault, so they fas
tened the outside door and ran to
the waiting automobile and speeded
away.
In the bank with Miller were: Lil
lian Hiller. Mary Manley, Miller H.
Koch and E. J. Jackson.
The bandits in gathering together
their loot placed much worthless
paper in the bags, being in such a
hurry to make their getaway that
they did not examine what they
were taking.

EDITION
BIG SIKORSKI
PLANE BURSTS
INTO FLAMES
Lieut. Fonck, U. S<
Aide Escape
Death.
BY PAIL W. WHITE.
ROOSEVELT FIELD, WEST
BURY, N. Y.—Rene Fonck's long
heralded attempt to fly with three
companions from New York to Parß
started today amid the acclaim of
a thousand people and three min
utes later it ended, the plane In
flames and two of the crew dead.
Charles Clavier of France, radi«
mau, and James Islamoff, the Rus*
sian mechanic, were burned to
death, when the running gear of
the plane gave way and it plunged
into a gulley.
Fonck and Lieut. Lawrence W.
Curtin, United States navy, hll
second in command, escaped unin
jured.
Doors Had Jammed.
The bodies of Clavier and
Islamoff were found in the ruins ot
the plane, partly buried in the ashes
of the cockpit. They were side by
side. The bodies were almost un
recognizable.
Apparently the doors of the cock
pit had jammed as the plane struck
and the two men were trapped,
forced to die an agonizing death.
Fonck and Curtin were thrown
clear of the wreckage and only
dazed by the crash.
Fonck announced last night that
he would make his start at 5:30
a. m. today.
Had Some Delay.
There was some delay in gettinf
ready for the start but soon after
6 a. m. Fonck and Curtin climbed
into the plane, where they joined
Clavier, who was at his radio act,
and Islamoff. Fonck took the con
trols with Curtin behind him.
The engine was speeded up and
slowly moved away’ down the field
while a thousand people sent up a
lusty cheer.
Finally the plane lifted a little
from the ground and settled back.
Again It came up some four feet but
could not maintain it, and again
dropped.
The plane was off the ground four
or five feet where there was a sud
den, muffled explosion. The plane
onreened at a giddy angle and fell
into a gully which separates
Roosevelt and Curtis flying fields.
Burst Into Flames.
Just as it fell, spectators on one
side of the field said, Curtin and
Fonck were seen to be thrown from
the plane.
Hardly had the plane struck the
ground than smoke poured from It
and then tongues of flame leaped
up. Soon it was apparent that the
plane would probably be a loss and
it was certain that Clavier and
Islamoff could not escape.
The crowd surged down the field,
about three-quarters of a mile to the
spot where the plane had fallen, but
could not approach nearer than a
few hundred yards on account of
the danger of explosion.

Termination of Water Contracts With Suburbs Is Sought
COUNCIL ASKED

THAN COST RATE
Law Does Not Bar
Adequate Rate,
Is View.
Termination of the contract under
which North Milwaukee, Shorewood
and West Allis are receiving water
from Milwaukee's municipally
owned water works system at less
than cost, will be terminated if the
common council acts favorably upon
a recommendation made late yester
day by its public utilities commit
tee.
Must End Contract.
In 1905 the city entered into a
contract to furnish these suburbs
with water at a rate of 6 cents per
100 cubic feet. The city, in 1921,
served notice on the suburbs that
their rate would be increased to 10
cents per 100 cubic feet, but the
suburbs obtained an injunction re
straining the city from increasing
the rate in view of the then exist
ing contract
Mr. Mattison explained that the
city must now terminate this con
tract. with the suburbs, upon which
they will be legally free to enter
into a new contract.
There is nothing in the law to pre
vent the city charging an adequate
rate. Assitant City Attorney Walter
J. Mattison advised the committee.
Sell at Profit.
He pointed out that the relation
between the city and the suburbs
obtaining the water is that of one
utility to another In view of the
fact that all of the suburbs are ob
taining their water supply from Mil
waukee at. a rate which enables
them to sell it to their consumers at
profit.
In view of this, Mr. Mattison de
clared the suburbs, in reality, are
utilities and the rate charged them
Is not classifiable by the rail com
mission ns a consumer's rate.

WEATHER HALTS
AERIAL PROJECT
CHICAGO —The difference in the
seasons in the northern and south
ern hemispheres makes impractical
the plan for aerial communication
between New York and Buenos
Aires, in the opinion of Maj. Ed
uardo Olivero, navigator of Ber
nardo Duggan’s New York-Buenos
Aires flight, who has arrived here
after three months of fighting bad
weather, according to a copyrighted
Buenos Aires story in The Daily
News. The party flew a total
9,000 miles, of which 7,000 wore in
rain or wind storms.
Olivero says it is impossible to
escape unfavorable weather condi
tions by choosing a departure date,
because no matter when the start is
made, the fliers will encounter bad
conditions in either the northern or
the southern hemisphere.
The mechanic, Ernesto Campa
nelli, who will accompany De Pinedo
around the world, described the
New York-Buenos Aires flight as
the worst in his experience.

MADISON—The Republican par
ty platform convention meets in the
assembly chamber, Capitol Bldg.,
here today, as required by law. The
Republican party is uncertain
whether the convention will dis
close a Ku Klux Klan domination
of the party councils or not.

took precedence over other matters

dates nominated In the recent pri
mary met previous to the opening
of the convention.
Get Dry Greeting.
The Campaigner, official prohi
bition organ in Wisconsin, wel
comed the Republicans to Madison
with the statement that the nomina
tion of Zimmerman, indorsed by
the Anti-Saloon league and The
Campaigner, is gratifying. Further
more the prohibition organ declared
that the state legislature will be
drier than ever as the result of the
dry wave which carried Zimmer
man to victory.
“Zimmerman looms as a new
state leader,” “Zimmerman’s vic
tory is gratifying,” “Fred R. Zim
merman is clearly the man of the
year in this state,” enthusiastic
comments in the latest issue of The
Campaigner, the dry organ.

Republicans even morp than the
wet and dry issue, if such a thing

ment is available, there are reports
in the capital that the La Follette
leaders have affidavits which show
that Zimiherman was a member of
the Klan, but that this evidence

mary election.

fidavits, and the discussion gener

THE SOCIAL CENTER.
Someone once said:
“Tell me how you spend your leisure time and I’ll
tell you what kind of a man you are.”
Of all the opportunities that the social center offers,
the most important is to spend our spare time. In our
social center we have a demonstration of the wholesome
results that can be wrought when play and work are
merged in one.

It was before 1910 that an organization of women
(The Woman’s Club of Wisconsin) established a social
center as an experiment in the schoolhouse on 4th and
Galena Sts.
At about the same time the common council con
ducted an investigation, instigated by the Socialist aider
men, into the causes of delinquency. No report was
rendered because of the widely conflicting evidence as to
causes and remedy. But the investigation stirred the
public interest in the experiment of these women.

The bureau of efficiency and economy obtained Mr.
Rowland Haynes, a man of national reputation, to make
a recreation survey for the child welfare commission and
the Milwaukee school board. The report (Bulletin 17)
was published in March, 1912.
The common council passed a resolution to determine
by a referendum the question of raising a special
tax for establishing and maintaining social centers.
Meanwhile, the school board appropriated the money
to conduct two centers, one on the nor^h side and one on
the south side, from January to April, 1911, the purpose
being to give the voters a better understanding of the
nature of the work.
This work was so well received by the people that
the referendum carried with a handsome majority.
Legislation was obtained authorizing the school
board to carry on this work and providing for a method
of raising the money necessary, thus assuring its con
tinuance and removing it from meddlesome interference.
The two experimental centers were now made per
manent and a third one opened at the school on 14th and
Galena Sts.
The first building used exclusively for social center
work was built by the park board at Lapham park, on
Bth and Walnut Sts. But the park board had not the
means to carry on this work and so the building was
turned over to the school board.

There are now maintained, under the supervision of
the extension department of the public schools, 13 of
these social centers. And the people have responded in
a way that has been an inspiration to the earlier pioneers.
Here they come—thousands upon thousands, to
spend their leisure hours. Of all ages and all colors, of
many tongues and every creed, of all stations and from
every walk of life they gather—to play, study, learn—to
search, laugh, act—to sew, knit, hammer, weave, cook,
nurse, bake, dance and work—busy as ants, musical as
birds, cheerful as sunlight—active, intent, alive.

“How do you get them to come?” I asked of Miss
Enderis, who is in charge of the extension department
of the public schools.
“Why, she smiles, “we try to understand the
people, particularly the young. What a lad wants is to
show his prowess—to exercise his strength—to blow off
his excess energy. What a lass wants is to grace herself
—to plan, nurse, rule with tenderness—to dream of her
future. What both, lad and lass, want, is to see one an
other, for they are good to look upon.”
“Lads come in. They want to show their muscle.
We have a room (they call it ‘rough-house’) where they
can be free to cuff, wrestle, box, turn, jump, play to their
heart’s content and do no injury. After that they are
ready for a shower. Now they can go to another place
for more quiet activities —billiards, pool, table games,
reading, study, work, etc., etc. We have nine branch li
braries connected with our centers, subscribe to the daily
papers, keep on file 22 magazines, have 40 different table
games, have gymnasiums, work rooms, etc., etc.”
I was given a circular (which is passed out by the
many thousands) that contains a list of the many activ
ities carried on at the social centers. Following are but a
few: Applied arts, cabinet making, china painting, cook
ing, home nursing, making lamp shades, millinery,
neddlework, personal health and care, etc., etc.
Among the musical and literary activities are: Bands,
orchestras, glee clubs, debating, speaking, dramatics, etc.
The civic and social organizations include: Parent
teacher associations, mothers’ clubs, men’s community
clubs, dancing classes, etc.

One of the tragedies, following in the wake of mod
ern industrial life, is the utter helplessness of the in
dustrial worker, who finds himself without a jo>\ and
without a master to order him around.
Tne “sluggard” of other days, who, with a jackknife
and a piece of white pine, could sit for hours—whittling,
whittling, whittling, basking in the sunshine while his
hands turned the piece of pine into most cleverly shaped
objects, was a gem of skill when compared with the mis
erables of today who have been trained to work at ma
chines only.

And there they slouch—on the corners, the curb, over
the stair rail—in singles, twos, threes—idly gadding, but
for the most part staring, staring—not a glint of intellect
in the eye—masses of muscular flesh, heavy bones, strong
limbs, and pent-up energy—waiting, waiting—they know
not for what—.
This is the tinder that is being heaped up by the
hundred-thousands, the millions in our land.

Man is not made to find gratification of his yearning
in aimless indolence. And yet, a man who is made to do
but one thing—serve a machine eight hours, nine hours,
10 hours a day—every day, seven days a week—s 2 weeks
a year—has but one ambition left—to get away, away
from the “damned” soul-killing beast—the machine.
And when he’s free, he’s more helpless than a dog
or a canary turned loose—the machine has wrecked his
life.

This is the meaning of play, the playground, the

LONDON The Briand-Strese
man plan for Franco-German co
operation was the chief topic of in
terest in British political circles
yesterday. While Downing Street
expresses unlimited delight over the
new developments which seem to be
leading toward peace between
France and Germany and making
f >r m United Europe, there are in
dications. nevertheless, that the
piospects of such a continental un
derstanding will cause serious mis
giving in some sections of British
political thought.
In any case, the scheme is being
used for the launching of another
onslaught against the allied debts
and revision of the Dawes scheme
of reparations payments, and it is
almcst openly admitted here that it
is the first step toward an organ
ized revolt against the financial
hegemony of New York and London.
Britain Must Choose.
Great Britain must choose one of
two paths. Li the first she would
back the Franco-German economic
entente, which would enable strong
representations, if not actual de
mands, to be made to Washington
for a scaling down of the war debts,
in which case Great Britain natur
ally would benefit. The second would
follow the older school of British
diplomacy, which is traditionally op
posed to all continental groupings.
The following remarkable state
ment of the British view of the
Franco-German negotiations was
given yesterday by a prominent pol
itician, a member of a circle having
an inner knowledge of foreign af
fairs:
“Certainly we are delighted to see
a favorable development In the
Franco-German conversations for a
final settlement of all debatable
points. All this is conducive to
peace in Europe.
Depends on U. S. Help.
“But the United States should
know that the final Franco-German
settlement is impossible without its
help, because Germany is expected
to give France financial compensa
tion for political concessions. This
compensation inevitably will take
the form of stabilization of the
franc on the one hand and advance
installments on the Dawes payments
on the other hand. This cannot be
done without the aid of Wall Street
and the American treasury.
“So we confidently expect the lat
est developments between Paris and
Berlin to bring to a head again the
whole question of the revision of
the Dawes scheme of payments and,
co-jointly, of the interallied debts.
Phis is unavoidable.”

Found in Italy, Lies

CASERTA—A huge monster, gen
erally thought to be the fossilized
skeleton of a mastodon, was recently
discovered near here and visitors
from all over Italy, as well as many
tourists, are crowding every day to
lee the bones of the giant beast
The Caserta mastodon has two
tusks nearly eight feet long, one of
which is perfectly preserved, though
the other is broken, probably owing
to the work of the excavators.
The skeleton lies at a depth of
some 20 feet below the ground, and
Is so far only partly excavated, the
work having been temporarily sus
pended in order to allow the gov
ernment experts to decide on the
best method of raising it.
The proprietor of the land where
the mastodon was brought to light is
stated to have become quite unbal
anced by his find, and lives in dread
that the precious brute will be car
ried off. He sleeps beside it at
night in the field where it lies, with
a gun by his side, and during the
day pockets the small fee he asks to
visit the mastodon from the crowds
of curious visitors.

MEXICAN LABOR BODY ASKS
QUESTION ON CHURCH FIGHT
Leader Special Service.
MEXICO —The Mexican Federa
tion of Labor asks the following
questions concerning the war be
tween the Catholic hierarchy and
the Calles government: “Is the
church to be permitted to become a
power capable of successfully op
posing the state? Is the church to
be permitted to oppose the demands
of modern democracy and industrial
progress?”
The Mexican Federation of Labor
emphatically answers “No” to both
questions. It pledges its loyal sup
port to the Calles government in the
effort to enforce respect for the con
stitution of the Mexican republic.
Seize Favorable Occasion.
Among the principal reforms in
which Mexican labor is interested
are the regulations for the enforce
ment of oil and property laws. These
caused a tense diplomatic situation
between the Washington and Mexico
governments and for a whole seemed
to bring on a serious crisis.
According to the Mexican News
service, the church hierarchy seized
this occasion as favorable for the
refusal to comply with the consti
tution of 1917. The state could not
act immediately Ijecause the consti
tution did not provide any penalties
for such offenses.
But on July 2, the Mexican par
liament enacted an amended penal
code, effective from Aug. 1,192 G, in
order to deal effectively with such
offenses. And as the diplomatic dif
ficulties between the Washington
and Mexico governments over oil
and property laws had been
straightened out for the moment,
the Calles government found itself
at last in a position to act firmly
against the hierarchy.
Must Obey Laws.
The laws which the hierarchy re
fuse to obey are easy to understand.
All that is asked of the priests is
that they shall register with the
municipal authorities. But the Mex
ican archbishops and bishops argue
that such action implies their sub
mission to the civil authorities.
Rather than submit, they ordered
all priests to withdraw from re
ligious service, hoping thereby to in
cite the religiously minded citizens
to revolt against the Calles govern
ment.
But the people disappointed the
hierarchy. Very little disorder re
sulted from the withdrawal of the
priests from the church services.
The municipal authorities took the

churches over and kept them open in
charge of community committees of
10. Tb<e services went on without
the priests.
The hierarchy then asked Presi
dent Calles to overlook the rebellion
of the priests. Calles replied that
they must register, as prescribed by
law.
Tried Violent Revolution.
The hierarchy then tried to start
a violent revolution about the be
ginning of August, Enrique Estrada,
a former Mexican general, who act
ed in behalf of the hierarchy, was
stopped at the Mexican-American
border.
The Mexican Federation of Labor,
known by its Mexican initials as the
CROM (Confederacion Regional
Obrera Mexicana), organized a pub
lic demonstration in favor of Pres
ident Calles in Mexico City on Aug.
1. More than 100,000 men and wom
en paraded through the streets of
the capital on that occasion.
In connection with this demon
stration, the CROM stated that it
was nonsectarian, did not wish to
meddle with matters of religious
faith or dogma, but would not per
mit religious sects to interfere in
the orderly processes of political
government.
The Mexican workers demand
secular education in the public
schools, freedom from priest rule
in education, and that religious serv
ices be administered only by na
tive Mexican citizens.
The Catholic hierarchy has long
tried to organize Catholic labor
unions against the bona fide federa
tion of labor, but failed.

KEY TO PEACE
Leader Special Service.
BRUSSELS Phil Snowden,
chancellor of the exchequer in Rain
say MacDonald’s labor government,
calls attention in Le Peuple to the
fact that Germany’s entry into the
league of nations brings the Locarno
pacts into full effect.
A Franco-German accord is the
key to the peace of Europe, ho
writes. The big business leaders of
France and Germany appreciate this
fact mere and more and strive to
act upon it.
Good relations between the two
nations, however, cannot be pro
moted without friction, so long as
large provinces of Germany remain
occupied by allied troops. The Lo
carno pacts took this into account
and provided for the gradual re
duction of the forces of occupation.
Must Reduce Occupation.
So far this provision of the Lo
carno pacts has not been put into
effect. There are in fact more for
eign troops in Germany nt this time
than there were a year ago. A be
ginning must now be made to reduce
these forces.
The additional occupation has
made a lot of bad blood. The Ger
mans are naturally very touchy on
this subject and insist upon the ful
fillment of the Locarno agreements.
Another question that must now
be definitely tackled is a thorough
revision of the Dawes plan. None of
the business leaders or statesmen
of the two nations believe that the
plan can or should l>e carried out as
it now stands.
Some of them still hesitate to
push the inquiry vigorously, but
economic as well as psychological
considerations press for an early
settlement of this problem.
Consider Interallied Debts.
However, the British and French
governments still insist that a re
vision of the Dawes plan carries
with it inevitably a revision of the
interallied debt settlements, and this
question still bids fair to delay a
thorough all around arrangement
that would work towards interna
tional amity.
Snowden argues that ^uch a settle
ment would do away with French
resentment against the demand to
pay tribute to London for the next
two generations, and would also re
move the German resentment
against foreign finance control.

ago he returned, and officers an
nounced he had reconsidered his re
fusal to stay in the service.
Backs Out Again.
But yesterday, following a long
conference with both Rear Admiral
Louis M. Nulton, superintendent of
the naval academy, and Curtis D.
Wilbur, secretary of the navy,
Zierkle again refused to become a
commissioned officer in the navy.
Naval officers are at a loss to
account for the midshipman’s atti
tude.
They pointed out that Zierkle, or
dered to ea as a midshipman, would
draw less pay and enjoy fewer priv
iliges than as an ensign.
Zierkle claims that while a mid
shipman he developed conscientious
objections against continuing in the
service. He tried to resign but it
was not accepted, and ui>on gradua
tion he was not allowed to get out
of the service. As he would not be
come an officer, he remained a mid
shipman.
Grad Must Sene.
The position of the navy depart
ment is that it objects to setting a
precedent by which any midshipman
could get out of the service upon
graduation. Some time ago the de
partment adopted the rule that a
graduate must serve two years as
an officer before his resignation
would be accepted. It is not felt
that it can recede from that posi
tion.
Zierkle must remain a midship
man indefinitely and his present
status has never been paraleled in
the navy. He is not under arrest or
restriction. It is thought he will
be allowed to resign after he has
served two years, as the spirit of the
regulation will then have been car
ried out.

Compete for Honors

state were here today to compete
in a contest which places a premium
on their freckles.
The contest is a feature of the
Tulare county fair, which opened to
day. Any boy can enter who is un
der 15 and has at least one freckle.
"Spec" O’Donnell, juvenile film
Mar, and king of the fair, will de
cide the winner.
Announcement of the contest was
made before the vacation period
started and many boys have spent
the summer cultivating their
freckles instead of applying lotions
to remove them.

The split, between Congressman
Jolin C. Schafer, 4tb district, and
the railroad labor organizations
which put him in office again was
widened by an announcement in the
Sept. 18 issue of Labor, the official
organ of the 1G railroad labor or
ganizations, Including the brother
hoods.
Labor comments as follows on the
congressional situation in the 4th
and sth district, of Milwaukee:
“In two districts of Wisconsin,
both in Milwaukee, the 4th and sth,
the progressives had one candidate,
Victor L. Berger, Socialist, who was
renominated in the sth district and
will bo opposed in November by Wil
liam Stafford, a lame duck Repub
lican of the old guard type.
Repudiated Platform.
‘•John C. Schafer, who first came
to congress in 1922 as a La Follette
progressive, is the candidate in the
4th district. Schafer announced
himself for renomination this year
as a La Follette progressive, but.
after the last day for the filing of
candidates in the primary, repudi
ated the progressive platform and
the candidacy of Blaine and Ekern.
He wound up the campaign by
taking the stump for the Lenroot
and Zimmerman forces which were
working hand in glove throughout
the fight.
“Schafer was repudiated by his
own mother and by his own labor or
ganization, the Brotherhood of Loco
motive Firemen and Enginemen.
Press Indorses Melms.
“Edmund Melms, former sheriff
of Milwaukee county, and a staunch
friend of labor, is the Socialist can
didate in the 4th district. He has
already been indorsed by The Madi
son Capital Times, the only La Fol
lette progressive newspaper in Wis
consin.’’
The heading of the paragraph on
Schafer’s desertion of his former
principles is “Schafer Proves Him
self a Traitor.” This indicates the
bitter feeling of the railroad organ
izations against the former progres
sive congressman.

MacDonald's is one of these, neither
better nor worse than the run of
houses in this lesser and unpreten
tious part of Lossiemouth. It is not
an encouraging approach, but the
small veranda, which fronts not to
ward the street, but toward a more
enheartening stretch of sea and
sweep of heath, is more reassuring.
A housekeeper opens the door and,
showing you into a sober, white
little sitting room, agrees to tell Mr.
MacDonald you are there. Soon he
comes —serious, quiet, simple, neith
er very forbidding nor very cordial.
He is distinguished, even handsome,
with a fine head and earnest, sen
sitive face. But he is not hearty.
Becomes Friendly Spirit.
Only gradually as you talk with
him do you feel more at ease. It
is difficult to say why, but there is
so great a detachment about the
man that he is disconcerting. Al
most it seems as if one has the bur
den of proof to show one's own sin
cerity. But once that difficulty is
surmounted, MacDonald becomes a
friendly, simple spirit, whose great
est interest in life is the Socialist
movement, whose strength is an al
most clairvoyant political acumen;
whose passion is sincerity.
Everything about MacDonald ex
presses his contempt for tawdry
show. He attends the bare Scotch
kirk of Lossiemouth each Sunday,
though, he confides, it “offers no red
carpeted way to heaven.” He scorns
any attempt to make the clever re
marks which “great men” often feel
obliged to do. He speaks thought
fully, shrewdly, but not brilliantly,
in private conversation, though it
is said of him that he is capable of
stirring eloquence in public speech.
He mistrusts all flashy mass action
—economically as well as politi
cally.
Respected in All Circles.
He is even something of a Puri
tan. And perhaps because of this
he is respected in all circles. Even
the most Tory of aristocratic ladies,
who confidently believe that the
chief objective of the Labor party
is to flood the streets with blood,
have a reluctantly admiring word
for MacDonald. It is quite possible
that he is auspicious of frivolity.
It is almost certain that he thinks
of the subject of divorce with a
squeamish aversion.
But for all of that he is much too
simple, much too tolerant, to be
hard. He is apt to tell a funny
story about himself, and through his
conversation runs a quiet, sly hu
mor. Particularly when he is re
minded of some comical experience
“while we were in power” his eyes
twinkle with amusement.
No Boasts; No Complaints.
However, it is his austerity, his
great simplicity, which keep him
from boasting or from complaining.
He never plays the martyr, and he
detests heroics, though there has

Shy of Press.

And he would rather suffer out

And then there is his impersonal
detachment in all things. It keeps
him, somehow, from close associa

the Labor movement. One suspects
that its source is a Scotch dislike
of intimacy—perhaps a “complex” of
repression. Its effect is to make
him a man apart—one with whom
others are uneasy, and there are
those who resent his aloofness. Some
men charge that he is too timid, or

Walking Major Pleasure.

at 59 he has only a moderate income,

that his integrity has never been
challenged, that he is unfalteringly
courageous—these things are com
mon knowledge.

diction on ratification of the French
debt agreement by the French par

closer view of political complica
tions affecting the French situation
Mr. Mellon seemed less confident of
favorable action by that government
than before he went to Europe.

tions, remarking that he had found
he saved himself a good deal of
trouble by avoiding such comments
while abroad.

Carolina, ranking minority member

a tax reduction during the coming
winter’s session of congress of more
than $500,000,000, Secretary Mellon
expressed the opinion that such a
raggestion was premature.

ment as being disloyal and disre

being heavily guarded.

STICK TO THE VOTE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
The automobile is resjionsible in
a large degree for the failure of
Americans to take advantage of the
franchise privilege.
The idea of a holiday on election
day makes people think not of cast
ing the ballots, but about where
they can go in their automobiles.
There was a very small vote cast
at the recent primaries. Even those
who did not get off from work to
vote did not have enough interest in
the outcome to go to the polls.
The automobile has produced a
nomadic population which not only
causes the voter to be away from
home on election day but causes him
to lose interest in local affairs.
I read some figures recently which
demonstrate this very clearly. They
were compiled by Simon Michelet of
the National Get-Out-the-Vote club.
In the presidential elections of
1876 to 1896, before the first auto
mobile. 80 per cent of Americans
qualified to vote went to the polls
and voted for president. In 1900,
when only about 5,000 automobiles
were made, there was little change

TEX RICKARD TAKES OUT

AGAINST ATTACHEMENT
BY HENRY L. FARRELL.
Staff Correspondent
The Lnitwl Press
PHILADELPHIA, Pa. This is
the first of those hectic days which
seem the inevitable prelude to
every world's heavyweight cham
pionship fight, when the boys who
had ambition to cut in upon the
luscious melon which only Tex
Rickanl, the master gardener,
knows how to raise, try their best
to get their share.
Before this excited city was fair
ly awake, there could be seen march
ing on the city hall, topi>ed by its
effigy of the benevolent William
Penn, a little army of legal lights,
following in the eager footsteps of
that fistic genius, Jack Kearns.
Seek to Attach Profits.
They were bent upon attaching
the profits of the forthcoming battle
of the Sesquiccntennial, in the name
of those who were disappointed that
Jack Dempsey, besides being world’s
champion, had proved himself to be
a good business man.
While fight fans, gathering from
near and far, were just beginning
to swarm the sidewalks and hotel
lobbies of hotels with their talk of
who would win the fight, John R.
K. Scott and Arthur N. Saeger, at
torneys, were busy with affidavits,
pleas and other legal paraphernalia,
bent upon seeing that the cham
pion's former manager won at least
$333,333.33 out of the affair.
Whatever the merits of the re
spective candidates in this heavy
weight championship fight which
now looms less than 72 hours away,
the fact exists that the worry about
this preliminary injunction business
is confined to the champion's camp.
Jack Dempsey, having renounced
active training for the affair, pro
fesses not to be worried, but he is
too much of a business man not to
have an ear attuned to these legal
proceedings which will occupy most
of the day in Philadelphia.
On the other hand Gene Tunney
appears like an amateur contestant.
The challenger has nothing to
worry him.
All efforts to stop the fight have
ceased. Tunney and Billy Gibson,
his astute manager, are assured of
their share of the proceeds, which
have been fixed at $200,000.
Rickard Posts Bond.
Tex Rickanl, aside from sundry
other difficulties which always con
front the promoter of a $2,000,000
affair, is doing a little worrying of
his own about these threatened
suits.
Rickard has posted a SIOO,OOO
bond whereby Dempsey will be per
mitted to leave the state of New
Jersey and journey here for next
Thursday’s fight.
Kearns brought suit In Atlantic
City to attach Jack’s share of the
purse.
The champion’s former manager
Is making his main fight in Phila
delphia, however, and it is here
that the legal difficulties in the way
of this battle of the Sesquicenten
nial will be Ironed out.
Rickard also took out $1,000,000
worth of insurance to guarantee the
match against “attachment or any
thing else.”

Christoph, last spring named fresh
man athletic mentor at Lawrence
college, came to the local campus
this month to find himself cast for
a new role. Christoph will act as
director of all Lawrence athletics
and varsity basketball coach while
A. C. Denney, who now holds two
offices, attends Columbia university
the ensuing year, on a year’s leave
of absence.
Christoph is himself an old Law
rence athlete, having won letters in
both football and basketball during
his intercollegiate days. It was in
the latter sport, however, that he
shone at his best, for he proved one
of the greatest defensive and offen
sive guards the Blue has ever
known. He was in the season of
1923-24 captain of the Lawrence
quintet. The past two years he has
been coach at Neenah High school
where his basketball teams won him
state-wide renown.

turn to Lawrence from his furlough
in the fall of 1927. Christoph will
be assisted by Don Gebhardt, who
acted as aide to Denney last school
year.

RING SPORT
LACKSSTRONG
ORGANIZATION
BY HENRY L. FARRELL.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
NEW YORK—“Why is it,” a cor
respondent asks, “that a boxing
champion can get away with any
thing? A baseball team, a tennis
player, a golf player and track and
field athletes have to defend their
title every year or give it up. Why
shouldn’t a boxing champion do it?”
Boxers should^ do it, and they are
violating the rules and regulations
of the New York boxing commission
when they do not accept the chal
lenge of a recognized challenger at
the end of every six months.
Strict Ruling Lacks.
They do not do it, however, be
cause they can’t be forced to do it,
and they can’t be forced against
their will because boxing is not or
ganized as well as other amateur
and professional sports.
Amateur boxing is well regulated
and no national champion can hold
a title by ducking opponents. He
has to defend his championship once
each year in the national champion
ships or give up the title.
Golf, tennis and athletics are per
fectly organized b ’ause the United
States Golf Assn., the United States
Lawn Tennis Assn, and the Amateur
Athletic Union not only control
their sports all over the United
States but because they are affiliated
with international organizations
which respect the majority vote of
their organizations.
Co-operation Fails.
Boxing will never be so perfectly
organized because the mon asso
ciated with the game are not of the
type that lend themselves to organ
ization or to supervision.
The lack of co-operation among
state boxing commissions, which is
the only present form of supervision,
was shown in the controversy about
the Jack Dempsey-Gene Tunney
heavyweight championship fight.
The New York commission said that
Dempsey and Tunney couldn’t fight
in New York, and the Pennsylvania
commission said, in words to the
effect—“ Come down to Philadelphia
and fight.”
This case is being used merely as
a recent example, and it may not be
pertinent, as the New York license
committee may have overstepped its
authority, or may have been guilty
of stubborn vindictiveness or poli
tics.
Set Rules Needed.
To be successful as au organized
sport, any sport has to be properly
organized and wisely administered.
Boxing can never be organized until
there are a standard set of rules.
As long as there are different rules
in New York, New Jersey, Pennsyl
vania, Illinois, California, Wiscon
sin and other big centers, the game
can be administered only according
to the rules and the champion <in
pick the state where the rules are
most to his liking.
Under the existing circumstances,
rules cannot be enforced because
there is no penalty that can be en
forced for a violation. No law can
be enforced unless something more
than a conscience pang happens to
the violator.

clared today in an interview.

hurt the champion by hammering
away at his nose, he will be wasting
his punches.”

statement of Dr. Peoria, noted

In the shivering blasts of winter
some folks marvel at the way
other folks go about half clad and
yet keep warm and well. The old
folks generally marvel at the
young folks, and more particularly
the old fogies marvel at the way
the girls do not dress nowadays.
In the witherng blasts of mid
summer suns and the stifling hu
midity of the dog days the old
folks lay off of their favorite in
door winter sport and try to tell
why the girls and women seem to
keep nice and cool when the rest
of us are suffering with the heat.
It is intuition that explains it.
Feminine intuition.
A couple of Dutch savants tell
us all about it in Nederlandsch
Tijdschrift vs. Geneeskunde. E.
Sluiter and G. van Uijnberk de
vised an electric thermoscope for
the study of the temperature of
the skin, both covered and un
covered. They observed with the
help of this instrument wide dif
ferences in the radiation of heat
from different regions of the body,
and they noticed that more heat
was radiated from surfaces near
large blood vessels, though not
invariably so. They found that
the radiation of heat is particu
larly intense whenever the skin
lies close to a bone surface.
According to the studies of
these men radiation of heat is
greatest from the skin over the
sprine, the breast-bone, the fore
head and the shin bones. Radia
tion is lowest over surfaces of skin
covering soft flesh.
So there you are. The women
have been keeping their spines,
foreheads, breastbones and shin
bones exposed, while the men have
been keeping theirs covered up.
The women have enjoyed comfort
through the hottest and humidest
weather and the men have fumed
and sweated and watched the
thermometer.
Radiation of heat proved ex
ceptionally low over skin cover
ing nice soft layers of subcutane
ous fat. We have always suspect
ed that the panniculus of adipose
which gives the feminine form
that softness and roundness also
helped to keep the body nice and
warm. The measurements made

care, give way under daily strain.

to run, year after year, without
supervision or overhauling—a dis
regard which would not be given
the cheapest monkey-wrench.

ern hill, nnd all the Star Crea

HAIR
Bl’ JEANNE RUERE.
Beauty Specialist.
I jEEP your hair beautiful—
fl J for the old adage about a
hgyjhj&l woman’s hair being her
crowning glory is as true
today as of yore. To do this, how
ever, it is not only necessary to
nourish and care for the hair, but
also to correct and neutralize a dis
eased condition—the presence of
gray, faded and streaked strands.
Medical science considers gray hair
a disease, calling it “canities.”
Hair, as seen under the micro
scope (Figure 1) is a long slender
stem with a lustrous covering. The
number of individual hairs in a sin
gle scalp is approximately 120,000,
but the number, size and length of
the hair differs greatly with indi
viduals. The normal rate of growth
is about a half inch a month and
there is more rapid growth in the
summer than winter.
Every hair has essentially the
same structure. Underneath the
covering there is a layer of fibers.
In these fibers nature puts its color.
Thus, the natural color of hair, as
it appears to us, is color seen
through the lustrous, almost trans
parent covering of hair. The color
is due to tiny granules of pigment
and the exact shade of hair is in
fluenced by the number of these
granules.
When hair turns gray it simply
means that nature no longer sup
plies colon to the inner layer of
fibers. The natural color of the in
ner hair substance is grayish and
it is seen through the lustrous
translucent covering the hair.
It is impossible to duplicate the
natural color of hair by applying
dye on the outside surface. This is
merely painting over which actual
ly hides the natural lustrous shell
of the hair. However, this is ex
actly what the old-fashioned dyes
and restorers did, giving the hair
a garish appearance. It proved un
satisfactory, for it made a hard,
flat and palpably artificial effect.
Science comes to the front, solv
ing the problem with a synthetic
dye which colors hair inside as na
ture does. The color pigment goes
inside the hair, placing the color
under the lustrous surface in the
inner fibers. Through this treat
ment the hair once again assumes a
clear, lustrous sheen which defies
detection.
This is brought out in the dia
gram, which illustrate a cross-sec
tion of a hair as seen under a mi
croscope. Figure 2 shows how na
ture distributes the color through
the layers of fibers beneath the outer
covering. Figure 3, a gray hair,
showing that the color is gone from
the layer of fibers underneath the
outer covering. Figue 4, a gray hair
ns colored by a coating dye, illus
trating the crust around the outside.
Figure 5, a hair recolored by the
synthetic dye, indicating that color
is again in the layer of fibers under
neath the outer coating, exactly as
in Figure 2 of natural colored hair.
Too much care cannot be taken
in the selection of hair dye. Par
ticular caution should be taken to
see that the dye restores the color
In the fibers of the hair and not
merely coats the outer shell.

RAIN, WITH JEANNE EAGELS, CUTS
DEEPLY INTO HEART AND MIND
BY KARL SCHAUERMANN.
The veneer of Puritan hypocrisy
fails to hold water in the John Col
ton-Clemence Randolph play which,
after years of patient waiting, ar
rived last night at the Davidson.
Puritan hypocrisy fails as dismally
as does Sadie Thompson in her en
deavor to become a “good woman.”
Floods of rain wash both Sadie and
her puritanical “savior” into the
gutter, and pagan drums, in
rhythmic symphony with the ele
mental forces of nature, chant a
hymn of victory.
Of course, the victory is not as
clean and triumphant for the poor
human beings who are caught be
tween the two opposing forces of
nature on one hand and the suppres
sion of natural instincts on the
other. It’s a victory that leaves a
woman, who had meant to climb out
of the destructive milieu surround
ing her into a better world, more
bitter than ever in her life, a woman
who turns from us with the abject
cry: “I guess I’m sorry for every
body in the world. Life Is a quaint
present from somebody—there’s no
doubt about that.” And the end
also leaves a would-be-savior lying
in the street, razor clenched in hand.
Rain has been put into the cate
gory of unpleasant plays, which
means it is neither musical comedy
nor revue. If these forms of the
atrical endeavor are your kind, you
will not like Rain. But if you can
appreciate the pleasure of bing pre
sented with a seriously worked out
comedy of life enacted by a com
pany in which character and im
personator are, in almost every in
stance, one, you will want to see
this week’s performance at the Da
vidson. The company includes sev-
ticeable sister of Hazel and Eleanor
DavWi, selected some songs with a
view to exhibiting to best advantage
her strong and exceptionally clear
voice. As added praise to Miss Ro
maine, her enunciation was some
thing to be desired. Perhaps the
most understandable of her efforts
was the potpourri of songs with
which she closed her act.
Headline position should be far
away for Chaney and Fox and com
pany, who have sponsored a color
ful dancing revue in which the girls
seem to have been chosen for grace
as well aS facial beauty and color
ing. A breezy affair, unfolded with
much waving of scarfs, is well bal
anced by some energetic stepping by
an ambitious titian-haired miss.

Billy and Dolly open the show
and sing a song reminiscent of the
Duncan Sisters. Neat gowns helped
to make this offering one not to be
expected in an opener.

And, as boys go to college to learn

Brown of the Davidson theater has
arranged for another week of the

Oct. 3.

illusions employed during the first

It need not cost much to make a
girl’s room beautiful, according to
some of the clever ideas suggested
by Alice Van Leer Carrick, author
of The Next-to-Nothlng House, In
the October McCall’s. Here are some

J. P. C.
“If your rooms faces northerly,
you can stress the warm colors of
rose-red and orange and yellow, and
If it gives on the south, take advan
tage of the cool charm of blues and
greens.

marquisette, ruffled at the edges

bordered with the figured material,
make very agreeable bureau scarfs
and tea table covers.”

U.S. CREDIT MEN
OPENMEETING
ATLANTIC CITY —Planning to
consider general business and credit
problems, as well as association af
fairs, the board of directors of the
National Association of Credit Men
opened its annual six days’ meeting
yesterday.
The directors’ program includes
such economic and credit problems
as installment sales, public debts,
commercial crime, agricultural cred
its, compromise settlements with
bankrupts, business conditions, in
dustrial and commercial waste, the
McFaddon bill and the proper func
tions of the trade and business asso
ciation. The opening meeting was
presided over by the president, Wil
liam H. Pouch, president of the Con
crete Steel Co.
“Our directors,” Mr. Pouch said,
"come from every section of the
country to discuss and plan ways
and means of safeguarding the ac
counts receivable of American busi
ness. Because a large majority of
people are honest and intend to pay
their just debts, business executives
are often lax in guarding against
losses on credit risks. In the aggre
gate, business failures amount to
extraordinary figures during the
course of a year, and this fact chal
lenges the ingenuity of those direct
ing business affairs to find methods
to decrease this waste. The public
must pay the bill, and it is a worthy
effort to attempt to eliminate a
8500,000.006 annual waste from our
cost of doing business.
“Several years ago we heard a
great deal about frozen assets, and
this meant that the ‘accounts reseiv
able’ items on a company’s financial
statement was not liquid. We hope
that the lessons of 1920-21 were suf
ficiently learned so that such a con
dition will not again prevail.”

ALL RAILROADS

The August earnings statements
of the railroads which will be forth
coming within the next few days
are expected to show a substantial
improvement over the same month
last year.
The Kansas City Southern road,
the first carrier to report earnings
for August, showed gross revenues
amounting to 81.578.798 as com
pared with $1,836,570 last year,
while the balance after taxes to
taled $505,177 against $495,985 last
year. For the first eight months
the total gross revenues were $14,-
638,993 against $13,788,460 and the
balance after taxes $4,031,044
against $3,226,856.
While the reports of nearly all
the carriers are expected to register
increases over last year, the largest
gains will undoubtedly be made by
the carriers operating in the central
western and southwestern districts
where there has been an unusually
heavy movement of agricultural and
petroleum products.
The Atchison, Topeka Sama Fe
railway is expected to show an in
crease of 50 per cent over the rail
way operating income of $5,054,865
in August last year, while the Rock
Island and Union Pacific will show
gains over last year when the rail
way operating income amounted to
$2,049,141 and $3,454,312 respect
ively.
The report of the Burlington, it
is understood, will show a slight
increase over the net railway oper
ating income of $3,670,352 in August
last year. On account of adverse
crop conditions in the northwest,
the earnings of the North Western
and the Milwaukee probably will
be about the same as last year,
when the ralway operating income
amounted to $3,339,361 and $2,633,-
726 respectively.

MILWAUKEE, TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 21, 1926
U. S. Bankers Will
Have Say in German
$125,000,000 Offer
BERLIN—It is recognized here
that American bankers will have
the final say in the German offer to
place $125,000,000 in preferred
shares of German railroads at the
disposal of France and Belgium.
The ndidtional credit so obtained
would be utilized in stabilizing the
currency of the two countries. The
consideration which Germany would
demand involves release of allied
military pressure in the Saar,
Eupen and Rhine areas.
It is believed that unless Amer
ican bankers came forward, the Ger
man railway securities vould have
little marketable value and that
their demand and possibilities for
sale in Europe would be small.
SPECIAL STAINS
MARK SEEDS
FROM ABROAD
Bootlegging is not confined to
moonshine. Profits that rival the
returns from “moon” are reported
to have been made in the illegal sale
of cheap and inferior grade of clover
and alfalfa seed to unsuspecting
farmers who thought they were buy
ing high quality stock.
“Seeds imported from foreign
countries where they have been
grown under conditions vastly dif
ferent from ours will not give satis
factory results in the states,” points
out A. L. Stone, seed specialist of
the state department of agricul
ture of the College of Agriculture.
Although the contraband seed ap
pears identical with home-grown
stock, most of it, he avers, cannot
survive the hard winters.”
In its fight against inferior seed,
the United States department of
agriculture has perfected a plan
that includes the coloring of a por
tion of all imported seeds before
they are unloaded in this country.
About 10 per cent of a shipment is
given a special stain. Red colors
are ai>plied to clover seed from
Italy and alfalfa seed from Africa
and Turkestan. Other colors, in
cluding orange, blue, and iridescent
violet are used to mark seed from
other countries.
“Seed grown in Wisconsin or in
states where climatic conditions are
similar to ours, is the safest to
buy,” asserts Stone.

with them they extend the tulip sea
son continuously from April till to
wards the end of June. They bridge
th-i gap that usualy comes between
the single earlies and the late tu
lips. The flowers are larger than
the single earlies and as they open
flat give the impression of a peony.
The double tulips like a richer
soil than the singles as they need
more plant food to perfect their
huge blooms, but manure is sure
death to tulip bulbs so the beds
need to be prepared some months in
advance if manure is to be used.

for bulbs and after they are planted

CATTLE RAISERS
HOLDING STEADY
DECATUR, Ill—All the talk
about higher prices for feeder cat
tle, which are expected to come with
the killing frosts that may hit the
corn crop early in October, has not
stampeded veteran feeders of cen
tral Illinois into filling up their
feed lots with expensive steers. Hot,
sunny days with thermometers
playing above the 96 mark last
Thursday and Friday has made cat
tle men more independent than they
were a week or two ago.
Feeder prices, farmers say, put
the cattle feeding business on the
dollar swapping basis. C. A. Ewing,
a grain and livestock farmer of Mc-
Lean county, says that farmers
must have a difference of at least
2% cents a pound in the price they
pay for feeders and what they get
for fat cattle.
Farmers in this part of the state
realize that there is an unbalanced
condition between the corn and live
stock situation, but they are hope
ful that damaging frosts will stay
away long enough for corn to ma
ture. They expect to take care of
a big supply of corn this fall by
holding their steers and porkers
in the feed lots a little longer.
