“new YORK—When the subject
of returning assets of the American
Metal Co. was first taken up with
the alien property custodian it was
done in the form of a hypothetical
case and no names were mentioned,
John Foster Dulles, New York attor
ney. testified at the Daugherty-
Miller conspiracy trial today.
Dulles, as attorney for Richard
Merton, who came here to obtain re
lease of the property, said he put
the matter before the alien property
custodian purely on a theoretical
basis and did not reveal that it was
American Metal Co. property that
was concerned.
Dulles was under cross-examina
tion by attorneys for former Atty.
Gen. Daupherty and former Alien
Property Custodian Thomas W. Mil
ler, who are accused of conspiracy
to defraud the government in con
nection with the return of the
American Metal Co. assets.
Merton’s Statement Questioned.
Richard Merton’s statement that
the return of $7,000,000 in American
Metal Co. stocks to his company in
1921 was a bona fide transaction
was attacked.
U. 8. Atty. Buckner, in a new at
tack on that testimony, introduced
evidence to show the metal com
pany stock was still the property
of its pre-war German owners in
1918, more than a year after Mer
ton had declared the Germans had
turned over the stock to neutral
Swiss.
The federal attorney's attack was
the high point of the day’s session
of the trial of conspiracy charges
against Harry M. Daugherty, attor
ney general at the time the $7,000,-
000 was paid, and Col. Thomas W.
Miller, then alien property custo
dian.
Berlin Clean City
Says Business Man
NEW YORK —Berlin today is
probably the cleanest city in the
world, according to John Bradley,
retired New York business man.
who returned on the Hamburg-
American liner Westphalia. He said
that traveling through Germany
was as comfortable now as it was
in pre-war days, with railroads run
ning on time and great courtesy
shown to American tourists. Mr.
Bradley found the Germans more
contented and optimistic than at
any time since the war, though most
of them were still short of the
money they used to have.

CO OPERATION HAS MANY SIDES
The other evening we listened to a plea for co-opera
tion between parents and teachers. It was delivered by a
teacher. Her idea of co-operation was that the state
teachers should follow the directions of their national com
mittee, and that the parents should follow the advice and
directions of the teachers.
This teacher was rather amused at the idea that the
parents might have something to contribute to this co
operation aside from meek acquiescence in the directions
of the teachers.
This is really the kernel of the whole co-operative
problem. People who have been brought up in the idea
of obeying without independent thinking are precisely the
great obstacle which now prevents successful co-operation.
This teacher’s idea of co-operation did not differ much
from Mussolini’s His idea is: I give orders, you carry
them out. Her idea is: We teachers give hints, you parents
carry them out.
That is the old class-rule idea of co-operation. But
this idea is failing so fast that the big business leaders
themselves are nervously striving to establish a more dem
ocratic sort of co-operation between themselves and their
employes. A modern industry is so complicated that it
cannot succeed, as it should, unless all its employes ha\e
some inkling of its complexities and can intelligently and
voluntarily co-operate to make it a success.
So industrial democracy is the thing that the most
far-seeing men of affairs are now reaching out for. But
because there has never been any training in this direction
before, and because hatred and distrust has been habitual
between employers and employes, it is very difficult to in
troduce a more democratic system without friction and
losses.
Co-operators must co-operate, but in order to make
real co-operation possible, there must be intelligent in
itiative on all sides. The specialists know some things very
well, the others know a great many things that the special
ists know' badly.
Co-operation will not be a real success, until the rank
and file of the co-operators have acquired the necessary
experience and training, and until their officers learn to
fit themselves into a system of popular democracy.
THE LEGION’S UNFINISHED TASK
We hear that there is a great deal of bad blood in the
American legion over recent French, British and Italian
attacks on Uncle Sam. The graves of Americans in
France have been desecrated. British newspapers have
called Uncle Sam bad names. Italian Fascists have
slugged American officials and tourists.
Now there is some talk of boycotting Paris. Next
somebody will want to boycott London and Rome. But
running around in the same old tit-for-tat circles will not
mend matters.
The other day, French, Belgian and German war vet
erans met near Paris. They pledged themselves to peace
and to the cause of labor. They overlooked all the provo
cations of royalist, Fascist, Nationalist hoodlums. Their
Idea was that the task which they undertook in 1914 will
not be finished, until all causes of war have been abolished.
The American legion can become a force for social
progress. The meetings of the legion abroad can become
instruments of international understanding. So long as
they are merely reunions of soldiers rehashing their old
lives, drinking and girl hunting, they remain tools of war
nrofiteers.
A SOP TO DAYTONISM
Prof. Westenhofer has started the old party editors
on one of their usual rounds of idiotorial brain storms.
He revives the old hint that the apes may be degenerated
men rathef than offspring of the same primitive type as
man. Immediately the advocates of Daytonism jump into
the debate, with all throttles open, and let loose a volley
of drivel.
We don’t know what possessed the professor to re
cast the old suggestion. We don’t even know whether he
meant it as a sop to the Daytonites, in order to make them
more inclined to look upon the theory of evolution with
favor. But the effect of his hint has certainly been to
make science ridiculous.
Darwin suggested long ago that evolution means not
only development upward, but also development down
ward. Some are improved, some debased in the processes
of nature.
But Darwin never made any concession to those ene
mies of the idea of evolution who posed as superior beings
for the simple reason that they had locked their brains
into a theological or metaphysical cell.

PERPLEXED WORLD SAVIORS
When the allies started out in 1914 to save the work'
from the kaiser, they didn’t know that they would have
to keep on saving it. But that is just what happened.
It is now beginning to dawn on some of their statesmen
that they bit off more than they can chew.
They were still hard at the job of saving the world
from the kaiser, when all of a sudden it became necessary
to save it from I^enin. Uncle Sam was dragged into the
mess. So the war to save democracy from the kaiser
turned into a war to save Russia for the czar.
It took so much of Uncle Sam’s money and men to
dispose of the kaiser that Lenin got away with Russia
and his friends still keep it. So no sooner had the kaiser
been ditched, than Germany had to be saved from Spar
tacus and Hungary from Bela Kun.
Before the job was fairly finished, Kemal Pasha ran
away w’ith Turkey. The allies tried hard to save it from
the Turks and paid the Greeks a pretty penny to get it
back, but that enterprise fell down like the raid on Russia.
France and Spain then had to rush in and save Mo
rocco from Abd-El-Krim. They did, but they are now
fighting to save it from Krim’s successor. The French
have been saving Syria for some time from the Syrians.
The job is not done yet. But the British managed to save
Egypt from the Egyptians and Mesopotamia from the
Turks.
There is more saving to be done, however. China
bids fair to fall into the hands of the Chinese, and that
would be awful for democracy and civilization, if we can
believe Mussolini and Morgan. It looks as if the Chinese
would get hold of their own country, if they keep on.
Uncle Sam is thinking hard, now, how he can save
Mexico from President Calles and the Moros from the
Filipinos. Some of us would like to save Uncle Sam from
Volstead and from Morgan, but of course that would hurl
the whole world back into Sodom and Gomorrah.
John Bull has saved the world from so many things
that it takes a whole encyclopedia to tell about it. What
is worrying John most at home is the question: How can
I save Great Britain from the Labor party and the trade
unions? If anybody knows the answer to this question,
the Bank of England will pension him for life.
The point of all this banter is that the whole war
propaganda has turned into a boomerang for its inventors.
The slogans that lured uninformed boys into the shambles
have become battle cries of rising classes and rising nations
that aim to throw off the yoke of native and foreign cap
italists.
The false cry of saving the world from one iuler has
assumed the true ring of a demand for saving the world
from all rulers. The allies started out by fighting one sur
face effect of capitalist evolution, and thereby aroused
movements which challenge the fundamental principles
of all capitalist business.
Much of the nationalist outcry against foreign im
perialism is animated by reactionary motives, of course.
Much of it is also utopian, not only in the sense that eco
nomic progress will not tolerate the narrow-minded na
tionalism any longer, but also in the sense that its eco
nomic aims cannot be realized.
But nevertheless all this effort to free classes and na
tions from capitalist control, which is so perplexing to the
leaders of big business, is the result of their owm doings.
They have shaken their own world from its moorings.
A JEFFERSONIAN VIEW
There is a curious passage in a letter of Thomas Jef
ferson written to Joseph Cabell in 1816 which will be
found in The Best Letters of Jefferson published by
Houghton, Mifflin Co. Jefferson was opposed to placing
the public schools in the hands of the state governmer
and wished to give control to the local communities. “1^
the principle one step further,” he wrote, “and amend the
bill so as to commit to the governor and council the man
agement of all our farms, our mills and merchants’ stores.
No, my friend, the way to have good and safe government
is not to trust it all to one, but to divide it among the many,
distributing to every one exactly the functions he is com
petent to do.”
Jefferson was right—for his time and place, but his
opinion shows how the social and political views of human
beings are limited to the environment with which they are
acquainted. Jefferson went on to say that he would divide
and sub-divide the governing powers until they “end in
the administration of every man’s farm by himself.” A
democracy of collective industry could not be visioned in a
society where small farms were the main basis of society.
The multitude of small proprietors suggested the division
and sub-division of government functions among thou
sands of small communities.
But in the highly complex industrial society of today
it would be impossible to adapt this Jeffersonian idea to
the needs of society. The roads, shops and mills have
become collective transportation systems and industries.
As well, think of pygmies controlling the tides as for
hundreds of thousands of small governing communities
controlling large-scale industry. Socialism is possible to
day, but it was not in Jefferson’s day. He was right then
but wrong now, right for his age but not for ours, yet there
is not one Jeffersonian Democrat in a thousand who can
understand this. They have no comprehension of what
evolution means.—The New Leader.

ALBINSON LETS
WISCONSIN VIEW
HIS PAINTINGS
An exhibition of the oils of E.
Dewy Albinson, Minneapolis, which
opened this week at the Milwau
kee Art institute, is, in its way, re
ciprocal.
Mr. Albinson acted as one of the
three out-of-the-state judges at the*
annual exhibit of Wisconsin paint
ers and sculptors last April, so that
now, after having seen and judged
the offerings of Wisconsin artists,
he is in turn allowing Wisconsin art
lovers to have a look at what one
Minnesota artist is doing.
Holds to Realism.
He has sent, among his 20 can
vases, three more or less distinctive
kinds of things—a few portraits
and an almost equal number of tap
es try like and distinctively patterned
things.
Albinson is both interested and
happy ir his patterns, which hold
the core of a very modern achieve
ment in realism.
In his Village and Chateau, a pil
ing up of grays, creams and greens
in small mass treatment produces
almost a tapestried effect which be
comes increasingly lovely with dis
tance. In several others the use of
somewhat higher lighting, and bits
of vivid color add to an impression
of realism to compensate for the
loss of textile effect. Taylor’s Falls,
with some reds, hay color and
warmth; Town, with a touch of the
color of spring about it, greens and
yellows, and Minneiska Hills, with
its satisfying composition augment
ed with color variations all lend
themselves ns examides of what Al
binson has chiefly carried over from
his background of study in Paris
and Munich.
Warms to Indians.
From northern Minnesota, which
forms the background of most of Al
binson’s American work, come many
theires from the St. Croix river dis
trict, where the artist studied the
Indians in their reservation life. In
these he manages to become very
warm and cheerful without the use
of much specific color.
This exhibit will continue through
September.

HELP FLORIDA,
HORN’S PLEA
Mayor Daniel W. Hoan today ap
pealed to Milwaukeeans to contrib
ute to the fund which the American
Red Cross is raising for the relief
of the victims of the recent Florida
hurricane.
In a proclamation he points out:
“The sad news has been brought
to our attention that a large area
in Florida has- been devastated by
hurricane and flood. Hundreds are
dead, thousands are injured, vastly
greater numbers are homeless. Dis
ease, pestilence and famine threaten
to increase the agony and loss.
“The whole nation is responding
in furnishing funds to alleviate in
part the indescribable suffering of
the helpless.
“Milwaukee must respond. We
have never failed to do our part.
Let us give generously to so worthy
a cause.
“Send all contributions to Mil
waukee chapter, American Red
Cross. 128 Grand Ave.”
PRAYERS OPEN
AFRICAN CHURCH
DISTRICT MEET
Prayers and choral communion
opened the annual Chicago district
conference of the African Methodist
Episcopal church, today in the Mil
waukee Auditorium.
Singing, without instrumental ac
companiment, by the congregation
while 300 pastors and as many lay
members from Wisconsin and parts
of Illinois, Indiana and lowa, re
ceived the eucharist, filled Engel
mann hall and flowed out to the
street in harmonic beauty.
Business Session Held.
A business session followed lunch
eon served by a ladies’ auxiliary
society of St. Marks, local African
M. E. parish, in which reports of
home missions by the various visit
ing pastors, were begun. With a
total of almost $15,000 collected by
the local African M. JT. parish, St.
Mark’s church is expected to take
a place near the top when reports
of mite boxes are complete. The
African M. E. Church conducts its
educational as well as its religious
activities under one organization,
it was pointed out, and is, therefore,
the largest one-race religious organ
ization in the world.
Mayor Daniel W. Hoan will make
the welcoming address to the con
ference at a banquet tonight, 7, In
Market hall. He will tie followed
by the Rev. Harry S. Wise, secre
tary, Milwaukee Council of
Churches.
The first day of the conference
will close with a reception in the
evening in Engelmann hall. Ses
sions will continue through Sunday.
The climax of the conference will
be the Young People’s Service Sun
day for which 3.000 persons are ex
pected. A si>ecial train will bring
1,000 Chicago African Methodists
and a caravan of more than 50 mo
tors also is expected.
Thrte Sessions Daily.
Upon the arrival, Friday, of
Bishop Sampson Brooks, educator
from the Negro republic of Liberia,
an hour will be set for the latter’s
address upon the work which is be
ing done in the college of which he
is head to teach the students to de
velop their country industrially sim
nltaneously with tbeir classic educa
tion.

day of the conference, according to

St. Marks, Milwaukee, in charge of
conference arrangements. Music

tendance indicate that this confer
ence will attain unexpected propor

FOOD STORES CO.
CREDITORS WIN
Another phase of the Union Food
Stores Co. case was disclosed in fed
eral court today when Judge F. A.
Geiger upheld the claim of creditors
of the company that a SIO,OOO insur
ance policy, held by the late Joseph
D. Talpin, former president of the
Waukegan Tea Co., which later
merged with the Union Food Stores
Co., should be placed among the as
sets of the latter company.
Albert K. Stebbins, counsel for
Henry R. King, receiver for the
Waukegan company, maintained
that as the Waukegan company had
gone into receivership in the state
courts at about the same time that
the Union Food Stores Co. went
bankrupt that the federal court had
no jurisdiction in the matter.
Judge Geiger ruled that the fed
eral court decision took precedence
over that of the state court in a
bankruptcy case of this type.
The Waukegan company took out
the insurance policy for Taplin and
made the payments on it while he
was president. The company also
used the policy as a basis for a
$9,000 loan from the Racine Na
tional bank.

We had something of a political

we now need another. The winning
slogan then was “anti-slavery”—
a slogan which men more humane

How about, “anti-supreme court
dominance over the laws!” I be
lieve that by organizing to defeat
such candidates for office as stand
for the present excess of power in
the supreme court, we, in effect, will
duplicate the results of the 60’s.
As a political machine, the su
preme court performs an indispens
able part in the robbery of labor
at the behest of big business. If
the anti-plutocrats do not know
this already, it is only because they
are lacking in satanic wisdom.
It will have to be the common
people or those few among the
higher-ups who are most truly in
sympathy with them, to start this
defeat.
Those nearest the throne of pi
ratical power are laggard? on the
democratic line of progress but it
behooves us to observe that our own
class is also laggard, on the in
dustrial line. The higher-ups in
sist that we are wrong. It will he
bad for us if we underestimate
their strength. They may make
concessions in the hope of prolong
ing their power and we mar fail at
first but even though we do not
wholly win one election, we will
gain prestige and preparedness for
future elections.
Due to the workings of economic
determinism, those now nearest the
throne of piratical power nre as
good as bribed to stand for its con
tinuance. Not nil of them, of
course, will stand for this
bribery. Some prefer equal rights
for nil rather than the bribe for
themselves. But how about the
common people? Wo offer them
freedom from piratical exploitation
on condition that they unite with
us. And that is as good as money
to them. And so. just as there is
money consideration to hold the
higher-ups to the plutocracy, there
Is also a money consideration to
cause the romon people to unite
for their deliverance from that ex
tortion.
All things considered, why would
it not be well to ask all candidates
for congress where they stand upon
such a question? It is to he ex
pected that but few will declare
themselves promptly and that most
of them will be noncommittal. Btft
once let it be understood that we
intend to get together in earnest
to defeat for election those most
hesitant to decide 1 favor of this
Idea, and the man on the fence

would end bis hesitancy. Yes, and

LOS ANGELES—Deputy district
attorneys questioned Mrs. Edith
Holmes, woman juror on the recent
ly dismissed 1926 county jury, and
later announced that she would be
an important witness for the state
in the preliminary hearing next
Monday of the McPherson kidnap
ing hoax charges.
Mrs. Holmes’ name, some weeks
ago, was dragged into accusations
connected with the sensational and
unexplained “loss” of McPherson
case evidence. The disappearance
of evidence, which consisted of two
sheets containing handwriting, oc
curred in the midst of the grand
jury’s secret sessions and ended in a
furor of factionalism among the 17
grand jurors previous to the papers
disappearance down a drain pipe in
one of the women jurors’ retiring
rooms.
10 Days in Cottage.
The handwriting samples were
said to prove the main possibility
for conclusive identification of the
woman who spent TO days in a
Carmel love cottage last May. That
woman gave her name as “Mrs.
George Mclntire.”
According to Kenneth Ormiston,
who confessed in a Chicago affidavit
that he was the “Mr. Mclntire” of
the cottage, bis companion was
“Miss X.” According to half a dozen
Carmel residents who saw the wom
an, “Mrs. Mclntire” bore a perfect
resemblance to Mrs. McPherson and
they made depositions to that ef
fect.
The questioning of Mrs. Holmes
provided several “leads” for prose
cutors. It is reported she admitted
having seen both Mrs. Lorraine
Wiseman and Atty. Roland Rich
Wooley, agents for Mrs. McPherson
In her efforts to obtain persons who
would come forward with testimony
In rebuttal of the Carmel identifica
tions.
Woman Was Accused.
Mrs. Holmes admitted, according
to the prosecutors that she had been
accused by fellow grand jurors of
making away with the handwriting
samples, but she declr.red, “I later
was exonerated by a vote of all
members of the grand jury.”
Mrs. McPherson and her mother,
Mrs. Minnie Kennedy are under $2,-
500 bonds for trial next Monday.

MINNEAPOLIS—Thomas John
son, found guilty of one of the 14
murders to which he confessed, was
to be sentenced today to life im
prisonment.
A jury deliberated less than three
hours and took three ballots to con
vict Johnson, “the man of many
crimes,” of killing Leonard Erdall,
Minneapolis attorney and former
University of Minnesota football
star, during a holdup.
Was Found Sane.
Johnson walked into a Seattle po
lice station last July and began his
series of confessions in which he
admitted the 14 murders, including
ErdaU’s and 1,750 robberies.
A commission found Johnson
sane, but County Attorney Floyd Ol
sen charged that by his conduct the
slayer was attempting to feign in
sanity.

its case, including the introduction
of two confessions, Johnson inter
rupted frequently to denounce de
fense witnesses as “black liars and
perjurers,” declaring he would “con
fess to anything” and ha-1 a mania
for confession, and pound a table
to obtain attention.
Would Rather Die.
After the trial, Johnson comment
ed that he would have preferred
to have been taken to lowa, which
has capital punishment, in order to
be executed for one of his murders.
“I’d rather be dead,” Johnson
said.

BIG FLOATING
UNIVERSITY TO
LEAVE SOON
NEW YORK—The floating uni
versity on board the S. S. Ryndam
will leave here Saturday with a
student body of 450, a faculty of
50 and an additional personnel of
40, necessary to care adequately
for those on board. The college
cruise about the world will travel
westward, with a stop at Los An
geles on Oct. 9 and will spend the
early winter in the Orient.
Some time in February, Constan
tinople will be reached, and the
remaining three months will be
spent in Europe. The return to
New York is to be in May, in time
for the cruising students to revisit
at commencement the land-locked
universities they formerly attended.
The purpose of this year of itiner
ant study is primarily educational,
in the broadest sense. The students
are to be given an opportunity to
develop an ability to think in world
terms, to cultivate an intelligent in
terest in foreign affairs and to
strengthen themselves in interna
tional understanding and good-will.
To Meet Leaders.
To further these ends students
will establish first-hand contact
with places, peoples and problems,
and will meet the leaders of
thought and action in many sig
nificant centers of culture and of
social and political development.
The response from the countries
to be visited has been gratifying to
the faculty. Governments in cer
tain cases will regard the students
as guests and will afford them ex
ceptional opportunities to learn the
characteristics of the country vis
ited and to investigate important
phases of national life. The Dutch
East Indies government has ap
pionted A. T. Keen of the Prinz
Hendrick school to represent it.
He is to meet the vessel at Man
ila and be with the students about
two weeks. The king of Siam has
sent an invitation to the group to
be his guests at Bangkok for four
days. This will be the first time
any round-the-world excursion has
visited Siam.
The general plan and organiza
tion of the cruise will be under
the direction of Dr. Charles F.
Th wing, president emeritus of West
ern Reserve university. Other of
ficers of administration are Albert
K. Heckel, Ph. D., professor of his
tory and dean of men, University
of Missouri; George E. Howes, Ph.
D., professor of Greek and dean,
Williams college; William E.
Haigh, M. I)., N. R., C. S., L R. C.
P., F. R. C. S., English Diploma
Tropical Medicine. Liverpool, phys
ical welfare, British medical unit,
league of nations; Daniel Chase, A.
M., chief of bureau of physical edu
cation of the state of New York.
Have 30 Courses.
The educational activities and
the welfare of the students are
organized under five departments.
The department of instruction will
offer 90 courses of college grade
under the direction of various co
operating colleges and universities.
The department of health protec
tion will include physicians, den
tists, dietitians and nurses. The
ship has a hospital, >but the depart
ment will rely chiefly on preventive
medicine.
Physical education and recreation
are under the direction of Daniel
Chase, chief of the bureau of phys
ical education of New York. His
staff includes expert instructors in
swimming, boxing, fencing and
other sports. Arrangements have
been made for athletic meets with
universities en route.
Activities in music, dramatics, de
bates, photography, as well as en
tertainments, are in charge of the
department of student life. The de
partment of shore trips and shore
excursions has planned its part
carefully and in many countries
visits are to be under the guidance
of local universities or communities
of citizens.
Plan For Comfort.
The Ryndam has been equipped
for this educational voyage with
classrooms, library, gymnasium and
swimming pool, and will be op
erated on the basis of a college
dormitory and commons. Comfort
and economy have both been
stressed.
Geography and geology are to be
studied in field and laboratory.
Students interested in foreign
trade, those interested in journal
ism, archaeology, the classics, eco
nomics, government, history and
languages will go in different direc
tions and visit places and persons
helpful to their specialized studies.

SETTLEMENT
ON NATIONAL
BASIS SOUGHT
Intimate Baldwin
Sold Out to
Owners.
LONDON—Observers in closest
touch with the coal situation
abandoned hopes yesterday for any
immediate settlement of the strike.
It is believed the controversy will
last three months more.
The miners’ officials sent a letter
to Prime Minister Baldwin yester
day rejecting the government’s pro
posals for ending the strike by be
ginning work on district agree
ments, followed by adjournments
through a national arbitration
board.
Is Flat Rejection.
The miners’ reply constituted a
flat rejection of the scheme on the
grounds that it absolutely abolishes
recognition of the national interests
of the miners.
The miners’ reply is a reasoned
argument pointing out that the
miners have done their part In offer
ing to arbitrate, but charging that
the government has gone back on
the promise made to them through
Chancellor Winston Churchill. The
notes intimate that Mr. Baldwin
has sold out to the mine owners.
Following receipt of the miners’
note several members of the cabi
net and the miners’ leaders were
summoned to Mr. Baldwin’s office.
The outcome of the parley will be
vital, not only with regard to the
coal settlement, but also for the eab
in< t. which is far from being a
happy family.
Slit Is Widened.
The split between .Mr. Baldwin
and Chancellor Churchill has
widened further as a result of the
pointed shafts contained in the
miners’ reply.
It was openly mentioned in cer
tain circles that Chancellor Church
ill is so disgruntled he may resign.
In any case, he has expressed his
avowed dissatisfaction at the man
ner in which he was “turned down”
by his chief.

ance to the cyclone. Roofs wore car

Posada also are providing relief fa-
cilities and have established hos
,^tal bases for the injured. The Ar
gentine president has asked offi
cials of Misiones province to extend
nil possible aid to the stricken city.

CITES GROWING
WAR BETWEEN
POPE, FASCISTS
Leader Special Service.
PARIS—The Paris correspondent
of The London Daily Herald here
reports that the growing conflict be
tween the Roman pope and the Fas
cist government had the effect of
Interfering with a proposed meeting
of French and Belgian gymnasts in
Rome.
The French federation of gym
nasts received a telegram from its
Italian brother organization stating
that “by the will of the holy see, and
for reasons of exceptional gravity,
which will be published later by the
papal authorities, the meeting is sus
pended.”
The thousands of gymnasts who
have learned that the loss of their
holiday was due to Mussolini’s hos
tility toward the pope are now
arousing French Catholics against
the dictator.
Recall Sad Incidents.
The Vatican has advised the juve
nile Catholic sporting federations of
Europe to refrain from holding their
international congress in Rome, “be
cause, in the opinion of the ecclesias
tical authorities, it is not advisable
for Catholic youths to gather in
numbers after the sad incidents
which have occurred lately in some
Italian towns.”
The reference is to the wrecking
of the Catholic Boy Scouts’ clubs in
Mantua and Macerata.
It appears that the prefect of
Mantua issued last week a decree
stating that the existence in that
province of Catholic boy scouts had
given occasion to “grave incidents,”
and that the members of such Cath
olic organizations were responsible
for “deplorable acts” amounting to
political manifestations and “open
provocation.” He therefore ordered
the dissolution of all Catholic boy
scouts’ associations in the province.
Fascists Attack Boys.
The “deplorable acts” consisted,
as a matter of fact, in a very peace
ful procession of Catholic boy scouts
in the streets of Mantua Aug. 25.
An eye witness gives an account
of the events.
The scouts, he says, marched in
an orderly way toward their head
quarters, and there was nothing
provocative about them. There was
no visible sign that they carried
weapons.
But there had been a warning
from the local Fascist! to the effect
that if the scouts “dared show their
faces in the streets they would re
pent it.”
The threat was not an empty one.
Fascist!, who had been waiting in
ambush in a side street near the
Catholic Boy Scouts’ quarters ad
vanced to the attack. The boy
scouts’ quarters and dubs were in
vaded and wrecked, after which the
Fascist! paraded the streets carrying
pieces of wrecked furniture and a
portrait of the pope hung on a stick
as trophies of victory.
Scouts Revenge Themselves.
It was only after this that the
Catholic Boy Scouts invaded the
Fascist headquarters and took re
venge on their enemies by setting
fire to the Fascist banners and to
a portrait of Mussolini.
This provoked more fierce re
prisals from the Fascisti, and a
number of houses belonging to Cath
olics were attacked and their occu
pants bludgeoned.
At Macerata a congress of Cath
olic societies was being held. Father
Cordovan!, a teacher in the Catholic
university of Milan, and the bishop
of Macerata were attending the con
gress when the hall was invaded by
the Fascisti. Scenes of violence fol
lowed, during which many congress
men were beaten. The Catholic
clubs in this town also were invaded
by Fascists and wrecked.

SCHOOL HISTORY
BIASED, DREARY,
SAYS EDUCATOR
NEW YORK—“History as it is
taught in the schools is too much,
from the point of view’ of the na
tion to which the child happens to
belong,” declares Helen Taft Man
ning, daughter of ex-President Taft,
and Dean of Bryn Mawr college.
Pointing out that this is serious in
retarding the interests of peace, Dr.
Manning says:
“History has been taught so much
from the point of view of the na
tion to which the child happens to
belong that it would seem that all
the good men and all the great
deeds had belonged to that partic
ular country. For each war the im
pression is given that all the men
on one side were heroes and that all
the enemy were villains.
“The story of wars has occupied
a number of pages out of proportion
to the space devoted to the other
activities of mankind. Boys and
girls studying history have often
gained the impression that there
was nothing to learn except a
dreamy succession of kings and the
wars which each king made on his
neighbors. Such historical narrative
soon becomes monotonous, and while
it may not and probably will not
give children any great enthusiasm
for war, it certainly gives them too
little idea of the real achifevements
of mankind.”
FINANCE HEAD IN
MEXICO QUITS
MEXICO CITY—The semi-official
organ, El Imparcial, yesterday an
nounced the resignation of Alberto
Pani, finance minister, and tells of
the split between Senor Pani and
the minister of labor, Luis Morones.
It is said the senor twice previously
presented his resignation, which
President Calles refused to accept.
Senor Pani was one of the two
strongest members of the cabinet.
His financial ability is held largely
responsible for the reconstruction
of finances and the savings which
enabled the government to pay in
terest on the foreign debt, construct
several thousand rural schools and
build much needed highways.
El Imparcial asserts that after
President Calles finally accepted
Senor Pani's resignation, Senor
Pani yesterday assembled the em
ployes of the department of finance,
after which 300 heads of depart
ments also resigned.

BRITAIN MIGHT
RECOGNIZE ALL
CHINESE CHIEFS
LONDON The British cabinet
has under consideration proposals
for a reversal of the policy fol
lowed in China during the last two
years. The essence of these pro
posals consists of full recognition of
all de facto provincial Chinese gov
ernments, especially the Cantonese
bolshevik regime.
It means that the local diplomatic
consular authorities would be given
power to deal with any situation
which arises. The Conservatives
are opposing the plan actively.
Be Figure Head.
Such a policy, if adopted, means
a rejection of the fiction of the
central Peking government as head
of China. The proposed policy
would make the British minister to
the Peking government little more
than a figure head.
Opposition to the proposals comes
from the Hongkong authorities, who
represent diehard ideas, and believe
only rigorous measures and a force
ful blockade can be effective when
dealing with the Chinese chaos.
Hongkong resists the new Cantonese
offer to withdraw the boycott
against customs dues in its favor.
No Reply Sent.
Additional opposition comes from
the British director of Chinese cus
toms, Mr. Agly, who refused to con
sider the British interests and as
trustee of the nominal Chinese cen
tral government, and oppose any
alienation in favor of Canton, even
on the part of customs duties.
The cabinet must decide these is
sues at tomorrow’s meeting. AZ yet
no reply has been sent by the Brit
ish to the Cantonese proposal to
levy certain extra taxes in return
for lifting the boycott and it is
realized the situation needs han
dling with much discretion. Though
Great Britain has not recognized
the Cantonese, proponents of that
step in the cabinet argue that any
thing is better than a continuation
of the boycott.
LONG ARM OF
MUSSOLINI HITS
FRENCH SHOW
PARIS—The long arm of Premier
Mussolini’s censorship reaches even
to the Parisian theaters. It was
learned last night that the Mou
lin Rouge was forced to cut part
of its show when the Italian dicta
tor protested to the French police
through his embassy at Paris.
The new show had a skit in which
the manners of American, English,
Spanish, Argentine, German and
Italian tourists are satirized bit
ingly.
Rome heard of this and the em
bassy at Paris was ordered to pro
test to the police, which ordered the
act cut to save the feelings of the
Italians. So the Italian was made
a Corsican, but the embassy again
protested, saying the actor still
spoke with an Italian accent; then
he was made up as a tourist from
Marseilles, but again the embassy
protested for the same reason, and
this time the entire act was or
dered suppressed.

AUTO ORDER OF
COUNCIL WILL
BE ENFORCED
The ban on the use of city owned
ears for anything but official busi
ness is in reality a ban and applies
to department heads as well as sub
ordinate city employes, Mayor
Daniel W. Hoan, demonstrated yes
terday when he conferred with Fire
Chief I’eter J. Steinkellner in pro
test against the latter’s use of a
fire department automobile in going
to and from a cottage at Fox Lake,
where he spent his summer vaca
tion.
Must Include All.
“If we are going to enforce the
common Council’s order against us
ing city cars for anything but offi
cial business, we will have to in
clude department heads and all de
partment heads,” said Mayor Hoan,
following the conference.
“Chief Steinkellner is very agree
able to the order and explained that
he took his car with him on his
vacation only because he is subject
to call at any time and as a matter
of fact he did return to the city three
times during his vacation upon sum
mons from the fire department.
“Nevertheless, in mj' opinion, this
is not sufficient justification for
taking a city car out of the city on
an errand that is purely personal
pleasure.”
Mayor Hoan explained that he
has requested Chief Steinkellner, in
the future, to make arrangements
with a private garage or a taxi line
to bring him to the city at such
times as he jnay be summoned to
duty while enjoying a vacation or
an outing.
Caused 11l Feeling.
“This banning of the use of city
cars for anything but official busi
ness has caused much hard feeling
among city department heads and
we must enforce it stringently,” said
the mayor.
Chief Steinkellner declared he is
heartily in accord with the mayor’s
desire to enforce the order unbiased
ly and explains that he took his car
to Fox Lake merely because he
thought that the ability to respond
promptly to a call from Milwaukee
was .of service to the city.

Staff Correspondent

MADISON, Wis. Fred R. Zim
merman, Republican gubernatorial
nominee, failed to control the Repub
lican state platform convention here
yesterday and today finds himself
burdened with a party platform
practically identical with that of
Atty. Gen. Herman L. Ekern, whom
he defeated for nomination.

forces were in control throughout
the session, which lasted until late
last right, and Ekem’s announce
ment of an independent candidacy
is anticipated as a result.

The sole amendment to the ma
jority report of the resolutions com
mittee which drafted the platform
was the adoption of the Izaak Wal
ton league proposal for taking the
conservation commission out of
politics and placing its activities
under the direction of a non-salaried
board.
Virgil H. Cady, Democratic
nominee for governor forced his
own platform, opposing repeal of
the personal property tax, through
to final approval by the Democratic
convention.
No Party Strife.
Socialist and Prohibition assem
blies held at the same time were
without party strife.
Zimmerman’s first defeat yester
day was in the election of Lieut.-
Gov. Henry A. Huber of Stoughton
as temporary chairman of the con
vention over Senator Charles B.
Casperson of Frederic, who was
nominated by Zimmerman. Then
in the district caucuses which
named the members of the resolu
tions and state central committee’s
the gubernatorial nominee lost
again.
Attempts to substitute the Zim
merman platform for the Ekern
platform submitted to the commit
tee by Senator R. B. Johnson of
Superior, were defeated 13 to 3 in
the committee and 52 to 42 on the
floor of the convention, where Zim
merman read his own platform as
a minority report.
Name Blaine Man.
Senator John B. Chase of Oconto,
choice of the Blaine-Ekern-La Fol
lette group, was elected chairman
of the state central committee on
the first ballot, receiving 47 votes.
Clinton B. Ballard, intimate friend
of the late Senator La Follette and
identified with the La Follette
movement throughout its existence,
was Zimmerman’s nominee and got
24 votes. Senator Harry B. Dag
gett of Milwaukee, stalwart Repub
lican nominee, was given 18 votes.

I am an American-born woman,
writes Mary K. Das in an article,
A Woman Without a Country, in
The Nation.
My ancestors came from England
to America in the year 1700. By the
existing double standard of the
American government, I am not only
undered alien, but a stateless alien.
My husband, a Hindu, was a nat
uralized American citizen when I
married him. He had secured his
certificate of naturalization from a
United States district court in 1914,
having previously resided in the
United States for eight years.
The United States state depart
ment three times gave him pass
ports with which he traveled all
over the world. He still holds his
American naturalization certificate,
hut today be is told by the state
department that he was never an
American citizen, because “the
judges, who during the last quarter
of a century or more naturalized
Hindus to American citizenshi.p, by
due process of law, did not know the
meaning of the United States natu
ralization laws, and so these judges
from all parts of the United States
acted illegally.” This interpretation
Is based upon a recent decision ren
dered by a United States supreme
court judge who is himself a nat
uralized citizen, wl^o held that
“high-caste Hindus are not white
I>ersons according to the commonly
accepted meaning of the term, and
thus are ineligible to American citi
zenship.”
Still Has Papers.
Before we were married my hus
band went to several lawyers and
asked if I stood the least chance
of losing my citizenship in marrying
him. These legal experts, one a
former adviser to the state depart
ment, told him that this could never
happen, because the United States
could not and would never apply a
supreme court decision retroactively.
Last year when I asked the state
department for a passport to go to
Europe my request was refused on
the ground that I was “no longer
an American citizen, having lost my
American citizenship by (my) mar
riage with an alien ineligible to cit
izenship.” This I disclaimed, and
still disclaim, for at the time of my
marriage and up to the present day
my husband is in possession of his
naturalization papers. But by fiat
of the state department my hus
band and I are stateless.
The amazing stand taken by the
United States authorities is “that
Hindus who are deprived of their
American citizenship revert to their
former British status.” Is this
stand due to total ignorance of the
British law? The British law says
that any British subject who re
nounces British nationality will
ingly, by naturalization into any
other country, cannot revert to
British citizenship automatically, in
case the said subject wishes to do
so; but must be naturalized accord
ing to British law, after living at
least five years in some British ter
ritory. Now, it is apparent that
without a passport an alien cannot
enter British territory for the pur
pose of taking up residence; and
there is no record of British author
ities offering safe conduct to an In
dian who has become an American
citizen and then been deprived of
American citizenship, to-go to Brit
ish territory, under promise of re
naturnlizntion in the course of
time.
Takes Our Safety.
Requests to the British govern-
ment to enter British territory,
made by Indians who have lost
their American citizenship, have
either been refused or no notice has
been taken of them. So when the
American government arbitrarily
takes from us (American women
and Hindus naturalized as Amer
ican citizens) our American citi
zenship and protection, violating
scraps of paper given us in the
form of naturalization certificates,
it takes from us our safety and our
standing in any community no mat
ter where we may take refbge.
According to the Cable act, an
American woman marrying an alien
Ineligible to citizenship loses her
American citizenship. An American
man may marry a Japanese, Chi
nese. Hindu—any woman he pleases.
To do so does not lose him his citi
zenship. But an American woman
is penalized when she exercises this
right granted the American man.
She may marry a Negro from Africa
and not lose her American citizen
ship, but if she marries a Hindu,
Chinese or Japanese, however high
his reptuation as a scholar, she loses
her American citizenship. I feel
that an American woman should not
be penalized for marrying the per
son she loves. Marriage Is not a
matter of convenience; it has a spir
itual bearing and none has the right
to dictate the inner life of an indi
vidual.
Hit in Congress.
The National Woman's party has
sought to temedy the situation by
amending the Cable act, but the
house immigration committee re
fused to report out the bill. Some
represenentatives and senators, mem
bers of the immigration committees
of the two houses of congress, hold
that the ideal of Americanism should
keep any American woman from
marrying any foreigner, particularly
an Asiatic. One senator said that
he would do all he could to defeat
any amendment to the Cable act
which would give the right of Amer
ican citizenship to any American
woman marrying any foreigner. The
American patriots who think that
such provincialism is Americanism
would do well to remember what
Theodore Roosevelt said on an allied
topic:
Our nation fronts on the Pacific,
just as it fronts on the Atlantic. We
hope to play a constantly growing
part in the great o6?an of the
orient. We wish, as we ought to
wish, for a great commercial de
velopment in our dealings with
Asia; and it is out of the question
that we should permanently have
such development unless we freely
and gladly extend to other nations
the same measure of justice and
good treatment as we expect to re
ceive in return. I ask fair

STRIKES CONDUCTED, FINANCED
ON REAL BIG BUSINESS BASIS
NEW YORK —Labor unionism, in
the garment trades at least, has
reached the magnitude of big busi
ness. Its machine runs night and
day during a strike to match the
employers’ strategic activities. A
corps of trained men directs opera
tions with an efficiency and a dis
cipline that an army officer might
commend. The management, ma
neuvering and financing of 40,000
cloakmakers on strike require high
skill in leadership.
In the present upheaval, finances
seem to be the least of the union
chiefs’ worries. Apparently the high
cost of strikes has not yet become a
factor for serious consideration.
Not only are the cloakmakers
counting on their own ample re
sources, but they have also been
handed blank checks by the other
needle trades unions to fill out
when more funds are required.
Machinery for the conduct of the
strike is designed to meet every
need of the strikers and to cover a
wide range of emergencies. From
the time the worker leaves the shop
until he returns to it after the con
clusion of the walkout he is part
of a system that has been elabo
rated to the last detail.
Well Cared For.
The individual striker is sheltered
by a hall committee. He receives
emergency relief and finally strike
benefits from a relief committee.
He goes to concerts and to the the
ater free, thanks to prearrange
ments by the entertainment com
mittee. Strike orators and lectur
ers are obtained for him by the
speakers’ bureau. In case of arrest
capable legal protection is provided,
so that he is quickly bailed and
counsel assigned to his case. If he
wants information, there is a spe
cial bureau to tell him what he
wants to know, about his shop or
any other related subject.
Strike periods, contrary to ex
pectations, are not times of finan
cial stringency at union headquar
ters. On such occasions a vast
amount of currency flows into the
union treasury from many sources
and goes out in numerous channels
to make the strike machinery func
tion effectively. The amount of
financial support it can command
and its credit with other labor or
ganizations makes one infallible test
of a labor organization’s strength.
An ample treasury is vital, for with
out money no strike could last very
long.
Strikes Are Costly.
Garment strikes are especially
costly. The needle trades unions
usually count on spending $1,000,000
in a major struggle. Frequently they
end a 10 weeks’ contest stronger
financially than when they began,
and usually the morale of the mem
bership has been raised by the con
flict.
The present strike has been in
progress eight weeks, and thus far
has been financed out of the cloak
makers’ war chest of about $1,000,-
000. The labor leaders are count
ing on another million becoming
available to carry on the struggle
well into the fall if necessary. There
have been years when the Interna
tional Ladies’ Garment Workers’
union and its locals disbursed be
jtween $5,000,000 and $6,000,000.
practically all on the organizing end
or for the direct cost of the adjust
ment of wage conditions in an in
dustry concentrated in a half dozen
cities. This is in favorable contrast
to the early days of the union in
1903; then the international presi
dent feared to go to his office be
cause the organization was half a
year in arrears for the rent.
Big Fund Raised.
Older eloakmakers can recall the
days when the public helped finance
treatment for the Japanese, as I
would ask fair treatment for Ger
mans. Englishmen, Frenchmen, Rus
sians, or Italians.
In Bad Way.
I am not pleading today for the
right of Asiatics to become Ameri
can citizens. But I hold that the
attitude of the United States gov
ernment toward Hindus who were
naturalized before the adverse su
preme court decision is worse than
the alleged attitude of Soviet Rus
sia or the Mexican government,
against which the United States
state department so bitterly com
plains, in enacting retroactive laws
depriving Americans of their vested
rights. The state department, de
claring that Hindus who were nat
uralized by United States judges
according to due process of law. to
whom naturalization certificates
were given upon the authority of
the United States government, are
no longer American citizens, is vio
lating a solemn contract. Ilas the
American government fallen to such
a state of degradation that to.it
the civil rights of its citizens have
less value than property rights?

their strikes, especially that of 191 G
in the lockout following the abro
gation of the protocol of peace. The
citizens’ committee raised more than
$140,000 at that time, Jacob H.

sums.
Long experience with strikes—
which recur like waves and usually
spread from city to city, involving
almost every one of the garment cen
ters —has made for an almost per
fect strike organization. "With the
calling of a strike the New York
joint board, representing all the
locals of the international here, be
came the general strike committee.
Its functions are divided among
nine committees. Upon these re
sponsibility is fixed for various
duties connected with the exigencies
of industrial welfare.
Men trained by years of expe
rience in picketing, organizing, legal
aid or relief are put in charge, with
veterans of the organisation to help
them in committee work. They act
under the direction of the general
strike chairman, who in the present
struggle is Louis Hyman, manager
of the joint board. They are re
sponsible to the general strike com
mittee, composed of about 130 mem
bers, including the managers of the
20-odd local unions, the executive
boards of the affiliated local unions,
the general officers of the joint
board and the 15 shop chairmen of
the block and building committees,
a new link in the elaborate strike
organization of the cloakmakers’ or
ganization.
Tax Is Levied.
Preparations for this strike began
just as soon as the employers indi
cated their determination not to
grant the union’s demands for a 44-
hour week, registration and limita
tion of subcontractors, a wage in
crease and other improvements in
working conditions. A tax of S2O a
member was levied to create the
strike fund. When the strike pros
pect became certain there was about
$350,000 in the treasury of the joint
board, according to Joseph Fish, the
secretary and treasurer, who is in
charge of all disbursements of funds
during the general strike. A full
$1,000,000 is due from the strike as
sessment, which it is expected will
be ample for the time being.
The 1921 cloakmakers’ strike,
which lasted 10 weeks, cost the
union all of $1,000,000, of which the
major portion was spent for strike
benefits. Single men got $5 a week
and married men $7. The 1916 con
troversy, one of the most bitter be
cause it involved the existence of
the union, was waged 11 weeks and
cost more than $1,000,000.
Have Plenty Aid.
It usually happens in a cloak and
suit strike that after the first six
or seven weeks enough workers go
back to settled shops under union
conditions to pay. through a tax on
their earnings, substantial amounts
into the union coffers while the rest
of the union remains on strike. At
present nearly $25,000 a week (15
per cent of their wages) is being
paid by such workers to the joint
board. Several thousand strikers
who have found work in other
trades are paying into the treasury
about $5,000 more—lo per cent of
what they earn. These assessments
gradually mount up, until frequent
ly a strike becomes self-sustaining.
The main strength of the striking
cloakmakers, however, is the sup
port of the other needle trades
unions, which they have helped in
similar crises and that are ready
and eager to aid their sister union.
Already the fur workers, who have
just ended a 17-weeks’ strike of
their own, have pledged a day’s
pay. This should amount to nearly
SIOO,OOO. In the background stands
the Amalgamated Clothing Workers
of America, representing the work
ers in the men’s clothing Industry,
which can readily donate or lend
5250.000 if the cloakmakers need it
to win. Other reserves prepared
to be called on are the capmakers,
pocketbook makers and similar
craftsmen, not to mention the lo
cals of the International Ladies’
Garment Workers in other cities
and the international or carer.t or
ganization itself.
Have Own Bank.
Tn past years the cloakmakers
were also able to get loans from
banks, aften without •mllateral.
Bankers rated the union's dues-pay
ing membership as sound security;
as the goodwill of a corporation of
standing that maintains a large
bank balance. Now the union has
its own bank, its own tellers.
Transactions are carried through
with speed and dispatch.
The Unemployment Insurance
fund maintained in the industry for
the last two years has unexpectedly
helped the union in the present sit
uation. Thq strain, upon the strike

NINE
CONDITION OF
BRITISH MINERS
CALLED PITIFUL
LONDON—Two weeks ago we de
•ided the only way to find out
vnether the miners were starving
or not was to go through the mining
ar<-as and see for ourselves. Mr.
Baldwin says the government alone
is spending £1,000,000 a month to
feed the strikers’ families; that
“there is no starvation or even mal
nutrition,” and that in many cases
the children, being fed in the schools
nre better off than they were before
the strike.
The miners’ organizations report
there are about 1,000,000 miners,
and common sense shows there must
be at least four dependents on each
•—at. least, since families of 12 chil
dren are not uncommon in the coal
districts, and we hear of one family
with 211 So the £1,000,000 a month
for 1,000,000 mining families works
out at 5 shillings a week for a
family. There is a little outside re
lief, private charity that is, and
Russian mon^y, the amounts differ
ing according to the violence of the
partisanship of the reporting papers.
Baldwin All Wrong.
Mr. Baldwin is wrong. There is
starvation and there is malnutrition,
and if it is true many children are
better fed now than before the
strike, so much the worse for pre
cttrike wages. We drove through the
Forest of Dean and into Wales, to
the west coast, then back to Eng
land and north through the Mid
lands and the Black Country into
York. Our way went through some
of the loveliest scenery in all Europe,
but wherever a vein of coal existed
under the hills they were ruined by
the filthy slag heaps that poured
down their sides, and their valleys
were made hideous by the crowded
streets of desolate, ugly little houses
packed into them.
Indeed, the most depressing thing
alsjut the whole depressing journey
was the vast amount of unnecessary
ugliness. The valley of the Rhondda
In South Wales is typical; for miles
and miles to its head one village
runs into another without a break,
a long drawn out gray wall of house
fronts on either side, all built to one
box-like pattern, a door and three
windows opening on to the pave
ment. The heather covered hills
•ower hundreds of feet above them,
without a house; in the towns the
children play in the tram tracks
and there is scarcely a garden any
where; indeed, some of the houses
aave other houses built in their
cellars.
As for starvation, it stared at us
In almost every home. Women and
men, too, swayed from weakness as
•hey talked. They live on bread and
•ea while the money from the Poor
Law Relief lasts, after that they go
without. As the rate of relief varies
:n each district, and ns the way it
:s administered depends on the offi
cials in charge, some families practi
cally starve, others exist just at the
itarvatlon line.
The children on the streets look
well enough, in the odd assortment
♦f rags and garments they are now
wearing—for none have had clothes
lor nearly four months now, and
Khoes especially have given out. But
the children of school age have one
nnd often two meals in their class
rooms, at least during week days.
And some schools, but by no means
nil are to go on giving them a daily
meal during the holidays.
But the tiny brothers and sisters
nt home were the most pathetic, for
♦hey didn’t play like normal, robust
ildren, and though I saw hundreds
J^hbies, I don’t remember one that
miled. They were dirty—bread is
more necessary than soap when you
get down to a primitive struggle for
life —but it was often hard to tell
whether tt<eir gray skins were due
to dirt or malnutrition.
Shocked by Sight.
At first the condition of some of
the families we visited shocked me.
1 remember a woman so poor that
when her baby was born she lay
naked, without a nightgown, with
<ut even a sheet to cover her. But
we found other families as badly
off. I remember a “case,” as the
local relief workers call them, where
there was not only nothing to cover
the mother when the child was born,
but not even a rag to wipe the new
born baby with, nor anything to
wrap it in. Of course there was no
food.
I remember a pretty little lame
girl of 14. who was patching her
skirt with a piece of bag, who began
crying to herself when her mother
Faid in a tone of complete and calm
hopelessness that toey would lose
her before the strike was over. She
needed more than the bread and tea
they got to live on, and she was not
strong enough to stand the foodless
days.

HOTEL AND BAR
TO BE BUILT ON
CANADIAN LINE
GLACIER NATIONAL PARK—
At the head of Glacier National
park, perhaps a day's ride by bus,
a few hours by motor, is Waterton
lake, which sits in the lap of the
Rocky mountains.
Waterton lake is bisected by the
international boundary line, and
part of the lake thus lies in Canada.
Just north of the Canadian bound
ary the Glacier Park hotel company,
a subsidiary of the Great Northern
railway company, which serves the
park, next summer will have com
pleted,it is expected, a new hotel
costing about $500,000.
It is unlikely that, when the hotel
is completed, the Great Northern
will advertise that a handsome bar
will, as you view it, either adorn of
detract from the hotel, yet the bar
will be there and there is reason
to l>elieve that it will be well nigh
impossible to buy a glass of re
freshing near-beer in the place.
The northern end of Waterton
lake is in the province of Alberta.
The new hotel will be in Alberta, or
at any rate that part of the hotel
where the population will scoff at
lemonades. Alberta is wet, quite
wet Beer parlors are allowed. Gov
ernment liquor stores are main
tained.
So far as can be learned the Great
Northern railway has not yet made
out the lists of guests who will be
invited to the opening of the new
hotel, which will compare favorably
with the good hotel at Many Glacier
camp, not far away. Getting in at
the Army-Navy game in comparison
may be a sinecure.

RELATES TALE OF TERRIBLE
SUFFERING IN MIAMI AREA
FORT PIERCE, Fla. Kirby
Jones, representative of the Ameri
can Bakeries Co., who left Miami on
the first train out after the storm,
described yesterday conditions in
that city during the hurricane.
“The storm started at 1 a. m., Sat
urday,” he said, “and raged until
2 p. m., Saturday. It started with
a terrific wind, followed a few min
utes later by heavy rains.
“About 7 a. m., Saturday, both
wind and rain abated. It was this
lull which indirectly caused most of
the casualties. Hundreds of persons,
believing the storm was over, start
ed for work, but about 8 a. m. the
rain began again and the wind grew
more and more violent.
“The city was covered with dark
ness which obscured everything. Be
tween 9 a. m. and noon the wind
velocity reached its maximum. Thou
sands of homes were ripped from
their foundations and the air was
filled with flying timbers.
“I was in a building seeking shel
ter from the storm when the roof
cared in. There were about 150
other people with me at the time.
All of us fled to a schoolhouse a
block away.
“It was a pitiful sight to see that
crowd running through the driving
rain, barely able to make headway
against the terrific force of the
wind. Women were crying hyster
ically and old men whimpering that
they did not want to die, their voices
almost inaudible in the roar of the
wind. And all the while flying tim
bers and glass were falling all
about us.
“We reached the schoolhouse and
remained there until noon. Then the
storm abated once more, and three
hours later it stopped.
“The city was without water be
cause mains everywhere had burst
and the authorities were compelled
to cut the water off.
“I saw people catching rain water
in saucepans as it dripped from the
roof in order to make coffee.
“Late in the afternoon I went
down town to survey the damage.

Colored Boy a Hero.
SEBRING, Fla.—A Negro boy in
the field hospital, his wrists bound
to ease pain from cuts and bruises,
told of a dozen rescues he had made,
but broke down after recounting his
inability to save two white children.
“God knows I tried to get to those
white folks,” he sobbed.
He said the children were on a
bridge which threatened to collapse.
Just as he reached the girders they
loosened, and the bridge went down,
carrying the children with it.

BIG SCOREBOARD
FOR 150-MILE
RACE HERE
A new scoreboard. 76 feet in
length, which will be manned by 20
scorers, is being erected at State
Fair park directly across from the
grandstand for the 150-mile na
tional championship motor race,
which will be staged by the Wiscon
sin Speedway Assn, over the his
toric West Allis race course Sun
day.
The board, which can be plainly
seen from the most distant scat in
the stands, will show the progress
of the titular event, and as Director
Grover Horn will have an expert
staff of sheetmen in charge there
will be no chance for a mixup such
as marred several races i eld on the
track this season.
Among the entries received Tues
day night was that of Jack Mattes,
former state champion, who cap
tured the first 100-mile race held
over the track. Mattes will wheel a
high powered Frontenac. He has
not been so successful in the sprint
and short distance events, but he
has never failed to finish in the
money in the long grinds. In fact
some of Jack’s Polish friends have
gathered a purse of .SSOO which they
will wager on his chances to win if
they can get the proper odds.
The entry of Mattes brings the
total of cars nominated up to 14.
Among those entered are some of
the leading dirt track stars of the
middle west, including the sensa
tional Louis Schneider, national 100-
mile champion, who will come here
to try for the 150-mile title.
The race will start at 2 p. m.

HAGEN, SARAZEN
MAY CLASH
FOR TITLE
GARDEN CITY, L. I.—lt looked
like Walter Hagen against Gene
Sarazen for the finals in the an
nual play for the professional golf
ers’ crown here, after the first
round had eliminated many of the
foremost contenders.
Yesterday was a bad day for the
stars, among those falling along the
fairways nnd greens being Jim
Barnes, Joe Turnesa, Al Watrous,
Al Espinosa, Freddie McLead, Bol>-
by Cruikshank and Harry Cooper.
Hagen wasn’t ou his best game
yesterday, but he did not have to
be to eliminate Turnesa, who
seemed to be under the spell of
Hagen charm. Both Barnes and
Sarazen played indifferent golf for
the first 18 holes of their match,
then little Gene cut loose with the
sensational play that carried him
to the heights of golfdom in 1922
and 1923, goipg out in 32 —four un
der par—for his first nine in the
afternoon and being even fours of
the five concluding holes which
ended the play five up and four
against Barnes.

Gene Normille, Dempsey’s busi

"We are not worried about all

TUNNEY MAY
HAVE KEARNS
AS SECOND
By The United Preus.
PHILADELPHIA When Jack
Dempsey walks in the ring tomor
row night to defend his heavyweight
championship against Gene Tunney
he may find in the other corner,
back of his opponent, Jack Kearns.
Billy Gibson, manager of the ma
rine challenger, hasn’t announced
his staff of seconds and Kearns
hasn't said anything more definite
than —“I'll be at the fight, you can
bet that.”
For other than the demoralizing
effect that the presence of his for
mer manager in his opponent’s cor
ner might have on Dempsey, Kearns
would be a handy man to have
around and in times of stress good
seconds are needed almost as much
for Gibson as for his fighter.
Mitchell Fight Recalled.
Never will those forget who saw
it, the face of Mr. Willum Gibson
one night in old Madison Square
Garden when Richie Mitchell clipped
Benny I*onard on the chin and
flopped him for the count of nine.
Gibson’s face turned almost green,
his eyes popped and his mouth made
all the motions of talking but not a
word came out.
It was Leonard who kept his head
and motioned to the panic stricken
Gibson that he was not in danger.
Leonard was fully recovered in a
few moments but Gibson didn’t get
over it for a month.
It was Leonard also who'shouted
to his manager to keep quiet when
he was being beaten all over the
ring by Lew Tendler in their first
fight. Leonard, it will he recalled,
was in very bad shape but he kid
ded Tendler out of what was a great
chance to win by a knockout.
Leonard probably will be one of the
seconds in Tunney’s corner.
Kearns isn’t the great second that
he thinks ho is but when he hasn’t
a million dollar fighter of his own
to take care of he may not become
so excited.
Bottle Story Disputed.
Kearns, in his memoirs, says that
his quick thinking saved Dempsey
between the first and second rounds
of his memorable fight with Luis
Firpo. Kearns says that Dempsey
was out on his feet and flopped so
heavily on the stool in the corner
that he knocked the bottle of smell
ing salts out of his manager’s hand.
The bottle smashed on the floor but
Kearns thought quickly, reached
down ami dipped the sponge in the
ammonia and held it under Demp
sey's nose and his head cleared.
If memory serves correct, and the
pictures proved it, Kearns did noth
ing of the kind. The bottle didn’t
fall to the floor and break. It re
mained all during the intermission
in his hands and the only nose un
der which it was applied was Mr.
Kearn’s nose!
It is doubtful what effect the pres
ence of Kearns in the opposite cor
ner would have on Dempsey. It
certainly wouldiVt surprise him. In
fact he would be surprised if he
didn’t find his former manager tell
ing him how to boat the champion.
Delaney Upset Jeffries.
Jim Jeffries was terribly dis
turlied when he saw Billy Delaney,
his former manager, liehind Jack
Johnson but Jeffries was in such a
state of nerves that the slightest an
noyance would have upset him.
Dempsey isn’t of that temperament.
Instead of bothering him it might
arouse him to a fury.
His feelings, although he is very
sensitive about some things, aren’t
easily hurt. lio was worked into
a frenzy when the crowd razzed him
before the Cnrjientier fight and he
could have murdered anyone within
reach when Tom Gibbons kept him
waiting 20 minutes in the corner in
Shelby.

ELEVEN
|A LAWYER-COACH
Law and sports seem to go hand
in hand of late, and I don't refer to
the various attachments, Injunc
tions, writs of mandamus, habeas
corpus, and hokus pokus which have
popped up in connection with the
recent activities of Tex Rickard,
Jack Dempsey and Jack Kearns.
Monte Munn, the big Nebraska
legislator, has put the combination
of the law and the ring before the
public quite satisfactorily of late.
But down nt Old Nassau for these
many years, a prominent lawyer
and lawmaker has been mixing his
Blackstone with his football, and
with great success too.
For Coach Bill Roper of the
Princeton football team has been n
prominent Philadelphia lawyer and
a member of the city council, at the
same time whipping the ambitious
undergraduates into well-drilled,
hard-fighting gridiron machines.
Bill is so good a politician that
he has been mentioned for mayor of
the City of Brotherly Love, and even
for governor of the state that took
the Dempsey-Tunney fight away
from New York. In fact, Roper has
one of the keenest legal minds in
the profession, and annually he de
cides that he must retire from the
field of sports to devote all his time
and energy to his business.
What will Bill Roper do at
Princeton this year? Will the threat
of being dropped from the Harvard
schedule in 1927 cause the ferocious
Tigers to rise to greater heights
than ever in their annual battle
with the Crimson? Last year, it
will be remembered. Princeton was
tied by the lowly Navy and then
whitewashed by Colgate on succes
sive Saturdays, but came on finely
to score G 1 points against Harvard
and Yale, thus winning the undis
puted championship of the "Big
Three.”
Bill Roper played at Princeton
from 1899 to 1901 and has been
coaching his Alma Mater for over

nals play one game with Brooklyn

A Page For Women and the Home
“Just think of it, Walter,” said
Constance, “we have known each
other for a year; we have been
engaged for three months—and we
haven’t had a single difference.
Those stories we read about in
romantic fiction of 'lovers’ quar-
rels’ are all nonsense—aren’t
they?”
“They are, they are,” replied
Walter; “when two persons really
love each other they don’t quarrel.
They can’t; they are too consid
erate of each other.” And then he
went home to pack his bags.
The very next afternoon Con
stance was in a tearoom drinking
lukewarm water, tea-flavored,
and eating when she saw a young
man come in escorting a young
lady with fluffy golder hair!
Constance half rose from her
chair, gazed and then sank back
again, feeling dizzy. Tbe couple
took a table across the room and
began chatting and laughing in a
most friendly and intimate man
ner.
“Why Constance!” cried one of
the young ladies who were with
her, “isn’t that Walter Bodwin
over there? It surely is. What’s
the matter? Ue looked right nt
you just now and didn't even
bow. Have you had a quarrel?
Oh, do tell us about it.”
“We have had no quarrel,” re
plied Constance struggling for
self-command, “we nre not on
speaking terms just now—that is
all.”
“No quarrel nnd not on speak
ing terms,” piped up another girl.
“How mysterious! Come now.
having excited our curiosity you
really owe us the details.”
“They would he too prosaic for
you, Paula,” snapped Constance:
“your own well-known imagina
tion will doubtless evolve some
thing much more interesting”—
and changed the subject. She
tried her best not to look toward
the table occupied by the recreant
one and his fluffy-haired com
panion but, in spite of herself,
she could not help stealing one or
two fleeting glances in that direc
tion. Walter was dressed as she
had never seen him dressed before
—rather loudly, she thought;
probably to harmonize with the
rather loudly dressed young lady
upon whom he was in attendance.
Somehow she got through with
her tea and hastening home sought
refuge alone In her room to think
things over. So Walter Bodwin
had not departed for the east, on
the midnight train the night be
fore. He had stayed over to meet
that fluffy-haired girl. Was he
going to N^w York at nil?—or
had that story been told her for a
blind? And he had cut her dead
in the tearoom! Of course he
must realize that all was over be
tween them now—and he had in
tended it to be so. Oh, it was all
very hard! i
A servant brought up a letter
which had just been delivered by
a district messenger. Constance
recognized the handwriting of the
address and opened the envelope
saying: “If Jhe messenger has not
gone tell him to wait.” The letter
read:
“Dearest: I did not have to go
east after all. Orders revoked nt
the last minute; so, I shall see
you tonight, as usual.”
He had written from his office,
on office letterhead. She took a
pencil and wrote at the bottom of
the page. “I do not wish to see
you tonight; or at any other
time;” folded It, sealed it in an
envelope, addressed ft —the mes
senger hoy having been caught in
time—dispatched the missive to
Mr. Walter Bodwin.
The next afternoon, at one of
the big department stores, Con
stance ran into Paula Bancroft.
“Oh, you, Constance!” i gushed
Paula, “how you did fool us all
yesterday. That man we took for
Walter Bodwin was his twin
brother from San Francisco —here
on his honey moon. I met him at
the Ringgolds’ last night. And you
knew it all the time and didn't
let on!” Of worse Constance
knew Walter had a brother in
“Frisco;” and remembered now
that Walter had mentioned that
ho was a twin. But San Fran
cisco was a long way off. Bow
was she to know that the Cali
fornia twin was in New York?
However, a hasty note, promis
ing explanation, summoned Wal
ter to her side and of him she de
manded “Why didn’t you toll me
your brother was in New York?”
You didn't give me a chance.”
expostulated Walter meekly. “I
only knew it myself this morn
ing."
“Well, I forgive you this time.
Walter.” said Constance; “it is
impossible to be angry with you
tery long.”

VARIETY OF FOOD
GIVES BALANCE
TO THE DIET
“Many a woman who constantly
feels ill and bemoans her fate would
change her outlook on life if she
balanced her diet,” says Dr. E. V.
McCollum, famous diet authority of
Johns-Hopkins university, in tho
October issue of McCall’s. The rules
for a balanced diet are really sim
ple to apply, declare the scientists,
and even the mysterious vitamins
are easy to get if you know where,
which is also revealed. Here are
the secrets of a balanced diet:
“By ‘balancing the diet,’ we mean
the proper adjustment of the
amounts cf the various food ele
ments we eat. The essential prin
ciples in the diet are protein, carbo
hydrate, fat, mineral matter, vitam
ins and water. All or nearly all of
these are found in most of our nat
ural foodstuffs, but in very different
proportions in each kind of food.
Proteins Necessary.
“It is not possible to sny thAt any
certain amount of protein is neces
sary in the daily diet, for some pro
teins are better than others. We
know, however, that the average
daily amount of protein should be
three to three and a half ounces.
Nutrition experts agree that one can
get enough protein by eating one to
two eggs, one quart of milk and
one fairly liberal serving of meat,
fish or fowl every day, together with
the protein contained in such bread,
potatoes and other foods as one
would naturally eat.
“Many women do not eat enough
protein-rich food. They live inac
tive lives, eat sweets between meals,
suffer from indigestion due to fer
mentation end constipation and
seek relief in eating but little food.
They acquire an appetite for fancy
foods with pronounced flavors and
avoid the more substantial ones such
as meats, eggs and milk. All these
individuals feel cold, are anemic
and have but little endurance and
little capacity for rest and recupera
tion. They would find a better bal
ancing of their diet very beneficial.
Vitamins in Fatty Foods.
“Both fats and carbohydrates
(starches and sugars) are sources
of energy and have but a secondary
place in building body structure,
which is the unique work of protein.
Some fats are carriers of vitamins,
but no carbohydrate eaten in a fair
ly pure form contains any vitamin.
The three vitamins contained in cer
tain fats are A, D and E. Vitamins
B and C do not occur in fats. The
distribution of the vitamins is very
interesting.
“No vegetable fat or oil contains
appreciable amounts of vitamin .A,
although it is to be found in small
amounts in many plant tissues. It
is abundant in fish oils, especially in
cod liver oil. Butter fat, cream or
whole milk, the fats of egg yokes
and the invisible fats in such gland
ular organs of animals as liver, kid
ney and sweet-breads, contain vi
tamin A in abundance. Although
all the leafy vegetables commonly
eaten in this country are very poor
in fats, they contain considerable
amounts of vitamin A.
“Vitamin B is never found in any
fats or oils of either animal or vege
table origin, but is the most widely
distributed of the vitamins, abun
dant in many of our common food
stuffs. Vitamin C, which protects
from scurvy, is abundant only in
fresh, raw. or perhaps better, un
cooked foods. The fruits are prob
ably all of some value as scurvy
preventives. but their values differ
greatly. The citrous fruits are
best, lemons having a greater
amount of vitamin C than oranges.
Vitamin D, which has such a re
markable effect in insuring the child
against abnormal bone growth and
rickets, unfortunately is not to be
found in more than mere traces in
even our most nearly complete agri
cultural foods. The only good
source of this vitamin is fish oil.
Mineral Element in Milk.
“Calcium or limo is the most im-
portant of the mineral elements
which are absolutely necessary to
jiood health. Most foods contain too
little calcium. In fact, only milk
and the leafy vegetables are rich in
it.
“What we have called the ‘protec
tive foods’ —milk and leafy vege
tables, are so constituted that they
make good the deficiencies of almost
everything else we eat. It is only
necessary to include enough of each
of these In the daily diet to make
our eating safe. We should eat, in
addition, some raw fruit such as
oranges and raw vegetables such as
cabbage, lettuce, celery and so forth,
every day or at least frequently, to
get the vitamin C. It is necessary,
too. especially in the case of chil
dren. to give every once in a while
a teaspoonful of cod-liver oil to sup
ply vitamin D.”
