few and far between. Later they
become more or less continuous.
The victims of asthma, it is
found, have a weakness toward cer
tain substances, when breathed in,
or taken as food, drink or medicine.
Among the substances breathed in,
which may cause astnma are
dander from all animals, cats, dogs,
rabbits, horses; also birds or furs;
house dust, flour, mustard, paper,
face powder. Various pollens of
flowers, grasses, weeds, trees, may
cause asthmatic attacks associated
with hay fever.
These facts make it unwise for
asthmatic people to work at any of
the dusty trades.

cially important in children) include
the entire dietary list and particu
larly milk, eggs, nuts and cereals.
Medicines, such as asperin, quinine,
or ipecac may also produce au at

quake and fire and the Japanese
earthquake.

structed, should and will withstand
a 150-mile an hour hurricane.

shown at the eighth annual Steel
and Machine Tool exhibition here,
make it possible to construct a steel
skyscraper In one great solid piece,

SALES CLIMB,
EXPORTS JUMP
NEW YORK —Industrial activity
on a large scale is reflected in the
upward trend of sales in machinery
and machine tools, American Ma
chinist reports. Earlier predictions
of a good fall business are borne out
by the volume of orders and the
number of inquiries reaching the
market. Moderate improvement in
export business has been reflected in
the sales made so far this month.
Demand Is Good.
Cincinnati has experienced con
tinued improvement in sales.
In Detroit the demand for ma
chine tools has increased and the
outlook for the fall is favorable.
Trading in the Chicago district is
quiet, but inquiries pending are ex
pected to open up after the ma
chinery exposition. The call for mis
cellaneous shop equipment is better
in the Indianapolis market.
Canada Shows Better.
In New England the machinery
manufacturers are working to ca
pacity. The New York market pre
m nts nothing out of the ordinary.
Industrial activity in Canada has
increased and has afforded much in
the way of contracts for industrial
machinery.
Canada Enters Upon
Period of Great
Industrial Activity
NEW YORK Canada has en
tered upon a period of great indus
trial activity in which American
manufacturing companies and
American capital are playing a no
table part, according to William
Phillips, manager, industrial de
partment of the Canadian National
Railways here today.
"There has been a very remark
able impetus to industrial develop-
ment in Canada during the past
year,” Mr. Phillips said, “and a sur
vey of the situation made by rep
resentatives of the Canadian Na
tional indicates that there is every
promise that this industrial growth
will continue upon an even larger
scale during the coming year.
“Power is becoming a more and
more important factor in industrial
development and Canada by its
fortunate situation in regard to
water power has a peculiarly ad
vantageous position. The available
power in Canada was increased by
719,000 horsepower during 1925,
bringing the total installation in the
dominian to 4.290,000 horsepower.”

LOAD ON TRACKS
UP 30 PER CENT
CHICAGO —The railroad tracks
of this country are now bearing
daily a load more than 30 per cent
greater than they did in 1921 as a
result of the increase in traffic and
the use of larger and heavier
equipment, R. 11. Aishton, president
of the American Railway Assn, told
the 44th annual convention of the
Railway Roadmasters and Mainte-
nance of Way Assn, at the Audi
torium hotel yesterday.
“The steel rail purchased last
year by the carriers, if laid end to
end in a single line, would extend
27,000 miles, which is equivalent to
the distance around the world at
the equator and 2,700 miles over.
“You are hearing continually
about the future of waterways, mo
tor truck and motor busses and
oven of airplane transportation in
competition with the railways. The
answer to all these things is a con
tinued increase in efficiency, to
gether with the necessity for con
tinuing to render more and more
adequate service to the public at the
lowest possible cost. If these things
are done, you need not fear the fu
ture of the railways.”

CABINET TELLS
OF PROSPERITY
WASHINGTON—-President Cool
idge today held his first cabinet
meeting since his return from White
Pine Camp. Many of the cabinet
members were able to report on ob
servations made during summer
trips and it was generally agreed
that conditions through the country
are favorable.
Secretaries Hoover and Wilbur
had both visited the Pacific coast
and were well pleased with the con
ditions they found there. “The
Rocky Mountain and Pacific states
are all in a very optimistic and
cheerful mood. Nobody is discour
aged or despondent,” Mr. Hoover as
serted. Question later regarding re
ports of his part in a new proposal
for agricultural financing, he said
he had never heard of a $100,000,000
farm aid fund being raised in New
York or anywhere else.”
Secretary Jardine said that farm
troubles in the middle west seemed
to be righting themselves, as he ob
served them on a vacation trip.
Secretary Mellon was the only
cabinet member who brought to the
meeting first-hand Information on
foreign affairs.

DI SON—Perhaps the most
dramatic incident in the state Re
publican convention here was the
denunciation of the late Senator
Robert M. La Follette by Otto
Werkmeister, Republican candidate
for the assembly, 21st ward, Mil
waukee.
After tAvo platforms Lad been pre
sented to the convention, both prais
ins La Follette, Werkmeister leai>ed
to his feet and declared:
“This praise of La Follette in two
platforms makes me sick. In a few
years the name of La Follette will
be only a memory.”
Attack Is Answered.
Later Senator Harry Sauthoff.
Dane county, and a close personal
friend of the late Senator La Fol
lette, obtained recognition from the
chairman, and pointing at Werk
meister said:
"Long after the person who just
insulted the memory of La Follette
has crumbled into dust the name
of La Follette will lie honored, and
will be an inspiration in American
political life.”
For Dry Ticket.
Werkmeister, with other Milwau
kee Repub’icans, voted for a bone
dry ticket; for Senator Casper son
for chairmanship of the Republican
convention; for a bone-dry chair
man of the Republican state central
committee and against Senator
Chase, wet, and for A. E. Smith.
Vernon county, dry, candidate for
secretary of the Republican conven
tion, and against John Eber, Mil
waukee, wet.
Other Milwaukee Republican
nominees for the assembly support
ed the dry ticket in an effon to put
over the Zimmerman slate.

Division Seeking
Jobs for Students
Giving a job to a University of
Wisconsin extension division stu
dent is equivalent to giving a schol
arship, according to Guy A\ertz, in
charge of the employment bureau,
University of Wisconsin, in Milwau
kee.
“We want more employers to be
Interested in giving genuine yart
time positions,” said Mr. Wertz to
day. “The type of student who is
willing to earn his way through a
university course is the very best.
He should be offered a real job with
a real opportunity."
Last year about 50 university ex
tension students were placed In real
jobs and the university expects to
continue this service this year.

FINANCE AND UNEMPLOYMENT
The Wall Street press informs us that President
Green of the American Federation of Labor had luncheon
with President Coolidge and told him: Twenty-five per
cent of the members of the federation are out of work,
and the best way to deal with this evil is to pay high wages
and reduce the hours of labor.
The repor* does not state what methods President
Green suggested to bring his remedy into effect, nor what
“The Spokesman” had to say to it, if anything.
We fully agree with President Green, but we doubt
that President Coolidge does. Our main reason for this
doubt is that Coolidge is the man who permits big bankers
to waste American money abroad instead of forcing them
to spend it at home in making the United States safe for
American citizens.
The war debt settlements and the private loans of the
American bankers to foreign governments and corpora
tions are the principal cause of American unemployment.
This policy, if pursued any further, will make more un
employment, not less, and will therefore militate most
strongly against higher wages and shorter hours.
There is no indication that President Coolidge in
tends to abandon or modify the Mellon policies, which
force the mass of the taxpayers to put up the money for
:he payment of the Liberty and Victory bond holders and
mables foreign military governments to employ their own
jobless on war industries.
This transaction is very profitable to the big bankers,
but unprofitable for the majority of American citizens.
It enables the bankers to draw from 8 to 14 per cent in
terest from foreign governments on new private loans
Awhile the mass of the American citizens must pay the in
terest on war bonds that the foreign governments are
allowed to cancel on the plea that they cannot pay from
3 to 4 per cent.
The Dawes plan compels Germany to compete with
the United States in tie control of foreign markets, and
uses American money to enable Germany to de it success
fully.
So we see no sense in telling Coolidge that he should
be interested in high wages and short hours, while at the
same time enabling him and his Repo-Democratic machine
to put the opposite policy into effect. And we wish Pres
ident Green would tell us what he proposes to do abcut it.

THE PLEA OF THE LOOTERS
The Paper Trade Journal prints an article by Charles
R. Berry which boldly recommends letting nature do her
own reforesting instead of interfering with her wise
methods by human efforts at conservation.
Berry claims that he does not mean to discourage
scientific methods of reforestation, but thinks neverthe
less that this conservation policy is as yet a mere experi
ment, none too worthy of approval. Nature can do it
much better than man, is his thesis.
If the looters would leave nature alone, it might be
a good plan to let her do her own reforesting. But so
long as they loot nature mercilessly, and then add insult
to injury by wasting her fine trees to make paper for such
articles as that one of Berry’s, it seems reasonable for
men to try to undo some of the harm that the looters have
done.
It is simply the old plea of “let us alone,” served up
in a new 7 sauce, and it is poorly disguised behind a lot of
quotations from Prof. Grondal of the forestry college of
Washington university. It is time for the looters to under
stand that their unrestrained freebooting raids on nature
are about over.

The Need of Control
BY ARTHUR CALHOUN
It ought to be apparent that
if the whole problem of the pro
duction and distribution of goods
continues to be left to chance, to
be carried haphazardly according
to the whims of a host of uncon
nected and irresponsible business
groups, progress toward an effec
tive administration of economic
affairs will be slow and bungling.
There must be more system, more
control.
The fact is realized by those
that hold the key position in the
business world—the financiers.
They would be quite willing to as
sume responsibility for heading
up the whole economic life under
the jurisdiction of a money trust,
control to be exercised through the
granting or withholding of credit
and ultimately through the inter
locking in the hands of the finan
ciers themselves of all the stra
tegic directorates, so that the
business world could move as a
unit and operate according to
system.
There is considerable merit in
such a scheme. Only persons with
a large familiarity with the broad
relations and general workings of
production and distribution the
world over can be in a position to
control effectively the scope and
direction of new investment and
of the operation of the system as
a whole. If no better plan for gen
eral control can be devised, then
we shall have to let the bankers
handle the job. In that event it
may be just as well to have a few
labor bankers more or less on the
inside in order to know at least
a little of what is going on,
though they can not expect to
have any considerable influence.
It is hardly likely, however, that
the workers will be i>ermanently
content to have things run by
financiers over whom no one can
have any real control. Sooner or
latter we shall have to look else
where for an effective administra
tion of the economic system.—

OLD DEBTS AND NEW WARS
Ex-Dictator Pangalos of Greece boasts that he ha^
made a deal with Dictator Mussolini to start a war on
Turkey this month, and that French influence back of
Gen. Kondylis queered this plan by a successful revolution.
If the ex-dictator tells the truth, several questions
suggest themselves. For instance, did Mussolini and Pan
galos act on their own hook, or did they act with the
knowledge of some foreign power? Did American bank
ers back them financially and promise them the help of
that foreign power?
Furthermore, would Germany have been taken into
the league, and would the Locarno pacts have taken effect,
if Mussolini and Pangalos could have started their war
on Turkey before the* league of nations met in Geneva?
It takes money to go to war. Everybody knows that
the Mussolini and Pangalos governments did not have the
money. Were the debts of Italy cancelled and was Pan
galos financed by American bankers for the purpose of
enabling them to attack Turkey?
We are naturally very much interested in the Amer
ican angle of this affair. We know that some American
interests still foment all the trouble that it is in their
power to stir up for Kemal Pasha’s government. W'e
know that they are in touch with those American bankers
who were most active in securing the cancellation of the
Italian war debts. Did these Same American bankers
authorize Mussolini to lend 200,000,000 lire to the Averescu
government in Rumania? Did they sanction his deal with
Pangalos and undertake to finance a war on Turkey?
A bankrupt government like that of Dictators Mus
solini or Pangalos cannot undertake such moves without
the backing of foreign bankers. The only bankers that
under present circumstances would be most likely to back
such a move are those American money lenders who fought
Kemal Pasha since the war, and who financed Mussolini
and Pangalos.
We don’t suspect British bankers of this deal, be
cause British oil interests in Albania, Mesopotamia and
Persia adjusted their differences with the Albanian and
Turkish nationalists. But the American interests that
Morgenthau has been representing in the Near East have
been befjting for a long time on Mussolini and Pangalos to
upset the barely established pacts in the Balkans and
Asia Minor.
This is only one flagrant instance of the way in which
the American taxpayer is robbed by the war debt settle
ments. He has to pay to the Liberty bond holders the 75
per cent which were knocked off the Italian war debt,
Mussolini, relieved of the obligation to pay back $2,000,-
000,000, spends this money on military preparations, dip
lomatic bribes and plots against the barely established
peace of the world.
The war debt settlement with Greece is also a series
of crooked deals which are a blot on the American govern
ment. Loans have been made, stopped, reopened, stopped
again and reopened according to the fluctuations of the
political scale in Greece, and the American taxpayer has
had to bear all the risk and loss of these underhanded
plots, in which Mr. Morgenthau has played a major role.
Pangalos, deposed and angry, gives a part of these
plots away and proves, what we have often maintained,
that the peace of the world is not secure, that war may
be started over night, as it was in 1914, even while all the
governments solemnly avow their sincere love of peace.
Can anybody blame us, under these circumstances, if
we do not believe that Germany in the league, or the grov
ing accord between Germany and France, or the Locas.
pacts, really make peace more secure?
WEATHER CHARTS SENT TO SHIPS
BY RADIO
Another step was taken the other day in the direction
of making travel by sea even safer than it is at present
when the experiments which have been conducted of late
of transmitting weather maps by radio to ships at sea were
declared a success. Indeed, during the oast few days
nearly a dozen weather charts furnished by the weather
bureau at Washington, D. C., have been sent from the
powerful naval station at Arlington, Va., and satisfactor
ily picked up by the bureau. It appears that the impulses
emanating from the Virginia station were caught and in
terpreted by a special machine, which recorded by an ink
stylus on a specially constructed drum the lines of the
map and indicated all the regular data depicted on the
usual daily charts.
Incidentally, the station at Arlington is of sufficient
power to make contact with ships in all sections of the
northern Atlantic, and it is announced that those in a po
sition to speak authoritatively give it as their opinion that
the experiments which have been conducted mean that it
will not be long before the regular meteorological chart of
the Washington bureau will be made available daily to
ships therein. And these same officials believe that vast
possibilities will open out before this field of marine
weather forecasting. This is how the results expected
have been outlined in one descriptive article concerning
this new activity:
“It will enable ships at sea to receive exactly the
same weather service as Uncle Sam now affords land
stations, and officials have asserted that the ability to re
ceive accurate daily weather maps showing the movement
of storms, areas of high and low pressure, thermal lines
and wind directions will be invaluable to meteorological
investigators on naval and merchant vessels especially
in time of impending disturbances.”
All such methods of constructive advancement in the
activities of human experience are to be welcomed—
Christian Science Monitor.

RESERVATIONS
BY HENRY WOOD.
Staff Correspondent
The tnited Press
GENEVA The conference of
world court signatories was to meet
today for final consideration of the
American reservations to court
membership.
A formula proposing acceptance
of all the senate’s reservations, with
one provision was to be acted upon.
The proviso is that the United
States shall negotiate an under
standing with the league of nations
council about the manner of ex
pressing American consent to the
rendition of advisory opinions.
To Submit Formula.
The formula was to be submitted
to the plenary session by a commit
tee of 14 appointed to find a way of
accepting reservations.
The committee yesterday adopted
the following eight specifications as
the formula:
1. Authorization for American
partiepation on a basis of equality
in all meetings of.the league of na
tions council or assembly for the
election of court judges.
2. Recognition that no amend
ment of the court’s statutes shall be
possible without the consent of the
United States.
3. Guarantee that the court shall
render all advisory opinions in pub
lic sessions.
4. Provisions that the manner in
which the United States shall con
sent to the court’s rendering an ad
visory opinion shall be the subject
of an understanding to be reached
with the United States government
and the league council.
5. Recognition of the rights of the
United States to withdraw at any
time from the court.
G. Provision that the court pro
tocol shall liecome effective only
when all signatories have ratified it,
including the United States, and it
is deposited with the league.
7. Provision for a reciprocity
clause whereby other signatories by
a two-thirds decision shall be en
titled to withdraw their acceptance
of the protocol should it fail to give
desired resmts.
8. Provision for the protocol to
remain open for signatures of other
nations which may later join the
Right to Withdraw.

sacola, battered by hurricane and

worse.

railroad roundhouse and the
wharves were badly damaged.

planes at the air station. The

Telegrams and letters, relating ex

in the hurricane which devastated a
portion of Florida, continued to ar

the anxiety of relatives.
The first to he received here, was

Palm Beach, to his mother, Mrs.

tearing planks from buildings and
boring them flying through the air,”
wrote Dr. Schwalble. He wrote that
the 130-mile an hour gale disabled
the water plant and the only avail
able drinking water was that which
leaked through the roof where the
storm had blown off shingles.
A similar letter, describing con
ditions, was received by Dr. and
Mrs. A. E. Mieding. 279 17th St.,
from F. C. Billings, formerly of Mil
waukee. who resided in Miami with
his wife and two sons, Henry and
Earl.
“The roof on our apartment house
was torn off by the terrific wind
and many windows were broken, but
fortunately no one was killed,” he
wrote.

Sacco and Vanzetti Await Outcome of Plea For New Trial
SHOW PROOF

Story of Mitchell’s

BOSTON—Nicola Sacco and Bar
tolomeo Vanzetti have made their
final motion for a new trial. Hear
ing of affidavits and argument on
the motion occurred before original
trial Judge Webster Thayer here.
The judge now has the case under
advisement.
Throughout the hearing, defense
counsel William G. Thompson em
phasized that he had urged on the
state joint examination of all wit
nesses in the presence of a public
stenographer so that there would
not be a “vulgar competition” of af
fidavits and counsel quibbling over
what was or was not said,
Slxtythree affidavits supported
the defense motion; 27 the state’s
opposition. The deposition of Ce
lestine Madeiros, whose confession
was the basis for the now trial mo
tion, was read into the record, to
gether with certain correspondence
Thompson deemed essential to show
his stand throughout the prepara
tion of the case.
Served Five Years.
The main facts of Madeiros’ con
fession were already known: That
he and a gang identified in other
affidavits as. the Morellis’ of Provi
dence, R. 1., committed the South
Braintree payroll robbery which re
aulted in the murder of the two
guards, Rerardelli and Parmenter.
Sacco and Vanzetti were convicted
of first degree murder for this
crime and have spent over five
years in the shadow of the electric
chair while their friends have car
ried on a momentous battle for their
lives.
Besides the confession and sup
porting evidence implicating the
Morellis ns the real criminals. the
most startling disclosures of the de
fense were contained in affidavits'
of former department of justice
agents. Fred J. Weynnd, now work
ing for Maine's attorney general,
and Lawrence Let herma n. employed
by Beacon Trust Co., both swear
that department of justice agents
took an important part in framing
np Sacco and Vanzetti on the mur
der charge because they could pot
get. sufficient evidence against two
Italian workers as radicals to de
port them.
United States Has Facts.
Weynnd insists that the Boston
office of the department of justice
has files of correspondence between
Dist. Atty. Frederick (J. Katzmann
and William J. West, federal agent
regarding the Sacco-Venzetti frame
up. Katzmann was chief prosecutor
of the two Italians. lie entered no
denial of the federal agents’ charge
His assistant. Harold Williams, is
now United States district attor
ney but has made no move to have
the Boston files opened to prove or
disprove the assertions of Wcyant
and Letherman.
Defense Counsel Thompson ap
pealed to L’. 8. Atty. Gen. Sargent,
upon advise of Senator William M.
^Butler, for aid in securing access to
the Boston department of justice
tiles. Neither Butler nor Sargent
succeeded in getting the informa
tion. Sargent did not even write
an answer to Thompson's request,
id though Thompson is a fellow Re
publican and head of the Massa
chusetts bar's grievance committee.
Is Called Tyranny.
The suppression of this evidence
by federal authorities, regardless of
what it might show, is cause
enough for the granting of a new
trial. Thompson argued effectively.
Disregarding Madeiros and the Mo
rellis, the unanswered charges of
Weynnd and Letherman are enough
to warrant setting Sacco and Van
zetti free. Asst. Atty. Dudley I*.
Ranncy admitted for the state, and
attempted to justify, the existence
of secrets in lioth federal and state
governments.
“A government that has to value
its secrets more than the lives of
its citizens has become tyranny!”
retorted defense counsel.
Followed Red Raids.
The Sacco-Vanzetti case is the
aftermath of the Balmer red raids
of 1920, Defense Counsel Thompson
related. Federal agents were balked
by Judge Anderson from easy depor
tation proceedings against suspect
ed and hounded aliens and radicals.
The conviction of Sacco and Van
zetti, whose names had been on de
partment of justic laioks for
months, for murder was regarded
as "one way of disposing of their
case
The two Italian workers lied,
tarried weapons and showed that
“consciousness of guilt” so noted by
Judge Thayer when identification
broke down at the first trial, be
cause they were radicals and knew
the fate of their friends in that
hectic spring of 4920 when A. Mit
chell Palmer was trying to climb
from the postion of United States
attorney general to the presidency.
The pitching of Andrea Salsedo
from the 14th floor department of
justice office to Park Row, New
York, after being held incommuni
cado without formal arrest and tor
tured for weeks, was fresh in the
minds of Sacco and Vanzetti when
arrested and quizzed about their
radicalism.

PASTOR SCORES
BRUTALITY OF
PASSAIC COPS
PASSAIC, N. J.—Declaring that
there are two Passaics, one clean,
tree-lined with luxurious homes, the
other dirty, with narrow streets
and dark, miserable homes, the Rev.
Norman W. Pendleton, pastor of the
Rutherford Congregational church,
Rutherford, in his sermon last eve
ning scored the mill owners for
their cold-hearted attitude towards
their workers and criticized the
Protestant churches Lr the un
worthy part they have played in the
big strike.
Rev. Pendleton told his congrega
tion he had seen with his own ejes
the unnecessary brutality of the po
lice and had watched the strikers
peacefully picketing the mills.
Strikers’ Action Harmless.
“I have watched the strikers
march, at a snail’s pace along the
sidewalks; many of them boys and
girls, singing their songs of ‘Broth
erhood and Solidarity,’ harmless as
a Sunday school picnic.
“I have watched the unnecessary
brutality of uniformed officials. I
listened to the Rev. John Hayes
Holmes make an eloquent plea for
the triumph of true Americanism
and the vindication of constitution
al rights, and saw a nervous sheriff
lose self-control and make himself
foolish. And through it all I Lave
marveled at the power of these peo
ple to hold themselves in, to hold
their peace, when it would seem
that there was almost evident pur
pose to drive them to violence.
“I tell you that if any group of
ministers or business men had been
meted such treatment there would
have been something doing!
A Great Divergency.
“One things stands out very clear
ly in mj’ mind. There are two
Passaics. One is clean, tree-lined,
beautifully homed. Americans in
hours of highest idealism may well
be proud of this Passaic. But there
is another Passaic. The two are
divided by railway tracks. The sec
ond Passaic is dirty; its streets are
narrow; its homes are dark; the
narrow streets are full of little
children. There are conditions here
of work and play of which no true
American can be proud.”

MOVE TO UNTIE

IS CONSIDERED
Demands for Change
Tn Constitutions
to Be Made.
OTTAWA, Ont.—Canada's atti
tude toward the London imperial
conference last night overshadows
all other political issues. This is
due to the announcement that
Henry Bourassa, nationalist leader
of Canada, will visit Desmond Fitz
gerald of the Irish Free State be
fore going to the empire conference.
Following his talks with the Irish
leaders Mr. Bourassa will cross to
London and meet Premier Hertzog
of South Africa. The meetings be
tween Messrs. Bourassa, Fitzgerald
and Hertzog will have to do with
the drafting of certain resolutions
involving changes in the dominions’
constitutions. It is hoped by the
Canadian Liberals that Canada,
South Africa and the Irish Free
State will stand united in backing
these demands in the imperial con
ference sessions. They also are ex
pected to act together in insisting
upon certain limitations on the func
tions of the king's representative in
a dominion and in defending of the
independent political status of the
dominions.
King May Attend.
Conservative leaders of parlia
ment announce they are willing to
give the incoming MacKenzie King
Liberal government every possible
co-operation and speed up parlia
mentary proceedings in order to al
low the new prime minister io lie
Canada's representative at the em
pire conference.
While it has been stated in semi
official circles that Mr. King will
not attend the imperial conference,
the Liberal leader has never said he
will not go.
Some Conservative chieftains as
sert Mr. King is seeking to avoid
attendance and unless he does at
tend or sends a man of equal status,
such as the minister of justice, they
are of the opinion that the disin
tegration of the British empire is
in sight.
Britain Is Alarmed.
LONDON Downing Street and
the colonial office are seriously per
turbed by the unexpected change in
the Canadian government due to
the victory of the Liberals in the
recent election. They fear it will
react unfavorably on the policies to
De propounded at the coming impe
•ial conference.
The return of MacKenzie King,
leader of the Liberals, as premier
has thrown a monkey wrench into
the machinery and upset the British
plans to keep Canada from joining
.South Africa in the claim for equal
status with the mother country.
The situation is more embarrassing
for the British government now be
cause Mr. King is silent as to
whether he will attend the empire
conference, which is only a month
distant.

pared to fight the reactionary Na

ward a culmination of the agree

eign Minister Rriand of France at

fice.

demands with the French refusal to
surrender certain definite benefits,
along with withdrawals from the
Rhineland and Saar, which already

tee’s work will be conducted entirely

government when he attempted to

the Russian telegram with feelings
of surprise and indignation, because
it gave to the British labor leaders
instructions as to what to do in re
gard to the miners and how to con
duct their affairs.

reply to Tomsky, telling him that

ers.”

of mine owners,” Tomsky rants.

have dared despoil the miners of the
seven-hour day.”

kee each year?

largest on the Great Lakes.
Question: Is Milwaukee a healthful city?

healthful cities. Milwaukee’s climate is pleasant
and invigorating; the seasonal temperature ex
tremes are such as to prevent monotony. Milwau
kee’s death rate is the second lowest of any city of
equal or greater size in the United States.
Question: Why has Milwaukee the lowest crime rate

courts with celerity, certainty and finality. There is
hearty co-operation between Milwaukee’s police de
partment and Milwaukee courts. Wholesome Mil
waukee home life and the absence of a large float
ing population are likewise big factors in keeping
Milwaukee’s crime record at a minimum.

kee?

JUDGE ADMITS
BREAD, WATER
DIET IS TOUGH
HARTINGTON, Neb. County
Judge W. F. Bryant, 75, foe of liq
uor law violators in Cedar county,
after three of his self-imposed five
day sentence on bread and water,
has decided the diet should be given
only in “severe cases.”
Today the veteran judge admitted
It was "a pretty hard job to live on
bread and water,” although he went
about his court business with his
usual alacrity and breakfasted,
lunched and dined on good shares of
rye bread and water.
Judge Was Hungry.
“I get, pretty hungry,” Judge Bry
ant said. "At nights I dream that
1 am having a big feast, only to
wake up and find my only available
food is rye bread and water. I
guess 10 days is quite a long time
to give a prisoner such a diet, but
I am going to give it in serious cases
of liquor law Infraction, as I believe
it will bring home to the prisoner
what it means to violate the law.”
Judge Bryant said he has been
giving bread and water diet sen
tences for 14 years, ranging from
3 to 10 days. He said that any
prisoner would starve on a 10 days’
diet if it was not changed from one
Wind of bread to another.
They Need Change.
“If you take the crust off and
feed the prisoner just white bread,
he is likely to starve to death on
the diet if held to it for 10 straight
days,” he said. “However, if you
give him white bread one day, rye
another, and whole wheat and gra
ham the next, why, he probably
will lie pinched with hunger, but
just enough to make his law infrac
tion acquainted with his stomach.”

“GET INTO PARTY,” SLOGAN.
To the Editor of The Leader:
A great deal of buncombe is be
ing put out by “Get Out the Vote”
advocates. Getting out the vote is
a very superficial part of practical
citizenship work. At the polls on
election day the voter has only an
opportunity to choose between tick
ets which he may regard ns equally
bad. In that event, he can go off
and play golf, but that will not help
the cause of good citizenship very
much. Nor can he do much more
by simply attending the primary,
especially where he is handed a
“slate” already printed. The only
way in which he can really count
in the matter is by joining his po
litical club or local association and
participating in the caucuses where
the primary tickets originate.
Of what value is it for a citizen
to cast his vote at a primary and
then have it counted out by crooked
or ignorant election officials as in
Chicago only last month, where
more than 80,000 votes had to be
thrown out because of juggling on
the part of judges and clerks? The
same thing has happened in other
large cities.
Instead of a “Get Ont the Vote”
slogan we ought to have a “Get
Into the Party” slogan.
There is no point to getting out
the vote where the result is a fore
gone conclusion. There is always
a struggle, however, in choosing can
didates within a party. If this ap
plies more to the Republican and
Democratic than to the Socialist
primaries, that fact does not alter
my conclusion that the place whore
interest counts Is not so much the
polls on election day as the caucuses
before the primaries are held.
Milwaukee. P. T. B.

LUMBERJACKS WRONGLY AC
CUSED.
To the Editor of The Leader:
I recently read “The Old Time
Lumberjack Passes,” by James
Stevens in The New York Times. I
thought he was going to tell the
story of modern machinery logging,
and it would be my pleasure, there
fore, to pass In on the lumbermen
up north whom I know.
The big picture of forest devasta
tion and the linos under it. “What
the country looks like after the lum
bermen have passed,” gave me the
first inkling that this would not be
so good.
As the loggers put it: “God had a
grudge against the whole tribe of
timber savages when he made this
ground and stuck them big trees nil
over the mountains.” The trees are
heavy and the ground is good for
nothing but growing more trees.
Get them all off, so the sun can
shine in and another crop comes
right up.”
Trees grow to maturity and are
cither logged, burned or decline and
die like the rest of us. Properly
logged, many types reproduce them
selves within a few years. Logging
hastens the regrowth. Loggers
burn the ground lightly (by state
law in most states) removing most
of the unsightly debris. Within two
years the ground is covered with a
carpet of young trees if fire is kept
out.
Some day the lumberman is going
to get mad at public misunderstand
ing nnd go to raising cabbages and
potatoes. J. B. F.

000 for missions, education and the

welcoming program will be given.

rpeak.

Elizabeth George, Mary Byard,

Borchers and Helen Keeler.

year.

BY EDWIN GREER,
(President, Greer College of Automotive
and Electrical Trades, Chicago, Hl.)
A peculiar thing. The worst tire
in the world can be made to look
exactly like the best tire in the
world. The gyp manufacturer uses
the poorest grade of rubber; even
reclaimed rubber vulcanized on a
carcass made of rotten fabric, but
to all outward appearance that tire
appears as would the best tire.
And the only protection the tire
buyer has is the name of the maker
branded in the rubber of the casing.
The name of the maker and serial
number is the only real assurance
of a quality tire.
When you read a sign: “Tires at
Half Standard Prices” beware.
Don’t get the feeling that here is a
chance to get a first class tire for
half. It isn’t done by the fellow
who want to save money. And just
as surely as yon do buy that cheap
tire —just as surely will that tire
blow out when a third of half the
mileage is put on it. And then when
you go back to get an adjustment
you will find that your dealer has
“gone out of business.”

buying nothing but standard makes
and paying the market price for
them. A cheap tire is—just that,
and the man who buys them is al

Some of the reputable tire manu
facturers do put out certain quan
tity of what are known as “sec
onds.” This means a tire that is
slightly defective. I once bought two
cassings which had been overcured.
They had been left too long in the
vulcanizer—the heat bad been too
intense. I got about 2,000 miles
from one and 1,500 from the other.

the price I paid for them, but I
would have beaten the game—and
saved two brand new tubes —had I
purchased two standard tires.

with the maker’s name and serial
number on it. Pay the top price
and you will get service that will
repay you for the money spent. A
good tire will give a minimum of
8.000 miles. Keep a record of the
tires on your machine and you will
be surprised at the smallness of the
item. But buy a gyp tire—and you
will remember the time when Erwin
Greer tried to help you save money.

Fined $5 Instead
Robert Mueller, 1117 Maiden
Lane, was haled into district court
yesterday for having been drunk
and disorderly Tuesday night. Police
testified to the disturbance he was
creating in his home when neighbors
called them.
“What shall I do with him?”
Judge A. J. Hedding asked his
wife.
“Give him life, judge,” she replied.
He has been drunk since the day
wo were married. He hasn’t con
tributed a cent to the house since
then, either.”
“I can’t give him life, but I’ll fine
him $5,” said the judge.
“I guess that will have to do,” the
wife replied.

tract a capacity crowd. The Dart
mouth-Chicago game last fall was
talked of for weeks in advance of
the date it was played.

game is the only struggle of great
importance to be played in the mid
dle west as elevens of this section

GARDS BOOST
LEAD TO 21-2
GAMES
NEW YORK—The thrilling race
between St. Louis and Cincinnati
for the National league pennant and
the right to play in the world series
had lost much of its thrill today.
By reverting to their earlier form
and defeating Brooklyn, 15 to 7,
while Cincinnati was idle, the Cardi
nals attained a two and a half game
lead over the Reds.
The Cardinals have three more
games to play—two with the Giants
and one with rhe Reds in Cincinnati
Sunday. By taking two of the three
games they cinch the pennant, even
if the Reds win all of the four
games still on their schedule. The
Reds meet the Phillies today in the
first of a three-game series before
the final game with St. Louis.
Even if the Cardinals win only
one of their three games, and Cin
cinnati wins four, the Reds will only
be tied and a playoff will be neces
sary.
The American league race was
somewhat closer. By beating the
Boston Red Sox, while the New
York Yankees were being defeated
by Chicago, Cleveland cut the Yan
kees’ lead to two games. Both teams
have four games to play. By win
ning four straight the Indians can
force a tie if the Yankees break
even.

English Girl Starts
3rd Channel Swim
CAPE GRIS NEZ, France—Swim
ming under the assumed name of
“Jane Darwin,” Miss Lorna Mar
riott of Barnstaple, Devonshire, be
gan another attempt at 9 p. m. last
night to swim across the English
channel with the hope of beating
the record set up by Gertrude Ed
erle. Except for a mist, channel

eter college, has made two unsuo
cessful attempts to swim the chan
nel—on Sept. 9 and 16.

Hundreds of college girls are
earning their way through school by
doing housework in the private
homes of local residents. The duties
vary from kitchen work to care of
the children, and the usual require
ment is four hours of work per day
in return for board and room. Over
time is generally paid at a rate of
about 35 cents per hour. If a girl
is experienced in domestic work and
is physically strong, housework of
this sort will pay the largest item
of her college expense, and at the
same time lend a feeling of security
for her college career. Some college
men do the same kind of work, in
cluding cleaning: they usually re
ceive about 40 cents an hour.

WHAT WILL DEMPSEY
SAY IF HE LOSES
TITLE TO TUNNEY
NEW YORK—(United Press)—Jim Jeffries said after he had lost
the world’s heavyweight championship to Jack Johnson that he had been
drugged by a double-crossing friend in his camp.
Johnson said he lost his title to Jess Willard because he knew “there
wasn’t no use in getting up.” He only smiles when asked why he bad
put his hands over his eyes to keep the sun out when he was on the floor.
Willard when he was knocked out by Jack Dempsey in Toledo, said
that Dempsey had his hands packed and that he wasn’t trained enough.
What Will Jack Say..
The records are not clear that,
with the exception of John L. Sul
livan’s “I’m glad the championship
remains in America” any defeated
heavyweight champion advertised
that he was beaten by a better man.
The thought follows—what excuse
will Jack Dempsey have if he loses
his title to Gene Tunney?
Perhaps he may say that he was
out of the ring too long but he
doesn’t look it and he has taken
better care of himself and lived
stricter during the period of his
temporary retirement than any
other fighter ever did.
He can’t say that he was drugged,
but he is surrounded by a shock
proof entourage of friends and em
ployes.
He won’t say that he was beaten
by loaded hands because he isn’t
that type. He won't say “it* was no
use to get up,” because he will get
up by instinct if his legs will hold
him.
It is very likely that he will say
that he was beaten by a better man.
Dempsey No Braggart.
Dempsey never has been a brag
gart. He admits that he is good,
but he has the record to show for
it and does not have to quote his
personal opinions.
A heavyweight champion always
is surrounded by “yes men,” but
Dempsey never has been influenced
by "yessing.”
They told him that Carpentier
was a setup, that Firpo was a pa
luka, and they are telling him now
that Tunney can’t break a window
glass.
“No man can stand up under a
punch or enough punching In the
right place.” is Dempsey’s answer
to all. “I know that some day I'm
going to be hit hard enough and
then I’ll be through.”
There are the usually silly stories
going around that the “fight is in
the bag,’’-and that Tunney will win-
The story has been passed around
New York and bounced back from
nearly every section of the country.

Louis Schneider, king of dirt
track stars, who will lead the in
vasion of out of town stars here
Sunday for the 150-mile national
automobile championship, is the
bolder of three world’s records.
These marks, which were made over
the Winchester, Ind., speedway, were
clocked off by the same mount,
which the noted Hoosier pilot will
drive over the State Fair track Sun-;
day.
Schneider did all his record break- j
ing in one day. He started by turn
ing the fastest lap ever made on a
half-mile track, traveling the half
mile at the dizzy speed of 2G 4-5 sec
onds. He then proceeded to set a
new world’s record for 15 miles, his
mark being 13 minutes 52 seconds.
Not satisfied with this he estab
lished a new record for 25 miles go
ing the distance in 22 minutes 44
seconds.
Schneider, whose name has be
come as famous as those of Ralph
De Palma, Barney Oldfield, De I’ao
lo and Sig Haugdahl, has cleaned up
nearly everything in sight this sea
son on the dirt ovals of the country.
Nearly every fast car in the middle
west will be matched against him
here Sunday while the cream of
Wisconsin drivers will also try to
throw their dust in his goggles.
The race, the longest held in Wis
consin since the Vanderbilt and
Grand Prix were held north of the
city in 1912. haS attracted state
wide attention and thousands of mo
torists plan to drive here for the big
classic. About 200 followers of
Schneider will come here from In
dianapolis to see him try to annex
the 150-mile crown.

Long ago I learned that it is dif
ficult if not impossible to get away
with any demonstrable errors of
logic, fact or allusion in this
column. A doctor, being ac
customed to burying his mistakes
quietly, finds it a little embarrass
ing here sometimes and envies the
privacy enjoyed by the gold fish.
A Duluth reader writes:
“If your article entitled Keep
Your Hair On you credit Shake
speare for the lines running ‘Vice
is a monster of such horrid mien,’
etc. Was not Pope the author of
these lines?”
A Long Island reader confesses
that he really enjoys Doctor
Brady’s something or other (I
can’t make out the name he gives
my stuff) but his quoting ought
to be checked up. Remember, my
Jamaica friend says, what Byron
wrote in English Bards and
Scotch Reviewers: “"With just
enough learning to misquote.”
The quotation which these two
readers refer to was made in a
letter from another reader, who
wrote this:
“Jim is right—and then some.
So is Doctor Angell at Yale and
so was Shakespeare when he said,
‘Vice is a monster of such horrid
mien as to be hated needs but to
be seen, but when familiar with
his face we first endure, then pity,
then embrace’
At the time I printed this letter
about Jim’s views I remember I
took the precaution of looking the
quotation up in Bartlett’s famil
iar Quotations, saw that the cor
respondent had it all wrong, and
let it go as he quoted it. I don’t
know how I failed to notice that
it was credited to Shakespeare.
Pope wrote it thus:
Vice is a monster' of so fright
ful mien, as to be hated needs but
to be seen; yet seen too oft,
familiar with her face, we first
endure, then pity, then embrace.
Quite a while ago I said some
thing here, about the Scriptural
injunction to “Know thyself.” A
dozen readers promptly challenged
me to cite the verse and chapter,
and a few of them kindly in
formed me that this quotation
was from Pope. These were the
first batch of corrections. A little
later came the second batch from
learned readers who desired to
tell me tht this quotation came
originally from Plutarch. Still
later a third batch of letters from
erudite persons to whose attention
the matter had been brought, in
nearly every Instance, by some
idle third person, and they begged
to state that the saying was
J’lato’s. Thon trickling along week
after week came a succession of
batches from antiquarians, atti
tudinnriAns, archeologists and
such folk crediting the remark to
Pythagoras, Socrates, Thales et
al. I have been searching Scrip
ture ever since and I still stick to
my error some day I’m going to
find the yer.se and chapter. I have

tunately, in recent years, there has

woman.

relieved by medical and surgical
measures.

inated from human thought as a
spiritual problem and has become,
instead, a medical matter amenable
to medical practice. In other words
childlessness is simply another
manifestation of bad health, which
usually can be corrected by proper
measures.

waste of child life.

applied to pigs or calves of the
nation, there would be a wail from

Frozen Peach Salad.
Three peaches, one-fourth cup nut
meats, one tablespoon canton ginger,
two tablespoons ginger syrup, one
half cup cream, one and one-half
tablespoons lemon juice, one cup
salad dressing. Lettuce.
Cut peaches, nut meats and ginger
in small pieces. Add remaining in
gredients. pack in small cans such
as baking powder cans and surround
with two parts ice nnd one part
rock salt. After two hours unmould

Molasses Dumplings.
Make a good baking powder bis
cuit dough. Make the dough into
balls size of walnuts and place in a
well-greased dripping pan to raise.
Meantime cook together for a few
minutes, one cup of water, one
tablespoon butter, one tablespoon
sugar, and one cup of molasses. Be
fore placing the dumplings in the
oven pour this sauce over them and
bake in a moderate heat. Serve the
dumplings with the molasses sauce
about them for dessert. These dump
lings may also be made of bread
dough that has a little butter or
lard added for shortening.
Tomato Toast.
Trim edges of sliced bread or cold
biscuit and cover with medium thick
slices of fresh tomatoes. Sprinkle
sparingly with salt and pepper, and
generously with sugar. Dot over
with butter and place in shallow
pan and bake until toast is browned
and tomatoes well cooked. Serve
hot. This is a nice dish for break
fast or lunch.

EVERYDAY FOOD.
A meat loaf is often the most suit
able way of serving meat to the
family, and when properly seasoned
and prepared is a tasty main dish.
Meat Loaf.
Chop one pound of fresh pork and
veal and two pounds of beef. Mix
and add one cupful of bread crumbs,
one cupful of milk, one tablespoon
ful of salt, one-eighth teaspoonful
of pepper, and three eggs slightly
beaten. Shape into a loaf, put into
a baking pan and cover the top with
thin strips of fat salt pork. Roast
one end one-half hours, basting
every 10 minutes with one-half cup
ful of water and the fat from the
pan. Remove to the platter; pour
around the loaf a tomato sauce and
garnish with parsley.
Pimento Potatoes.
Season three cupfuls of hot riced
potatoes with three tablespoonfuls
of butter, one-half cupful of cream
and salt to taste. Add one and one
half cans'pimentoes cut into small
pieces and forced through a sieve,
then beat until well blended. Re
heat and pile on a hot dish.
Coffee Junket.
A dessert which is wholesome,
easy to prepare and dainty to
serve: Take one junket tablet,
crush and dissolve in a tabiespoon
ful of warm milk, then add to a
quart of lukewarm milk. Reserve
half a cupful of milk and pour boil
ing hot water over two tablespoon
fuls of coffee; let stand until well
infused, then strain and cool before
adding to the milk. Let stand in a
warm place on ice to chill Serve
with whipped cream.
Banana Ice Cream.
Peel and mash six bananas, add
the strained juice of half a lemon,
one and one-half cupfuls of sugar,
beat to a cream. Add three pints of
rich milk and freeze.
Velvet Lemon Sherbet.
This is one of the most popular
of desserts. Take the juice of three
lemons, add two cupfuls of sugar
and one quart of rich milk, cream
and all. Freeze. The mixture will
curdle when being combined but will
freeze so that it is as smooth as
velvet.—Nellie Maxwell.
Vegetable Bouquet.
Procure a rather small cauliflow
er which is perfect in shape, tie it
up in a thin, clean cloth and boil
in salted water until about half
done.
Boil four or five medium sized
carrots or sweet potatoes in salted
water until they are beginning to
l>e tender, and at the same time boil
a cupful of rice in the same way.
In the center of a good sized cas
serole or baking pan place the cauli
flower after you have carefully re
moved it from the cloth; surround
it with the carrots or sweet potatoes
which have been sliced unifornfly;
surround the circle of these with the
rice in neat manner, and around
all place quartered portions of ripe
red tomato. Cover the bouquet with
grated cheese and finish baking in
a moderate oven until the top is
nicely browned, when the vegetable
will be found to be separate and dis
tinct in appearance but blended in
flavor, making a very attractive and
palatable dish.
Candied Sweet Potatoes.
Boil six medium sized sweet po
tatoes until they are slightly tender,
then place them evenly in a baking
dish and cover the top of them gen
erously with light brown sugar and
bits of butter here and there. Then
spread over them a half cupful of
slightly crushed pecan meats and
then pour over all the liquid in
which the sweet potatoes were
boiled, until the baking dish is half
full. Place in a rather hot oven and
bfkke until a golden brown, when the
potatoes will have become crystal
lized in the syrup.
Hamburger Slteak With Macedoine
Garnish of June Vegetables.
Arrange steak with an imitation
bone of suet down center and broil
delicately. Tut the meat on a grid
dle or old cookie sheet under the
flame. Slip onto a hot platter, butter
and salt it (never salt before cook
ing), add a tablespoon or two of
boiling water to start the gravy,
and surround with a mixture of any
suitably cooked vegetables in sea
son. with mounds of new potatoes
made in balls at the ends, sprinkled
with finely minced parsley. Vege
tables may Include peas, tiny onions,
tiny or diced carrots, small string
beans, diced or shredded half ineh
bits of asparagus. Arrange small
hotter balls rolled in paprika among
the vegetables and serve at once.
If one has a garden this dish, an
entire course, makes a handsome
and delicious dinner.
Green Beans and Bacon.
Kentucky Wonder Pole beans are
the best for canning. Wash, string,
and put beans in glss jars that have
previously been thoroughly washed
and sterilized. Fill jars as full as
possible and in the center of each
jar place a strip of good bacon. Fill
with cold salted water. Place a
wooden rack, slats, or straw in the
bottom of a wash boiler; put in cold
water to within two inches of top
of jars, replacing with boiling water
as it boils away. See that jars do
not touch each other and that they
are full of water. Boil three hours,
keeping boiler covered. Partly screw
lids on for boiling and when done
screw tightly and keep in dark
place, handling as little as possible.
Orange Nip Punch.
One part orange nip. two parts
grape juice, six parts water.
Mix and serve in tall glasses with
chopped ice in each glass. A maras
chino cherry and a few sprigs of
mint may be added to each glass if
desired.

NET INCOME
$14,296,611;

Cars Travel Greatest

Year.
The annual report of the Pullman
Co., issued yesterday, shows that in
number of sleeping car passengers,
average distance traveled, and In
earnings, all previous records were
broken in the company’s fiscal year
ended July 31.
“During the year, 36,231,488 rev
enue passengers were carried in
Pullman cars, an Increase of 1,719,-
223 over the preceding year,” Presi
dent E. F. Carry says.
“These passengers traveled in the
aggregate 14,479,249,784 miles, an
Increase of 1,056,938,251 miles. This
is an average distance of 400 miles
per passenger. The daily average
of Pullman travel was 99,264 pas
sengers, an Increase of 4,702. Each
car traveled an average of 154,102
miles during the year, or 422 miles
a day.”
Gross Receipts Up.
Gross receipts from car operations
wer $90,831,274, compared with $83,-
927,749 in the preceding year. Net
income, after all charges, was $14,-
296,611, equivalent to $10.59 a shaie
on the $135,000,000 capital stock.
In addition, the company’s equity in
undisturbed earnings of the Pull
man Car Manufacturing Co.
amounted to $3,826,629. equivalent
to $2.83 a share on Pullman stock,
making a total of $13.42 a share. In
the prece<ling year, Pullman’s net
income was $13,771,976, or $10.20 a
share, and an equity m Pullman
Car earnings was $3,566,996, or
$2.04 a share, making a total of
$12.84 a share on Pullman stock.

tons. The rails will be ordered for

Defends Railroad
Consolidation Plan
WASHINGTON—In n statement
filed with the interstate commerce
commission yesterday by attorneys
for Henry Ford, the Detroit auto
mobile manufacturers’ railway con
solidation plans were defended. Mr.
Ford’s proposal to combine the De
troit, Toledo Iron Mountain sys
tem with the Detroit Ironton road
is being opposed by minority stock
holders of the former.

only an “infinitesimal interest,”
the brief sets forth.

right or authority to consider the
protest. The merger is essential,
the brief adds, in order that bonds
may be issued to finance improve

TWELVE
TIRE PLANTS
ARE RUNNING
AT CAPACITY
Tire plants around Milwaukee are
operating near capacity, and one of
them is running on. a double s^ift
basis, according to reports yester
dny from tire manufacturers at
Cudahy and Racine.
More stable prices are looked for
from now on.
The use of balloon tires on auto
mobiles now being manufactured has
diminished somewhat the output of
jiigh pressure tires, tire makers say,
although this trend is not as pro
nounced as might be expected on ac
count of the greater number of auto
mobiles being used today, many of
them with nonballoon tires.
The Federal Rubber Co., Cudahy,
is operating about at a capacity of
12.000 castings and 20,000 tubes a
day, with a force of about 2.200 men,
about the same as a year ago.
Officials of the Ajax Rubber Co.,
Racine, stated rhat the plant is run
ning night and day, has been op
erating at capacity of from 8.000 to
9,000 tubes and 4.200 tires a day all
of last month, and expects to con
tinue so for at least another month.
The plant employs 1,500 men. Prices
declined some time ago, but if
weather continues fair it is expect
ed they will hold at present levels
until the end of the year.
Horseshoe Sales Off.
Sales have been off some at the
plant, of the Racine Horseshoe Tire
Co., Racine, it was announced, and
production has been cut a little this
week on account of a slight depres
sion that is looked upon as seasonal,
but increased orders and output are
expected to be in evidence in Octo
ber. when work will be started on
next spring’s business. This plant
has about 225 men at work, turning
out 700 tires a day and 1,500 to 1,800
tubes, slightly fewer than a year
ago.
Lisman Car Plan
Backers Must Be
CHlCAGO—Frederick J. Lisman,
New York, must reveal the names of
the principal backers of his plan for
operating Chicago’s traction lines
before serious negotiations are be
gun, it was made clear yesterday
by members of the city council sub
committee in charge of the New
York proposal. John Maynard Har
lan, attorney for the Lisman inter
ests, will have a draft of an ordi
nance embodying the Lisman plan
ready by tomorrow, It was an
nounced, and a meeting of the sub
committee was called for that time
by Chairman Thomas F. Byrne.
“Before the committee under
takes to work out an ordinance on
the basis of the skeleton which Mr.
Harinn is to submit, I believe we
should have definite assurance of
Mr. Lisman and his associates’ fi
nancial ability to carry to comple
tion any scheme involved,” Aid.
Joseph B. McDonough, chairman of
the local transportation, said.
“While I have full confidence in
Mr. Lisman, I believe the committee
owes it to itself to insist on know
ing who is associated with him. If
the committee did not do so, it
would lav itself open to the charge
of having wasted valuable time if
it later develops that the financial
hacking behind the plan was insuf
ficient.”

Experts Meet to
Wage Fight on
European 'Borer'
CHlCAGO—Alarmed at the de
structive work of the European corn
borer, entomologists, farmers, and
engineers of the United States and
Canada open a t^ree-day interna
tional conference at Detroit today
to see what can be done to control
the pest which has advanced 75
miles nearer the heart of the corn
belt this season.
Dean C. F. Curtiss, Ames, Ta.,
chairman of the national corn borer
committee, called the conference and
has invited experts from all parts
of the corn belt states and Canadian
provinces. Today and tomorrow
trips will be made through the in
fested sections of Ohio, Michigan
and Ontario. A final conference will
be held Saturday.
The pest has been found this sum
mer in four counties in Indiana, lit
tle more than 100 miles from the
Illinois line.

ALLOY STEEL UP
IN 15 YEARS
CHICAGO A remarkable in
crease in the use of heat treated
steel has been recorded in recent
years, according to members of the
American Society for Steel treating
in convention this week in Chicago.
Production figures in alloy steel
show a sharp increase in the last
15 years. In 1911 the ratio of car
bon steel to alloy steel output was
approximately 50 to 1. At present
it is something like 20 to 1 and is
steadily gaining.
Alloy steel production in 1911 to
taled 481,459 tons in the United
States, according to figures com
piled by the bureau of railway eco
nomics, Washington. The steady
increase in its use is shown by the
following record: 1912, 792.501
tons: 1913, 714,357 tons; 1914, 646.-
953 tons; 1915, 1,021,147 tons; 191 G,
1.302,147 tons; 1917, 1.644,335 tons:
1918, 1.787.852 tons: 1919, 1,481.188
tons; 1920, 1,060.292 tons: 1921.
509.548 tons: 1922, 1.073.490 tons;
1923, 2,100.489 tons: 1924, 2,026,409
tons and 1925, 2.432.973 tons.
Reasons set forth for the sharp
increase are numerous, one of the
most important being greater re
sistance against fatigue.

THIRTEEN
VESTA TEMPLE
IN ROME TO
BE REBUILT
NEW YORK Funds are being
<ised by public subscription fur the
immediate reconstruction of the
Temple of Vesta, one of the most
ancient buildings in Rome, its foun
dation dating back to the epoch of
the Reman kings; according to copy
righted story in The World. This
temple is not the spurious Temple of
Vesta rising near the Temple of ir
ile Fortune on the banks of the
Tiber, but the true Temple of Vesta
in the Fortun. three graceful Corin
thian columns supporting a gigantic
fragment of highly carved marble
cornice, one of the most character
istic landmarks of the Forum.
Use Old Pieces.
Plans for reconstruction of the
temple were made by Senator Roni.
It is proposed to carry out his proj
ect as homage to the memory of the
I’ornm's great excavator on the an
niversary of his death. The inten
tion is to build a rough skeleton of
the temple, as it appears on an
cient coins, out of Travertine stone.
On this skeleton will be applied all
the existing fragments of the an
cient temple now lying on the
ground at the base of the three ver
tical columns.
The fragments are not sufficient
for Complete reconstruction, but
there are enough to give a good idea
of the graceful elegance of this mas
terpiece of Roman architecture.
The Temple of Vesta was, accord
ing to tradition, first built by King
Numa Pompolius, the successor to
Romulus. Since then it has been
destroyed and rebuilt at least three
times. The last time it was rebuilt
by Emperor Septimus Severus, to
whose epoch the majority of existing
fragments belong.
Virgins Fed Fire.
It was a circular building, sur
rounded by a graceful colonnade of
Corinthian columns rising on a plat
form raised about eight feet above
the general level of the Forum. In
side there was a cubicle where ves
tal virgins continually fed the un
dying fire with teakwood. The ex
isting fragments, experts declare,
should suffice to rebuild about half
of the colonnade and the exquisite
cornice it supported.
It is hoped to be able to complete
the partial reconstruction with an
outlay of about $5,000. About this
sum was subscribed on the first day.
New Magazine to
Take Up Problems
Of Parenthood
NEW YORK—Under the sponsor
ship of 60 eminent specialists in
children’s health, education, and
welfare, a new national periodical
called “Children, The Magazine for
Parents.” made Its initial appear
ance today.

nounced by George J. Hecht, presi

Assn., under whose auspices it is is
sued, “will have no propaganda pur
pose, being dedicated soley to

and child welfare agencies, private,
public and governmental.
GOLF COURSES
'TO BE FREED
OF SMALL BOYS
To curb the activities of small
boys who are said to roam Grant
and Greenfield park golf courses in
search of stray balls, the county
park board decided, today that only
golfers Qnd others to whom special
permits have been given will be per
mitted on the courses in the future.
To facilitate enforcement of the
rule, that portion of the Greenfield
course lying next to the highways
will lie separated by a fence.
In the future, under the board’s
decision, anyone found upon the
course with neither a player's or
visitor's permit will be subject to
arrest.
The district attorney will be
asked to immediately make the nec
essary legal arrangements for the
enforcement of the rules.
The board adopted a detailed plan
for the development of an addi
tional portion of. the county park
way system, which will extend from
North Ave. to Lake St.

COMBINE HULA,
CHARLESTON IN
LATEST DANCE
BY EVERETT R. HOLES.
Staff Correspondent
The United I’ress
CHICAGO—Wave your arms and
wiggle —that's the new Hula
Charleston, picked by the first in
ternational jazz congress to be next
winter’s ballroom craze.
It’s a simple “gesture” dance, A.
F. Shcan, director of the congress,
said today in explaining the dance.
Here's how. Standing in one
place, kick your feet, sway your
body and wave your arms above
your head in time to the music.
That’s the way 10 of Gilda Gray's
dancing girls demonstrated the
“steps” to the advisory board of the
Jazz Assn.
Gilda, creator of the American
Hula, invented the Hula Charles
ton to revolutionize jazz dancing,
she told officials of the association,
holding its congress in Chicago this
week.
Other dances introduced are the
Black Bottom and Chicago Loop,
variations of the Charleston.
Dances with plenty of gestures
found the greater favor among
those exhibted to the advisory
board for approval.
Braves Death to
Save Rabbit's Life;
Woman Injured
I don’t mind shooting rabbits but
to hit them with a two ton ear
isn’t sporting,” declared Mrs. Joseph
M. Hopp, 2031 Grand Ave., when
she recovered consciousness in a
roadside ditch near Marinette, Wis.,
yesterday.
In trying to avoid running over a
rabbit in the road. Mrs. Hopp
swerved her automobile too far.
The machine ran into a ditca throw
ing her through the windshield.
A motorcycle officer took her to
Wausaukee where she received
treatment for cuts and bruises to
her face.

THE SPOKESMAN’S OUTLOOK
The return of President Coolidge to the white house
in Washington is anything but a triumphal entry. “The
Spokesman” kept mum on the results of the primary elec
tions, of course. He would have swallowed his Adam’s
apple rather than committed himself on that subject. But
jiobody can claim that he came back from his vacation a
proud victor.
He cannot have misunderstood the meaning of the de
feat of more world court senators. Even the inspired press
reports pretending that the powers in the league of nations
would accept all American reservations without hesitation
did not add a single leaf to the Coolidge laurel.
Unless all present indications are misleading, there
will be no Coolidge majority in the next United States
senate after the votes have been counted this fall. Whether
the house of representatives will remain his, is also doubt
ful. The revolt against the drys has taken its victims as
well as that against the world court.
Unfortunately the loss of the Coolidge machine can
not be counted as a gain for the majority of the citizens.
As usual the voters have merely exchanged one set of old
party statesmen for another, and will do so this fall.
Voting for wet and anti-world court statesmen on old
party tickets is no royal road to a policy of getting out
of the imperialist swamp or of escaping from the morass
of Volsteadism,
The American voters have a naive habit of assuming
even after a generation of proofs to the contrary that an
old party political promise means a political program.
About the only promising change that we can observe
is the dawning realization in certain progressive Repub
lican and Democratic circles that Socialist candidates are
really more reliable and more responsive to the expressed
wishes of the voters than all others.
From “The Spokesman’s” point of view, however, this
does not add any silver lining to the black clouds which
are gathering over the Coolidge machine.
SOME FOOLISH LITERATURE
An Associated Press report from Boston relates that
Theodore Roosevelt, Sr., left among his private papers
some letters of Kaiser Wilhelm. They were written, says
the report, while Roosevelt was president of the United
States. Then how can they be private papers?
This is an introduction to a press notice for a book
by William Dana Orcutt, entitled “In Quest of the Perfect
Book,” in which the author claims that Roosevelt told him:
These letters, if published at the time they were written,
would have brought on a world war.
Maybe these letters are all that Roosevelt and Or
cutt claim for them. The kaiser was foolish enough to
write that sort of stuff to the head of a foreign power.
But we would not put that sort of drivel into a book that
is advertised as a crowning result of 35 years of research
for the perfect book.
If this advance notice is authentic, we would say that
it is advertising the perfect foolishness of its author and
raising suspicions, not only of his sanity, but also of his
purpose.
OUR VANISHING MERCHANT FLEET
We still have government-owned merchant ships with
American names left, but President Coolidge’s packed
board of experts is doing its utmost to get rid of them
before the revolt of American businessmen against selling
out to the British can stop the fraud.
It is typical of old party mentality that even this be
lated and rather ineffective revolt does not find fault with
Coolidge’s policy because it is injurious to the economic
machinery of the United States, but because it would leave
Uncle Sam without a reserve of merchant ships in case of
another war.
The argument is merely that Uncle Sam found him
self at the mercy of John Bull when he needed a merchant
fleet in the last war, and that a patriotic regard for the fu
ture should prevent the recurrence of such a disaster.
When will the voice of reason be strong enough in old
party circles to make Uncle Sam’s participation in another
war impossible instead of misusing even the controversy
over the government merchant marine as a new basis for
war propaganda?
THE SUPER-FACTORY
Henry Ford expects American industries to develop
into super-factories. He means factories in which effi
ciency engineering exceeds the profit motive in mass pro
duction. But he does not say in what manner the profit
motive is to yield. For the present, the Ford method of
mass production shows no lack of profit motive, and man
is more the slave of the machine than he has ever been
in all human history. Neither has Ford shown any in
clination to give to his employes a voice and vote in the
management of his super-factories. Far from it. Nor
has he distributed profits and proved that mass efficiency
for the common good is his predominating motive. So we
still expect more from the organization of the workers
than from him.

His face darkened as he spoke of

tions.
We agreed to meet for lunch a

I had a chance to verify him at

ful laughter at people he disliked

DOLLAR DIPLOMACY AT BAY
The war front of dollar diplomacy in Central Chin,
has broken down. The Cantonese have taken Wuchang in
addition to Hankow and Hanyang. They now hold the
great strategic triangle on the central Yangtse river.
Wu Pei-fu, the Chinese general acting for the foreign pow
ers under the Peking puppet government, has been driven
out of these positions, leaving the British and American
gunboats to face the Cantonese alone.
The British and American gunboats that got into
trouble with “pirates” on the Yangtse river have no treaty
rights there. The official reports claiming that foreign
powers have such rights are pure fiction. Besides, the
“pirates” that attacked British and American boats belong
to the forces of Gen. Wu Pei-fu, the ally of the foreign
powers.
British and American propaganda now claims that it
may be necessary for the British and American govern
ments to make war on the Cantonese, in order to punish
'them for attacks made by rebellious sections of
Wu Pei-fu’s armies. That would be about as logical as
making war on Mexico in order to punish the Calles gov
ernment for attacks of its enemies on Americans in
Mexico.
The British and American gunboats on Chinese
rivers are the enemies of the majority of the Chinese
people who back the Cantonese. If British and American
troops in China join forces against the Cantonese, then
the American government will be automatically involved
in all the results arising from their actions.
So far the foreign powers have maintained the fiction
of dealing with the Peking government. But this govern
ment has nothing more to say in the biggest and most pop
ulous part of China. In a little while, Cantonese troops
will again enter Peking. Then the powers will have to
make up their minds whether to recognize the uantonese
government as the regular one, or to pretend that there is
no responsible government for them to deal with.
To make the Cantonese responsible for the attacks of
their enemies on British and American gunboats would
mean to give official recognition to the Canton government.
In fact, the British in Hongkong have been making war
on the Canton government for a long time, whereas the
Canton government has shown a lamb’s patience with Brit
ish arrogance. Some day, when the Cantonese decide that
they, have stood enough, there will be a grand cleanup
that will put the British out of Hongkong.
Meanwhile shelling unfortified Chinese towns will not
increase the friendship of the Chinese for the foreigners
nor impassion the folks at home to a frenzied support of
a foreign invasion into China.
The winter is coming on. The campaign on the Mon
golian front, long heralded as a grand success for
Wu Pei-fu and Chang Tso-lin, seems to remain barren of
tangible gains.
The foreign powers will face a new year with the
dismal prospect of finding the Chinese people in a better
position than ever to defy the foreign devils.
In the Near East, in Afghanistan and Thibet, things
have not moved according to the imperialist Hoyle, either.
On the contrary Soviet Russia and China are making gains
also along that important front.
The American government can find 16 good reasons
for letting the British do their own dirty work in China
for every one that seems to make a British-American war
on China profitable. Let us hope that Washington will
see those 16 points.

age corporation last year made 5 cents net profit on each
dollar of gross receipts. But companies engaged in bank
ing, insurance and related lines made 16 cents net profit
out of each dollar of gross receipts.
That fact explains why millionaires cluster in New
York—which is also the home of the only billionaire that
Mr. McCoy found; and had he analyzed closer, he would
have found most of the superrich men of New York state
centered in the city of the same name. For all its great
volume of manufacturing. New York is primarily a per
centage town, not a producing one. It gathers and re
distributes capital—and takes its toll.
The big rewards do not go to labor. They do not go
to the combination of labor and capital found in farming.
They go to capital invested in manufacturing, and the big
gest money of all goes to those who handle other people’s
money.
While such a condition prevails, one can hardly ex
pect universal satisfaction with the so-called industrial
“system” that prevails today.—Labor.

TWO
SOCIALISTS OF
ITALY EXPOSE
FASCIST POLICY
Leader Special Service.
ROME—The United Italian So
cialist party bas issued a pamphlet
entitled “The Financial Policy of
the Fascist Government” which ex
poses the swindle of Mussolini's al
leged success as a stabilizer and
savior of Italian economy.
The Socialist party declares that
the Fascist claim of having taken
charge of a completely bankrupt
treasury and having put It on a
sound foundation is just a bluff.
The truth is rather that the gov
ernments preceding the Mussolini
regime had decided to raise taxes
and to start a policy of deflation.
As a result, conditions had shown
a turn for the better when the Fas
cits took control in October, 1922.
Fascists Falsify Records.
Long before Mussolini strutted on
the scene, the pamphlet explains,
the circulation of paper money had
been reduced. The exchange value
of the lira was on the mend. Prices
were coming down. The Italian bal
ance of trade was getting active.
The budget deficit was being re
duced.
Fascism today boasts of billions
of surplus in the national treasury,
but this is swindle. The Fascists
have falsified the ijatlonal book
keeping. They have juggled the bil
lions of cancelled war debts in their
favor and have also done the same
with about 290,000,000 lire paid by
Germany.
In this way they have “saved”
nearly a billion lire, but only on
paper. On the other hand, the Fas
cists have made fraudulent entries
of the war expenses which were
carried over into the peace budgets,
and so there should have been a
real surplus of three billion lire
where they can show only a paper
surplus of one billion.
Waste Money on War.
The national budget has been
actually improved by the low quo
tation of the lira, and the duties
are payable in gold, so that there
was a difference of about a billion
and half between last year’s and
this year's revenue from duties. But
the Fascists have wasted billions on
war preparations instead of using
them to improve economic condi
tions.
Instead of reducing government
expenses, the Fascists have actually
wasted five billion lire and raised
taxes by four billion, especially the
indirect taxes which fall most
heavily on the poorer classes of con
sumers.
When Mussolini took charge of
the government, the lira was quoted
at 20 to the American dollar. He
promised to make a dollar worth
10 lire. Today it takes 30 lire to
buy one dollar.
The actual buying power of wages
in Italy is the lowest in all Europe,
with the exception of Esthonla. The

First Jazz Band
Played for Nero’s
Petting Parties
ROME —Nero reclined with his
wine and women to the languid and
erotically charged strains of an or
chestra of primitive saxophones, ac
cording to records just revealed by
Prof. Federico Celentano, famous
Latin scholar. Exciting “jazz,” or a
forerunner of it, enlivened the ec
centric emperor’s Bacchanalian
feasts.
Even as far back as 753 B. C.
during the rape of the Sabine wom
en the Romans played gaily on the
tiblcius thusci as they called them.
These instruments were imperfect
saxophones, forerunners of the mod
ern instrument.
Instead of the modern polyphonic
orchestra of mixed Instruments, the
Romans had groups of musicians all
flaying the same Instrument. These
bands were called colleges and were
used mostly Wr military purposes.
King Servio Tullio had a band of
200 musicians of different colleges
all playing together daring the bat
tles.
The Romans borrowed many of
their instruments from the Greeks
and the Egyptians, among which
was the lyre. Nero was a champion
of the lyres. It was this instrument
that he played during the burning
of Rome instead of the Addle as Is
commonly supposed.
Coal Strike Helps
Modernize Homes
LONDON The coal strike is

Never has there been so lively
A demand for gas and electric

ported now by the dealers. Gas
stoves and gas ovens are replacing
the old-fashioned coal ranges over
which British women have toiled
for generations. Electrical equip
ment is appearing on hundreds «f
British breakfast tables, to simpli
fy housekeeping and avoid the
shortage of coal. Gas furnaces are
also being installed in many homes.
A shortage of domestic servants
has also helped to accelerate the
demand for labor-saving and time
saving household equipment. Eng
lish wires are adopting the Amer
ican way of doing their own work
and they inevitably demand all the
modern comforts and assistances
available.
