Native Customers
Favored By French
PARlS—Tourists may or may not
be aware of it but they pay more in
Paris restaurants for a meal than a
Frenchman pays.
The scheme is ingenious. In a
restaurant overlooking the Seine
much frequented by foreigners two
Frenchmen were dining. The waiter
brought the bill amounting to 190
francs. The guest glanced at it and
noticed chat 10 per cent was taken
off. He eyed the waiter inquiringly.
"It’s like this,” said the attendant.
“The manager knows you are
Frenchmen and on account of the
drop in the franc you cannot be ex
pected to pay like the Americans or
British. As we have no right to
make two prices we settle the diffi
culty by giving you the same check
as a foreigner would get but in your
case we deduct the 10 per cent.”

FAILS TO HELP
THOSE IN NEED
Leader Special Service.
VIENNA The Geneva corre
spondent of The I ienna Arbeiier
Zeitung writes that those who most
need the help of the league of na
tions don’t even get a hearing, let
alone relief from injustices inflict
ed under the authority of the
league.
"The idea of colonial mandates is
one of the most promising germs of
an international law,” he contin
ues. "It is true that it arose from
a war lie. The allies had solemnly
declared during the war that they
wanted no annexations. So, when
it was time to divide the loot, the
German colonics and some Turkish
territories were annexed and called
"mandates.”
“But such forms of law. once that
they have become established, have
a tendency to make themselves in
dependent and to assume a life of
their own.
Started New Departure.
“The idea was that one country
should no longer be the possession
of another, but should merely be
held in thist by all powers, together
for the purjiose of being guided
along the right paths in its develop
ment, until it could stand on its own
feet.
“This was a departure from the
old feudal principle of foreign rule
in international law. This new es
sence of the future theory of man
dates is a,t war in present society
with the actual law practice which
uses a mandate merely as a dis
guise for imperialist exploitation.
“Naturally it should be a part of
the mandate theory that the league
of nations, which bestows a man
date, should also supervise its exe
cution. This is the function of the
mandates* commission which con
venes from time to time.
Took Office Seriously.
“Recently one of the meetings of
the mandates commission decided
to take its office seriously and to
exercise the functions wliich had
been entrusted to it. So it sent the
Swedish Socialist Unden to the
council of the league of nations
with a report to this effect.
‘•The commission suggested that
the questionnaire, or question blank
addressed to the mandate powers,
should be enlarged. And as many
organizations and representatives of
people ruled under a mandate were
addressing the mandates commis
sion with complaints against the
powers exercising the mandate over
them, the commission wanted to
know whether it had the right to
take down the personal testimony of
the complainants.
“Immediately the representatives
of the powers exercising mandates
raised a row. The well-bred Cham
berlain used very sharp words
against the mandates commission’s
suggestion. He said it was trying
to exceed its functions. The league
of nations is a fine thing, but it
should not meddle with such matters

“Jovial Briand gave a drastic de
scription of the sort of intriguing
complainants, who would have a
free field for their intrigues, if the
league—which is otherwise so free
from intrigues—opened its doors to
them. He may have thought of
some Syrian “knockers,” against
whose complaints the French gov
ernment prefers to use the more ef
fective remedy of a hempen rope.
“The Socialist Vandervelde de
fended the right of the complainants
to petition the league for a redress
of just grievances. But he admit
ted that his practical experience
with international politics taught
him the difficulties which stand in
the way of a personal touch with
deputations of complainants.
"So a compromise was the out
come. Chamberlain and Briand took
back their reproaches against the
mandates commission. Unden with
drew his report and presented it
later in an amended form. The ex
tension of the question blank was
authorized.
Recognize Petition Right.
“The league council also recog
nized on principle the right of the
mandates commission to listen per
sonally to the complaints from man
dated areas. But it was set down
as a reservation that such personal
complaints should be heard only
after the power exercizing the man
date had been duly notified and en
abled to have a representative of
its own attend the hearing.
“As for a reorganization of the
whole procedure of the mandates
commission, the mandate powers are
to be consulted first and asked for
an opinion as to whether they con
sider any change of procedure prac
ticable.
“It is still a long way to the point
where the people ruled under the
authority of the league will be en
abled to voice their complaints
against injustices which are com
mitted against them in the name
and by the orders of the league of
nations.”

CANADA RUM
WORTH MILLION
SENT TO U. S.
OTTAWA, Ont.—Official figures
of the Canadian government statis
tics bureau, made public last night,
show that in the 12 months just end
ed Canada has exported legal’y $27,-
852,408 worth of hard liquor, beer
and ale. Of this, the figures show.
$24,690,470 worth was given legal
Canadian customs clearance for ex
port to Uncle Sam’s domain.
During Canada's last election cam
paign rum running between Canada
and the United States played a
prominent part in the speeches of
the leading politicians.
Simultaneously with the an
nouncement that Gen. Andrews of
the United States prohibition forces
is expected in the Canadian capital
to seek aid to stop the flow of Cana
dian “wet goods” to the United
States, statistics showing that in the
Inst 12 months the value of hard
liquor exported from Canada to the
United States was $5,186,065. and
that beer and ale legally shipped
out of Canada to the'United States
had a value of $19,604,405, were re
ceived.
It also is contended that illicit
shipments of hard liquor and beer
from Canada to the United States
will be as high or higher than the
value of tye legal shipments, and
that of the remainder of the $27,-
852,408 worth of liquor legally ex
ported from Canada much went to
the United States, having been short
circuited from Mexico and Latin
American countries.
The Canadian department figures
credit the United States with con
suming in 12 months 3,946.380 gal
lons of beer and ale and 889,395 gal
lons of whisky.
With the Meighen administration
due to hand over the government
reins to Mackenzie King today, it is
now announced that once the new
government gets its machinery func
tioning, the prohibition leaders of
Canada will ask that Canada offer
the United States every possible
support to stamp out the liquor and
beer running traffic between this
country and a friendly nation.

Vienna Scientist
Claims His Ability
To Split Electron
BERLiN Following the an
nouncement that a German scientist
had perfected a cure for malaria
which was successful in every one
of 134 cases, the international phy
siciains’ congress at Dusseldorf yes
terday heard the Viennese scientist.
Prof. Ehrenhaft, announce he has
succeeded in splitting the electron.
Ever since the American scientist,
Rutherford, succeeded in splitting
the atom, scientists have been hop
ing to produce light, beat and en
ergy by breaking down the electron,
which until now has been the small
est unit of electricity. Prof. Ehren
haft says he is able to discern the
component parts of the electron,
namely, platinum, gold, silver, nick
el and selenium.
Ee used in his experiments a
magnet with poles two millimeters
apart. The electron., under a pow
erful microscope, appeared to have
component parts of a diameter of
one hundred-thousandth of a centi
meter each. These were ball
shaped. When electrified they pos
sessed only half the amount of
electricity of an electron.

Socialists Denied
Entrance to Russia,
Says German Paper
l.eadcr Special Service.
BERLlN—Vorwaerts, the central
organ of the German Socialist
party, reports that its expert on
political economy, Kurt Helnig, who
wanted to study conditions in Soviet
Russia, has been denied permission
to enter Russia. No explanation
was vouchsafed by the soviet gov
ernment.
Vorwaerts comments: “One may
therefore brand as untrue all asser
tions to the effect that Socialists
and bona fide trade unionists are
free to enter Russia whenever they
want to. Only those are admitted
into Russia who are presumed to
make inspired reports of pre
arranged celebrations. But such a
prepared and prearranged method
of reporting cannot inspire any con
fidence.”
Vorwaerts adds that capitalist
newspaper writers have long been
admitted into Russia. Only Social
ists are still excluded.

FOUR
SURPLUS WILL
SEAT ESTIMATE,
MELLON SAYS
WASHINGTON —A surplus for
the fiscal year 1927 considerably in
excess of $185,000,000 is now in
prospect, according to Secretary of
the Treasury Mellon. The $185,000,-
000 estimate was announced by
President Coolidge in his budget ad
dress in June, but revenue has been
pouring into the treasury since that
time at such a rate as to make it
evident that this total will be ex
ceeded.
See Big Surplus.
Secretary Mellon made no pre
diction as to the exact surplus, but
on the basis of September Income
tax receipts and customs receipts
the surplus might easily run $25,-
000,000 or more above the $185,000,-
000 total. Septeml>er income tax re
ceipts. which are estimated at about
$440,000,000, are about $15,000,000
ahead of the original estimate, while
customs receipts thus far are about
$10,000,000 ahead of last year.
Notwithstanding evidences of a
greater surplus than anticipated,
Secretary Mellon indicated that it
would still be inadvisable to attempt
any reduction in taxes at the coming
session of congress. There is no cer
tainty, he pointed out, as to expendi
tures during the fiscal year, and fac
tors might easily develop between
now and July 1, 1927, which would
greatly reduce the prospective sur
plus.
Would Be Unwise.
With congress adjourning in
March, several months in advance of
the close of the fiscal year, it would
be unwise, he thinks, to attempt any
tinkering with the revenue law at
this time. Furthermore, it was
pointed out, until the new revenue
law has been in operation for at
least a full year it will be difficult
to forecast the situation which will
exist during the fiscal years 1928
and 1929.

GREAT FUTURE
FOR STEEL MEN
CHICAGO —Charles M. Schwab,
old steel master, as he called him
self, talked last night to the steel
men of today, and he told them
that steel is riding on a great crest
of national prosperity into an era
of increased production never be
fore paralleled.
“Never before was there greater
promise for steel than in this mar
velous country of ours today,” Mr.
Schwab declared in his talk before
the American Society for Steel
Treating. “On all sides, in all walks
of life, there is reflected a well
being and a prosperity that is good
to behold.
“You men know that I have ever
been the optimist in business, that
I have built mill after mill when
others doubted, and I say to you
that none of them was able to meet
the demand. It is even more ap
parent today.”
Untimely Deaths

vention of the American Association
for Medico-Physical Research at the
Congress hotel. Less starch and
more natural food, such as fruits, is
the key to health, be said. Dr. Jones
described the human system as
similar to a fermenting vat, in
which the body is paralyzed if ex
cessive starch foods are eaten.

CROUP AFTER

Led by Dist. Atty. Eugene Wen
gert and Asst. Dist. Atty. George
A. Rowman, 22 members of the Re
publican county committee bolted
from the committee meeting in the
Republican hotel last night and or
ganized their own campaign com
mittee.
A. J. Beyer was elected chairman,
11. M. Blume secretary and W. E.
Tubesing treasurer.
Bolt Is Climax.
The bolt was the climax of scenes
of turmoil, starting when Mr. Wen
gert demanded that Frank E. Da
vidson be deposed as county chair
man. lie charged that disposal of
money collected by him for the Len
root. Perry and county candidates’
campaign had not been reported.
Mr. Rowman read a statement
signed by county candidates in
which they declared that they re
gard Mr. Davidson “as totally un
fit to conduct oi»r campaigns,” and
in which the candidates withdrew
nny authorization he had to collect
funds or spend money in their be
half.
Mr. Wengert read a long list of
contributions and charged that this
money had been collected two years
ago but never reported. He dis
played several $49.50 checks given
in the primary campaign this year
and asserted that though they had
been indorsed by Davidson, they
had neither been acknowledged nor
had any report been made of the
expenditure of the money.
Davidson Is Re-elected.
He asked that the committee de
pose Davidson and elect a man in
whom the candidates had confi
dence.
The committee, by a vote of 26
to 22, re-elected Davidson. The
county candidates’ committee men
then left the room.
The fight opened when Davidson
declared that the meeting was an
executive session and wanted to ex
clude newspaper representatives
from the room. Mr. Wengert object
ed and opened the battle by demand
ing of Davidson what he had done
with the money.
Atty. Frank Mackut, Jr., in the
course of the fight, declared that he
was there in Mr. Davidson’s de
fense and explained that the money
collected had been used to distribute
The National Republic, national
newspaper of the Republican party.
Produced INo Evidence.
Under questioning, Mr. Mackut
admitted that the subscription
price of the paper was $1.50 and
that he handled the solicitors. He

JUDGE IS WISER
AFTER DIET OF
BREAD, WATER
HARTINGTON, Neb. Declaring
himself a wiser man after five days
on a bread and water diet. County
Judge Wilbur F. Bryant, 75, vowed
that “hereafter I will regulate my
diet during the term of my natural
life.”
Judge Bryant, who in the last 14
years has affixed more than 100
sentences to be served on a bread
and water diet for infractions of
the liquor law or other ordinances,
today said he would not continue
his fast although he was in perfect
health.
The judge decided last week to
accept the challenge of his critics
to “p. actice what he preached,” and
subsequently started the diet Mon
day. Today is the last day of the
limited fare. He has lost eight
pounds.
“I hope my critics are satisfied,”
said the judge, “that I have dis
proved their theory that such a diet
is injurious to the health.”
Judge Bryant declared he discov
ered through the five days’ fare of
rye bread and water that “I have
been stuffing my stomach with too
much food for the last 50 years.”

OF WRECKAGE, IS
.FRANK’S BELIEF
MADISON—After a year as head
of the University of Wisconsin,
President Glenn Frank has reached
the definite conclusion that the in
tellectual fabric of American univer
sities and colleges is “a pile of
wreckage.”
Yesterday he repeated the charge
in a discussion of the case of Wil
fred C. Cross, whose articles on
the morality of undergraduates re
cently caused a storm of dispute
among educators.
Dr. Frank apparently held with
Cross, maintaining that a humpty
dumpty mass of knowledge is un
loaded Into students’ minds “which
cannot be put together again by all
the kings’ horses and all the king s
men.”
“Until we have tried to recover
the lost unity of knowledge we have
no right to quarrel with the super
ficiality and scrappiness of the
minds of our undergraduates.”
President Frank declared that
American universities must free
themselves from the ancient absur
dity of putting half-wits and geni
uses into the same classroom, lock
stepping them through freshman,
sophomore, junior and senior years,
and graduating them with the same
recognition.”

COUNTRY COPS
FOR DRY FORCE,
ANDREWS’ AIM
WASHINGTON—LincoIn C. An
drews, czar of the dry army, yester
day called upon his administrators
to enlist county authorities in the
nation-wide drive against ruin.
Only county officials in states
having local dry laws would be
mobilized. They would not be fed
eralized. Neither would they snoop
for the government. Their work
would be simply to enforce locally
the state dry laws.
As outlined by Mr. Andrews, the
work of the administrator will be to
inspire the county authorities to ac
tion. He would have them persuade
county officials that it would pay
them to enforce rigidly state dry
laws.
Leave Agents Free.
Acting through sheriffs, con
stables and other law enforcement
officers, the county officials, in the
opinion of Mr. Andrews, should be
able to take care of all the ordinary
police court type of dry law viola
tions, leaving the federal agents
free to go after higher-ups.
The work of Sam I. Johnson, San
Francisco administrator, in lining
up county authorities in California
was held up as an example.
Mr. Johnson reported that 40
counties had collected $434,000 in
fines at an expense of only .$.>1,000,
a dear profit, as he explained it,
of $383,000.
Provide Tax Relief.
“Such a record should be an in
centive, from a purely mercenary
viewpoint, to all county officials,”
Mr. Johnson asserted. “Money col
lected in fines relieves the taxpayers
of taxes.”
Mr. Andrews then highly com
mended another feature of the re
port.
“Mr. Johnson's report discloses.’
he said, “that in most cases county
authorities make their raids at
night. No matter how late the raids
are made, the local judges wait up
until the prisoners are brought in.”

ARREST BATHER
WHO DIDN’T USE
COMMON SENSE
NEW YORK Jersey justice,
which expresses itself in novel
ways, took a new turn yesterday
when a man was arrested on the
beach at Lavallette on a charge of
violating “the law of common
sense.”
If Allen Roesch, 23, of Philadel
phia, had been bitten by a shark
or had drowned, the officials
wouldn’t have been concerned, but
because he made others risk their
lives by rescuing him in a heavy sea
he was arrested and must appear
before Mayor Enoch Titus Van
Camp of Lavallette today.
When Roesch went out to swim
off the beach, a.most directly in
front of the heme of Henry Stev
ens, a prominent figure in the Hall-
Mills case, he found himself caught
in the undertow. There was noth
ing to do but call for help.
James Nebille, a life guard, and
three others jumped into a boat and
went to Roesch's rescue. The sea
was choppy and they had difficulty
rescuing the man. When Roesche
was brought to shore he was con
fronted by Mayor Van Camp and
Town Marshal Peter Bloom.
“Arrest the man,” the Mayor said
to Bloom.
“On what charge? For being res
cued?” asked Bloom.
“Well, if there isn’t any law cov
ering his case, at least he violated
the law of common sense by going
out swimming on a day lik'e this,”
said the mayor.
But in view of the fact that
Roesch was in his bathing suit and
also because there isn’t any jail in
Lavallette, he was allowed to go to
the home of friends with the under
standing he will show cause iu
court why a man should go in swim
ming when the water is rough.
EXPLOSIONS OF
GRAIN DUST RUN
MOTOR ENGINE
NEW YORK—Predictions of a fu
ture shortage in gasoline have led
to experiments which prove that a
gasoline engine can be operated with
waste, such as grain and flour dust,
powdered coal and other carbonace
ous substances as fuel. In the cur
rent issue of Power, experiments
made with a Ford engine are de
scribed. With minor alterations,
the motor was made to run on floor
sweepings from a grain elevator.
In preparation for the experi
ments, the carburetor of the engine
was ta’cen off and to the intake
manifold was attached a metal tube
which connected the engine with a
chamber. This chamber was
equipped with a small fan and re
circulating pipes, so that air could
be drawn out of the top and blown
in at the bottom, thus producing an
updraft designed to keep the grain
dust in suspension. Check valves
were placed in the tube to safeguard
against back-fire. To avoid hand
cranking, an electric motor was
used to drive a pulley on a shaft
connected at the rear of the engine.
The manifolds were removed and
the dust fuel fed by hand through
a tube to the intake valve port.
With this arrangement, the dust ex
ploded readily and frequently.
“It cannot be said,” says the de
scription. “that the engine made any
prolonged continuous run, but cer
tainly enough power was developed
to turn it over many times. If a
system of feeding a continuous,
measured quantity of dust to the
engine could be developed, better
operation might be expected. How
ever. the engine used for the ex
periments, although probably not
the right type for a dust engine,
gave encouraging results, which in
dicated the possibility of designing
an engine to use grain dust as the
source of fuel.”

WHEREAS, At the biennial ses
sion of the legislature for the year
1923, an amendment to the consti
tution was proposed and agreed to
by a majority of the members elect
ed to each of the two houses, which
proposed amendment Is as follows:
“Resolved by the Senate, the As
sembly concurring, That a new sec
tion be added to article XIII of the
constitution to read: (Article XIII)
Section 12. The qualified electors
of the state or of any county or of
any congressional, judicial or leg
islative district, may petition for
the recall of any elective officer
after the first year of the term for
which be was elected, by filing a
petition ■with the officer with whom
the petition for nomination to such
office in the primary election Is
filed, demanding the recall of such
officer. Such petition shall be
signed by electors equal In number
to at least twenty-five per cent of
the vote cast for the office of gov
ernor at the last preceding election.
In the state, county or district from
which such officer Is to be recalled.
The officer with whom such peti
tion is filed shall call a special elec-
tion to be held not less than forty
nor more than forty-five days form
the filing of such petition. The of
ficer against whom such petition
has been filed shall continue to per
form the duties of his office until
the result of such special election
shall have been officially declared.
Other candidates for such office
mav be nominated in the manner as
is provided by law in primary elec
tions. The candidate who shall re
ceive the highest number of votes
shall be deemed elected for the re
mainder of the term. The name of
the candidate against whom the re
call petition is filed shall go on the
ticket unless he resigns within ten
days after the filing of the peti
tion. After one such petition and
special election, no further recall
petition shall be filed against the
same officer during the term for
which he was elected. This article
shall be self-executing and all of
its provisions shall be treated as
mandatory. Laws may be enacted
to facilitate its operation, but no
law shall be enacted to hamper, re
strict or impair the right of recall.”
Resolved by the Senate, the As
sembly concurring, That the fore
going amendment to the constitu
tion of the state of "Wisconsin be
and the same is hereby agreed to
by this legislature.
NOTE.—This amendment. If ap
proved. will add to the constitution
a self-executing provision for the
recall of elective public officers by
the direct vote of the people of the
state or of any county or of any
congressional, judicial or legisla
tive district, under the conditions
and in the manner therein set forth.
It will apply to officers elected by
the people of the following classes
only: State officers, county officers,
congressional officers, judicial offi
cers, and legislative officers, and
will enable the people to recall any
officer in the classes named, at any
time after he has served one year
of the term for which he was elect
ed, and to elect another person in
his place for the remainder of such
term.

URGES MUSIC
CURE BE GIVEN
TO PATIENTS
NEW YORK Of recent years
hospital authorities have been
studying the therapeutic value of
music on patients placed under their
care. The proper presentation of
music is considered of such impor
tance that the Natioal Association
for Music in Hospitals, founded in
December, 1925, has just announced
that it will offer scholarships to mu
sicians willing to be trained in the
work of giving appropriate concerts
for the sick.
Although it has been customary
to permit singers, violinists and
pianists to visit hospital wards, it
is only in comparatively recent
years that music has been looked
upon as a valuable aid to the physi
cian in his effort to heal the patient.
For the ilrst time courses are being
given in “organized music” —the
term originated by Mrs. Isa Maud
Ilsen, musical director of the as
sociation.
It is held that “right music right
ly presented” may be of inestimable
assistance in the curing of the sick,
while “wrong music wrongly ren
dered” may be equally harmful. The
classes Mrs. Ilsen has organized are
not to instruct performers in the
technique of their art (this they
are supposed to have mastered be
fore coming to her), but to teach
them what type of music is accept
able and the correct manner in
which to interpret it for this pur
pose.
Chosen With Care.
When Mrs. Ilsen speaks of “or
ganized music,” she implies that the
music must have certain well-de
fined qualities. The words of songs
must be chosen with care; the char
acter of the composition, its tone
color, rhythm, repetition—all must
be combined in such a way that
they may bring hope to the listen
ers, soothe rather than excite,
arouse interest in life. The artists
who give of their talents must be
“possessed of a personality to bring
cheer; able to go through their part
undaunted by any emergency that
may arise in the ward.”
Dress plays an important part in
the director’s talks with her women
students. “It must not be too flap
perish, nor yet too sombre,” she be
lieves. Performers must have poise
and sympathy; must above all be
able to reach the invalids—in the
words of the actor, “to get across
the footlights.”
The making up of a program for
a hospital ward is no less important
then is the choosing of a program
for Carnegie hall. In fact, Mrs. Ilsen
would say that much greater
thought must be expended on the
former. Two forms of musical^ex
pression, if they can be called that
—jazz and doleful hymns—are abso
lutely taboo. The former is too
jerky and unrestful; the latter too
solemn and tearful.
Must Be Quiet.
The student is urged to bear in
mind the fact that his music must
quiet, yet at the same time whole
somely stimulate the mentality of
his adudience. The pieces played
must be such as will tend to
arouse the vital functions of the
body, says Sirs. Ilsen. The same
attention ought to be given to the
rhythm of music played in hospitals
that is given to music used to ease
the burden of marching troops.
“The vital functions of the body are
all rythmic when in a perfect state
of health, and to this state the
rhythm should accord.
It is because of the highly sensi
tive psychological state of the sick
that such caution Is taken in train
ing performers. The response of
patients is almost immediately no
ticeable. Artists of the association
often give more than one concert in
a hospital, going from ward to ward.
As a rule, the duration of a pro
gram is half an hour.
Though the National Association
for Music in Hospitals is still in its
infancy, it has over 30 institutions
on its list in Greater New York and
neighboring states. From all over
the country calls are being received
for information and instruction.
Tennessee has recently introduced
“organized music” in nine of its
hospitals.
Of Great Value,
Doctors increasingly recognized
music to be of value in hospital
treatment; though they have not an
yet given it formal recognition as a
vanquisher of aches and pains.
many are welcoming it as an all.v
in their tight on disease.
Since the days of ancient Greece
the healing power of melody has
been spoken of and written about.
After Florence Nightingale sought

American tourists, said that the
cases in Belgium would close at mid
night every night after Oct. 1 as
part of an economy program to build
up the franc.
Among the passengers was Miss
Ruth Askenas, Brooklyn, w’ho has
been blind since she was 2 years
old. She returned from a tour
through France, Switzerland and
Italy. She won a travel scholarship
from the New York Association for
the Blind, and went abroad under
the escort of Miss Louise Cavell!
and Miss Kate Accurso.
Miss Capelli said that Miss
Askenas displayed a wonderful
knowledge of literature and history,
which made the tour most interest
ing and instructive. “To travel with
an alert blind person is like seeing
the fourth dimension,” she said.
Miss Askenas spoke of the places
of interest they visited as if she had
seen them all.* “Italy is to be found
in miniature in the shops,” she said.
“When I visited the fine palaces and
ancient buildings. I would trace the
columns, the facades and the
statues with my fingers and then I
could create the structure in my
own mind. In Venice I heard the
swish of the long oars of the gon
dolas, with the music stealing over
the waters of the Grand canal, and
I thought of Byron and Shelley and
Keats, and needed no eyes. I know
I was in the famous square of St.
Mark when the pigeons came all
around me to eat grain from my
hand.”
In Paris Miss Askenas visited the
Lighthouse for the Blind, estab
lished by Mrs. Winifred Ilolt
Mather.*

DEBTS NOT SOLE
REASON U.S. IS
HATED ABROAD
NEW YORK —The official Brit
ish attitude toward M. Clemenceau's
letter to President Coolidge is one
of reticence, says a copyrighted dis
patch to The Times from London.
It is regarded as the appeal of a
distinguished Frenchman to Amer
ican public opinion, and therefore
not a matter in which England has
any direct concern.
However, conversations in the
British capital reveal certain gen
erally held ideas. One is that M.
Clemenceau allowed enthusiasm for
his cause to lead him too far: First,
in charging indirectly that America
planned to get French colonial pos
sessions in return for her loan—for
which the British see no justifica
tion in any official Washington
word or action; and second, his
comparison of America’s separate
treaty with Germany with the Rus
sian soviet’s separate peace with the
"common foe.”
See No Parallel.
It at once occurs that the soviet
peace was made in wartime, cost
ing the allies much blood and treas
ure, whereas the American separate
peace was made two years after the
victory had been won.
However, one senses In London
the idea that President Coolidge’s
reply as published by the after
noon's papers to the effect that the
debt matter is a closed Incident does
not answer M. Clemenceau's letter.
It is felt that the Tiger has placed
his appeal on a higher plane and in
larger scope than the mere consid
eration of international debts. The
French war premier’s real meaning
is seen in the last paragraph of his
letter, where he refers to his hopes
that America would assume the
moral leadership of the world and
his suggestion that the United
States “pass judgment on itself.”
Debts Mere Incident.
The British are essentially an in
ternationally minded people and,
like all Europeans who turn their
minds to the consideration of inter
national affairs, regard the retro
gression of America from its su
preme world position as vastly over
shadowing the debt issue, which is
regarded as a mere incident in a
larger story. And, furthermore,
even with regard to the debts, it
must not be forgotten that Britain’s
world position is that the debts
should have been all canceled, but
that this program was made impos
sible by the refusal of the United
States to adhere to it.
M. Clemenceau’s final appeal,
taken with the British reaction,
emphasizes the fact that the debts
do not form the only basis of the
European attitude toward the
United States. It is convenient to I
talk about debts, but from the larger
point of view the withdrawal of
America from the position of in
fluence, responsibility and domina
tion she had seven years ago looms
in the European mind bigger and
more important and therefore more
worthy of serious criticism than her
debt policy, which forms only one
point in the foreign program of the
United States in recent years which,
for what that is worth, is regarded
on this side of the Atlantic as ego
istic and nationalistic.
More Criticism Soon.
Next month, when Germany is due
to be admitted to the league of na-
tions by the league assembly, one
more occasion will arise for the ab
sence of America to give opportunity
to voice this dissatisfaction with
her. Despite everything which
Washington has or has not done, or
has not said, it remains true that
the American position has been woe
fully poorly presented to other na
tions, and, generally speaking, Amer-
ica is credited with no other motives
than those of selfishness. And the
vast majority of European states
men really agree fundamental!/with
M. Clemenceau's recommendation
that America give second thought
to her international record since the
war.

UNIQUE PRIZE
OFFERED IN
DX CONTEST
JOHANNESBURG, South Africa
—A silver replica of an African
springbok, a variety of small ante
lope, and the national symbol of
South Africa, has been offered by
The Rand Daily Mail, of this city,
as the prize to the United States,
Canadian, or Hawaiian amateur
who effects the greatest number of
two-way contacts on short waves
with South African amateurs dur
ing the months of September and
October.
The tests are being held under the
auspices of the American Radio Re
lay league, of Hartford, Conn., and
the South African Radio Relay
league, with headquarters in this
city.
Amateurs Are Eligible.
Any amateur in either country
with a transmitting station is eli
gible to participate, and the only re
quirement of the contest that each
American, Canadian or Hawaiian
station work just as many South
African amateurs as possible dur
ing the two months. If an American
station vtorks the same South Afri
can amateur more than once in a
given week, only one contact will be
counted toward the total. The mak
ing of schedules between stations is
prohibited, in addition.
Will Collect Records.
At the close of the contest period
the two national organizations will
collect the records in their respec
tive countries nnd submit them to
the contest judges. The board of
judges is composed of the editor of
The Rand Daily Mail; the editor of
QST, the magazine of the American
Radio Relay league: the communi
cations manager of the ARRL; the
secretary of the South African Ra
dio Relay league, nnd the chief en
gineer of the broadcast station lo
cated here.
For about a year, various Amer
ican amateurs have been talking
with a limited number of South
African amateur radio stations, but
this communication has been con
fined to a few of the more promi
nent stations both in this country
and America. It was to overcome
this condition and get a large num
ber of stations in each country to
communicate with each other that
the contest was planned, and al
ready the preliminary returns show
that a far greater number of con
tacts are being effected than ever
before.

To the Editor of The Leader:
Reading in Thursday’s Leader
that the Milwaukee Art institute
1 will become the property of the city
with in a few years, it occurred to
me that the city should be consider
ing some centralization of this and
its allied activities.
Would it not lie better to have
all such activities—the library, the
museum—under the same roof
where possible? Each would then
gain visitors by reason of the pres
ence of the others?
Books, historical specimens,
painting, sculpture—all have much
in common. The cultured person’s
interests play broadly among all of
these.
There would also seem to me to
be some economy connected with
joining forces and organizations in
presenting those departments of the
city’s cultural activities.
F. S.
Milwaukee.

part in the elections, so the ministry
now simply becomes a business
cabinet.

euphorbia tree yields a sap or latex

pounds of latex. Attempts at vul
canizing are said to have been quite
satisfactory.

MANIFESTO ASKS
LEAGUETOBAN
CONSCRIPTION
CHICAGO—The league of nations
is to be asked to propose the aboli
tion of military conscription
throughout the world as a first step
toward disarmament in a manifesto
issued here and signed by some very
prominent people belonging to 14
different countries, says a copy
righted dispatch reprinted by The
Tribune from The New York Times.
The manifesto, which is published
by a committee specially appointed
for the purpose, reads:
Text of Manifesto.
During the war people in all the
countries determined to throw off
forever the yoke of militarism, and,
when peace came, the league of na
tions was welcomed as the offspring
of this hope. It is our duty to see
that the terrible suffering of the
war does not recur.
We call for some definite step to
ward complete disarmament and
the demilitarizing of the mind of
civilized nations. The most effective
measure toward this would be the
universal abolition of conscription.
We therefore ask the league of na
tions to propose the abolition of
compulsory military service in all
countries as a first step toward true
disarmament.
It is our belief that conscript
armies, with their large corps of
professional officers, are a grave
menace of peace. Conscription in
volves the degradation of human
personality and the destruction of
liberty. Barrack life, military Grill,
blind obedience to commands, how
ever unjust and foolish they may
be, and deliberate training for
slaughter undermine respect for the
Individual, for democracy and hu
man life.
Calls It Debasing.
It Is debasing human dignity to
force men to give up their lives or
to inflict death against their will or
without conviction as to the justice
of their action. The state which
thinks itself entitled to force its citi
zens to go to war will never pay
proper regard tn the value and hap
pinecs of their lives in peace.
'Moreover, by conscription the mili
tarist spirit of aggressiveness is im
planted in the whole male popula
tion at the most impressionable age.
By training for war men come to
consider war as unavoidable and
even desirable.
By the universal abolition of con
scription war will be made less easy.
The government of a country which
maintains conscription has little dif
ficulty in declaring war, for it can
alienee the whole population by a
mobilization order. When govern
ments have to depend for support
upon the voluntary consent of their
peoples they must necessarily exer
cise caution in their foreign policies.
Plan of Wilson.
In the first draft of the covenant
of the league of nations, President
Wilson proposed to make conscrip
tion illegal in all affiliated coun
tries. It is our duty to restore the
original spirit which created the
league, a spirit shared by many of
those who fought In the war, ant.
professed by many Of the statesmen
of the countries concerned.
By the universal abolition, of con
scription we can take a decisive step
toward peace and liberty. We there
fore call upon all men and women
of good-will to help create in all
countries a public opinon which will
Induce governments and the league
of nations to take this definite step
to rid the world of the spirit of
militarism, and to open the way to
a new era of freedom within na
tions and of fraternity between
them.

GIRL TEACHER
ANTIGO, Wis. Police with
bloodhounds failed yesterday to
establish whereabouts of Alice A.
Diehl, 23. Necedah, a teacher here,
who disappeared mysteriously
Wednesday .following a bridge party.
According to information given to
police, Miss Diehl went to her room
after the card party and retired
for the night. Her roommate, how
ever, awoke about 5:30 a. m.
Wednesday and found Miss Diehl
gone. She apparently had changed
clothing and had been in bed.
Bloodhounds were brought to the
house and took up a trail leading
to a bridge over a pond. When the
dogs reached the bridge they lost
the trail.
5 Democrats Fail
To Get Names on
Election Ballot
MADISON. Wis. —Five Demo
cratic candidates in the primary
election failed to secure sufficient
votes to insure their appearing un
der the party banner on the general
election ballot in November, reports
from the state canvassing board
showed yesterday.
They will appear on the ballot as
independent candidates.

Jr., Platteville, candidate for attor
ney general; A. H. Schubert, La
Crosse, candidate for congressman
from the seventh district; R. J.
Walsh, Plainfield, candidate for
congressman from eighth district;
Oscar F. Roessler, Jefferson, can
didate for state senator, and Frank
B. Becker, Berlin, candidate for as
semblyman.
The Wisconsin law requires a
primary candidate to secure 5 per
cent of the total vote cast by his
party for governor in the preceding
general election.

One man was fatally injured and
four other prominent Milwaukee
shipping men were hurt late yester
day', when the automobile, in which
they were riding, Skidded into a
ditch and overturned twice on High
way 15, 14 miles north of Sheboy
gan.
The dead:
William C. Cunliffe, 71, 13G Ju
neau Ave., retired general agent,
Grand Trunk railroad system.
The injured:
James F. Taylor, 1156 12th St.,
■urveyor for the American Bureau
of Shipping.
Henry W. Pless, 2723 Chestnut
St., general agent.
J. A. Hunter, 779 54th St., freight
agent.
Capt C. E. MacLaren, manager,
marine department, Grand Trunk.
Mr. Cunliffe was pinned beneath
the demolished machine. His neck
was broken. The remaining four,
thrown clear from the wreckage,
were taken to a Sheboygan hospital
for treatment. Hunter, who was
driving, escaped with slight in
juries.
The accident happened as Hunter
was about to pass a motor truck,
driven by Charles Grinner, Sheboy
gan. The road, a narrow stretch of
macadam, was slippery from the
all-day rain.
The body of Cunliffe was removed
to the Kroos funeral parlors in She
boygan.
Cunliffe is survived by his wife,
a son, Russell W. Cunliffe, city
chemist, and a daughter, Mrs. L. J.
Mueller, Jr., 424 Kane place.

SOCIftLCLINIC
HERE OCT. 3-6
What will be in fact a social and
civil clinic for Wisconsin will be
held in Milwaukee, Oct. 3,4, 5 and
6. under the leadership of the Wis
consin Conference of Social Work.
Citizens from all parts of the
state, including men and women
from all walks of life —farmers,
ministers, business men, club wom
en, mothers, municipal officials,
labor leaders, social workers, physi
cians, editors —have met for the
past few years to discuss prob
lems wltich confrent them in their
cities, towns and villages.
There will be divisions on com
munity health, municipal govern
ment, poor relief, dependent chil
dren, recreation, boys’ work, indus
try problems, mental hygiene, rural
social work, crippled children, and
civic and social organization prob
lems.
“What these conferences of civic
and social leaders aim to do is to
obtain use of scientific and humane
methods in the every-day business
of living,” declared Justice M. B.
Rosenberry, state supreme court,
of the conference.

the fervor and intensity which
marks the deliberations of youth
and idealism, and the frilled and
dour ancestors who preside in great
gilt frames at solemn intervals
about the walls, have never wit
nessed, for all their antiquity, such
desperate ardor, and withai, such
friendly tolerance as is exhibited
by these moulders of England's des
tinies.
After the lecture and discussion,
luncheon, and then the afternoon
and loveliest of England lies before
the group. Tennis, swimming,
books, conversation, even a trip to
exquisite and stately Cambridge
all of these are quite within the
range of posibility.
Americans Made “At Home.”
After dinner there is another lec
ture, followed usually by what is
known as a “social evening.” This
involves Pat Dolan, enhanced by a
scarlet jacket, acting as master of
ceremonies, and with inimitable wit,
satirizing the personalities of the
leaders and convulsing a receptive
audience with mockeries of their
theories. On such evenings the glee
"ul strains of “wage the class war
strictly, put the job through quick
ly” must shock the painted ears of
the venerable Warwick ancestors
and the abandon of the romping
folk dancing, be difficult for their
somber dignity.
Always, before the Auld Lang
Syne closing, comes the tribute to
the American guests—“ Does the
Spearmint lose its flavor on the bed
post overnight? If you chew it in
the morning, will it be too hard to
bite?” etc., sung in high merriment
and with a secret conviction that
now, indeed, these Americans must
feel at home.
Able Men Invited.
The ablest political leaders of
Liberal and Labor policy ate invit
ed to the summer school at Easton
to present to the students their par
ticular specialties. So, during the
first fortnight of the sessions, such
men as John Maynard Keynes, in
ternationally known financial ex
pert, spoke, as did such Labor lead
ers as Hon. John Wheatley, minis
ter of health in the late Labor cab
inet Hugh Dalton, member of par
liament, and Oswald Mosley, one
of the most important of the young
er men.
Leaders and representatives of
the rank and file wrestled over the
problems of policy together.
It was an exciting morning, for
instance, when as part of a general
discussion on internationalism, Fen
ner Brockway, pale, sensitive, fine
of face, the secretary of the Inde
pendent Labor party, put the cause
for absolute pacifism and roused
the scorn and the choleric argument
of Pat Dolan, who challenged the
idyllic Brockway to protect the Brit
ish food supply with moral suasion.
And there was the evening Keynes
came w-ith his flower-like wife, Lo
pokova, a Russian dancer, to cope
with the sharp satire and quick
brilliance of Mosley, with the vola
tile fervor of Pat Dolan, with the
bombastic wordiness of the occa
sional self-important adolescent,
with all the enthusiasm and class
consciousness of this group of pros
eletizers—Keynes, sleek and well
bred and behaved, in the midst of
persons without reverence and with
out awe, persons defiant of prestige,
persons who were simply and avid
ly hungry for the promised life.

cialist.
If one personality dominated

There were at Easton a few out
croppings of those bits of fanaticism
which so lend themselves to carica
ture that they have become the ear

on the whole it was not a very ec
centric group which dealt so sol
emnly with national destiny at Eas

ELECTION WILL
DECIDE ISSUE
OCTOBER 15
Voters’ League Hears
Seidel Score
Incorporation.
Nearly unanimous opinions
against incorporation of the town
of Milwaukee into a city was ex
pressed at a meeting, called by the
Taxpayers and Voters’ league, to
discuss the subject in Community
hall, Green Bay and Green Tree
roads, last night. About 850 per
sons attended.
The voters will be called upon to
decide if they wish to incorporate
inta a city, to be known as the city
of Lincoln Park, at the special elec
tion, Oct. 15.
“We must remember that we are
all citizens of a larger unit than
the city or town in which we live,
that our interests and problems
reach way beyond our own borders
merging with those of the county,
state and nation.” Emil Seidel, for
mer mayor of Milwaukee, said In
addressing the meeting.
Need Larger Units.
He pointed out, as an example,
that while the Milwaukee river
drains an area of over 600 miles,
problems due to the presence of the
river are common to all persons
living within that area, although at
the present time they must lie met
to a large decree by various town,
municipal and county governments.
“Because of the extensiveness of
our problems it is advisable to form
larger, rather than smaller units of
government,” he stated. “At pres
ent there are 16 villages, city and
town governments within the
county.”
Mr. Seidel emphasized the dupli
cation of costs which would result
if the town is incorporated into a
city. He also illustrated the many
advantages which a large city like
Milwaukee offers to all those in the
county, such as libmry extension
service and use of parks, museums
and social centers, without charge.
Pastor Calls It “Unfair.”
The Rev. Peter Dietz, jiastor, St.
Monica’s Catholic church, Whitefish
Bay, said that incorporation was a.
“question of honor,” and that it
would be unfair to the city of Mil
waukee. He explained that dis
tricts such as the surrounding town
ships were enjoying most of the
benefits offered by Milwaukee, and
that to incorporate into a separate
city would prevent Milwaukee’s
growth and expansion. Prosperity
of adjoining territory depends jipon
the growth and prosperity of Mil
waukee, he added.
W. N. Voorhees, is chairman of
the league. H. R. Gmham and
Henry Ripple, real estate dealers,
also spoke.

WILL PARADE
ON OCTOBER 2
The rules for the pet animal pa
rade which will be conducted Oct.
2, 2 p. m., by the Wisconsin Humane
society, were given out today by
Walter J. Dethloff, superintendent.
The parade is being held as part
of the dedication ceremonies of the
society’s new animal shelter and
headquarters, 299 sth Ave.
The rules are as follows: All boys
and girls of grade and high school
age are eligible to enter; all kinds
of pets may be entered; no dogs
should be required to pull any small
vehicles such as a coaster wagon.
Anyone entering a pet animal, ex
cept a pony, harnessed to a small
wagon, will reduce his chances for
winning a prize. They may be
drawn in any small vehicle with or
without enclosure; decorations are
permissible.
Prizes will be awarded. The fol
lowing points will be taken into con
sideration by the judges: General
condition of animal; idea conveyed
for kindness to animals; careful
handling of animals.
All types and breeds of animals
will be considered on equal terms.
All entrants are requested to call
at the society headquarters in per
son, or telephone Hanover 5274, in
order to get a number for position
in the parade.
The i>arade committee consists of
F. A. Vaughn, William Wirth. R. V.
Ahrens, J. C. Castlemann and J. E.
Partington. The judges are: Mrs.
F. A. Vaughn, Mrs. George D. Bai
ley, Mrs. George F. O’Neil, H.
Froehlich and Dr. F. W. .Milke.
The dedication ceremonies will
open Oct. 1 with a dinner in the
new building.

TRADE LARGE
Many farm co-operatives are
qualified to give lessons in efficient
marketing.
“They have made an enviable
record in getting and holding busi
ness and in marketing farm prod
ucts so they bring the greatest re
turns to farmers,’’ explains Theo
dore Macklin, economist at the Wis
consin College of Agriculture.
Among the ordinary provisions
that enter the kitchen of the Ameri
can home, Macklin points out that
many of the most popular brands are
marketed by co-operative organiza
tions. These Include the Sunkist and
Sealdsweet oranges, Land o’Lakes
butter, Tillamook, Mello-Creme and
Federation cheese, Red Star pota
toes, Diamond walnuts, Eatmore
cranberries, Sunmaid raisins and
“Sunsweet prunes. All of these
brands are well known for their
consistent high quality.
“These particular products have
been sold to better advantage by co
operative associations than by other
methods of trade,” he declares.
“This is shown by the fact that
those co-operatives which started
out in a small way have since in
creased until they now handle, in
many cases, from one-tenth to nine
tenths of the products of a single
branch of the farm Industry. The
annual business of these associa
tions ranges from $2,000,000 to $70,-
C 00.000.”
Not only have the co-ops supplied
consumers with the highest quality
products but they have set a stand
ard which other organizations have
followed.

EXPORTS OF
FARM PRODUCE
ON INCREASE
WASHINGTON Exports of
agricultural products, excluding for
est products from the United States,
during the fiscal year 1925-26 de
clined in vaule 17 per cent from the
total of previous years, although
they were larger than in any other
year since 1921-22. The figures,
analyzed by the department of agri
culture, show total agricultural ex
ports, excluding forest products,
amounted to $1,892,000,000.
These products constituted 41 per
cent of our total exports, against
48 per cent in 1924-25 and 44 per
cent In 1923-24. Grain, grain prod
ucts and cotton showed the greatest
falling off. Exports of tobacco and
friuts increased, with forest prod
ucts included in the the total of
agricultural exports the proportion
of our agricultural to ou. total ex
ports was 44 per cent, against 51
per cent in 1924-25.
Grain and grain products, ac
counted for $264,202,000 of the agri
cultural export trade, against $522,-
575,000 in 1924-25. In this 50 per
cent drop, declines In wheat, grain
and flour exports were particularly
noticeable. Corn was the only grain
the exportation of which increased
appreciably in the fiscal year. Ex
ports of corn totaled 23,137,000
bushels, against 8,460,000 bushels
in 1924-25, although the export
price averaged only 92 cents a
bushel, against $1.25 a bushel dur
ing 1924-25.
68,000 PHONE
CABLE REELS
USED YEARLY
With more than 5,000,000 miles of
telephone conductor wire added to
the system each year a tremendous
number of wooden reels are used
in the shipment of this wire from
factory to various points of use.
A large percentage of wire is now
made up in lead covered cables
which are shipped on reels varying
in diameter ^from 2^ feet, weighing
perhaps 15 pounds, to those feet
in diameter, weighing almost 300
pounds. While these reels are used
over many times, at least 1,000 new
ones are manufactured in one fac
tory each month to keep up the
shipping facilities, which total 68,-
000 every year
Originally these reels were made
by hand, but the necessity for
stronger and more durable material
resulted in the development of
special machinery for the manufac
ture of these reels, which are usually
made of three piles of wood nailed
in one operation by a special ma
chine, trimmed to a circular shape
by a band saw, and then clamped
together over the drums by machin
ery prepared for that purpose.

FOREIGN STEEL
PACT ACCORD
IS EXPECTED
WASHINGTON Formation of
the International Steel Syndicate to
which Germany, France, Luxem
burg and Belgium will be the prin
cipal parties is expected to come
within a few days in spite of the
objections raised by Belgian inter
ests on account, of the size of her
quota allotment, according to ca
bled advices sent the department of
commerce by Acting Commercial At
tache Miller at Paris.
It is accepted from Mr. Miller’s
reports that the other three coun
tries at interest are preparing to of
fer concessions satisfactory to the
Belgians. Negotiations to this
end, it is said, are being continued
and are expected to result in estab
lishment of the syndicate soon.
The syndicate, it is said, will not
limit production, but rather assess
penalties iu steel produced by va
rious countries over the allotments
agreed to. It will leave prices free,
it is claimed, on the theory that un
der the plan production will be lim
ited automatically and prices kept
at a reasonably high level.
The general scheme is to provide
for the entrance into the syndicate
of smaller producing countries of
Europe after the four principal na
tions have gotten the matter under
way. Austria, which already has
made arrangements with Geramny
and Hungary, has indicated a de
sire to join, while it is reported
that Poland and Czecho-Slovakia
would probably follow.

COTTON CROP
ESTIMATE UP,
SAYS REPORT
WASHINGTON —An estimated
cotton crop of 15,810,000 bales of
500 pounds gross weight is indi
cated by the Sept. 16 condition of
the crop, which was 59.5 per cent of
a normal, the department of agricul
ture announced today.
Unusually warm weather during
the first half of September favored
fruiting and enabled the cotton crop
to partially overcome its late start,
the department of agriculture stated
in announcing an indicated total pro
duction of 15,810,000 bales of 500
pounds gross.
Crop Slightly Less.
The improvement in the crop
amounted to 644,000 bales between
Sept. 1 and 16 and indications now
are for a crop only 293,679 bales
smaller than last year's. Declines
in prospects were reported from only
two states, Missouri and Tennessee,
since Sept. 1. Elsewhere the in
creasing damage from boll weevil
and leaf worms has been more than
offset by the increased fruitfulness,
that is now apparent, the crop re-
porting board stated.
Cotton of this year’s growth ginned
prior to Sept. 16 totaled 2.511,317
running bales, counting 61,584 round
bales as half bales and excluding
linters.
Yield 160 Pounds.
Upon the preliminary estimated
area remaining for harvest, 47,207,-
000 acres, the indicated crop would
approximate a yield of 160 pounds
of lint cotton per acre.
A crop of 15,166.000 bales was in
dicated by the Sept. 1 condition.

capitalization of the company from
$35,000,000 to $45,000,000.

States in the first six months of
1926 amounted to 16,415,395 dozen,
an increase of 3,000,000 dozen over
the exports in the corresponding pe
riod of 1925, according to the food
stuffs division of the department of
commerce.

1925 amounted to 24.998,502 dozen
and in 1924 to 28,117,102 dozen. The
largest markets for eggs exported
from the United States are Cuba.
Mexico, Argentina, Canada and
Panama, in the order named. In
1925 Cuba took 45 per cent of the
exports, Mexico 17 per cent, Argen
tina 14 per cent, Canada 10 per
cent, and Panama 4 per cent.
United States imports of eggs in
the shell are negligible, but imports
of egg products have been increas
ing in recent years. The value of
these imports in 1924 was $5,G72,-
070 and in 1925, $8,824,805. The
greater part of these products is
imported during the second half of
the year. The value of the imports
has increased from $942,082 in the
first half of 1924 to $1,990,643 in
the first half of 1925 and to $2,428,-
786 in the first half of 1926. China
and Hongkong are the source of
these imports, the imports recorded
as coming from England being
doubtless transshipments of Chi
nese products. z

FLOODS SWEEP
AWAY CROPS
PEORIA, Ill.—Loss of $1,000,000
on corn alone in the valley of the
Illinois river between Peoria and
Grafton in the recent flood is the
sum placed by James R. Fuller, as
sistant United States engineer. His
estimate is placed after a tour of
the stricken district. Eleven levee
districts were partly or wholly
flooded. The land flooded is placed
at 54,000 acres, practically 70 per
cent of which was planted to corn.
The destruction, the report says,
was caused by small streams over
flowing their levees. No levee of the
Illinois river gave way.
The condition at La Grange is
also menacing. The federal locks
and dams here are submerged and
water is overflowing the state dam
at Copperas creek. Browning in
Brown county, Liverpool in Fulton,
Florence in Pike, and Hardin and
Kampsville in Calhoun are also
flooded. Additional rainfall will
greatly increase the damage, reports
from army officers who made the
inspection said.

United Fruit Co.
To Let Employes
Purchase Stock
BOSTON—The United Fruit Co.
has decided to adopt a program of
employes’ stock ownership and
stockholders will be asked to ap
prove the plan at a special meeting
scheduled for Oct. 27. The direc
tors propose to offer employes of
three years’ continuous service the
right to purchase an amount of
United Fruit Co.’s stock equal to
annual salary, taking shares at SIOO
each. The purchase price is to be
$96. Payment to be made from
monthly salaries at the rate of $2 a
month for the four-year period of
operation of the plan. It is esti
mated that shares to be subscribed
for will not exceed 100,000 shares.
It the plan is approved the first al
lotments will be made Jan. 1, 1927,
and provision will be made for quar
terly entrance of employes becom
ing eligible up to Jan. 1, 1931.

Stuffed with Oysters.
Beef tenderloin, one cup oysters
with liquor, four tablespoons butter,
melted; one cup cracker crumbs,
celery salt, salt, pepper.
Split the tenderkin, lengthwise.
Season with salt IXI pepper. Mix
the oysters with the cracker crumbs
and melted butter. Season with salt,
pepper and celery salt. It there is
not enough of the oyster liquor to
moisten the dressing, add a little
stock or hot water. Put the dress
ing between the pieces of tender
loin and sew together. Roast for
20 to 40 minuteSj basting often.

Planked Sirloin Steak.
Sirloin steak, one and one-half
Inches thick, mashed potatoes, salt,
pepper.
Wipe steak with a damp cloth.
Broil for about 10 minutes. Lay on
a hot plank. Pipe hot well-seasoned
mashed i>otatoes around. Put in the
oven until well heated, about 10
minutes. Garnish with parsley and
slices of lemon.
Margaret Grishman of Marshall,

Roast Beef and Dressing Balls.
Rib roast of beef, one-half loaf
stale bread, milk, seasonings.

dressing made as follows: Break
the bread into small pieces and
moisten with milk. Season with salt,
pepper, sage, and minced onion or
celery. Form into balls. Baste the
meat and dressing balls. Serve
roast on a platter surrounded by
the balls of dressing.

I BREAKFAST DISHES THAT TEMPT I
Breakfast strikes the keynote of
the day, and should, therefore, be
made as tempting, satisfying and
pleasant as possible. Start the day
with a well Ailed satisAed stomach
and you start the day with a smile
that will help you win success and
happiness.
Fruit, preferably orange juice,
should be served. Sliced peaches,
a bunch of grapes, a ripe juicy pear,
cantaloupe, or any other fruit in
season may be the first course of a
well planned breakfast.
A combination of eggs and bacon,
bacon and waffles, wheat cakes or
mush with marmalade, make tempt
ing, breakfast dishes. Puffy omelet
served with strips of bacon, while
poached eggs served on rounds of
toast garnished with bacon curls
will make hubby beam with delight.
Bacon with baked eggs is popular
especially during the fail and winter
months when hot breads are a part
of the morning meal. Put one and
one-half teaspoonfuls of milk or
cream in individual baking dishes,
break one egg in each. Springle
with salt and pepper and cover with
two slices of cooked bacon chopped
fine. Bake in a hot oven until the
eggs are set.
Scrambled Eggs and Bacon.
Two eggs, one teaspoon onion, cut
One; two slices bacon, cut fine; one
tablespoon green pepper (if de
sired) two tablespoons milk, one
third teaspoon salt, dash of paprika.
Beat the eggs, add the milk, salt
and paprika. Fry the chopped
bacon, pour off some of the drip
pings, then add the green pepper
and chopped onion. Cook a few
minutes before pouring in the beaten
chopped suet, ice cold water, one
teaspoon baking powder.
Filling.
One and one-half pounds round
steak, one-half beef kidney, two
tablespoons flour, one teaspoon salt,
one-third teaspoon pepper, cold
water.
Sift together the flour, salt and
baking ponder; add suet and
moisten with cold water. Cut off a
small piece of the dough and set it
aside. Roll the remainder out thin
ly and use to line a well-oiled bak
ing dish.
Prepare the meat by cutting it
into thin strips. Roll each of these
in the flour, salt, and pepper mixed
together; then roll up the strips of
meat putting a small piece of kid
ney in each portion. Pack these into
the pastry lined bowl, two-thirds
full of water. Wet the edges of fie
crust and cover with reserved crust
rolled out to fit the top of the bowl.
Tie a floured cloth over the top,
place in a sauce pan containing
enough boiling water to come
two-thirds of the way up the side of
the bowl and boil at least three
hours, adding more water as that
in the pan boils out. Turn out and
cut a hole in the crust and add one
cup water to form additional gravy.

business begins tomorrow.

are still living and nine grandchil
dren are now in the ranks.

Spring St., now Grand Ave., which

boy, Jacob.

versary sale.

ordinary day,” said Vincent Pace,
manager of the Milwaukee store.

SCRIMMAGE ON
U.W. PROGRAM
TOMORROW
By The United Frew.
MADlSON—Scrimmage is on the
program tomorrow for the Univer
sity of Wisconsin football squad
and, rain or shine, the football fans
will gather along the sidelines to
gather dope on this year's chances
for the Big Ten title.
Ten players, seven veterans and
three sophomores, appeared yester
day in the Cardinal jerseys which
coach George Little awards for pre
season accomplishments.
Punting Is Stressed.
With Shaw and Hall tossing
passes, Cameron, Bnrrus, Muegge
and Rose tried plucking them from
the air, while a squad of others at
tempted to prevent completion of
the aerial plays. Shaw also did
some flesky work snatching and
carrying passes.
“Red” Kreuz, veteran fullback,
and Van Horne, former fresh back
field player, did some punting under
the personal supervision of Little,
who stressed the importance of be
ing able to place the kick where
ever the booter desired. Other
backs, including Capt. Harmon,
Crofoot, Hall, Shaw, Rose and Mc-
Glveran. took turns in going down
under the punts along with the
ends and in returning them from
safety position.
Lieb Drills Linemen.
Linemen under Tom Lieb had a
long, tough session on the ground,
with the coach joining in the shov
ing and pushing to demonstrate his
ideas on line play.
A session on the tackling dummy
for both backs and linemen ended
the two-hour drill to which the
squad is limited since the opening
of the school term of the university.
ESTELLE THIES
NOT TO HEAR
BAD NEWS
FORT WAYNE, Ind.—Estelle
Taylor, who no longer is the wife
of a world’s heavyweight champion,
tried not to listen to newspaper men
who sought to tell her that her hus
band had lost the crown when she
passed through here last night en
route to join Jack Dempsey at
Philadelphia.
All curtains in her stateroom on
the Pennsylvania Limited had been
drawn and there was no response to
insistent knocking on her door while
the train paused here briefly.
There was no question but that
the screen actress knew what had
happened, however, as the shouts of
the reporters were so hearty they
aroused the entire car.
Estelle was due in Philadelphia
at 3 p. m. today.

TUNNEY WOULD
GIVE DEMPSEY
RETURN BOUT
PHILADELPHIA—Gene Tunney
said last night: “In advance of my
battle with Dempsey I determined
to fight in defense of my title as
soon as I had a reasonable rest. I
have promised Tex Rickard to meet
any opponent against whom the pub
lic wishes me to appear. If Demp
sey wants a return bout I think
he is entitled to it and I will tie
glad to meet him.
“Outside the ring we are good
friends and I have a high regard
for Jack personally.
“There was not a knockout. Of
course, I think there would have
been over a longer route, for I felt
I was growing better and Dempsey
weaker as the battle progressed. I
fought according to the plan I had
mapped out. Jack, however, may
think he is entitled to another
chance because neither of us was
flattened for the count, and that I
am willing to grant.
“Jack was game. He showed he
could take it. None of Lis blows to
the head hurt me. Several of his
body blows had a sting, but I did
not at any time feel any paralyzing
effect from them. Of course, I'm
very happy to be a champion.”

coal mine at Sedgeley, England,
which he works single handed. For

pit and worked it alone, his mine
being probably the only one in the
world that has never been inter
rupted by a strike.

NEW TITLE HOLDER WINS
10 ROUND FIGHT
WITH EASE
BY HENRY L. FARRELL.
Staff Correspondent The United Tress.
PHILADELPHIA —There is a new heavyweight cham
pion of the world.
Gene Tunney won the heavyweight championship of the
world and the richest prize in the sporting world when he
was awarded a 10-round decision over Jack Dempsey here
last night.
In these more modern days of the prize ring since Tex
Pickard started offering millions of dollars to fighters, it
has been the opinion of those close to the game that the
heavyweight title never would be passed on a decision.
But the title passed last night before a crowd of 130,000
spectators and there was not one voice of protest from the largest
crowd that ever saw an athletic event in the United States.
Eight Rounds to Tunney.
Tunney won eight of the 10 rounds by a mile- Two
might have been awarded to Dempsey only through the
countesy that might be conceded to a champion. If two
ham and eggers had been fighting the first -and fourth
rounds, in which Dempsey made his best showing, would
have been called even rounds. And they were the only
rounds in which Dempsey looked like the champion who
murdered Jess Willard, stopped Carpentier with ease and
outslugged Firpo in what the old timers called a “back
room fight.”
The Question first asked here to
’day was:
“Why did Dempsey lose?”
Those who thought that Dempsey
couldn't lose and who had bet 3 to
1 that he would retain the cham
pionsblp, recalled the fact that all
the race track money in New York
had been planted on Tunney to win
and that the fight was in the bag.
Not Dempsey of Old.
But any unprejudiced spectator
who saw the fight last night knows
that Dempsey lost because he wasn’t
the Dempsey of old and that he
wouldn’t have taken a dive for all
the money in the world.
A little tout from the New York
race tracks, who came up to the
press pit after the fight, offered in
typical language the solution of the
problem why did Dempsey lose?
when he said:
“Wait till Dempsey see’s his face
in glass in the morning. He’ll feel
worse than losing the championship,
because the wife is going to be in
town.”
Dempsey's friends know that he
had a pride in his title, and in the
statements made on his first trip
to England by some nobles that hb
looked more like an athlete than
ii prize fighter.
Dempsey didn't have the punch
nnd Tunney found, after the first
round, that he could take the cham
pion's best and he gained courage
nnd confidence round by round.
Dempsey Fights Foul.
In the fifth round Tunney started
marling at Dempsey and in the
’inches he began to out-wrestle and
out-rough Dempsey. The losing
champion committed fouls time after
time. He pulled rabbit punches and
Sidney blows that were barred by
the rules of the Pennsylvania com
mission, but Tunney didn’t com
plain or protest.
lie punched Dempsey out of the
clinches and countered him so
viciously that for the first time
since he has been the champion,
Dempsey smarted holding.
The description of the fight was
probably the easiest to write since
the old days of John L. Sullivan,
the original Jack Dempsey and Jack
McAuliffe.
Dempsey, as he always has fought,
tore into Tunney at every step of
every round but for the first time
cince Toledo, Dempsey found an op
ponent who could not he stopped
.with his right and left body punches.
Tunney was hurt several times
end was in danger as many times
but he always came back and was
forcing Dempsey back with punches
that didn’t knock him down but that
wore him down.
Gene Stands Test.
The actions of the passing cham
pion during the first few seconds
of each round after the first,
showed the way things were going.
Jack rushed, almost leaped, from
his corner at the first bell to carry
Tunney clear across the ring with
the momentum of his charge.
He looked like the Dempsey of
Toledo for a moment, and like a
real champion, he tore at his dial
longer. Jack landed on the chal
lenger’s jaw. Jack charged in again
and One slugged him on the chin.
Then Gene let loose with his right
fist thrice and Jack sought to jab
him away. But Gene was not go
ng away last night. He stood up to
"'Jack the man killer,” and in an
exchange of mighty blows the chal
lenger thudded either fist against
the champion’s jaw until Jack was
dizzy. Gene bled a bit from the
mouth and Jack seemed to be hurt,
lack’s round, perhaps, because of
aggressiveness, hut otherwise even.
The champion opened the show
hgaln in the second with another
rush, but Jack was missing and
Gone was hitting. A stiff blow to
The body moved the former marine
backward and Jack was on him in
an instant, only to be jarred away
by blows to the bead. Rain was
falling. Jack slammed his right to
Tunney’s body and it hurt. Gene
returned a blow^with each fist just
before the bell. Gene's round.
Champ Slowed Up.
In the third round the effect of
Gene’s punches had slowed the
champion. Rights and lefts ham
mered against Dempsey’s jaw and
«ttgg»red him. pene s round*
The fourth round may have been
Dempsey's. Jack had his rush with
him when he came out and landed
a right which unbalanced the chal
lenger. It hurt Gene and he
sought the comfort of distance
fighting, poking with his left to
keep Jack away. Thenceforth it
was Gene’s fight.
In the fifth the mauler was being
mauled. Gene began roughing it
with Dempsey.
Jack was still slower in the sixth,
seventh and eighth, although still
able from time to time to hurt Tun
ney with heavy blows to the body.

A veneer of new vitality covered

Dempsey Is Groggy’.
He came out apparently eager
and started a right too soon to

WHARF FIGHT
GAVE GENE
HIS START
NEW YORK—Greenwich Village,
known more for writers and artists
and fakirs than boxing celebrities,
contributed James Joseph Tunney.
He was born, the son of a long
shoreman, May 15, 1898, and
launched upon his pugilistic career
by accident rather than purpose.
Like many other children of New
York’s most famous neighborhood
he played on the wharves, went to
parochial school and got into boy
hood scraps.
It was one such scrap, defending
his personal rights, that started him
on his path to the championship
battle. He licked one Goo Goo De
laney and Goo Goo’s big brother
licked Tunney. Thus he took up
what is known as the manly art of
self-defense. He boxed in a Green
wish Village gymnasium and at
tended the fights of the old Na
tional Sporting club while he was
contributing to the family exchequer
from his employment as a freight
clerk of the Ocean Steamship Co.
at $22 a week.
Gene Joins Marines.
He won prestige in his neighbor
hood and finally earned a chance in
a preliminary bout at the Fairmont
A. C., where Billy Gibson was
matchmaker. His present manager
was not particularly impressed with
the stripling, who weighed 155 and
would not even leave his desk to see
him at the behest of Tunney’s
sponsor, who believed sincerely in
his protege.
It wasn't long after this that the
war started and Tunney joined the
marines. Athletic activities are, of
course, part of the service’s train
ing, and Tunney made an impres
sion as a boxer when he trained at
Quantico, Vs.
Tunney served overseas, and
after the armistice he boxed for the
benefit of the wounded In France.
This culminated in his winning the
light heavyweight title of the A. E.
F. in Pershing stadium in the in
terallied games.
Beaten By Greb.
His time earned him little when
he got back, so he set about grow
ing and developing himself system
atically into a full fledged heavy
weight. He has fought 61 battles
since the war. One he lost to Harry
Greb, and another left a smudge
upon his otherwise worthy record.
In 1922 he and Jack Renault were
ordered from the ring in Philadel
phia for “not trying.”
His claim to honors is based upon
his conquests of Tommy Gibbons,
Bartley Madden, and Georggs Car
pentier, chiefly his knockout of
Tommy Gibbons who went 15 rounds
with Dempsey in Shelby.
Tunney Different Champ.
Meantime, he had added a new
personality to the list of boxers
Jack Dempsey has met. Georges
Carpentier, a Frenchman; Luis bir
po, the Wild Bull of the Pampus,
each had their place in the public
imagination, much for the char
acterizations applied to them. Tun
ney, as if marked by the atmosphere
of his native Greenwich Village, ap
pears in the limelight as a studious
person who rolls off long sentences
and mental attitudes.
However, Tunney’s simplicity and
sincerity are contained in his own
story of how he obtained the name
Gene. A baby sister had trouble
saying bls given name. Jim. and so
his ring name became Gene Tunney.

Gordon McComas found his call
upon Diane something of an irri
tation and he rebuked her with
bis eyes when he took his de
parture early in the evening. For
when McComas arrived Diane had
ingeniously shooed the entire Col
fax family to the veranda, and
when either Mother or Father
made half-hearted preparations to
withdraw and leave her with her
visitor she protested with con
vincing energy.
“I don’t believe Mr. McComas
enjoyed talking to Dad about
credits and risks,” mused Diane’s
mother as she watched McComas
disappearing down the street.
“You didn’t put yourself out much
to eatertain him.”
“Is ho supposed to be courting
me?” Done demanded tartly. “If
he is, he may save himself the
bother. McComas rather bores
ine, Mother.”
And with this Diane withdrew
to her room, where, for an hour,
before she finally dropped off to
sleep, she reflected upon the ador
able cowlick spang in the center
of Phil Osborne’s forehead. That’s
how much McComas counted now
with Diane.
But Mrs. Colfax did not find it
so easy to dismiss this strong, im
pressive young man from her
thoughts and hazy half-formed
calculations. In the privacy of
their bedroom, after the lights had
been snapped off and Judson Col
fax had buried his head in the
grateful bosom of his pillow, she
meditated upon what she consid
ered her daughter’s strange per
versity.
“Sometimes I think Diane is not
like other girls,” she said to her
husband.
“That’s an original idea for a
mother to hold,” was hia muffled
rejoinder.
"Don’t be sarcastic, Jud. I’m
really worried about Diane. I
don't think she takes the proper
interest in these nice fellows who,
you can see with half an eye, are
seriously interested in her.”
Father yawned noisily and set
tled himself more comfortable.
“Don’t worry about Diane. She’s
only a kid yet. If she was the
kind of girl who goes crazy every
time a new man smiles at her
you’d have cause to worry.” A
tentative pause. “Diane Is an in
telligent girl and her head sits
mighty straight on her shoulders.”
Another pause. “She gets that
from me.”
Mrs. Colfax deigned no reply to
this beyond a genteel snort.
The Colfax clan slept.

The next day the news of the
arrival of Capt. Jean D’Armand
saturated the whole fabric of the
city. Small boys played hooky to
haunt the old Arena building
which had been chosen to house
the riding association’s venture,
which was considered the most
fashionable European diversion.
More than a dozen beautiful ani
mals with satin coats and fas
tidious footing were on view to
these privileged spectators. Two
flunkeys were tremendously busy
forking enormous piles of tanbark
evenly upon the surface of the rid
ing ring, and its acrid scent
stirred the passions of passersby
as the odor of sawdust inflames
the heart and soul of the visitor
to an old-fashioned circus. So far
in the proceedings, however, the
figure of Capt. Jean D’Armand
had not projected itself upon the
scene. Perhaps like a true artist,
he held himself in reserve to make
his entrance against a fitting
background and before an impor
tant audience.
News of all this was brought to
the dinner table of the Colfaxs
that night and eager ears awaited.
“It’s going to be a great suc
cess.” declared Mr. Colfax, judici
ously, selecting a maraschino
cherry from the colorful fruit
salad which was the tour de force
of the meal. “It means something
to the bank, too.”

their slick policy and pay honest
ly for the service pupil nurses
render in the two or three years

more like the Chinese chop suey.

THE GAME OF DIMINISHING.
One mother says:
This is a simple campfire or
bedtime game that is instructive
and that children of various ages
can enjoy together. The leader
starts with a word such as “cen
tury” and the child next to him
must diminish it by saying
“year.” The next says “month,”
the next “fortnight," “week.”
“day,” etc., down to “second.” If
a diminisher is omitted, the one
who sees the mistake and corrcts
it has an extra turn. The new
cycle is started by the child who
completes the last. “Forest, grove,
tree, limb, bough, branch, twig,”
would be an example, and “house,
barn, garage, shed, chicken
house, dog-kennel,' doll-house,”
another.
