SKIRTS, HAIR, TO
REMAIN SHORT,
SAYS PARIS
“For months French styles have
been returning to more ‘feminine’
things and the new season’s modes
will continue the trend,” declares
Anne Rittenhouse, acknowledged in
ternatioual style authority, in Mc-
Call's for October. Here is her de
scription of what we are to wear,
as Indicated by McCall's Taris rep
resentatives
"Again our frocks flutter in the
breeze. The fashionable woman
is slimly contoured, but the differ
ence lies in a subtly introduced full
ness. Paris having determined on
this silhouette, we should take care
to follow it. Skirts are full enough
to run in, which is a comfortable
thought. Hopeful prophets who
said skirts and hair would be
longer this fall missed their guess.
Both keep short. That is the fash
ion no matter what each individual
may choose. Jenny breaks the skirt
line with circular flounces at the
back or petal panels in front. Pa
tou adds flaring tunics and a soft
draped collar. Ruffles and jabots
further break the lines.
"The openings in Faris convince
us that pleats are to remain. The
American dressmakers have count
ed 15 different kinds that can be
used on skirts alone. The new
gowns seem to put emphasis on fine
knife pleats and wide box pleats.
Both go to extremes in size.
"Further to decorate our frocks,
Paris sends us models like these
with bows in front and girdles
that swathe the hip. This trick of
fashion serves to flatten the hip line
so the stout may have no fears.
Worth’s new ensemble copies the
prevailing beach costume. Its
blouse is belted to a pleated skirt.
Jenny uses the gypsy girdle. Many
new models feature the smart
bloused silhouette. It is the verdict
from Paris that if a frock cut in
one piece has something to break
the line at the hip, it is smart. The
new tendency as evidenced at the
Paris openings is to try to keep the
two-piece sports frock for country
wear.
“The severe neckline without a
touch of relieving while has gone
in partial eclipse. It has become
more important to frame the neck
line with becoming collars. White
is used in great abundance in every
thing, from chiffon to satin. The
softer the fabric, the softer the ef
fect.
"The effort to achieve movement
in new frocks is so persistent that
Paris has created cloud-like dra
peries to wear in the evening. It is
a most artistic idea, and a very
feminine one. These frocks nre
built of cloudHke fabrics that cling
in slenderizing folds. Chiffon and
georgette, triple voile and mousse
line de sole are so light and airy
they swing with every movement.
Wing draperies and the scarf, petal
tunics and flounces, float about us
in a riot of loveliness.”

CAN MUSSOLINI
NATIONALIZE
STYLES?
BY HEDDA HOYT.
Written for The I nited Preus,
NEW YORK—Stylists are won
dering whether the Italian women
will accept the nunlike dresses
which Premier Mussolini suggests
in his newly-formed League of Na
tionalization of Women’s Clothes.
The league. which Is headed by the
Italian queen, sponsors dresses
which will protect Italian women
from the "immodesty” of modern
times.
The kowns accepted by the league
cover the figure from neck to hem
and they have sufficient width to
conceal the outlines of the body.
This movement for Italian-made
clothes for Italian women has cre
ated quite a furor in the fashion
centers of Paris, London and New
York. The better class of Italian
women have heretofore found
French styles much to their liking
and it is very doubtful whether they
will accept a national uniformity of
dress. Poorer may find the new
mode economical and practical and
may accept Mussolini’s command.
Some of the French countries are
already turning out French gowns
of Italian inspiration to meet the
situation in Italy. This may mean
that before long we shall have
Italian designs and colors in Amer
ica. When Russian women gave irp
all thought of style after the Revo
lution we immediately turned tn
styles of pre-Revolution days in
Russia. For instance, wide sleeves
embroidered, tunics, high collars and
smocks were examples of Russian
influence.
It is very doubtful whether nnv
country where the smart women are
cosmopolitan will accept a national
mode of dressing. We have recently
witnessed the discarding of veils by
Turkish women. Many of them now
wear modern dress. Flappers of
China are growing up with unbound
feet and many of them wear bobbed
hair and modern frocks. In many
instances women nre at their best
when dressed in their native cos
tumes but one must travel far these
days to find a place where a mod
ern trend in dressing is not found.

FRANK WALSH
NAMED HEAD
OF WAR VETS
Frank A. Walsh, 2601 Cedar St.,
elected commander in chief of the
Grand Army of the Republic late
yesterday in the GOth annual en
campment in Des Moines, la., has
the distinction of being the first
Wisconsin man who hns held the of
fice since Col. A. G. M eissert was
elected in 1888.
Mr. Walsh was opposed by candi
dates representing four other states
and Washington, D. C.
Lived Here 44 Years.
Mr. Walsh has been active in state
and national veterans’ organizations
throughout the greater part of his
life and has been mentioned promi
nently for national commander for
25 years. He was born in East
Greenwich, R. 1., July 9, 1849.
He hns been a resident of Mil
waukee 44 years, bringing the Walsh
Canning Machinery Co. here in 1882,
which he founded in Chicago in
1878. In 1901 the company was eon
■olidated with the American Can
Co. and was moved to Chicago. Mr.
Walsh retired in 1903. but retained
an Interest in the business.
Was Senior Vice-Commander.
Mr. Walsh was mustered in E. B.
Wolcott Post No. 1, G. A. R., Aug.
23, 1889. and was elected senior
vice-commander of the post in 1899,
commander in 1903, inspetcor in
1908 and department commander of
Wisconsin in 1910.
He was appointed inspector gen
eral at the national encampment at
Washington in 1902 and received a
vote of thanks for his efficient serv
ice and splendid report at the ex
piration of his term of office.
In 1923 Mr. Walsh was elected
senior vice-commander of the na
tional G. A. R. In the encampment
in Milwaukee.
Talk Disbandment
Of Grand Army
BY I. I. FEMRITE.
Staff Correspondent
Th« United Press
DES MOINES—The specter of
disbandment was present today at
the final session of the 192 G G. A.
R. reunion.
The band of ex-soldiers, who in
their youth fought the war of the
rebellion, now is reduced to a f *w
thousand white-haired and greatly
feebled old men. Many are unable
to march in the annual review—the
peak of every G. A. R. encampment.
Each year of late has seen the
ranks of the veterans thinning.
Each year has seen the march in
front of the commander a little less
animated.
This year there was outspoken
talk of disbanding the G. A. R.
There was opposition, however,
from the younger of the veterans,
one of whom said “we have at least
eight years left for meetings.”

THEORY VERSUS PRACTICE
C. W. Barron, financial expert and owner of the lead
ing financial papers in the United States, the other day
told a New England textile lord that decreased production,
lower wages and poverty are not the right way to build up
the textile industry.
“I believe,” he said, “that full employment can be
had within our own country with full consumption, and
lam not a great believer in foreign markets. The United
States is becoming a law, indeed a planet, unto itself.”
The textile industry does not need more capital, but
more brains, Barron added, pointing out that a concern
like the Amoskeag mills has more than $25,000,000 of
government bonds in its treasury.
The report did not state what the textile lord, thus
attacked on the score of insufficient brains, replied to
Barron. He would have had a good enough come-back
by telling Barron that it is easy for the big bankers to
talk, who make 16 per cent profit on every unit of their
investments compared to the manufacturers’ 8 per cent.
And he might have pointed out that one of the main
reasons for the slump in the world market is the wildcat
speculation of the big bankers in dollar diplomacy, which
wastes a lot of American capital in foreign adventures
while advising the manufacturers to neglect foreign
markets.
It is a general human failing to see the splinter in
the other fellow’s eye, but to deny the beam in one’s own.
The banker can see where the manufacturer could use
more brains and less money, and the manufacturer can
give tit for tat to the banker, but both of them refuse to
see that they are hurting themselves and the whole na
tion most by robbing the pockets of the farmer and wage
worker.
If the bank employes tried to take Barron at his word
and to make an organized demand for higher wages, would
he make his practice fit the theory which he recommends
to the manufacturer?
If the farmers acted on his advice and demanded di
rect farm loans without any rake-off to private bankers,
would he say: Amen?
And the farmers themselves, will they realize that
high wages for the city workers and farm laborers are
the foundations of farm prosperity?
THE GREAT CRIME OF 1919
A national survey of conditions under Volsteadism
in the last five years stamps the ratification of the 18th
amendment on Jan. 16, 1919, as the great American war
crime committed against the American people.
This survey, published by The Moderation League,
is based upon authentic police figures. It shows a steady
increase of drunkenness, crimes of carelessness, lawless
ness under Volsteadism.
The report of The Moderation League concludes that
the Volstead act “has failed utterly to do what it was in
tended to do, namely promote temperance and sobriety.
Moreover, since conditions have become worse, not better,
each year with the ‘next generation’ drinking as never be
fore, there seems to be no hope that the Volstead act in
Its present drastic form, can ever accomplish its purpose.”
To this just judgment we add that in our opinion the
hidden mind back of Volsteadism never intended this act
to work for temperance, but merely used sentimental
morality phrases to give the national executive unwise
powers and to enable the party in power to increase its
own machine gang at the public trough.
EMBARRASSED WORLD COURTERS
President Coolidge seeks to hide his embarrassment
over the hedging of the league of nations on the fifth
American world court reservation by a standpat posture
md a threat to withdraw, unless the European powers ac
;ept the whole American attitude.
This threat may make some impression on the Euro
peans who have their eyes on the American pocketbook,
but it will not convince the American majority which has
roted against the league and the world court.
Coolidge cannot get out of embarrassment by such
gestures. The mere fact that the league considers whether
it wants to accept the American reservations to the world
:ourt shows that the world court is a part of the league.
If this were not enough, the speeches of the league
members emphasize it sufficiently, for all of them insist
that the world court was created by the league, is main
tained by it, and must remain a part of it.
The president’s dilemma is further increased by the
fact that if his lame duck senate does not dispose cf the
matter before adjournment in March, 1927. the next sen
ate in the fail of 1927 will bury it.

A MOVEMENT OF GREAT PROMISE
At this moment, the great promise of mankind is in
that despised proletarian, Socialist or Social-Democratic,
movement which is rising everywhere in strength, youth
ful power, vigor of new ideals, and clear-toned assertion of
a demand for the abolition of all classes, the giving of all
sources of life into the keeping of society, and the provid
ing for all who live the means of a decent life. It is one
of the very greatest movements the world has ever seen,
and, though only a half-century old, makes old thrones
tremble, old customs hide their head, old ideals fear so?
their existence, and old tyrannies take their flight The
rising up of the w’orking-class to conceptions the noblest
and most far-reaching men have ever devised is a magnifi
cent spectacle, the most inspiring, and, of all the world
now offers, the most promising for the future.
I am sometimes inclined to criticize Socialism severely,
to dwell upon its faults, to condemn its spirit of class
antagonism, to call in question its theoretical develop
ment; but when I contemplate this great movement in
its actual accomplishments, and in its promise for the
future, I can but bow down before it in unrestrained
admiration and approval. It is a glorious tribute to the
capacities of the toilers of all countries to realize in
mass action, some of the loftiest ideals and results of
combined efforts the world has recorded on the pages
of history. In the moments when I most worthily realize
what this movement is, and what it means for the coming
ages, I no longer see its limitations, and I forget its de
fects, in my joy of its promises of peace, fellowship and
common social action.
In such moments all criticism of its class-hatred and
antagonism seems petty and contemptible, quite unworthy
of thinking men and women. I cannot forget that intel
lectual and aristocratic Rome looked on in like spirit when
Christianity was rising out of the dregs of society to the
conquest of the empire and all the lands it held under its
control. When I forget the seeming defects in the Social-
Democracy, I am glad to turn to its demand for an inter
national unity of the working classes of the world, as the
basis of the realization of peace and unity amongst all
nations. Its demand for the abolition of all wars aj sav
age, cruel and unnecessary, meets with my entire approval.
This despised Social-Democracy has already done more to
banish from civilized countries the barbarism of the duello
between nations, than all The Hague conferences and
peace societies which the modern world nas produced. If
I am not mistaken in my reading of current events, it
promises today the only real assurance for the abolition
of the degrading spectacle of great nations settling their
differences by resort to arms.
Then again, Social-Democracy makes war on pov
erty, which it assures us ought not to exist, and need not
exist if we will to abolish it from our midst. The very
conception that ever-present poverty is unnecessary, and
can be put away by methods we clearly understand,
methods sanctioned by all social science, is one to inspire
confidence and co-operation on the part of every one who
wishes well to mankind.
The only party in the world w r hich has dared to stand
forth to assure to women equal rights with men in all
directions is this same despised Social-Democracy. Other
parties may make the same promises, but this is the only
one which everywhere and always stands by its conviction,
that women should be recognized and lifted up to the
place where they belong.
I may confess to an ever-growing admiration for the
democracy of the toilers, who labor with the ideal of the
common good before them, and like Atlas, carry the world
of reform and progress on their shoulders. lam assured
that these men have before them only their own advantage,
the bringing of more wealth into their own store; but
even if it were so, -what a vast change and Ad^ic* from
the old time when the worker dared not to look up or to
ask for anything for himself. I do not find it true, how
ever, that the Social-Democracy is concerned only for
individual advantage, and merely for more of the loaves
and fishes out of the world's store. On the contrary, J
find self-sacrifice, large conceptions of the social proce^ c
and eagerness to toil that others may reap the advantage
in the days to come, w’hich I find nowhere else in the same
measure.
As in the days of old, out of the company of the de
spised and outcast, a new world is in the process of being 1
born, a w’orld fairer and richer than any we have known
before. It is out of no enthusiasm, but out of a study of
society, an earnest inquiry into its forces making for prog
ress, that comes this conviction of mine. I stand gladly
with the new movement, for out of it I am confident will
come things rich with hope and joy of mankind. The very
fact that many millions of men and women have been
gathered solidly together to further this new ideal, this
fresh conception of life and its social processes, gives as
surance that what they desire will be realized through
their loyalty and devotion to the democratic demand.—
George Willis Cooke.

We read in the papers of a proposed measure of the
Mexican government which “would be more harmful to
American interests in Mexico than the alien land and pe
troleum law’s,” which have aroused so much indignation in
the breasts of Washington. What is this bill, about which
we are now expected to get excited as conflicting with our
interests? Its main features are enforcement of the eight
hour day and adequate workmen’s compensation, a mini
mum w’age to be determined by workers’ committees, a
share in profits or a fixed bonus for workers, and author
ity for union committees to examine employers’ books and
fix the amounts of profits to be divided. The bill is de
manded by Mexican organized labor.
If you, Brother Union Man, think that your interests
are endangered by improved conditions for Mexican work
ers and the strengthening of their labor movement, you
w’ill w’ave the flag and join the hue and cry for a “stern
attitude” in dealing w r ith Mexico. But if you are sane, you
will tell those who holler about “American interests” in
Mexico to go to, and w’ill look to your ow r n interests by
standing by the Mexican workers.—The Illinois Miner.

Chinese warfare.

“A company of young monkeys were taken to
a secluded hut, where the trainer was the only
human being they saw. Before the hut were
little flags of different colors—red, blue, and
yellow. They were fastened to little sticks that
were thrust into the ground.
“The training began by tying a cord round
the reck of a monkey, so that it could not escape
from the trainer. The creature was allowed to
run out to the flags, where its naturally mis
chievous disposition made it seize a flag and
carry it back to the hut. If the monkey was be
ing trained against an enemy blue flag he was
petted and fed when he brought back a flag of
that color; if he brought back a flag of a differ
ent color he was punished.
“As the training proceeded the monkey made
no mistake, and, shrieking fiercely, would eagerly
bring in a flag of a certain color. After a time
the cord was removed, and a monkey would bring
in the right flag from rs distance of two miles or
more.

Shoes of Topmost Importance in Woman’s Get-Up
Some Women Wish for Simpler Shoes, But They Wish
in Vain.—Russian Boot, Only Sort of High Shoe
Seen Nowadays, Not Much Worn in This Country.—
Oxfords Chosen for Serviceable Shoe.—Feet Look
Slender, and Shoemakers Are Skillful in Devising
Ways of Minimizing Foot’s Size. —Navy Blue Shoes
Are Worn With Matching Frocks.—Straps Are
Placed in Comfortable Position on New Shoes.
By Mary Marshall
BUYING shoes today is as interesting and complicated a busi
ness as buying hats. At the smart shops where shoes are
made to order there is a bewildering array of colored kids,
luxurious brocades and new and curious trimming devices. There
are women who would welcome back an era of simpler shoes.
They cling to the old feeling that, however striking one’s frock
or hat may be, good taste calls for inconspicuous shoes. But
this surely is a minority opinion. However, you may be as
simply shod as you like and still be in the picture. Some women
are choosing simple slippers—sans straps or buckle —in colored
kid for evening. With black patent leather for afternoon.
What we Americans caMd “high
shoes” and our English cousins
spoke of as their “boots’* have en
tirely passed from the stage. To
be sure you find them in some of
the shoe shops—kept there for the
benefit of older women, who feel
some prejudice or other against the
lower type of shoe. They fear they
will catch cold on chilly days if
they wear low shoes or that they
will sprain their ankles if they at
tempt to walk much without some
only fear that they will sacrifice
slenderness of ankles if they wear
low shoes or slippers all day long.
Anyway they want to wear high
shoes despite the present fashions
and so high shoes persist, in some
of the shops.
Russian Boots
From the point of view of fash
ion, the only sort of high footwear
fa the Russian or Wellington boot.
For some reason or other this has
never been generaly esteemed here
in America. You may have heard
women refer to it as rather com
monpace. But commonplace it cer
tainly never has been in this coun
try because it has not been worn
enough for that. Perhaps in mat
ters of taste in dress we are tem
peramentally nearer Paris than
London. In London the Wellington
boot has enjoyed immense favor.
In France it has never been re
ceived with much enthusiasm. The
French woman explains that this is
because she adores fine stockings
and shapely ankles and hates to
hide them. Stil you know very
well that there are women in Paris
who habitually wear substantial
cotton stockings and have indiffer
ent ankles who wouldn't want to
wear a Welington boot.
Black Satin Oxfords
Black satin oxfords were worn
by a number of smart Parisians at
the races this summer but the
fashion was not spread You would
have had difficulty in finding a
shoe of this type ready made at
any of the shoe shops in Parts.
Women who followed this fashion
apparenty had them made to order.
There are a number of oxfords
among the new shoes for autumn.
But It Is as a serviceable sort of
shoe that the oxford seems to find
favor. American women will choose
it to accompany their tailored
street coetumes rather than for the
more formal sort of afternoon wear.
You may have heard that heels
were going to be lower. Possibly—
but it seems much more probable
that women who have been wear
ing moderate heels will go on wear
ing them, while those who have
become accustomed to the higher
sort will stick to them. Fortunate
ly there is very little inclination
even on the part of the school and
college girl to wear the extremely
fiat sport heel—save for actual
sports wear.
Our feet must follow the fashion
of our figures—and appear to be
slender even when they are not.
The **svelt silhouette” is as impor
tant in the cut of shoes as it is in
the cut of frocks and wraps. But
mere skinniness is no more to be
desired in feet than in body. There
rust be a graceful contour withal.
Shoes Seem Slender
To the end of attaining the
affect of such graceful slenderness
the shoemakers have shown great
Ingenuity in the fashioning of the
new shoes. The extremely pointed
last has been discarded because
after all thia does not produce just
the result we desire. It accentuates
the breadth of the middle of the
toot and adds much additional
length. The very long foot even
when slender has never been espe
cially admired in Paris and the
ornamentation of many of the new
shoes copied from French models
Is placed across the lower part of
the instep in a way that detracts
from the length of the foot without
making it look chubby. The ex
tremely low-cut vamp is no longer
characteristic of French shoes —the
vamp section is fairly long but it
curves gracefully to the instep and
tn that way eliminates the effect of
flatness.
Whether shoes should match the
frock or not —this is a question that
has been much discussed by fash
ion observers. Shoes of beige or
gray with stockings to match are
still worn with frocks of other
colors by well-dressed women, but
many women are following the
fashion of having shoes exactly
matching the frock. For the navy
blue costume you will find charming
navy blue shoes —and there is no
longer anything extreme in their
appearance. There are shoes of
various shades of mauve for the
convenience of the woman who has
an afternoon frock of this color.
You will find that the straps on
new strap-pumps are quite narrow
and even when there are two of
them they are placed both rather
high—toward the ankle. The strap
that crosses over the full part of
the Instep is as rare now as it. was
usually uncomfortable.
SLENDER ANKLES FOR ALL
PARIS
Slender ankles are now within
the reach of all —without the
discomfort of dieting or exercis
ing. The device is very simple.
The would-be slender plump
woman simply dons a pair of the
new stockings Invented by some
clever Frenchman. and presto!
her ankles are as slender as
those of any classic dancer.
These stockings are cleverly
painted so that the effect of
shadow appears in the region of
the ankles, giving the effect of
tapering contour.
Great strides have been made
in the making of apparel for
stout women since the war.
Some people say this is directly
due to the war when the cam
ouflage artists made a thorough
study of the art of optical
illusion.

on their toes, ready to dash toward
the center. As the last note sound
ed, they made a concerted rush—
that is, all except the Sophomores,
who hovered back awaiting Bob
Manley’s signal. The other three
factions met with a clash that
echoed through the Quadrangle—a
clash that must have sounded sim
ilar to that of listing knights in
the days of King Arthur’s court.
The battle was on. Freshman
against Senior, Senior against Jun
ior, pushing and scrambling and
shouting with glee. Still Bob Man
ley’s Sophomores held back, though
they were aching to get into the
fray.
Soon there was such a mix-up on
the field that one hardly knew the
other. It was then that Bob gave
the much-wanted signal. A solid
mass of boys, with a 150-pounder
as the point of the wedge, came
hurling its way toward the center,
cutting sharply through those w’ho
blocked its way. In its center, not
using too much of his energy for
he knew he would need it all with
in the next few minutes, trotted
Bob, the Sophomore flag rolled and
tucked under his arm.
By this time the fight was so
general that few realized this
wedge was a concerted action. Op
ponents crumpled before the Soph
omores as they went on. Nearer
and nearer they came to the flag
pole.
If Bob had had the whole foot
ball team on his side, victory would
have been simple. As it was, he
fought without the power of his
teammates. Close to the flagpole,
where the most feverish fighting
centered, was Steve Waters, a star
football player and a boy familiar
with quick thinking. He saw the
flying wedge as it battered its way
closer, and saw, too, the victory
that seemed imminent for the
Sophomores.
“Rally, Seniors! Bust up the
wedge!” he cried. “Tear it to
pieces.” A little group of Seniors
rallied around him, hurling against
the oncoming group—slowing them
up a trifle. But still they ad
vanced, intent on squirming their
way around the staff, and forming
a guard for Bob Manley.
Summoning all his strength,
Steve Waters rushed at the wedge,
having strategy enough to hit it
on the side, instead of in front
It gave way, and he found himself
in the center, close to Bob. “Ho,
my buck-o,” he breathed, and
lunged at Bob to tackle him. But
Bob saw an opening on the other
side; he sidestepped, and reached
the flagstaff.
It was his chance to climb with
his flag. Suddenly he felt a pair
of arms seize him. Roughly, he
threw them off, and turning his
head to see who had attempted to
stop him, looked into the face of
“Dude” Rimley. And in that brief
moment, an expression of pain
spread over “Dude’s” face, and
screaming once, as though in mor
tal agony, the boy Bank to the
ground.

This Turtle Is “Picky”
“Billy Bowlegs” is a turtle who
lives with Pam Wolfe of Salt Lake
City, Utah. He is called Billy for
short. Pam claims that he is un
usually intelligent. When he is
fed, he will only eat what he likes
and will not touch any food he
does not care for. In order to be
taken out of his bowl of water,
Billy swims around the bowl three
or four times and then stops in
front of Pam and pokes out his
head from underneath his hard
shell coat. Pam says that when
ever Billy gives this little per
formance, it is a signal that he
wants to get out of the bowl and
crawl around on the floor. After
walking around the room a couple
of times, he will crawl into a cor
ner where there is little light and
take a nap.

A Spitz That Likes Ice Cream
Marie Wilkinson of Poelton,
Tennessee, has a white Spitz dog
for her pet. His name is “Ponta”
and he is two and one-half years
old. He is especially fond of
candy, ice cream, and oranges.
When he hears anyone pass by the
house, he will stand up on his hind
legs and walk to the fence to see
who it is. If he does not know the
passerby, he will bark and run
back and forth between the fence
and the house. He can do many
tricks. Marie says that he can
iump four feet into the air. Ponta
is a dandy pet and it is never
lonesome when he is around.

sideration the years he has
spent in perfecting his work.

hours he spend in keeping fit
—for the leader KEEPS FIT

the future success of each one
of us depends on the start wc
give ourselves NOW. Straight
thinking and, above all,
straight LIVING are just
as essential to US as to the
leaders we admire. Let’s
KEEP FIT ALL THE TIME!

Special to The Leader.
LONDON —The recent meeting of
the British trade union congress at
Bournemouth discussed among oth
er things the idea of One Big Union,
reports The Daily Herald.
The discussion turned on a resolu
tion of the National Union of Gen
eral and Municipal Workers, which
declared that existing craft unions
failed to meet the demands of mod
ern industrial concentration.
This resolution urged the con
gress “to approve every movement
to reduce the number of unions and
to discourage the formation of new
organizations, in order that the
amalgamation of kindred unions
should be continued with the object
of One Big Union being reached as
the ultimate goal of working class
organization.”
Quote Ford’s Example.
The mover of the resolution,
Dukes of Manchester, pointed to
Henry Ford’s control of 42 indus
tries and asked: Would the most
efficient way to barter with him
be by 42 unions? The line of ad
vance, he claimed, lay in the direc
tion of one big union.
An amendment to this resolution,
offered by Tomkins of London, sug
gested that the congress should ex
press regret at the little advance
made in the direction of industrial
unionism, and that it should instruct
the general council to call a confer
ence of the trade groups in order
to arrange for the merging of the
separate unions within these groups
into industrial unions.
Among those supporting the reso
lution was A. J. Cook, the secretary
of the British miners’ federation.
Want Scientific Strength.
“I want this conference to recog
nize that we have to meet science
with science,” Cook said. “We can
not do that unless we are scientifi
cally organize!. There can be no
united front unless we all unite.”
There were many of the older
and more cautious leaders, however,
who emphasized some of the diffi
culties which stood in the way of a
rapid realization of the one big
union.
Among these was Ernest Bevin,
of the General and Transport Work
ers. who said that this subject re

had learned by long experience that

ing organizations, and that it was
futile to try to destroy craft unions.

over t<» the general council for
study and recommendation. They
could not impose amalgamation from

CHICAGO—Mars, neighbor to the
world, again is to approach near to
our sphere, offering once more a
possible solution of that great
query: Are there living Martians?
Astronomers will dust off their
giant eye pieces Oct. 27, pointing
them at the tantalizing planet of
war, for then Mars will be dropping
by for a visit, a mere 42,600,000
miles from the world, according to
Prof. E. B. Frost, of the University
of Chicago’s Yerkes observatory.
Another field day of watchful
waiting will come on Nov. 4, for on
that day astronomical conditions in
the heavens will be ideal, I’rof.
Frost declares.
Will Tune In.
Radio scientists also will strive
to tune in on Mars, for in the fall
of 1924, when the planet cam^ the
closest in a century, numerous ra
dio listeners set the land agog with
the claim they had hoard strange
signals.
And from the housetops all may
see the great fiery red planet, glow
ing as the brightest orb in the fir
mament.
Although Mars will he some 7,100,-
000 miles farther away than in
1924, when 35,500,000 miles spanned
rhe gap between, observers in the
northern hemisphere will be blessed
with a better view, for it will ap
jtear north of the celestial equator
instead of south, as Jiefore.
No Hope for Life.
“Mars thus will be much higher
above the mists of the southern
horizon,” I’rof. Frost explained.
"The air should be more transparent
and more steady, so that the image
of the planet’s disk should tremble
Jess as a result of the atmospheric
waves.”
I’rof. Frost holds forth no hope of
animal life on the planet Mars.
I’rof. Schaer, in charge of the Jung
frau observatory in Switzerland,
however, says that two years ago
his telescope revealed conditions on
Mars which make habitation on the
planet possible.
A new apparatus for attachment
to the 40-inch telescope at the
Yerkes observatory at Williams
Bay, Wis.. which will photograph
the planet with a new color process,
now is being perfected by Prof.
Ross of the observatory.

LANE TRAFFIC ETIQUETTE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
Double lane traffic is a wonder
ful system for the motorist, but:
Why do some motorists persist in
making a right turn when they are
in the left traffic lane and a left
turn (where they are permitted)
when they are in the right lane?
Why do the traffic officers permit
this practice? It is obviously
hazardous and always results in a
tieup of the traffic flowing through
the intersection. I have noticed
that the practice is apparently
tolorated at Wells and West Water
Sts. and at State and 3rd Sts., two
of the most congested corners in
the city.
If a few motorists were forced to
go around the block when they get
into the wrong lane and attempt a
turn, the practice would soon be
abandoned.
Milwaukee. L. P. S.

this SI,OOO as a nest egg for next
year’s pageant,” Thomas M. Dun
can, executive secretary, pageant
committee, explained today.

Hartney of the Argonauts, the or
ganization sponsoring the flight, had
had been called as a witness.

charged that Capt. Rene Fonck was
incompetent to handle the plane.
Capt. Fonck was questioned by
Dist. Atty. Elvin Edwards, with
Robert C. Crete as interpreter.
Col. Hartney, in an affidavit, re
vealed that it was over his opposi
tion to Capt. Fonck as the pilot for
the ocean hop that lie resigned from
his office in the Argonauts.
“Irresponsibility” and “poor
pilotage” were the reasons he gave
for his stand against the French war
ace.
He charged also that when the Si
korsky taxied across Roosevelt field
the tail of the ship had not been
lifted, so that a take-off was imuos
sible.

IF WOMEN PROPOSE.
To the Editor of The Leader:
When ministers talk about the
falling off of marriages, it occurs to
me that the reason is not so much
that people do not wish to marry,
as the ministers assert, but that
they do not meet or recognize the
right mates.
Why not let women, as well as
men, propose? Women’s tendencies
toward bearing 50 per cent of life’s
burdens, should include 50 per cent
of life’s choice of mates.
Of course, there could be no more
assurance that the men to whom
women propose would accept them
than there now is that the women
to whom men propose will accept.
Women as well as men must be pre-'
pared to take that chance.
But at least there is ft chance
that the intuition and other qual
ities of acumen for which women
are famed, would have an effect
upon cutting down the work of the
divorce courts.
“Love is blind” has been an
axiom as long as man’s prerogative
to propose. Perhaps its truth would
be somewhat modified with women
on the proposing job. It is only
false pride that keeps women back.
They might, if they chose, establish
a custom that would make for good
to many and add myriads of happy
hearts.

PREDICT RECORD
The fourth Wisconsin redio ex
position opened today with exhibits
vaued at a half million dollars on
display.
The evening session again will be
opened by the Zinkepators who will
offer their concert at 7:30, followed
by the Radio Revue at 8:30, which

sisting of console radio receivers,
will be presented tonight. A prize
will be given away each evening,
and the grand prize will be given
on the closing night of the show.
Record attendance is predicted. The
exposition is sponsored by the Wis
consin Radio Trade Assn.
Consoles will predominate. Ac
cording to rumors that have crept
out, many of the 1926-27 models of
the best-known makes are of almost
entirely new design and are scarcely
recognizable as the familiar sets of
past seasons.
In spite of the fact that this
year's exposition is being held some
six weeks earlier than those of past
years, this does not in any way
affect the completeness of the ex
hibits. Whereas in past seasons
many of the new models did not
make their appearance until the
latter part of October or early in
Novemlier, this year manufacturers
have so advanced the season that
all of their new sets are ready for
exhibition.
WHA, University
Radio Station, Has
Been Reconditioned
MADlSON—Station WHA, radio
mouthpiece of the University of Wis"
consin. will go on the air Oct. 15
with improved equipment and pro
grams. after a summer quiet period
for rebuilding, Prof. E. M. Terry of
the physics department and Prof.
W. 11. Lighty, program director, an
nounced today.
The station equipment is being
completely rebuilt, Prof. Terry said.
Four new amplifiers, and a crystal
control frequency stabilizer are in
cluded in the new equipment.
The amplifiers, one on power, one
on intermediate power, one for the
studio, and one for out-of-studio
broadcasting, will be put into use
when the station reopens. Output
will be increased from 625 to 750
watts.
The new crystal control fre
quency stabilizer is being built in
the physics laboratories of the uni
versity.
Plan Ad Campaign

Dress Consciousness
PHILADELPHIA In a resolu
tion adopted yesterday at the con
vention of the National Association
of Clothiers and Furnishers, adver
tising to arouse “dress conscious
ness” in men was advocated.
The advertising campaign will be
coiiducted nationally and locally
“to eliminate slovenly habits of at
tire among men, and to make them
realize that neat, correct and fash
ionable attire is a great factor in
achieving success in life.”
J. Duncan Williams, Chicago, ad
dressing the convention, asserted
that the boy of today was stepping
out snappily in the matter of
clothes.
“The boy Is no longer distin
guished by the made over garments
of his father or big brother,” he
said. “It used to be thought the
boy had little to say in regard to
the suit selected for him. His
mother did the job and he wore
what was given him. Little atten
tion was paid to style or pattern.
But things are different today. The
boy has lots to say about the clothes
he wears and his preference is con
sidered by his parents.”

cans speak, but oddly enough do
not. And the result is so thin as to

is so characteristic of his manner,
of his bearing, that it became the
basis of an interview not long ago
at his home at Grove Lodge. Hemp

work, including the Forsyte Saga,
the most recent addition to which,
The Silver Spoon, is reviewed in

Old English, which George Arliss is

The interview is by Irma Kraft.
The man who wrote The Silver
Spoon has evolved a personal
philolophy. vastly interesting, which
is reflected in characters of his fic
tion and drama as widely different
as Lord Miltourn, Courtier Baba
and John Soams. But it is in the
person of the stoic, as George Ar
liss portrays him in Old English,
that one catches the clearest gleam
of that vast tolerance underlying
everything John Galsworthy does
or writes.
I had been asking why he did not
“do” the Forsyte Saga into drama.
He dreamed awhile and then olc
served:
“But this Saga can go on. as no
play does—on and on—as life it
self. There are things which lurk
only in printed pages—the qualities
which no one can inject into drama
—the tolerance which must animate
life.”
“And yet your Old English had
little tolerance with other people's
viewpoints 1”
“Right. In that lay Old English’s
failure. Because of his lack of tol
erance he could not understand his
daughter, his business associates
his friends—he could not pull him
self out of the morass which ended
him.”
“When you see things so very tol
erantly, doesn’t it Income increas
ingly difficult to take sides?”
“But must we take sides?” He
stared dreamily into the fire. “My
audiences would be far happier if
I settled things for them. But how
can I? Dare I or any one? The
l>est art can do is to present the
question and then leave it, gently to
its fate.”
“To do its own work?”
“Precisely. If it is well enough
presented, it will.”

Miss Hawthorne tells the story of
this new life in her usual free and
simple style—a style that is espe
cially adaptable to young people,
girls. Throughout the story it's the
girls who are most in evidence—the
boys seeming to be there chiefly to
lend color to the doings of and to

there is one) resembling one long
picnic, with dad and the princess
serving as safety valves to their

aura of pleasant mystery that keeps
one turning the pages, even should
the trivialities peculiar to children's
lives make for slight boredom. And
everything is rosy as the novel ends;

CHILD’S GIFT BOOKS.
Four Times Once Upon a Time. Ry
Margaret Baker. Published bv
I >uffield Co.
Irresistible in its covers of green
and tangerine, with each of its four
fairy tales imprinted upon pages of
its own color, Four Times Once
Upon a Time must surely please the
child both visually and audibly.
Lovely green pages like the deep
woods in midsummer, form the
background for the story about Bid
dy and Paddy O’Flannigan, the
moral of which is that dishes won't
wash themselves. Soft apricot
pages relate the doings of The
Broomstick. In addition, thqre is
a tangerine story of The Three Old
Wives, and a i>ower blue background
for a tale of The Lassie and the
Goblins.
Besides the colors which make
this one of the most interesting of
child's books, there are silhouette
illustrations which make every page
a surprise. The story runs along
one side and on the other side the
black and blue gnomes, or the black
and tangerine old ladies with their
big noses very big as they rock and
discuss who is the prettiest girl in
the village. The old donkey and
the black cat and the witch with
her dusting cloth look particularly
intriguing in black and apricot,
while silhouettes of little boys lean
ing against big tree trunks and gaz
ing at little people of the earth are
all the more fascinating against
deep forest green. The illustrations
are by Mary Baker, who does them
as though she were in spirit at least
a little girl herself.
Beside the appeal of the looks of
this book, there are the piled up ad
jectives and the repetitions so dear
to the child listener. The three
drops of cream for the third little
old lady, the two drops for the sec
ond and the one drop for the first
come up again and again whenever
the important function of sipping
tea accompanies their whispered
confidences.
Four Times Once Upon a Tima
would make a lovely gift book for
any child.

FIVE
DECIDE CANCER
NOT HEREDITARY
NOR CONTAGIOUS
LAKE MOIIONK. N. Y. When
the world’s recognized authorities
on the disense put into a single
Btatement all the basic knowledge
they have of the subject, an impor
tant weapon in combating cancer
wns mode ready for use yesterday.
The statement, regarded ns the
most important pronouncement on
cancer ever made, was adopted at
the closing session of the four-day
symposium on cancer control, which
was attended by more than 100 can
cer specialists of the United States
end several European countries.
"Although the present state of
knowledge of cancer is not suf
ficient to permit the formulation of
such procedures for the suppression
of this malady as have been success
fully employed for the suppression
of infectious diseases,” said the
statement, "there is enough well
established fact and sound working
opinion concerning the prevention,
diagnosis and treatment of cancer
to save many lives if this informa
tion is carried properly into effect.
Is Not Contagious.
"Although the causation of can
cer is not completely understood, it
may be accepted that for all prac
tical purposes cancer is not to be
looked upon as contagious or in
fectious.
"Cancer itself is not hereditary,
although a certain predisposition or
susceptibility to cancer is apparent
ly transmissable through inherit
once. This does not signify that be
cause one’s parent or parents or
other members of the family have
suffered from cancer, cancer will
necessarily appear in other persons
of the same or succeeding genera
tions.
"The control of cancer, so far as
this subject can be understood nt
the present time, depends upon the
employment of measures of personal
hygiene and certain preventative
ami curative measures, the success
of which depends upon the intelli
gent co-operation of patient and
physician.
Only One Cure.
"The cure of cancer depends upon
discovering the growth before it has
done irreparable injury to a vital
part of the body and before it has
spread to other parts. Therefore, ef
forts should be made to improve the
methods of diagnosis in these vari
ous locations and the treatment of
the cancers so discovered.
“The public must be taught the
earliest danger signals of cancer,
which can be recognized by persons
without a special knowledge of the
subject, and induced to seek com
petent medical attention when any
of these indications are believed to
be present
Three Methods Used.
“The most reliable forms of treat
ment, and, in fact, the only ones
thus far justified by experience and
observation, depend upon surgery,
radium and X-rays.
"Efforts toward the control of
cancer should be made in two prin
cipal directions, the promotion of
research in order to increase the ex
istent knowledge of the subject and
the practical employment of the in
formation which is at hand. Even
with our present knowledge many
lives could be saved which are sac
rificed to unnecessary delay.”
After a brief morning session the
specialists went to New York city,
where tonight they were the guests
of the American Society for the
Control of Cancer.

WORKERS STRIKE
Special to The Leader.
WAUKEGAN. 111. —One hundred
employes of the Garnert Roths
child, a tailoring company, are on
strike here as a result of the dis
missal by the company of 11 em
ployes who attempted a public meet
ing. The meeting was called to dis
cuss the advantages of organized
labor and was open to anyone in the
city. The next day five employes
who had attended the meeting, some
of them women, were discharged. A
protest meeting was then held, and
six other employes of the firm who
attended that meeting also were dis
charged. The company manufac
tures overcoats and topcoats for
Chicago firms. The strikers demand
reinstatement of the 11 employes
and recognition of the principle of
collective bargaining. The strike is
conducted by the Amalgamated
Clothing Workers of America. Maud
McCreery, of the Federated Press,
Is locally in charge.
Sues Apartment
House Owner for
Removal of Trees
Belief that Arthur Strauss Co.,
owners of the Devonshire apartment
house, are responsible for the re
moval of trees and shrubs that
formed a wall around the garden
in the rear of the Surf hotel, 130
Prospect Ave., has prompted Mrs.
Jeanette Nicholson, owner of the
Surf, to Institute a damage action
against the realty firm.
Mr. Strauss is said to have admit
ted that a gardener, under instruc
tions of the company, removed cer
tain trees and shrubs from the hotel
premisis. The action has been re
corded with Court Commissioner
James Stover, but the amount of
damages ‘o be asked has not been
determined, according to George
Ballhorn, attorney for the Surf.
The complainant charges that the
destruction ruined the property’s
commercial and artistic value and
th^t it will take 16 years to repair
the damage. The trees and shrubs
hid the North Western road tracks
'"which pass to the east of the prop
erty.
Atty. W. D. Corrigan
Weds Libby Miller
Marriage of Atty. W. D. Corri
gan, 50, and Miss Libby Miller, 452
Van Buren St., by Rabbi Samuel
Ilirshberg was revealed late yester
day.
The marriage, it is said, took
place several days ago, following
which the couple left Milwaukee
for a wedding trip.
Mendel Miller, father of the
bride; her brother, Samuel Miller.
Chicago, and two close friends of
the groom attended the ceremony.

at 177 14th St., is a member of the
law firm of Glicksman, Gold Cor
rigan. His bride for several years
has been proprietress of a public
stenographer's office in the Under
writers’ Exchange Bldg.
Bar Fixing Quiz
Dismissed; Charge
Hearsay, Judge Says
After six weeks inquiry into re
ports of activities of “fixers” for
saloonkeepers, bribery, misfeasance
in office of city ana county officials
and charges against the common
council license committee, Judge
Michael Blenski yesterday dismissed
the district court John Doe proceed
ings as groundless.
"After due and careful consider
ation of all of the testimony and
records presented to me, I find that
the charges were based on hearsay;
that they were groundless, and in
some instances malicious, and,that
there is not sufficient legal evi
dence on which a warrant should
issue.”
Electrical Body
Secretary Named
Subject to the approval of the
common council, Buildingrlnspector
W. D. Harper yesterday announced
the appointment of Archie Middle
mas as secretary of the electrical
license examining committee and at
the same time announced the reap
pointment of four members of the
committee for terms of four years
each.
The reappointments are for Allen
C. Schultz and William A. Rech,
representing citizens not engaged in
the electrical business: Edwin Herz
berg, representing the contractor
dealers, and Joseph Keating, repre
senting the union journeymen elec
tricians.
Their terms will expire May 17,
1928.

Date; Gets Divorce
Mark Goetzman, 34, electrician,
and his wife, Helen, 30, celebrat
ed their sixth wedding anniver
sary yesterday in the divorce
court of Circuit Judge John J.
Gregory.
Mrs. Goetzman was granted a
decree on a counterclaim, charg
ing cruel and inhuman treatment.
She told the court that her hus
band had been of a quarrelsome
disposition, had nagged and found
fault with her all the time.
They were married Sept. 24,
1919.

I PERFECT MALE
SOUGHT BY 125
DIOGENESSES
ST. LOUlS—Modern young men.
among other things, lack ambition,
courtesy, Christianity, energy and
respect for women. They care more
for jazz than the classics. All they
want of life is plenty of moonshine,
dancing and smoking.
At least that is the indictment of
the modern young male made by
125 St. Louis young women as re
ported bv Rev. A. E. Halter, pas
tor of the Salem M. E. church in
St. Louis.
The 125 young women who made
the investigation, Rev. Halter de
clares, were on the lookout for the
ambitious, good-looking, character
ful young fellow. Instead, the in
vestigators found “parlor puppies,”
most of whom were full of "gin and
deceit.”
"They even let the girls do the
wooing,” Rev. Halter reported one
feminine complainant as saying.
"And that,” said Rev. Halter, who
was inclined to agree with the girls,
“certainly is a mark of weakness.”

Certification of a list of eligibles

for a certification of eligibles at its
next meeting Friday night.”

chief, a new captain, to succeed the
one made chief, and a new lieuten
ant to succeed the captain.

of three eligibles certified.

m REAMS of C. C. Pyle about the possibility of open or professional
tennis in the United States will prove more of a nightmare to
the officials of the United States Lawn Tennis Assn, since Mary
K. Browne, former American champion, joined Mlle. Suzanne
Lenglen under Pyle’s management, writes 11. L. Farrell. The
thought behind the present deliberations of the association is not the
immediate effect of the desertion of the amateur ranks by two such
high ranking women players but the influence it will have on other stars,
especially if Pyle’s experiment proves a success.
“I have worked enough for tennis. Ix»t tennis work some for me.”
Mlle. Lenglen said when she accepted the offer to turn professional. Miss
Browne expressed the same feeling in almost the same words and if
other high ranking players decide to let tennis contribute openly to their
support, the big stadium at Forest Hills will have to be made available
for open or professional tennis or it will almost have to have a curtain
for movies.
When Pyle announced front Paris
that he had signed a contract with
Mlle. Lenglen, the association
laughed it off. “Where will she play
in the United States and against
whom will she play?” they asked.
When Pyle added the announce
ment that he would recruit a whole
team of players for an invasion of
the United States, the idea was
again ridiculed and a list of the
high ranking players that he could
not get was called.
Wut when the announcement fol
lowed that Miss Browne had decid
ed to turn professional, official ten
nis was horrified and refused to
comment. The intimation was of-'
sered that Miss Browne had been
too close to the game, its officials
and its best players to make any
kind of a statement that might of
fend her.
Pyle started something when he
got the idea that star tennis play
ers in the professional field could
make as much money for him and
for themselves as Red Grange did
on the football field. And it looks
now as if Pyle will be able to finish
what he started.
Amateur tennis in the United
States can offend Mlle. Lenglen, but
it cannot offend Miss Browne be
cause the tennis public thinks just
as much, if not more, of Mary
Browne than it thinks of the asso
ciation.

down in the books as one of the

chese brothers top the list of Badger

ors fear the husky Mattes, who has

MADISON, Wls.—Starting his
second year as athletic director and
bead football coach at the Univer
sity of Wisconsin, George E. Little
has gathered about him a high cali

er, who signed as assistant at

i

western athletic chiefs when he

paired, and there were those who

by beating Johnny Farrell, 6 and 5,
in the semi-finals yesterday, while
Diegel just barely won his semi-final
match from Johnny D. Golden of
Paterson by winning the final hole.

ST. LOUlS—(United Press)
Armistice day with all its noise, its
hilarity and its enthusiasm was re
enacted in St. Louis last night, not
in commemoration of the end of the
World war, but in celebration of the
end of the National league baseball
battle, an end which saw the St.
Louis Cardinals winners of the pen
nant for the first time and gave St.
Louis its first pennant in 38 years.
Traffic Demoralized.
Bedlam reigned in the streets
from the time the news was
flashed over the wires in the after
noon until late at night. Traffic
was demoralized. Impromptu par
ades were formed. Straw bats,
saved for the occasion, were de
stroyed by the hundreds.
Confetti, paper streamers and
even leaves from telephone books,
thrown In a drenching rain which
fell most of the evening, soon filled
downtown streets with an inch of
paper slush.
228,000 Phone Calls.
The Cardinals’ victory was
greeted by 228,000 .telephone calls,
swamping all of the city’s switch
boards^md making it necessary to
call in all operators who where off
duty.
Long distance calls doubled in
volume.
Many were for hotel reservations.
NEW YORK—Jolly Bogers Horns
by and his crack crew of Cardinals
from the state of excitement that is
known as St. Louis were on top of
the heap today.
Beating the Giants while the Reds
suffered defeat, the Cardinals won
their first pennant yesterday and
earned n chance to face, probably
the Yankees, for the championship
of the baseball world.
The victory climaxed the most
closely contested race the old major
circuit has ever known. The contest
was so hot that at one time any
one of six clubs could have stepped
out in front.
A couple of ex-sandlotters, one of
whom John McGraw appraised as
“not strong enough” for his team
last spring when he traded him to
the Cardinals, showed veterans how
strong they were and led the card
sluggers to victory from a three run
handicap.
The heroes were George Toporcer,
who never got a chance in his home
town, and Billy Southworth, former
Giant outfielder.
Homer Wins Game.
Toporcer came to bat as a pinch
hitter in the second inning and ham
mered out a two base hit with two
men were on, to tie a three-run lead.
Then came Billy. He slammed out a
long home run to score Toporcer,
and that headed the Giants. This
from a couple of “boys not strong
enough”—McGraw's own words, for
his vaunted team of Giants.
The boys were so happy today It
was whispered Jolly Bogers was
going to hire an aggregation of cro
quet players to go down to Cincin
nati to play the closing game of the
season with the Reds, who lost all
chance when they dropped one game
of i double bill. Hornsby wants
to save his regulars for the series.
That’s where his mind is now.

GALSWORTHY’S OLD SINNER LIVES
THROUGH ART OF ENGLISH STAR
George Arliss appears in W’in
throp Ames’ production of John
Galsworthy's Old English at the
Davidson theater for one week only,
beginning Monday night. As Syl
vanus Heythrop, the rare old sinner,
Mr. Arliss seems to have made even
a greater appeal to popular favor
than in his famous Disraeli, and the
Rajah of Rukh in The Green God
dess, or in Alexander Hamilton, in
which he last appeared in Mil
waukee.
Old English shows Sylvanus Hey
thorp, octogenarian shipowner, a
staunch, alert, shrewd, unscrupulous
fellow, about to reap the tares he
has sown in his own garden. Prizing
independence above all things in life,
he sees his freedom threatened and
he makes an heroic effort to save
himself. He has two grandchildren,
acquired “under the rose,” whom he
tenderly loves. To provide for their
future he enters upon a somewhat
dubious scheme. A pagan at heart,
he has lived freely and fully. When
the end arrives he faces it as in
evitable, without self-pity, with un
repentant soul. The banquet scene
which closes the play, and shows
Old English dining in solitary gran
due r, already has become a classic
in the record of great acting in the
English-speaking theater.
Irby Marshal, a prominent Aus
tralian actress, is leading woman
for Mr. Arliss. In the company are
Molly Johnson, Elnor Johnson, Dora
Lennox, Henrietta Goodwin, Lillian
Brennard. Ivan F. Simpson. Murray
Kinnell, Henry Morrell, Alan Trot
ter, Guy Cunningham, M. Murray
Stephens, Lewis A. Sealy, Perry
Norman, Thomas Donnelly, Arthur
Villars. George Harcourt. Harry
Kendall, Peter Jacot and Martin
Daniel.

Short Cuts to Art.
Every now and then some enter
prising teacher of music distributes
circulars telling how good his par
ticular method is and on what sci
entific principles it is based. While
this is against professional ethics
as practiced by Grade 1 teachers,
there are those in any profession
who are carried away by the popu
larity of sensational advertising.
The better teachers make an
nouncements in papers, periodicals
and elsewhere and this is quite in
order. But some persist in sending
out circulars proving how the whole
art can be mastered in a half dozen
lessons.
One such just received is an ideal
specimen. It announces a course of
six lectures on the “Techni-Esthetic
Mastery of the Piano." The expla
nation of the procedure requires
four pages of heavy scientific terms.
Thus Lecture A discusses “the su
periority of conscious knowledge of
all the natural technical proce
dures.” B tells about nerve forces,
C physiology and anatomy. Anoth
er is headed psychology and neurol
ogy, touching on the subconscious.
Finally there is the esthetics of
piano playing and an explanation of
how the student can analyze him
self.
Why is it that the word science
is used most freely where it is least
justified? Why should it be
claimed that so intimate an affair
as playing the piano can be taught
by science or by analysis? What is
this constant blurting about es
thetics in teaching music?
The idea of esthetics as an exact
science has nnt 'been long in vogue
but it seems to have contained pre
cisely the amount of ambiguity re
quired by questionable artists. It
has never been a science and it
shows no indication at present of
attaining that status. It is merely
a term used to describe certain the
ories of what constitutes heauty.
The expression “techni-esthetic mas
tery of the piano” has no meaning,
but it sounds good.
The Old Method.
The piano was well aiastered be
fore the use of these scientific terms
became known. There were dozens
of prominent pianists in the past
century and there are hundreds
who have accomplished their ends
without theory and without bunk.
They can explain their means eat
ily without recourse to science.
once can build the piano and the
player-piano but it cannot build the
player. Physiology, anatomy, psy
chology, nerve forces all play their
part in any natural act but to bo
an artist one either has them in the
right arrangement or not.
Without good ground no instru
ment can be played. Without nat
ural ability added no amount of
teaching of this sort will make a
great artist. With a small amount
of natural ability in the pupil, the
teacher can accomplish a good deal
more by encouragement, suggestion
and interest than by the use of any
theory. Th? teacher who require!
remote words to act for solid lir
struction ought not ba encouraged.

Fits, convulsions, spasms,
cramps, spells, seizures, nervous
attacks, spinal irritation, are vari
ous names for grand mal epileptic

Railroads Carry Greatest Freight Traffic inHistory
BUSINESS DONE
WITHOUT DELAY,
CAR SHORTAGE
Total Freight Move
ment Tops Optimis-
tic Forecasts.
WASHINGTON —The country’s
railroads are carrying the greatest
freight traffic in history, the car
service division of the American
Railway Assn, reported yesterday.
This record movement is being
handled without delay and without
car shortage, the report said.
As a barometer of the nation's
prosperity, 3G,881,938 freight cars
were loaded during the first 37
weeks this year, an increase of
1,208,648 cars, or a gain of 3.4 per
cent over the best previous record,
made last year. It is a 10 per cent
increase over 1924.
Little Repair Need.
The total freight movement for
the period this year was 1,177,552
cars, or 3.3 per cent over the opti
mistic estimates made last spring
by the car service division, the re
port said. It added:
“Not only are fewer locomotives
and freight cars in need of repairs
this fall than at any time in the
past four years, but the railroads
have approximately 5,000 service
able locomotives in good repair and
In storage.
“They have also nearly 142,000
surplus freight cars in serviceable
condition which can be placed in
use whenever needed.
Winter Wheat Up.
“In the record freight traffic that
has been handled this year, loading
of every commodity shows an in
crease over last year except live
stock and forest products.
“The movement of winter wheat
in the southwest this season estab
lished a new high record for rail
road performance. With the larg
est number of grain cars ever as
sembled in the loading district and
surplus locomotives to give the
loads prompt handling, the south
western railroads were never bet
ter prepared for record movement
than in 1926.’’
ROAD EQUIPMENT
SALES INCREASE
CTIICIGO—From a standpoint
of both orders and inquiries, the
last week was one of the most ac
tive In some time for the railroad
equipment business. It is estimated
that rolling stock valued at more
than $18,000,000 appeared last week
in the form of inquiries and orders.
With the budgets of the carriers for
next year nearing completion, it is
expected that inquiries for a sub
stantial number of cars will be made
in the near future.
In view of the fact that railroads
are handling the largest volume of
freight in history, together with the
increasing tendency on the part of
the carriers to replace obsolete
equipment with the more modern
type, the equipment trade is looking
forward to a buying movement of
large proportions. The feature last
week was the announcement that
the North Western road had author
ized the purchase of 2,500 freight
cars and 133 passenger cars, and
the order placed by the American
Refrigerator Transit Co., for 2,000
refrigerator cars.
The car loadings of the Pennsyl
vania road continue to show a
marked increase over last year. In
the week ended Sept. 10 the road
loaded 187,887 revenue freight
cars as compared with 165.962 in the
preceding week and 176,312 in the
same period last year. Since Jan.
1. the car loadings totaled 6,166,012
against 5,948,243 in the same period
last year. The Chicago, Burlington
Quine” in the first 21 days of
September handled 117,002 revenue
freight cars as compared with 119,-
909 in the same period last year.
Locomotives in need of repair on
Sept. 1 totaled 9,031 or 14.4 per cent
of the number on line, according to
the American Railway Assn. This
was a decrease of 402 locomotives
under the number reported.
The retiring directors of the Cen
tral railroad of New Jersey have
been re-elected.

ed here today by the board of di
rectors of the National Association
of Credit Men at the final session
of its annual meeting.

and the reduction of waste, rather
than more credit, are necessary,”
the board declared.

equalization plans and mere credit
facilities will not prove a perma
nent relief.

received by the farmers and prices
paid by consumers indicates very
clearly the amount -f w’asteage oc
curring somewhere in between, and
this Is the place where intelligent
and persistent attacks should be
made.”

tural industry, the gross Income
from which during this year was
?12.500,000,000, “must not lose its
commanding position in our nation
s’ economy.”

months will be even better than at
this time was the expressed opin
ion of a majority of the board, in
a formal statement.

Record Shipment

NEWTON, la. —The largest ship
ment of manufactured merchandise
ever to leave a factory will be sent
out of here Oct. 6 and 7, when the
Maytag Washing Machine Co. will
send a fleet of five trains, loaded
with 12,000 washing machines, to
its Philadelphia branch. Another
fleet of trains, three in number, will
leave today, two destined for the
California branch and one intended
for Portland. The value of the Phil
adelphia shipment will be over $2,-
000,000, and the Portland shipment
will raise the value to $3,500,000.

Decline in 1926
The exports of both live nnd dead
poultry from the United States in
1925 amounted to 5,813.951 pounds
valued at $1,890,750, according to

partment of commerce. Tn 1924 the
figures were 4,802.411 pounds valued

4,188,406 pounds in the first half of
1924 to 5.034.261 pounds in the first
half of 1926 and dropped to 3.269.-
523 pounds in the first half of 1926.
Live poultry is shipped from the
United States mainly to Mexico,
Cuba, Canada and the United King
dom.
The United Kingdom is the prin
cipal market for the dead poultry
exported from the United States,
nnd takes from 83 to 88 per cent of
the total exports from this country.

WHOLESALE PRICES DOWN AS
SEPTEMBER NEARS CLOSE
WASHINGTON —Check payments
in the third week of September, in
dicative of the general volume of
trade, although lower than a year
ago, were higher than at any time
in almost two months, according to
the weekly statement of the depart
ment of commerce.
The volume of goods moving into
consumption continued to record an
increase over a year ago. New build
ing contracts awarded during the
third week of the month were on
practically the same level as a year
ago. The output of petroleum, al
though lower than in the previous
week, was higher than during the
corresponding period of 1925. The
production of bituminous and bee
hive coke during the second week
of the month was also closer than
a year ago.
Wholesale prices during the third
week averaged lower than in the
previous week and a year ago.
Loans and discounts of federal re
serve member banks continued to
mount and at the end of the third
week were the highest on record.
Interest rates on both time and call
money showed no change from the
previous week, but each averaged
higher than a year ago. Prices of
stocks on the New York Stock Ex
change averaged lower than in the
previous week, but were still well
above last year.
Great Britain.
The week ended Sept. 18 was
featured in Great Britain by fur
ther strenuous efforts to find a
basis for ending the coal deadlock,
but it appears that no progress was
made toward a settlement of the dif
ficulty.
Belgium.
There is a noticeable increase in
optimism in business circles, at
tributed primarily to the vigorous
financial policy of the government.
The economic position of Belgium Is
generally much stronger now than
a month ago. Little public protest
has been aroused by the forced con
solidation of the internal loan and
the distribution of railway stocks.
The August retail price index
showed a further noticeable increase
in the cost of living. Automobile
sales are very dull. Although the
wheat and rye crops are slightly
below normal, other important crops
are quite good.
The Netherlands.
The usual summer calmness in
the Netherlands has been succeeded
by an improvement in general busi
ness conditions. Crops are on the
whoie satisfactory, but the animal
industry has been hard hit by the
British import embargo on meat.
Norway.

ports from 129,415,000 crowns dur
ing Julv, 1925, to 72,091,000 crowns

1 15,000 ATTEND
TOOL EXPOSITION
CHICAGO The eighth annual
Steel and Alachine Tool exposition
came to a close at the Alunicipal
Pier last night. The show, as well
as the convention of the American
Society for Steel Treating, under
whose auspices the steel exhibition
was held, were the most successful
in the history of the society, officers
said.
It is estimated that more than
115,(XX1 persons visited the pier dur
ing the exhibition. Every conceiv
able variety of machinery, fur
naces, treating devices and record
ing apparatus were on display, 75
per cent of them being in actual
operation.
According to J. Fletcher Harper,
Alilwaukee, new president of the so
ciety, the feature of the show this
year is the development of lighter
steel without the sacrifice of
strength. Through the invention of
new treating processes, Air. Harper
said, compactness of machinery has
resulted in a great saving of space
and a consequent reduction of fixed
charges in machine shops. One of
the most noticeable examples of this
is the new turbine engines, which
now replaces the old fashioned
steam engines which used to take
up almost as much space as a com
plete machine shop does now.
Next year’s convention will be
held in Detroit, Sept. 19 to 23.

Wood Waste Hit
At Forestry Meet;
Staffs Inadequate
Information gathered at univer
sities, in government laboratories,
and by private foresters was
brought to bear upon the problem
of utilization methods employed by
industry to use and prevent wood
waste at the second annual Forest
School conference hold at the Unit
ed States Forest Products labora
tory at the University of Wisconsin.
The purpose of the conference
was to harmonize research on forest
products as carried on by the For
est Service nt the Wisconsin labora
tory and by the various schools of
forestry and to promote the ex
change of information between
these agencies.
It was pointed out that the com
bined staffs of the local Forest
Products laboratory and the state
and privately supported schools of
forestry are inadequate to carry on
the full program of research on
wood utilization that present day
economic problems demand.

WINTER TIME FOR
LIMITED TYPES
BUILDING WORK
WASHINGTON Construction
statistics indicate a gradual shift in
volume from residential and office
buildings to industrial commercial
buildings. The building industry, it
would appear, must look to factory
and mills construction for a good
part of its activity through the
coming winter. "With this in mind,
it is not too early to remind builders
and Industrial executives of the pos
sibilities of winter construction in
this field.
The additional expenditures In
volved in winter construction, if in
deed there are such added costs, are
relatively less important for large
industrial buildings than dwellings.
The cost of a watchman to keep
heating appliances in operation, or
the additional plant to warm mate
rials is a more important factor for
a house, than for a large structure,
where a night-watchman usually is
employed at any time of the year,
and where the ratio of value to
heating plant costs is high.
Industrial plants of certain types
are nlso less subject to winter dam
age than the dwelling, with its thin
masonry walls and long period of
plastering. Both structural steel
and heavy timber framework,
through difficulty of erection on
particularly stormy days, are prac
tically immune to frost. Thick
plank floors, much used for mill
and factory buildings, can be in
stalled regardless of temperature,
and do not need to be protected for
a considerable period before
strength is attained.
Rapidity of construction is of
much more importance In winter
construction when working days are
relatively fewer than in summer,
and advantage must be taken of
every opportunity to complete the
structure. From this viewpoint
heavy timber construction presents
a marked advantage, for the build
ing can rise as rapidly as men can
lay brick and drive nails. One story
does not need time to gain strength
before another is placed upon it. and
the connections of beams and col
umns are so simple that they can
be made very rapidly. Complete
exclusion of piaster and fireproofing
from such buildings also makes for
speed of construction. As the work
is confined to a few building trades
crafts the problem of labor relat
tious is comparatively simple.

Recent rapid progress in north
west side real estate development
will make that section of the city
the scene of great building activity,
in the opinion of L. W. Brueggeman,
realtor, whose most recent subdivi
sion, “Irvington,” on Lisbon Ave.,
near Lake Blvd., is meeting with
favor by homesite seekers and specu
lators.
More than 40 lots in the sub
division already have been sold and
such interest is being shown in the
subdivision that a branch office has
been erected on the grounds for the
convenience of buyers and salesmen.
Lot sales are being held every Sat
urday and Sunday.
“Land is the only permanent
wealth,” said Mr. Brueggeman. “This
was illustrated in Germany after
the war when landholders suffered
little by the depression.
“That population is the basis for
land values is proven by the his
tory of boom towns. In Milwaukee,
which has a steady growth in popu
lation and industries, land values
have been constant.”

COOLIDGE OPENS HIS MIND
President Coolidge opened his mind to Bruce Barton
for the space of two front page columns on nothing in par
ticular. It is always pleasant to find that a man is really
human, only that tells us nothing about his public policies.
Coolidge is a nice little man. Is that worth two front page
columns at a time when the fate of the Republican party
hangs in the balance and the whole American nation is
dragged back and forth between foreign and native im
perialists?
If a skipper on a ship in a hurricane headed for the
rocks should open his mind to the radio man to the extent
of telling him to tell the world that he was born on a farm
and liked his eggs well done, it would not be an equivalent
for the S O S which he should send out in the interest of
the ship, the crew and the owners.
The only remarkable thing about such a message
under such conditions would be that a skipper should
think it a matter of importance to send that sort of drivel
over the air. And that is precisely the effect of Coolidge’s
message to the American people via Bruce Barton.
American citizens who take their national and inter
national problems seriously will read Coolidge’s mental
effusion and say: Good Lord, is he as empty as all that?
What’s his idea in opening his mind and showing chat there
is nothing in it? Or does he imagine that any serious
mind will take such stuff in place of the frank statesman
ship that every citizen is entitled to?
The league of nations tells the president and the
United States senators that no matter whether they admit
it or not, the world court is a part of ths* teague and no
amount of American interpretation can change that fact.
Coolidge shrugs his shoulders and tells us that he used to
ride a horse as a boy.
The Cantonese drive the foreign powers and their
Chinese war lords into a corner. The British cry out for
American help as they did when the Germans pushed them
into the North sea. Everybody is anxious to krow what
Coolidge intends to do about it. He says that his boyhood
ambition ■was to keep a store. We wish he did.
It is just as Upton Sinclair wrote in “The Spokes
man’s Secretary.” Bruce Barton plays the role of the
manicure girl who tells the secretary what the “Spokes
man” should tell the American people about themselves.
The only striking difference between the manicure girl and
Barton is that he knows better and plays the game, fully
aware of offering to the American people a dish of Polly
anna bunk in place of the solid political truth to which
they are entitled.
THE SELFISH PROFIT MIND
The Milwaukee Journal and The Chicago Tribune
are exchanging uncivil civilities over the waterways
question. They are discussing a grave problem of na
tional welfare with the tricks of college debate in the spirit
of Babbitism.
New York profiteers want no water route or only a
waterway from Chicago to New York, but not a waterway
from Chicago down the Mississippi or down the St.
Lawrence. Chicago wants a waterway down the Missis
sippi, but begrudges Milwaukee and other lake cities a
waterway down the St. Lawrence. Milwaukee profiteers
try to play New York against Chicago and to put over the
St. Lawrence route before any of the others can be started.
Each set of profiteers thinks only of its own private
pocket and wants to use its whole financial and political
pull to beat the others. None thinks of the social angle
of these projects. In the selfish dog-eat-dog spirit of pri
vate capital the leading exponents of Babbitism pervert a
great social enterprize into a prize fight. But at the same
time they pose as grand examples of enlightened civic
virtue.
There is no reason why all three projects should not
be built, except the worship of The Golden Calf. One
American business lord wants to outdo the others as a
Black Pirate holding up and robbing the ship of public
welfare.
THE EMPTY PROMISE
Milwaukee voters who back the standpatters for the
alleged reason that this is the only way to secure lower
taxes will be disappointed by a recent article in Barron’s
Weekly, which declares that tax reduction by the present
congress is impossible, and that a tax cut will be unwise
even later for the reason that it might mean a deficit in the
national treasury.
So the empty promise of the Wisconsin standpat can
didates and of those progressives who have flocked to the
Zimmerman standard is revealed by the inspired mouth
piece of Wall Street.
Promises of old party statesmen mean nothing, any
way, and they mean less than nothing when the organ of
eastern standpat Republicanism exposes their emptiness in
these words: “What must be considered in advocating a
tax cut is not what has happened, but what is likely to
happen. And before the treasury or any one else can tell
what is likely to happen, it must have some experience on
which to base predictions.” That’s just what The Leader
has been telling the taxpayers all the time.

infliction of suffering upon our

ings is evidence of a low state of

The North American Indians
