fication of those assembled at the
bloody festival.
The modern man or woman of
ordinary culture reads of these
ghastly ceremonies with a sense of
sickening revolt. The more abun
dant our culture the more vio
lent is our revulsion from these
actions of the human animal, yet
somewhere in the line of our an
cestors we will find ancient rela
tives who enjoyed these savage
rites. Where they appear in mod
ern society we may be sure that
they represent either a reversion
to or a survival of primitive bar
barism.
In the United States there are
large patches of territory which
have not advanced beyond this
barbaric stage of human progress.
The nation is like a human body
well developed but marred by
numerous and hideous sores.
There are regions where masses
of men, women and children glut

physical torture on their fellows.
They are barbarian zones outside
the current of modern progress.
Here primitive superstitions pre
vail and it is these very regions
which produce legislation intend
ed to outlaw the teaching of mod
ern science.
Almost the whole southern
section of the United States rep
resents this savage survival with
splotches here and there in the
west. Occasionally there is a
temporary relapse into barbarism
in large urban centers of the
north when Negroes are hunted

DEMPSEY AND TUNNEY
It started back in 1917. Jack Dempsey, heavyweig'
boxing champion, would not fall for the Northcliffe
propaganda. The “Neanderthaler” had sense enough to
laugh at the war lies. Maybe it was his Irish-Indian
blood that balked at the British propaganda. Or it was
the natural habit of the fighter who sees through the
feints of his antagonist straight into his ey^s. Or some
Socialist ideas lit up the scene for him. Perhaps he also
had looked behind the scenes enough through his personal
touch with some of America’s “big men” to understand
what they were up to.
The paytriots were stung in their most sensitive part,
their vanity. Their champion would not take them se
riously. He saw through the game. It was just like the
•whole fighting game, a money-making proposition in which
the mob puts up and the principals get the aough. It
wasn’t his fight, he had no stake in it.
So the paytriots got sore. Their champion wouldn’t
fight for “their ideals.”' He was “a slacker.” And he hurt
their conceit deliberately by posing for his photograph in
patent leather shoes handling a riveting machine on one
of our over-night auxiliary merchant steamers.
When Morgan’s men organized the American legion in
Paris for purposes that were anything but profitable and
wholesome for the majority of the American citizens, the
official spokesmen of war heroics took up the hunting cry
against Dempsey. They wanted a “hero” for a boxing
champ. You can’t make war propaganda with a champion
•who refused to fight for Wall Street. They looked about
for a war veteran who could lick the champion.
So they picked Gene Tunney. He was a marine, a
“leatherneck,” and everybody knows that Pershing saved
France and Morgan’s $500,000,000 “with the help of God
and a handful of marines.” If Tunney could lick “that
slacker,” the conceit of the paytriots would get its badly
needed balm, and the war mongers could have the right
kind of an idol to inflame some more ignorant boys for
the next big parade.
The propaganda for Tunney started and kept it up
till the present. Tunney was painted not only as a great
fighter and patriot, but also as a man of intellect, a sort of
a Cro-Magnon compared to the “brutish Neanderthaler.”
Like all propaganda, this is a lie. Tunney’s mental at
tainments, in our opinion, fall far short of Dempsey’s,
but few people realize it and the Tunney propaganda fools
the mob.
Well, the big fight is over. The paytriots have the
sort of a champ that they can use. But it will always
remain a sting for their pride that Tunney couldn’t knock
out a Dempsey Who did not fight like his old self. Jack
says himself that “he just couldn’t get started,” but we
fancy he chuckled inwardly as he said it. He had made
up his mind long ago to quit the silly game. He let Tunney
hit him in the face, knowing all the time that the new
champ couldn’t knock him out. He put up a good enough
scrap to please the fans and let Tunney win a decision on
points.
“OUR” INTERESTS IN CUBA
“The finding of dead bodies of active union men is a
daily occurrence both in the city and in the village,’’ writes
a Cuban worker speaking of the aftermath in Cuba of the
recent railroad strike. “By order of the dictator Machado,
all union men known to be active are expelled from the
country.” Seventeen workers were killed during the strike
for their part in it, two of the strike leaders have been
killed since, and any liberal or labor paners printing ar
counts of the terrorism against the workers have b&
suppressed.
All of this reads like the palmiest days of the Fascist
terror in Italy, but this time it isn’t in a country the other
side of the Atlantic from which America can remain self
righteously aloof. It is in little Cuba, one of the brood
chicks of American imperialism, and the men in whose in
terests this terror is enacted are our own capitalists. The
Cuban railroads are owned by American capital and Pres
ident Machado has been acting in their behalf in suppress
ing the strike against them with blood and iron.
Our interests as workers in lands where American,
capital is invested are the interests of the workers em
ployed by that capital. The interests in whose behalf we
hear so much talk in favor of American intervention are
the interests of our enemies.—Oklahoma Leader.

DRY LAW BAN

A probability that the national
administration itself will obtain a
modification of the Volstead act
prior to the next national campaign
was the claim of John Rader, inter
national secretary, Brewery and
Cereal Mill Workers’ union, whose
home is in Milwaukee and who has
returned from the convention of the
union just closed in Cincinnati, The
convention is held every three years.
Senators Are Beaten.
“The prohibition question natur
ally was uppermost in the meeting,”
he said.
“The situation was regarded as
favorable, especially when consider
ing the procession of political de
feats of national lawmakers, not
withstanding their standing with
the present administration. Every
one of them, despite administration
backing, were knocked out on the
wet and dry question, even including
the senator from Georgia.
“With the headway made in de
feating dry candidates and in elect
ing those in favor of modification
it would not be a surprise if the na
tional administration would be
forced to modify the Volstead law
prior to the presidential election.”
All Officers Re-elected.
Mr. Rader said the convention
was absolutely harmonious.
All the officers were re-elected,
subject to the customary referen
dum, including Charles Nickolaus,
Milwaukee, fourth vice-president.
The union has had no strikes of
any importance in the last three
years, in spite of adverse conditions,
he said.

SUPPLY HERE
Milwaukee’s entire milk supply

beginning Friday, it was announced
today by the health department.

chief of the department’s food di
vision, approximately 98 per cent of
the cows are now tested and the
remaining ones will have undergone
the test before the date set for the
exclusion of all but tested milk.
Milwaukee receives 74,121 gallons
of milk daily which Is distributed
by 19 dealers. It is obtained from
3,750 herds.
Milwaukee has had pure milk
since 1921 when complete pasteuri
zation was demanded of city deal
ers, Dr. Pilgrim explained. The
tuberculin test merely will supple
ment the former assurance.
According to Dr. Pilgrim, most of
the owners in the Milwaukee dis
trict had subjected their herds to
the tuberculin test before the Mil
waukee health department ruled for
tested milk.

Can student government in a
school of 2,250 pupils be successful?
Some schools iu the country main
tain firmly that it cannot.
But Washington High school has
proved beyond doubt that it can.
Begun last February on an intensive
scale, the system has proved such
a success that the officers connect
ed with it believe it will never be
supplanted.
The prihcipal object of the self
government is to give practical
training in civic affairs. There are
no “laws” or “courts,” as in some
schools, but a clear-cut set of rules
which are necessary toward the
maintenance of good behavior in the
school.
Most schools, the officers point
out, which established “courts” to
punish offenders are forced to aban
don their government. The main
reason given is that pupils do not
like to tell on their fellow students.
The latest and most potable example
of such failure was that at the
University of Wisconsin.

says.

arrests for driving while intoxicated

cago, with 476 per cent; and most
of the larger cities of the country.
Minreapolic was a close second

For the first time in the history
of the American labor movement a
delegation of the imtiou’s most
prominent trade union executives
intend to investigate lnlior and eeo«
noxuic conditions in England, Italy,

ing to an announcement made pub
lic today by President L. E. Shep

neers Journal, its secretary. Chair

known lenders of the American la
bor movement, was npitointed by
the president three years ago on a
somewhat similar mission to in
vestigate labor conditions in the
Hawaiian islands for the federal
government.

to secure accurate facts about la
bor's status in Soviet Russia, under

tor Mussolini.

rely merely on personal observation,
but is to take along a complete staff
of economic experts headed by Dr.
"VV. Jett Lirtfck of Washington, D. C\,
who has repeatedly served ns a con
sulting economist for the railroad
brotherhoods and the United Mine
Workers of America. Frank I\
"Walsh, former joint chairman of
the United States war labor hoard
with Chief Justice Taft, will act as
legal adviser to the party.
According to announcement, the
delegation will cover not only the
largest countries of western Europe,
hut also Holland, Denmark, Sweden,
Czecho-Slovnkin and Austria where
it will meet the leaders of the trnde
union, Labor Party and co-operative
movements, and ascertain what or
ganized labor in these lands is now
achieving and planning for the fu
ture. Special meetings are to be
arranged with the British Labor
Party, the International Labor Of
fice of Geneva, and the Federation
of Trnde Union Headquarters in
Amsterdam, as well ns with the ac
credited leaders of the Italian and
Russian labor movements. The dele
gation intends to leave early next
July and return during September."

MADISON —If the state of New
York can cut its diphtheria loss in
half within five years, ns it has suc
ceeded in doing, Wisconsin with far
less population congestion can do as
well.
This summarizes the stand of the
Wisconsin state board of health in
advocating the universal immuniza
tion of children against diphtheria.
The hoard announces that the sub
ject is receiving special emphasis in
all states during September and Oc
tober.
Rests With Parents.
The Empire state proposes to
abolish the disease entirely by 1030.
The agencies are at hand for W is
consin to roach the same goal, ac
cording to the board of health of
our state, within a few years if
parents demand this protection for
their children. The case rests with
the narents, the board states.
Records show that more than
2.000 died in Wisconsin from diph
theria in 1880, when the population
was but half of today’s, while at
present these deaths usually arc
from 200 to 400 per year, with about
3,000 cases reported. This down
ward tendency began with the dis
covery of diphtheria anti-toxin and
throat tests, followed by the advent
of the preventive treatment —toxin-
antitoxin.
Immune For Life.
“The greatest hope for eliminating
diphtheria altogether,” declared the
atate board, “lies ia the agent toxin
antitoxin, by which children are
vaccinated against the disease and
rendered immune, probably t or life.
“In the process of immunizing the
child, a trifling quantity is intro
duced into the arm once a week for
three weeks. This makes about 80
per cent of these children immune.
A test (known as the Schick test)
applied a few months later will tell
whether the child is still suscept
ible. If found susceptible, more
doses can be given until entire im
munity is established.
“No barm follows this vaccina
tion. Ia many thousand doses given
in New York city, no bad results
came to anyone. The discovery of
this agent for protecting childhood
from a standing foe should be of
great interest to all parents,” the
•tate board declares.
Child's Own Right.
“The greatest mortality from
(diphtheria is in children under
school age, and there are many
deaths also later in life. To use
this agency upon children 1 year
old and upwards, is conferring a
right to which every child should
be entitled.
“Vaccination against diphtheria
can be administered by any physi
cian, and it is hoped that before
many years the great majority, if
not all, of Wisconsin children will
be fully protected against this dev
astating malady. It should be re
garded as a communal measure,
since the prevention of cases pre
vents the further spread of the dis
r se from those sources.”
The board warned against con
fusing toxin-antitoxin, a preventive
agent, with antitoxin, which is used
in actual cases of diphtheria, and
which if applied the first day will
cure almost any case.
Is Often Confusing.
“In the confusion between symp
toms of diphtheria and common
coids or croup,” the state health de
partment states, “a good many cases
are neglected, often unwittingly, but
with fatal results. If diphtheria did
not so closely simulate sore throat
and croup, the disease would be un
der much better control.”

service, operated by the Inland Wa

yesterday.
Almost since it was begun the
Mississippi end of the service has
shown a profit, but the Warrior
service always has shown a deficit.
This year, according to figures
based on eight months of operation
and estimated results for the last
four months, there will be a com
bined profit of $347,032.
Last year’s deficit was approxi
mately $53,000; in 1023 the deficit
was almost $1,000,000. An actual
profit of 26 cents per ton will be
made on all goods handled in 1926.*
The total net income on the Mis
sissippi increased $1.15 per ton in
1026 over 1923 by changing a loss
of 49 cents per ton in 1923 to an
estimated profit of OG cents per ton
in 1926.
On the Warrior the net deficit
was decreased $1.47 per ton in 1926
as compared to 1923.

ical Research here.

moving the mineral content,” Dr.

elements remained.' Wheat and
nearly all food grains now are de
natured.”

figures showing that 1,000,000 chil
dren in the United States are suf
fering from tuberculosis, 400,000

have spinal curvature, 4,000,000 are

000 have defective teeth.
Need Balanced Diet.
“A balanced diet with substitutes
for the mineral ground out of the
grain will remedy the situation,” he
continued.
“Four ounces of proteins, or such
foods as meat, milk or beans is nec
essary for a proper ration.
“Of carbohydrates or starchy
foods a little over one pound is need
ed to produce energy and heat. Ap
proximately two ounces of fats are
required.
Dr. Ilinhede, a Danish nutrition

dvring the World war by forcing

THEY DON’T BELIEVE IN SIGNS
To the Editor of The Leader:
We have “eat-more-apples week”
and “education week” and “be kind
to animals week” and various other
periods of strenuous activity too
numerous t<r mention. Why not
sponsor a “read-the-signs week”? It
seems necessary.
The other night I clambered
aboard a Sherman Bird, bus at the
North Western depot. We started
up the avenue aud proceeded with
out interruption until commanded
to stop by the imperious wave of a
female hand. The bus screeched to
a stop and the owner of the hand
stuck her head in the door.
“Does this bus go to Washington
park?” she inquired in a voice that
dared the driver to say “no.”
“I’m afraid not, mndam,” replied
that unassuming person. “The sign
on the front says ‘Sherman.’
She stepped back aud we careened
on our way until, two blocks fur
ther on, an elderly gentleman, ap
parently possessed of average intel
ligence, halted our progress and de
manded to go to 16th St. The driv
er again explained that his vehicle
did not pass 16th St., and the last
I saw of our would-be passenger he
was standing on one foot gazing ma
lignantly after our tail light.
At West Water St. and the ave
nue, traffic wouldn’t let us by, and
as we screamed to a stop, the driver
opened the door to admit a young
couple, who got ready to drop tlieir
dimes before inquiring casually,
“Does this bus go to 25th St.?”
Once again we were forced to de
cline their company and they de
scended just in time for us to end
the traffic procession west.
We rocked on up the avenue with
out further incident until the red
light halted us at 6th St. Here a
rather rotund woman of uncertain
years,, planted one foot firmly on
the step plate and popped her head
inside to utter:
“This is a Serman bus, isn’t it?”
Receiving an affirmative answer
from our smiling driver, she
went on:
“Well, I want to get off at 39th
St. and Grand Ave. Can I do it?”
And once again our host was
forced to remind her that the Sher
man park bus turned north on 14th
St., and she finally removed her
pedal extremity In time to prevent
us from being shut in by the chang
ing light.
And all this despite the fact that
our bus had “Sherman” in big let
ters on its front— distinguishable a
block or more away. Maybe these
people think The Electric Co. is
kidding them! They ought to have
some excuse. B. B.
for civic encouragement.

To the Editor of The Leader:
I note with approval that inter
section traffic officers are now mak
ing an effort to prevent the turning
left by motorists in a right traffic
lane and the turning right by motor
ists who are in a left traffic lane, a
practice which I have several times
seen weged in the readers’ column of
The Leader.
I myself was caught by a long
line of street cars the other day, and
was forced to approach an intersec
tion presided over by an officer in a
right lane or else be delayed until
the street cars moved along.
When I tried to make a left turn,
I was stopped, reprimanded, and al
lowed to go round the block to
reach the corner I had hoped to
reach directly.
Traffic laws are made in order to
give every motorist the greatest
possible help without Imposing on
any one. Though ray proposed turn
would have inconvenienced no one,
I suppose it is too much to expect
an officer to display judgment and
make a decision based on the factors
of the situation.
That they are enforcing a general
procedure which is correct is worthy
of commendation and worth the oc
casional spleen an unnecessary call
ing-down provokes. H. N. P.

Paul's, London, in an analytical sur
rey of the empire published yester

ous authors on “the modern world,”
forecasts the early passage of Great
Britain ns a world power.

of “the gloomy dean,” he sees “great
danger, not only in the internation
al situation but even more from the
conquest. The main problem there
is anti-social and class sectionalism
which is the cure of industrial civ
ilization, especially dangerous in a
country situated as we are.”
Time of Trial.
“The main danger is interior to
the empire,” declares the dean. “The
omens at present are very unfavor
eble
“Everything points to a coming
time of trial for the nation and the
empire. It seems for every reason
unlikely that our position ns ft
world power will endure much
longer. Much depends upon the
friendliness of the United States on
which we certainly cannot count, al
though we should not despair.
“The cordial friendship which
many Englishmen enjoy with indi
vidual Americans rnpst not blind us
either to the intense concentration
of the American people at large
upon what they consider their own
interests, or to the prevailing un
friendliness of America as expressed
by its politicians and journalists to
this country.
Hits At U. S.
“If in the future we are attacked
by a European coalition we may take
It ns probable that the United
States will leave us to our fate, un
less, Indeed we are invaded by a
Mack army.”
“There are no occasions of war at
present between the British empire
and the United States, says the
dean, “since our government in
variably give way.”
“Americans insisting upon repay
ment of the vast debt incurred for
France to which we rashly put our
names have secured that we shoul 1
remain permanently tributary to
themselves.”
Among the specific “problems” he
lists the immigration exclusion
policy, “which can only be main
trined while It is possible to exclude
by force,” and the fact that the
loyalty of the colonies “is less
wholehearted than an Englishman
could wish.
“The future of Canada is prob
lematical. Its chief safeguard is

Sees Big Combine.
“If the British flag was hauled

nent, It’s more than possible the na
tions of Europe, enraged by bloated
propserlty nnd airs of superiority
of ‘the man who won the war,’

teeth.
“The future of India lies on the
nees of the gods. Democratic insti-
.ilons have thrown power into
iinnds of most pernicious agitators.

quieter than British India.

BIG BIZ ASKS
SOCIALIST AID
FOR GERMANY
Leader Special Service.
BERLIN—Dr. Silverberg, chair
man of the national organization of
big business in Germany, said at the
Dresden convention of the organi
zation that the leaders of big busi
ness must support the republic,
keep the Nationalist-Monarchist out
of the government, and invite the
Socialist party to share the re
sponsibilities of government.
The Berlin Vorwaerts, speaking
for the majority of the German So
cialist party, declined to walk into
the parlor of big business, but ad
mitted that Silverberg’s speech
marked a new turn in the policies
of big business.
Shocks Old Reactionaries.
“The conclusion from this reali
zation, to the effect that there can
be no longer a stable government
without the workers and their po
litical instrument, the Socialist
party, is doubtless a complete re
versal of former ideas. It explains
both the pained surprise of the
press of the right and the reserved
attitude of the trade unions and So
cialists towards Silverberg’s
speech,” Vorwaerts thinks.
On the other hand, Vorwaerts Is
not surprised at the violent uproar
raised against Silverberg in the
ultra-reactionary press published by
Hugenberg, who owns such papers
ns Der Tag and The Berlin Lokal
Anzeiger.
Vorwaerts recalls that seme of
the lending big business men have
been for some time trying to shake
off Hugenberg and his ultra-reac
tionary following.
Catholics Favor Socialists.
While the reactionary chorus
barks at the Socialists and declares
them unfit for the companionship of
the old parties, the leading Catholic
paper, Germania, declares that it
has no objection to working with
the trade unions or the Socialist
party.
“On the contrary.” writes The
Germania, “the Catholic* party
agrees with Dr. Silverberg, having
taken the position long before him
that it is highly desirable to make
no attempt to work without the
trade unions or without tho Social
ist party.”
The Democratic press, led by The
Berliner Tageblatt welcomes Sil
verberg s support of the republic
and hopes that this will mean the
end of the policy of boycotting Re
publican civil servants, voters and
workers.
Nationalists Will Lose.
The Berliner Tageblatt recalls
that all during recent years German
big business financed anti-Repub
lican societies and secret conspir
acies against the republic.
“We hope that we can take it for
granted after the Dresden conven
tion that this sort of financing will
be definitely dropped,” writes The
Tageblatt.
The chorus of the German So
cialist press unanimously declares
that there is no basis for any co
operation with big business except
that of political and industrial de
mocracy. Until then the class war
must continue and the power of
trade unionism and Socialism must
decide the political policies of the
workers.
The Socialists are much amused
by the antics of the Communist
edifors. who say that big business
is calling upon the Socialists to stop
the mighty attacks of Communism
—which has no appreciable follow
ing left in Germany.

AID BUSINESS

has decreed that no more gold ore

Bank of Mexico.

having more than two grains of gold
to the ton shall be manifested be
fore the government nssayers nnd
at the customs house when leaving
the country. After being exported,
the exporters are to be given a
month in which to return to Mexico
the equivalent of the gold exported,
in the form of gold bullion or for
eign cold coin. If they fail to do
this they will be liable to a fine of
10 per cent of the value of the
gold exported. It is expected the
decree will discourage the exporta
tion of gold.

business, which has been depressed
since the first of the year, and has
grown considerably worse sinee the
Catholics began their boycott as a
protest against the religious laws.

which announced that in July and
August they had paid expenses for
the first time in 10 years, now are
suffering from the general depres
sion which brought a heavy decrease
iu freight.

NOTED PERSONS
CONTEND LAW
IS HARMFUL
Cite Proofs That
Drinking Is on
Increase.
CHICAGO—A greater degree of
temperance could be attained by a
wise restrictive law,” rather than
by a bone dry statute, is the con
clusion announced yesterday by of
ficials of the Moderation league, an
organization opposed to Volstead
lsm, following its national survey
of prohibition conditions during the
year 1925. The survey was released
simultaneously in various cities
from the headquarters In New York,
Under Its banner, The Restoration
of Temperance, the league lists ns
directors and members of its ad
visory board a number of nationally
known figures drawn from every
walk of life. Among them are the
Rev. Charles Warren Raldwin; F.
N. Brown, president of the Frisco
railroad; Newcomb Carlton, presi
dent of the Western Union Tele
graph Co., and Archibald Douglas, a
trustee of Columbia university.
Many Prominent Men.
Other familiar names among the
directorate are: Kermit Roosevelt;
the Rt. Rev. Charles Fiske, bishop
of central New York; Haley Fiske,
president of the Metropolitan Life
Insurance Co.; Alexander C. Hum
phreys, president of Stevens univer
sity; Charles A. Fenbody, president
of the Mutual Life Insurance Co.;
Francis K. Pendleton, former justice
of the New York supreme court;
William C. Redfield, former secre
tary of commerce; Dr. George David
Stewart, president, New York Acad
emy of Medicine; Elinu Root, and
Owen Wister, nationally known
novelist.
“When we consider that drunken
ness generally has increased to the
pre-prohibition level, and that
drunken drivers and drunken chil
dren have increased far above any
thing ever known before in this
country,” declares the report, ‘‘we
cannot escape the conclusion that
the Volstead act has failed utterly
to do what it was intended to do,
namely, promote temperance and so
briety.
No Hope Seen.
‘‘Moreover, since conitions have
become worse, not letter, each year,
and with the next generation drink
ing as never before, there seems to
be no hope that the Volstead act, in
Its present drastic form, can ever
accomplish its purpose.
“From the experience, before na
tional prohibition, of the states
which had restrictive laws, from the
experience of the whole country dur
ing the restrictive years 1918-1919,
and from the experience of the Ca
nadian provinces and the Scandina
vian countries, we believe that a
greater degree of temperance can
be attained by a wise restrictive law
than by a bone dry law which does
not command the respect of a large
part of the people.
“We are also of the firm convic
tion that such n policy of wise re
striction would have the incidental
advantage of eliminating almost en
tirely the scandalous corruption and
bribery of public officials, would
Stop the growth of the bootlegging
millionaire class, would check dis
respect for law, and would, in addi
tion, produce a handsome national
revenue.”
Show Big Gain.
After citing figures indicating that
under Volsteadism the greatest in
crease in drunkenness has been in
the states which formerly had their
own dry laws, the report says:
“Perhaps one reason for this
greater increase In drunkenness in
the dry state* is that most of these
so-called dry states were not really
so, but were, in the main, merely
restrictive. It is not generally
known that at the time the 18th
amendment was ratified, Jan. IG,
1919, only six states, containing 4.2
per cent of the population of the
United States, were bone dry by
popular vote: six other states, with
7.6 ]>er cent of the population, were
bone dry by legislative act, and 18
states, with 55.7 per cent of the
population, were wet. The remain
ing IS states, with 52.5 per cent of
the population, were neither wet nor
dry in any Volsteadian sense.
“Of the 12 states which had bone
dry laws, all of them acquired these
laws after the World war began.”
A startling increase in consump
tion of bootleg spirits in 1925 over
1924 is cited, the league basing its
conclusion upon police figures cover
ing arrests for drunkenness submit
ted from representative cities in
every part of the nation.
“Drunkenness increased about
twice as fast in 1925 as it did in
11>24,” declares the report. “In 5G4
places arrests for drunkenness in
creased 21.000 in 1924 over 1923. and
in 1925 such arrests increased 36,241
over 1924.”
Comparative figures from Atlanta,
Ga., and Birmingham, Ain., are cited
to indicate that Volsteadism proved
a lame substitute under state re
strictive measures previously in
vogue in those cities.

WASHINGTON Substantial in
creases in nearly all tax collections
were reported during the fiscal year
1920, according to an analysis of
revenue made public today by the
internal revenue bureau.
Collections of internal revenue
from all sources during the fiscal
year which ended June 30 were $2,-
835,999,892.19, or an increase of
$251,859,023.95 over that of the
fiscal year 1925 of $2,584,140,205.24,
Income Tax Increases.
Income taxes showed an increase
of $212,445,091.82, of which $178,-
747,037.15 consisted of greater rev
enue from the tax on corporation
earnings, while $33,095,054.07 was
in the form of greater Individual
tax returns.
There was greater revenue from
the individual income tax, notwith
standing a substantial cut in rates
which affected payments in March
and June of 1920.
The revenue from the estate tax
increased by $14,019,209.39, collec
tions from this source amounting to
$110,041,030.09, as compared with
$101,421,700.20 in the fiscal year
1925. Revenue, from the gift tax,
which was repealed effective Jan.
1, 1920, fell off from $7,518,129.32
in the fiscal year 1925 to $3,175,-
338.73 in 1920.
Other boosts in tax revenue in
cluded an increase of $25,419,227.91
in revenue from tobacco taxes, $14,-
574,028.51 from excise, stamp and
special taxes, and $553,514.16 from
distilled spirits. There was an in
crease of about $18,000,000 in the
revenue from automobile taxes.
Big Corporation Tax.
The capital stock tax on corpora
tions, which was repealed, effective
July 1,192 G, yielded $97,385,755.G1
in the fiscal year 192 G, or an in
crease of $7,383,161.05 over 1925,
when the total was $90,002,594.50.
Collections from nil miscellaneous
taxes showed a net increase of $39,-
414,532.
One of the principal decreases in
miscellaneous tax collections was
from the admission tax to theaters
and other places of amusements,
which fell off by $6,927,132.43, total
collections from this source being
$23,980,07G.6G, as against $30,907,-
509.09. This was more of a decrease
than anticipated.
Refunds during the year of taxes
illegally collected totaled $174,156,-
597.01,
Expenditures in administering the
internal revenue tax laws for the
fiscal year 1920 were $34,948,483.37,
not including expenditures for re
funding internal revenue collections
and tnxes illegally collected. The
cost of operation for the fiscal year
1920 was $1.23 for each SIOO col
lected, compared with $1.44 for each
SIOO collected for the fiscal year
1925, or a reduction of 14.6 per cent.

NEW YORK—William De Rosa, a
painter employed In the Staten
Island plant of the Procter Gam
ble Co., has been elected by popular
vote to represent bis fellow workers
on the company’s board of directors
in Cincinnati. Similar elections
were held in Cincinnati and Kansas
City where the company operates
factories.
The employe-director plan began
with the formation of an employes
conference committee at the Cincin
nati factory several years ago. The
purpose of this committee was to es
tablish closer relationship between
employer and employe. From this
conference committee developed the
idea of having a representative of
the employes ou the board of di
rectors of the company.
There are 12 directors, and three
of these represent the employes of
the company’s three main plants.
This was a radical departure in in
dustrial organization, but it has
been succesful and has done much
to cement the tie between the man
agement and the workers.
The employes who are members
of the profit sharing plan are guar
anteed a minimum of 48 weeks’
work in the year.

England More Sober
Than Dry America
Despite Volstead
CHlCAGO—Comparing America
and prohibition with England and
liquor freedom, the National As
sociation Opposed to Prohibition
yesterday issued a letter sent to
22,000 bankers, manufacturers, and
other heavy tax payers in the
country.
The association cites statistics to
prove that arrests for drunkenness
in England and Wales shrank from
185.577 in 1813 to 77,05)4 in 1923.
In Plymouth, a city of 210,000, the
arrests for drunkenness average 87
per year, while in Atlanta, Ga., a
city of similar size, more than 7,000
drunks are arrested annually, de
spite the prohibition law.
The United States treasury loses
$1,500,000,000 annually in taxes
which could be collected from
brewers and wine makers, the asso
ciation states.
“While Great Britain is reducing
drunkenness, emptying its jails and
filling its treasury,” says the letter,
“our own government pursues its
course of criminal folly. The bil
lions shunted away from the trea
sury become a harvest for law
breakers.”

U. W. INDORSES
VACCINATIONS
FOR HAY FEVER
The University of Wisconsin in
dorses vaccinations for the fighting
of liny fever.
Posters are being employed by its
extension department to disseminate
Information concerning hay fever
vaccines throughout the state.
In opposition to those who doubt
the efficacy of liny fever innoeuln
tions, is this statement of the exten
sion division:
“Relief can often be obtained
through a series of vaccinations if
the particular pollen causing the
trouble is known.
"A skin test is used to determine
one’s sensitivity to particular pol
lens. A little of the pollen is rubbed
into a slight scratch in the skin. If
one is sensitive there is a reaction
in from 5 to 30 minutes. It usually
fades In from one to three hours.”
The accompanying illustration is
a photograph of one of the univer
sity’s se\eral charts devoted to hay
fever and kindred summer affec
tions, displayed in one of Its ex
hibits at the State Fair.

DATE OF BIRTH
Observance of the 42nd anniver
»ary of the opening of the Schuster
atores was begun by a 13-day sale
today.
Ed. Schuster first came to Mil
waukee from Hamburg. Germany, in
1854. but returned to Germany, com
ing back to America in 1882.
Schuster was employed by Jacob
Poss in a dry goods store at 32th
nnd Walnut Sts. for one year, and
then with A. F. Friedmann, another
former employe of Poss, went Into
business at 047 3rd St.
“At that time lower 3rd St. was
“down town,” and Prairie and
Chestnut Sts. were lending business
thoroughfares, Mr. Friedmann re
calls. “The business and sales force
consisted of one clerk, a salesgirl,
Mr. Schuster and myself.
“Store hours were from 7 :30 a. m.
to 0 p. in., Sundays from 8 a. in. to
12 m. Today the hours are from
8:30 a. m. to 5:30 p. m., with no
Sunday work.”
Several years after the first store
Was established It was moved to 3rd
St. and Garfield Ave., and is known
now ns the 3rd St. store.
The 32th St. store, at 32th and
Yliet Sts., was established in 1804
and in 3014 the store at Gth Ave.
and Mitchell St. was built.
The store force, originally four
persons, has grown until now the
three stores employ 2.300 persons.

Young Actor Had Stage
In the Apple Orchard.
Straight to the apple orchard ran
Glenn Hunter, a book under his
arm. lie bad just been reading a
thrilling story, and, as always, bis
one idea wa3 to act out the part of
the hero.
There was a gentle slope in the
orchard, and at the foot of this
slope, in an open space, was his
“stage.” He was safe there from
any prying eyes, and could play at
being an actor as long as he chose.
lie put down the book and
stepped out on the stage. In his
imagination he was the character
in the 1 book. He began acting out
one of the scenes in the exciting
tale, making up words to suit the
actions as he went along. For him
the open space In the orchard was
really a stage, and the nodding
trees had become an audience.
It wasn’t any wonder that a boy
who started acting because be just
couldn’t help himself became one
of the leading young actors of the
American stage. Nearly everyone
has seen him in Merton of the Mov
ies, his first big success on the
stage or screen. Glenn Hunter adds
another year to his age today.

BLEYER CITES
NEED UF CRIME
NEWS IN PRESS
The necessity for newspapers
printing crime news and the limita
tions tiiey should place upon them
selves in regard to their description
were detailed by Prof. Willard G.
Bleyer, director of the journalism
department, University of Wiscon
sin, before the luncheon meeting of
the Optimists’ club today in the
Milwaukee Athletic club.
Must Guard Selves.
“If a sneak thief is in our neigh
borhood, or bank robbers working in
our town, we must know about them
in order to protect ourselves,” Dr.
Bleyer said.
“And if we did not read of their
work in the newsimpers, how could
we tell whether our police depart
ment, our prosecuting attorneys and
our courts are functioning prop
erly?”
Dr. Bleyer then named four ways
In which newspapers may wrongly
deal with news of crime: by creat
ing sympathy for the undeserving;
making a hero of a criminal; pre
senting evidence which will preju
dice those who try the case, nnd giv
ing n distorted picture which feeds
morbid minds.
Class Shows Gain.

per cent increase in new students
in his department, 135 freshmen
registering this fall, as against 80
a year ago.

thers in the second pro game of the season at Athletic park
yesterday, 6 to 0, via the field goal route.
Two place kicks, with Don Curtin doing the booting,
one from the 30-yard line and another from the 35-yard
mark, accounted for the scoring. Both were made during
the second quarter when the Badgers were showing their
best wares.

turned Ashmore’s kick to the Pan
ther 30-yard line. The visitors were
unable to make downs and were
forced to punt.

when Dilweg intercepted a pass on

on his teammates with the result
that the oval was worked down to
the Panther’s five-yard lir..* The
Detroit delegation heid, however,
and pulled themselves out of dan
ger.

however when Neacy clamped
down two successive passes, one for
a 30-yard gain, the other for six
yards as the quarter ended.
Milwaukee was again held and
Curtin relied upon his toe for the
first score.

made possible through gains netted
by forward passes. Dilweg. after
catching a 15-yard pass, ran 25
yards before he was stopped, and
two plays later caught a 25-yard
pass. Both wore thrown by
Ileimscb.
The third quarter saw a return
of the midfield game, but in the last
peiod the Panthers clenly outplayed
the Badgers and started a drive
that was stopped only on Milwau
kee’s 10-yard line.
Dilweg, Bryan, Neacy and Ash
more starred for the locals. Vick,
Donne, Cohzelman and McNamara
for the visitors. About 2,500 at
tended the game.

Grimes’ head at first.

ARTIE BRACH
CAPTURES 150
MILE RACE
Artie Brach, Milwaukee racer,
emerged victor from a field of a
score of contestants in the 150-mile
dirt track championship race yester
day In the State Fair park. It was
one of the best races ever staged on
the Fair track.
In addition to winning the event,
Brach established a new world’s
record for 150 miles on a dirt track
—finishing In 2 hours 4 minutes
and 2-5 of a second.
Ten thousand persons witnessed
the races. Out of the 20 contest
ants entered in the event, only 10
finished, the race being marred by
several mishaps. Brach, after the
73rd lap, remained in front.
He was given keen competition by
Louis Schneider, considered the best
of the outside drivers.
Bill Laudon, Milwaukee, finished
second; Frank Brisko, third; Tudy
Mnrchese, fourth, and Russell Tru
dell, fifth.
Otto lost control of his
machine while rounding the north
turn, plunging through the fence.
His racer was demolished, but he
only suffered slight injuries.
F. Luppo lost a wheel directly In
front of the grand stand. The
wheel careened down the track, nar
rowly missing Policeman G. Baskin,
and struck a post.

centennial.

DETROIT—Tyrus Cobb will re
turn next year at the helm of the
Detroit Tigers, and, if he can get
the pitchers, will be right up in
the midst of the pennant fight, he
told the United Press.
“We have a young team.” Ty said,
“just a bunch of kids. They made
more hits than any other club and
drove in nearly as many runs. But
we didn’t have the pitching.
“Remember, when you see a team
having extended losing streaks, nine
times out of ten it’s the pitching,
because good pitchers will win now
and then even with poor batting.”
Cobb indicated he would play as a
“reserve” next season, if “needed.”

After two weeks of preliminary
work at the Lake Beulah training
camp, the Marquette university
football squad arrived in Milwaukee
today to continue workouts in the
university stadium.
While Coach Frank Murray has a
large aggregation of men out to
make the team, he is experiencing
great difficulty in the selection of
ends and tackles.
At Appleton Saturday.
Most of the week’s work will be
taken seriously in prei>aration for
the game with Lawrence college at
Appleton next Saturday. The Law
rence college warriors have long
looked forward to this game and ex
pect to give the Marquettters a stiff
argument.
Marquette alumni and friends are
making final plans for an intensive
ticket sales campaign for the 1920
home games.
The drive officially gets under
way tomorrow night ns the members
of the campaign teams and those in
charge of the undertaking get to
gethcr at a dinner at the Milwaukee
Athletic chib at 0:30. Conrad M.
Jennings, the Marquette athletic di
rector, will preside at the gathering
and Walter J. Abel, secretary,
Alumni Assn., is handling the ar
rangements.
Five Home Games.
Marquette has five home games
this fall, and all of them, three in
particular, should be stirring grid
battles. After meeting Lawrence
at Appleton next Saturday, the Hill
toppers return to Milwaukee to pre
pare for their reception of Grinnell
college of Grinnell, la., here Oct.
9. This will be a newcomer on the
Hilltop schedule, and the Hawkeye
eleven usually is one of the strong
est in the Missouri valley and last
season defeated Kansas. St. Mary's
college of Winona, Minn., will be
here Oct. 23.

6, again will be provided by the
flashy Kansas Aggies, who earned
a 2 to 0 decision over Marquette
here last year. North Dakota, said
to be stronger than ever, invades
Milwaukee Nov. 20, and the Oregon
Aggies, who scored a 67 to 0 victory

will come here Thanksgiving day,
Nov. 25. The Aggies on Saturday
scored more points on Multnomah
than they had accumulated in the
12 previous years, and yet reports
say they used but a few simple
plays.
Campaigners will offer a season
ticket for $7, and the order will call
for the same seat all season so that
the early buyers will get the choice
locations. Headquarters will be at
the Marquette gymnasium and
tickets may be purchased there.

The children and Jerry camp at
Indian Falls.
CHAPTER. Y.
Behind the Falls.
“Now we are in a fine fix,”
cried Jolly Jerry when they found
all their food supplies were gone.
“We haven’t a thing to eat.”
The children looked glumly at
him and at each other. Then
Jerry’s face brightened.
"I can gather berries! They
will help to fill us.”
"Hurrah!” shouted Jack. “Clyde
and I can catch more fish. We
will not starve.”
They ran for their rods. Jolly
Jerry joined them. Once more
they began to climb down the
cliff. L’ut Jack, who was ahead,
paused suddenly. “Look!” he
whispered as Janet had done the
night before.
All three did look. Dimly
through the mist appeared a fig
ure dressed like an Indian. It
seemed to come out of the falls.
It vanished into the depths of the
gorge. It came and went so quick
ly and so indistinctly that all
three wondered if their eyes, too,
had been playing tricks.
“Humph!” said Jolly Jerry
after they had stared several min
utes and seen nothing more. “It
Is foolish for us to be thinking
we are seeing things when we are
not. Come. Let’s get busy fish
ing or we will be mighty hungry
before we catch our breakfast.”
But though Jerry talked as
though he thought they had seen
nothing, the children noticed that
he carried his hunting ax, and he
made Janet go with them into the
gorge instead of remaining above
to pick berries.
Again the fishing proved good.
They quickly caught a fine mess
for breakfj.st.
Again Jack gave a cry os he
bent over the ground where he had
found the footprint the day be
fore. There were two prints now
where there had been one before.
“Humph!” said Jolly Jerry.
“There is a prowler about here.”
“The spirit of Chief Look-at-the-
Sky?” whispered Janet.
“Guarding the waterfalls from
white persons?” added Jack.
“Humph!” said Jolly Jerry.
“I'll bet we find this spirit is alive
and spry.”
“The thing we saw coming out
of the falls surely looked like a
spirit and an Indian spirit, too,”
insisted Clyde. “How could any
thing but a spirit come through
the water that way? That was
very strange.”

of falling water. “Humph! I
wonder!” said he. “Whatever I
have come upon anything very

had some simple explanation be

Janet’s face brightened,

closer look.”
Jolly Jerry clambered over the
rocks at the base of the falls. lie
got close to the tumbling waters.
He looked this way and that.
The children, at his order, hung
back and watched him. He
climbed up the bank a bit. And
suddenly, as their eyes were upon
him, he vanished.
“Oh!” screamed the children
together. “What has happened?”
As abruptly as he had vanished,
Jolly Jerry appeared again, seem
ing to come out of the water as
the mysterious figure had done.
He was grinning broadly. He mo
tioned them to join him, pointing
to the path he had climbed.
They scrambled up the slippery
rocks and stood beside him. He
turned and followed a path. They
saw to their astonishment that
the path rnn behind the falling
water. It led to a large cavern
behind the falls. The water came
down like a curtain in front of
the cavern, but none came inside
of it t!RI
But this was not the only sur
prise they got. In the cavern
were their food supplies, neatly
piled in a heap.
“Ha Ha laughed Jolly Jerry,
raising his voice so as to be
heard above the roar of the falls.
“Whoever haunts this cavern has
a big appetite, and I never heard
of a spirit beng hungry.”
How they learn the secret of
the falls will bo told in the next
chapter.

n note under the door of the girl’s

J. E. O'Hern, Chief
Of Armour Co.
Plants Is Dead
CHICAGO—A heavy cold which
developed into pneumonia caused
the death yesterday of John E.
O’Hern, general superintendent of
Armour Co. plants in the United
States. Mr. O’Hern had been ill in
St. Luke’s hospital several weeks.
Mr. O’Hern came to Chicago 40
years ago from Lawrence, Kan.,
where he was born. He entered the
employe of Armour Co. at the
age of 17 as a laborer. He was
sent to Omaha as plant superin
tendent in 1900, where he remained
12 years. He was promoted to gen
eral superintendent of plants and
returned to Chicago to live.
Mr. O’Hern’s social affiliations in
cluded membership in the Elks’
lodge, the Ilidge and South Shore
country clubs, the Saddle and Sir
loin club and the Knights of Colum
bus.
lie Is survived by his widow, two
brothers, Jnmos and Joseph, and
two sisters, Mrs. Charles A. Mc-
Mahon, and Sister Mary Gonzaga,
Sister of Mercy.
Serivce will be held Wednesday.

St. Louis railroad in favor of a

poned for at least 30 days.

looper that “leasing the Big Four to

diction and that the minority hold
ers should file their protest with the
interstate commerce commission.

poses to lease the Big Four at an

WASHINGTON Reorganization
of the Milwaukee road on the basis
proposed by Kuhn, Loeb Co., and
the National City Co., if approved
in the current fiscal year, will add
$50,000,000 to the United States
treasury receipts for the year and
increase by that amount whatever
surplus there is available at that
time.

ment $55,000,000. Of that amount
$20,000,000 is due the director gen
eral of railroads and $33,000,000 the
secretary of the treasury on account
of loans certified by the interstate
commerce commission.
James C. Davis, formerly director
general of railroads, declines to ap
prove the proposed settlement of
the $20,000,000 debt. Secretary
Mellon of the treasury, however, it
is understood, looked with favor on
the offer, and he now is director
general of railroads, so the offer of
the $20,000,000 rests with him.

CHICAGO—The early touch of
winter which swept over the middle
west over the week end continued to
day, according to reports of the
,weather bureau here.
In Chicago the temperatures re
mained low following the Sunday
touch of frost. The lowest tem
perature recorded Sunday was 38
degrees.
Frost was reported through the
greater portion of northern Illinois
Sunday, extending as fur south as
Peoria. Ice was reported on many
small streams,
The lower temperatures were gen
eral over a great portion of the agri
cultural region, the weather bureau
reported today. Corn suffered a con
siderable loss as a result of the pre
season freezes.

HOW WISCONSIN CAN LEAD
In order to retain its leadership in social progress,
Wisconsin should lead ail other' American states in So
cialism. Every attempt to make social progress by a de
tour around the Socialist program inevitably leads back
into the old party corral.
The Socialist party is here to stay and to grow. It
is rapidly recovering from the slump which the war psy
chology and left-wing fanaticism Inflicted on it. In pro
portion as this party gains strength in Wisconsin, the
progressive elements in the old parties will need its sup
port against the standpat machines.
We welcome the present realignment in the camp
of old party progressivism as a healthy sign of mental
growth. We believe that the majority of the Wisconsin
progressives want to get out of old party rut and clean
their ranks of standpat adventurers sailing under a pro
gressive flag.
The Socialist party does not expect the progressive
voters to become Socialists over night. We know very
well that new ideas grow slowly. We don’t value a sudden
conversion. But we put it to the progressive voters who
realize that they need the help of the Socialists to beat the
standpat adventurers whether good judgment and honest
politics do not demand that they should familiarize them
selves with the ideas of the Socialists more than hereto
fore.
In the coming years, the same fight whjch the honest
progressives are now forced to face against Zimmerman
and his standpat helpers will always crop up again in
some form. Again and again the progressive voters will
be called upon to make up their minds whether to vote for
a standpatter sailing under progressive colors or for a
real progressive on the Socialist ticket.
The Socialist party has proved again and again that
it knows how to distinguish between honest progressives
and false progressives. It has never abandoned a real pro
gressive. Naturally it supports its own candidates, whom
it knows well, rather than outsiders whom it -does not
know through long association. But where its own candi
dates have been out of the running, the Socialists have
always backed real progressives against the standpatters.
We are convinced that future party battles will bring
real progressives and Socialists closer and closer together.
But that is not enough to insure social progress in a con
structive direction. We believe that many progressives
realize this already and will vote for Socialist candidates
with the firm resolve to get better acquainted with Social
ist principles and methods. For this reason we are en
couraged to believe that Wisconsin will lead the other
states in Socialism.
THE SPOKESMAN’S STANDARD
President Coolidge lets it be known that he will not
recognize, the Moscow government, until it rules “in ac
cordance with our standards.” If that's all he wants, he
can recognize Soviet Russia right away.
The Washington government claims to represent de
mocracy, liberty and modern enlightenment, but it ex
cluded Count Karolyi for the benefit of the American
millionaires whose daughters are married to Hungarian
reactionaries. The Moscow government claims to be the
most advanced and fairest government in the world, but it
excludes Socialist press writers for the benefit of foreign
and native concession hunters.
We don’t see any difference between these two
“standards." They look to us like twins. Besides, both
the Washington and Moscow governments have identical
economic and political interests in China. Both of them
conceal their selfish interests in China under the identical
phrases of sentimental friendship.
Anyway, there is already so much American money
invested in European and Asiatic Russia and in their
common neighbor China, that “our standards" of govern
ment will find it extremely convenient to stress that
identity of interests more and more. The Spokesman can
take another hitch in his tight mind and play the coy
beauty, but Moscow and Washington will get together
soon just as they did when the czar of all the Russias
and Teddy Roosevelt swapped yarns with W. J. Bryan.

Hell-Maria Dawes, who wants to cut down the range
of hot air in the United States senate by a gag rule for
the anti-standpatters, suddenly blossoms forth as a cham
pion of free air for all radio users. What great fi.'ticn
writers some statesmen would make!
There is no free air for radio users. The radio trust
has already fixed things so that only its own standpat
crowd can ride the radio waves with its bunk, and e\cry
opponent of standpatism finds himself gagged, either by
refusals to broadcast or by interference from high-power
stations. We will believe that Dawes believes in free radio
when we hear his opponeuk; as freely as his barking.

als of this limitation.
A crowd is like an exaggerated

Intelligent questioning that

tioner special knowledge can bring

Fear of making some such ef
fect deters many questioners.

ardice manifest like courage. Peo

THE RED HAND OF CAPITAL
A recent appeal of the Lithuanian government to the
league of nations warns Europe that the Polish govern
ment is preparing for a new attack on its Baltic neighbor.
Whether this warning is voluntary or inspired, based upon
facts or imaginary, it emphasizes the fact that the Baltic,
like the Mediterranean, is a sporting ground of secret
diplomacy.
The Leader reported from time to time that British
and French diplomacy were contending for supremacy
along the eastern and southern borders of European Rus
sia. British diplomacy made Finland, Latvia and Es
thonia its strategic bases against Soviet Russia.
The French influence has not yet given way to the
British in Poland. French naval squadrons visited the
Danzig zone while British maneuvered in the same region.
The efforts of the Danzig people to free themselves from
Polish dictation succeeded only in part.
In proportion as French and German statesmen and
business leaders try to get together on common ground,
the British influence over continental Europe loses its
strategic points. The British influences did not succeed
in forcing Lithuania into a British-controlled Baltic en
tente. The little country remained a natural overland
link between*Germany and Soviet Russia.
The British front in China has collapsed. Soviet in
fluence has made progress in Afghanistan, Kashmir and
Thibet. The French position in Cochin-China makes the
Singapore naval and air base insecure in case of a war
against two fronts.
It becomes more and more a matter of life and death
for British imperialism to create a diversion against Soviet
Russia in Europe. If British diplomacy can use Poland
as a cat’s-paw to attack Lithuania and cut the overland
route between Germany and Russia, the British position
in the Baltic will be stronger.
So the red hand of capital reaches into the heart of
Europe and stirs two nations into enmity which have the
same great political and economic interests. United with
a French-German-Russian entente, Poland and Lithuania
would guarantee the peace of Europe. Pitted against
each other, they become a menace to the peace of the
whole world.
The interests of all classes of American citizen can
be served best by promoting peace in Europe and refusing
to back the British intrigues. This is also the best way to
get out of British entanglements in China.
The American people can gain nothing but a chance
to waste more men and money by saving British imperial
ism from its inevitable fate. Our future relations with
Canada, Australia, Central and South America will be
more friendly and mutually helpful by forcing British
foreign policy to adjust itself to the trend towards the
national independence of China and the peaceful economic
progress of Soviet Russia.
During the world war, the Wilson government as
sumed the obligation to be a collector of tribute for British
imperialism in Mexico and Central America. Wilson did
the dirty work for the British imperialists also in East
India on the false theory that the British navy protected
American interests.
It is different now. American capitalism has a stake
in Germany and Russia that it dare not sacrifice for the
benefit of British imperialism. Perhaps this will save V
American people from the folly of a war which the Brk
foreign office would like to wage at the expense of tn
American taxpayer.

“Educate” the worker, cries the anti-unionist, who
would now control the worker’s mind.

militia, the clubber and the injunction judge. Books with
out number are being written on the new system and its
value to anti-union employers who are striving to have
employes acquire their economic viewpoint.
Behind the assumed candor and simplicity of latter
day Pecksniffs looms the fact that employes are denied
the right to select their own representatives. They must
bargain with spokesmen the employer approves.
There is but one answer to this policy. Eventually,
tradition must yield, as it has before. But that time will
not automatically come, no more than did the eight-hour
day, free school books, compensation statutes, safety laws,
passing of the company store and a nation-wide opposition
to child labor.
Regardless of its disguise, reaction must surrender
its control of workers’ lives. This control is backed by
the most ancient traditions. The lines of this hoary con
cept must be broken along its entire front. The trade
unions have won maip'' positions in this long struggle to
establish new viewpoints. It must continue to do so.
Tradition will yield to experience in proportion to
the education and agitation of unions.—American Federa
tion of Labor News.

RUMOR BLIND
MOVE HERE TO
GET PENSIONS
Hints that the blind of Wisconsin
are being colonized in Milwaukee to
get the benefit of its blind pension
liberality, were made late yesterday,
by members of the county board
committee on county and state insti
tutions, following a session in which
14 blind pensions were approved
and added to a list that is already
larger than was dreamed of when
the county set up the system.
"Of course it is only a suspicion,
and I have no tangible proof,” said
one supervisor.
"But there is a strong suspicion
that some agency is at work induc
ing blind people in the state to re
move to Milwaukee, live here long
enough to acquire a legal residence
and then apply for a pension. We
hope we are wrong, but there were
never such a lot of blind living in
Milwaukee as now, and the number
seems steadily on the increase.”
Under the law a county can elect
to pay blind pensions and the state
agrees to re-emburse the said county
to the extent of one-third of the
cost, provided the fund set up by
each legislature has not become ex
hausted.
Many counties have not gone In
on the proposition, nnd thus become
less favorable places of residence
for those afflicted with loss of their
sight.

fessional Women's club, worked
night as well as day superintending

clothing, food and medical supplies
in the stricken area.

wrote that coast residents were

That building houses the Continuation school. It was there always for it is a new building. For merly this square was occu pied for the most part by a number of factory buildings and shacks—a stove foun dry. Continued education for our youth is a recent ven ture in the United States. In Germany the continua tion school (Fortbildung’s Schule) has been a part of the educational system for more than 40 years. It is said that the “Fort bildung’s Schulen” in that country deserves much credit for the part they have played in the training of high class mechanics for which Germany is noted. During the years that followed the first Socialist victories in 1904, one of the Socialist aidermen never missed an opportunity to present to his audiences the following word picture of the injustices done to our chil dren by the school system of Milwaukee. He said in part: “We men an J women of Milwaukee send cur chil dren to the public schools from about 6 years of age to 14 years. During that time we spend on each child each year $24. At about 14 years of age they graduate. “When they graduate, we separate them into two groups. (Of course it must be groups, since we have no classes.) Of each 100 children we pick 80, which we send to the high schools. On each one 'of these that we send to the high schools we now spend S4B instead of $24 every year. “There is nothing wrong with that. If there is one thing that we owe to our children and to which they are entitled, that thing is an education. “But what do we do to the other 80 out of every 100? “We send them to the factories, the mills, and the shops; we make them produce wealth, eight hours, nine hours, 10 hours a day, six days a week and 52 weeks a year. Then we assess the wealth they produce and col lect taxes therefrom. Then we take the money we have collected from the wealth produced by the 80 of every 100 children and spend it for the education of the 20 of every 100. “But we do not spend another cent for the education of the 80 children out of every 100. We boast of our democracy, our civilization, our Christianity; but we are not democratic, neither are we civilized, nor are we Christian so long as we do one thing to the 20 and an other thing to the 80 of our children.” It was this simple description of a crying social in justice (together with the exposes of other equally great wrongs) which stirred the voters to express their dissatisfaction with things as they were. In 1908 the city of Milwaukee came within a few thousand votes of being carried by the Socialists. In 1909 the legislature finally appointed a committee of five Wisconsin citizens, prominent in educational mat ters, to study the question and report to the legislature. In 1910 the Socialists carried the municipal and county elections and also elected a congressman. At the very next session of the legislature in 1911, the Contin uation school law was passed. TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 28. 1926 THE MILWAUKEE VOCATIONAL SCHOOL Prior to the time that this law was passed, the school laws and educational practice were concerned chiefly with those who could attend school full time, or in the day time. The Continuation school is to serve the purpose of giving the boy and girl, who are obliged to go to work when they graduate from the elementary school an opportunity to continue to get an education. The Wisconsin law is very broad and permits a latitude wide enough to serve all the needs of its pupils. In that way it is an aid to the boy and girl who has chosen a vocation; it can aid the boy and girl, who have no vocation, to find themselves and it can aid all others to find something in life that will give that life a content. R. L. Cooley, who is the director of the school, has a broad understanding of the problem confronting this institution; of the practical needs that it should supply, and a keen vision of a cultural goal that he aims at. Above all, he loves his work and the youth that seeks his aid. Good will toward all radiates from his words when he says: “I think it is a fair conclusion to say that, in the interest of everybody, those who leave school early must be given further opportunity. Those who have their plans interfered with by unexpected responsibilities must be given a chance. Those who develop late must be given a chance. Those who start wrong and find it out on time must be given a chance. Those who have a chance and need assistance must be given help. Those who have had a chance and need another must be given it.” And again he says: “The wealth of our nation lies in its manhood and womanhood, not in some indirect, remote and fanciful way, but positively, directly, and, in a way, sus ceptible of mathematical demonstrations. That nation prospers most that best conserves and develops its hu man element.” The Continuation school was not handed to the city of Milwaukee as a gift on a platter, conceived and born from the brain of a few intellectual leaders. It grew out of the voice in the wilderness, that reverberated in the thousands of votes which protested against the par tiality shown the 80 out of every 100. Encouraging as are the results that have already been attained, the institution has only begun its work and has yet a great field to cover. No one realizes this better than does Mr. Cooley. climax last night with Gen. Primo

fluence to establish a republic.

to decide whether he will indorse
Dictator de Rivera’s plan and con
tinue the present military dictator
ship, appoint a new dictator, or try
to bring about a parliamentary gov
ernment as the party leaders de
mand.

professors, educators, doctors and
lawyers, is anti-constitutional and
that the constitution of Spain pro
vides for a parliamentary assembly,
and none other will be satisfactory.

ously refrained from the controversy
now are also protesting against the
proposed assembly, and when they
learn it is planned to make it a
patent farce, it is expected they will
demand that King Alfonso remove
Gen. de Rivera.

cates he intends to apply a rigid
censorship of speech as well as pub
lication of proceedings of the assem
bly, adopting the principles of Pre
mier Benito Mussolini's iron rule.

lessly for the king to make his de

IN DIAN APO LIS, I nd.—Revela
tion of a super-government within
the state over which David C. Steph
enson, at the zenith of his power as
grand dragon of the Hoosier Ku
Klux Klan, held sway, was promised
today by Thomas Adams, Vincennes,
head of a probe committee of the
Indiana Republican Editorial Assn.
The committee has been delving
for months into the political activ
ities of Stephenson, who is now serv
ing a life sentence in the state pris
on at Michigan City for the murder
of Miss Madge Oberholtzer, of In
dianapolis.
“Controlled Courts, Too.”
Documents of an astrounding na
ture, letters, pictures and other evi
dence have come into possession of
the committee which show conclu
sively that Stephenson’s “word was
law in Indiana” that he manipulat
ed appointments and forced courts
to do his bidding under threat of
political destruction, Adams said,
lie claims many of Stephenson's
former workers assisted in the
probe.
Some of these former lieutenants
or “Klockards” have made signed
statements, Adams announced, re
vealing for the first time the story
of Stephenson’s mysterious political
power built on the foundation of the
Kn Klux Klan organization.
Tell of Frameup.
These confessions, according to
Adams, tell of “framed” charges
against the state highway commis
sion of corruption methods in the
last session of the state legislature,
of the sale of various bills and who
got the money and of contracts
made in writing to control the acts
of public officials, both in city and
state government in Indiana.
Serious charges have already been
placed with the American Bar Assn,
against certain officials and lawyers
as a result of the investigation,
Adams announced.
The information obtained by the
Investigators will be placer! before
state and federal grand juries with
a demand for a thorough house
cleaning of the Stephenson faction
in Indiana politics, Adams said.

No One Minds Weather.
Or they all gather in the huge
library, an enormous and elegant
room lined from floor to painted
ceiling with yellowed and inviting
volumes. It is an even choice, and
no one minds inclement weather.
The while, Taft looks every ounce

on the table, and yet another King
Edward VII lends a reminiscently

Tea in the garden at 4:30, more
likely than not, is attended by the
Countess of Warwick herself, still
showing evidence of her former
beauty and giving substance to the
stories of early days, when being
a Socialist in England was not the
easy thing it now is, and when, al
though she was the king’s friend,
Lady Warwick daringly espoused
the perilous cause and won for her
pains the contempt of a large part
of the British aristocracy and the
grateful devotion of thousands of

Still “Picture Lady.”
She is still the “picture lady”—
pretty, perfumed, powdered
though she must be over GO, and
she drifts graciously about among
the textile workers and miners, a
fairj- god-mother smile on her face,
touching the scene always, with an
air of unreality.
The whole bouse has been given
over to the use of the Independent
Labor party, and Lady Warwick
has converted the stables into rooms
for herself. There, with a dozen or
more dogs of every kind and de
scription, she lives in theatrically
picturesque state. A preposterous
collection of great divans covered by
rare tapestries, fur rugs, oil paint
ings and outrageously decorated
walls make a desperate effort to
convert the huge and unrecogniz
able stables into an incongruous sul
tana's bower. At the far end of
one long room is a magnificent can
opied bed, raised like those in ex
travagant stage settings, on a little
platform. And everywhere, in this
profusion of luxuries, there yelp and
sniff and scamper the lady’s dogs.

Legend swathes this noblewom
ans life in the most romantic and

us beautiful as always, and cour
ageous—at once the king s great

tically at the remote end of the

come upon it at all is rare, and to

el. and studded with pointed leaded

ries.

puzzled today over the disappear
ance of John Cooper—its cherished

Tells of Gift.
Cooper, after many weeks spent

pulpit of the first Presbyterian
church Sunday that he had de
posited checks in two Kewanee
banks for the construction of the
new church and nurses home.
The checks were drawn on a De
troit bank which he said held the
first $200,000 of the estate.

The Kewanee bankers investi
gated and found that Cooper did
not have an account In the Detroit
bank and today the checks were
forwarded there for identification.
Immediately afterward Cooper
left town.
“Wait and see,” was Cooper’s
parting shot as he drove away in
an expensive automobile.

“On the basis of the estimated yield of gasoline by
straight distillation in 1925, it would have required
approximately 287,000,000 barrels, additional, of
crude oil to furnish the gasoline made by cracking
processes.”
This quotation from a circular published by the
U. S. Bureau of Mines, indicates the extent of the
sendee rendered by the Standard Oil Company
(Indiana) in discovering and developing commer
cially successful prdeesses for cracking gasoline.
The widespread use of the cracking processes,
effecting a saving of 287,000,000 barrels of crude
in 1925, is largely the result of the action of the
Standard Oil Company (Indiana) in leasing its
processes to competitors.
The Standard Oil Company (Indiana) did not
maintain a monopoly of the processes it discovered,
because unwavering loyalty to the people of the
Middle West and an unfaltering integrity of pur
pose in serving them, prohibited such a course.
Ultimately, it is the people who benefit from the
widespread use of cracking processes.
Without the widespread leasing of these processes,
the motorists of the country would have been
forced to shoulder the cost of "bringing in” 287,-
000,000 additional barrels of crude oil, or of going
without the use of their cars.
Moreover, it is extremely doubtful if 287,000,000
additional barrels of crude oil could have been
produced in 1925, regardless of the money expended
to discover it.
The importance of the process for producing gas
oline by cracking in conserving an essential natural
resource of the nation cannot be estimated.
Its importance to the future of oil conservation is
suggested by the Bureau of Mines’ circular which
says: "There is probably no one factor that is
more important with regard to a future supply of
motor fuel than a more extended use of thecrack
ing process in the refineries of the country."
The conservation of 287,000,000 barrels of crude
resulting, directly and indirectly, from scientific
work in the research laboratories of the Standard
Oil Company (Indiana) is a sensational saving.
Yet it is but one far-reaching result of the quiet,
unpretentious work that is going on every day in
the laboratories of this Company. It is but one of
the fruits of steady, untiring labor and persistent
effort.
This sensational economy was made possible by
the ordinary, every-day integrity that governs the
Standard Oil Company (Indiana) in all its activi
ties —an integrity that has made the name of the
Standard Oil Company (Indiana) a guarantee of
dependability.
The reputation of the Standard Oil Company (In
diana) is due to no sudden or spectacular effort.
It has been built slowly and solidly by the simple
process of hard work, animated by the desire to
serve the thirty million people of the Middle West
sincerely and efficiently.

fessional standing on the managers

BIG TEN FROWNS
ON LONG GRID
JOURNEYS
CHlCAGO—Officials of Big Ten
universities will discourage mass
migrations of students to football
games this fall, but not because
Wilfred O. Cross made an alleged
expose of what happened on such
trips.
Prof. O. F. Long, chairman, ath
letic committee, Northwestern uni
versity, said yesterday that the mat
ter was discussed nt a Big Ton
meeting last May and it was decid
ed then that no college would take
any hand in promoting trips to out
of town games. He added that no
large blocks of tickets were to be
set aside for visiting students.
At the University of Chicago,
Vice-president Frederick Woodward
said the Cross attack had nothing
to do with the rule. There had been
complaints of disorder on such jour
neys, he admitted, and several stu
dents traveling in automobiles had
been injured, but the decision to
advise against the mass movements
was made months ago, he added.
There is no definite bar against
students making trips on their own
initiative, both university officials
declared. Loss of time in classes,
they said, was serious when the
trips were too long.
Form Athletic Club
For Girls at
Washington High
Wahiat, Washington High school's
girls’ athletic club, has been organ
ized for the year and plans for an
active season of sports among the
girls.
If enough girls sign up, a bowling
club will be organized.
The Wahiat basketball league will
function as usual this winter, with
the classes divided into teams and
in the end deciding a faculty-stu
dent championship.
The officers of the Wahiat for the
next term are: Evelyn Jaeschke,
president; Bernadette Van Dyke,
vice-president; Sylvia Khimb, sec
retary: Dorothy Erickson, treas
urer Nellie Havens and Adele Falk,
faculty advisors.
Snaplock Dummy at
Washington High
Coach Lisle Blackbourn of Wash
ington High has instituted several
new ideas in training his team for
the 1926 race. One of the features
of Blackbourn’s equipment is the
snaplock dummy, which enables the
tacklers to put some snap and spirit
into their work without fear of
hurting themselves.
He also Is emulating the baseball
managers, in that he holds skull
practice sessions every day before
school starts. Everyone connected
with the team, even the manager,
attends these brain periods.

Sunrise A. C. Cops
Volley Ball Title
The Sunrise A. C. representing
the Cleveland Ave. playground, won
its fourth All-City volley ball cham
pionship by defeating decisively the
Auer A. C. of the Auer Ave. play
ground by the scores of 15 to 2 and
15 to 8, in the championship game'
at the Scott St. playground.
The Sunrise A. C. went through
the 1926 season without losing a
single game.
Five teams, all of which won the
sectional championship in their sec
tions, were entered in the champion
ship games. Sunrise A. C. and Auer
A. C. by eliminating the other teams
met in the final game for the city
championship.
Medals were awarded the cham
pions by the extension department
of the Milwaukee public school
board.
