Pitching Advantage With Cardinals in Coming Series
ST. LOUIS ALSO HAS
BEST CATCHER IN
808 O’FARRELL
NEW YORK—Since the days when the champion Chi
cage White Sox were the hitless wonders, through suc
cessive years to the Brooklyn Robins of 1920 and until the
era of the lively ball, the importance of a battery was fully
realized.
Even through the mad home run days of the “rabbit
ball,” the spectators at a ball game were interested chiefly
in—who’s going to pitch.”
Now that some of the life has been taken out of the
ball, the battery strength of baseball teams has gained in
importance and in the coming series when two slugging
teams are to battle for the world series, the comparative
strength of the batteries is of vital importance.
The catchers can lie disposed of
easily.
O’Farrell Leads Catchers.
With Bob O’Farrell working l>e
hind the plate for the St. Louis Car
dinals, ths National league cham
pions will be fortified much strong
er than the Yankees.
O’Farrell not only is regarded ns
the best catcher of the year in the
major leagues, but he is the rank
ing candidate for the National
league’s most valuable player prize.
He worked in 14(5 games for the
Cardinals during the regular sea
son and there is no doubt that he
will be able to last through the se
ries.
The Yankees will have to depend
upon old Hank Severeid, who is a
good mechanical catcher, but not a
star. Benny Bengough had a weak
arm all season that finally was
broken in Cleveland. Pat Collins
has a terrible throwing arm and
when he began to lose games the
Yankees claimed Severeid on waiv
ers from the Washington Senators.
Cards Have Best Pitchers.
w Behind the bat—a most vital spot
—the Cardinals wiil be at least 25
j>er cent stronger than the Yan-
kees.
Both teams have good pitchers,
but St. Ixniis has more good pitch
ers than the Yankees have and
while the Yankees have good re-,
serve pitchers they may have to be
used oftener.
In Haines. Rh'un. Reinhart, Alex
ander and Sherd el the St. Louis
club has a more dependable start
of pitchers than the Yankees hare
in Pennock, Shocker;Reuther, Hoyt,
Jones and Shawkey.
Miller Huggins always Las neon
strong on pitching and he would
have had his favorite “five-star”
staff this year if Hoyt’s arm had not
gone bad, if Jones had not dHap*
pointed and if Shawkey had not
lieen injured.
ReutiM'r May Star.
As it stands now the Yankees
have only two dependable pitchers,
Pennock and Shocker, but Dutch
Reuther may prove to be the man of
the hour. For some reason Bucky
Harris wouldn’t use him for Wash
ington In the series last year and to
wards the tail of the season this
year he asked waivers on him. Hug
•rins grabbed him- and he may use
m in the series.
Reuther, one of the best pitchers
the game, is on the threshold
headed toward the minors and he
certainly ought to have sufficient in
ducement to work if he is called
upon to pitch.
Rogers Hornsby is much better
off with Haines, Rhem, Alexander
nnd Rbordel. Alexander’s average
doesn’t look as inspiring as the
others but with Bob O'Farrell catch

Alex Strengthens Cards.
Chicago released Alex because he

Some of the critics, who favor
might above skill, say that the Cin

the Yankees in battery strength.

been destroyed by recent floods,

hunters, men of ordinary means,
will enjoy duck shooting for the
first time in several years.
Thousands of acres of cornfields
along the Mississippi, Illin'ois, San
gamon and other rivers are now
covered with water varying In
depth from one to 10 feet or more.
It is doubtful if much of this corn
will mature sufficiently to make
even duck feed. But in every corn
field there is an abundance of
smartweed nnd other natural food,
he pointed out.

fore, In view of father’s bland
admonition, mother swathed her
self in an overall apron and gave
herself exactly four hours of busy
preparations in the kitchen dur
ing the course of which every
piece of silver was polished, the
best china set was brought out,
and culinary exercises brought
into play virtually every pot, pan
and other implement, down to
the last mixing spoon.
It was into this hive of indus
try that Diane ushered herself,
after her early departure from
the office, which had made pos
sible her escape from Phil Os
borne’s proffered entertainment.
“I don’t need a bit of help,”
her mother bad exclaimed, with a
nod of satisfaction, as she ex
plained that^Capt. D’Armand was
to lie fetched home by father to
dinner.
“Heavens!” murmured Diane.
She did not view the prospect of
Capt. D’Armand’s appearance
with the least bit of enthusiasm.
The truth was, that she had been
fearfully let down by what had at
first seemed her idle conversation
with Dr. Sam Patrick. Now, she
believed that he had intentionally
sought to warn her against asso
ciating with Phil Osborne. But
surely, Osborne was not so dan
gerous that she stood in need of
warning. Had this come from
any but Dr. Patrick, she would
not have thought twice about the
matter. But she could not doubt
his intention and she could not
question his judgment. The whole
business had left a bitter taste in
her mouth and she felt in no mood
to smile sweetly and say polite
nothings to Capt. D’Armand. She
wondered aguely if he would
smell of horses and if he would
wear a horseshoe of brilliants in
his necktie.
“Now, Diane, you go right up
stairs and get dressed,” said Mrs.
Colfax busily, whipping the may
onnaise. “Better fix your hair
up a little, too.”
“You'd think the Prince of
Wales was coming," Diane
laughed carelessly.
“Well, I know father sets a lot
of store by Capt. D’Armand,” her
mother said, “and I want every
thing to be real nice.”
Diane negligently went upstairs
and satisfied herself with a very
casual toilette.
It was rather curious how Capt.
D’Armand struck them, the mem
bers of the Colfax clan, that night.
In the first place, the captain was
not at all what the Colfax women
had painted him. He was by no
means an exquisite nor a per
fumed dandy. He looked more
like a successful young lawyer, or
perhaps one given to a pursuit of
the arts, but in a wholesome,
rugged way, rather than against

was something about him which

Capt. D’Armand allowed no

“How many times were you
shot?” demanded Richard.
“Eight,” answered the captain,
solemnly.
“Aw—Alex Anderson, he works
down In Ringling’s Smoke Shop—
he’s got 51 holes in him. Shrap
nel. He had about a million op
erations, and beside that, he got
two fingers shot off and a glass

“Richard!”
Dick exchanged glances with his
mother.
“Aw. Well.”
Capt. D’Armand was lyrically
optimistic about the prospects for
the popularity and success of the
riding association’s venture. He
intimated that he had only accept
ed the appointment as permanent
master of ceremonies (that is the
title he permitted himself) with
the greatest reluctance.
“You see, Madame, I have

Mrs. Colfax nodded sympathet
ically.

a side glance at Diane. He
thought he detected a sign of
sympathy there. “My family was
deprived of its fortune, which was
very large. Not that we have lost

Diane studied the man’s face

it was the strange foreign air

seemed so beautifully polite with

could pay compliments and make

thing, Diane thought, he always
makes such a botch of it. Yes,
she liked the captain—and he

He took his departure after cof

“Please remember, madame,”
he said with his adieu to Mrs.
Colfax, “that I shall place at your
disposal the two very best horses
we have and my services will ever
be at your disposal.” He turned
to Diane with his finished Con
tinental bow. “And your’s, tou,
mademoiselle.”
The family sat silently for a
moment as he stepped gracefully
through the gate and turned into
the street with a final salute in
their direction.
“I think that fellow will make
a hit in this town,” said father.
“I shouldn’t be surprised," Mrs.
Colfax answered in a curious way.
She seemed undecided about Capt.
D’Armand, but her unfailing in
stinct that is a part of mother
hood was fermenting within her.
“He hr harming manners,

“Aw, he’s stuck on himself. He
makes me sick.”
“Richard—such language,” from
mother in a weary voice. She
turned to Diane and said with a
little more interest: “So you think
rather well of our importation?"
Diane felt a barb that irritated
her.
“Well, he's at least a gentle
man.’’ she answered. And then
added wickedly: “And he’ll be
rich some day.”
“Maybe.” replied her mother
cryptically.

Health Talks
BY WILLIAM BRADY, M. D.
COLLOID.IL lead treat
ment OF CANCER.
Fifteen years ago Wassermann
and Keysser found that the salts
of tellurium and selenium would
destroy cancer cells when injected
into the cancer, hut when doses
sufficient to do this were injected
into the blood stream the effect
was as likely to prove lethal to
the host. The idea of these and
many other scientific investiga
tors was to find a remedy which
would destroy cancer cells when
administered through the blood
stream, yet not attack the normal
cells of the body.
Colloidal copper, colloidal sil
ver, colloidal gold, colloidal sele
nium, colloidal sulphur and vari
ous combinations of these have
been tested by research workers,
both on animals and on human be
ings, and these observations and
experiments have warranted at
least the hope that some remedy
might be found which, when in
jected into the blood stream,
would attack or destroy or even
impair the vitality of cancer
cells without seriously injuring
the normal body cells.
In 1920 Dr. Blair Bell of Liver
pool began the treatment of hu
man cancer by injections of col
loidal lead into the veins. The
colloidal form of lead was select
ed because various lead compounds
had been found too poisonous, to
the host.
Out of 227 patients with other
wise hopelessly advanced cancer,
that is, cancer advanced beyond
the hope of any relief by the one
remedy we have today, surgery,
this treatment with colloidal lead
has to its credit 50 patients who
have lived from one to five years
with complete arrest of the can
cer.
Speaking of this extraordinary
record, Dr. Francis C. Wood, di
rector of the institute of cancer
research, says: “For the first
time a substance has been found
that will arrest the growth of
cancinoma for a period of from
one to five years, and this in pa
tients both inoperable and beyond
the power of irradiation to effect
a cure.”
Bell himself says much remains
to be done in order to diminish
the danger of this treatment. The
injection of colloidal lead in the
method Blair devised is a highly
dangerous procedure, for it is
necessary to approach a lethal
dose to the host, and this calls
for the highest skill and judg
ment as well as special clinical
experience on the part of the phy
sician.
In animals the injection of the
colloidal lead preparation causes
intense congestion of the cancer
for 24 hours, with subsequent cap
illary thrombosis, necrosis and
shrinkage. In human beings a
great deal of pain occurs in the
first 24 hours after injection,
then the patient becomes more
comfortable. Doses are given
about once a week for three
months. However, Bell feels
from his own experience that
“the time is not yet ripe for the
general employment of lead.” Sci
entific students of cancer every
where are working on this line
now, and there is some ground
for hope that a weapon may be
found which will be of some use
against this most baffling of
modern plagues. That Bell has
no illusions about the colloidal
lead treatment being a specific
“cancer cure” is evident in his
practice of operating on all oper
able cases, as he believes that of
fers the best chance, reserving the
colloidal lead treatment for car
cinoma or sarcoma cases which
are beyond hope of surgery.

VALUE OF FRUITS.
The healthfulness of fruit is so
well known that while we may not
support the claims of those who be
lieve we should subsist on fruits
and vegetables entirely, we are will
ing to credit them with great vir
tue. It is also interesting to know
what is said about them.
Lemons and limes were found so
necessary for the health of the
sailors that as far back as 18G3
England passed a law requiring all
her ships to carry sufficient lime
or lemon juice so that each member
of the crew might receive a daily
ration of one ounce, to prevent
scurvy.
We turn to lemons and oranges
in time of sickness, their acidity
and refreshing qualities often being
the one thing that a feverish patient
craves.
Lemon juice is used as a bleach
to soften the skin and remove stains.
Mixed with buttermilk it is said to
dispel freckles.
Lemon juice applied to bites and
stings of insects will relieve at once.
As a mouth wash, lemon juice in
a glass of water dissolves tartar on
the teeth and sweetens the breath.
When washing the hair a lemon
rinse takes out the last remnant of
soap and leaves the hair soft and
lustrous.
A glass of lemonade without sug
ar, taken the first thing in the
morning is a fine remedy for that
tired feeling.
Lemon juice and salt will remove
rust stains if laid in the sun.
Grapefruit is said to contain a
substance similar to quinine. This
fruit has been recommended in case
of grippe and flu, and is also good
for that tired feeling. Those who
know say that the proper way to
prepare it for medicine is to grind
it, pulp, seeks, skin and all, cover
with boiling water and let stand un
til the mixture gets cold. Strain
aiul take in small doses three times
a day. Those who like quinine will
probably enjoy this. —Nellie Max
well.
Apple Butter.
Take two gallons of sweet cider
and boil down to six quarts or one
quarter. Wash one-half bushel of
good tart apples, cut them up and
cover but do not peel. Put with
cider in a large preserving kettle,
cook all day, stirring frequently, to
prevent scorching. When dark red
and smooth put the mass through
a colander to remove skins, add two
cups sugar (more if desired), four
teaspoons cinnamon, two teaspoons
clover, one-half teaspoon allspice,
cook a little longer and put in jars.
Will keep without sealing.
Burnt Caramel Cake.
One-half cup butter, one cup
brown sugar, two eggs, four table
spoons burn caramel, one-half cup
buttermilk, four tablespoons corn
starch, two teaspoons baking pow
der, one-half teaspoon soda, two
cups flour and vanilla. Cream but
ter and sugar, add eggs one at a
time, beat well after adding each
egg. Then the caramel. Sift the
dry ingredients together about four
times, then add milk and dry ingre
dients one at a time alternately,
beating after each addition, and
bake in a sheet pan or two layers.
One cup nuts, chopped, and added,
improves it. and use a peanut butter
icing or O-llenry icing. Way to pre
pare burn caramel is: Put one cup
dry sugar over fire and cook until
black, stirring constantly, then pour
one cup of water into it and let boil
until a sirup, and pour into a pitch
er or glass and set aside for use.
Buttermilk Pie.
One-half cup sugar, two eggs, one
heaping tablespoon flour, one pint
fresh buttermilk, one tensjtoon
lemon extract. Put sugar and flour
in pan and make a paste of it with
a little of the buttermilk, then add
the yolks of two eggs and stir well.
Add the rest of the buttermilk, cook
in double boiler until thick, then re
move and stir in the lemon extract.
Make an icing of the whites of eggs
and one-half cup sugar and spread
on top and brown in oven.

DOWN MADDEN LANE.
BY JANE OSBORN.
“Well, if you don't go with Jim,
how in the world nre you going to
get to the dance?” said Dora,
who, nt 24, felt herself quite the
sensible, old married woman.
Her sister Julie, sitting beside
her before the spacious fireplace,
pouted by way of answer.
‘‘Do I have to go?” she asked at
length.
“Certainly,” was the elder sis
ter's decision. “Jim Mapes will
be there, and everyone will say
you didn’t come because you
didn’t have anyone to come with.
If Bert weren’t going to work all
the evening I'd get him to go with
you.”
“As if I'd go with a brother-in
law,” scorned Julie. “I’ll go by
myself—in Bert’s runabout, if you
don't mind. I’ll get there early bo
no one will especially notice that
I have come alone, and there are
always loads of the men who
come stag and before the dancing
has begun I’ll have my dances all
promised—and I won't give one
to Jim.”
A few hours later Julie, a
charming little figure in pink chif
fon, paused to bld her sister good
night.
“You’ll dodge a lot of traffic
if you go right, down Madden
lane,” Dora told her.
So Julie started out, and as she
sat there with her wee golden
slippered feet and gleaming white
hands regulating the speed and
direction of her brother-in-law’s
car she wondered to herself just
why she had come. She felt su
premely miserable. Jim and sho
had been engaged for several
weeks. Then, when some rather
trivial question had come up about
the announcement of the engage
ment, Julie had taken offense and,
without qiute knowing how it had
happened, she told Jim that she
felt she could not marry him.
Down Madden lane sped Julif
and her ear, cautiously keeping
to the middle of the road to avoid
the soft sand at the edges which,
since a recent rain, was heavily
water-soaked. For a short
stretch the road was wide enough
fo^ only a single cur, but it was
unfrequented, and Julie had little
thought of meeting craft coming
in the opposite direction. Sud
denly at a curve in the lane Julie
heard what she took to be sounds
of approaching traffic, and with
out waiting for further develop
ments she swerved to the right.
As she did so she felt the wheels
softly skid in the sand for a few
Inches. Then she stopped and
waited. What she had heard
had been only a remote railroad
whistle. Julie tried to go forward
into the firm purt of the rond,
and then she tried to make it by
backing, but whatever she did
seemed to become hopelessly in
volved in that soft, rain-soaked
sand. Even if she had some bur
lap, which she hadn’t, how could
she get out and remedy matters
dressed as she was?
It was while she was still mak
ing such plans that she heard
sounds of an approaching ear
coming from the same direction
that she had come, and then she
saw the car, which stopped at
sight of her plight.
“I’m stuck in the sand,” she
said, hailing the stranger; then,
when she saw the lone masculine
figure, she wondered whether she
ought to ask him to give her a lift
to the nearest telephone. The
stranger proved to be Jim, who
seemed at first quite elated at
her predicament. Jim said he
would turn about and go to the
farmhouse to tell them they were
leaving a car on the road and
then they could go on to the dance
together. But Julie stoutly re
fused to go with him. So Jim
went a little forward to make
his turn, stopped short, made a
few false starts and declared
that he, too, had stuck in the
sand.
What happened seemed rather
absurd as Julie reviewed it later.
Jim carried Julie back in his
strong arms to the farm. There
she sat in the dimly lighted, stuffy
farmhouse “parlor” while Jim
talked to the farmer, who subse
quently went forth saying that he
would try to drag the cars out
of the stand with the tractor.
After three-quarters of an hour,
in which Jim and Julie sat to
gether quite shyly, the farmer re
turned and announced his inabil
ity to budge either of the cars.
Then Jim went to another room
to telephone for help and shortly
came back with the information
that the telephone seemed to be
out of order. Julie suggested
that the farmer might drive them
to the dance nnd the farmer in
formed them that the tractor was
the only motor conveyance he pos
sessed. His son would be back
with a car along toward midnight,
he said.
So Jim and Julie sat in the lit
tle parlor alone, and before mid
night came they had made up so
satisfactorily that Julie forgot
how the spat had begun. Then
Jim led the way. not to the sup
posed car of the farmer's son. but
back to his own roadster. With a
rope he had brought from the
farmer he tied Julie’s car to his
own and, side by side, they drove
home to Julie’s sister's in Jim's
car.
“My car was not stalled, really.”
ho announced, before they parted,
“and yours could easily have
been got out. The farmer didn’t
try to get thorn out nnd he had a
ear in his garage all the time and
the phone wasn't out of order.
But I'll never lie to you again.
Julie, dear. I did it all because T
didn't want to go to that dance
until ve had had time to make
up,”

FUTURES ACT
WASHINGTON Charging that
the Armour Grain Co., Chicago, had
attempted to manipulate the market
price of grain violation of the grain
futures act, Secretary of Agricul
ture Jardine yesterday ordered the
company to appear before a referee
on Oct. 11 and show cause why it
should not be denied trading privi
leges by every contract market in
the country.
Fred Lees was designated as ref
eree by Secretary Jardine and or
dered to conduct the investigation.
Two Grounds Given.
In the citation issued Secretary
Jardine alleged that the Armour
Grain Co. violated Section 5 of the
grain futures act. Two grounds for
this charge are stated, namely, that
the Armour company had a quan
tity of rye screenings mixed with
No. 2 rye in a public warehouse
and had warehouse receipts issued
for this material as No. 2 rye, and
that it caused to be reported as parr
of the public regular elevator
stocks of grain in Chicago a quan
tity of rye as No. 2 rye, a grade de
liverable on futures contracts
which, in effect, was not of a grade
deliverable on such contracts.
Mr. Jardine stated that this ac
tion on the part of the grain com
pany violated a clause in the grain

Royal Mail Line
Is 87 Years Old
CHICAGO—The Royal Mail line
has celebrated its 87th anniversary.
The company is among the oldest
of the great British shipping com-
panies. having been incorporated
Sept. 26. 1839, by a royal charter
granted by Queen Victoria at the
outset of her long reign. The his
tory of the company’s progress and
development is closely allied to that
of the British shipping industry. In
1839, paddle steamers, fully
equipped with sails, were the latest
fashion on the seas. The then new
ly organized Royal Mail Co. started
at once to build a fleet of 14. It in
augurated the first regular service
to the West Indies.
In 1925 Royal Mail steamers tra
versed over 17.350,000 miles, made
57,576 entries into ports all over
the world, carried 1.170.000 passen
gers and over 12.000,000 tons of
cargo, while the average number of
employes afloat and ashore num
bered 50,000.

was a decrease of 120,265 cars under
the preceding week, which was the
largest in the history of the coun
try”s’ railroads in the volume of
traffic handled. Had it not been
for the holiday the week of Sept. 11
would undoubtedly have shattered
all records.

week last year, which also included

Sept. 11 this^year was an increase
of 55,5.82 cars, but it was a decrease
of 30,700 cars under the correspond
ing week in 1924, which week, how
ever. did not Include Labor day.

with the preceding week in the total
loadings of all commodities, but all
except the southern reported in
creases compared with the corre
sponding week last year. The east-
ern. Allegheny and central western

creases compared with ?he corre

TEXAS COTTON
LOAN PROPOSAL
FACES CRITICS
NEW YORK Opinion among
New York cotton brokers as to the
feasibility of the plan formulated
by 100 Texas bankers to withdraw
1,000,000 bales of the 1926 crop from
the market by lending $100,000,000
on the withheld staple seemed di
vided teday as prices sagged again.
Some brokers predicted that the cot
ton farmer would not be bound by
any agreement to reduce acreage,
commenting that reduction cam
paigns of that kind had usually
failed in the past owing to lack of
co-operation among growers of cot
ton.
On the other hand, some other
cotton men were enthusiastic in
support of the plan. A. B. Bowen,
a member of the cotton firm of the
M. H. Thomas Co., said he
thought the plan was not only fea
sible but that it would be put into
effect.
Price Is Down.
“The price of cotton today is- be
low the cost of production,” said
Mr. Bowen. “Under the plan the
bankers would loan money on cot
ton on the basis of SSO a bale, er the
equivalent of 10 cents a pound.
That cotton would l>e held off the
market until the new crop came in.
The plan calls for reduction of acre
age by 25 per cent by al! who ob
tain cotton loans.
“English rubber producers were
successful in restricting the amount
of rubber put on the market and
benefited largely by the advance in
price which resulted. India jute
growers have similarly controlled
the market for jute. I see no rea
son why American cotton growers
cannot in like manner restrict tbe
market for cotton.”
Bankers Not Enthusiastic.
Bankers were not enthusiastic
over the suggestion. One banker
whose institution lends money both
to cotton dealers and to the textile
industry, said that he did not doubt
that cotton could be held off the
market. He pointed to the success
of copper producers a few years
ago in holding copper off the mar
ket with the aid of bank money.
However, this same banker ques
tioned the advisability of restrict
ing the market for cotton and put
ting the price up.

hoover’spijblic ideal
Secretary Hoover, by profession a mining engineer
and like most technical men a champion of co-operative
idealism and an opponent of political Socialism, wants
the American government to undertake huge public worka
on a nonpartisan basis, in order to eliminate the political
pork barrel from public enterprise.
We would wish him success, if we did not know that
he is demanding the impossible. His own department of
commerce does not live up to this ideal. It cannot, because
the two old parties serve special interests which fatten on
the public.
Private capitalism and imperialism need the co-oper
ation of the nation, but always misuse it for private gain
at public expense. The old party statesmen who make
laws for these private interests naturally expect to get a
share in the spoils, in accord with the biblical injunction:
Don’t muzzle the ox that thrashes the grain.
The old party pork barrel supplies the oil that keeps
the old party machines well greased. Stop the pork bar
rel, and you stop the machine. The great business and
political leaders of capitalism teach their subordinates
the virtue of unselfish service, but for themselves they pre
fer selfish gain. They teach the jesuitic axiom: Follow
my theory, not my practice.
Hoover’s own commerce department continually is
sues garbled crop forecasts for the benefit of the insiders.
It helps the sugar, fruit, tobacco, grain, cotton and other
lords of industry, commerce, finance and agriculture to
trim the suckers. Hoover’s appeal to the old party states
men to abolish the pork barrel therefore sounds to us like
the appeal of a highwayman to rob the people honestly.
It is impossible to eliminate private and party greed
from public enterprise while supporting the practices of
private capitalism and of old party machine politics. Un
selfish public service and old party politics are antipodes.
One might as well expect a whale to fly.
The experience of unselfish idealists in the old parties
has always been the same. They went in as unsophisti
cated enthusiasts and came out as confirmed sceptics and
cynics. And that’s what will happen to those idealists
who follow Hoover’s lure. They will find themselves
balked at every turn by private contractors, old party
bribers, political trimmers and paid wreckers.
A GREAT SUCCESS—MAYBE
Yes, fellow citizens, the farm loan board is a great
success—for the banks. The farm loan board announces
that banks lending money to “farmers” have undivided
profits of $2,678,346.32. Joint stock land banks had an
earned surplus on Aug. 31 of $1,412,674.45.
The report shows that these profits were made by the
banks in loans to tobacco raisers, fruit and vegetable can
neries, raisin driers, wool dealers, cotton jobbers, alfalfa
seed companies, coffee, olive oil, rice and wheat dealers.
The joint stock land banks made their money clapping
mortgages on farms and furniture, shaving government
bonds, notes and sheriff’s certificates, and collecting in
stallments.
Nothing is said in the report about what happened to
the farmers whose homes were mortgaged and whose
products were handled by the fellows that borrowed
money from the banks. Evidently the farm loan board is
convinced that the less said about that subject, the better

VOCATIONAL GUIDANCE
A symposium of “leaders of American thought”—
meaning those who believe in things as they are—bitterly
complains about the lack of forethought displayed by the
educational institutions of the United States in giving boys
and girls the right kind of guidance in picking a suitable
profession.
Boys and girls are wasting the best years of their
lives trying to find out what sort of work is their real
vocation. It is a very old complaint of capitalist “leaders
of thought.” And it always neglects the other half of the
problem, namely making sure that the new generation
finds enough steady jobs for which they are best fitted.
What good would even the best vocational guidance
do, if the boys and girls who receive it cannot be assured
of a place in the line that is naturally theirs? And how
is such security to be achieved for them, so long as the
“leaders of thought” support a social system which ex
poses everybody to insecurity?
The Milwaukee Leader

At the next congress, which

scribing the flight, he wrote:
“We fl _v in the form of a tri
angle, with the back corners high.
We fly pretty close to
gether and have a set of signals.
If the leader is going to turn
sharp, he drops his wing on that
side. If he is going to dive steep,
he holds up his arm. If he wants
us to come up close or wants to
call our attention to something,
he shakes both wings. If he means
•yes,’ he bobs his nose up and
down, and if he means ‘no,’ he
shakes his wings. If he
has trouble and wants us to go on,
he fires a red light from his Very
pistol. If he wants us to follow
him out of sight, he fires a white
light. If he wants to signal the
other flights, he fires a green
light.

TRIBUTE FROM AN OPPONENT
“It used to be said that one cannot govern against,
the workers. It would be more correct to say that one
cannot govern without the workers. Business men should
draw the right conclusion from this truth. The German
government cannot stand without the Social Democracy
which the overwhelming majority of the German workers
regard as their own political party. The German Social
ist party must learn to work with the government. Un
less the party does that, it will fail.”
Who said that? Sounds like the speech of a So
cialist leader exhorting his friends of the left wing. But
it isn’t. It was said by Dr. Hugo Silverberg, chairman
of the national association of German big business, a close
friend of the late Stinnes. It was said to the leaders of
German big business. It was a flat repudiation of the
Nationalist-Monarchist plea for an exclusion of the So
cialist party from government.
Can you imagine a chairman of an American big
business convention talking like that? Yet in Germany
it was warmly seconded by the elite of German capital
ism. Although a few ultra conservatives raised a row’
about it and spoke for the Nationalist-Monarchist coali
tion, most of the big business leaders affirmed their loyal
ty to the republic and admitted that they must come to
a working agreement with the Socialist party.
And w’hat do the German Socialists say to that?
Simply: No thank you. We want to take part in the gov
ernment, but not in the way that you invite us to do it.
You tried for the last years to smash the trade unions
and the Socialist party. You couldn’t do it. Now you
want us to pull your cart out of the mud, but to let you
run the government -while you tell us where ano how to
co-operate. Nothing doing.
Vorwaerts, the central organ of the German Social
ists, acknowledges .the compliment which Silverberg pays
to the Socialist party, but makes it plain that the execu
tive of the party has a different idea of its position in
the government than he.
“If a political co-operation between workers and cap
italists is possible,” Vorwaerts explains, “it can be only,
upon the basis of real democracy. Not leaders and led,
but human beings and managers of industry meet on
common ground, knowing full well how far their inter
ests are identical, w’here they diverge, and to w’hat extent
they can travel the same road for co-operation.
“We can leave the settlement of our differences to
the development of the actual conditions of our relative
power. The workers have good reasons for trusting to
the strength of their organizations.
“The Socialist party, which according to Silverberg’s
own confession represents the overwhelming majority of
the German workers, will shape its political decisions by
the light of the necessities to which it owes its existence.
It will protect the interests of the manual and mental
workers without regard to any inviting gesture- of the
employers or to the yells of the Communists.
“If the employers desire a co-operation with the
workers, well turned phrases will not do the ti'Ck. The
employers will have to prove by the deeds of their polit
ical parties and by practical respect for the claims of the
workers that the rights of the working class will receive
due consideration in such a joint collaboration.
“The speeches of the industrial capitalists so far
have shown some good intentions on their part, but r
a realization of the requirements which, how’ever lx’
for big business to meet, are the indispensible conditic
which must be fulfilled before any co-operation is pos
sible.”

CLOSING ANOTHER BREACH
Close on the heels of the admission of Germany .int'
the league of nations, the Washington conference of t'
International Union of Pure and Applied chemistry E.
paved the way for the re-admission to membership in that
body of chemists from Germany and the other central
European nations.
Since 1914, delegates from these countries have been
excluded. It will be a matter of surprise to most people
that a scientific organization should have retained such
restrictions for nearly eight years after the armistice.
As the president of the American Medical society said at
the opening of the conference this week, science is inter
national and the fruits of its research should be the com
mon property of the world.
The restoration of this association of chemists to a
truly international status is a wholesome step, both for
science and for better world relations. A gathering of the
world’s chemists with no Germans present is a very in
complete gathering indeed. —The New York World.

CASE ARGUED
BY E. W. LEWIS.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
NEW Y ORK Attorneys today
argued in chambers before Federal
Judge Julian Mack over the legal
points involved in the trial of
Thomas W. Miller, former alien
property custodian, and Harry M.
Daugherty, former attorney general,
for alleged conspiracy to defraud
the government. The jury was ex
cused.
Has Made Ruling.
It was understood that Judge
Mack already had made a tentative
ruling that George E. "Williams, as
sistant to Miller in the alien prop
erty custodian's office, was not a
party to any conspiracy. Such a
ruling would form a basis for a de
fense motion to strike out the evi
dence all testimony regarding con
versations between Richard Merton
and Williams, which were an im
portant portion of the government
case.
Merton had testified it was Wil
liams who gave him valuable infor
mation about the method to follow
in his efforts to secure return of $7,-
000,000 worth of property seized by
the government during the war.
Ready to Fight.
The government indicated it was
ready to fight to retain in the record
that portion of the evidence even
though it were ruled Williams had
no knowledge of a conspiracy. Wil
liams was named in the indictment.
The defense motion to dismiss' the
charges also was before Judge Mack
and part of today's discussion was
in connection with that motion.

“Unawed by Influence and Unbribed by Gain”
THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 30, 1926.
NO RACE, CREED
PREJUDICE AT
U., FRANK SAYS
Will Not Consent to
Discrimination,
He Says.
MADISON—There will be no
racial prejudice at the University of
Wisconsin, and complaints of racial
discrimination will be investigated
by President Glenn Frank person
ally, as an outgrowth of claims
made by Milwaukee Jews that Alex
Stern had been denied a position in
the university library because of his
faith.
Stern, a Milwaukee student at the
university, applied for a position in
the library with high recommenda
tions from M. S. Dudgeon, Milwau
kee public librarian.
Mr. Dudgeon received a reply
from Miss Alice V. King, university
employment officer, which declared
that no Jewish students are ac
ceptable.
Miss King, when interviewed to
day, refused to comment about the
letter she had written. She declared
she had not communicated with the
student and that her correspondence
had been with Mr. Dudgeon only.
She asserted that she had nothing to
say and that any information must
come from President Frank.
President Frank was emphatic in
his declaration that there can be no
racial or religious discrimination at
the university and that no such
policy exists in any branch of the
university.
“It was a case of some one em
ploye expressing a personal policy
rather than a university policy, and
as far ns I can tell there has been
no general racial discriminatic-i,”
President Frank said.
“I have found that considering
the number enrolled. Jewish stu
dents have more than their quota
of jobs in the university service.
“I made it very clear to one or
two persons in the library that
there could be no racial discrimina
tion in the university. I will per
sonally continue the investigation of
this case.”
President Frank today wrote to
a Bernhard Cohen of the Gymal
Doled club of Milwaukee, giving the
university policy on racial and xe
ligious points. Mr. Cohen had
lodged a complaint with President
Frank concerning the letter written
by Miss K»«g.
Won’t Be Permitted.
“Nowhere in the organization of
the University of Wisconsin are
racial prejudices permitted with my
consent,” President Frank declared
in the letter to Mr. Cohen.
“The University of Wisconsin has
not. will not, and must nqt know e
distinction between Jew or Gentile,
Catholic or Protestant. Supported
by all. the university is the servant
of all.”
Stern is still at school here and
lives in Tripp hall. It could not be
learned today whether he would
again apply for a job at the library.

BY A. W. FOLGER.
Staff Correspondent
The United Press
MEXICO CITY —A hurricane and
tidal wave has swept historic Vera
Cruz, perched perilously near sea
level on the'Gulf of Campeche. Life
and property loss is feared, accord
ing to fragmentary reports coming
out of the ravaged city by crippled
communication facilities.
The wind, accompanied by heavy
rains, swept westward over the
mountains. Buildings in its path
were wrecked and it is feared that
many Indians lost their lives. The
property loss was put at $2,500,000.
Four Ships Sunk.
The tail end of the storm struck
here late yesterday and the barom
eter dropped, but the; wind did not
reach hurricane force.
Four ships were sunk in Vera
Cruz harbor. The crews of the
Anahuac and the San Juan, small
steamers, were lost, according to
reports.
Messages received at railway of
fices say that many persons were
killed in the poorer districts where
wooden houses collapsed, burying
the occupants.
New Storm Feared.
Another storm was expected hour
ly, railroad advices said.
The conductor of a train which
left Vera Cruz said that great dam
age had been done all along the line

Drill Tearing Into

BULLETIN.
By The United Frees.
IRONWOOD, Mich.—-No word
of encouragement has come from
the G. Pabst mine where 42 men
have been entombed since a cave
in Friday. The 110th hour of
their imprisonment came and
passed at 11:30 a. m. today. Of
ficials of the Oliver Mining Co.
had predicted that there was no
hope for the men beyond the 110th
hour.
IRONWOOD, Mich.—With no ad
ditional signals from below for 24
hours, rescue workers pushed for
ward today in the nope that they
may reach some of the 42 men im
prisoned in the G. Pabst mine be
fore nightfall.
The rescue has become a grim
struggle which death already may
have won. Human effort has done
its utmost, but it is a slow ordeal to
overcome the resistance of the walls
of rock which hold the miners im
prisoned and many precious hours
had been lost in changing tactics
of abandoning work already started.
Somewhere 780 feet below the
surface are 40 of the miners, known
to be without food, their carbide
lamps long since burned out, their
water supply perhaps only what
seeps through the rocks and pure
air uncertain.
Cling to Hope.
Still another 500 feet beneath
them are either two or three other
miners, whose circumstances are
identical, but who may lie the first
to lie reached.
There are some who cling to the
hope that the men are alive.
Faint tappings sounded on air
pipes early Tuesday, but whether
they were sounds made by the res
cue crews has not been determined
and since, the noises have not re
curred.
Even the women at the mine
mouth are losing hope. As late as
Tuesday, they welcomed every scrap
of information from the rescuers,
but now, as the shifts change at half
hour intervals, they are silent and
sad.
May Reach Tomb.
It is possible the rock prisons may
lie readied today, lint no one can
sjieak with certainty. The best
progress has been made in working
upward from the 26th level where
two of the miners are known to have
been working. The crew engaged
in this attempt has had less ob
stacles than any other.
The shaft that is expected to be
the first to reach the 40 men on the
eighth level is being .driven at an
angle from the Aurora mine adjoin
ing. The entire distance is about
280 feet and it is estimated half that
has been conquered.
One or two other attempts at tun
neling inet with a slow start. It is
the 2^-inch hole that a diamond
drill is tearing into the ground to
provide a channel for communi
cating with the men on the eighth
level and passing down concentrated
food. This operation is speedy, but
it got a late start.
Clearing of Shaft
The other work is the clearing of
the shaft which was blocked by the
cavein Friday. Retimberlng is neces
sary to protect the rescue workers
and the removal of debris has fur
ther delayed the work.
The men now have been impris
oned for 110 hours —20 hours less
than the time officials set as the
maximum that they could survive.
Dr. E. IL Madajesky, mine phy
sician, believes, however, that the
men can live for another eight or
nine days, provided they have fresh
air and water.

Rumors that a filling station
would be built on the northwest cor
ner at Grand Ave. and 11th St. were
denied today by Richard Oberst,
who holds a 99-year lease on the
property and who has instituted
mandamus proceedings in the cir
cuit court in an attempt to force
the building inspector's office to
grant a permit for the erection of
a 10-story apartment hotel on the
site.
Denies Filling Station.
Building Inspector William D.
Harper admitted today that a Mil
waukee oil company, whose identity
he refused to disclose, has been
making inquiries as to legality of
building a filling station on this
site.
“Under the zoning ordinance, it
would be legal but I strongly ad
vised. them against it,” declared Mr.
Harper.
“There is no prospect of a filling
station being built on this site,” de
clared Mr. Oberst when questioned
as to any possible negotiations to
ward that end.
“I have a 99-year lease on this,
property and I am confident that the
courts are going to permit me to
erect the hotel which I plan.”
Legal Question Arises.
There is a legal question as to
whether this site is located in the
so-called “125-foot district” or the
“S5-foot district” designated by the
zoning law. If it is in the 125-foot
district Mr. Oberst’s plans are per
missible.
Another obstacle to the plans,
however, is the action now pending
before the common council by means
of which the city proposed to con
demn a triangular piece of this site
with a 120-foot frontage on Grand
Ave. and a 3G-foot frontage on 11th
St.
The acquisition of this strip
would permit the partial straighten
ing of Grand Ave. at this point, and
the removal of the “jog” caused by
the protruding of this block into
Grand Ave.

SOCIALIST AND
LABOR PRESS
DISCUSS OFFER
Leader Special Service.
BERLIN—The invitation of the
big business leaders of Germany to
the trade unions and the Socialist
party to co-operate with the capital
ists in the government has started a
lively discussion in the German La
bor and Socialist press.
Theodore Leipart, the president of
the German Federation of Labor,
declares that “the responsible lead
ers of the trade unions, in the vast
majority, are in favor of practical
Socialist co-operation with the old
party government.” On the other
hand, a great deal of reserve and
opposition manifests itself against
this policy in many Socialist papers.
Advise Cautious Policy.
Even moderate Socialist papers
like The Frankfurt Arbeiter Zeitung
warns against too optimistic and
rash conclusions and points out that
the policy of making concessions
and co-operating with the capitalists
has not done the workers much
good.
It is true that the trade unions
and the Socialist party of Germany
have recovered from their after-war
slump, but now the capitalists, hav
ing failed to crush the workers’ or
ganization, want to weaken them
by friendship, hints this paper.
The capitalists have also learned
that a republic gives them even bet
ter chances for exploitation than a
monarchy, in which the aristocracy
and the princes play the main role.
Catholics Need Socialists.
The Leipziger Volkszeitung points
out that the left wing of the Cath
olic party needs the help of the So
cialists very much, because the
Catholic party suffers so long as the
Socialists remain in opposition to
the government parties.
The capitalists also need a recon
ciliation with the Socialist trade
unions, because the Catholic labor
unions have become more and more
radical and imbued with Socialist
ideas.
What the capitalists want is not

W. Virginia Gets

Business.
CHICAGO Only indirectly
through price influences are Illinois
coal operators concerned in the
rising tide of American coal exports
to Britain and to the markets usual
ly supplied by British mines.
The Black Diamond, coal trade
weekly published here, reports that
something like 700,000 tons of
American coal was ship]>cd from
Hampton Roads ports last week, and
the movement of coal to United
Kingdom ports continues heavy. A
strong demand from Italy, usually
supplied from England, is felt in the
American markets and “In fact, in
quiries have come in from ail mar
kets, which under existing condi
tions should be reached by American
coals,” The Black Diamond says.
It was recalled in Chicago yester
day that, in days past, Illinois op
erators thought of using the Ohio
and Mississippi to reach South
American markets. Nothing came
of it—no coal moves on that route,
and the down river traffic to south
ern states markets which once
amounted to 40,000,000 tons a year
from the Pittsburgh district has de
clined.
Exports Are Heavy.
Railway figures show exports of
American coal from Hampton Roads,
for the period of Aug. 23 to 2S,
amounted to 324,799 tons: Aug. 30-
Sept. 4, 303,178 tons; Sept. 6-11,
342.505 tons.
Total exports from Hampton
Roads, Jan. 1 to Sept. 18, as report
ed by the bureau of mines, were
6,080,292 tons, against exports of
3.338,997 tons for the same period
of 1925. Exports from all American
tidewater ports from Jan. 1, 1926. to
Aug. 31 were 8,833,216 tons, against
3.895,188 tons for the same period
of 1925. Exports for the month of
August, 1926, alone amounted to
2,826,639 tons, 70 per cent as much
as all last year’s exports up to
Aug. 31.
The increase of American exports
amounting to 4,938,028 tons in eight
months is, however, but a small part
of the increase of coal production
this year caused by domestic pros
perity. Up to Sept. 11, American
soft coal mines produced 374,753,000
tons, against 336,108,000 for the
same period last year—a gain of
48.645,000 tons, nearly 10 times the
amount of tlfe gain in exports.
Gets Lion’s Share.
West Virginia appears to be get
ting the lion's share of the export
business caused by the British
strikes. Production of that non
union state for the five weeks end
ing Labor day was, by weeks, 2,920,-
000, 3,110,000, 2,972,000, 2,600,000,
and 1,777,000 tons. The drop the
last week was due to the influence
of the holiday.
In the same weeks the production
of Illinois mines was 1,230,000,
.1,320,000, 1,280,000, 1,400,000’ and
1,218,000 tons. A few years ago
Illinois and West Virginia were run
ning neck and neck in tonnage. Just
at present, however, the surprisingly
large production of the Illinois
mines is a feature of the coal trade.
Illinois, which long sagged below
non-union Kentucky, has again
taken the lead over that state. In
the five weeks production race Kon
tuckv’s tonnage was 1,147,000,1,205,-
000, 1,168,000, 1,148,000 and 814,000,
Illinois leading every week.
Fourth of Demand.
WASHINGTON American coal
exports to the United Kingdom are
going forward at a rate sufficient to
supply approximately one-fourth of
its present consumption, according
to the latest figures of the depart
ment of commerce.

JUDGE'S VIEW
CHICAGO —In nn address before
some 500 members of Hadassah, nn
organization of Jewish women af
filiated with the Zionist movement
for the reclamation of Palestine,
Judge Harry Fisher at the Congress
hotel late yesterday revealed condi
tions in that ancient land ns con
siderably less flourishing and far
Jess encouraging than reports have
painted them. Judge Fisher has
just returned from a tour of Pales
tine.
Optimism Exaggerated.
Jews of America have listened
during the last 15 years to scores of
returned travelers from Palestine,
the majority of whom have substi
tuted triumphs of oratory for hard
facts, and have glossed over, grossly
misjudged or completely misstated
the situation, Judge Fisher asserted.
And because of the exaggerated op
timism such propaganda instilled in
the public mind Palestine Itself has
suffered immeasurable detriment.
As nn example of this misdirected
promotion of the potentialities of
the country, he cited the Instance of
the city of Telavlv, which during
1925 experienced a period of in
flation only comparable to the
Florida land boom. Between $15,-
000,000 nnd $25,000,000 wns invested
there in 1925 by individuals who ex
pected to realize a large profit quick
ly. Now the city stands with fine
houses and paved streets, and pov
erty all about it, whereas the same
amount of money, invested in indus
tries or agriculture, would have re
turned a profit nnd established real
prosperity.
Work Will Be Slow.
“We must realize,” Judge Fisher
said, “that Palestine is not ripe for
the 50,000 immigrants we tried to
crowd into it in a year. This work
must proceed slowly if It is to go
ahead in a practical way. It is peo
ple we need with the spirit of pio
neers. who will till the soil and pre
pare the ground for others.”
College Moralist
In Divinity School
MIDDLETOWN, Conn.—Wilfred
O. Cross, student moralist, who
wrote of pa jama dances participated
in by students of both sexes, now
is a student at Berkley Divinity
school in this city, where he will be
gin a year of communistic relation
ship with students and professors.
At Berkley the entire student body
participates at odd moments in
manual tasks to earn money, what
ever their means. All that is earned
is put into a common purse, from
which each draws according to his
needs.
The professors also contribute all
that they earn, aside from their
salaries. Each student does that
particular manual work to which he
is best fitted.

STATE FILES
SUGGESTIONS
ON BOUNDARY
WASHINGTON—Ideas for chang
ing the boundary line between Wis*
consin and Michigan, under the de
cision of the supreme court at its
last term, were filed with the court
yesterday by Wisconsin.
The decision fixed the general lo
cation of the boundary line and left
it to the two states to suggest the
form in which the final decree defi
nitely fixing the line should be pre
pared.
Under Wisconsin's plan, the boun
dary would begin in the middle of
Lake Michigan, opposite the most
usual ship channel leading into
Green Bay, and proceed to the mid
dle of the most usual channel in the
bay. It then would follow the mid
dle of the channel north of Rock
Island and north and west of Cham
bers Island to the main channel of
Menominee river, and along that
channel and the Brule river to Lake
Brule.

by Prof. Heberlein, of the Nether
lands service. The skull was found
at the same place where Prof. Eu
gene Dubois of Amsterdam univer
sity discovered in 1892 the upper
part of a skull, two teeth and a
thigh bone, from which was recon
structed the previously unknown
apelike human designated as Pithe
canthropus erectus.

By Elwin Robert Petre
THE GREAT DOLOMITE ROAD.
There is surely much for which
Italians are not grateful to Aus
trians, but on every side I heard
praise for the fine road which the
Austrians built in the pre-war days
from Bolzano eastwards to Cortina
and on to Dobbiaco, DO miles of
travelway amid the world’s most
entrancing scenery. The surface is
smooth and gives good motoring,
but I chose the slower gait of doing
the road in stages by horse car
riage. It wound through magnifi
cent gorges, grassy uplands, and
lovely woods of larch and pine, over
mountain passes, two of them over
7,000 feet high, and at every turn
a new view of the amazing Dolo
mite peaks presented itself for ad
miration. 1 suppose, to enjoy the
great Dolomite road to the best, it
should be traveled from both direc
tions, for natural beauty faces all
points of the compass. Never mind
the day when you start the Dolo
mite road. I have traversed be
neath proverbial Italian skies, but
also beneath cloud. When it lacks
color, it gains impressiveness and
when the clouds roll away, its
shades and tinges make it an art
ist’s highway.

Walter Polakowskl, Socialist
‘state senator from the 3rd district,
and father of the resolution calling
for the beer referendum in the Nov.
2 election, referring to the fact that
the state supreme court had denied
nn injunction restraining the ref
erendum, today declared: “The de
cision is what I expected.
“Before I proposed the reso'iu:ioi
I satisfied myself that it would
be presented in a legal niann :r.
“As all legislative power, ac
cording to the state constitution,
rests in the senate and assembly, it
did not seem possible that the su
preme court could have given any
other decision.
“Where Wc Stand.
“A referendum on the question
of 2.75 per cent beer will let the
entire country, as well as our own
lawmakers, know just where Wis
consin stands on this subject.
“Aside from the Socialist can
didates, few candidates for state
and national offices have ever ex
pressed themselves. The referen
dum will i>oint the way and will
force candidates to recognize it.”
The question, which is embodied
in Senator PolakowskTs resolution
and which the voters shall an
swer is:
Here’s the Subject.
“Shall the congress of the United
States amend the Volstead act so
as to authorize the manufacture
and sale of beer for beverage pur
poses, of an alcoholic percentage of
2.75 per cent by weight, under gov
ernmental supervision but with the
provision that no beverage so pur
chased shall be drunk on the prem
ises where obtained?”
The referendum was ordered by
last year’s session of the legisla
ture through the resolution, be
cause the time limit for the intro
duction of bills had passed.
The legality of the resolution was
challenged by 8. A. Fulton, West
Allis, official of the Anti-Saloon
league, who asked for the injunc
tion which would have prevented
the referendum. lie contended that
as the action required the expendi
ture of money it should have been
ordered by a bill instead of a reso
lution.
To Cost sl6.
It is believed that the- expendi
ture involved will total about sl6.
The Socialist party is the only
one which has taken definite stand
in both its national and state plat
forms on the question. In its 1924
platform it went on record for beer
and light wines, while the 1920 plat
form reaffirms this stand. The
1926 platform, which anticipated
the supreme court’s recognition of
the legality of the legislature’s reso
lution follows:
Dry Law Failed.
“In the failure of prohibition en
forcement in the United States, the
Socialist party sees the result of
blind, blundering legislative meth
ods so characteristic of Republican
and Democratic politicians. As the
one sane solution of this serious
problem, the Socialist party advo
cates legislation that will permit of
domestic use of light wines and
beer, and the manufacture for sale
of alcoholic beverages by the fed
eral government alone under strict
safeguards and proper restrictions.
“Wisconsin is the first state in
the union to obtain the sentiment of
the people on prohibition by the
1926 fall referendum. This referen
dum was made possible by a resolu
-ion introduced by a Socialist leg
islator and the people would not
have been allowed to express their
opinion on this subject had there
been no Socialist in the legislature."

before they finish the grades, I
think children need all the sleep
they can get, and it is necessary for
them to have an early bedtime hour.
If a child cannot learn, in school
hours, what the curriculum states
he should in one semester, then I
think the curriculum should be re
arranged, and children take a year
longer in going through grade
school. They will be better off in
the end than if they study every
evening instead of romping and
playing and getting their blood up
in good, old-fashioned little girl add
boy style.
But I do not think any such re
arrangement necessary. I think
children can learn enough in school
hours to pass every grade and fin
ish in the same number of years as
they do now.
What do other mothers think
about this?” I should like to hear
from others who feel as I do, or
else hear some arguments I have
not thought of which would justify
the home work which children are
now required to do in the evenings.
I can remember taking my spell
ing book or reader or arithmatic
home, when I was in grade school;
but I always seemed to need a great
deal of sleep and invariably grew
so heavy-eyed my parents insisted
that I go to bed. The result was,
I never did any home work to speak
of. And I never flunked, either.
Whether that home work had really
been required by my teacher or
whether I just felt that I should
do a little by myself, I cannot re
member. The important point, any
way, was that I neither studied at
night nor failed to pass when the
time came. I went to a school, too,
where examinations, no matter the
pupil’s grades, were required.

BARNUM PASSES
TEST; TO PLAY
WITH BADGERS
MADISON, Wis.—Cheer has been
brought to the Wisconsin football
camp by the announcement that Rol
lie Barnum. veteran halfback, has
passed eligibility requirements.
Coach Little is driving his squad
harder each succeeding day and
seems to be concentrating on the per
fection of an over-head attack.
BLOOMINGTON, Ind. Coach
Pat Page is shifting his lineup for
the Depauw game Saturday, moving
Frank Silbey from end, where he
has played for two years, to quarter
back. Silbey is known as a cool
player and Page believes he will
make an ideal field general.
CHAMPAIGN, lll.—Ted Marriner,
a regular tackle on last year’s var
sity, has appeared for practice and
greatly bolstered Illini strength in
the line. Marriner was unable to re
port earlier localise he was study
ing for a special examination to be
come eligible.
CHICAGO Minor injuries to
some of his regulars have forced
Coach Stagg to slow up his practice
sessions of the University of Chi
cago team which meets the Univer
sity of Florida Saturday.
EVANSTON, Ill.—Coach Thistle
thwaite is looking for a punter on
his Northwestern squad for early
season. Moon Baker, an excellent
kicker, is to be kept out of the early
games except for a few minutes anil
the squad is shy on substitute
kickers.

Prior to the opening of classes Sept.
22. the men were driven through two
drills at Camp Randall stadium daily,
and are now well hardened for the dif
ficult schedule that faces them.
Hundreds of fans have thronged to
the practice fields to view the three
scrimmages held to date. Four teams
have been taught a few plays and forma
tions and are sent in to battle each other
for 15 to 18 minutes.
A quartet of first string men have yet
to write examinations before being elig
ible to compete this fall. The grldders
with scholastic blots on their records are
Rollie Barnum. star back; Gene Rose,
sophomore quarterback from Racine; J.
J. Kurth, a Madison lineman of great
promise, and Bob Kaslske, guard on last
year’s eleven.

Larson, bulky lineman of ’.wo years’ ex
perience. Larson was injured in an ac
cident this summer and wrenched his
leg in the first day’s practice. He will
not be in fit condition to work until late
next week.

back, who ripped the Chicago Une to
threads last fall, will be shifted to half
back. Little has several promising full
backs who have shown well in scsim
make thus far. Kreuz, Kreske and
Mansfield are all good plungers, Inter
ferers and defenders.

brought to light unusual quarterback
possibilities in a pair of youngsters, bat
tling for berths of the 19z<5 eleven.

Rose. The former is a light boy. very

‘FIGHT A FAKE?
LOOK AT FACE,'
SAYS JACK
NEW YORK—“Was that fight
faked? Just look at my face.”
Thus did Jack Dempsey, former
heavyweight champion, after play
ing hide and seek with the press fol
lowing his arrival here last night,
answer ugly rumors anent Gene
Tunney’s accession to the heavy
weight throne.
Wild Stories Circulated.
It had been whispered about since
Jack lost his title to Gene last
Thursday night in Philadelphia that
Dempsey, of his own accord, tossed
his crown into Gene’s hands, there
by reaping a fortune by betting
against himself at the prevailing
odds.
The story was that a group of
gamblers promised Jack a betting
profit of $2,000,000 if he would let
Tunney win. The story further was
that Tunney was ignorant of the al
leged deal —not a party to it.
We looked Jack over.
“Now, hen.” said the ex-cham
pion, “there would have been an
easier way to get out of a framed
fight, don’t you think?”
Won’t Discuss Future.
Jack declined to state whether he
would try for a comeback or retire
from the ring, but added that he
might have something to say along
that line in a day or two.
Dempsey had intended holding off
the members of the press until this
morning, but with the arrival of
Gene Normile, his manager, he re
ceived them in the former’s suite.
He merely exhibited his battle
scarred features as exhibit A to
wards proving the honesty of his ef
forts against Tunney.
“I am going to try and put an end
to those rumors.” he said, “and take
in tfie world series. I also have
some business matters to take care
of.”

challenging the present champion,

MADISON, Wis.—With the open
ing engagement of his 192 G football

Signal drill is given priority over

elevens driving through new and
old plays daily. The regulation
game that was held at Camp Ran
dall practice field Saturday brought

departments of play, and are being
rapidly ironed out by Little and his
staff.
Stars Are Saved.
The Cardinal backs, who have
been so popular with the railbirds
in the early scrimmages, did not
produce many of their spectacular
stunts in Saturday’s battle. Tom
Lieb had whipped his line material
Into such shape that the offensive
attacks of both’elevens were futile.
Neither goal line was crossed dur
ing the afternoon’s entertainment.
Neither Capt. Harmon nor Rollie
Barnum have been engaging in
much rough work, as the coaches
have been eyeing the younger men
at every opportunity. “Sol” Kreuz,
the stocky little fullback, has shown
a decided improvement over last
season, and undoubtedly will start
at fullback Saturday. His punting
is far better than a year ago. If
Barnum is used at all this week it
will be at a halfback position.
Kresge, hard-hitting sophomore
back, is fast rounding into form,
and should prove a dependable un
derstudy at fullback.
Wagner at Guard.

brought to light some first rate line
men of such caliber that the vets in
the forward wall are becoming un
easy. Ralph Wagner, Paul Schuette
and Bob Carney look to be confer
ence caliber, while Horwitz. Gostein,

shown well. With Wilke and Wil-
son fighting for the post of pivot
man, Big Wagner has been shifted
to guard.

had poor breaks in his first year of
eligibility for varsity competition,
being kept from scrimmage because
of a minor injury. He is a rugged
back, and is awaiting a chance to
show his wares under fire. Rose,
Hall, Shaw, Bartlett, Barr and
Muegge are the outstanding recruits
for backfield duties, and are being
tried in various combinations.

wings, under the care of the pop

string of victories that have been

joice at the opportunity of oppos

physicians.

BY WILLIAM BRADY, M. D.
INDIGESTION IS SERIOUS.
Chicago woman paints a vivid
word picture of her indigestion—a
picture which might furnish good
material for the professional testi
monial writer if I should publish
it—and then asks whether I think
it will result in anything serious
eventually.
Indigestion, before we become
further involved, never happens.
However, I think it is rather a
serious matter when anybody gets
the obsession that he has indi
gestion.
Having indigestion is very much
like contracting a “slight cold”
or drifting into a “run down con
dition” or suffering a “nervous
breakdown” from “overwork,”
that is, if anybody takes these
spurious terms seriously.
Indigestion is in some respects
worse than autointoxication. Half
informed folk who cherish the de
lightfully morbid delusion of au
tointoxication generally haven’t
anything the matter anyway and
find considerable diversion experi
menting with colon therapy. Mis
informed folk who suffer with the
indigestion obsession often have
something really the matter with
them, and while they are fooling
with “aids to digestion” or “care
ful diet” the unrecognized disease
may go on to a dangerous condi
tion.
Wh^n I say there is no such ail
ment, disease or abnormal condi
tion as “indigestion” I mean what
I say I do not mean that there are
not a million deluded folk who
fatuously ascribe their ailments
or disease to “indigestion.” Nor
do I wish to intimate that I can
tell anybody what his trouble is
if it isn’t indigestion.
I recall a great lesson in diag
nosis imparted by a fine teacher,
Dr. Delancey Rochester. Prof.
Rochester presented to his med
ical class a group of patients with
early tuberculosis, each patient il
lustrating a different mode of on
set—in one case the disease be
gan with what resembled ordi
nary bronchitis, in another with
anemia, in still another with
what purported to be indigestion
and stomach trouble, and so on.
In a great many instances of
heart disease, cardiovascular de
generation, Bright’s disease, the
victims drift along for months or
years monkeying with their “poor
indigestion.”
The practice of ascribing the
effects of infection or disease of
the gall sac, with or without gall
stones, to “indigestion” is almost
universal.
Although a neurotic or hypo
chondriac may complain of a
choice selection of subjective sym
toms of “indigestion,” such a per
son cannot so readily make a phy
sician believe he has any objective
symptoms or signs of such a hy
pothetic illness. A subjective
symptom is something which the
patient feels or observes; an ob
jective symptom is something the
physician can determine or ob
serve for himself. It should be ob
vious, then, that in any case a
diagnosis of “indigestion” is made
by a physician only as a matter of
courtesy or convenience, sort of
an alibi for the patient or a mask
to conceal the physician’s ignor
ance. Newspaper fatalities from
“acute indigestion” are generally
affairs of courtesj-; lies given the
public in order to conceal what
really caused death. Of course no
physician would seriously record
“indigestion" as a cause of death.
This is the idea I am driving
at: Whenever your “indigestion"
becomes annoying enough to call
for treatment, it is high time to
bid your doctor find out what ails
you.

he tried, and again. His own fail
ure made him the more eager; al
most in a frenzy, he toiled at it.
The rough stone tore his hands;
he slipped in the slimy water,
struck his face against the wall so
hard that it bled. For a moment
he was dazed then, the moment his
head cleared he returned to his
task.
Night came and moonlight, a tiny
ray of which pierced the cell's dark
ness. Once Juan had thought that
the stone moved a little, and more
frantically than ever he strove to
move it again. There were steps
in the corridor. The steps of those
coming to lead him to his death,
perhaps. He knelt there in the wa
ter until they had passed, then with
a final effort that took all his
strength he hurled himself at the
stone.

MILWAUKEE RD.
TO BE PUT ON

CHICAGO—The property of the
Milwaukee road, which has been in
receivership since March, 1925, will
be placed on the auction block, Nov.
22, to be sold for not less than $122,-
500,000. pursuant to a decision hand
ed down yesterday by Federal Judge
Wilkerson in the United States dis
trict court.
The sale will be cond icted by
Special Master Herbert A. Lumlahl
at the main entrance of the railway
station at Butte, Silver Bow county,
Mantana, 11 a. m.
The court further stipulated that
the buyer must take over with the
road $154,000,000 of the mortgage
refunding bonds of the system”s
chief subsidiary, the Chicago, Mil
waukee Puget Sound railway.
Upset Price Given.
The announcement was made
after the court denied the bondhold
ers’ defense committee permission
to file an amendment and supple
mental petition to intervene in the
receivership proceedings. The upset
price, pursuant to the terms of the
decree, was set at $122,500,000, as
follows:
Parcel I. Puget Sound prop
erty 42,500,000
Parcel 11. Property subject
to refunding mortgage
other than Puget Sound
bonds 67,500,000
Parcel 111. The aggregate
of the sums required as
to parcels I. and 11.
Parcel IV, Unpledged assets. 12,500,000
Parcel V. The aggregate of
the sums required as to
parcels 1., 11. and IV 122,500,000
It had been understood by in
vestors that the Puget Sound rail
way bonds would not be disturbed
under the reorganization, and the
court’s action in this regard came
as a surprise.
Deny Sale Delay.
In explaining the upset price, the
court pointed out that $250,000,000
had been argued as a minimum
figure by the Jamieson committee,
while only $1,000,000 had been asked
by the committee representing over
80 per cent of the refunding and
Puget Sound bonds.
In denying further delay in the
sale of the property, the court main
tained that the interest of all se
curity holders would be protected
by the right to make objection to
any bids which may be made for
the property. To hold up the sale
for the purpose of the expert ex
amination of the properties and the
accounting records of the railway
would, in the court’s opinion, re
quire too much additional time.

SOUTH GLOOMY
OVER COTTON
CHICAGO—With cotton selling at
the lowest level since 1922, it is not
strange that the south is feeling a
bit pessimistic just now, declared
Oscar Wells, president of the Ameri
can Bankers’ Assn., who arrived in
Chicago yesterday en route to the
annual convention of the association
in Los Angeles Monday.
Mr. Wells is president of the First
National bank of Birmingham.
“To some extent the size of the
cotton crop, which will be one of
the largest ever raised, will offset
the drop in price,” Mr. Wells de
clared. Mr. Wells expressed him
self as optimistic on the general
business situation.
Several hundred banker-delegates
from the oast and south left for the
coast last night in four special
trains, two of which were routed
over the North Western and two
over the Burlington. A fifth train
will leave tonight on the Santa Fe.
The five trains will carry approxi
mately 600 delegates, of which 150
are from Chicago.
British Coal Strike
Cuts Production;
Steel Is Scarce
NEW Y’ORK—Describing the de
crease of British manufactures as a
result of the coal strike, The Lon
don Economist reports that “manu
facturers are obtaining better sup
plies of coal, both from home and
foreign sources: but they are ex
periencing considerable difficulty in
obtaining supplies of continental
steel.
“Continental manufacturers have
recently advanced their prices, but
the position is confused, and while
a number of the foreign steel mak
ers are quoting high prices and are
disinclined to accept orders, others
are showing a greater disposition to
do business; but in all cases the pe
riod required for delivery has heen
extended into the autumn. The con
tinental situation has been made
more difficult by the movements of
the exchanges and by efforts to
form international associations to
maintain prices.
“By the aid of foreign and out
crop coal a considerable volume of
work is being carried on in the
lighter branches of the steel trade,
and unemployment tends to de
crease. The shortage of steel ma
terial, however, becomes more ac
centuated every day. causing stop
pages of operations here and there.
A few crucible furnaces have been
started on Westphalian coke, which
is extremely expensive. Nearly the
whole of the crucible plants, how
ever, are idle.”

EVOLUTION OF
GERMS PUZZLE
TO SCIENTISTS
ITHACA, N. Y.—Evolution in its
beginning stages may be the thing
we see under the microscope when
we look at a slide of bacteria that
have been growing so long in one
tube that they have begun to get
soured on existence and are chang
ing their shapes.
Dr. Ralph R. Mellon of Rochester,
N. Y., has made a study of these
minute disease carriers, and he
thinks that when they change their
shapes from rod-like to spherical or
Legin to put forth branches as prop
erly behaved germs should not do,
they are not necessarily old or sick
bacteria, which has long been the
common opinion.
They may be that, or they may
be evolving into other kinds of bac
teria he told his fellow bacteriolo
gists in the International Congress
of riant Sciences at their session
here. He has taken specimens of
these freakish, supposedly old or
sick bacteria, and used them as the
starting points of new cultures, and
he found that these new cultures
behaved like entirely new brands of
bacteria; for example, some of
them, from virulent disease-causing
strains, had become much less mali
cious in their action.
And he thinks it quite as possible
for a hitherto mild and harmless
breed of “bugs” to go through a
change in the opposite direction, and
become dangerous parasites.

CLEVELAND—Pig iron is more
active in the middle west, sales dur
ing the last few days in St. Louis
territory being heavier than in any
similar period in four or five
months. While so far sales have
reached close to 10.000 tons, mostly
for fourth quarter delivery, live in
quiry approaches a like quantity.

ducers’ selling efforts because of the

eral. pig iron sales are such ns to

Ernest Byfield
Succeeds Dad as
Sherman Hotel Head
CHICAGO—The distinction of be
ing the youngest hotel president in
any metropolitan district in the
United States yesterday was con
ferred on Ernest L. Byfield, who
was chosen head of the Hotel Sher
man Co., succeeding his father, the
late Joseph Byfield.
The diretcors of the company
elected other officers as follows:
Eugene Byfield, vice president:
Frank W. Bering, vice-president and
managing diretcor, and A. L. Bering,
secretary-treasurer.
Ernest L. Byfield, 36. becomes the
chief executive of a company con
trolling approximately $20,000,000 in
properties, outstanding among which
are the Hotel Sherman, the Ambas
sador and the Fort Dearborn hotel.
Mr. Byfield served 15 years as secre
tary-treasurer of the company.

Revenue Collections
Show Big Increase
WASHINGTON —The upward
trend in internal revenue collections
shown in the last fiscal year despite
reduced tax rates appears to be con
tinuing in the present fiscal period
as the curve of the Ration’s business
prosperity mounts. Figures for the
first 25 days of September, made
available by the internal revenue
bureau today, show that income tax
and miscellaneous revenue during
that time aggregated $475,814,006,
against $416,496,000 for the same
period of 1925. This is an increase
of $59,318,000, or equivalent to $2,-
372,720 a day and $864,670,000 a
year. In the fiscal year ending
June 30, 1926, the total internal
revenue increase over the fiscal year
of 1925 was $251,859,624.
