GAINS OF PUBLIC OWNERSHIP
A record of steady increase in public functions along
many lines could be given in detail, but that is too long a
story for one short column, so we shall confine our observa
tions to that sector of the struggle for public ownership
which pertains to municipal light and power plants.
The private ownership prevaricators have for several
years been spreading propaganda to the effect that hun
dreds of municipal light and power plants have failed and
have therefore had to go back to private ownership. Ap
parently the old theologians were correct in sajing theie
is a devil who inspires men to meanness. This damnable
demon’s name is private profit.
The census takers gather the figures on electric plants
every five years, and as it takes time to compile and pub
lish them, the figures always lack a little of being strictly
up to date.
However, the census figures show that in 1881, the
municipally-owned plants were 12.5 per cent of the total
there were only eight plants altogether at that time, and
the installation of such plants began to increase greatly
right after that. In 1885, the municipal plants were 9.5
per cent of the total. In 1890, they were 13.5 per cent of
the total. In 1895, they were 18.5 per cent of the totaL
In 1900, they were 22.02 per cent of the total. In 1905,
they were 24.3 per cent of the total. In 1912, they weie
30 per cent of the total. In 1917, they were 35.43 per cent,
of the total. In 1922—the last year for which the figures
are available —they were 40.6 per cent of the total.
And there is no reason to believe that this steady up
ward march of municipal ownership has changed since
then. Yet the damnable demon keeps on inspiring the
prevaricators to prevaricate about it. Undoubtedly a few
plants have been sold or abandoned, but that does not af
fect the general trend.
Among the municipal plants listed as having failed
is that of Pasadena, Calif. It is listed as having “failed”
because it bought over 11,000,000 kilowatts from private
companies during 1924. But it generated over 27,000,000
kilowatts itself in the same year. It is a fine example of
successful municipal ownership. Why shouldn’t it buy
current when it needs it, if its own facilities are not yet
sufficient to supply all it needs?
Another municipal plant listed as having failed
was that of Eagle River, Wis. At the La Crosse meeting
of the Wisconsin League of Municipalities in July, the
mayor of Eagle River and the superintendent of the elec
tric plant at that place reported that the plant is highly
successful.
And so on. The Public Ownership League riddles the
claim that municipal ownership is going backward.
But the big fellows are after the super power plants
and they will get them if the people do not watch out.
Vote the Socialist ticket—that’s the best way to head them
off.
OUR SOUTHERN NEIGHBOR
An American living in Mexico and having large busi
ness interests in that country tells us, what we already
knew, that the tales of disorders in Mexico are faked.
This needs to be told to many Americans, although
we did not need it. There are newspapers in America
which take particular pains to lie about our national
neighbor to the south, representing it to be customarily in
a state of chaos from which the United States will some
day have to rescue ic. Such newspapers are the minions
of big business persons who, unlike the one mentioned
above, are desirous of having Uncle Sam take control of
Mexico in order that American exploiting interests may
have a free hand to gobble up all the Mexican resources in
sight.
There is crime in Mexico, of course, but if there is any
place on earth where there is. more violence and disorder
than the United States we should like to have it pointed
out. Some of our cities are hotbeds of criminality. Amer
ican newspapers would do well to clean up the cities in
which they are published before they undertake the task
of overturning the liberties of a neighboring country.

WAYS OF THE WORLD
At a concert the other day I re
ceived a greeting from a woman
with an exceedingly frank and
pleasant face. Though I knew 1
had seen her before 1 couldn’t re
call where and I couldn’t recall
her name.
However, in our common enthu
siasm for the singer, we bad
some exchanges of talk, with very
intelligent comments on her part.
Vaguely my mind was groping
about for a clew to her identifi
cation. Of course, I ought to
have had sense enough to tell
her frankly I didn’t know her
name and to ask where we’d met.
‘•Some pleasant association,” I
said to myself.
It occurred to me that wher
ever she went she created pleas
ant associations, through her
friendliness of manner, her meet
ing the world on terms of good
humor and candor.
How lucky some people are to
be born themselves.
That woman, whoever she was,
had probably brought into the
world an outgoing disposition,
quick to tie up with the sympa
thetic forces, perhaps the great
est of all gifts.
She was entirely different from
those with the consciousness
seemingly isolated, imprisoned in
a fortress, looking out at the
world as from a distance, through
an atmosphere of mistrust, chal
lenge and fear.
She wasn’t concerned with her
self. Apparently she thought
about herself not at all. She was
absorbed by the interests outside.
The ingrowing people, how they
do suffer. They keep burrowing
in farther and farther, away from
the world where they have to
function. Though their trouble
seems to lie in their attitude to
ward what’s outside, it really
comes from an overemphasis on
themselves, from overstimulation
of the egotism that, through its
very exactions, continually leads
to wrong adjustment and defeat.

Have you ever noticed the dif
ference in voices on the tele
phone? Of course you have.
We’ve all noticed.
Eagerly, happily, some voices
speed over the wire. They enjoy
relating themselves to whatever
may be out there, far from sight.
They aren’t afraid of it; they are
free, in tune.
Lucky are you if you have one
of those voices, reflecters of the
consciousness that can meet the
world, even the world not seen,
with confidence and readiness to
be friendly.
But those voices, on their
guard, remote, suspicious, calcu
lating, how the mere sound of
them can operate as a disturbance
and a warning.
Always they come from the ego
ists, the shut-ins.
Consider the man who leads an
iregular life. His relation to the
world, his relation even to him
self, is irregular. He has to be
watchful. When the telephone
rings for him or when he rings
the telephone, what does the
sound celebrate?
Does it celebrate anything like
what the telephone bell celebrates
in the mind of the woman whose
name I couldn’t recall at the con
cert
For her, obviously, the tele
phone echoes her happy associa
tion with her kind, her success.
What does the telephone mean
to the most pathetic of all the
shut-ins, the criminal, unhealthy
in all his attitudes, unhealthiest
in his attitude toward himself?
It means at once something use
ful and dangerous, a partner and
a menace, to be treated adroitly,
covertly, to be spoken over in a
low voice, with words guarded,
often of double meaning.
The voice has an inexorable
habit of giving us away and it is
never more clear in its betrayals
than when it sounds over the tele
phone, stripped of distractions,
subjected to the concentrated at-
ceedingly bitter as well as irritat
ing, and presumably poisonous; at
any rate, stock will not eat it, so
that it stands up in pastures,
along with ragweeil, jimpsonweed
and a few other ill growths, long
after the last of the grass has
been cropped close. A survival of
the fittest —from the weeds’ point
of view.
It is perhaps a trifle odd that
such an ill-favored, foul-flavored
weed should be close kin to the
fragrant chamomile, the basis of
one the innumerable “teas” with
which our careful grandmothers
dosed us when we were young.
Both plants belong to the same
genus, known to modern botanists
as “Anthemis,” the name it bore
in the days of Hippocrates and
Galen. For the traditional medi
cines of our grandparents had an
cesters, many of them, that ran
back to Greece and Egypt. Not
much curative virtue in chamo
mile, perhaps; but it had rather
a pleasant taste, which in itself
was unusual among old-fashioned
medicine, and it is was a painless
way of swallowing hot water in
considerable quantities.

Though the notion that crimi

often been shown to be false, it’s

There’s something about con
sciousness that reveals itself
through the intricacies of per
sonality. And in the voice it
meets its most subtle urges to be
trayal. It’s as if through that
live expression it took on exagger
ated life, with its character ex
posed.
In this matter of expression we
are likely to go astray by caring
too much about what is on the
surface. The important consid
eration is, naturally, what’s
within.
The assumed voice of frank
ness, the pretended heartiness, all
the artifical ways, we know how
quickly they can proclaim their
insincerity.
The only way really to seem
frank is to be frank. The only
way to be open is to have nothing
to hide.
The only way to be in harmony
with people is to approach them
with good will.
If we are detached we celebrate
our detachment. We keep warn
ing people against ourselves. We
let them know that we consider
we are different, usually supe
rior. For our self-flattery we im
pose on others exactions they re
sent.
Those who, at some period of
life, don’t realize that, essentially,
they are like the rest of the world
and that the thing for them to do
is to blend in and to make the
best of their situation, mins what
is perhaps the greatest discovery
of life. Through their preoccu
pation with themselves, their im
portance, their rights, their ad
vantages, they are always out of
accord with the currents that
keep life flowing. In their fail
ures of adjustment they make
their situation worse by putting
the blame outside themselves, in
stead of putting it where it be
longs.
In the game of living they are
inevitable losers.
The reason is that they never
learn how to play.

How Trees Grow
A tree grows in two places each
year; the topmost tips grow
longer and climb a little higher
into the air; at the same time the
trunk grows thicker, the tree puts
on another of its “annual rings,”
a woody growth. Which happens
first? When a tree wakes up some
spring morning, does it first
stretch out its fingers in the sun
light or does it first let out its
belt another hole?
An answer comes from the ex
periments of Dr. D. T. McDougal
of the Carnegie Institute of Wash
ington. The doctor has invented
an instrument which takes the
waist measure of the tree very ac
curately indeed. Even a hun
dredth of an inch enlargement of
the tree’s belt is as obvious to Dr.
McDougal and his instrument as a
foot or two would be in your belt
or mine. And by putting a ruler
against the tree tops and his in
strumental tape measure around
the belt, Dr. McDougal finds that
the tips begin to grow weeks,
sometimes months, before the
trunk begins to enlarge.
This is quite as it should be.
Remember that trees get part of
their food from air and from sun
light. They must stretch out ling
ers for a breakfast or two, and
we all know what happens to the
waistline of folks who eat hearty
breakfasts.—From “Keeping Up
With Science”; Edited by Edwin
E. Slossin. Published by Har
court, Brace Co.

Doggone It
IF THEY COULD THINK AHEAD
Dean Inge, of St. Paul’s, London, brightened up con
siderably on his recent visit to the United States. He
thawed out enough in the genial atmosphere of a new
York summer to say that it was all wrong to call him “the
gloomy dean,” because he was really a very optimistic
a..J cheerful soul.
But it seems that things look different to the dean
after spending some time back in the London fogs. We
have not read a more gloomy forecast for the British
empire than that written by the dean for a “modern
world” series.
The dean, who was a great war fan, now admits
that the World war was the greatest misfortune -which
ever befell Britain. He sees now, after it is too late to
do anything about it, that the World war ended the in
dustrial and naval supremacy of Britain capitalism.
Submarines and air forces throw “the tight little isle”
wide open to foreign attack. Continental European
pools and American finance overshadow British capital.
Old England is no longer sure that Canada, South
Africa or Australia will go to war for British Toryism
and capitalism. And the rise of the trade unions and
Labor party as a power in home affairs makes the dean
even gloomier.
Not only the dominions, but also the United States
will no longer fight for England, says the dean. And
that means an early end of the British empire.
Well, it is too late now to cry over the spilled milk
of British capital. The time to do this kind of thinking
was before 1914, when British Toryism had a chance to
pay the kaiser a fair price for an understanding which
would have pooled the British and German navies and
armies.
When Grey helped the czar and Poincare to break
down the only European power that could co-operate
with British capital all over the world, he laid the ax at
the root of British power and of all capitalist rule.
Now the organized workers of Great Britain and Ger
many will soon be the ruling powers and will tackle the
job which Grey fumbled and which Chamberlain tries to
fumble still more.
The sooner Labor secures the power to begin work
on this job of international co-operation, the better it
will be for all human beings on this mismanaged globe.
If the dean had acquired a little more ability to look
at the world without Tory spectacles, and to look ahead
a bit without Tory prejudices, beyond the narrow old
party horizon, he could get a glimpse of the fact that the
internal troubles which he deplores so much are the be
ginning of England’s salvation.
No nation can be prosperous and happy so long as
it tries to rule other nations. No nation can be happy
under capitalist rule, because it is a divided nation, and
because it promotes division and strife everywhere.
To fight Labor, to make English men and women
work long hours for low pay, to fight other nations’ cap
italists, to beat them out of a shilling, to fight backward
races and steal their country, cannot lead to liberty, hap
piness and welfare. That’s what the British ruling class
has done, setting a pace for all the others.
The dean should have known even without some So
cialist intelligence that the British ruling class must reap
what it sowed. He should have raised his voice, as Th'
Carpenter did, against these things. Instead he ex
doned them and cheered the British exploiters on to con
quer the world. Now he has to be gloomy about it.
The British Labor leaders are not gloomy. They
have good reasons for looking into the future with opti
mistic cheerfulness. They may lose the British empire,
but they will gain England and with it the good will of
the human race.
PRODUCE THE RECORD
You never in this world can convince the common
sense of mankind it is justifiable to send these two
men to the electric chair when it stands uncontra
dicted and unchallenged that there is documentary
evidence in the possession of the national govern
ment having th,e greatest possible bearing on the in
nocence of these men and the methods by which they
were entrapped which responsible officers of the gov
ernment refuse to produce.
This is from the address to the court made by Wil
liam G. Thompson, counsel for Nicola Sacco and Bartol
omeo Vanzetti, at the hearing to determine whether a
new trial is to be granted these two condemned radicals.
The point could not be better expressed. John G. Sar
gent, attorney general of the United States, has so far
refused to open the files of his department to disclose the
truth; and President Coolidge is reported disinclined to
do anything about it until Mr. Sargent has decided
whether the evidence is pertinent.
Mr. Sargent’s opinion really will not do. His depart
ment is seriously involved, and the more damaging the
evidence the stronger the motive of his inferiors to con
vince him that secrecy should be maintained.
What the record shows we do not know. But the
case has become so notorious that the record is the only
thing which will satisfy public opinion. Furthermore
the case is so notorious that any officer of the govei
ment who lends himself to further compounding of tht
plot will find himself involved past all hope of extrica
tion—New York World.
